================================================================================
  STAGE 10: UNDERGRADUATE — YEARS 2-3 — QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
  Core pure and applied mathematics
================================================================================

How to use this file (note for the parent / teacher)
----------------------------------------------------
- There are 49 topics (10.1 to 10.49, the same as in topic.txt), in four
  strands: Analysis (10.1-10.14), Algebra (10.15-10.24), Geometry and
  topology (10.25-10.31) and Applied and computational mathematics
  (10.32-10.49).
  Each topic has:
    * WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN   the checklist of definitions, theorems
                                  and methods in that topic
    * PART A — DESCRIPTIVE        12 questions (D1-D12): proofs,
                                  explanations, derivations and worked
                                  numerical problems, each with the answer
                                  and "Teacher explains" (the method step
                                  by step as a teacher shows it on the
                                  board, common mistakes, and a "Now you
                                  try" question)
    * PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY  12 questions (M1-M12): pure drills with
                                  answers. Most have many parts (a, b,
                                  c ...) so that EVERY case of the topic is
                                  practised, from the easiest to the
                                  hardest — every test, every kind of
                                  integral, transform and equation, every
                                  small group and ring, every decomposition
                                  and algorithm — not just one example.
    * TEACHING TIPS               what to do if the student struggles, and
                                  how to make it harder
- In total: 588 descriptive + 588 mathematical questions, then a mixed
  revision test (equal descriptive and mathematical parts, two questions
  from every topic in each part) and a readiness checklist for Stage 11.
- Level: second- and third-year university mathematics: Real Analysis II,
  Metric Spaces, Complex Analysis, Fourier Analysis and Transforms, Group
  and Ring Theory, Fields and Galois Theory, Linear Algebra II, Topology,
  Differential Geometry, Algebraic Topology (introduction), PDEs,
  Dynamical Systems, Numerical Analysis, Probability II, Statistics,
  Optimisation and Operations Research, Game Theory, Mechanics, Calculus
  of Variations, Combinatorics, Logic, Computation, Cryptography,
  Modelling, Financial Mathematics and the History of Mathematics.
- What is new in Stage 10: STRUCTURE. The student now studies whole
  theories: completeness and compactness as the engines of analysis;
  analytic functions and the residue theorem; groups, rings and fields as
  abstract systems with their homomorphism theorems; spaces described only
  by their open sets; curved surfaces measured from the inside; and the
  big applied toolkits (PDEs, numerical methods, statistical inference,
  optimisation) that turn models into numbers.
- Conventions: N = {1, 2, 3, ...} unless 0 is stated; log means the
  natural logarithm ln; i² = −1; vectors are columns unless written as
  rows; matrices are written [[a, b], [c, d]] (rows); Zₙ = Z/nZ; ≅ means
  isomorphic; □ or ∎ ends a proof; angles are in radians; exact answers
  first, decimals with ≈.
- Method: for every theorem know its hypotheses and a counterexample when
  one of them is dropped; for every computation know which theorem
  justifies it. Use Python/SageMath to CHECK calculations and to explore,
  and write solutions in LaTeX.
- Do 2-3 hours a day: 2 descriptive questions (write the full proof or
  solution) and 2 drills per session, plus weekly mixed revision. The
  strands can be studied in parallel (one analysis, one algebra and one
  applied topic at a time), as in a university timetable.
- Revise Stage 9 (A9.txt) whenever the student finds something difficult;
  especially 9.1-9.6 (proof, sets, sequences, series) before 10.1-10.6,
  9.9-9.11 (multivariable and vector calculus) before 10.7-10.8 and
  10.27, 9.13-9.18 (linear algebra) before 10.15-10.24, 9.19 (ODEs) before
  10.13-10.14 and 10.32-10.33, and 9.23 (probability) before 10.35-10.37.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.1 — REAL ANALYSIS: COMPLETENESS, SEQUENCES, BOLZANO-WEIERSTRASS,
CAUCHY SEQUENCES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - BOUNDS: u is an UPPER BOUND of A ⊆ R if a ≤ u for all a ∈ A. The SUPREMUM
    (least upper bound) sup A is an upper bound with sup A ≤ u for every
    upper bound u; the INFIMUM inf A is the greatest lower bound. A MAXIMUM
    is a supremum that belongs to A. sup A need not be in A (sup [0, 1) = 1).
    Conventions: sup A = +∞ if A is not bounded above; sup ∅ is not used.
  - ε-CHARACTERISATION: s = sup A ⇔ (i) a ≤ s for all a ∈ A and (ii) for
    every ε > 0 there is a ∈ A with a > s − ε. Similarly for inf. Equivalently
    there is a sequence aₙ ∈ A with aₙ → s.
  - COMPLETENESS AXIOM (least upper bound property): every NON-EMPTY subset of
    R that is BOUNDED ABOVE has a supremum in R. Q fails it:
    {x ∈ Q : x² < 2} has no supremum in Q. Consequences: every non-empty set
    bounded below has an infimum (inf A = −sup(−A)); √2 exists.
  - ARCHIMEDEAN PROPERTY: N is not bounded above; for every ε > 0 there is n
    with 1/n < ε; for x > 0 and any y there is n with nx > y. DENSITY: between
    any two reals x < y lie a rational (m/n with 1/n < y − x, m = ⌊nx⌋ + 1)
    and an irrational (e.g. a rational multiple of √2).
  - SUP ALGEBRA (A, B non-empty, bounded): sup(A + B) = sup A + sup B,
    sup(cA) = c·sup A for c > 0, sup(−A) = −inf A, sup(A − B) = sup A − inf B,
    sup(A ∪ B) = max(sup A, sup B), and A ⊆ B ⇒ sup A ≤ sup B.
  - NESTED INTERVAL PROPERTY: if I₁ ⊇ I₂ ⊇ ... are CLOSED BOUNDED intervals
    [aₙ, bₙ] then ⋂ Iₙ ≠ ∅; if also bₙ − aₙ → 0 the intersection is a single
    point. Fails for open intervals ((0, 1/n)), unbounded ones ([n, ∞)) and
    in Q. Used for BISECTION and to prove R is uncountable.
  - SEQUENCES: aₙ → L ⇔ ∀ε > 0 ∃N ∀n ≥ N : |aₙ − L| < ε. Limits are unique,
    convergent sequences are bounded, limits respect +, ×, ÷, ≤, and the
    SQUEEZE rule. MONOTONE CONVERGENCE THEOREM (MCT): a monotone sequence
    converges iff it is bounded; an increasing bounded sequence tends to
    sup{aₙ}. Recursions: prove bounded and monotone by INDUCTION first, then
    solve L = g(L).
  - SUBSEQUENCES: (a_{n_k}) with n₁ < n₂ < ... (so n_k ≥ k). If aₙ → L every
    subsequence → L. If a₂ₙ → L and a₂ₙ₋₁ → L then aₙ → L. A number is a
    SUBSEQUENTIAL LIMIT (cluster point) iff every neighbourhood of it contains
    aₙ for infinitely many n. PEAK LEMMA: every real sequence has a MONOTONE
    subsequence.
  - BOLZANO-WEIERSTRASS THEOREM (BW): every BOUNDED sequence in R has a
    CONVERGENT subsequence (proofs: peak lemma + MCT, or bisection + nested
    intervals). Set version: every bounded INFINITE subset of R has an
    ACCUMULATION point.
  - LIMSUP AND LIMINF: limsup aₙ = lim_{n→∞} sup{aₖ : k ≥ n} = inf over n of
    the tail sups (the LARGEST subsequential limit); liminf is the smallest.
    Always liminf ≤ limsup, and (aₙ) converges ⇔ limsup = liminf (finite).
    limsup(aₙ + bₙ) ≤ limsup aₙ + limsup bₙ (strict inequality is possible).
  - CAUCHY SEQUENCES: ∀ε > 0 ∃N ∀m, n ≥ N : |aₘ − aₙ| < ε. Convergent ⇒
    Cauchy; Cauchy ⇒ bounded; a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence
    converges. CAUCHY CRITERION: in R, Cauchy ⇔ convergent (proof by BW).
    In Q a Cauchy sequence may have no limit (decimals of √2). 'aₙ₊₁ − aₙ → 0'
    is NOT enough (√n, ln n, Hₙ).
  - CONTRACTIVE SEQUENCES: if |aₙ₊₂ − aₙ₊₁| ≤ c|aₙ₊₁ − aₙ| with 0 < c < 1 then
    (aₙ) is Cauchy, and |L − aₙ| ≤ cⁿ⁻¹|a₂ − a₁|/(1 − c). Series: ∑aₖ
    converges ⇔ ∀ε ∃N ∀m > n ≥ N : |aₙ₊₁ + ... + aₘ| < ε.
  - EQUIVALENT FORMS OF COMPLETENESS (in an ordered field that is
    Archimedean): least upper bound property ⇔ MCT ⇔ BW ⇔ every Cauchy
    sequence converges ⇔ nested interval property. Each one fails in Q.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find sup, inf, max and min (where they exist) of
    A = {1 − 1/n : n ∈ N},  B = {(−1)ⁿ + 1/n : n ∈ N},  C = {x ∈ Q : x² < 3},
    and prove your claims for A using the ε-characterisation of sup.
    Answer: A: sup 1 (no max), inf = min = 0. B: sup = max = 3/2, inf −1 (no
    min). C: sup √3, inf −√3, neither attained (and neither exists in Q).
    Teacher explains: First LIST terms, then GUESS, then PROVE.
       A: 0, 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, ...         increasing, creeping up to 1
       B: n odd:  0, −2/3, −4/5, −6/7, ... → −1  (from above)
          n even: 3/2, 5/4, 7/6, ...     → 1   (from above)
    For A: (i) 1 is an upper bound, since 1 − 1/n < 1 for every n. (ii) Let
    ε > 0. By the Archimedean property choose n with 1/n < ε; then
    1 − 1/n > 1 − ε, so 1 − ε is NOT an upper bound. Hence sup A = 1; since
    1 − 1/n ≠ 1 for all n, 1 ∉ A and A has no maximum. The least element is
    0 (n = 1), so inf A = min A = 0. For B: every odd term is > −1 and the
    odd terms −1 + 1/n come within any ε of −1, so inf B = −1, not attained;
    the largest term is 3/2 (n = 2), because odd terms are ≤ 0 and even terms
    1 + 1/n ≤ 3/2. For C: x² < 3 ⇔ −√3 < x < √3, and by density of Q there
    are rationals as close to ±√3 as we like; sup C = √3 ∉ Q, so in the
    universe Q the set C has upper bounds (2, 1.8, 1.74, ...) but no LEAST
    one. Common mistakes: saying 'sup B = 1' because the even terms tend to
    1 (the sup is about ALL terms, not the limit); confusing sup with max.
    Now you try: sup and inf of {n/(2n + 1) : n ∈ N}. (increasing from 1/3:
    inf = min = 1/3, sup = 1/2, not attained)

D2. Using only the completeness axiom, prove (a) the Archimedean property:
    N is not bounded above; (b) for every ε > 0 there is n ∈ N with 1/n < ε;
    (c) between any two reals x < y there is a rational number; (d) between
    any two reals there is an irrational. Find the rational given by the
    proof for x = 2/7, y = 3/10.
    Answer: proofs below; the construction gives 21/71 ≈ 0.29577.
    Teacher explains: (a) Suppose N were bounded above. By completeness
    s = sup N exists. Then s − 1 is not an upper bound, so some n ∈ N has
    n > s − 1; but then n + 1 ∈ N and n + 1 > s, contradicting that s is an
    upper bound. (b) Apply (a) to 1/ε: some n > 1/ε, i.e. 1/n < ε. (c) Choose
    n with 1/n < y − x (by (b)), i.e. ny − nx > 1. Put m = ⌊nx⌋ + 1, the
    least integer greater than nx (it exists by the Archimedean property).
    Then
       nx < m ≤ nx + 1 < ny     so     x < m/n < y.
    (d) Apply (c) to x/√2 < y/√2 to get a rational r ≠ 0 between them (if the
    rational found is 0, apply (c) again to (0, y/√2)); then r√2 is
    irrational and lies in (x, y). Numbers: y − x = 3/10 − 2/7 = 1/70, so
    we need n > 70: n = 71. Then nx = 142/7 = 20.28..., m = 21, and
       2/7 = 0.285714... < 21/71 = 0.295774... < 0.3 ✓
    Common mistakes: taking m = ⌊nx⌋ (that is ≤ nx, too small); 'proving'
    the Archimedean property by 'n eventually passes any number', which
    assumes it. Now you try: find the rational the proof gives between 0.1
    and 0.11. (n = 101, m = ⌊10.1⌋ + 1 = 11: 11/101 ≈ 0.10891)

D3. Let S = {x ∈ R : x ≥ 0, x² < 2} and s = sup S. Prove that s² = 2. Explain
    why the same set taken inside Q has no supremum in Q, so Q is not
    complete.
    Answer: s² < 2 and s² > 2 both lead to contradictions, so s² = 2.
    Teacher explains: S ≠ ∅ (1 ∈ S) and S is bounded above by 2 (x > 2 ⇒
    x² > 4), so s exists and 1 ≤ s ≤ 2. Rule out both inequalities.
    Case s² < 2: we look for a slightly bigger element s + h ∈ S. For
    0 < h < 1,
       (s + h)² = s² + 2sh + h² < s² + h(2s + 1) ≤ s² + 5h
    so choosing h = min(1/2, (2 − s²)/5) gives (s + h)² < 2, i.e. s + h ∈ S
    with s + h > s: contradicts s being an upper bound.
    Case s² > 2: we look for a slightly smaller upper bound s − h. For
    0 < h < s,
       (s − h)² = s² − 2sh + h² > s² − 2sh ≥ s² − 4h
    so with h = (s² − 2)/4 (which is < s since s² − 2 ≤ 2 < 4s) we get
    (s − h)² > 2; then every x ∈ S has x² < 2 < (s − h)², so x < s − h: a
    smaller upper bound, contradiction. Hence s² = 2. In Q: if a rational q
    were sup(S ∩ Q), the SAME two arguments (h can be chosen rational) show
    q² = 2, impossible since √2 is irrational. So Q lacks the least upper
    bound property. Common mistakes: using √2 in the proof (we are proving
    it exists); forgetting h < 1 when estimating h² < h. Now you try: which
    step changes to prove that every a > 0 has a square root?
    (S = {x ≥ 0 : x² < a}, bounded by max(1, a); the same estimates with 2
    replaced by a)

D4. State and prove the nested interval property. Show by examples that each
    hypothesis (closed, bounded, nested) is needed, and that it fails in Q.
    Use it to prove that R is uncountable.
    Answer: If [a₁, b₁] ⊇ [a₂, b₂] ⊇ ... then ⋂[aₙ, bₙ] ⊇ [sup aₙ, inf bₙ] ≠ ∅.
    Teacher explains: Nesting means a₁ ≤ a₂ ≤ ... ≤ b₂ ≤ b₁. Every bₘ is an
    upper bound for all aₙ (for n ≤ m, aₙ ≤ aₘ ≤ bₘ; for n > m, aₙ ≤ bₙ ≤ bₘ).
    So a = sup aₙ exists and a ≤ bₘ for every m. Also aₙ ≤ a. Hence
    a ∈ [aₙ, bₙ] for every n. If bₙ − aₙ → 0 and x, y both lie in every
    interval then |x − y| ≤ bₙ − aₙ → 0, so x = y. Counterexamples:
       open:        (0, 1/n)                 ⋂ = ∅
       unbounded:   [n, ∞)                   ⋂ = ∅
       not nested:  [n, n + 1]               ⋂ = ∅
       in Q:        Q ∩ [√2 − 1/n, √2 + 1/n] ⋂ = ∅ in Q (only √2 ∉ Q)
    Uncountability: suppose R = {x₁, x₂, x₃, ...}. Choose a closed interval
    I₁ of positive length with x₁ ∉ I₁; split I₁ into three closed thirds
    and let I₂ be one not containing x₂; continue, Iₙ₊₁ ⊆ Iₙ with xₙ₊₁ ∉ Iₙ₊₁.
    The intersection contains some x, and x ≠ xₙ for every n since xₙ ∉ Iₙ.
    So the list misses x: contradiction. Common mistakes: thinking the
    intersection of shrinking open intervals is always a point; forgetting
    that the argument needs CLOSED intervals. Now you try: find
    ⋂ [1 − 1/n, 1 + 1/n²] and ⋂ (1 − 1/n, 1]. ({1}; {1})

D5. Let A, B be non-empty bounded subsets of R. Prove sup(A + B) =
    sup A + sup B and sup(−A) = −inf A. Deduce sup(A − B) = sup A − inf B.
    Check with A = [−1, 3), B = (2, 5]. Show that sup(AB) = sup A · sup B can
    fail, where AB = {ab}.
    Answer: sup(A + B) = 3 + 5 = 8, sup(A − B) = 3 − 2 = 1; for these sets
    sup(AB) = 15 = 3·5, but A = B = [−2, −1] gives sup(AB) = 4 ≠ 1.
    Teacher explains: Put α = sup A, β = sup B. Upper bound: a + b ≤ α + β for
    all a ∈ A, b ∈ B. Least: given ε > 0 choose a > α − ε/2 and b > β − ε/2;
    then a + b > α + β − ε. By the ε-characterisation sup(A + B) = α + β.
    For −A: x ≥ inf A for all x ∈ A ⇔ −x ≤ −inf A, so −inf A is an upper
    bound of −A; and x < inf A + ε for some x ∈ A gives −x > −inf A − ε.
    Then A − B = A + (−B) and
       sup(A − B) = sup A + sup(−B) = sup A − inf B.
    Check: A + B = (1, 8), so sup 8 ✓; A − B = [−6, 1), sup 1 ✓ (inf B = 2,
    not attained, which is why 1 is not attained). Products break the
    pattern because multiplying by a negative number reverses order:
    with A = B = [−2, −1], AB = [1, 4], sup = 4, while sup A · sup B =
    (−1)(−1) = 1. For sets of POSITIVE numbers sup(AB) = sup A · sup B does
    hold. Common mistakes: 'sup(A − B) = sup A − sup B' (it is inf B that is
    subtracted); forgetting that the ε must be split between the two sets.
    Now you try: with A = [−1, 3), B = (2, 5] find inf(A + B) and sup(−2A).
    (−1 + 2 = 1; −2·inf A = 2)

D6. Prove the monotone convergence theorem. Apply it to x₁ = 2,
    xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ + 3/xₙ)/2: show the sequence is decreasing and bounded below,
    find its limit and compute x₂, x₃, x₄.
    Answer: xₙ ↓ √3; x₂ = 1.75, x₃ = 97/56 ≈ 1.7321429, x₄ ≈ 1.7320508.
    Teacher explains: MCT: let (aₙ) be increasing and bounded above. By
    completeness s = sup{aₙ} exists. Given ε > 0, s − ε is not an upper
    bound, so some a_N > s − ε; then for n ≥ N,
       s − ε < a_N ≤ aₙ ≤ s,   so |aₙ − s| < ε.
    Hence aₙ → s (decreasing bounded below → inf similarly). For the
    recursion: bounded below by AM-GM, for n ≥ 1,
       xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ + 3/xₙ)/2 ≥ √(xₙ·3/xₙ) = √3    (and x₁ = 2 > √3)
    Decreasing: xₙ − xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ² − 3)/(2xₙ) ≥ 0 because xₙ ≥ √3 > 0. By MCT
    xₙ → L ≥ √3 > 0, and letting n → ∞ in the recursion, L = (L + 3/L)/2,
    so L² = 3 and L = √3. Numbers:
       x₂ = (2 + 1.5)/2 = 1.75
       x₃ = (1.75 + 1.7142857)/2 = 1.7321429       (= 97/56)
       x₄ = (1.7321429 + 1.7319588)/2 = 1.7320508  (√3 = 1.7320508...)
    The number of correct digits roughly doubles each step (Newton's method).
    Common mistakes: solving L = (L + 3/L)/2 and choosing L = −√3; writing
    the fixed-point equation before proving the limit exists. Now you try:
    x₁ = 1, xₙ₊₁ = √(3xₙ + 4). (increasing, bounded by 4: L² = 3L + 4 gives
    L = 4)

D7. Prove the peak lemma: every sequence of real numbers has a monotone
    subsequence. Illustrate on aₙ = (−1)ⁿ/n and on aₙ = sin(nπ/2) + 1/n.
    Answer: Proof below; for (−1)ⁿ/n the even terms 1/2, 1/4, ... form a
    decreasing subsequence (all peaks); for the second, a₁, a₅, a₉, ...
    (the values 1 + 1/n) is a decreasing subsequence.
    Teacher explains: Call m a PEAK if aₘ ≥ aₙ for every n > m (nothing later
    is higher). Two cases.
    Case 1: infinitely many peaks m₁ < m₂ < m₃ < .... Each is a peak, so
       a_{m₁} ≥ a_{m₂} ≥ a_{m₃} ≥ ...
    a decreasing subsequence.
    Case 2: finitely many peaks. Let n₁ be beyond the last peak. n₁ is not a
    peak, so some n₂ > n₁ has a_{n₂} > a_{n₁}; n₂ is not a peak either, so
    some n₃ > n₂ has a_{n₃} > a_{n₂}; and so on: a strictly increasing
    subsequence. Examples: for aₙ = (−1)ⁿ/n = −1, 1/2, −1/3, 1/4, ... every
    even n is a peak (1/n beats all later terms, which are < 1/n), so
    Case 1 gives 1/2 ≥ 1/4 ≥ 1/6 ≥ .... For sin(nπ/2) + 1/n the values at
    n = 1, 5, 9, ... are 1 + 1/n, and each is a peak (every later term is
    ≤ 1 + 1/(n + 1) < 1 + 1/n), giving 2, 1.2, 1.111..., decreasing to 1.
    Common mistakes: thinking the monotone subsequence must be increasing;
    forgetting that the indices must increase. Now you try: find a monotone
    subsequence of 1, 1/2, 1, 1/3, 1, 1/4, .... (the constant subsequence
    1, 1, 1, ...; or 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, ...)

D8. Prove the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem in two ways: (a) from the peak
    lemma; (b) by bisection. Apply the bisection proof to the bounded
    sequence aₙ = (−1)ⁿ + 1/n on [−2, 2] for three steps.
    Answer: (a) monotone + bounded ⇒ convergent (MCT). (b) choosing the
    right half whenever it qualifies: [−2, 2] → [0, 2] → [1, 2] → [1, 3/2],
    homing in on 1, the limit of the even-indexed terms.
    Teacher explains: (a) By the peak lemma (aₙ) has a monotone subsequence;
    it is bounded because (aₙ) is; by MCT it converges. Done.
    (b) Let all aₙ lie in I₀ = [a, b]. Halve it; at least ONE half contains
    aₙ for infinitely many n; call it I₁. Halve I₁, keep a half with
    infinitely many terms, I₂, and so on. Choose n₁ < n₂ < ... with
    a_{n_k} ∈ I_k (possible because each I_k holds infinitely many terms).
    The Iₖ are nested closed intervals of length (b − a)/2ᵏ → 0, so they
    shrink to one point L, and |a_{n_k} − L| ≤ (b − a)/2ᵏ → 0. On the example
    (terms 0, 3/2, −2/3, 5/4, −4/5, 7/6, ...):
       I₀ = [−2, 2]
       halves [−2, 0], [0, 2]: both hold infinitely many terms; take the
         right one, I₁ = [0, 2]
       halves [0, 1], [1, 2]: [0, 1] holds only a₁ = 0 (odd terms after it
         are negative, even terms exceed 1); [1, 2] holds every even term:
         I₂ = [1, 2]
       halves [1, 3/2], [3/2, 2]: [3/2, 2] holds only a₂ = 3/2, while
         [1, 3/2] holds every even term: I₃ = [1, 3/2]
    and the process homes in on L = 1 (the even-term limit). Choosing the
    LEFT half I₁ = [−2, 0] instead homes in on −1. Both are subsequential
    limits. Common mistakes: claiming the whole sequence converges; keeping
    a half that contains only finitely many terms (the chosen half must
    contain aₙ for INFINITELY MANY n, otherwise we cannot pick n₁ < n₂ < ...).
    Now you try: does aₙ = n·sin²(nπ/2) (= n for odd n, 0 for even n) have a
    convergent subsequence although it is unbounded? (Yes: the even terms
    0, 0, 0, ...; BW gives a SUFFICIENT condition only.)

D9. Define limsup and liminf. For aₙ = (−1)ⁿ(1 + 1/n) compute the tail sups
    sₙ = sup{aₖ : k ≥ n} and tail infs, hence limsup and liminf, and compare
    with sup and inf. Prove that aₙ → L iff limsup aₙ = liminf aₙ = L.
    Answer: sₙ = 1 + 1/n (n even), 1 + 1/(n + 1) (n odd) → 1; tail infs
    → −1. limsup = 1, liminf = −1; sup = 3/2, inf = −2.
    Teacher explains: The terms are −2, 3/2, −4/3, 5/4, −6/5, 7/6, ....
    Tail sups: the largest term from index n on is the first EVEN-indexed
    term at or after n:
       s₁ = 3/2, s₂ = 3/2, s₃ = 5/4, s₄ = 5/4, s₅ = 7/6, ...   ↓ 1
    Tail infs: the first odd-indexed term at or after n:
       i₁ = −2, i₂ = −4/3, i₃ = −4/3, i₄ = −6/5, ...           ↑ −1
    The tail sups DECREASE (a smaller set has a smaller sup), so by MCT
    limsup aₙ = lim sₙ = inf sₙ always exists in [−∞, ∞]. Here limsup = 1 and
    liminf = −1, the largest and smallest subsequential limits (even and odd
    terms). sup = 3/2 and inf = −2 are different: they see the early terms,
    limsup and liminf only see the long run. Proof of the criterion: iₙ ≤ aₙ ≤
    sₙ. (⇐) If sₙ → L and iₙ → L, squeeze gives aₙ → L. (⇒) If aₙ → L then
    for n ≥ N all aₖ (k ≥ n) lie in (L − ε, L + ε), so L − ε ≤ iₙ ≤ sₙ ≤ L + ε;
    hence both limits equal L. Common mistakes: 'limsup = sup'; thinking
    limsup is the limit of a subsequence chosen arbitrarily (it is the
    LARGEST one). Now you try: limsup and liminf of aₙ = cos(2nπ/3).
    (values −1/2, −1/2, 1 repeating: limsup 1, liminf −1/2)

D10. Define a Cauchy sequence. Prove: (a) every convergent sequence is
     Cauchy; (b) every Cauchy sequence is bounded; (c) every Cauchy sequence
     in R converges. For aₙ = 1/n and ε = 0.01 find an N that works. Show
     that the harmonic sums Hₙ = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n are not Cauchy.
     Answer: N = 100 works for 1/n; H₂ₙ − Hₙ ≥ 1/2 for all n.
     Teacher explains: (a) If aₙ → L, choose N with |aₙ − L| < ε/2 for n ≥ N;
     then for m, n ≥ N
        |aₘ − aₙ| ≤ |aₘ − L| + |L − aₙ| < ε/2 + ε/2 = ε.
     (b) With ε = 1 there is N with |aₙ − a_N| < 1 for n ≥ N, so
     |aₙ| ≤ max(|a₁|, ..., |a_{N−1}|, |a_N| + 1). (c) By (b) and BW some
     subsequence a_{n_k} → L. Given ε, choose N with |aₘ − aₙ| < ε/2 for
     m, n ≥ N, and k with n_k ≥ N and |a_{n_k} − L| < ε/2. For n ≥ N:
        |aₙ − L| ≤ |aₙ − a_{n_k}| + |a_{n_k} − L| < ε.
     The point of the Cauchy criterion: we can prove convergence WITHOUT
     knowing the limit. For 1/n with m, n ≥ N: |1/m − 1/n| < max(1/m, 1/n)
     ≤ 1/N, so 1/N ≤ 0.01, i.e. N = 100, works. For Hₙ:
        H₂ₙ − Hₙ = 1/(n + 1) + ... + 1/(2n) ≥ n·1/(2n) = 1/2
     so with ε = 1/2 no N works: take m = 2n. Note Hₙ₊₁ − Hₙ = 1/(n + 1) → 0,
     so consecutive terms getting close is NOT the Cauchy condition. Common
     mistakes: checking only |aₙ₊₁ − aₙ| < ε; in (c) forgetting that BW needs
     boundedness (that is why (b) comes first). Now you try: show that
     aₙ = √n is not Cauchy although √(n + 1) − √n → 0.
     (a₄ₙ − aₙ = √n ≥ 1 for all n)

D11. A sequence is CONTRACTIVE if |aₙ₊₂ − aₙ₊₁| ≤ c|aₙ₊₁ − aₙ| for all n, with
     a fixed 0 < c < 1. Prove every contractive sequence is Cauchy, with
     |L − aₙ| ≤ cⁿ⁻¹|a₂ − a₁|/(1 − c). Apply this to x₁ = 1,
     xₙ₊₁ = 1/(2 + xₙ): find c, the limit, x₂ to x₅, the error bound for x₅
     and the least n for which the bound is below 10⁻⁶.
     Answer: c = 1/4, L = √2 − 1 ≈ 0.41421; x₂ = 1/3, x₃ = 3/7, x₄ = 7/17,
     x₅ = 17/41; bound for x₅ = 1/288 ≈ 0.00347; n = 11.
     Teacher explains: Iterating, |aₖ₊₁ − aₖ| ≤ cᵏ⁻¹|a₂ − a₁| = cᵏ⁻¹d. For
     m > n, by the triangle inequality and the geometric series,
        |aₘ − aₙ| ≤ d(cⁿ⁻¹ + cⁿ + ... + cᵐ⁻²) < dcⁿ⁻¹/(1 − c) → 0,
     so (aₙ) is Cauchy and converges (completeness). Letting m → ∞ gives the
     error bound. For the example, all xₙ > 0, so
        |xₙ₊₁ − xₙ| = |1/(2 + xₙ) − 1/(2 + xₙ₋₁)|
                    = |xₙ − xₙ₋₁|/((2 + xₙ)(2 + xₙ₋₁)) ≤ |xₙ − xₙ₋₁|/4
     giving c = 1/4. The limit satisfies L = 1/(2 + L), L² + 2L − 1 = 0,
     L = −1 + √2 (the positive root). Terms: x₂ = 1/3, x₃ = 1/(7/3) = 3/7,
     x₄ = 7/17, x₅ = 17/41 ≈ 0.414634 (these are continued-fraction
     approximations of √2 − 1). With d = |1/3 − 1| = 2/3:
        |L − x₅| ≤ (1/4)⁴(2/3)/(3/4) = (8/9)/256 = 1/288 ≈ 0.00347
     (true error 0.00042). Bound < 10⁻⁶ ⇔ 4ⁿ⁻¹ > 8·10⁶/9 ≈ 888889; 4⁹ = 262144,
     4¹⁰ = 1048576, so n − 1 = 10, n = 11. Common mistakes: using
     |aₙ₊₁ − aₙ| → 0 as if it were contractive; forgetting to show xₙ > 0
     before bounding the denominators. Now you try: x₁ = 1, xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ + 1)/3.
     (c = 1/3, L = 1/2, xₙ = 1/2 + (1/2)(1/3)ⁿ⁻¹)

D12. Show that, for an Archimedean ordered field, 'every Cauchy sequence
     converges' implies the least upper bound property. Then give, in Q,
     (a) a Cauchy sequence with no limit in Q, (b) an increasing bounded
     sequence with no limit in Q, (c) a bounded sequence with no subsequence
     converging in Q. Summarise the chain of equivalent completeness axioms.
     Answer: bisection argument below; (a), (b), (c): the decimal
     truncations 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, ... of √2 serve for all three.
     Teacher explains: Let A be non-empty and bounded above; pick a₀ ∈ A
     (not an upper bound, unless it is the max, in which case we are done)
     and an upper bound b₀. Repeatedly bisect: if the midpoint is an upper
     bound of A make it the new b, else the new a. Then aₙ is never an upper
     bound, bₙ always is, and
        0 ≤ bₙ − aₙ = (b₀ − a₀)/2ⁿ → 0      (Archimedean: 2ⁿ ≥ n)
     Both sequences are Cauchy (|aₘ − aₙ| ≤ (b₀ − a₀)/2^min(m,n)), so they
     converge, to the same s. s is an upper bound: x ≤ bₙ for all n and
     x ∈ A, so x ≤ s. s is least: if u is an upper bound, since aₙ is not,
     some x ∈ A has x > aₙ, so u > aₙ for all n and u ≥ s. Chain:
        LUB ⇒ MCT (D6) ⇒ BW (D8) ⇒ Cauchy converge (D10) ⇒ LUB (above),
     and nested intervals sit in the chain too. In Q take qₙ = √2 truncated
     to n − 1 decimals: 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, 1.4142, ... It is increasing,
     bounded by 2, Cauchy (|qₘ − qₙ| < 10^(1−n)), and every subsequence tends
     to √2 ∉ Q. So MCT, Cauchy completeness and BW all fail in Q. Common
     mistakes: thinking Q is 'almost' complete because it is dense; forgetting
     that the Archimedean property is needed (there are non-Archimedean
     fields where Cauchy sequences converge but LUB fails). Now you try:
     using sₙ = ∑_{k=0}^{n} 1/k!, which tends to e, explain why (sₙ) is Cauchy
     in Q but converges only in R. (e is irrational; sₙ ∈ Q is increasing
     and bounded by 3)

M9. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
    a) Every bounded sequence converges.
    b) Every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.
    c) Every sequence has a monotone subsequence.
    d) Every sequence has a convergent subsequence.
    e) An unbounded sequence has no convergent subsequence.
    f) If a₂ₙ → L and a₂ₙ₋₁ → L then aₙ → L.
    g) If a₂ₙ → L and a₃ₙ → L then aₙ → L.
    h) If a₂ₙ, a₂ₙ₋₁ and a₃ₙ all converge then (aₙ) converges.
    i) A monotone sequence with a convergent subsequence converges.
    j) A sequence taking finitely many values has a constant subsequence.
    k) Every bounded sequence of rationals has a subsequence converging to a
       rational.
    l) If (aₙ) is bounded and every convergent subsequence tends to 0 then
       aₙ → 0.
    m) If every convergent subsequence of (aₙ) tends to 0 then aₙ → 0.
    n) Every bounded infinite subset of R has an accumulation point.
    o) N has an accumulation point in R.
    p) If |aₙ| → |L| then aₙ → L.
    q) If aₙ → L then |aₙ| → |L|.
    r) limsup aₙ ≤ sup aₙ for every bounded sequence.
    s) If limsup aₙ = liminf aₙ = 5 then aₙ → 5.
    t) The set of subsequential limits of a bounded sequence can be empty.
    Answers:
      a) F: (−1)ⁿ       b) T (BW)        c) T (peak lemma)
      d) F: aₙ = n      e) F: n for odd n, 0 for even n
      f) T              g) F: aₙ = 1 if n is prime, 0 otherwise
      h) T (a₆ₙ links the even and a₃ₙ; a₆ₙ₋₃ links the odd and a₃ₙ)
      i) T (the subsequence bounds the monotone sequence)
      j) T (pigeonhole)  k) F: decimal truncations of √2
      l) T              m) F: n for odd n, 0 for even n
      n) T              o) F
      p) F: (−1)ⁿ with L = 1              q) T (||aₙ| − |L|| ≤ |aₙ − L|)
      r) T              s) T             t) F (BW gives at least one)

M11. Contractive sequences. Give a contraction constant c (as found by the
     standard estimate) and the limit L.
     a) x₁ = 1, xₙ₊₁ = 1/(2 + xₙ)
     b) x₁ = 1, xₙ₊₁ = 1/(1 + xₙ)   (terms lie in [1/2, 1])

     d) x₁ = 0, xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ² + 2)/5   (terms lie in [0, 1])
     e) x₁ = 2, xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ + 3/xₙ)/2 (terms lie in [√3, 2])
     f) x₁ = 1, xₙ₊₁ = cos xₙ        (terms lie in [0, 1])
     g) x₁ = 1, xₙ₊₁ = e^(−xₙ)       (terms lie in [1/e, 1])
     h) x₁ = 0, xₙ₊₁ = 2 + xₙ/4
     i) in a): the bound (8/9)(1/4)ⁿ⁻¹ on |L − xₙ| for n = 5
     j) in a): least n with (8/9)(1/4)ⁿ⁻¹ < 10⁻⁶
     k) in c): a formula for xₙ
     l) in h): least n with the bound cⁿ⁻¹|x₂ − x₁|/(1 − c) < 0.001
     Answers:
       a) 1/4, √2 − 1 ≈ 0.41421
       b) 4/9, (√5 − 1)/2 ≈ 0.61803
       c) 1/3, 1/2
       d) 2/5, (5 − √17)/2 ≈ 0.43845
       e) 1/8 (|g′(x)| = (1 − 3/x²)/2 ≤ 1/8), √3 ≈ 1.73205
       f) sin 1 ≈ 0.84147, ≈ 0.73909
       g) e^(−1/e) ≈ 0.69220, ≈ 0.56714
       h) 1/4, 8/3
       i) 1/288 ≈ 0.00347 (true error ≈ 0.00042)
       j) 11
       k) xₙ = 1/2 + (1/2)(1/3)ⁿ⁻¹
       l) bound = (1/4)ⁿ⁻¹·2/(3/4) = (8/3)(1/4)ⁿ⁻¹ < 0.001 ⇔ 4ⁿ⁻¹ > 2667:
          n = 7 (4⁶ = 4096)

M12. Cauchy criterion for series. sₙ = ∑_{k≤n} aₖ. Using the given bound
     |sₘ − sₙ| < B(n) (m > n), find the least N with B(N) ≤ ε.
     a) aₖ = 2⁻ᵏ, B(n) = 2⁻ⁿ, ε = 10⁻³
     b) aₖ = 1/(k(k + 1)), B(n) = 1/(n + 1), ε = 0.01
     c) aₖ = 1/k², B(n) = 1/n, ε = 0.001
     d) aₖ = 1/k³, B(n) = 1/(2n²), ε = 10⁻⁴
     e) aₖ = 1/k!, B(n) = 2/(n + 1)!, ε = 10⁻⁶
     f) aₖ = (−1)ᵏ⁺¹/k, B(n) = 1/(n + 1), ε = 0.001
     g) aₖ = 0.9ᵏ, B(n) = 10·0.9ⁿ⁺¹, ε = 0.01
     h) aₖ = 3⁻ᵏ, B(n) = 3⁻ⁿ/2, ε = 10⁻⁵
     i) aₖ = 1/k: compute s₂ₙ − sₙ for n = 1, 2, 3, and say whether any N
        works for ε = 1/2
     j) aₖ = 1/√k: show s₄ₙ − sₙ ≥ 3n/(2√n) and decide
     k) aₖ = 1/(k(k + 1)): the exact value of s_∞ − s₁₀
     l) aₖ = 2⁻ᵏ: the exact value of s₂₀ − s₁₀
     Answers:
       a) 10     b) 99     c) 1000   d) 71     e) 9 (10! = 3628800 ≥ 2·10⁶)
       f) 999    g) 65 (0.9⁶⁶ ≈ 0.000955 ≤ 0.001)   h) 10 (3¹⁰ = 59049)
       i) 1/2, 7/12, 37/60 — all ≥ 1/2, so no N: not Cauchy, diverges
       j) each of the 3n terms is ≥ 1/√(4n) = 1/(2√n), so s₄ₙ − sₙ ≥ (3/2)√n
          → ∞: not Cauchy
       k) 1/11          l) 2⁻¹⁰ − 2⁻²⁰ = 1023/1048576 ≈ 0.000976

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw every set on a number line and mark the candidate sup
  with an open or closed dot; always write the two clauses of the
  ε-characterisation ('upper bound' and 'nothing smaller is') as separate
  lines. For recursions, compute four terms numerically before proving
  anything, and insist on 'bounded and monotone FIRST, then L = g(L)'. For
  limsup, make a two-row table of tail sups and tail infs. Stress that
  Cauchy means ALL pairs m, n beyond N, not neighbours. Harder: prove that
  the least upper bound property implies the nested interval property and
  conversely (with the Archimedean property); show that the set of
  subsequential limits of any sequence is closed; prove limsup(aₙbₙ) ≤
  limsup aₙ · limsup bₙ for positive sequences and find a case of strict
  inequality; show that liminf aₙ₊₁/aₙ ≤ liminf aₙ^(1/n) ≤ limsup aₙ^(1/n) ≤
  limsup aₙ₊₁/aₙ; prove Cesàro: aₙ → L ⇒ (a₁ + ... + aₙ)/n → L; and
  construct R from Cauchy sequences of rationals, checking that the
  resulting field is complete.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.2 — CONTINUITY, UNIFORM CONTINUITY, DIFFERENTIABILITY (RIGOROUS)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - CONTINUITY at a ∈ D: ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0 ∀x ∈ D : |x − a| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(a)| < ε.
    δ may depend on ε AND on a. At an isolated point of D every f is
    continuous; at a limit point, continuity means lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a).
  - SEQUENTIAL CRITERION: f is continuous at a ⇔ for EVERY sequence xₙ → a
    in D, f(xₙ) → f(a). To prove DIScontinuity find ONE sequence xₙ → a with
    f(xₙ) ↛ f(a), or two sequences with different limits of f(xₙ).
    Sums, products, quotients (denominator ≠ 0) and COMPOSITIONS of
    continuous functions are continuous.
  - DISCONTINUITIES: REMOVABLE (lim f exists but ≠ f(a) or f(a) undefined),
    JUMP (one-sided limits exist and differ), ESSENTIAL / second kind (a
    one-sided limit fails to exist: oscillation like sin(1/x), or infinite
    like 1/x). A MONOTONE function has only jump discontinuities, at most
    countably many. Examples: DIRICHLET 1_Q is nowhere continuous; x·1_Q(x)
    is continuous only at 0; THOMAE's function (1/q at p/q in lowest terms,
    0 at irrationals) is continuous exactly at the irrationals.
  - INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM (IVT): f continuous on [a, b] and y between
    f(a) and f(b) ⇒ ∃c ∈ [a, b] with f(c) = y (proof: c = sup{x : f(x) < y}).
    Consequences: odd-degree polynomials have a real root; a continuous
    f : [a, b] → [a, b] has a FIXED POINT; the continuous image of an
    interval is an interval; BISECTION halves the root interval each step.
  - EXTREME VALUE THEOREM (EVT): f continuous on a CLOSED BOUNDED [a, b] is
    bounded and ATTAINS its max and min (proof by Bolzano-Weierstrass). Each
    hypothesis is needed: 1/x on (0, 1], x on [0, 1), arctan on R.
  - UNIFORM CONTINUITY (UC) on D: ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0 ∀x, y ∈ D :
    |x − y| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(y)| < ε — ONE δ for the whole set. Not UC ⇔
    ∃ε > 0 and sequences xₙ, yₙ ∈ D with |xₙ − yₙ| → 0 but
    |f(xₙ) − f(yₙ)| ≥ ε. x² is UC on [0, 2] but not on R; 1/x and sin(1/x)
    are not UC on (0, 1).
  - LIPSCHITZ: |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ K|x − y| ⇒ UC (take δ = ε/K). A bounded
    derivative, |f′| ≤ K, gives Lipschitz with constant K (by the MVT). √x is
    UC on [0, ∞) (|√x − √y| ≤ √|x − y|, δ = ε²) but not Lipschitz near 0.
  - HEINE-CANTOR: continuous on a closed bounded interval (compact set) ⇒
    uniformly continuous. UC maps CAUCHY sequences to Cauchy sequences; f is
    UC on (a, b) ⇔ f extends to a continuous function on [a, b].
  - DERIVATIVE: f′(a) = lim_{h→0} (f(a + h) − f(a))/h. Equivalently
    (CARATHÉODORY) f(x) − f(a) = φ(x)(x − a) with φ continuous at a,
    φ(a) = f′(a). Differentiable ⇒ continuous (not conversely: |x| at 0).
    Product, quotient and CHAIN RULE (g ∘ f)′(a) = g′(f(a))f′(a); inverse
    function rule (f⁻¹)′(f(a)) = 1/f′(a) when f′(a) ≠ 0.
  - x²sin(1/x) (f(0) = 0) is differentiable everywhere, f′(0) = 0, but f′ is
    NOT continuous at 0. For |x|ᵖ sin(1/x): continuous at 0 ⇔ p > 0,
    differentiable ⇔ p > 1, C¹ ⇔ p > 2.
  - FERMAT: an interior local extremum with f′(c) existing has f′(c) = 0.
    ROLLE: f continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), f(a) = f(b) ⇒
    ∃c ∈ (a, b), f′(c) = 0. MEAN VALUE THEOREM (MVT): f′(c) =
    (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). CAUCHY MVT: (f(b) − f(a))g′(c) = (g(b) − g(a))f′(c).
  - CONSEQUENCES: f′ = 0 on an interval ⇒ f constant; f′ ≥ 0 ⇒ increasing;
    f′ > 0 ⇒ strictly increasing; inequalities like |sin x − sin y| ≤
    |x − y|, eˣ ≥ 1 + x. L'HÔPITAL's rule (0/0 or ∞/∞) follows from Cauchy's
    MVT. f′(a) > 0 alone does NOT make f increasing near a.
  - DARBOUX: a derivative has the intermediate value property (even if
    discontinuous), so derivatives have NO jump or removable discontinuities
    (sgn x is not a derivative). TAYLOR with LAGRANGE REMAINDER:
    f(x) = ∑_{k≤n} f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)(x − a)ᵏ/k! + f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c)(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)!.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove from the ε-δ definition that (a) f(x) = x² is continuous at 3,
    (b) g(x) = 1/x is continuous at 2, (c) h(x) = √x is continuous at 4.
    For ε = 0.1 give the δ your proof produces in (a) and the largest δ that
    works.
    Answer: (a) δ = min(1, ε/7); for ε = 0.1, δ = 1/70 ≈ 0.01429; largest
    δ = √9.1 − 3 ≈ 0.01662. (b) δ = min(1, 2ε). (c) δ = 2ε.
    Teacher explains: The method: factor |f(x) − f(a)| as |x − a| times
    something, BOUND the something near a, then choose δ.
    (a) |x² − 9| = |x − 3||x + 3|. First restrict |x − 3| < 1, so
    2 < x < 4 and |x + 3| < 7. Then |x² − 9| < 7|x − 3|. So
       δ = min(1, ε/7):  |x − 3| < δ ⇒ |x² − 9| < 7·ε/7 = ε ✓
    (b) |1/x − 1/2| = |x − 2|/(2|x|). With |x − 2| < 1 we have x > 1, so
    |1/x − 1/2| < |x − 2|/2 < ε when also |x − 2| < 2ε: δ = min(1, 2ε).
    (c) |√x − 2| = |x − 4|/(√x + 2) ≤ |x − 4|/2, so δ = 2ε works (for x ≥ 0).
    Largest δ in (a) with ε = 0.1: we need |x² − 9| < 0.1, i.e.
    √8.9 < x < √9.1, and the interval (3 − δ, 3 + δ) must fit inside:
       √9.1 − 3 = 0.016621,   3 − √8.9 = 0.016713   ⇒ δ_max = √9.1 − 3
    Any smaller δ (like 1/70) also works: δ is not unique, and a proof only
    needs SOME δ. Common mistakes: letting δ depend on x ('δ = ε/(x + 3)');
    forgetting the first restriction that makes |x + 3| bounded. Now you
    try: prove x³ is continuous at 1 and give δ. (|x³ − 1| = |x − 1||x² + x + 1|
    < 7|x − 1| when |x − 1| < 1; δ = min(1, ε/7))

D2. Prove the sequential criterion for continuity. Use it to show:
    (a) f(x) = sin(1/x) cannot be defined at 0 so as to be continuous;
    (b) Dirichlet's function 1_Q is discontinuous everywhere; (c) f(x) =
    x·1_Q(x) is continuous at 0 and nowhere else.
    Answer: (a) xₙ = 1/(2nπ + π/2) and yₙ = 1/(nπ) give limits 1 and 0.
    (b), (c) below.
    Teacher explains: (⇒) If f is continuous at a and xₙ → a: given ε pick
    δ; for n ≥ N we have |xₙ − a| < δ, so |f(xₙ) − f(a)| < ε. (⇐) Suppose f is
    NOT continuous at a: some ε > 0 has no δ; with δ = 1/n there is xₙ with
    |xₙ − a| < 1/n but |f(xₙ) − f(a)| ≥ ε. Then xₙ → a but f(xₙ) ↛ f(a).
    (a) f(xₙ) = sin(2nπ + π/2) = 1 and f(yₙ) = sin(nπ) = 0 for all n, while
    xₙ, yₙ → 0. Whatever value c we give f(0), both sequences would have to
    tend to c: impossible. The discontinuity is ESSENTIAL (oscillation).
    (b) Let a ∈ R. Q and R − Q are both dense, so there are rationals
    qₙ → a and irrationals rₙ → a, with 1_Q(qₙ) = 1 and 1_Q(rₙ) = 0: the two
    limits differ, so 1_Q is not continuous at a. (c) At 0: |f(x) − 0| ≤ |x|,
    so δ = ε works. At a ≠ 0: rationals qₙ → a give f(qₙ) = qₙ → a, and
    irrationals rₙ → a give f(rₙ) = 0 → 0 ≠ a. Common mistakes: using a
    single sequence to prove continuity (the criterion needs ALL sequences);
    thinking that 'continuous at only one point' is impossible. Now you try:
    where is f(x) = x on Q, 1 − x off Q continuous? (only at x = 1/2, where
    x = 1 − x)

D3. Thomae's function is T(p/q) = 1/q for p/q in lowest terms (q ≥ 1, so
    T(0) = 1), and T(x) = 0 for irrational x. Prove T is continuous at every
    irrational and discontinuous at every rational. Classify the
    discontinuity of: ⌊x⌋ at 1; (x² − 1)/(x − 1) at 1; e^(1/x) at 0; T at 1/2;
    1/(1 + e^(1/x)) at 0.
    Answer: Proof below. ⌊x⌋: jump; (x² − 1)/(x − 1): removable (limit 2);
    e^(1/x): essential (right limit ∞); T at 1/2: removable (limit 0, value
    1/2); 1/(1 + e^(1/x)): jump (left limit 1, right limit 0).
    Teacher explains: The key fact: for a fixed ε > 0 and a bounded interval,
    only FINITELY many rationals p/q in it have 1/q ≥ ε (q ≤ 1/ε, and for each
    such q only finitely many p). Continuity at irrational a: fix ε; in
    (a − 1, a + 1) list the finitely many rationals with 1/q ≥ ε; none equals
    a, so let δ be less than the distance from a to the nearest of them.
    For |x − a| < δ, either x is irrational (T(x) = 0) or x = p/q with
    1/q < ε; in both cases |T(x) − T(a)| = T(x) < ε ✓. Discontinuity at
    rational r = p/q: T(r) = 1/q > 0, but irrationals rₙ → r give T(rₙ) = 0 →
    0 ≠ 1/q. In fact lim_{x→a} T(x) = 0 at EVERY a, so each rational is a
    REMOVABLE discontinuity. The other examples:
       ⌊x⌋ at 1:            left limit 0, right limit 1       JUMP
       (x² − 1)/(x − 1):    = x + 1 → 2, f(1) undefined       REMOVABLE
       e^(1/x) at 0:        left limit 0, right limit +∞      ESSENTIAL
       1/(1 + e^(1/x)):     x → 0⁻: e^(1/x) → 0, limit 1;
                            x → 0⁺: e^(1/x) → ∞, limit 0      JUMP
    Common mistakes: calling every discontinuity 'a jump'; forgetting that
    T(0) = 1 (0 = 0/1). Remark: no function is continuous exactly on Q (the
    continuity set is always a G_δ set, and Q is not). Now you try: classify
    sgn(x) and x·sin(1/x) (value 0) at 0. (jump; continuous)

D4. Prove the intermediate value theorem. Deduce that every polynomial of
    odd degree has a real root and that every continuous f : [0, 1] → [0, 1]
    has a fixed point. Perform three bisection steps for x³ − 2x − 5 on
    [2, 3].
    Answer: Intervals [2, 2.5], [2, 2.25], [2, 2.125]; the root is ≈ 2.09455.
    Teacher explains: Let f be continuous on [a, b], f(a) < y < f(b) (the
    other case uses −f). Put S = {x ∈ [a, b] : f(x) < y}; a ∈ S and S is
    bounded, so c = sup S exists, c ∈ [a, b].
      f(c) < y impossible: by continuity f < y on some [c, c + δ) (and c < b
        because f(b) > y), so points beyond c lie in S, contradicting c = sup S.
      f(c) > y impossible: by continuity f > y on (c − δ, c], so no point of
        S lies there, and c − δ/2 would be a smaller upper bound.
    Hence f(c) = y. ODD DEGREE: p(x) = xⁿ + ... with n odd has p(x) → +∞ as
    x → ∞ and → −∞ as x → −∞, so p takes a negative and a positive value on
    some [−R, R], and the IVT gives a root. FIXED POINT: g(x) = f(x) − x has
    g(0) = f(0) ≥ 0 and g(1) = f(1) − 1 ≤ 0, so g(c) = 0, f(c) = c. BISECTION
    for f(x) = x³ − 2x − 5: f(2) = −1 < 0, f(3) = 16 > 0.
       f(2.5)   = 15.625 − 5 − 5         = 5.625 > 0    → [2, 2.5]
       f(2.25)  = 11.390625 − 4.5 − 5    = 1.890625 > 0 → [2, 2.25]
       f(2.125) = 9.595703 − 4.25 − 5    ≈ 0.3457 > 0   → [2, 2.125]
    After n steps the error is at most 1/2ⁿ. Common mistakes: applying IVT
    to a function with a jump (sgn x takes no value 1/2); concluding
    'exactly one root' from IVT alone. Now you try: show that eˣ = 3 − x has a
    root in (0, 1). (g(x) = eˣ + x − 3: g(0) = −2, g(1) = e − 2 > 0; root
    ≈ 0.79206)

D5. Prove the extreme value theorem. Show by examples that it fails if the
    interval is not closed, not bounded, or f is not continuous. Find the
    maximum and minimum of f(x) = x³ − 3x on [−2, 3].
    Answer: Proof below; max f(3) = 18, min f(−2) = f(1) = −2.
    Teacher explains: Step 1 (bounded): if f were unbounded, pick xₙ ∈ [a, b]
    with |f(xₙ)| > n. By Bolzano-Weierstrass a subsequence x_{n_k} → c, and
    c ∈ [a, b] because the interval is CLOSED. Continuity gives
    f(x_{n_k}) → f(c), a finite number, but |f(x_{n_k})| > n_k → ∞:
    contradiction. Step 2 (max attained): M = sup f exists by Step 1. Pick
    xₙ with f(xₙ) > M − 1/n; again a subsequence tends to some c ∈ [a, b]
    and f(c) = lim f(x_{n_k}) ≥ M, so f(c) = M. Counterexamples:
       (0, 1],  f = 1/x        unbounded              (not closed)
       [0, 1),  f = x          sup 1 not attained     (not closed)
       R,       f = arctan x   sup π/2 not attained   (not bounded)
       [0, 1],  f = x on [0, 1), f(1) = 0  sup 1 not attained (discontinuous)
    Computation: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1. Compare critical points and
    endpoints:
       f(−2) = −2,  f(−1) = 2,  f(1) = −2,  f(3) = 27 − 9 = 18
    max 18 (at 3), min −2 (at −2 and 1). Common mistakes: checking only
    critical points (here the max is at an endpoint); using EVT on an open
    interval. Now you try: max and min of x e⁻ˣ on [0, 2]. (max 1/e at x = 1;
    min 0 at x = 0)

D6. Define uniform continuity and explain how it differs from continuity.
    Prove: (a) f(x) = x² is uniformly continuous on [0, 2] but not on R;
    (b) g(x) = 1/x is not uniformly continuous on (0, 1); (c) h(x) = √x is
    uniformly continuous on [0, ∞).
    Answer: (a) δ = ε/4 on [0, 2]; on R use xₙ = n + 1/n, yₙ = n. (b) xₙ = 1/n,
    yₙ = 1/(n + 1). (c) δ = ε².
    Teacher explains: In continuity δ may depend on the POINT; in uniform
    continuity one δ must serve every pair of points: '∀ε ∃δ ∀x ∀y' against
    '∀ε ∀x ∃δ ∀y'. (a) On [0, 2], |x² − y²| = |x + y||x − y| ≤ 4|x − y|, so
    δ = ε/4 works everywhere. On R:
       xₙ = n + 1/n, yₙ = n:  |xₙ − yₙ| = 1/n → 0,
       xₙ² − yₙ² = 2 + 1/n² ≥ 2
    so with ε = 2 no δ can work: the graph gets steeper and steeper.
    (b) |1/n − 1/(n + 1)| = 1/(n(n + 1)) → 0 but |g(xₙ) − g(yₙ)| = 1 for all
    n. (c) For 0 ≤ y ≤ x: (√x − √y)² ≤ (√x − √y)(√x + √y) = x − y, so
    |√x − √y| ≤ √|x − y|, and δ = ε² works on all of [0, ∞). Note √x is UC
    but NOT Lipschitz: (√x − 0)/x = 1/√x → ∞. Common mistakes: 'the
    derivative of x² is unbounded, hence not UC' is only a heuristic
    (√x has unbounded derivative near 0 and IS UC); forgetting that in the
    negation the two sequences must get close. Now you try: is sin(x²) UC on
    R? (No: xₙ = √(nπ + π/2), yₙ = √(nπ) are close, |sin xₙ² − sin yₙ²| = 1)

D7. Prove the Heine-Cantor theorem: a continuous function on [a, b] is
    uniformly continuous. Prove also that (a) a Lipschitz function is UC;
    (b) a UC function maps Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences; (c) hence
    sin(1/x) is not UC on (0, 1), while x·sin(1/x) is.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: Heine-Cantor by contradiction. If f is not UC there
    are ε > 0 and xₙ, yₙ ∈ [a, b] with |xₙ − yₙ| < 1/n but
    |f(xₙ) − f(yₙ)| ≥ ε. By BW a subsequence x_{n_k} → c ∈ [a, b]; then
    y_{n_k} → c as well (|y_{n_k} − x_{n_k}| < 1/n_k). By continuity at c,
       f(x_{n_k}) − f(y_{n_k}) → f(c) − f(c) = 0,
    contradicting ≥ ε. (a) If |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ K|x − y|, take δ = ε/K.
    (b) Let (xₙ) be Cauchy and ε > 0; take the UC δ, then N with
    |xₘ − xₙ| < δ for m, n ≥ N; so |f(xₘ) − f(xₙ)| < ε. (c) xₙ = 1/(nπ/2) =
    2/(nπ) is Cauchy in (0, 1) (it converges to 0), but sin(1/xₙ) = sin(nπ/2)
    = 1, 0, −1, 0, 1, ... is not Cauchy, so sin(1/x) is not UC. For
    F(x) = x sin(1/x), set F(0) = 0: then F is continuous on the CLOSED
    interval [0, 1] (|F(x)| ≤ |x|), hence UC there by Heine-Cantor, hence UC
    on (0, 1). General rule: f is UC on (a, b) ⇔ it extends continuously to
    [a, b] (i.e. the one-sided limits at a and b exist). Common mistakes:
    applying Heine-Cantor on open or unbounded intervals; thinking UC fails
    whenever the domain is unbounded (sin x is UC on R). Now you try: is
    f(x) = x ln x UC on (0, 1)? (Yes: x ln x → 0 as x → 0⁺, so it extends
    continuously to [0, 1])

D8. (a) From the definition find f′(a) for f(x) = x³ and show that
    f(x) = |x| is not differentiable at 0 while g(x) = x|x| is, with
    g′(x) = 2|x|. (b) Prove that differentiability implies continuity.
    (c) Prove the chain rule using Carathéodory's formulation.
    Answer: f′(a) = 3a²; |x| has one-sided derivatives −1 and 1; g′(0) = 0.
    Teacher explains: (a) (a + h)³ − a³ = 3a²h + 3ah² + h³, divide by h:
       3a² + 3ah + h² → 3a²  (h → 0).
    For |x| at 0: (|h| − 0)/h = 1 for h > 0 and −1 for h < 0: the one-sided
    limits differ, no derivative (a CORNER). For g(x) = x|x| at 0:
    g(h)/h = |h| → 0, so g′(0) = 0; for x > 0, g = x², g′ = 2x; for x < 0,
    g = −x², g′ = −2x: altogether g′(x) = 2|x|, which is continuous but not
    differentiable at 0. (b) f(x) − f(a) = ((f(x) − f(a))/(x − a))·(x − a) →
    f′(a)·0 = 0. (c) Carathéodory: f is differentiable at a ⇔ there is φ
    continuous at a with f(x) − f(a) = φ(x)(x − a); then f′(a) = φ(a) (put
    φ(x) = (f(x) − f(a))/(x − a) for x ≠ a, φ(a) = f′(a)). For g ∘ f: write
    g(y) − g(b) = ψ(y)(y − b) with b = f(a), ψ continuous at b. Then
       g(f(x)) − g(f(a)) = ψ(f(x))(f(x) − f(a)) = ψ(f(x))φ(x)(x − a)
    and x ↦ ψ(f(x))φ(x) is continuous at a with value ψ(b)φ(a) =
    g′(f(a))f′(a). This avoids the classical gap of dividing by
    f(x) − f(a), which may be 0 for x near a. Common mistakes: 'continuous ⇒
    differentiable'; computing only a one-sided limit. Now you try: from the
    definition, differentiate √x at a > 0. ((√(a + h) − √a)/h =
    1/(√(a + h) + √a) → 1/(2√a))

D9. Let f(x) = x² sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0, f(0) = 0. Show f is differentiable
    everywhere but f′ is not continuous at 0. Then classify, for p > 0,
    fₚ(x) = |x|ᵖ sin(1/x) (fₚ(0) = 0): when is it differentiable at 0, and
    when is fₚ′ continuous at 0?
    Answer: f′(0) = 0, f′(x) = 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x) for x ≠ 0, which has no
    limit at 0. fₚ is differentiable at 0 ⇔ p > 1, and C¹ near 0 ⇔ p > 2.
    Teacher explains: At 0 use the DEFINITION (rules do not apply there):
       (f(h) − f(0))/h = h sin(1/h),   |h sin(1/h)| ≤ |h| → 0,
    so f′(0) = 0. Away from 0 the product and chain rules give
    f′(x) = 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x). Along xₖ = 1/(kπ):
    f′(xₖ) = −cos(kπ) = (−1)ᵏ⁺¹, alternating between 1 and −1, so
    lim_{x→0} f′(x) does not exist: f′ has an ESSENTIAL discontinuity at 0
    (by Darboux it cannot be a jump). General p:
       at 0:  fₚ(h)/h = |h|ᵖ sin(1/h)/h → 0 iff p > 1   (for p ≤ 1 it
              oscillates or does not shrink)
       x ≠ 0: fₚ′(x) = p|x|ᵖ⁻¹ sgn(x) sin(1/x) − |x|ᵖ⁻² cos(1/x)
    The second term → 0 iff p > 2. So: p ≤ 1 not differentiable at 0;
    1 < p ≤ 2 differentiable with discontinuous derivative; p > 2 C¹.
    (Continuity at 0 needs only p > 0.) Common mistakes: computing f′(0) by
    substituting x = 0 into the formula for f′(x) (it is undefined there);
    concluding 'f′(0) does not exist' from 'lim f′(x) does not exist'. Now you
    try: is g(x) = x³ sin(1/x) (g(0) = 0) twice differentiable at 0?
    (g′(x) = 3x² sin(1/x) − x cos(1/x), g′(0) = 0; g′(h)/h = 3h sin(1/h) −
    cos(1/h) has no limit: no)

D10. Prove Fermat's theorem, Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem.
     Use the MVT to prove |sin x − sin y| ≤ |x − y| and ln(1 + x) < x for
     x > 0, and find c in the MVT for x³ on [0, 2].
     Answer: Proofs below; c = 2/√3 ≈ 1.15470.
     Teacher explains: FERMAT: if f has a local max at interior c and f′(c)
     exists, then (f(c + h) − f(c))/h ≤ 0 for small h > 0 and ≥ 0 for small
     h < 0; the limit f′(c) is both ≤ 0 and ≥ 0, so f′(c) = 0. ROLLE: by EVT,
     f attains a max and a min on [a, b]. If both are at the endpoints,
     f(a) = f(b) makes f constant and f′ ≡ 0. Otherwise one of them is at an
     interior c, and Fermat gives f′(c) = 0. MVT: tilt the graph. Let
       g(x) = f(x) − f(a) − ((f(b) − f(a))/(b − a))(x − a)
     so g(a) = g(b) = 0; Rolle gives g′(c) = 0, i.e.
     f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). Applications:
       sin x − sin y = cos(c)(x − y), |cos c| ≤ 1 ⇒ |sin x − sin y| ≤ |x − y|
       ln(1 + x) − ln 1 = x/(1 + c), 0 < c < x ⇒ ln(1 + x) < x
     For x³ on [0, 2]: slope (8 − 0)/2 = 4 = 3c², c = 2/√3 ≈ 1.1547 ∈ (0, 2) ✓.
     Common mistakes: using Rolle when f(a) ≠ f(b), or when f is not
     differentiable inside (|x| on [−1, 1] has no horizontal tangent);
     forgetting that c is strictly inside. Now you try: MVT for √x on
     [1, 4]. (slope 1/3 = 1/(2√c), c = 9/4)

D11. Prove: (a) if f′ = 0 on an interval then f is constant; (b) if f′ > 0 on
     an interval then f is strictly increasing; (c) Cauchy's mean value
     theorem; (d) L'Hôpital's rule for 0/0 at a point. Evaluate
     lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³ and lim_{x→0} (1/x − 1/sin x). Show that
     f(x) = x + 2x² sin(1/x) (f(0) = 0) has f′(0) = 1 but is not increasing on
     any interval around 0.
     Answer: 1/6; 0; f′(x) = 1 + 4x sin(1/x) − 2cos(1/x) takes the value −1
     arbitrarily near 0.
     Teacher explains: (a), (b): for x < y in the interval, MVT gives
     f(y) − f(x) = f′(c)(y − x): = 0 in (a), > 0 in (b). (c) Put
        h(x) = (f(b) − f(a))g(x) − (g(b) − g(a))f(x);
     then h(a) = f(b)g(a) − g(b)f(a) = h(b), and Rolle gives
     (f(b) − f(a))g′(c) = (g(b) − g(a))f′(c). (d) If f(a) = g(a) = 0,
     g′ ≠ 0 near a and f′/g′ → L, then for x near a Cauchy's MVT on [a, x]
     gives f(x)/g(x) = f′(c)/g′(c) with c between a and x; as x → a, c → a,
     so f(x)/g(x) → L. Examples (apply three times while 0/0 persists):
        (x − sin x)/x³ → (1 − cos x)/(3x²) → sin x/(6x) → 1/6
        1/x − 1/sin x = (sin x − x)/(x sin x) → (cos x − 1)/(sin x + x cos x)
                      → −sin x/(2cos x − x sin x) → 0
     Last part: f′(0) = lim (h + 2h² sin(1/h))/h = 1. For x = 1/(2kπ),
     f′(x) = 1 + 0 − 2 = −1 < 0, so f decreases near points arbitrarily
     close to 0. Common mistakes: using L'Hôpital when the limit is not 0/0
     or ∞/∞; differentiating the quotient f/g instead of f and g separately.
     Now you try: lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1 − x)/x². (→ (eˣ − 1)/(2x) → eˣ/2 → 1/2)

D12. Prove Darboux's theorem: if f is differentiable on [a, b] and
     f′(a) < y < f′(b), then f′(c) = y for some c ∈ (a, b). Deduce that sgn x
     is not the derivative of any function. Then state Taylor's theorem
     with Lagrange remainder and estimate the error of approximating e^0.5 by
     its degree-3 Maclaurin polynomial; find the degree n that guarantees
     |eˣ − Pₙ(x)| < 10⁻⁶ on [0, 1].
     Answer: P₃(0.5) = 1.6458333, error ≤ 2(0.5)⁴/24 ≈ 0.0052 (true error
     0.00289); n = 9.
     Teacher explains: Darboux: let g(x) = f(x) − yx. Then g′(a) =
     f′(a) − y < 0 and g′(b) = f′(b) − y > 0. g is continuous on [a, b], so it
     has a minimum at some c (EVT). g′(a) < 0 means g decreases just after a,
     so the min is not at a; g′(b) > 0 means g increases just before b, so
     it is not at b. Hence c is interior and g′(c) = 0 (Fermat): f′(c) = y.
     No continuity of f′ was used! sgn x takes the values −1 and 1 on
     [−1, 1] but never 1/2, so it has no antiderivative on R. TAYLOR: if f
     is n + 1 times differentiable,
        f(x) = Pₙ(x) + f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c)(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)!   (c between a and x)
     For eˣ at 0: P₃(0.5) = 1 + 0.5 + 0.125 + 0.0208333 = 1.6458333, and
        |R₃| = e^c(0.5)⁴/4! < 2 × 0.0625/24 ≈ 0.0052   (e^0.5 < 2)
     True value e^0.5 = 1.6487213: error 0.00289 ✓. On [0, 1],
     |Rₙ| ≤ e/(n + 1)! < 3/(n + 1)!; we need (n + 1)! > 3·10⁶: 9! = 362880 is
     too small, 10! = 3628800 works, so n + 1 = 10, n = 9. Common mistakes:
     thinking a derivative must be continuous; bounding e^c by e^0 = 1 (c is
     between 0 and x, so e^c ≤ eˣ). Now you try: the degree-2 Taylor
     polynomial of √(1 + x) at 0 and a bound for its error at x = 0.2.
     (1 + x/2 − x²/8; |R₂| ≤ (3/8)(0.2)³/6 = 0.0005; P₂(0.2) = 1.095,
     √1.2 ≈ 1.095445)

       n) none: f′(x) = (2/3)x^(−1/3) ≠ 0 (not differentiable at 0)
