       p) (e² − 1)(−e⁻ᶜ) = (e⁻² − 1)eᶜ ⇒ e²ᶜ = e², c = 1

M11. Evaluate (L'Hôpital or Taylor).
     a) lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³      b) lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/x²
     c) lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1 − x)/x²     d) lim_{x→0⁺} x ln x
     e) lim_{x→1} (ln x)/(x − 1)      f) lim_{x→0⁺} xˣ
     g) lim_{x→0} (1/x − 1/sin x)     h) lim_{x→0} (tan x − x)/x³
     i) lim_{x→∞} x²/eˣ               j) lim_{x→∞} (1 + 2/x)ˣ
     k) lim_{x→0} (x − ln(1 + x))/x²  l) lim_{x→0} (arcsin x − x)/x³
     m) lim_{x→0} (cos x − 1 + x²/2)/x⁴                 n) lim_{x→∞} x^(1/x)
     o) lim_{x→0} (2ˣ − 3ˣ)/x         p) lim_{x→0} ((sin x)/x)^(1/x²)
     q) lim_{x→0} (sin 3x)/(sin 5x)   r) lim_{x→π/2} (1 − sin x)/cos x
     Answers:
       a) 1/6    b) 1/2    c) 1/2    d) 0      e) 1      f) 1
       g) 0      h) 1/3    i) 0      j) e²     k) 1/2    l) 1/6
       m) 1/24   n) 1      o) ln(2/3) ≈ −0.40547         p) e^(−1/6) ≈ 0.84648
       q) 3/5    r) 0

M12. Taylor's theorem and Darboux's theorem.
     a) Maclaurin polynomial P₃ of eˣ
     b) P₃(0.5) for eˣ and the Lagrange bound (use e^0.5 < 2)
     c) P₅ of sin x and its error bound at x = 0.5 (|R| ≤ x⁷/7!)
     d) P₃ of ln(1 + x), its value at 0.1 and the bound x⁴/4
     e) P₂ of √(1 + x), its value at 0.2 and the bound
     f) least n with 3/(n + 1)! < 10⁻⁶ (eˣ on [0, 1])
     g) P₄ of cos x
     h) Taylor polynomial of x³ − 2x + 1 about a = 1
     i) least n such that the bound 1/(n + 1)! for sin x on [0, 1] is < 10⁻⁴
     True or false:
     j) sgn x is the derivative of some function on R
     k) ⌊x⌋ is the derivative of some function on R
     l) 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x) (x ≠ 0), 0 at 0, is a derivative on R
     m) a derivative can have a removable discontinuity
     n) f differentiable on [0, 1], f′(0) = −1, f′(1) = 2 ⇒ f′(c) = 1/2 for
        some c
     o) f′ > 0 on (a, b) ⇒ f strictly increasing on (a, b)
     p) f′(0) > 0 ⇒ f is increasing on some interval around 0
     Answers:
       a) 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6
       b) 1.6458333; bound 2(0.5)⁴/24 ≈ 0.0052 (true error 0.00289)
       c) x − x³/6 + x⁵/120; 0.5⁷/5040 ≈ 1.55 × 10⁻⁶
       d) x − x²/2 + x³/3; 0.0953333; 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ (ln 1.1 = 0.0953102)
       e) 1 + x/2 − x²/8; 1.095; (3/8)(0.2)³/6 = 0.0005 (√1.2 ≈ 1.095445)
       f) 9           g) 1 − x²/2 + x⁴/24
       h) (x − 1) + 3(x − 1)² + (x − 1)³
       i) 7 (8! = 40320 > 10⁴, 7! = 5040 < 10⁴, so n + 1 = 8)
       j) F    k) F    l) T (it is the derivative of x² sin(1/x))
       m) F    n) T (Darboux)    o) T (MVT)    p) F: x + 2x² sin(1/x)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always start an ε-δ proof with 'scratch work' (factor
  |f(x) − f(a)|, restrict |x − a| < 1, bound the other factor), then write
  the clean proof with 'Given ε > 0, let δ = ...'. Draw pictures of an
  ε-band and a δ-window, and show how the window must shrink for x² far out
  on the axis (the heart of NON-uniform continuity). Collect the standard
  counterexamples on one card: |x|, x sin(1/x), x² sin(1/x), 1_Q, x·1_Q,
  Thomae, sin(1/x), 1/x on (0, 1). For differentiability at a special point
  always use the difference quotient, never the formula for f′(x). Harder:
  prove that a monotone function has at most countably many
  discontinuities; show that a continuous injective function on an
  interval is strictly monotone with continuous inverse; prove that f is UC
  on a bounded set iff it maps Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences; prove
  the Taylor theorem with integral remainder; show that e^(−1/x²) has all
  derivatives 0 at 0 (so its Taylor series does not represent it); and read
  about Weierstrass's continuous nowhere-differentiable function
  ∑ aⁿ cos(bⁿπx) (0 < a < 1, ab > 1 + 3π/2).


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.3 — RIEMANN INTEGRATION; RIEMANN-STIELTJES INTEGRAL
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A PARTITION P of [a, b] is a finite set a = x₀ < x₁ < ... < xₙ = b, with
    Δxᵢ = xᵢ − xᵢ₋₁ and MESH ‖P‖ = max Δxᵢ. For BOUNDED f put
    Mᵢ = sup f and mᵢ = inf f on [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ]; UPPER SUM U(P, f) = ∑ MᵢΔxᵢ,
    LOWER SUM L(P, f) = ∑ mᵢΔxᵢ. A RIEMANN SUM ∑ f(tᵢ)Δxᵢ (tᵢ any tag in
    the i-th interval) lies between them.
  - REFINEMENT: if P ⊆ P* then L(P) ≤ L(P*) ≤ U(P*) ≤ U(P). Hence
    L(P₁) ≤ U(P₂) for ANY two partitions. UPPER INTEGRAL = inf_P U(P, f),
    LOWER INTEGRAL = sup_P L(P, f); always lower ≤ upper. f is RIEMANN
    INTEGRABLE (f ∈ R[a, b]) when they are equal; the common value is ∫ₐᵇ f.
  - RIEMANN CRITERION: f ∈ R[a, b] ⇔ ∀ε > 0 ∃P : U(P, f) − L(P, f) < ε.
    Equivalently (Darboux's theorem) the Riemann sums converge as ‖P‖ → 0;
    then ∫ₐᵇ f = lim (b − a)/n · ∑ f(a + k(b − a)/n) (limits of sums).
  - INTEGRABLE CLASSES: CONTINUOUS functions (via uniform continuity);
    MONOTONE functions (U − L = |f(b) − f(a)|(b − a)/n on n equal parts);
    bounded functions with FINITELY (even countably) many discontinuities.
    LEBESGUE's CRITERION: a bounded f is integrable ⇔ its set of
    discontinuities has MEASURE ZERO. Dirichlet's 1_Q is NOT integrable
    (U = 1, L = 0); Thomae's function IS, with integral 0. Unbounded
    functions are never Riemann integrable.
  - PROPERTIES: linearity; monotonicity (f ≤ g ⇒ ∫f ≤ ∫g); additivity
    ∫ₐᵇ = ∫ₐᶜ + ∫ᶜᵇ; m(b − a) ≤ ∫ₐᵇ f ≤ M(b − a); |f|, f², fg, max(f, g) and
    φ ∘ f (φ continuous) are integrable; |∫f| ≤ ∫|f|; CAUCHY-SCHWARZ
    (∫fg)² ≤ ∫f²·∫g². Changing f at finitely many points changes nothing.
    MEAN VALUE THEOREM FOR INTEGRALS: f continuous ⇒ ∫ₐᵇ f = f(c)(b − a).
  - FTC I: if f ∈ R[a, b] then F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f is LIPSCHITZ (|F(x) − F(y)| ≤
    M|x − y|) and F′(c) = f(c) at every point c where f is CONTINUOUS. Chain
    form: d/dx ∫_{u(x)}^{v(x)} f = f(v)v′ − f(u)u′.
  - FTC II: if F is differentiable on [a, b] and F′ = f ∈ R[a, b] then
    ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a) (proof: MVT on each subinterval). F′ may exist yet not
    be integrable (x² sin(1/x²)). Integration BY PARTS and SUBSTITUTION follow.
  - RIEMANN-STIELTJES: for α INCREASING on [a, b], Δαᵢ = α(xᵢ) − α(xᵢ₋₁),
    U(P, f, α) = ∑ MᵢΔαᵢ, L(P, f, α) = ∑ mᵢΔαᵢ; f ∈ R(α) when
    inf U = sup L = ∫ₐᵇ f dα. Criterion: ∀ε ∃P, U − L < ε. f continuous
    (α increasing) ⇒ f ∈ R(α); also f monotone with α continuous.
  - STEP INTEGRATORS: if α jumps by jₖ at cₖ (and is constant between) and
    f is continuous there, ∫ f dα = ∑ f(cₖ)jₖ. So ∫₀ⁿ f(x) d⌊x⌋ = f(1) + ... +
    f(n): sums ARE Stieltjes integrals. A jump at the left endpoint a
    contributes nothing if α is right-continuous there.
  - SMOOTH INTEGRATORS: if α′ is Riemann integrable, ∫ₐᵇ f dα = ∫ₐᵇ f(x)α′(x) dx.
    Mixed α = smooth part + jumps: add the two contributions. Linear in f
    and in α; additive over [a, c] ∪ [c, b].
  - INTEGRATION BY PARTS: ∫ₐᵇ f dα + ∫ₐᵇ α df = f(b)α(b) − f(a)α(a) (one exists
    ⇒ the other does). f and α with a COMMON discontinuity on the same side
    (⌊x⌋ d⌊x⌋) have no Stieltjes integral. For α of BOUNDED VARIATION write
    α = α₁ − α₂ with α₁, α₂ increasing.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. For f(x) = x² on [0, 1] and the partition Pₙ into n equal parts find
    U(Pₙ, f) and L(Pₙ, f) in closed form, evaluate them for n = 4 and
    n = 10, and prove from the definition that ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3.
    Answer: U = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n²), L = (n − 1)(2n − 1)/(6n²); n = 4:
    U = 15/32 = 0.46875, L = 7/32 = 0.21875; n = 10: U = 0.385, L = 0.285.
    Teacher explains: The points are xₖ = k/n, all Δxₖ = 1/n. x² is
    INCREASING on [0, 1], so on [(k − 1)/n, k/n] the sup is at the right end
    and the inf at the left end:
       U = ∑_{k=1}^{n} (k/n)²·(1/n) = (1/n³)·n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
       L = ∑_{k=1}^{n} ((k − 1)/n)²·(1/n) = (1/n³)·(n − 1)n(2n − 1)/6
    n = 4: U = 30/64 = 15/32, L = 14/64 = 7/32. n = 10: U = 11·21/600 =
    0.385, L = 9·19/600 = 0.285. Now U − L = (1/n)·(f(1) − f(0)) = 1/n → 0
    (the sums telescope), so by the Riemann criterion f is integrable. Both
    U and L tend to 2/6 = 1/3, and
       L(Pₙ) ≤ lower integral ≤ upper integral ≤ U(Pₙ)
    squeezes the integral: ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3. Common mistakes: taking the sup
    at the left end (true only for decreasing functions); forgetting the
    factor Δx = 1/n. Now you try: U(Pₙ) and L(Pₙ) for f(x) = x on [0, 1].
    (U = (n + 1)/(2n), L = (n − 1)/(2n), both → 1/2)

D2. Prove: (a) refining a partition does not decrease L or increase U;
    (b) L(P₁, f) ≤ U(P₂, f) for all partitions P₁, P₂; (c) the lower
    integral is ≤ the upper integral; (d) the Riemann criterion: f is
    integrable ⇔ for every ε > 0 there is P with U(P, f) − L(P, f) < ε.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: (a) It suffices to add ONE point y to [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ]. The
    term Mᵢ(xᵢ − xᵢ₋₁) is replaced by
       M′(y − xᵢ₋₁) + M″(xᵢ − y)   with M′, M″ ≤ Mᵢ
    (sups over SMALLER sets), so U can only drop; symmetrically L can only
    rise. Add points one at a time. (b) Let P* = P₁ ∪ P₂ (a common
    refinement):
       L(P₁) ≤ L(P*) ≤ U(P*) ≤ U(P₂).
    (c) By (b) every lower sum is ≤ every upper sum; take sup over P₁, then
    inf over P₂. (d) (⇐) For every ε: 0 ≤ upper − lower ≤ U(P) − L(P) < ε,
    so upper = lower. (⇒) If both equal I, pick P₁ with L(P₁) > I − ε/2 and
    P₂ with U(P₂) < I + ε/2; for P = P₁ ∪ P₂, U(P) − L(P) < ε. The criterion
    is the working tool: it avoids computing the integral. Example: f = x on
    [0, 1] with P = {0, 1/2, 1}: L = 1/4, U = 3/4, and adding 1/4, 3/4 gives
    L = 3/8, U = 5/8 — the gap closes from 1/2 to 1/4. Common mistakes:
    thinking U(P) decreases for ANY change of partition (only for
    REFINEMENTS); comparing U(P₁) with L(P₂) without a common refinement.
    Now you try: for f = x² on [0, 2], P = {0, 1, 2}, compute U − L, then
    refine by adding 1/2 and 3/2. (U − L = 5 − 1 = 4; refined U = 15/4,
    L = 7/4, gap 2)

D3. Show that Dirichlet's function 1_Q is not Riemann integrable on [0, 1].
    Find the upper and lower integrals of g(x) = x for rational x, 0 for
    irrational x on [0, 1]. Explain why the Lebesgue criterion predicts both
    answers.
    Answer: For 1_Q: U(P) = 1, L(P) = 0 for every P. For g: upper integral
    1/2, lower integral 0: not integrable.
    Teacher explains: Every subinterval, however small, contains rationals
    and irrationals (density). So for 1_Q, Mᵢ = 1, mᵢ = 0 on every piece:
       U(P) = ∑ 1·Δxᵢ = 1,   L(P) = 0   for every P
    and U − L = 1 can never be made small. For g: mᵢ = 0 (irrational points)
    and Mᵢ = sup of rationals in [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ] = xᵢ. So L(P) = 0 and
    U(P) = ∑ xᵢΔxᵢ, which is an upper sum for h(x) = x. Its infimum over P
    is ∫₀¹ x dx = 1/2. Lower integral 0 ≠ 1/2 = upper integral. Lebesgue: 1_Q
    is discontinuous at EVERY point of [0, 1] (positive measure: length 1);
    g is continuous only at 0, so its discontinuity set (0, 1] also has
    positive measure. Contrast Thomae's function (D5): discontinuous only on
    the COUNTABLE set Q, measure zero, so integrable. Common mistakes:
    'the rationals are countable, so 1_Q is integrable' (the discontinuity
    set is ALL of [0, 1], not Q); thinking Riemann integrability depends on
    how f is defined on a measure-zero set in general (changing f on Q
    changed everything here). Now you try: upper and lower integrals of
    f = 1 on Q, 2 off Q on [0, 3]. (upper 6, lower 3)

D4. Prove that (a) every continuous function on [a, b] is integrable and
    (b) every monotone function on [a, b] is integrable. For f(x) = eˣ on
    [0, 1] find the least n such that the equal partition Pₙ has
    U − L < 0.001.
    Answer: Proofs below; U − L = (e − 1)/n, least n = 1719.
    Teacher explains: (a) By HEINE-CANTOR, f is uniformly continuous: given
    ε > 0 there is δ with |x − y| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(y)| < ε/(b − a). Take any P
    with mesh < δ. On each piece f attains its max and min (EVT) at points
    closer than δ, so Mᵢ − mᵢ < ε/(b − a), and
       U − L = ∑(Mᵢ − mᵢ)Δxᵢ < (ε/(b − a))·(b − a) = ε.
    (b) Say f is increasing; take n equal parts of width h = (b − a)/n. Then
    Mᵢ = f(xᵢ), mᵢ = f(xᵢ₋₁) and the sum TELESCOPES:
       U − L = h ∑ (f(xᵢ) − f(xᵢ₋₁)) = h(f(b) − f(a)) = (b − a)(f(b) − f(a))/n
    which is < ε for large n. Monotone functions may have infinitely many
    jumps, yet are integrable. For eˣ on [0, 1]: U − L = (e − 1)/n < 0.001 ⇔
    n > 1718.28..., so n = 1719. Common mistakes: in (a) using mere
    continuity (a δ that depends on the point cannot control all pieces at
    once); in (b) forgetting that the telescoping needs EQUAL widths (or at
    least mesh ≤ h). Now you try: least n for U − L < 0.01 with √x on [0, 4].
    (U − L = 2·4/n = 8/n; n = 801)

D5. Thomae's function T (T(p/q) = 1/q in lowest terms, T(irrational) = 0)
    on [0, 1]. Prove T ∈ R[0, 1] and ∫₀¹ T = 0. Prove also that a bounded
    function with finitely many discontinuities is integrable. State
    Lebesgue's criterion and use it to decide sin(1/x) (value 0 at 0) and
    the indicator of the Cantor set.
    Answer: Proofs below; both are integrable (∫₀¹ sin(1/x) dx =
    sin 1 − Ci(1) ≈ 0.50407; the Cantor-set indicator has integral 0).
    Teacher explains: THOMAE: every L(P) = 0 (irrationals everywhere). Given
    ε > 0, only finitely many points, say K of them, have T(x) ≥ ε/2 (those
    p/q with q ≤ 2/ε). Choose P so that these K points lie in pieces of total
    length < ε/2 (e.g. each inside a piece of length < ε/(4K); a point can
    touch two pieces). On the other pieces T < ε/2. Then
       U(P) < 1·(ε/2) + (ε/2)·1 = ε   (T ≤ 1)
    so U − L < ε: integrable, and 0 ≤ ∫T ≤ U(P) < ε for every ε gives ∫T = 0.
    FINITELY MANY DISCONTINUITIES c₁, ..., c_K with |f| ≤ M: enclose each cⱼ
    in a tiny interval of length η; these pieces contribute at most 2M·Kη to
    U − L. On the remaining closed intervals f is continuous, hence
    integrable (D4), so they can be partitioned with gap < ε/2. Choose
    η = ε/(4MK). LEBESGUE: bounded f is integrable ⇔ {discontinuities} has
    MEASURE ZERO (can be covered by intervals of total length < ε for every
    ε). Countable sets and the Cantor set (length (2/3)ⁿ → 0 at stage n) have
    measure zero. sin(1/x) is bounded with one discontinuity: integrable.
    1_Cantor is discontinuous exactly on the Cantor set: integrable, and
    its lower sums are 0, so ∫ = 0. Common mistakes: forgetting BOUNDEDNESS
    (1/x on (0, 1] has one 'discontinuity' but is not integrable); thinking
    uncountable discontinuity sets always prevent integrability (Cantor).
    Now you try: is f(x) = 1 at x = 1/n (n ∈ N), 0 elsewhere, integrable on
    [0, 1]? (Yes, discontinuities {0} ∪ {1/n} are countable; ∫ = 0)

D6. Prove: (a) if f ∈ R[a, b] then |f| ∈ R[a, b] and |∫f| ≤ ∫|f|; (b) f² and
    hence fg are integrable when f, g are; (c) the mean value theorem for
    integrals. Then show 4/3 ≤ ∫₀¹ e^(x²) dx ≤ e and find c with
    ∫₀³ x² dx = 3c².
    Answer: Proofs below; c = √3. (∫₀¹ e^(x²) dx ≈ 1.46265.)
    Teacher explains: (a) On every piece | |f(x)| − |f(y)| | ≤ |f(x) − f(y)|,
    so the oscillation of |f| is at most that of f and U(P, |f|) −
    L(P, |f|) ≤ U(P, f) − L(P, f). Then −|f| ≤ f ≤ |f| and monotonicity give
    −∫|f| ≤ ∫f ≤ ∫|f|. (b) With |f| ≤ M: |f(x)² − f(y)²| = |f(x) + f(y)||f(x) −
    f(y)| ≤ 2M|f(x) − f(y)|, so the gap for f² is at most 2M times that for
    f. Then fg = ((f + g)² − (f − g)²)/4 is integrable. (c) If f is
    continuous with min m and max M on [a, b], then m(b − a) ≤ ∫f ≤ M(b − a),
    so (1/(b − a))∫f lies between m and M, and the IVT gives c with
    f(c) = (1/(b − a))∫ₐᵇ f. Estimates: eᵘ ≥ 1 + u gives e^(x²) ≥ 1 + x², so
       ∫₀¹ e^(x²) ≥ ∫₀¹ (1 + x²) = 4/3 ≈ 1.333;   e^(x²) ≤ e on [0, 1] ⇒ ∫ ≤ e.
    The plain bound m(b − a) = 1 is weaker than 4/3. For x² on [0, 3]:
    ∫ = 9 = 3c², so c = √3 ≈ 1.732 ∈ (0, 3). Common mistakes: 'f integrable
    ⇒ f continuous'; forgetting that the MVT for integrals needs continuity
    (for sgn on [−1, 1], ∫ = 0 but only f(0) = 0 works, luckily; for f = 0 on
    [0, 1), 1 on [1, 2], mean 1/2 is never a value). Now you try: find the
    average value of sin x on [0, π] and a c where it is attained.
    (2/π; c = arcsin(2/π) ≈ 0.69011 or π − 0.69011)

D7. Prove the first fundamental theorem: for f ∈ R[a, b], F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f is
    Lipschitz, and F′(c) = f(c) wherever f is continuous at c. Illustrate
    with f = sgn on [−1, 1], and compute d/dx ∫ₓ^(x²) e^(t²) dt.
    Answer: F(x) = |x| − 1 for sgn; F is not differentiable at 0.
    d/dx ∫ₓ^(x²) e^(t²) dt = 2x e^(x⁴) − e^(x²).
    Teacher explains: With |f| ≤ M:
       |F(y) − F(x)| = |∫ₓʸ f| ≤ M|y − x|     (Lipschitz, hence continuous)
    At a continuity point c: given ε pick δ with |f(t) − f(c)| < ε for
    |t − c| < δ. For 0 < |h| < δ,
       |(F(c + h) − F(c))/h − f(c)| = |(1/h)∫_c^{c+h} (f(t) − f(c)) dt| ≤ ε.
    So F′(c) = f(c). For sgn on [−1, 1]:
       x ≤ 0: F(x) = ∫₋₁ˣ (−1) dt = −(x + 1)
       x ≥ 0: F(x) = −1 + ∫₀ˣ 1 dt = x − 1
    i.e. F(x) = |x| − 1: continuous everywhere (even though f jumps), with
    F′ = sgn except at 0, where F has a corner. Integration SMOOTHS: f has
    a jump, F a corner. For the variable limits, write
    G(x) = H(x²) − H(x) with H(u) = ∫₀ᵘ e^(t²) dt, H′(u) = e^(u²):
       G′(x) = H′(x²)·2x − H′(x) = 2x e^(x⁴) − e^(x²).
    Common mistakes: forgetting the chain-rule factor 2x; writing
    e^((x²)²) as e^(x²)·²; claiming F′ = f everywhere for discontinuous f.
    Now you try: d/dx ∫₀^(sin x) √(1 − t²) dt. (cos x·√(1 − sin²x) = cos x·|cos x|)

D8. Prove the second fundamental theorem: if F is differentiable on [a, b]
    and F′ = f is Riemann integrable, then ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a). Use it to
    derive integration by parts, and compute ∫₀¹ x²eˣ dx. Explain why
    F(x) = x² sin(1/x²) (F(0) = 0) shows that the hypothesis 'F′ integrable'
    cannot be dropped.
    Answer: ∫₀¹ x²eˣ dx = e − 2 ≈ 0.71828. F′ exists everywhere on [0, 1]
    but is unbounded, hence not Riemann integrable.
    Teacher explains: Take any partition P. By the MVT on each piece,
    F(xᵢ) − F(xᵢ₋₁) = f(tᵢ)Δxᵢ for some tᵢ, and summing (telescoping):
       F(b) − F(a) = ∑ f(tᵢ)Δxᵢ,   so L(P, f) ≤ F(b) − F(a) ≤ U(P, f).
    This holds for EVERY P, so F(b) − F(a) lies between the lower and upper
    integrals, which are equal: it IS the integral. Parts: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
    is integrable when u′, v′ are, so ∫ₐᵇ uv′ = [uv]ₐᵇ − ∫ₐᵇ u′v. Twice:
       ∫₀¹ x²eˣ = [x²eˣ]₀¹ − 2∫₀¹ xeˣ = e − 2([xeˣ]₀¹ − ∫₀¹ eˣ)
               = e − 2(e − (e − 1)) = e − 2
    For F(x) = x² sin(1/x²): F′(0) = lim h sin(1/h²) = 0, and for x ≠ 0
       F′(x) = 2x sin(1/x²) − (2/x)cos(1/x²),
    which is unbounded near 0 (at x = 1/√(2kπ) it equals −2√(2kπ)). An
    unbounded function is not Riemann integrable, so FTC II does not apply,
    although F(1) − F(0) = sin 1 is perfectly defined (as an improper
    integral it works). Common mistakes: 'every derivative is integrable';
    forgetting that FTC II needs F′ on the whole closed interval (one-sided
    at the ends). Now you try: ∫₀^(π/2) x cos x dx. (π/2 − 1 ≈ 0.5708)

D9. Use Riemann sums to evaluate the limits (a) lim ∑_{k=1}^{n} n/(n² + k²),
    (b) lim ∑_{k=1}^{n} 1/(n + k), (c) lim (1/n)∑_{k=1}^{n} (k/n)ᵖ (p > 0),
    (d) lim (n!/nⁿ)^(1/n).
    Answer: (a) π/4, (b) ln 2, (c) 1/(p + 1), (d) 1/e.
    Teacher explains: Since the Riemann sums of an integrable f converge to
    the integral when the mesh → 0, for continuous f on [0, 1]
       (1/n)∑_{k=1}^{n} f(k/n) → ∫₀¹ f(x) dx   (right-endpoint sums).
    The skill is to spot f by pulling out 1/n:
       (a) n/(n² + k²) = (1/n)·1/(1 + (k/n)²),  f(x) = 1/(1 + x²),
           ∫₀¹ = arctan 1 = π/4 ≈ 0.785398
       (b) 1/(n + k) = (1/n)·1/(1 + k/n),  f(x) = 1/(1 + x),  ∫₀¹ = ln 2
       (c) f(x) = xᵖ,  ∫₀¹ xᵖ dx = 1/(p + 1)
       (d) take logs: (1/n)ln(n!/nⁿ) = (1/n)∑ ln(k/n) → ∫₀¹ ln x dx = −1
           (improper but convergent; justify by monotonicity), so → e⁻¹
    Check (a) numerically: n = 10 gives ∑ 10/(100 + k²) ≈ 0.7600 and
    n = 100 gives ≈ 0.7829 (the right-endpoint sum is below for decreasing
    f, error ≈ (f(0) − f(1))/(2n) = 1/(4n)). Common mistakes: forgetting to
    factor out exactly 1/n; wrong interval (∑_{k=1}^{2n} 1/(n + k) is a sum
    over [0, 2], giving ln 3). Now you try: lim ∑_{k=1}^{n} k/(n² + k²).
    ((1/n)∑ (k/n)/(1 + (k/n)²) → ∫₀¹ x/(1 + x²) dx = (ln 2)/2 ≈ 0.34657)

D10. Define the Riemann-Stieltjes integral ∫ₐᵇ f dα for increasing α. Let
     H(x) = 0 for x < 0, 1 for x ≥ 0 (unit step). Prove: if a < c < b and f is
     continuous at c then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dH(x − c) = f(c). Deduce ∫₀ⁿ f(x) d⌊x⌋ =
     f(1) + ... + f(n) for continuous f, and evaluate ∫₀³ x² d⌊x⌋ and
     ∫₀^π sin x d⌊x⌋.
     Answer: ∫₀³ x² d⌊x⌋ = 14; ∫₀^π sin x d⌊x⌋ = sin 1 + sin 2 + sin 3 ≈ 1.89189.
     Teacher explains: The Stieltjes sums weight each piece by the INCREASE of
     α instead of its length:
        U(P, f, α) = ∑ MᵢΔαᵢ,  L(P, f, α) = ∑ mᵢΔαᵢ,  Δαᵢ = α(xᵢ) − α(xᵢ₋₁).
     For α(x) = H(x − c), Δαᵢ = 0 for every piece except the one [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ]
     with xᵢ₋₁ < c ≤ xᵢ, where Δα = 1. So
        U(P) = sup f on that piece,   L(P) = inf f on that piece.
     By continuity of f at c, refining P so the piece around c is tiny makes
     both → f(c): the integral is f(c). The integrator is a 'point mass' at
     c. ⌊x⌋ on [0, n] is H(x − 1) + H(x − 2) + ... + H(x − n) (for x ≥ 0), and
     the integral is linear in α, so ∫₀ⁿ f d⌊x⌋ = ∑_{k=1}^{n} f(k). Note: the
     jump at the right end n counts (⌊n⌋ − ⌊n⁻⌋ = 1), none at 0 (⌊x⌋ is
     right-continuous and starts at 0). Values:
        ∫₀³ x² d⌊x⌋ = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14
        ∫₀^π sin x d⌊x⌋ = sin 1 + sin 2 + sin 3 = 0.84147 + 0.90930 + 0.14112
     (jumps at 1, 2, 3 < π ≈ 3.14). Common mistakes: including a jump at 0;
     computing ∫ x² dx instead; thinking the Stieltjes integral is always
     'area'. Now you try: ∫₀^5 x² d⌊x/2⌋. (jumps at 2 and 4: 4 + 16 = 20)

D11. Prove: if α is increasing and α′ is Riemann integrable on [a, b], and f
     is bounded, then f ∈ R(α) ⇔ fα′ ∈ R, and ∫ f dα = ∫ f(x)α′(x) dx.
     Evaluate ∫₀¹ x d(x²), ∫₀^(π/2) x d(sin x), and ∫₀² x² d(x + ⌊x⌋).
     Answer: 2/3; π/2 − 1; 8/3 + 1 + 4 = 23/3.
     Teacher explains: Sketch: given ε, choose P with U(P, α′) − L(P, α′) < ε.
     By the MVT, Δαᵢ = α′(tᵢ)Δxᵢ for some tᵢ, and for ANY sᵢ in the same piece
     |α′(sᵢ) − α′(tᵢ)| ≤ oscillation of α′ there, so
        |∑ f(sᵢ)Δαᵢ − ∑ f(sᵢ)α′(sᵢ)Δxᵢ| ≤ M·∑ |α′(tᵢ) − α′(sᵢ)|Δxᵢ ≤ Mε.
     Hence the Stieltjes sums for (f, α) and the Riemann sums for fα′ stay
     within Mε; taking sups and infs over the sᵢ gives
     |U(P, f, α) − U(P, fα′)| ≤ Mε and the same for L, so the two integrals
     exist together and are equal. Computations: 'dα = α′(x) dx':
        ∫₀¹ x d(x²) = ∫₀¹ x·2x dx = 2/3
        ∫₀^(π/2) x d(sin x) = ∫₀^(π/2) x cos x dx = π/2 − 1  (by parts)
        ∫₀² x² d(x + ⌊x⌋) = ∫₀² x² dx + (1² + 2²) = 8/3 + 5 = 23/3
     In the last one α is split into a smooth part x and a jump part ⌊x⌋
     (jumps at 1 and 2), using linearity in α. Common mistakes: writing
     ∫ x d(x²) = ∫ x dx·2x 'at the end'; forgetting the jump at the right
     endpoint 2. Now you try: ∫₀³ x d(x² + ⌊x⌋). (∫₀³ 2x² dx + 1 + 2 + 3 = 18 + 6
     = 24)

D12. Prove the integration by parts formula ∫ₐᵇ f dα + ∫ₐᵇ α df =
     f(b)α(b) − f(a)α(a) (at the level of sums). Verify it for f(x) = x,
     α(x) = ⌊x⌋ on [0, 2], and show that ∫₀² ⌊x⌋ d⌊x⌋ does not exist.
     Answer: ∫₀² x d⌊x⌋ = 3 and ∫₀² ⌊x⌋ dx = 1, total 4 = 2·2 − 0 ✓.
     ∫₀² ⌊x⌋ d⌊x⌋: U − L ≥ 2 for every partition.
     Teacher explains: Summation by parts. For a partition with tags
     tᵢ ∈ [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ], put t₀ = a, tₙ₊₁ = b. Then
        ∑_{i=1}^{n} f(tᵢ)(α(xᵢ) − α(xᵢ₋₁)) = f(b)α(b) − f(a)α(a)
                                     − ∑_{i=0}^{n} α(xᵢ)(f(tᵢ₊₁) − f(tᵢ)),
     and the last sum is a Stieltjes sum for ∫ α df over the partition
     {tᵢ} (with tags xᵢ). As the partitions refine, if one side converges so
     does the other. Check: ∫₀² x d⌊x⌋ = 1 + 2 = 3 (jumps at 1 and 2, f
     continuous), ∫₀² ⌊x⌋ dx = 0·1 + 1·1 = 1, and 3 + 1 = 4 = 2·⌊2⌋ − 0 ✓.
     Now f = α = ⌊x⌋. Take any partition; the piece [xᵢ₋₁, xᵢ] containing 1
     with xᵢ₋₁ < 1 ≤ xᵢ has Δα = 1 and f takes the values 0 (at xᵢ₋₁) and 1
     (at 1): Mᵢ − mᵢ = 1. The piece ending at 2 has Δα = 1 (from 1 to 2) and
     f takes 1 and 2: again Mᵢ − mᵢ = 1. So U − L ≥ 1·1 + 1·1 = 2 for EVERY
     partition: not integrable. The culprit: f and α jump at the same points
     (from the left). General rule: f ∈ R(α) fails when f and α share a
     discontinuity from the same side. Common mistakes: 'evaluating'
     ∫ ⌊x⌋ d⌊x⌋ as ∑ ⌊k⌋·1 = 3; using the formula without checking that
     one of the two integrals exists. Now you try: evaluate ∫₀³ ⌊x⌋ d(x²)
     and check parts with ∫₀³ x² d⌊x⌋ = 14. (∫ 2x⌊x⌋ dx = 3 + 10 = 13;
     13 + 14 = 27 = 9·3 ✓)

M10. Riemann-Stieltjes integrals with smooth integrators (∫ f dα = ∫ fα′ dx).

     Answers:
       a) 2/3          b) 96/5          c) π/2 − 1       d) π/4
       e) (e² + 1)/2 ≈ 4.19453          f) (e² − 1)/2 ≈ 3.19453
       g) 1            h) 1/2           i) 128/5         j) 1
       k) −π           l) 1

M11. Mixed integrators, integration by parts and existence.
     a) ∫₀² x² d(x + ⌊x⌋)              b) ∫₀³ x d(x² + ⌊x⌋)
     c) ∫₀² eˣ d(x − ⌊x⌋)              d) does ∫₀² ⌊x⌋ d⌊x⌋ exist?
     e) ∫₀² ⌊x⌋ dx and ∫₀² x d⌊x⌋; check by parts
     f) ∫₀¹ x d(x²) via parts from ∫₀¹ x² dx
     g) ∫₀³ ⌊x⌋ d(x²)                  h) ∫₀³ x² d⌊x⌋ + ∫₀³ ⌊x⌋ d(x²)
     i) ∫₀¹ x² dα, α = x (x < 1/2), x + 1 (x ≥ 1/2)
     j) ∫₀² (x − 1)² d(⌊x⌋ + x³)
     k) ∫₋₁¹ x² d(sgn x)               l) ∫₀¹ x d(x²) + ∫₀¹ x² dx
     Answers:
       a) 8/3 + 1 + 4 = 23/3            b) 18 + 6 = 24
       c) (e² − 1) − (e + e²) = −1 − e ≈ −3.71828
       d) no: U − L ≥ 2 for every partition
       e) 1 and 3; 1 + 3 = 4 = 2·⌊2⌋ − 0·⌊0⌋ ✓
       f) 1·1 − 0 − ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3
       g) ∫₀³ 2x⌊x⌋ dx = 3 + 10 = 13     h) 27 = 3²·⌊3⌋ ✓
       i) 1/3 + (1/2)² = 7/12
       j) ∫₀² 3x²(x − 1)² dx + (0 + 1) = 16/5 + 1 = 21/5
       k) 0 (f(0)·2)    l) 1 = [x·x²]₀¹

M12. True (T) or false (F)? f, g bounded on [a, b].
     a) Every continuous f on [a, b] is integrable.
     b) Every bounded f on [a, b] is integrable.
     c) f integrable ⇒ |f| integrable.
     d) |f| integrable ⇒ f integrable.
     e) f² integrable ⇒ f integrable.
     f) f, g integrable ⇒ fg integrable.
     g) f integrable, g = f except at finitely many points ⇒ g integrable
        with the same integral.
     h) f integrable, g = f except at countably many points ⇒ g integrable.
     i) f integrable, φ continuous ⇒ φ ∘ f integrable.
     j) f, g integrable ⇒ f ∘ g integrable.
     k) every monotone f is integrable.
     l) every integrable f has an antiderivative (F′ = f everywhere).
     m) if f′ exists on all of [a, b] then f′ is integrable.
     n) f integrable ⇒ F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f is continuous.
     o) f ≥ 0 integrable with ∫ₐᵇ f = 0 ⇒ f = 0 everywhere.
     p) the discontinuity set of an integrable f has measure zero.
     q) f continuous and α increasing ⇒ ∫ₐᵇ f dα exists.
     r) U(P, f) − L(P, f) < ε ⇒ every Riemann sum over P is within ε of ∫f.
     Answers:
       a) T            b) F: 1_Q        c) T             d) F: 1 on Q, −1 off
       e) F: same example               f) T             g) T
       h) F: 0 and 1_Q                  i) T
       j) F: f = 1 on (0, 1], f(0) = 0, g = Thomae: f ∘ g = 1_Q
       k) T            l) F: sgn        m) F: x² sin(1/x²) (F′ unbounded)
       n) T (Lipschitz)                 o) F: Thomae (T if f continuous)
       p) T (Lebesgue) q) T             r) T

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the upper and lower rectangles for a few partitions and
  colour the gap U − L; for monotone functions show the gap rectangles
  sliding into one column of width Δx and height f(b) − f(a). Practise
  'spotting f' in Riemann-sum limits by always rewriting the summand as
  (1/n)·f(k/n). For Stieltjes integrals first split α into its smooth part
  and its jumps, list each jump with its size, and treat endpoints with
  care. Harder: prove Lebesgue's criterion (at least the 'measure zero ⇒
  integrable' direction); show that the composition f ∘ g of integrable
  functions can fail but φ ∘ f with φ continuous cannot; prove the
  Riemann-Lebesgue lemma ∫ₐᵇ f(x)sin(nx) dx → 0 for step functions and then
  for integrable f; prove the second mean value theorem (Bonnet); show that
  a function of bounded variation is a difference of increasing functions
  and compute ∫ x dα for α(x) = the Cantor function (answer 1/2).


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.4 — SEQUENCES AND SERIES OF FUNCTIONS; UNIFORM CONVERGENCE;
WEIERSTRASS M-TEST
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - POINTWISE CONVERGENCE on A: fₙ(x) → f(x) for each fixed x ∈ A, i.e.
    ∀x ∀ε ∃N(x, ε) ∀n ≥ N : |fₙ(x) − f(x)| < ε. Compute f(x) by freezing x.
    Pointwise limits can destroy continuity (xⁿ on [0, 1]), and integrals and
    derivatives need not pass to the limit.
  - UNIFORM CONVERGENCE (fₙ ⇉ f on A): ∀ε ∃N ∀n ≥ N ∀x ∈ A :
    |fₙ(x) − f(x)| < ε — one N for ALL x. Equivalent: the SUP NORM
    Mₙ = ‖fₙ − f‖∞ = sup_{x∈A} |fₙ(x) − f(x)| → 0. Uniform ⇒ pointwise.
  - METHOD: (1) find the pointwise limit f; (2) compute Mₙ = sup|fₙ − f| by
    calculus (differentiate, compare critical points and ends) or bound it;
    (3) Mₙ → 0 ⇒ uniform. NOT uniform ⇔ there are xₙ ∈ A with
    |fₙ(xₙ) − f(xₙ)| ↛ 0 (e.g. a 'travelling hump' at xₙ = 1/n). Uniformity
    depends on the SET: xⁿ ⇉ 0 on [0, a] (a < 1) but not on [0, 1).
  - CAUCHY CRITERION: (fₙ) converges uniformly on A ⇔ ∀ε ∃N ∀m, n ≥ N
    ∀x ∈ A : |fₘ(x) − fₙ(x)| < ε. The space of bounded functions with ‖·‖∞
    is complete.
  - CONTINUITY THEOREM: a uniform limit of CONTINUOUS functions is
    continuous (ε/3 argument). So a discontinuous pointwise limit of
    continuous functions PROVES non-uniform convergence. Also uniform limits
    of bounded (or uniformly continuous) functions are bounded (UC).
  - DINI'S THEOREM: fₙ continuous on a COMPACT set K, fₙ(x) MONOTONE in n for
    each x, and pointwise limit f CONTINUOUS ⇒ convergence is uniform. All
    three hypotheses are needed.
  - INTEGRATION: fₙ ∈ R[a, b], fₙ ⇉ f on [a, b] ⇒ f ∈ R[a, b] and
    ∫ₐᵇ fₙ → ∫ₐᵇ f (|∫fₙ − ∫f| ≤ (b − a)Mₙ). Counterexample without
    uniformity: fₙ(x) = nxe^(−nx²): ∫₀¹ fₙ → 1/2 but f = 0.
  - DIFFERENTIATION: if fₙ are differentiable on [a, b], (fₙ(x₀)) converges
    for ONE x₀, and fₙ′ ⇉ g uniformly, then fₙ ⇉ f uniformly and f′ = g.
    Uniform convergence of fₙ alone is NOT enough: sin(nx)/n ⇉ 0 but
    fₙ′ = cos nx does not converge; √(x² + 1/n) ⇉ |x|, not differentiable.
  - SERIES OF FUNCTIONS ∑fₙ: pointwise / uniform / absolute convergence
    means that of the partial sums Sₙ(x) = f₁(x) + ... + fₙ(x). Uniform ⇒
    fₙ ⇉ 0. Cauchy criterion: sup_x |f_{n+1}(x) + ... + fₘ(x)| → 0. Continuity,
    TERM-BY-TERM INTEGRATION and (with uniform convergence of ∑fₙ′)
    TERM-BY-TERM DIFFERENTIATION carry over from sequences.
  - WEIERSTRASS M-TEST: if |fₙ(x)| ≤ Mₙ for all x ∈ A and ∑Mₙ < ∞, then ∑fₙ
    converges ABSOLUTELY and UNIFORMLY on A (tail ≤ ∑_{k>n} Mₖ). Best choice:
    Mₙ = sup_A |fₙ|. The M-test is sufficient, not necessary:
    ∑(−1)ⁿ/(n + x²) is uniform on R (alternating bound 1/(n + 1)) but fails it.
    Dirichlet/Abel tests handle ∑ sin(nx)/n on [δ, 2π − δ].
  - POWER SERIES ∑aₙ(x − c)ⁿ with radius R (1/R = limsup |aₙ|^(1/n)): converge
    uniformly on every [c − r, c + r] with r < R (M-test with Mₙ = |aₙ|rⁿ),
    not necessarily on (c − R, c + R). The sum is continuous and may be
    differentiated and integrated term by term inside (same R). ABEL's
    theorem: convergence at an endpoint gives continuity there
    (∑(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n = ln 2, ∑(−1)ⁿ/(2n + 1) = π/4).
  - LANDMARKS: ζ(x) = ∑1/nˣ is continuous (even differentiable) on (1, ∞),
    uniform on [a, ∞) for a > 1 only; Weierstrass's ∑aⁿcos(bⁿπx) is
    continuous everywhere (M-test) but differentiable nowhere; the
    WEIERSTRASS APPROXIMATION THEOREM: every continuous function on [a, b]
    is a uniform limit of polynomials.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Let fₙ(x) = xⁿ. Find the pointwise limit on [0, 1]. Prove that the
    convergence is uniform on [0, a] for every a < 1 but not on [0, 1) or
    [0, 1]. For a = 0.9 find the least N with |fₙ(x) − f(x)| < 0.01 for all
    n ≥ N and all x ∈ [0, 0.9].
    Answer: f(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 1, f(1) = 1. On [0, a]: Mₙ = aⁿ → 0; on
    [0, 1): Mₙ = 1. For a = 0.9: N = 44.
    Teacher explains: Freeze x. If 0 ≤ x < 1, xⁿ → 0; if x = 1, 1ⁿ = 1. So
       f(x) = 0 (0 ≤ x < 1),   f(1) = 1   — a DISCONTINUOUS limit
    of continuous functions. On [0, a] with a < 1: |xⁿ − 0| ≤ aⁿ, with
    equality at x = a, so Mₙ = aⁿ → 0: uniform. On [0, 1): Mₙ = sup xⁿ over
    [0, 1) = 1 (xⁿ creeps up to 1 as x → 1⁻), so Mₙ ↛ 0: not uniform. A
    sequence witness: xₙ = 1 − 1/n gives fₙ(xₙ) = (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e, not 0.
    On [0, 1] the discontinuity of f already proves non-uniformity (D4).
    Numbers: 0.9ⁿ < 0.01 ⇔ n > ln 0.01/ln 0.9 = 43.7, so N = 44 (0.9⁴³ ≈
    0.01078, 0.9⁴⁴ ≈ 0.00970). Pointwise, at a fixed x, the needed N(x) =
    ⌈ln ε/ln x⌉ blows up as x → 1: exactly what uniformity forbids. Common
    mistakes: saying 'xⁿ → 0 uniformly on [0, 1)' because each point
    converges; computing sup at x = 1 when 1 is not in the set (sup is still
    1). Now you try: is fₙ(x) = xⁿ uniformly convergent on [−1/2, 1/2]?
    (Yes: Mₙ = (1/2)ⁿ)

D2. Let fₙ(x) = nx/(1 + n²x²). Find the pointwise limit on [0, ∞) and
    Mₙ = sup|fₙ − f| on [0, ∞) and on [a, ∞) (a > 0). Decide where the
    convergence is uniform. Compute M₁₀ on [1, ∞).
    Answer: f = 0; on [0, ∞) Mₙ = 1/2 (at x = 1/n): not uniform; on [a, ∞)
    Mₙ = na/(1 + n²a²) for n ≥ 1/a: uniform. M₁₀ on [1, ∞) = 10/101.
    Teacher explains: For x = 0, fₙ(0) = 0; for x > 0, fₙ(x) ≈ 1/(nx) → 0. So
    f = 0. Now maximise g(x) = nx/(1 + n²x²):
       g′(x) = n(1 + n²x² − 2n²x²)/(1 + n²x²)² = n(1 − n²x²)/(1 + n²x²)²
    zero at x = 1/n, where g = 1/2. g rises on [0, 1/n] and falls after.
       on [0, ∞):  Mₙ = g(1/n) = 1/2 for every n — NOT uniform
    This is a TRAVELLING HUMP: a bump of height 1/2 slides into x = 0. On
    [a, ∞), once 1/n < a (n > 1/a) the hump has left the set and g is
    decreasing there, so
       Mₙ = g(a) = na/(1 + n²a²) ≤ 1/(na) → 0 — uniform
    On [1, ∞) with n = 10: M₁₀ = 10/101 ≈ 0.0990. Common mistakes: finding
    the maximum point x = 1/n and then 'letting n → ∞ first' to get 0;
    forgetting that the max over [a, ∞) is at the END a once the hump has
    passed. Now you try: sup of fₙ(x) = x/(1 + nx²) on R. (max at
    x = 1/√n: Mₙ = 1/(2√n) → 0, uniform on R)

D3. State and prove the Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence. Use it to
    show that ∑_{n≥1} xⁿ/n is not uniformly convergent on [0, 1), while its
    partial sums converge pointwise there.
    Answer: Proof below; sup_{[0,1)} ∑_{k=n+1}^{2n} xᵏ/k ≥ 1/2 for all n.
    Teacher explains: (⇒) If fₙ ⇉ f, choose N with |fₙ(x) − f(x)| < ε/2 for
    n ≥ N and all x; then |fₘ(x) − fₙ(x)| < ε for m, n ≥ N, all x. (⇐) For each
    fixed x the sequence (fₙ(x)) is Cauchy in R, hence converges: call the
    limit f(x). In |fₘ(x) − fₙ(x)| < ε (m, n ≥ N, all x) let m → ∞:
    |f(x) − fₙ(x)| ≤ ε for all x and all n ≥ N. That is uniform convergence.
    Note the order: the pointwise limit is found FIRST, then the uniform
    estimate survives the limit m → ∞ (strict < becomes ≤). For the series,
    Sₙ(x) = ∑_{k≤n} xᵏ/k converges for each x ∈ [0, 1) (compare with ∑xᵏ),
    to −ln(1 − x). But the block from n + 1 to 2n satisfies
       sup_{0≤x<1} ∑_{k=n+1}^{2n} xᵏ/k = ∑_{k=n+1}^{2n} 1/k ≥ n·1/(2n) = 1/2
    (let x → 1⁻). So with ε = 1/2 no N works: not uniform. (Reality check:
    the sum −ln(1 − x) is unbounded on [0, 1), while each Sₙ is bounded; a
    uniform limit of bounded functions is bounded.) Common mistakes:
    thinking pointwise Cauchy for each x gives uniform Cauchy; forgetting
    the sup over x. Now you try: is ∑ xⁿ/n² uniformly convergent on [0, 1]?
    (Yes: M-test with Mₙ = 1/n², or the Cauchy block ≤ ∑_{k>n} 1/k² → 0)

D4. Prove that the uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
    Deduce again that xⁿ does not converge uniformly on [0, 1]. Give an
    example showing that a continuous pointwise limit does not imply
    uniform convergence.
    Answer: ε/3 proof below; example fₙ(x) = nxe^(−nx) on [0, ∞) (limit 0,
    Mₙ = 1/e).
    Teacher explains: Let fₙ ⇉ f on A, each fₙ continuous at a. Given ε,
    choose n with |fₙ(x) − f(x)| < ε/3 for ALL x ∈ A (uniformity used here),
    then δ with |fₙ(x) − fₙ(a)| < ε/3 for |x − a| < δ (continuity of this one
    fₙ). Then for |x − a| < δ:
       |f(x) − f(a)| ≤ |f(x) − fₙ(x)| + |fₙ(x) − fₙ(a)| + |fₙ(a) − f(a)|
                     < ε/3 + ε/3 + ε/3 = ε.
    For xⁿ on [0, 1] the limit (0 on [0, 1), 1 at 1) is discontinuous, so the
    convergence cannot be uniform: a one-line proof. But the converse is
    FALSE: fₙ(x) = nxe^(−nx) → 0 pointwise on [0, ∞) (for x > 0, e^(−nx)
    beats n). Maximising: fₙ′ = ne^(−nx)(1 − nx) = 0 at x = 1/n, where
    fₙ(1/n) = e⁻¹. So Mₙ = 1/e ≈ 0.36788 for every n: not uniform, though the
    limit 0 is as continuous as can be. Common mistakes: 'the limit is
    continuous, so the convergence is uniform'; in the ε/3 proof choosing n
    depending on x. Now you try: show fₙ(x) = x^(1/n) on [0, 1] does not
    converge uniformly. (limit 0 at 0, 1 on (0, 1]: discontinuous)

D5. State and prove Dini's theorem. Apply it to fₙ(x) = √(x² + 1/n) on
    [−1, 1], and check by computing Mₙ directly. Show that each hypothesis
    (compact domain, monotone in n, continuous limit) is needed.
    Answer: fₙ ↓ |x| uniformly; Mₙ = 1/√n (at x = 0).
    Teacher explains: DINI: let K be compact, fₙ continuous, fₙ(x) ≥ fₙ₊₁(x)
    for all x, n, and fₙ → f pointwise with f continuous. Put gₙ = fₙ − f ≥ 0,
    continuous and decreasing to 0. Given ε, the sets
    Uₙ = {x : gₙ(x) < ε} are OPEN, increase with n, and cover K (each x has
    gₙ(x) < ε eventually). By compactness finitely many cover K, hence the
    largest one, U_N, covers K. So 0 ≤ gₙ(x) ≤ g_N(x) < ε for n ≥ N and all x.
    Example: √(x² + 1/n) decreases in n and tends to √(x²) = |x|, continuous;
    [−1, 1] is compact: uniform. Directly,
       √(x² + 1/n) − |x| = (1/n)/(√(x² + 1/n) + |x|) ≤ (1/n)/(1/√n) = 1/√n
    with equality at x = 0, so Mₙ = 1/√n → 0 ✓. Each hypothesis is needed:
       not compact:     xⁿ on [0, 1), decreasing to the continuous 0; Mₙ = 1
       not monotone:    nxe^(−nx) on [0, 1] (hump), limit 0; Mₙ = 1/e
       limit not cont.: xⁿ on [0, 1], decreasing, limit discontinuous
    Common mistakes: applying Dini to sequences that are not monotone in n;
    confusing 'monotone in n' with 'monotone in x'. Now you try: does
    (1 + x/n)ⁿ ↑ eˣ uniformly on [0, 1]? (Yes by Dini: increasing in n,
    continuous limit, compact set; M₁₀ = e − 1.1¹⁰ ≈ 0.12454)

D6. Prove: if fₙ ∈ R[a, b] and fₙ ⇉ f on [a, b], then f ∈ R[a, b] and
    ∫ₐᵇ fₙ → ∫ₐᵇ f. For fₙ(x) = nxe^(−nx²) on [0, 1] compute ∫₀¹ fₙ, its limit
    and ∫₀¹ lim fₙ, and explain. Also treat gₙ(x) = xⁿ, where the integrals
    do converge correctly although the convergence is not uniform.
    Answer: ∫₀¹ fₙ = (1 − e⁻ⁿ)/2 → 1/2 ≠ 0 = ∫₀¹ 0. ∫₀¹ xⁿ = 1/(n + 1) → 0 = ∫ f.
    Teacher explains: Let εₙ = Mₙ = ‖fₙ − f‖∞ → 0. Then
       fₙ − εₙ ≤ f ≤ fₙ + εₙ,
    so the upper and lower integrals of f are within 2εₙ(b − a) of each
    other (they lie between ∫fₙ − εₙ(b − a) and ∫fₙ + εₙ(b − a)); letting
    n → ∞ they are equal: f ∈ R. And |∫fₙ − ∫f| ≤ ∫|fₙ − f| ≤ (b − a)εₙ → 0.
    Example: fₙ(x) = nxe^(−nx²). Pointwise: fₙ(0) = 0; for x > 0 the
    exponential wins: f = 0. But substituting u = nx²:
       ∫₀¹ nxe^(−nx²) dx = [−e^(−nx²)/2]₀¹ = (1 − e⁻ⁿ)/2 → 1/2
    while ∫₀¹ f = 0. Not uniform: max at x = 1/√(2n), value √(n/2)·e^(−1/2) →
    ∞ (a hump that grows while getting thinner, keeping area ≈ 1/2). For
    gₙ = xⁿ: ∫₀¹ xⁿ = 1/(n + 1) → 0 = ∫₀¹ f (f = 0 except at one point). So
    uniform convergence is SUFFICIENT, not necessary; bounded convergence
    (|gₙ| ≤ 1) is what saves xⁿ (Arzelà / dominated convergence). Common
    mistakes: swapping lim and ∫ without checking anything; 'pointwise limit
    0 ⇒ integrals → 0'. Now you try: fₙ(x) = n²x(1 − x²)ⁿ on [0, 1].
    (∫₀¹ fₙ = n²/(2(n + 1)) → ∞, although fₙ → 0 pointwise)

D7. State the theorem on differentiating a limit. Show why uniform
    convergence of fₙ alone is not enough, using (a) fₙ(x) = sin(nx)/√n,
    (b) fₙ(x) = √(x² + 1/n), (c) fₙ(x) = x/(1 + nx²).
    Answer: (a) fₙ ⇉ 0 but fₙ′(0) = √n → ∞; (b) fₙ ⇉ |x|, not differentiable
    at 0; (c) fₙ ⇉ 0 but fₙ′(0) = 1 for all n, so lim fₙ′(0) = 1 ≠ 0 = f′(0).
    Teacher explains: THEOREM: fₙ differentiable on [a, b], fₙ(x₀) converges
    for some x₀, and fₙ′ ⇉ g on [a, b]. Then fₙ converges uniformly to some
    f, f is differentiable, and f′ = g. (Proof idea: by the MVT applied to
    fₘ − fₙ, |(fₘ − fₙ)(x) − (fₘ − fₙ)(t)| ≤ |x − t|·sup|fₘ′ − fₙ′|, which gives
    uniform Cauchy for fₙ and controls the difference quotients uniformly.)
    The hypothesis is on the DERIVATIVES. Examples:
       (a) |sin(nx)/√n| ≤ 1/√n → 0 uniformly, but fₙ′(x) = √n cos(nx): at
           x = 0 it is √n → ∞. Wiggles get small in height but steep.
       (b) Mₙ = 1/√n (D5), fₙ smooth, limit |x| has a corner at 0;
           fₙ′(x) = x/√(x² + 1/n) → sgn x (with value 0 at 0): not uniform
           (limit discontinuous).
       (c) sup|fₙ| = 1/(2√n) → 0. fₙ′(x) = (1 − nx²)/(1 + nx²)² → 0 for
           x ≠ 0 but = 1 at x = 0: the limit of the derivatives exists
           everywhere yet differs from (lim fₙ)′ at 0.
    Common mistakes: thinking fₙ ⇉ f makes f′ = lim fₙ′; forgetting the
    condition 'fₙ(x₀) converges' (fₙ = n has fₙ′ = 0 ⇉ 0 but fₙ diverges).
    Now you try: check the theorem for fₙ(x) = (1 + x/n)ⁿ on [0, 1].
    (fₙ′ = (1 + x/n)ⁿ⁻¹ ⇉ eˣ, fₙ(0) = 1 converges, so f = eˣ and f′ = eˣ ✓)

D8. State and prove the Weierstrass M-test. Apply it to (a) ∑ sin(nx)/n² on
    R, (b) ∑ xⁿ/n! on [−R, R], (c) ∑ 1/(n² + x²) on R, (d) ∑ x²e^(−nx) on
    [0, ∞). Bound the error of the 10th partial sum in (a).
    Answer: Mₙ = 1/n², Rⁿ/n!, 1/n², 4/(e²n²): all uniformly convergent;
    error in (a) < 1/10.
    Teacher explains: If |fₖ(x)| ≤ Mₖ on A and ∑Mₖ converges, then for
    m > n and all x ∈ A:
       |∑_{k=n+1}^{m} fₖ(x)| ≤ ∑_{k=n+1}^{m} Mₖ → 0   (tail of a convergent series)
    so the partial sums are UNIFORMLY Cauchy; by D3 the series converges
    uniformly (and absolutely, since the same bound holds for |fₖ|). Applying
    it means finding sup_A |fₖ|:
       (a) |sin(nx)/n²| ≤ 1/n², ∑1/n² = π²/6 < ∞
       (b) |xⁿ/n!| ≤ Rⁿ/n! for |x| ≤ R, and ∑Rⁿ/n! = e^R < ∞. So eˣ's series
           is uniform on bounded sets (NOT on R: each xⁿ/n! is unbounded)
       (c) 1/(n² + x²) ≤ 1/n²
       (d) maximise x²e^(−nx): derivative xe^(−nx)(2 − nx) = 0 at x = 2/n,
           value (4/n²)e⁻²: Mₙ = 4/(e²n²), summable
    The limits are continuous by D4 since each term is. Error in (a):
       |S(x) − S₁₀(x)| ≤ ∑_{k>10} 1/k² < ∫₁₀^∞ dt/t² = 1/10   for every x.
    Common mistakes: using a bound that depends on x ('|xⁿ/n!| ≤ |x|ⁿ/n!' is
    not an Mₙ); forgetting to take the SUP over the set. Now you try:
    ∑ x/(n(1 + nx²)) on R. (sup x/(1 + nx²) = 1/(2√n), so
    Mₙ = 1/(2n^(3/2)): uniform)

D9. For ∑_{n≥0} xⁿ(1 − x) on [0, 1] find the sum, and decide whether the
    convergence is uniform. Compare with ∑_{n≥0} (−1)ⁿxⁿ(1 − x) on [0, 1] and
    with ∑_{n≥1} (−1)ⁿ/(n + x²) on R. Which pass the M-test?
    Answer: First: sum 1 on [0, 1), 0 at 1: not uniform. Second: sum
    (1 − x)/(1 + x), uniform (tail ≤ max xⁿ⁺¹(1 − x) ≤ 1/(n + 2)) but fails
    the M-test. Third: uniform on R, fails the M-test.
    Teacher explains: First series: telescoping,
       Sₙ(x) = ∑_{k=0}^{n} (xᵏ − xᵏ⁺¹) = 1 − xⁿ⁺¹ → 1 (x < 1),  0 (x = 1)
    Discontinuous limit of continuous partial sums: NOT uniform (D4).
    Second: an alternating geometric series, sum (1 − x)·1/(1 + x) for
    0 ≤ x < 1, and 0 at x = 1 (all terms 0) — consistent. For each fixed x the
    terms (1 − x)xⁿ decrease to 0, so the alternating-series bound gives
       |S(x) − Sₙ(x)| ≤ (1 − x)xⁿ⁺¹ ≤ max_{[0,1]} (1 − x)xⁿ⁺¹
                     = (1/(n + 2))((n + 1)/(n + 2))ⁿ⁺¹ ≤ 1/(n + 2) → 0.
    Uniform! Yet sup|(−1)ⁿxⁿ(1 − x)| ≈ 1/(e(n + 1)) and ∑1/n diverges: the
    M-test FAILS (in fact ∑|terms| is the first series, not uniform).
    Third: for each x, 1/(n + x²) decreases to 0, so the tail after n terms
    is at most 1/(n + 1 + x²) ≤ 1/(n + 1): uniform on all of R. But
    sup_x 1/(n + x²) = 1/n, not summable. Lesson: M-test ⇒ uniform AND
    absolute; uniform convergence of a conditionally convergent series needs
    alternating, Dirichlet or Abel tests. Common mistakes: 'fails the M-test,
    so not uniform'. Now you try: is ∑ sin(nx)/n uniformly convergent on
    [π/2, 3π/2]? (Yes by Dirichlet's test: |∑_{k≤n} sin kx| ≤ 1/|sin(x/2)| ≤ √2
    there and 1/n ↓ 0 uniformly; the M-test fails)

D10. Let ∑aₙxⁿ have radius of convergence R > 0. Prove it converges
     uniformly on [−r, r] for every r < R, and justify term-by-term
     differentiation and integration there. Use this to find ∑ n/2ⁿ,
     ∑ n²/2ⁿ, ∑ 1/(n2ⁿ), and (with Abel's theorem) ∑ (−1)ⁿ/(2n + 1).
     Answer: 2, 6, ln 2, π/4.
     Teacher explains: Pick s with r < s < R. The series converges at x = s,
     so aₙsⁿ → 0 and |aₙ|sⁿ ≤ C. For |x| ≤ r:
        |aₙxⁿ| ≤ |aₙ|rⁿ ≤ C(r/s)ⁿ = Mₙ,   ∑Mₙ < ∞ (geometric)
     so the M-test gives uniform convergence on [−r, r]. The derived series
     ∑naₙxⁿ⁻¹ has the same radius (n^(1/n) → 1), so it too converges uniformly
     on [−r, r]; by D7 the sum is differentiable with derivative ∑naₙxⁿ⁻¹.
     Integration: by D6, ∫₀ˣ ∑aₙtⁿ dt = ∑aₙxⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1). Computations from
     1/(1 − x) = ∑xⁿ (|x| < 1):
        differentiate:  1/(1 − x)² = ∑ nxⁿ⁻¹  ⇒ ∑nxⁿ = x/(1 − x)²
                        x = 1/2: ∑ n/2ⁿ = (1/2)/(1/4) = 2
        again:          ∑n²xⁿ = x(1 + x)/(1 − x)³;  x = 1/2: (3/4)/(1/8) = 6
        integrate:      ∑ xⁿ/n = −ln(1 − x);  x = 1/2: ∑ 1/(n2ⁿ) = ln 2
     For π/4: arctan x = ∑ (−1)ⁿx²ⁿ⁺¹/(2n + 1) for |x| < 1 (integrate
     1/(1 + t²) = ∑(−1)ⁿt²ⁿ). At x = 1 the series converges (Leibniz), and
     ABEL's theorem makes the sum continuous from the left at 1, so
     ∑ (−1)ⁿ/(2n + 1) = arctan 1 = π/4. Common mistakes: claiming uniform
     convergence on (−R, R) (∑xⁿ is not uniform on (−1, 1)); plugging an
     endpoint into a formula without Abel's theorem. Now you try: ∑ n/3ⁿ and
     ∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n. (x/(1 − x)² at 1/3: 3/4; ln 2)

D11. Show that ζ(x) = ∑_{n≥1} 1/nˣ is continuous on (1, ∞) although the
     convergence is not uniform there, and that ζ is differentiable with
     ζ′(x) = −∑ (ln n)/nˣ. Then show that the Weierstrass-type function
     W(x) = ∑_{n≥0} 2⁻ⁿcos(3ⁿπx) is continuous on R.
     Answer: M-test on [a, ∞) for each a > 1; W continuous by the M-test with
     Mₙ = 2⁻ⁿ.
     Teacher explains: Continuity is a LOCAL property: to prove ζ continuous
     at x₀ > 1 it suffices to have uniform convergence on some [a, ∞) with
     1 < a < x₀. There 1/nˣ ≤ 1/nᵃ = Mₙ and ∑1/nᵃ < ∞: uniform, so ζ is
     continuous on [a, ∞), hence at x₀. Not uniform on (1, ∞): the tail
       ∑_{k>n} 1/kˣ ≥ ∑_{k=n+1}^{2n} 1/kˣ ≥ n/(2n)ˣ → n/(2n) = 1/2 as x → 1⁺
     so sup of the tail ≥ 1/2 for every n (Cauchy criterion fails). For the
     derivative, the differentiated terms −(ln n)/nˣ satisfy
     |(ln n)/nˣ| ≤ (ln n)/nᵃ, and ∑(ln n)/nᵃ converges (ln n ≤ C·n^((a−1)/2)).
     So the differentiated series converges uniformly on [a, ∞), and D7 gives
     ζ′(x) = −∑ (ln n)/nˣ. Weierstrass-type: W(x) = ∑_{n≥0} 2⁻ⁿcos(3ⁿπx) has
     |2⁻ⁿcos(3ⁿπx)| ≤ 2⁻ⁿ = Mₙ, summable: uniform on R, hence W is continuous
     everywhere. With a = 1/2, b = 3 we do NOT have ab > 1 + 3π/2, so
     Weierstrass's original proof does not cover it, but by Hardy's theorem
     (ab ≥ 1 suffices) W is nowhere differentiable; term-by-term
     differentiation is not available, since the derived terms
     (3/2)ⁿπ sin(3ⁿπx) do not even tend to 0. Common
     mistakes: 'not uniform on (1, ∞), so not continuous there'; computing a
     derivative term by term without checking the derived series. Now you
     try: compute ζ(2) − ∑_{n≤10} 1/n² bounds using the integral test.
     (between ∫₁₁^∞ dt/t² = 1/11 ≈ 0.0909 and 1/10)

D12. Worked sup-norm study of fₙ(x) = x/(1 + nx²) on R: pointwise limit,
     Mₙ, uniformity, limit of fₙ′ and comparison with f′. Then for
     gₙ(x) = n²xe^(−nx) on [0, ∞) find the limit, Mₙ and lim ∫₀^∞ gₙ.
     Answer: fₙ ⇉ 0 with Mₙ = 1/(2√n); fₙ′(0) = 1 → 1 ≠ f′(0) = 0.
     gₙ → 0 pointwise, Mₙ = n/e → ∞, ∫₀^∞ gₙ = 1 for every n.
     Teacher explains: fₙ(0) = 0 and |fₙ(x)| ≤ |x|/(nx²) = 1/(n|x|) → 0: f = 0.
        fₙ′(x) = (1 − nx²)/(1 + nx²)²   = 0 at x = ±1/√n
        fₙ(1/√n) = (1/√n)/2 = 1/(2√n)     so Mₙ = 1/(2√n) → 0: uniform on R
     But fₙ′(0) = 1 for every n while fₙ′(x) → 0 for x ≠ 0: the derivatives
     converge pointwise to the DISCONTINUOUS indicator of {0}, not uniformly,
     and lim fₙ′(0) = 1 ≠ 0 = f′(0). For gₙ: fixed x > 0, n²e^(−nx) → 0, so
     g = 0. Maximum: gₙ′ = n²e^(−nx)(1 − nx) = 0 at x = 1/n, gₙ(1/n) = n/e:
     the humps get TALLER (Mₙ → ∞) and thinner. Area (substitute u = nx):
        ∫₀^∞ n²xe^(−nx) dx = ∫₀^∞ ue⁻ᵘ du = 1   for every n
     so lim ∫gₙ = 1 ≠ 0 = ∫ lim gₙ. On [a, ∞) with a > 0, though, for n > 1/a
     Mₙ = n²ae^(−na) → 0: uniform away from 0. Common mistakes: treating 1/√n
     as a fixed point when computing sup; forgetting that on unbounded
     intervals even uniform convergence does not allow ∫ and lim to be
     swapped (fₙ = 1/n on [0, n]: Mₙ = 1/n but ∫ = 1). Now you try: find Mₙ for
     hₙ(x) = x²e^(−nx) on [0, ∞). (max at x = 2/n: 4/(e²n²) → 0, uniform)
