M11. True (T) or false (F)? Give a counterexample for F.
     a) A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
     b) A pointwise limit of continuous functions is continuous.
     c) fₙ → f pointwise with f continuous ⇒ fₙ ⇉ f.
     d) Dini: fₙ continuous on [a, b], fₙ ↓ f pointwise, f continuous ⇒
        uniform.
     e) Dini's conclusion holds on [0, 1) as well.
     f) Dini's conclusion holds without monotonicity in n.
     g) fₙ ⇉ f on [a, b], fₙ integrable ⇒ ∫fₙ → ∫f.
     h) fₙ ⇉ f, fₙ differentiable ⇒ f differentiable.
     i) fₙ(x₀) converges and fₙ′ ⇉ g on [a, b] ⇒ (lim fₙ)′ = g.
     j) A uniform limit of bounded functions is bounded.
     k) fₙ ⇉ f and gₙ ⇉ g on R ⇒ fₙgₙ ⇉ fg on R.
     l) A power series converges uniformly on its open interval of
        convergence.
     m) ∑fₙ uniformly convergent on A ⇒ fₙ ⇉ 0 on A.
     n) ∑|fₙ| uniformly convergent ⇒ ∑fₙ uniformly convergent.
     o) ∑fₙ uniformly convergent ⇒ the M-test applies.
     p) Every continuous function on [0, 1] is a uniform limit of
        polynomials.
     q) fₙ ⇉ f on [a, b] with fₙ integrable ⇒ Fₙ(x) = ∫ₐˣ fₙ ⇉ ∫ₐˣ f.
     r) fₙ ⇉ f on R and each fₙ is uniformly continuous ⇒ f is uniformly
        continuous.
     Answers:
       a) T            b) F: xⁿ on [0, 1]
       c) F: nxe^(−nx) on [0, ∞)         d) T
       e) F: xⁿ on [0, 1)                f) F: nxe^(−nx) on [0, 1]
       g) T            h) F: √(x² + 1/n) → |x|              i) T
       j) T            k) F: fₙ = x + 1/n, gₙ = x (fₙgₙ − x² = x/n)
       l) F: ∑xⁿ on (−1, 1)              m) T             n) T
       o) F: ∑(−1)ⁿ/(n + x²)             p) T (Weierstrass approximation)
       q) T (sup|Fₙ − F| ≤ (b − a)Mₙ)    r) T

M12. Sup norms and 'least n' problems.
     a) ‖x² − x‖∞ on [0, 1]            b) ‖sin x + cos x‖∞ on R
     c) ‖xe⁻ˣ‖∞ on [0, ∞)              d) ‖x/(1 + x²)‖∞ on R
     e) least n with ‖xⁿ‖∞ < 0.01 on [0, 0.9]
     f) least n with ‖x/(1 + nx²)‖∞ < 0.01 on R
     g) least n with ‖sin(nx)/n‖∞ < 0.001
     h) least n with ‖√(x² + 1/n²) − |x|‖∞ < 0.001
     i) least n with ‖eˣ − ∑_{k≤n} xᵏ/k!‖∞ < 10⁻⁶ on [0, 1]
     j) least n with the M-test tail bound 1/n ≤ 0.01 for ∑ sin(kx)/k²
     k) ‖xⁿ(1 − x)‖∞ on [0, 1] for n = 1, 2, 3
     l) ‖nxe^(−nx²)‖∞ on [0, ∞) in general and for n = 2
     m) ‖eˣ − (1 + x/10)¹⁰‖∞ on [0, 1]
     n) ‖nx/(1 + n²x²)‖∞ on R
     Answers:
       a) 1/4          b) √2            c) 1/e           d) 1/2
       e) 44           f) 2501 (1/(2√n) < 0.01 ⇔ n > 2500)
       g) 1001         h) 1001
       i) 9 (e − s₈ ≈ 3.06 × 10⁻⁶, e − s₉ ≈ 3.03 × 10⁻⁷)
       j) 100          k) 1/4, 4/27, 27/256
       l) √(n/2)·e^(−1/2); for n = 2: e^(−1/2) ≈ 0.60653
       m) e − 1.1¹⁰ ≈ 0.12454 (at x = 1)                   n) 1/2

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always do the three steps in writing — pointwise limit (freeze
  x), Mₙ = sup|fₙ − f| (calculus on a fixed n), then n → ∞ — and sketch fₙ for
  n = 1, 2, 5, 10 to SEE travelling or growing humps. Keep a card of the
  standard examples: xⁿ, nx/(1 + n²x²), nxe^(−nx²), sin(nx)/n, √(x² + 1/n),
  ∑xⁿ(1 − x), ∑(−1)ⁿ/(n + x²), and what each one teaches. When applying the
  M-test insist that Mₙ contains no x. Harder: prove Dirichlet's and Abel's
  tests for uniform convergence and use them for ∑ sin(nx)/n on
  [δ, 2π − δ]; prove Abel's theorem on power series; show that the uniform
  limit of Riemann integrable functions is integrable using Lebesgue's
  criterion; prove the Weierstrass approximation theorem with Bernstein
  polynomials Bₙf(x) = ∑ f(k/n)C(n, k)xᵏ(1 − x)ⁿ⁻ᵏ; and construct a continuous
  nowhere-differentiable function via ∑ 4⁻ⁿ·dist(4ⁿx, Z) (Takagi-type).


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.5 — METRIC SPACES: OPEN/CLOSED SETS, COMPACTNESS, CONNECTEDNESS,
COMPLETENESS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A METRIC on a set X is d : X × X → [0, ∞) with (M1) d(x, y) = 0 ⇔ x = y,
    (M2) d(x, y) = d(y, x) (SYMMETRY), (M3) d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z)
    (TRIANGLE INEQUALITY). (X, d) is a METRIC SPACE; any subset Y ⊆ X with the
    restricted metric is a SUBSPACE. Reverse triangle inequality:
    |d(x, z) − d(y, z)| ≤ d(x, y).
  - STANDARD EXAMPLES: on Rⁿ, d₁(x, y) = ∑|xᵢ − yᵢ| (taxicab), d₂ (Euclidean),
    d∞(x, y) = max|xᵢ − yᵢ|, with d∞ ≤ d₂ ≤ d₁ ≤ n·d∞; the DISCRETE metric
    (d = 1 for x ≠ y); on C[a, b] the SUP metric d∞(f, g) = sup|f − g| and the
    L¹ metric ∫|f − g|; the sequence spaces ℓ¹, ℓ², ℓ∞; the Hamming distance
    on strings. If d is a metric so are min(1, d) and d/(1 + d).
  - OPEN BALL B(x, r) = {y : d(x, y) < r}; CLOSED BALL {y : d(x, y) ≤ r}.
    U is OPEN if ∀x ∈ U ∃r > 0 with B(x, r) ⊆ U; F is CLOSED if X − F is open.
    Open balls are open. ARBITRARY unions and FINITE intersections of open
    sets are open; arbitrary intersections and finite unions of closed sets
    are closed. ∅ and X are both open and closed ('clopen'). A set may be
    NEITHER ([0, 1) in R). Openness depends on the ambient space: [0, 1) is
    open in the subspace [0, 2].
  - x is a LIMIT (accumulation) POINT of A if every ball about x contains a
    point of A other than x; an ISOLATED point of A is a point of A that is
    not a limit point. INTERIOR A° = union of open subsets of A (largest open
    subset); CLOSURE Ā = A ∪ {limit points} (smallest closed superset);
    BOUNDARY ∂A = Ā − A°. x ∈ Ā ⇔ d(x, A) = 0 ⇔ some sequence in A tends
    to x. A is closed ⇔ A contains the limits of all its convergent
    sequences (SEQUENTIAL CHARACTERISATION). A is DENSE if Ā = X (Q in R).
  - CONVERGENCE xₙ → x means d(xₙ, x) → 0; limits are unique. f : X → Y is
    CONTINUOUS at a if ∀ε ∃δ: d(x, a) < δ ⇒ d(f(x), f(a)) < ε ⇔ xₙ → a
    implies f(xₙ) → f(a). f is continuous everywhere ⇔ f⁻¹(open) is open ⇔
    f⁻¹(closed) is closed. UNIFORMLY CONTINUOUS: δ independent of the point;
    LIPSCHITZ: d(f(x), f(y)) ≤ L·d(x, y) (Lipschitz ⇒ uniformly continuous ⇒
    continuous). Metrics d, d′ with c·d ≤ d′ ≤ C·d are EQUIVALENT: same open
    sets, same convergent and Cauchy sequences.
  - CAUCHY SEQUENCE: ∀ε ∃N with d(xₘ, xₙ) < ε for m, n ≥ N. Convergent ⇒
    Cauchy ⇒ bounded. X is COMPLETE if every Cauchy sequence converges IN X.
    Complete: R, Rⁿ, closed subsets of complete spaces, C[a, b] with the sup
    metric, ℓᵖ, every discrete space. Not complete: Q, (0, 1), R − Q, C[0, 1]
    with the L¹ metric, the polynomials with the sup metric. A subspace of a
    complete space is complete ⇔ it is closed. Completeness is NOT a
    topological property: R ≅ (0, 1) (homeomorphic) but only R is complete.
  - COMPACT: every OPEN COVER has a FINITE SUBCOVER. SEQUENTIALLY COMPACT:
    every sequence has a convergent subsequence (with limit in X). TOTALLY
    BOUNDED: for each ε > 0, finitely many ε-balls cover X. In a metric
    space: compact ⇔ sequentially compact ⇔ complete and totally bounded.
  - Compact ⇒ closed and bounded (in any metric space); a closed subset of a
    compact set is compact; finite sets are compact. HEINE-BOREL: in Rⁿ
    (any of d₁, d₂, d∞), K is compact ⇔ K is closed and bounded. This FAILS
    in general: an infinite discrete space, the closed unit ball of ℓ² or of
    C[0, 1] are closed and bounded but not compact.
  - CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS ON COMPACT SETS: the continuous image of a compact
    set is compact; a continuous real function on a non-empty compact set is
    bounded and ATTAINS its max and min (EXTREME VALUE THEOREM); a continuous
    function on a compact metric space is UNIFORMLY continuous; a continuous
    bijection from a compact space to a metric space is a HOMEOMORPHISM.
    LEBESGUE NUMBER: for an open cover of compact X there is λ > 0 such that
    every set of diameter < λ lies in one member of the cover.
  - CONNECTED: X is not the union of two DISJOINT NON-EMPTY OPEN sets
    (equivalently the only clopen sets are ∅ and X; equivalently every
    continuous f : X → {0, 1} is constant). A subset of R is connected ⇔ it
    is an INTERVAL. The continuous image of a connected set is connected
    (gives the INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM). The closure of a connected set is
    connected; a union of connected sets with a common point is connected.
  - PATH-CONNECTED: any two points are joined by a continuous γ : [0, 1] → X.
    Path-connected ⇒ connected; the converse fails (TOPOLOGIST'S SINE CURVE
    {(x, sin(1/x)) : 0 < x ≤ 1} ∪ {0} × [−1, 1]) but holds for OPEN subsets
    of Rⁿ. COMPONENTS are the maximal connected subsets; Q and the Cantor set
    are TOTALLY DISCONNECTED (components are points).
  - HOMEOMORPHISM INVARIANTS: compactness, connectedness, path-connectedness
    and 'the number of components after removing a point' are preserved by
    homeomorphisms; so R ≇ R², [0, 1] ≇ S¹, [0, 1) ≇ (0, 1). Completeness and
    boundedness are NOT preserved.
  - DISTANCES: d(x, A) = inf{d(x, a) : a ∈ A} (1-Lipschitz in x),
    d(A, B) = inf{d(a, b)}, diam A = sup{d(a, b)}. Traps: an infimum need
    not be attained; 'closed and bounded ⇒ compact' outside Rⁿ; the closure
    of B(x, r) need not be the closed ball; 'not open' does not mean
    'closed'.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Find d₁, d₂ and d∞ between P = (1, 2) and Q = (4, −2) in R². (b) Prove
    that d(x, y) = |x − y|/(1 + |x − y|) is a metric on R. (c) Show that
    ρ(x, y) = (x − y)² is not a metric on R. (d) Prove the reverse triangle
    inequality |d(x, z) − d(y, z)| ≤ d(x, y).
    Answer: (a) d₁ = 7, d₂ = 5, d∞ = 4. (b) Proof below. (c) The triangle
    inequality fails: ρ(0, 2) = 4 > ρ(0, 1) + ρ(1, 2) = 2. (d) Below.
    Teacher explains: (a) The coordinate differences are 3 and −4:
       d₁ = |3| + |−4| = 7,   d₂ = √(9 + 16) = 5,   d∞ = max(3, 4) = 4
    Note d∞ ≤ d₂ ≤ d₁, as always. (b) Put t = |x − y| and φ(t) = t/(1 + t).
    M1 and M2 are clear (φ(t) = 0 ⇔ t = 0; |x − y| = |y − x|). For M3, φ is
    INCREASING (φ(t) = 1 − 1/(1 + t)) and SUBADDITIVE:
       φ(s + t) = s/(1 + s + t) + t/(1 + s + t) ≤ s/(1 + s) + t/(1 + t)
                = φ(s) + φ(t)                            (s, t ≥ 0)
    So with a = |x − y|, b = |y − z|, and |x − z| ≤ a + b:
       d(x, z) = φ(|x − z|) ≤ φ(a + b) ≤ φ(a) + φ(b) = d(x, y) + d(y, z) ✓
    The same argument shows d/(1 + d) is a metric whenever d is; it is a
    BOUNDED metric (values < 1) with the same open sets as d. (c) M1 and M2
    hold for (x − y)², so the only hope is M3, and one counterexample kills
    it: squaring exaggerates large distances. (d) From M3,
    d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z), so d(x, z) − d(y, z) ≤ d(x, y); swapping x
    and y gives d(y, z) − d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y). Together:
    |d(x, z) − d(y, z)| ≤ d(x, y). Consequence: x ↦ d(x, z) is 1-Lipschitz,
    hence continuous. Common mistakes: checking M3 only for x ≤ y ≤ z;
    forgetting that d(x, x) = 0 must also be verified. Now you try: is
    d(x, y) = |x³ − y³| a metric on R? (Yes: it is |g(x) − g(y)| with
    g(x) = x³ INJECTIVE; injectivity gives M1, and M3 is inherited from |·|.)

D2. (a) Sketch the unit balls B(0, 1) in R² for d₁, d₂, d∞ and for the
    discrete metric. (b) Prove d∞ ≤ d₂ ≤ d₁ ≤ 2d∞ on R² and deduce that the
    three metrics have the same open sets. (c) In the discrete metric on a
    set X, which subsets are open, which closed? Which sequences converge?
    Answer: (a) d₁: diamond |x| + |y| < 1; d₂: disc; d∞: square
    max(|x|, |y|) < 1; discrete: B(0, 1) = {0} (and B(0, 2) = X). (b) Below.
    (c) Every subset is open and closed; a sequence converges ⇔ it is
    eventually constant.
    Teacher explains: (a) The diamond sits inside the disc which sits inside
    the square, reflecting d∞ ≤ d₂ ≤ d₁ (a bigger metric gives a smaller
    ball). (b) Let a = |x₁ − y₁|, b = |x₂ − y₂|, say a ≥ b. Then
       d∞ = a = √(a²) ≤ √(a² + b²) = d₂
       d₂² = a² + b² ≤ a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)² = d₁²
       d₁ = a + b ≤ 2a = 2d∞
    Now let U be d₂-open and x ∈ U, with B₂(x, r) ⊆ U. Since d₂ ≤ d₁,
    B₁(x, r) ⊆ B₂(x, r) ⊆ U, so U is d₁-open. Since d₂ ≤ 2d∞,
    B∞(x, r/2) ⊆ B₂(x, r) ⊆ U, so U is d∞-open. The same chain run backwards
    gives the other directions. Picture: each ball contains a SMALLER ball of
    the other shapes centred at the same point. General rule: if
    c·d ≤ d′ ≤ C·d, the metrics are EQUIVALENT and have the same open sets,
    convergent sequences and Cauchy sequences. (c) In the discrete metric
    B(x, 1/2) = {x}, so every singleton is open and hence every set (a union
    of singletons) is open; every complement is open too, so every set is
    closed. If xₙ → x then d(xₙ, x) < 1/2 eventually, i.e. xₙ = x
    eventually. Common mistakes: thinking the closed ball {y : d(0, y) ≤ 1}
    is the closure of B(0, 1) (discrete: closed ball = X, closure = {0});
    drawing the d∞ ball as a diamond. Now you try: in Rⁿ prove
    d₁ ≤ √n·d₂. (Cauchy-Schwarz: ∑|xᵢ − yᵢ|·1 ≤ √(∑|xᵢ − yᵢ|²)·√n.)

D3. Prove: (a) every open ball is open; (b) a union of any family of open
    sets is open; (c) an intersection of two (hence finitely many) open sets
    is open; (d) the corresponding statements for closed sets. Show by
    examples in R that an infinite intersection of open sets need not be
    open and an infinite union of closed sets need not be closed.
    Answer: Proofs below; ⋂ₙ (−1/n, 1/n) = {0} is not open;
    ⋃ₙ [1/n, 1] = (0, 1] is not closed.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let y ∈ B(x, r), and put s = r − d(x, y) > 0. If
    d(z, y) < s then by the triangle inequality
       d(z, x) ≤ d(z, y) + d(y, x) < s + d(x, y) = r
    so B(y, s) ⊆ B(x, r) ✓. (Draw it: the small ball fits because we used
    the room left, r − d(x, y).) (b) If x ∈ ⋃Uᵢ then x ∈ Uⱼ for some j, and
    some B(x, r) ⊆ Uⱼ ⊆ ⋃Uᵢ. (c) If x ∈ U ∩ V choose B(x, r₁) ⊆ U and
    B(x, r₂) ⊆ V and put r = min(r₁, r₂) > 0; then B(x, r) ⊆ U ∩ V. With
    infinitely many sets the minimum becomes an infimum which can be 0:
    that is exactly what happens in ⋂ (−1/n, 1/n) = {0}, and {0} is not open
    because no interval (−r, r) fits inside it. (d) Take complements with
    De Morgan: X − ⋂Fᵢ = ⋃(X − Fᵢ) is open, so ⋂Fᵢ is closed; and
    X − (F ∪ G) = (X − F) ∩ (X − G) is open. The union ⋃ [1/n, 1] = (0, 1]
    misses its limit point 0, so it is not closed. Common mistakes: thinking
    'closed' is the opposite of 'open' (Q is neither; R is both); forgetting
    that openness is relative to the space: [0, 1) is open in X = [0, 2]
    since [0, 1) = X ∩ (−1, 1). Now you try: show that a finite set in a
    metric space is closed. (Each {x} is closed: if y ≠ x then
    B(y, d(x, y)) misses x; a finite union of closed sets is closed.)

D4. For A = [0, 1) ∪ {2} in R find the interior, the limit points, the
    closure, the boundary and the isolated points. Do the same for Q and for
    S = {1/n : n ∈ N}. Then prove: A is closed ⇔ whenever aₙ ∈ A and aₙ → x,
    then x ∈ A.
    Answer: A: A° = (0, 1), limit points [0, 1], Ā = [0, 1] ∪ {2},
    ∂A = {0, 1, 2}, isolated point 2. Q: interior ∅, limit points R,
    closure R, boundary R, no isolated points. S: interior ∅, limit points
    {0}, closure S ∪ {0}, boundary S ∪ {0}, every point of S isolated.
    Teacher explains: Go point by point. For A: a point of (0, 1) has a small
    interval inside A, so it is interior; 0 is in A but every (−r, r) sticks
    out to the left, so 0 is not interior; 2 is not interior (nothing near 2
    except 2 itself is in A). Limit points: every x ∈ [0, 1] is approached by
    points of [0, 1); 2 is not (B(2, 1/2) ∩ A = {2}), so 2 is ISOLATED. The
    boundary = closure minus interior = {0, 1, 2}. For Q use DENSITY: every
    interval contains rationals and irrationals, so no point is interior and
    every real is a limit point. For S: the points 1/n are isolated (the gap
    to the neighbours 1/(n ± 1) is positive), and 0 is the only limit point.
    Proof of the criterion. (⇒) Let A be closed, aₙ ∈ A, aₙ → x, and suppose
    x ∉ A. X − A is open, so B(x, r) ⊆ X − A for some r; but d(aₙ, x) < r for
    large n, putting aₙ outside A: contradiction. (⇐) Suppose A contains all
    such limits and let x ∉ A. If no ball about x lay in X − A, then for each
    n pick aₙ ∈ A ∩ B(x, 1/n); then aₙ → x, forcing x ∈ A: contradiction.
    So X − A is open ✓. Common mistakes: listing 2 as a limit point of A;
    saying the boundary of Q is ∅ ('Q has no edges'). Now you try: find the
    interior, closure and boundary of (0, 1) ∪ (1, 2). ((0, 1) ∪ (1, 2),
    [0, 2], {0, 1, 2})

D5. (a) Prove: f : X → Y is continuous (ε-δ at every point) ⇔ f⁻¹(V) is
    open for every open V ⊆ Y. (b) Deduce that {(x, y) : x² + y² < 1} and
    {(x, y) : xy > 1, x + y < 5} are open in R² and that {(x, y) : xy ≥ 1}
    and the unit circle are closed. (c) Show that f(x) = x² is uniformly
    continuous on [0, 3] but not on R.
    Answer: Proofs below. On [0, 3], δ = ε/6 works; on R, ε = 1 fails with
    xₙ = n, yₙ = n + 1/n.
    Teacher explains: (a) (⇒) Let V be open and a ∈ f⁻¹(V). Choose ε with
    B(f(a), ε) ⊆ V; continuity gives δ with f(B(a, δ)) ⊆ B(f(a), ε) ⊆ V, so
    B(a, δ) ⊆ f⁻¹(V) ✓. (⇐) Given a and ε, V = B(f(a), ε) is open, so
    f⁻¹(V) is an open set containing a, hence contains some B(a, δ): that δ
    works. Taking complements, f is continuous ⇔ preimages of closed sets
    are closed. (b) The functions g(x, y) = x² + y², h(x, y) = xy and
    k(x, y) = x + y are continuous (polynomials), so
       {g < 1} = g⁻¹((−∞, 1))                       open
       {h > 1} ∩ {k < 5} = h⁻¹((1, ∞)) ∩ k⁻¹((−∞, 5))  open (finite ∩)
       {h ≥ 1} = h⁻¹([1, ∞)),  S¹ = g⁻¹({1})         closed
    This is the quickest way to classify sets in the drills: STRICT
    inequalities of continuous functions give open sets, weak inequalities
    and equations give closed sets. (c) On [0, 3]:
       |x² − y²| = |x + y|·|x − y| ≤ 6|x − y|
    so f is 6-Lipschitz and δ = ε/6 works for all x, y at once. On R take
    xₙ = n, yₙ = n + 1/n: |xₙ − yₙ| = 1/n → 0 but
       |yₙ² − xₙ²| = 2 + 1/n² > 1
    so no δ can serve ε = 1. Common mistakes: 'the image of an open set is
    open' (x² maps (−1, 1) onto [0, 1), not open); proving uniform
    continuity with a δ that depends on x. Now you try: show
    {(x, y) : sin(xy) > 0} is open and find a Lipschitz constant for
    d(·, A). (Preimage of (0, ∞) under a continuous map; L = 1 by D1(d)-type
    argument: |d(x, A) − d(y, A)| ≤ d(x, y).)

D6. (a) Prove that every convergent sequence is Cauchy and every Cauchy
    sequence is bounded. (b) Show that Q is not complete, using Newton's
    iteration xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ + 2/xₙ)/2, x₁ = 1. (c) Show that (0, 1) is not
    complete but [0, 1] is. (d) Prove: a closed subset of a complete space is
    complete, and a complete subspace of any metric space is closed.
    Answer: (b) x₂ = 3/2, x₃ = 17/12, x₄ = 577/408, ... is Cauchy in Q with
    limit √2 ∉ Q. (c) 1/n is Cauchy in (0, 1) with no limit there. (a), (d)
    below.
    Teacher explains: (a) If xₙ → x, given ε pick N with d(xₙ, x) < ε/2 for
    n ≥ N; then d(xₘ, xₙ) ≤ d(xₘ, x) + d(x, xₙ) < ε. Bounded: with ε = 1,
    all xₙ (n ≥ N) lie within 1 of x_N, and the finitely many earlier terms
    are at bounded distance, so all lie in B(x_N, R) with
    R = 1 + max(d(x₁, x_N), ..., d(x_{N−1}, x_N)). (b) Every xₙ is rational
    (the recursion uses only +, ×, ÷):
       x₂ = (1 + 2)/2 = 3/2,  x₃ = (3/2 + 4/3)/2 = 17/12,
       x₄ = (17/12 + 24/17)/2 = 577/408 ≈ 1.4142157
    In R the sequence converges to √2 (the Newton limit L satisfies
    L = (L + 2/L)/2, i.e. L² = 2), so it is Cauchy in R and therefore Cauchy
    in Q (the same distances). If it converged in Q, limits in R being
    unique, the limit would be √2, which is irrational. So Q has a Cauchy
    sequence with no limit IN Q: not complete. (c) 1/n is Cauchy, and its
    only possible limit 0 is not in (0, 1). In [0, 1] a Cauchy sequence
    converges in R (R is complete) and the limit stays in [0, 1] because
    [0, 1] is closed (D4). (d) Let F be closed in complete X and (xₙ) Cauchy
    in F. Then (xₙ) is Cauchy in X, so xₙ → x ∈ X, and x ∈ F as F is closed.
    Conversely let Y be complete and xₙ ∈ Y with xₙ → x ∈ X. Then (xₙ) is
    Cauchy, so it converges to some y ∈ Y; uniqueness of limits gives
    x = y ∈ Y: Y is closed. Common mistakes: saying '1/n converges to 0 so
    (0, 1) is complete'; forgetting that 'complete' always refers to limits
    INSIDE the space. Now you try: is N with d(m, n) = |1/m − 1/n| complete?
    (No: xₙ = n is Cauchy since d(m, n) ≤ 1/min(m, n), but it has no limit:
    d(n, k) → 1/k ≠ 0 for every fixed k.)

D7. (a) Prove that C[0, 1] with d∞(f, g) = sup|f − g| is complete. (b) Show
    that C[0, 1] with d(f, g) = ∫₀¹|f − g| is not complete, using the ramps
    fₙ(x) = 0 on [0, 1/2 − 1/n], fₙ(x) = 1 on [1/2, 1], linear in between
    (n ≥ 3).
    Answer: Proofs below; in the L¹ metric (fₙ) is Cauchy
    (d(fₘ, fₙ) = |1/(2n) − 1/(2m)|) but has no continuous limit.
    Teacher explains: (a) Three steps, which are the pattern for every
    completeness proof: find a candidate, show convergence, show it lies in
    the space. Let (fₙ) be Cauchy in sup. For each x,
    |fₘ(x) − fₙ(x)| ≤ d∞(fₘ, fₙ), so (fₙ(x)) is Cauchy in R and converges;
    call the limit f(x) (CANDIDATE). Given ε choose N with d∞(fₘ, fₙ) < ε for
    m, n ≥ N. Fix n ≥ N and x and let m → ∞ in |fₘ(x) − fₙ(x)| < ε to get
    |f(x) − fₙ(x)| ≤ ε for all x: fₙ → f UNIFORMLY (CONVERGENCE). A uniform
    limit of continuous functions is continuous (ε/3 argument), so f ∈ C[0, 1]
    (IN THE SPACE) ✓. (b) For m > n the graph of fₘ is a steeper ramp lying
    below fₙ, and the area between them is the difference of two triangles:
       d(fₘ, fₙ) = (1/2)(1/n)(1) − (1/2)(1/m)(1) = 1/(2n) − 1/(2m) < 1/(2n)
    so (fₙ) is Cauchy. Suppose fₙ → g in this metric with g continuous. On
    [0, a] with a < 1/2, fₙ = 0 for large n, so ∫₀ᵃ|g| = lim ∫₀ᵃ|g − fₙ| = 0,
    forcing g = 0 on [0, 1/2) (g is continuous). Likewise g = 1 on [1/2, 1].
    Then g jumps at 1/2: not continuous, a contradiction. The 'limit' is a
    step function, which lives in a bigger space (L¹). Common mistakes: in
    (a) forgetting to prove that the limit is continuous; in (b) concluding
    'not complete' just because the pointwise limit is discontinuous without
    ruling out every continuous candidate. Now you try: are the polynomials
    on [0, 1] with the sup metric complete? (No: the Taylor polynomials of eˣ
    are Cauchy in sup but the limit eˣ is not a polynomial.)

D8. (a) Define compactness by open covers. Show directly that (0, 1] is not
    compact, and that K = {0} ∪ {1/n : n ∈ N} is compact. (b) Prove that a
    compact subset of a metric space is closed and bounded. (c) Prove that a
    closed subset of a compact space is compact.
    Answer: (a) The cover {(1/n, 2) : n ∈ N} of (0, 1] has no finite
    subcover; for K, the member containing 0 contains all but finitely many
    points. (b), (c) below.
    Teacher explains: (a) K is COMPACT if EVERY open cover has a finite
    subcover (one bad cover is enough to show non-compactness). The sets
    Uₙ = (1/n, 2) cover (0, 1] since every x > 0 exceeds some 1/n; any finite
    subfamily has a largest index N and covers only (1/N, 1], missing 1/(N+1).
    For K, take any open cover. Some member U contains 0, and U ⊇ (−r, r)
    for some r > 0; all 1/n with n > 1/r lie in U. The finitely many
    remaining points 1, 1/2, ..., 1/N each need one more member: finite
    subcover ✓. (b) BOUNDED: the balls B(x₀, n), n ∈ N, cover K; a finite
    subcover means K ⊆ B(x₀, N). CLOSED: let y ∉ K. For each x ∈ K put
    rₓ = d(x, y)/2; the balls B(x, rₓ) cover K, so finitely many
    B(x₁, r₁), ..., B(xₖ, rₖ) cover K. With r = min rᵢ > 0 the ball B(y, r)
    misses every B(xᵢ, rᵢ) (triangle inequality), hence misses K. So X − K
    is open ✓. (c) Let F ⊆ K be closed and {Uᵢ} an open cover of F. Add the
    open set X − F: now it covers K, a finite subcover exists, and dropping
    X − F leaves finitely many Uᵢ covering F ✓. Common mistakes: 'every
    cover of (0, 1] has a finite subcover because (0, 1) ∪ (1/2, 2) works' —
    ONE finite cover proves nothing; compactness is about EVERY cover. Now
    you try: show [0, ∞) is not compact. (The cover (−1, n), n ∈ N, has no
    finite subcover.)

D9. (a) State the equivalent forms of compactness in a metric space and
    HEINE-BOREL. (b) Show that an infinite set with the discrete metric, and
    the closed unit ball of C[0, 1] (sup metric), are closed and bounded but
    not compact. (c) Show that the closed unit ball of ℓ² is not compact.
    Answer: (a) Compact ⇔ sequentially compact ⇔ complete + totally bounded;
    in Rⁿ compact ⇔ closed + bounded. (b), (c) below: in each case a
    sequence with all mutual distances ≥ 1 exists.
    Teacher explains: (a) In a metric space X the following are equivalent:
       (i)   every open cover has a finite subcover        (compact)
       (ii)  every sequence has a subsequence converging in X
       (iii) X is complete and TOTALLY BOUNDED (∀ε, finitely many ε-balls
             cover X)
    In Rⁿ a bounded set is automatically totally bounded (cover a big cube by
    small cubes), and a closed subset of Rⁿ is complete, which gives
    HEINE-BOREL: K ⊆ Rⁿ is compact ⇔ K is closed and bounded. (b) THE TOOL:
    if a sequence has d(xₘ, xₙ) ≥ c > 0 for all m ≠ n, no subsequence is
    Cauchy, so the space is not sequentially compact. Discrete X: take
    distinct points xₙ; d(xₘ, xₙ) = 1. X is closed (in itself) and bounded
    (diameter 1) but not compact; also the cover by singletons {x} has no
    finite subcover. In C[0, 1] let fₙ be the TENT of height 1 on
    [1/(n + 1), 1/n] (0 outside). The supports do not overlap, so
    d∞(fₘ, fₙ) = 1 for m ≠ n; all fₙ lie in the closed unit ball. (c) In ℓ²
    the unit vectors eₙ = (0, ..., 0, 1, 0, ...) satisfy
       ‖eₘ − eₙ‖ = √(1² + 1²) = √2        (m ≠ n)
    Again no convergent subsequence. Lesson: Heine-Borel is special to
    FINITE-dimensional spaces (Riesz's theorem: the closed unit ball of a
    normed space is compact iff the dimension is finite). What saves
    compactness in C[0, 1] is EQUICONTINUITY (Arzelà-Ascoli, topic 10.6).
    Common mistakes: using Heine-Borel in C[0, 1]; forgetting that R with
    the bounded metric min(1, |x − y|) is closed and bounded but not
    compact. Now you try: is the Hilbert cube {x ∈ ℓ² : |xₙ| ≤ 1/n} compact?
    (Yes: it is closed, and totally bounded because the tail ∑_{n>N} 1/n² is
    small, so only finitely many coordinates matter.)

D10. Prove: (a) the continuous image of a compact set is compact; (b) a
     continuous f : K → R on non-empty compact K attains a maximum and a
     minimum; (c) a continuous function on a compact metric space is
     uniformly continuous. Then (d) find the maximum and minimum of
     f(x, y) = x² − y² + 2y on the closed unit disc, and explain why they
     exist.
     Answer: (a)-(c) below. (d) Maximum 3/2 at (±√3/2, 1/2); minimum −3 at
     (0, −1).
     Teacher explains: (a) Let {Vᵢ} be an open cover of f(K). The sets
     f⁻¹(Vᵢ) are open and cover K, so finitely many f⁻¹(V₁), ..., f⁻¹(Vₖ)
     do; then V₁, ..., Vₖ cover f(K) ✓. (b) f(K) is a compact subset of R,
     hence closed and bounded; a closed bounded non-empty set contains its
     sup and inf. (c) Suppose not. Then for some ε > 0 and every n there are
     xₙ, yₙ with d(xₙ, yₙ) < 1/n but |f(xₙ) − f(yₙ)| ≥ ε. By sequential
     compactness a subsequence x_{n_k} → x; then y_{n_k} → x too. By
     continuity f(x_{n_k}) − f(y_{n_k}) → f(x) − f(x) = 0, contradicting ≥ ε.
     (d) The disc is closed and bounded, so compact, and f is continuous:
     max and min EXIST. Find them. Inside: ∇f = (2x, −2y + 2) = 0 at (0, 1),
     which is on the boundary, not inside. On the boundary put x² = 1 − y²:
        f = 1 − y² − y² + 2y = 1 + 2y − 2y²,   y ∈ [−1, 1]
     This is 3/2 − 2(y − 1/2)² with maximum 3/2 at y = 1/2 (x = ±√3/2) and
     minimum at y = −1: 1 − 2 − 2 = −3. Compare y = 1: 1. So
        max f = 3/2 at (±√3/2, 1/2),     min f = −3 at (0, −1)
     Common mistakes: forgetting the boundary; applying the extreme value
     theorem on an open disc (f(x) = x on (0, 1) has no max). Now you try: why
     does f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1] fail to be bounded, and which hypothesis of
     (b) fails? ((0, 1] is not compact: it is not closed in R.)

D11. (a) Define connectedness and prove that [0, 1] is connected. (b) Show that
     Q and R − {0} are not connected. (c) Prove that the continuous image of a
     connected space is connected and deduce the intermediate value theorem.
     (d) Show that every continuous f : [0, 1] → [0, 1] has a fixed point.
     Answer: Proofs below. For (b): Q = (Q ∩ (−∞, √2)) ∪ (Q ∩ (√2, ∞)) and
     R − {0} = (−∞, 0) ∪ (0, ∞) are separations.
     Teacher explains: X is CONNECTED if it is not U ∪ V with U, V open,
     disjoint and non-empty (a SEPARATION). (a) Suppose [0, 1] = U ∪ V is a
     separation (U, V open in [0, 1]) with 0 ∈ U. Let
        c = sup{t ∈ [0, 1] : [0, t] ⊆ U}
     If c ∈ U: U is open, so [c, c + r) ⊆ U for some r, and [0, c) ⊆ U, so
     (unless c = 1) the sup could be pushed beyond c, impossible; and if
     c = 1 then [0, 1] ⊆ U and V = ∅, impossible. If c ∈ V: V is open, so
     (c − r, c] ⊆ V, but points just below c lie in U by the definition of
     c: U ∩ V ≠ ∅, impossible. Either way a contradiction ✓. The same
     argument shows every interval is connected; conversely a non-interval A
     has a < b < c with a, c ∈ A, b ∉ A, and (−∞, b), (b, ∞) separate it.
     (b) Both displayed pieces are open in Q (intersections with open sets of
     R), disjoint (√2 ∉ Q) and non-empty. (c) If f(X) = U ∪ V were a
     separation, X = f⁻¹(U) ∪ f⁻¹(V) would be one. IVT: if f : [a, b] → R is
     continuous, f([a, b]) is a connected subset of R, i.e. an interval, so
     it contains every value between f(a) and f(b). (d) Put g(x) = f(x) − x.
     Then g(0) = f(0) ≥ 0 and g(1) = f(1) − 1 ≤ 0; by the IVT g(c) = 0 for
     some c, i.e. f(c) = c. (This is the 1-dimensional BROUWER fixed point
     theorem.) Common mistakes: in (b) using √2 as a split point inside Q;
     thinking 'connected' means 'path-connected' always. Now you try: show
     that a continuous f : [0, 1] → Q is constant. (f([0, 1]) is a connected
     subset of Q; the only ones are single points.)

D12. (a) Define path-connectedness and prove path-connected ⇒ connected.
     (b) Describe the topologist's sine curve T and explain why it is
     connected but not path-connected. (c) Use connectedness to prove that R
     is not homeomorphic to R², that [0, 1] is not homeomorphic to the
     circle S¹, and that [0, 1) is not homeomorphic to (0, 1). (d) Is the
     letter X homeomorphic to the letter T?
     Answer: (a) below. (b) T is the closure of a connected set, hence
     connected; no path reaches the segment from the curve. (c) Remove
     points and count components. (d) No: removing the centre of X leaves 4
     components, removing a point of T leaves at most 3.
     Teacher explains: (a) Suppose X is path-connected but X = U ∪ V is a
     separation, u ∈ U, v ∈ V. Take a path γ : [0, 1] → X from u to v. Then
     [0, 1] = γ⁻¹(U) ∪ γ⁻¹(V) is a separation of [0, 1] (open, disjoint,
     0 in the first, 1 in the second), contradicting D11(a). (b)
        T = {(x, sin(1/x)) : 0 < x ≤ 1} ∪ ({0} × [−1, 1])
     The curve part G is path-connected (continuous image of (0, 1]), so
     connected, and T = Ḡ (every point (0, y) with |y| ≤ 1 is a limit of
     points (x, sin(1/x)) where sin(1/x) = y). The closure of a connected set
     is connected. Not path-connected: a path γ(t) = (x(t), y(t)) from (1,
     sin 1) to (0, 0) would have a first time t₀ with x(t₀) = 0; just before
     t₀, x(t) → 0 through the curve, where sin(1/x) oscillates between −1 and
     1 infinitely often, so y(t) cannot be continuous at t₀. (c) A
     homeomorphism h : X → Y restricts to a homeomorphism X − {p} →
     Y − {h(p)}, so the number of components after removing a point is an
     invariant.
        R − {0}: 2 components;       R² − {p}: connected (always)
        [0, 1] − {1/2}: 2 components; S¹ − {p}: connected (an arc)
        [0, 1) − {0}: connected;     (0, 1) − {p}: 2 components (every p)
     So none of the pairs are homeomorphic. (d) Removing the crossing point
     of X leaves 4 arms; removing any point of T leaves at most 3 pieces.
     Common mistakes: thinking 'the closure of a path-connected set is
     path-connected' (T is the counterexample); in (c) removing a point from
     only one of the spaces. Now you try: explain why an open connected
     subset U of R² is path-connected. (The set of points reachable from a
     fixed u by paths is open (balls are path-connected) and so is its
     complement in U; connectedness forces it to be all of U.)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Compute the distances. For points in Rⁿ give d₁, d₂, d∞. For functions on
    [0, 1] give the sup distance d∞ and the L¹ distance ∫₀¹|f − g|.

    e) (1, 0, −1), (3, −3, 5)         f) (1, 1, 1, 1), (0, 0, 0, 0)

    i) f = 0, g = sin(πx)             j) f = 1, g = eˣ
    k) f = x, g = 1 − x               l) f = xⁿ, g = 0
    m) discrete metric: d(3, 7), d(3, 3)
    n) Hamming distance between 10110 and 11100
    o) ℓ¹, ℓ², ℓ∞ distances between (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ...) and 0
    p) SNCF (railway) metric on R² (d(x, y) = |x − y| if x, y lie on one ray
       from 0, else |x| + |y|): d((1, 0), (3, 0)) and d((1, 0), (0, 2))

      o) 1, 1/√3 ≈ 0.577, 1/2     p) 2, 3

M2. Is d a metric on the given set? If not, name an axiom that fails, with a
    counterexample.

    m) 0 if x = y, |x − y| + 1 if x ≠ y, on R

      f) yes    g) no, M1: d(1, 1) = 1 (also not symmetric)       h) yes
      i) yes (bounded metric)             j) no, d(1, 1) = 1; d(1, −1) < 0
      k) no, M1: d((0, 0), (0, 1)) = 0    l) yes
      m) yes    n) yes    o) no, M1: d(0, π) = 0                  p) no, M1:
      f = 0, g = x give 0    q) yes    r) yes    s) yes (t^(1/3) is
      subadditive)    t) no, M1: f = 0 and g = 0 except g(1/2) = 1 give 0

M6. Does the sequence converge in the given metric space? Give the limit, or
    say why not.
    a) 1/n in R                        b) 1/n in (0, 1)
    c) 1/n in R with the discrete metric
    d) (1/n, 1 − 1/n) in (R², d₂)      e) (1/n, n) in (R², d∞)
    f) fₙ = xⁿ in C[0, 1], sup metric  g) fₙ = xⁿ in C[0, 1], L¹ metric
    h) fₙ = x/n in C[0, 1], sup        i) fₙ = xⁿ/n in C[0, 1], sup
    j) fₙ = nxe^(−nx) in C[0, 1], sup  k) the same fₙ in C[0, 1], L¹
    l) eₙ (unit vectors) in ℓ²         m) eₙ/n in ℓ²
    n) (1, 1/2, ..., 1/n, 0, 0, ...) in ℓ²
    o) the same sequence in ℓ¹
    p) xₙ = n in R with d(x, y) = |arctan x − arctan y|
    Answers:

      c) no (not eventually constant)      d) (0, 1)
      e) no (unbounded)       f) no (pointwise limit is discontinuous)
      g) 0 (∫xⁿ = 1/(n + 1))  h) 0 (sup = 1/n)       i) 0 (sup = 1/n)
      j) no (sup = e⁻¹ at x = 1/n, pointwise limit 0)

      l) no (‖eₘ − eₙ‖ = √2)   m) 0 (norm 1/n)

      o) no (not Cauchy: distance ∑_{n<k≤m} 1/k is unbounded)
      p) no (Cauchy, but the limit would need arctan x = π/2)

M7. Is the metric space complete? (Y/N; usual metric unless stated.)
    a) R                              b) Q
    c) (0, 1]                         d) [0, 1]
    e) Z                              f) N with |1/m − 1/n|
    g) R with |arctan x − arctan y|   h) R with |x³ − y³|
    i) (Rⁿ, d₁)                       j) C[0, 1], sup metric
    k) C[0, 1], L¹ metric             l) polynomials on [0, 1], sup
    m) ℓ²                             n) finitely supported sequences, ℓ²
    o) any discrete metric space      p) {1/n : n ∈ N}
    q) {0} ∪ {1/n : n ∈ N}            r) the Cantor set
    s) R − Q                          t) C¹[0, 1] with the sup metric
    u) C¹[0, 1] with ‖f − g‖∞ + ‖f′ − g′‖∞
    v) [0, ∞) with d(x, y) = |√x − √y|
    Answers:
      a) Y   b) N   c) N   d) Y   e) Y   f) N (n is Cauchy)   g) N (n)
      h) Y (x ↦ x³ is an isometry onto (R, |·|))   i) Y   j) Y   k) N (D7)
      l) N (Taylor polynomials of eˣ)   m) Y   n) N ((1, 1/2, ..., 1/n, 0, ...)
      tends to (1/k) outside the space)   o) Y (Cauchy ⇒ eventually constant)
      p) N   q) Y   r) Y (closed in R)   s) N (rationals ≈ irrationals: √2/n
      → 0 ∉ R − Q)   t) N (C¹ functions tend uniformly to |x − 1/2|)   u) Y
      v) Y (x ↦ √x is an isometry onto [0, ∞) with |·|, a closed subset of R)

M12. True or false? For F give a counterexample.
     a) Every closed bounded subset of a metric space is compact.
     b) Every compact subset of a metric space is closed and bounded.
     c) A union of infinitely many closed sets is closed.
     d) An intersection of infinitely many open sets is open.
     e) A proper non-empty subset of a metric space can be both open and
        closed.
     f) Every Cauchy sequence is bounded.
     g) Every bounded sequence in R² has a convergent subsequence.
     h) Every bounded sequence in ℓ² has a convergent subsequence.
     i) The continuous image of a closed set is closed.
     j) The continuous image of a compact set is compact.
     k) The continuous preimage of a compact set is compact.
     l) The continuous image of a connected set is connected.
     m) Connected ⇒ path-connected.
     n) An open connected subset of Rⁿ is path-connected.
     o) A subspace of a complete space is complete ⇔ it is closed.
     p) The closure of B(x, r) is always {y : d(x, y) ≤ r}.
     q) (Ā)° = A° for every A.
     r) Continuous functions map Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences.
     s) Every compact metric space is complete.
     t) A complete bounded metric space is compact.
     u) A complete totally bounded metric space is compact.
     v) The boundary of any set is closed.
     w) A continuous bijection between metric spaces is a homeomorphism.
     x) Completeness is preserved by homeomorphisms.
     Answers:
       a) F (infinite discrete space)     b) T
       c) F (⋃[1/n, 1] = (0, 1])          d) F (⋂(−1/n, 1/n) = {0})
       e) T ([0, 1] in X = [0, 1] ∪ [2, 3])            f) T
       g) T (Bolzano-Weierstrass)         h) F (eₙ)
       i) F (arctan(R) = (−π/2, π/2); projection of xy = 1 to the x-axis)
       j) T      k) F (constant map R → {0})           l) T
       m) F (topologist's sine curve)     n) T         o) T
       p) F (discrete metric, r = 1: closure {x}, closed ball X)
       q) F (A = Q: (Q̄)° = R, Q° = ∅)
       r) F (1/x on (0, 1), xₙ = 1/n); true for uniformly continuous maps
       s) T      t) F (infinite discrete space; unit ball of ℓ²)   u) T
       v) T (∂A = Ā ∩ (X − A)‾, an intersection of closed sets)
       w) F (t ↦ (cos t, sin t) from [0, 2π) onto S¹); true if the domain
          is compact
       x) F (R ≅ (0, 1) via arctan-type maps; (0, 1) is not complete)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw everything. Sketch the three unit balls of R² and let the
  student see why a small square fits in a disc and vice versa; for 'open or
  closed?' first try the preimage rule (strict inequality of a continuous
  function ⇒ open; ≤, ≥, = ⇒ closed) and only then think about boundary
  points. For compactness keep a two-line check list: in Rⁿ use
  Heine-Borel; anywhere else look for a sequence with mutual distances ≥ c
  (discrete points, unit vectors eₙ, disjoint tents). For completeness always
  ask 'where does the Cauchy sequence want to go, and is that point in the
  space?'. For connectedness split the set by an open cut, or join points by
  a path. Harder: prove that a metric space is compact iff it is complete
  and totally bounded (use a diagonal argument for (⇐)); prove the Lebesgue
  number lemma and use it to show that continuous maps on compact spaces are
  uniformly continuous; prove the Baire category theorem (a complete metric
  space is not a countable union of nowhere dense closed sets) and deduce
  that R is uncountable and that Q is not a Gδ set; construct the completion
  of a metric space from Cauchy sequences; show that the Cantor set is
  compact, perfect, totally disconnected and uncountable.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.6 — CONTRACTION MAPPING THEOREM; ARZELA-ASCOLI; STONE-WEIERSTRASS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A map T : X → X on a metric space is a CONTRACTION if there is a constant
    k with 0 ≤ k < 1 and d(Tx, Ty) ≤ k·d(x, y) for all x, y (a Lipschitz map
    with constant k < 1). A contraction is uniformly continuous. x* is a
    FIXED POINT if Tx* = x*.
  - BANACH CONTRACTION MAPPING THEOREM: if X is a NON-EMPTY COMPLETE metric
    space and T : X → X is a contraction, then T has EXACTLY ONE fixed point
    x*, and for ANY starting point x₀ the iterates xₙ₊₁ = Txₙ converge to x*.
    ERROR ESTIMATES: a priori d(xₙ, x*) ≤ kⁿ/(1 − k)·d(x₀, x₁); a posteriori
    d(xₙ, x*) ≤ k/(1 − k)·d(xₙ₋₁, xₙ); also d(xₙ, x*) ≤ kⁿ·d(x₀, x*).
    Iterations needed for accuracy ε: n ≥ ln(ε(1 − k)/d(x₀, x₁))/ln k.
  - EVERY HYPOTHESIS MATTERS: completeness (x ↦ x/2 on (0, 1] has no fixed
    point); k < 1 uniform, not merely d(Tx, Ty) < d(x, y) (x ↦ x + 1/x on
    [1, ∞) has none); T must map X INTO X (x ↦ x/2 + 1 on [0, 1]). The
    conditions are sufficient, not necessary (1 − x on [0, 1] has the fixed
    point 1/2 but is not a contraction). If some power Tᵐ is a contraction,
    T still has a unique fixed point.
  - TEST FOR REAL FUNCTIONS (mean value theorem): if g maps a CLOSED interval
    I into itself and |g′(x)| ≤ k < 1 on I, then g is a contraction on I. To
    solve f(x) = 0 rearrange as x = g(x) with |g′| small near the root;
    NEWTON's method is the rearrangement g(x) = x − f(x)/f′(x).
  - The constant depends on the METRIC: for T(x) = Mx + c on Rⁿ, k is the
    maximum ROW sum of |mᵢⱼ| for d∞, the maximum COLUMN sum for d₁, and the
    largest singular value for d₂. JACOBI ITERATION for Ax = b converges when
    A is STRICTLY DIAGONALLY DOMINANT (k = maxᵢ ∑_{j≠i}|aᵢⱼ|/|aᵢᵢ| < 1).
  - INTEGRAL EQUATIONS: FREDHOLM x(t) = f(t) + λ∫ₐᵇ K(t, s)x(s) ds has a
    unique continuous solution when |λ|·sup_t ∫ₐᵇ|K(t, s)| ds < 1 (sup metric
    on C[a, b]); VOLTERRA x(t) = f(t) + λ∫ₐᵗ K(t, s)x(s) ds has a unique
    solution for EVERY λ (some power of the operator is a contraction).
    Degenerate kernels (K = ∑aᵢ(t)bᵢ(s)) are solved exactly by constants.
  - PICARD-LINDELÖF: if f(t, y) is continuous on R = {|t − t₀| ≤ a,
    |y − y₀| ≤ b}, |f| ≤ M there and f is LIPSCHITZ in y (|f(t, y) − f(t, z)|
    ≤ L|y − z|), then y′ = f(t, y), y(t₀) = y₀ has a unique solution on
    |t − t₀| ≤ h = min(a, b/M) (with Lh < 1 in the simplest proof). The
    solution is the fixed point of (Ty)(t) = y₀ + ∫_{t₀}^t f(s, y(s)) ds, and
    PICARD ITERATES yₙ₊₁ = Tyₙ converge to it uniformly. Without the
    Lipschitz condition uniqueness can fail (y′ = 3y^(2/3), y(0) = 0:
    y = 0 and y = t³).
  - A family F ⊆ C(K) (K compact metric) is UNIFORMLY BOUNDED if
    ∃M ∀f ∈ F : ‖f‖∞ ≤ M; POINTWISE BOUNDED if each {f(x) : f ∈ F} is
    bounded; EQUICONTINUOUS if ∀ε ∃δ (the SAME δ for all f and all x):
    d(x, y) < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(y)| < ε. A family of functions with a COMMON
    Lipschitz constant (e.g. |f′| ≤ L) or a common Hölder bound
    |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ C|x − y|^α is equicontinuous. {xⁿ} and {sin nx} are not.
  - ARZELÀ-ASCOLI: for K compact, F ⊆ C(K) (sup metric) is RELATIVELY COMPACT
    (closure compact; equivalently every sequence in F has a UNIFORMLY
    convergent subsequence) ⇔ F is uniformly (equivalently pointwise)
    bounded and equicontinuous. F is compact ⇔ closed, bounded and
    equicontinuous. Proof: DIAGONAL argument on a countable dense set plus
    equicontinuity. Uses: compactness of {f : f(0) = 0, Lip f ≤ 1}; the
    operator f ↦ ∫₀ˣ f is COMPACT; PEANO's existence theorem (f continuous
    only: a solution exists, maybe not unique).
  - WEIERSTRASS APPROXIMATION: every f ∈ C[a, b] is a uniform limit of
    polynomials. Constructive proof by BERNSTEIN POLYNOMIALS on [0, 1]:
    Bₙf(x) = ∑ₖ f(k/n)·C(n, k)xᵏ(1 − x)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, with Bₙ1 = 1, Bₙx = x,
    Bₙx² = x² + x(1 − x)/n; Bₙf → f uniformly; Bₙf(0) = f(0), Bₙf(1) = f(1).
  - STONE-WEIERSTRASS (real): K compact metric (Hausdorff), A ⊆ C(K, R) a
    SUBALGEBRA (closed under +, ·, scalar multiples) that CONTAINS THE
    CONSTANTS and SEPARATES POINTS (∀x ≠ y ∃f ∈ A : f(x) ≠ f(y)). Then A is
    DENSE: Ā = C(K). COMPLEX version: A must also be closed under COMPLEX
    CONJUGATION (self-adjoint). The polynomials in z are NOT dense in C(S¹):
    ∫₀^{2π} p(e^{iθ})e^{iθ} dθ = 0 for every polynomial p, but the same
    integral for z̄ = e^{−iθ} is 2π, so z̄ is not a uniform limit.
  - STANDARD CONSEQUENCES: polynomials in n variables are dense in C(K),
    K ⊆ Rⁿ compact; trigonometric polynomials are dense in the continuous
    2π-PERIODIC functions (C(S¹)); polynomials in eˣ, in x², in x³ are dense
    on suitable intervals exactly when they separate points; C[a, b] is
    SEPARABLE (rational polynomials); if ∫₀¹ f(x)xⁿ dx = 0 for all n ≥ 0 and
    f is continuous then f ≡ 0.
  - TRAPS: forgetting to check T(X) ⊆ X; using k = sup|g′| over the wrong
    interval; thinking equicontinuity is just 'each f is uniformly
    continuous'; forgetting the constants (polynomials with p(0) = 0 are not
    dense in C[0, 1]) or separation (even polynomials on [−1, 1]); in the
    complex case forgetting conjugation.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. State and prove the Banach contraction mapping theorem, including the a
    priori and a posteriori error estimates.
    Answer: If (X, d) is non-empty and complete and d(Tx, Ty) ≤ k·d(x, y) with
    0 ≤ k < 1, then T has a unique fixed point x*, xₙ = Tⁿx₀ → x* for every
    x₀, and d(xₙ, x*) ≤ kⁿd(x₀, x₁)/(1 − k), d(xₙ, x*) ≤ k·d(xₙ₋₁, xₙ)/(1 − k).
    Teacher explains: Four steps. STEP 1 (consecutive terms shrink):
       d(xₙ₊₁, xₙ) = d(Txₙ, Txₙ₋₁) ≤ k·d(xₙ, xₙ₋₁) ≤ ... ≤ kⁿ·d(x₁, x₀)
    STEP 2 (Cauchy): for m > n, by the triangle inequality and the
    geometric series,
       d(xₘ, xₙ) ≤ d(xₙ₊₁, xₙ) + ... + d(xₘ, xₘ₋₁)
                ≤ (kⁿ + kⁿ⁺¹ + ... + k^{m−1})·d(x₁, x₀) ≤ kⁿ/(1 − k)·d(x₁, x₀)
    which → 0 as n → ∞ because k < 1. STEP 3 (limit is fixed): X is
    COMPLETE, so xₙ → x* ∈ X. T is continuous (Lipschitz), so
    Tx* = lim Txₙ = lim xₙ₊₁ = x*. STEP 4 (uniqueness): if Tx* = x* and
    Ty* = y*, then d(x*, y*) = d(Tx*, Ty*) ≤ k·d(x*, y*), so
    (1 − k)d(x*, y*) ≤ 0 and x* = y*. ESTIMATES: let m → ∞ in Step 2 to get
    the a priori bound d(x*, xₙ) ≤ kⁿd(x₁, x₀)/(1 − k). Applying the same
    bound with xₙ₋₁ as the starting point (one step) gives the a posteriori
    bound d(x*, xₙ) ≤ k·d(xₙ, xₙ₋₁)/(1 − k), which uses the latest step and is
    usually much sharper. Where each hypothesis was used: k < 1 in Steps 2
    and 4, completeness in Step 3, T(X) ⊆ X to form the iterates at all.
    Common mistakes: proving only that d(xₙ₊₁, xₙ) → 0 (that does NOT make a
    sequence Cauchy: think of √n); forgetting uniqueness. Now you try: show
    that d(xₙ, x*) ≤ kⁿd(x₀, x*). (Induction: d(xₙ, x*) = d(Txₙ₋₁, Tx*)
    ≤ k·d(xₙ₋₁, x*).)

D2. Show by examples that each hypothesis of the theorem is needed:
    (a) T(x) = x/2 on (0, 1]; (b) T(x) = x + 1 on R; (c) T(x) = x + 1/x on
    [1, ∞); (d) T(x) = x/2 + 1 on [0, 1]. (e) T(x) = 1 − x on [0, 1] has a
    unique fixed point; does the theorem apply? What happens to the iterates?
    Answer: (a) no fixed point: X not complete. (b) none: k = 1. (c) none:
    d(Tx, Ty) < d(x, y) but no k < 1 works. (d) T(1) = 3/2 ∉ [0, 1]: T does
    not map X into X (its fixed point 2 lies outside). (e) No (k = 1); the
    iterates from x₀ ≠ 1/2 oscillate x₀, 1 − x₀, x₀, ... and never converge.
    Teacher explains: (a) |x/2 − y/2| = |x − y|/2, a contraction with
    k = 1/2, but x = x/2 only for x = 0 ∉ (0, 1]. The iterates 1, 1/2, 1/4,
    ... are Cauchy and want to converge to the missing point 0. (b)
    |Tx − Ty| = |x − y|: an isometry, k = 1, and x + 1 = x is impossible.
    (c) For 1 ≤ x < y, by the mean value theorem
       |Tx − Ty| = |1 − 1/c²|·|x − y| < |x − y|     (some c ∈ (x, y))
    but 1 − 1/c² → 1 as c → ∞, so no single k < 1 works. And Tx − x = 1/x > 0,
    so there is no fixed point; the iterates increase to ∞ (xₙ₊₁² = xₙ² + 2
    + 1/xₙ², so xₙ ≈ √(2n)). (d) k = 1/2 and [0, 1] is complete, but T is not
    a map from [0, 1] to itself. (e) |Tx − Ty| = |x − y|, k = 1: the theorem
    says nothing; the fixed point exists for another reason (IVT). REMARK:
    on a COMPACT space, d(Tx, Ty) < d(x, y) for x ≠ y IS enough for a unique
    fixed point (Edelstein's theorem) — case (c) fails because [1, ∞) is
    not compact. Common mistakes: checking only that |g′| < 1 pointwise
    (case (c)); forgetting the self-map condition. Now you try: does
    T(x) = x² on [0, 1/3] satisfy the theorem? (Yes: T maps [0, 1/3] into
    [0, 1/9], |T′| ≤ 2/3; the fixed point is 0.)

D3. Solve x = cos x by fixed-point iteration. (a) Show that T(x) = cos x is a
    contraction of [0, 1] and find k. (b) From x₀ = 1 compute x₁, ..., x₄.
    (c) How many iterations does the a priori estimate require for an error
    below 10⁻⁶? (d) Use the a posteriori estimate after x₄.
    Answer: (a) k = sin 1 ≈ 0.8415. (b) 0.5403, 0.8576, 0.6543, 0.7935.
    (c) n = 87 (in fact 32 iterations suffice). (d) error ≤ 0.739; the fixed
    point is x* ≈ 0.739085.
    Teacher explains: (a) Self-map: cos is decreasing on [0, 1], so
    cos([0, 1]) = [cos 1, 1] = [0.5403, 1] ⊆ [0, 1] ✓. Contraction: by the
    MVT |cos x − cos y| = |sin c|·|x − y| ≤ sin 1·|x − y| on [0, 1], and
    k = sin 1 ≈ 0.84147 < 1 ✓. [0, 1] is closed in R, so complete ✓.
    (b) Iterate (radians!):
       x₁ = cos 1 = 0.54030,  x₂ = cos 0.54030 = 0.85755,
       x₃ = 0.65429,          x₄ = 0.79348
    The iterates ZIG-ZAG around x* because T′ < 0 (a cobweb diagram
    spirals). (c) d(x₀, x₁) = 1 − 0.54030 = 0.45970. We need
       kⁿ/(1 − k)·0.45970 < 10⁻⁶  ⇔  n > ln(10⁻⁶·0.15853/0.45970)/ln 0.84147
                                  = (−14.88)/(−0.17260) ≈ 86.2
    so n = 87. The a priori bound is pessimistic: the true error falls
    below 10⁻⁶ at n = 32, since near x* the real rate is |sin x*| ≈ 0.674,
    not sin 1. (d) A posteriori after x₄:
       d(x₄, x*) ≤ k/(1 − k)·|x₄ − x₃| = 5.308 × 0.13919 ≈ 0.739
    (true error 0.054); these bounds are guaranteed, not sharp. Common
    mistakes: using degrees; taking k = 1 = sup|sin| over all of R (then the
    theorem does not apply); forgetting to check that [0, 1] is mapped into
    itself. Now you try: show that T(x) = e^(−x) maps [0.4, 0.7] into itself
    and find k. (T is decreasing: T(0.7) ≈ 0.497, T(0.4) ≈ 0.670, both in
    [0.4, 0.7]; k = e^(−0.4) ≈ 0.670; fixed point ≈ 0.5671.)

D4. The equation x³ + x − 1 = 0 has one real root r ∈ (0, 1). Compare the
    rearrangements x = 1 − x³ and x = 1/(1 + x²) on [0, 1]; iterate the good
    one from x₀ = 1. Then show that Newton's method for x² = 2,
    g(x) = x/2 + 1/x, is a contraction on [1, 2], and iterate from x₀ = 1.
    Answer: 1 − x³ has |g′| = 3x² up to 3: not a contraction.
    1/(1 + x²) has k = 9/(8√3) ≈ 0.650: iterates 0.5, 0.8, 0.6098, 0.7290,
    0.6530, ... → r ≈ 0.682328. Newton: k = 1/2, iterates 1.5, 1.416667,
    1.414216, 1.4142136 → √2.
    Teacher explains: The METHOD: write f(x) = 0 as x = g(x), check (i)
    g(I) ⊆ I and (ii) max|g′| < 1 on I. For g₁(x) = 1 − x³, g₁′ = −3x² and
    near r ≈ 0.68, |g₁′(r)| ≈ 1.40 > 1: iterates are pushed AWAY from the
    root. For g₂(x) = 1/(1 + x²) (write x³ + x = 1 as x(1 + x²) = 1):
       g₂([0, 1]) = [1/2, 1] ⊆ [0, 1]
       g₂′(x) = −2x/(1 + x²)²,  maximum of |g₂′| at x = 1/√3:
       (2/√3)/(4/3)² = 9/(8√3) ≈ 0.6495
    So g₂ is a contraction with k ≈ 0.65. Iterates from 1:
       0.5, 0.8, 0.60976, 0.72897, 0.65300, 0.70106, ...  → 0.682328
    For Newton on x² − 2: g(x) = x − (x² − 2)/(2x) = x/2 + 1/x, and
       g′(x) = 1/2 − 1/x² ∈ [−1/2, 1/4]  on [1, 2],  so k = 1/2
    g has minimum √2 at x = √2 and g(1) = g(2) = 3/2, so g([1, 2]) =
    [√2, 3/2] ⊆ [1, 2] ✓. Iterates: 3/2, 17/12 = 1.416667,
    577/408 = 1.414216, 1.4142136. Newton converges much faster than k = 1/2
    suggests because g′(√2) = 0 (QUADRATIC convergence: the number of
    correct digits roughly doubles). Common mistakes: judging a
    rearrangement by one step; forgetting that |g′(r)| > 1 makes the fixed
    point repelling. Now you try: for x = √(x + 2) on [0, ∞) find k and the
    fixed point. (g′ = 1/(2√(x + 2)) ≤ 1/(2√2) ≈ 0.354; g maps [0, ∞) into
    [√2, ∞); x* = 2.)

D5. (a) Show that the map T(x) = Mx + c on Rⁿ with the metric d∞ has
    Lipschitz constant equal to the maximum row sum of |mᵢⱼ|. (b) Use it to
    prove that Jacobi iteration converges for the system 4x + y = 6,
    x + 5y = 11; compute two iterations from (0, 0) and the exact solution.
    (c) Why does Jacobi fail for x + 2y = 3, 2x + y = 3, and how can it be
    rescued?
    Answer: (b) k = 1/4; iterates (1.5, 2.2), (0.95, 1.9); solution (1, 2).
    (c) k = 2: the iterates (3, 3), (−3, −3), (9, 9), ... blow up; swap the
    equations to get a diagonally dominant system (k = 1/2).
    Teacher explains: (a) For each i,
       |(Mx − My)ᵢ| = |∑ⱼ mᵢⱼ(xⱼ − yⱼ)| ≤ (∑ⱼ|mᵢⱼ|)·max|xⱼ − yⱼ|
    so d∞(Tx, Ty) ≤ (maxᵢ ∑ⱼ|mᵢⱼ|)·d∞(x, y); equality is attained by choosing
    xⱼ − yⱼ = ±1 with the signs of the largest row. (b) Solve each equation
    for its diagonal unknown:
       x = (6 − y)/4,   y = (11 − x)/5,   M = [[0, −1/4], [−1/5, 0]]
    Row sums 1/4 and 1/5, so k = 1/4 < 1 in the complete space (R², d∞):
    Jacobi converges from ANY start. From (0, 0):
       (x₁, y₁) = (6/4, 11/5) = (1.5, 2.2)
       (x₂, y₂) = ((6 − 2.2)/4, (11 − 1.5)/5) = (0.95, 1.9)
       (x₃, y₃) = (1.025, 2.01)
    Exact: substitute x = (6 − y)/4 into x + 5y = 11: 6 − y + 20y = 44, y = 2,
    x = 1. The errors shrink by about 1/4 or better per step (in fact by
    1/20 every two steps, since M² = (1/20)I). (c) x = 3 − 2y, y = 3 − 2x
    gives row sums 2: not a contraction, and indeed from (0, 0) the iterates
    are (3, 3), (−3, −3), (9, 9), ... Rewriting the system as 2x + y = 3,
    x + 2y = 3 gives x = (3 − y)/2, y = (3 − x)/2, k = 1/2, converging to
    (1, 1). Common mistakes: using column sums with d∞ (column sums belong
    to d₁); concluding 'not a contraction in d∞ ⇒ diverges' (another metric
    may work: M = [[1/2, 1/2], [0, 1/4]] has row sum 1 but column sums 1/2
    and 3/4). Now you try: 10x + y + z = 12, x + 10y + z = 12,
    x + y + 10z = 12. (k = 1/5; from 0: (1.2, 1.2, 1.2), then
    (0.96, 0.96, 0.96); solution (1, 1, 1).)

D6. Consider the Fredholm equation x(t) = t + λ∫₀¹ ts·x(s) ds on C[0, 1].
    (a) For which λ does the contraction theorem guarantee a unique solution?
    (b) Solve exactly for all λ. (c) For λ = 1 compute the Picard iterates
    from x₀ = 0 and compare.
    Answer: (a) |λ| < 2. (b) x(t) = 3t/(3 − λ) for λ ≠ 3; no solution for
    λ = 3. (c) x₁ = t, x₂ = 4t/3, x₃ = 13t/9, ... → 3t/2.
    Teacher explains: (a) Define (Tx)(t) = t + λ∫₀¹ ts·x(s) ds. Then
       |(Tx − Ty)(t)| = |λ|·|∫₀¹ ts(x(s) − y(s)) ds| ≤ |λ|·t·(1/2)·‖x − y‖∞
    so ‖Tx − Ty‖∞ ≤ (|λ|/2)·‖x − y‖∞, a contraction when |λ| < 2. C[0, 1]
    with the sup metric is complete (10.5 D7), so the theorem applies. (b)
    The kernel is DEGENERATE (a product t·s), so the solution must be
    x(t) = t + λct with the unknown CONSTANT c = ∫₀¹ s·x(s) ds. Substitute:
       c = ∫₀¹ s(s + λcs) ds = 1/3 + λc/3  ⇒  c(3 − λ) = 1  ⇒  c = 1/(3 − λ)
       x(t) = t(1 + λ/(3 − λ)) = 3t/(3 − λ)
    For λ = 3 the equation for c reads 0 = 1: no solution (λ = 3 is the
    reciprocal of an EIGENVALUE of the integral operator). The contraction
    theorem gave only |λ| < 2; the true condition is λ ≠ 3 — the theorem is
    sufficient, not necessary. (c) λ = 1: xₙ₊₁(t) = t + t∫₀¹ s·xₙ(s) ds. If
    xₙ = aₙt then ∫ s·aₙs ds = aₙ/3, so aₙ₊₁ = 1 + aₙ/3:
       a: 0, 1, 4/3, 13/9, 40/27, ...  → 3/2
    matching x = 3t/2 from (b) with λ = 1. The error |aₙ − 3/2| = (3/2)(1/3)ⁿ
    shrinks by 1/3 per step — better than the guaranteed k = 1/2, because
    the true operator norm (1/3 on this family) is smaller. Common mistakes:
    bounding ∫ ts ds by 1 instead of t/2; forgetting that c is a number, not
    a function. Now you try: solve x(t) = t² + (1/2)∫₀¹ ts·x(s) ds.
    (x = t² + ct/2 with c = 1/4 + c/6, c = 3/10: x(t) = t² + 3t/20.)

D7. State the Picard-Lindelöf theorem and prove it with the contraction
    mapping theorem. Compute the Picard iterates for y′ = 2ty, y(0) = 1, and
    identify the limit. Show that y′ = 3y^(2/3), y(0) = 0, has more than one
    solution, and say which hypothesis fails.
    Answer: Iterates 1 + t², 1 + t² + t⁴/2, 1 + t² + t⁴/2 + t⁶/6 → e^(t²).
    y = 0 and y = t³ both solve the second problem; f(y) = 3y^(2/3) is not
    Lipschitz at y = 0.
    Teacher explains: STATEMENT: let f be continuous on
    R = {|t − t₀| ≤ a, |y − y₀| ≤ b} with |f| ≤ M and
    |f(t, y) − f(t, z)| ≤ L|y − z|. Then the IVP has a unique solution on
    I = [t₀ − h, t₀ + h] for h = min(a, b/M) (we also take Lh < 1). PROOF:
    y solves the IVP ⇔ y(t) = y₀ + ∫_{t₀}^t f(s, y(s)) ds (integrate, FTC).
    Let X = {y ∈ C(I) : |y(t) − y₀| ≤ b}, a CLOSED subset of the complete
    space C(I), so complete. Define (Ty)(t) = y₀ + ∫_{t₀}^t f(s, y(s)) ds.
       T(X) ⊆ X:   |Ty(t) − y₀| ≤ M|t − t₀| ≤ Mh ≤ b
       contraction: |Ty(t) − Tz(t)| ≤ |∫ L|y − z| ds| ≤ Lh·‖y − z‖∞
    With Lh < 1 the theorem gives a unique fixed point = unique solution.
    (The restriction Lh < 1 can be removed with the weighted norm
    sup e^(−2L|t − t₀|)|y(t)|, or by showing Tⁿ is a contraction.) Example:
    (Ty)(t) = 1 + ∫₀ᵗ 2s·y(s) ds. From y₀ = 1:
       y₁ = 1 + ∫₀ᵗ 2s ds = 1 + t²
       y₂ = 1 + ∫₀ᵗ 2s(1 + s²) ds = 1 + t² + t⁴/2
       y₃ = 1 + t² + t⁴/2 + t⁶/6
    These are the partial sums of ∑ (t²)ᵏ/k! = e^(t²), which indeed solves
    y′ = 2ty, y(0) = 1. NON-UNIQUENESS: y = t³ gives y′ = 3t² and
    3(t³)^(2/3) = 3t² ✓, and y = 0 works too. The difference quotient
    |3y^(2/3) − 0|/|y − 0| = 3|y|^(−1/3) → ∞ as y → 0: no Lipschitz constant.
    (Peano's theorem, via Arzelà-Ascoli, still gives existence.) Common
    mistakes: forgetting the constant y₀ in each iterate; claiming global
    existence (y′ = y², y(0) = 1 gives 1/(1 − t), which blows up at t = 1).
    Now you try: Picard iterates for y′ = y, y(0) = 1. (1 + t,
    1 + t + t²/2, 1 + t + t²/2 + t³/6 → eᵗ.)

D8. Define equicontinuity. Decide whether each family on [0, 1] is uniformly
    bounded and equicontinuous: (a) fₙ(x) = xⁿ; (b) fₙ(x) = sin(nx);
    (c) fₙ(x) = sin(nx)/n; (d) F = {f ∈ C¹[0, 1] : |f(0)| ≤ 1, |f′| ≤ 3};
    (e) fₙ(x) = n. Show directly that (xⁿ) has no uniformly convergent
    subsequence.
    Answer: (a) bounded, not equicontinuous (at 1). (b) bounded, not
    equicontinuous. (c) both. (d) both (|f| ≤ 4, Lipschitz 3). (e)
    equicontinuous, not bounded.
    Teacher explains: F is EQUICONTINUOUS if for every ε > 0 there is ONE δ
    that works for EVERY f ∈ F: |x − y| < δ ⇒ |f(x) − f(y)| < ε. Each single
    continuous function on [0, 1] is uniformly continuous; the point is
    that δ must not depend on f. (a) Take ε = 1/2 and any δ. Put y = 1 and
    x = 1 − δ/2; then |fₙ(1) − fₙ(x)| = 1 − (1 − δ/2)ⁿ → 1 as n → ∞, so for
    large n it exceeds 1/2: NOT equicontinuous (the graphs get steeper near
    1). (b) Take x = 0, y = π/(2n): |sin(nx) − sin(ny)| = 1 while
    |x − y| = π/(2n) → 0: not equicontinuous. (c) |fₙ′| = |cos nx| ≤ 1, so
    |fₙ(x) − fₙ(y)| ≤ |x − y|: δ = ε works for all n. Bounded by 1. (d) By
    the MVT |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ 3|x − y| (δ = ε/3) and |f(x)| ≤ |f(0)| + 3x ≤ 4.
    (e) Constant functions: |fₙ(x) − fₙ(y)| = 0, perfectly equicontinuous,
    but ‖fₙ‖ = n is unbounded. For (xⁿ): a uniformly convergent subsequence
    would converge to the pointwise limit, which is 0 on [0, 1) and 1 at
    x = 1, a DISCONTINUOUS function; but a uniform limit of continuous
    functions is continuous. Contradiction. (Arzelà-Ascoli explains why:
    equicontinuity fails.) Common mistakes: thinking 'each fₙ is uniformly
    continuous' means equicontinuous; checking only at one point. Now you
    try: is fₙ(x) = cos(nx)/√n equicontinuous on [0, 1]? (Yes, although the
    Lipschitz constants √n are unbounded: |fₙ(x) − fₙ(y)| ≤ 2/√n < ε for
    n > 4/ε², and the finitely many remaining functions are each uniformly
    continuous: take the smallest of their δ's.)

D9. State and prove the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem for sequences in C[0, 1]: a
    uniformly bounded, equicontinuous sequence (fₙ) has a uniformly convergent
    subsequence.
    Answer: Proof by a diagonal argument on the rationals of [0, 1] plus an
    ε/3 argument; the converse also holds (relatively compact ⇒ bounded and
    equicontinuous).
    Teacher explains: STEP 1 (diagonal argument). List the rationals in
    [0, 1] as q₁, q₂, q₃, .... The numbers fₙ(q₁) are bounded, so by
    Bolzano-Weierstrass a subsequence f_{1,1}, f_{1,2}, ... converges at q₁.
    From it extract a further subsequence f_{2,1}, f_{2,2}, ... converging
    at q₂, and so on. The DIAGONAL sequence gₖ = f_{k,k} is (from the kth
    term on) a subsequence of every row, so gₖ(qⱼ) converges for EVERY j.
    STEP 2 (uniformly Cauchy). Let ε > 0. Equicontinuity gives δ with
    |x − y| < δ ⇒ |gₖ(x) − gₖ(y)| < ε/3 for all k. By compactness finitely
    many rationals q₁, ..., q_N (reordered) are δ-dense in [0, 1]. Choose K
    with |gₖ(qⱼ) − gₘ(qⱼ)| < ε/3 for k, m ≥ K and j = 1, ..., N (finitely
    many convergent sequences). For any x pick qⱼ with |x − qⱼ| < δ:
       |gₖ(x) − gₘ(x)| ≤ |gₖ(x) − gₖ(qⱼ)| + |gₖ(qⱼ) − gₘ(qⱼ)|
                        + |gₘ(qⱼ) − gₘ(x)| < ε/3 + ε/3 + ε/3 = ε
    STEP 3. So (gₖ) is Cauchy in the sup metric, and C[0, 1] is complete: gₖ
    converges uniformly to a continuous g. CONVERSE: if F has compact
    closure it is totally bounded; cover it by finitely many ε/3-balls about
    f₁, ..., fₘ, take a δ that works for these finitely many functions, and
    the ε/3 argument makes it work for all of F (and bounded is clear).
    The same proof works on any compact metric space K (it has a countable
    dense subset). Common mistakes: forgetting why the diagonal sequence
    converges at every qⱼ; using infinitely many qⱼ in Step 2 (compactness
    is what makes the list finite). Now you try: where exactly is uniform
    boundedness used? (Step 1: Bolzano-Weierstrass needs the numbers fₙ(qⱼ)
    to be bounded; pointwise boundedness is enough.)

D10. Use Arzelà-Ascoli to show: (a) F = {f ∈ C[0, 1] : f(0) = 0,
     |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ |x − y|} is compact; (b) the operator
     (Vf)(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt maps the closed unit ball B of C[0, 1] into a
     relatively compact set, although B itself is not compact; (c) the
     family {sin(cx) : c ∈ [0, 10]} is relatively compact but
     {sin(cx) : c ≥ 0} is not.
     Answer: (a) bounded by 1, equicontinuous (δ = ε), closed. (b) V(B) is
     bounded by 1 and 1-Lipschitz. (c) Lipschitz constant ≤ 10 for the
     first; the second contains sin(nx).
     Teacher explains: (a) BOUNDED: |f(x)| = |f(x) − f(0)| ≤ x ≤ 1.
     EQUICONTINUOUS: common Lipschitz constant 1, so δ = ε works. CLOSED: if
     fₙ ∈ F and fₙ → f uniformly, then f(0) = lim fₙ(0) = 0 and letting n → ∞
     in |fₙ(x) − fₙ(y)| ≤ |x − y| gives the same for f. Closed + bounded +
     equicontinuous ⇒ compact. Consequence: a function in F maximising a
     continuous functional (such as f ↦ ∫₀¹ f·g) EXISTS. (b) For ‖f‖∞ ≤ 1:
        |Vf(x)| ≤ ∫₀ˣ|f| ≤ 1,    |Vf(x) − Vf(y)| = |∫ᵧˣ f| ≤ |x − y|
     so V(B) ⊆ F from (a): relatively compact. An operator that maps bounded
     sets to relatively compact sets is called COMPACT; V is compact while
     the identity is not (B contains the disjoint tents with mutual distance
     1, 10.5 D9). (c) d/dx sin(cx) = c·cos(cx), |·| ≤ 10, and |sin| ≤ 1:
     bounded and equicontinuous. For c ≥ 0 unrestricted the subsequence
     sin(nx) is not equicontinuous (D8), so no subsequence of it converges
     uniformly. Common mistakes: forgetting to prove closedness when the
     question says 'compact' rather than 'relatively compact'; thinking the
     closed unit ball of C[0, 1] is compact because it is closed and
     bounded. Now you try: is {f ∈ C¹[0, 1] : f(0) = 0, ∫₀¹ f′² ≤ 1}
     relatively compact? (Yes: by Cauchy-Schwarz
     |f(x) − f(y)| = |∫ᵧˣ f′| ≤ √|x − y|·(∫f′²)^(1/2) ≤ √|x − y|, and
     |f| ≤ 1: a common Hölder bound.)

D11. (a) Define the Bernstein polynomials and compute B₁f, B₂(x²), B₃(x²) and
     B₂f for f(x) = |2x − 1|. (b) Show that Bₙ(x²) = x² + x(1 − x)/n, find the
     maximum error and the least n giving error < 10⁻³. (c) Sketch the proof
     that Bₙf → f uniformly for every f ∈ C[0, 1] (Weierstrass).
     Answer: (a) B₁f = f(0)(1 − x) + f(1)x; B₂(x²) = (x + x²)/2;
     B₃(x²) = (x + 2x²)/3; B₂|2x − 1| = 1 − 2x + 2x². (b) Max error 1/(4n)
     at x = 1/2; n = 251. (c) Below.
     Teacher explains: Bₙf(x) = ∑_{k=0}^n f(k/n)·C(n, k)xᵏ(1 − x)ⁿ⁻ᵏ: sample f
     at k/n and weight by the BINOMIAL probabilities pₖ(x) (the probability
     of k successes in n trials with success probability x). (a) n = 1:
     f(0)(1 − x) + f(1)x, the chord. For f = x², n = 2: samples 0, 1/4, 1:
        B₂(x²) = (1/4)·2x(1 − x) + x² = x/2 + x²/2
     n = 3: samples 0, 1/9, 4/9, 1:
        (1/9)·3x(1 − x)² + (4/9)·3x²(1 − x) + x³ = x/3 + 2x²/3
     For f = |2x − 1|: samples 1, 0, 1: (1 − x)² + x² = 1 − 2x + 2x².
     (b) Probabilistic view: if Sₙ ~ Bin(n, x) then Bₙf(x) = E[f(Sₙ/n)].
     E[Sₙ/n] = x and Var(Sₙ/n) = x(1 − x)/n, so
        Bₙ(x²) = E[(Sₙ/n)²] = x² + x(1 − x)/n
     (check n = 2: x² + (x − x²)/2 = x/2 + x²/2 ✓). The error x(1 − x)/n is
     largest at x = 1/2: 1/(4n). 1/(4n) < 10⁻³ ⇔ n > 250, so n = 251. (c)
     Given ε, uniform continuity gives δ with |s − x| < δ ⇒ |f(s) − f(x)| <
     ε/2. Split the sum: terms with |k/n − x| < δ contribute < ε/2; the rest
     have total weight P(|Sₙ/n − x| ≥ δ) ≤ x(1 − x)/(nδ²) ≤ 1/(4nδ²)
     (CHEBYSHEV), and there |f(k/n) − f(x)| ≤ 2‖f‖. So
        |Bₙf(x) − f(x)| ≤ ε/2 + 2‖f‖/(4nδ²) < ε    for n > ‖f‖/(εδ²)
     uniformly in x. On [a, b] rescale x = a + (b − a)u. Common mistakes:
     forgetting the binomial coefficient; expecting Bₙf = f for polynomials
     (only for degree ≤ 1). Now you try: compute B₂(x³) and B₂(sin πx).
     (x/4 + 3x²/4; 2x − 2x²)

D12. State the Stone-Weierstrass theorem (real and complex). Decide whether
     each algebra is dense: (a) polynomials in x² on [0, 1]; (b) the same on
     [−1, 1]; (c) polynomials p with p(0) = 0 on [0, 1]; (d) polynomials in eˣ
     on [0, 1]; (e) trigonometric polynomials in C(S¹); (f) complex
     polynomials in z on the unit circle. Finally prove: if f ∈ C[0, 1] and
     ∫₀¹ f(x)xⁿ dx = 0 for all n ≥ 0 then f = 0.
     Answer: (a) dense; (b) not (closure = even functions); (c) not (closure
     = {f : f(0) = 0}); (d) dense; (e) dense; (f) not (z̄ is not a uniform
     limit). Proof of the last part below.
     Teacher explains: THEOREM: K compact, A ⊆ C(K, R) a subalgebra that
     contains the constants and separates points ⇒ A is dense in the sup
     metric. Complex: add 'f ∈ A ⇒ f̄ ∈ A'. So for each example CHECK THREE
     THINGS: algebra? constants? separates points?
       (a) x² is injective on [0, 1], so x ≠ y ⇒ x² ≠ y²; constants in A:
           DENSE. (√x is a uniform limit of polynomials in x².)
       (b) every p(x²) is EVEN, so p(1) = p(−1): 1 and −1 are never
           separated. The uniform closure consists of even functions only;
           x is at sup distance ≥ 1 from every even g, because
           |1 − g(1)| + |−1 − g(1)| ≥ 2, so one of the errors at ±1 is ≥ 1.
       (c) contains no non-zero constants; everything vanishes at 0, and so
           does every uniform limit: f = 1 is at distance ≥ 1.
       (d) eˣ is injective: dense.
       (e) on S¹ (θ ↔ e^{iθ}) 1, cos θ, sin θ generate an algebra
           (product formulas), cos θ and sin θ together separate points:
           dense in the 2π-PERIODIC continuous functions (FEJÉR also proves
           this).
       (f) not closed under conjugation. Proof of failure: for every
           polynomial p, ∫₀^{2π} p(e^{iθ})e^{iθ} dθ = 0 (each term
           e^{i(k+1)θ} integrates to 0), but for z̄ = e^{−iθ} the integral
           is ∫ 1 dθ = 2π. If pₙ → z̄ uniformly the integrals would converge:
           0 → 2π, impossible.
     MOMENT RESULT: by linearity ∫ f·p = 0 for every polynomial p. Choose
     polynomials pₙ → f uniformly (Weierstrass). Then
        ∫₀¹ f² = lim ∫₀¹ f·pₙ = 0
     (|∫ f(f − pₙ)| ≤ ‖f‖·‖f − pₙ‖ → 0), and f² ≥ 0 continuous gives f ≡ 0.
     Common mistakes: forgetting to check the constants; in (b) thinking
     'x² separates 0 from 1, so it separates points'. Now you try: are the
     functions ∑ aₖcos(kx) (finite sums) dense in C[0, π]? (Yes: cos x is
     injective on [0, π] and cos products are sums of cosines. On [0, 2π]
     they are not dense.)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Is T a contraction on the given space? If so give the best constant k;
    if not, say why.
    a) T(x) = x/3 + 1 on R             b) T(x) = 2x on R
    c) T(x) = (sin x)/2 on R           d) T(x) = cos x on R
    e) T(x) = cos x on [0, 1]          f) T(x) = x² on [0, 1/3]
    g) T(x) = x² on [0, 1]             h) T(x) = 1/(1 + x) on [1/2, 1]
    i) T(x) = e^(−x) on [0.4, 0.7]     j) T(x) = √(x + 2) on [0, ∞)
    k) T(x) = x + 1/x on [1, ∞)        l) T(x) = arctan x on R
    m) T(x, y) = (x/2 + y/4, x/4 + y/3) on (R², d∞)
    n) T(x, y) = (x/2 + y/2, y/4) on (R², d∞)
