                                 at 0; deform to the unit circle)

M10. Stokes and divergence theorems in R³.
     a) ∮_{∂S} z dx + x dy + y dz, S = upper unit hemisphere, outward
     b) ∫_S d(−y dx + x dy) for any oriented surface S whose boundary is the
        unit circle in the xy-plane traversed counterclockwise
     c) ∫_{S²} x dy∧dz + y dz∧dx + z dx∧dy
     d) ∫_{∂C} x² dy∧dz, C = [0, 1]³
     e) ∫_{S²(R)} z dx∧dy
     f) ∫_{∂C} x dy∧dz + y dz∧dx + z dx∧dy, C = [0, 1]³
     g) ∮ y dx + z dy + x dz round the unit circle in x + y + z = 0,
        counterclockwise seen from (1, 1, 1)
     h) ∫_{S²} x³ dy∧dz + y³ dz∧dx + z³ dx∧dy
     i) ∫_{S²} dω for any smooth 1-form ω
     j) ∫_{∂B} (x dy∧dz + y dz∧dx + z dx∧dy)/r³ for a ball B containing 0;
        for a ball B not containing 0
     k) ∫_{∂K} z dx∧dy, K the solid cylinder x² + y² ≤ 1, 0 ≤ z ≤ 1
     l) ∫_{∂S} xy dz, S = [0, 1]² × {0} (a square in the xy-plane)
     Answers:
       a) π        b) 2π       c) 4π       d) 1        e) 4πR³/3
       f) 3        g) −√3π     h) 12π/5    i) 0
       j) 4π; 0    k) π (the volume)       l) 0 (dz = 0 on the boundary)

M11. Fill in (dimensions, degrees and signs).
     a) dimension of the 1-forms on R³ (at a point)
     b) dimension of the 2-forms on R³
     c) dimension of the 3-forms on R³
     d) dimension of the 2-forms on R⁴
     e) dimension of the 3-forms on R⁵
     f) total dimension of all forms on R⁴
     g) the k-forms on Rⁿ for k > n
     h) β ∧ α in terms of α ∧ β: α a 2-form, β a 3-form
     i) the same for two 1-forms
     j) the same for a 1-form and a 3-form
     k) the degree of dω for a k-form ω
     l) d(α ∧ β) for a 1-form α
     m) dx₃∧dx₁∧dx₂ in the increasing basis
     n) dx₂∧dx₁∧dx₄∧dx₃ in the increasing basis
     o) dx₄∧dx₃∧dx₂∧dx₁ in the increasing basis
     p) Is dx₁∧dx₂ + dx₃∧dx₄ a product α ∧ β of two 1-forms?
     Answers:
       a) 3        b) 3        c) 1        d) 6        e) 10
       f) 16       g) 0        h) +α ∧ β   i) −α ∧ β   j) −α ∧ β
       k) k + 1    l) dα ∧ β − α ∧ dβ      m) +dx₁∧dx₂∧dx₃
       n) +dx₁∧dx₂∧dx₃∧dx₄     o) +dx₁∧dx₂∧dx₃∧dx₄ (6 inversions)
       p) no: (α ∧ β) ∧ (α ∧ β) = 0 but ω ∧ ω ≠ 0

M12. The vector calculus dictionary in R³ (F = (P, Q, R)).
     a) df corresponds to ...          b) d of a 1-form corresponds to ...
     c) d of a 2-form corresponds to ...
     d) d(df) = 0 says ...             e) d(dω) = 0 for a 1-form ω says ...
     f) curl (yz, xz, xy)              g) curl (−y, x, 0)
     h) div (x², y², z²)               i) curl (x²y, yz, xz)
     j) the 2-form for F = (x, y, z)   k) the 1-form for grad(xyz)
     l) Stokes for a 0-form on a curve m) Stokes for a 1-form on a region
                                          in R²
     n) Stokes for a 1-form on a surface in R³
     o) Stokes for a 2-form on a solid in R³
     p) Stokes for a 0-form on [a, b]
     Answers:
       a) grad f                        b) curl F
       c) div F (times dx∧dy∧dz)        d) curl grad f = 0
       e) div curl F = 0                f) (0, 0, 0)
       g) (0, 0, 2)                     h) 2x + 2y + 2z
       i) (−y, −z, −x²)                 j) x dy∧dz + y dz∧dx + z dx∧dy
       k) yz dx + xz dy + xy dz
       l) ∫_C ∇f·dr = f(B) − f(A)
       m) Green: ∮(P dx + Q dy) = ∬(Q_x − P_y) dA
       n) Kelvin-Stokes: ∮ F·dr = ∬ curl F·dS
       o) Gauss: ∯ F·dS = ∭ div F dV
       p) FTC: ∫_a^b f′(x) dx = f(b) − f(a)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: drill the three rules dx∧dx = 0, dy∧dx = −dx∧dy and
  d(f dx_I) = df ∧ dx_I until they are automatic; have the student write
  every wedge in increasing (or cyclic) order immediately. For each integral
  insist on the routine 'parametrise, check orientation, pull back,
  integrate'. Keep the dictionary grad/curl/div on the board, and after
  each Stokes computation ask which classical theorem was just used. Draw
  the boundary orientation (outward normal first, surface on the left).
  Harder: prove d² = 0 and the Leibniz rule in general; prove that pullback
  commutes with d; prove the Poincaré lemma for 1-forms on a star-shaped set
  with the formula f(x) = ∫₀¹ ω(tx)(x) dt and for k-forms by the homotopy
  operator; show that the de Rham cohomology H¹(R² − {0}) is
  one-dimensional (spanned by the winding form); compute the flux of the
  electric field of a point charge (Gauss's law) with σ; and show that
  Maxwell's equations become dF = 0, d⋆F = J in the language of forms.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.9 — COMPLEX ANALYSIS: ANALYTIC FUNCTIONS, CAUCHY-RIEMANN EQUATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A COMPLEX FUNCTION f(z) = u(x, y) + i v(x, y) (z = x + iy) is a pair of
    real functions of two variables: u = Re f, v = Im f. Write every function
    in this form: z² = (x² − y²) + i(2xy), 1/z = (x − iy)/(x² + y²),
    eᶻ = eˣ cos y + i eˣ sin y.
  - LIMIT: lim (z→z₀) f(z) = L means ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0 : 0 < |z − z₀| < δ ⇒
    |f(z) − L| < ε. z may approach z₀ from EVERY direction; two paths giving
    different values prove the limit does NOT exist (z̄/z → 1 along the real
    axis, → −1 along the imaginary axis). f is CONTINUOUS at z₀ if
    lim f(z) = f(z₀) (⇔ u and v are continuous). Limits at ∞ use w = 1/z.
  - DERIVATIVE: f′(z₀) = lim (h→0) [f(z₀ + h) − f(z₀)]/h, h COMPLEX. The
    usual rules (sum, product, quotient, chain, (zⁿ)′ = nzⁿ⁻¹) hold, and
    differentiable ⇒ continuous. z̄, Re z, |z| are differentiable NOWHERE;
    |z|² is differentiable only at 0.
  - ANALYTIC (= HOLOMORPHIC) at z₀: differentiable at EVERY point of some
    disc around z₀. Analytic on an open set: differentiable at each point.
    ENTIRE: analytic on all of C (polynomials, eᶻ, sin z, cos z). A point
    where f stops being analytic is a SINGULAR POINT (z = 0 for 1/z).
    Differentiable at a point or on a line is NOT analytic there.
  - CAUCHY-RIEMANN (CR) EQUATIONS: if f = u + iv is differentiable at z₀
    then u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x there, and f′ = u_x + i v_x = v_y − i u_y.
    Complex form: ∂f/∂z̄ = ½(f_x + i f_y) = 0. CR alone are NOT sufficient
    (√|xy| satisfies them at 0 but is not differentiable).
  - SUFFICIENT CONDITION: if u_x, u_y, v_x, v_y EXIST, are CONTINUOUS near
    z₀ and satisfy CR at z₀, then f is differentiable at z₀. CR + continuous
    partials on an open set ⇔ analytic there. Method: compute the four
    partials, solve u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x; the solution set is where f
    is differentiable; f is analytic on its INTERIOR only.
  - POLAR CR (z = re^(iθ), r > 0): u_r = (1/r) v_θ, v_r = −(1/r) u_θ, and
    f′(z) = e^(−iθ)(u_r + i v_r). Use for Log z, zⁿ, √z.
  - HARMONIC functions: u_xx + u_yy = 0 (Laplace's equation, Δu = 0). Real
    and imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic. v is a
    HARMONIC CONJUGATE of u if u + iv is analytic (then −u is a conjugate of
    v). On a simply connected domain every harmonic u has a conjugate,
    unique up to adding a real constant; find it by integrating v_y = u_x,
    v_x = −u_y.
  - MILNE-THOMSON METHOD: f′(z) = u_x(z, 0) − i u_y(z, 0) (given u), or
    f′(z) = v_y(z, 0) + i v_x(z, 0) (given v); integrate in z. Given u − v,
    work with F = (1 + i)f, whose real part is u − v.
  - CONSEQUENCES of CR on a DOMAIN (open, connected): f′ ≡ 0 ⇒ f constant;
    Re f, Im f, |f| or arg f constant ⇒ f constant. Where f′ ≠ 0 the level
    curves u = c and v = d cut at RIGHT ANGLES (∇u · ∇v = 0).
  - EXPONENTIAL: eᶻ = eˣ(cos y + i sin y); |eᶻ| = eˣ, arg eᶻ = y; eᶻ ≠ 0;
    e^(z+w) = eᶻe^w; PERIOD 2πi; (eᶻ)′ = eᶻ. eᶻ = w has solutions
    z = ln|w| + i(Arg w + 2kπ) for every w ≠ 0.
  - TRIG/HYPERBOLIC: sin z = (e^(iz) − e^(−iz))/(2i), cos z = (e^(iz) +
    e^(−iz))/2, sinh z = −i sin(iz), cosh z = cos(iz). sin z = sin x cosh y +
    i cos x sinh y, cos z = cos x cosh y − i sin x sinh y,
    |sin z|² = sin²x + sinh²y, |cos z|² = cos²x + sinh²y. Zeros of sin, cos
    are only the real ones; sin and cos are UNBOUNDED on C.
  - LOGARITHM: log z = ln|z| + i arg z (infinitely many values, differing by
    2πi). PRINCIPAL value Log z = ln|z| + i Arg z, −π < Arg z ≤ π; Log is
    analytic on C − (−∞, 0] (the BRANCH CUT) with (Log z)′ = 1/z.
    e^(Log z) = z always, but Log(eᶻ) = z only if −π < Im z ≤ π, and
    Log(z₁z₂) = Log z₁ + Log z₂ can fail by 2πi.
  - POWERS: z^c = e^(c log z); principal value e^(c Log z). c integer: one
    value; c = p/q in lowest terms: q values; otherwise infinitely many.
    i^i = e^(−π/2 − 2kπ), all real. (z^c)′ = c z^(c − 1) on the cut plane.
  - POWER SERIES ∑ aₙ(z − a)ⁿ: radius R with 1/R = limsup |aₙ|^(1/n)
    (CAUCHY-HADAMARD), or R = lim |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| when it exists. Absolutely
    convergent for |z − a| < R, divergent for |z − a| > R, anything on the
    circle. The sum is ANALYTIC in the disc, differentiable term by term,
    and the derived series has the same R.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. (a) Prove from the definition that lim (z→2i) z² = −4. (b) Show that
    lim (z→0) z̄/z does not exist. (c) Is f(z) = z·Re z/|z| (f(0) = 0)
    continuous at 0? (d) Find lim (z→∞) (2z + i)/(z − 1).
    Answer: (a) δ = min(1, ε/5) works. (b) The limit is 1 along the real
    axis and −1 along the imaginary axis. (c) Yes. (d) 2.
    Teacher explains: The definition is the real one with |·| now the
    distance in the plane. (a) Factor the distance:
       |z² − (−4)| = |z² + 4| = |z − 2i|·|z + 2i|
    Keep z near 2i first: if |z − 2i| < 1 then
       |z + 2i| = |(z − 2i) + 4i| ≤ |z − 2i| + 4 < 5
    So |z² + 4| < 5|z − 2i|. Given ε > 0 take δ = min(1, ε/5): then
    0 < |z − 2i| < δ gives |z² + 4| < 5·ε/5 = ε ∎.
    (b) In the plane z can come from infinitely many directions. Put z = x
    (real, x ≠ 0): z̄/z = x/x = 1. Put z = iy: z̄/z = −iy/(iy) = −1. Two
    paths, two values: the limit does not exist. (In fact along the ray
    z = te^(iθ), z̄/z = e^(−2iθ), a different value for each direction.)
    (c) For z ≠ 0, |f(z)| = |z|·|Re z|/|z| = |Re z| ≤ |z| → 0 = f(0), so f
    is continuous at 0 by the squeeze principle. (d) Divide by z:
       (2z + i)/(z − 1) = (2 + i/z)/(1 − 1/z) → (2 + 0)/(1 − 0) = 2
    (formally: put w = 1/z and let w → 0). Common mistakes: testing only
    along the two axes and concluding that a limit EXISTS (the two axes can
    agree while the line y = x disagrees); forgetting that |z + 2i| must be
    bounded before δ is chosen. Now you try: show that lim (z→0) xy/(x² + y²)
    does not exist. (0 along the axes, 1/2 along y = x.)

D2. Using only the definition of the derivative, (a) find the derivative of
    f(z) = z²; (b) prove that f(z) = z̄ is differentiable nowhere; (c) show
    that g(z) = |z|² is differentiable at 0 only. (d) Prove that a function
    differentiable at z₀ is continuous at z₀.
    Answer: (a) f′(z) = 2z. (b), (c), (d) below; g′(0) = 0.
    Teacher explains: The difference quotient is [f(z + h) − f(z)]/h with h
    a COMPLEX number tending to 0 in any manner. (a)
       [(z + h)² − z²]/h = (2zh + h²)/h = 2z + h → 2z
    whatever the path of h. (b) For f = z̄:
       [conj(z + h) − z̄]/h = h̄/h
    h real: h̄/h = 1; h = ik imaginary: h̄/h = −ik/(ik) = −1. The quotient has
    no limit, at ANY z. So the harmless-looking z̄ = x − iy (smooth as a map
    of R²) has no complex derivative anywhere. (c) For g = z z̄:
       [|z + h|² − |z|²]/h = [(z + h)(z̄ + h̄) − z z̄]/h
                          = z̄ + h̄ + z·(h̄/h)
    At z = 0 this is h̄ → 0, so g′(0) = 0. At z ≠ 0 the terms z̄ + h̄ → z̄, but
    z·h̄/h takes the value z along real h and −z along imaginary h: no limit.
    (d) For h ≠ 0,
       f(z₀ + h) − f(z₀) = {[f(z₀ + h) − f(z₀)]/h}·h → f′(z₀)·0 = 0
    so f(z₀ + h) → f(z₀). The converse fails (z̄ is continuous everywhere).
    Common mistakes: letting h → 0 along the real axis only (that is just a
    partial derivative); thinking 'a polynomial in x and y is always
    differentiable'. Now you try: find where f(z) = z·Re z is differentiable.
    (Quotient at 0 is Re h → 0, so f′(0) = 0; elsewhere not differentiable;
    confirm with CR in M4 l).)

D3. Derive the Cauchy-Riemann equations and the formula for f′, and state
    the sufficient condition for differentiability. Use them to show that
    f(z) = x² − y² + 2ixy is entire and to find f′.
    Answer: u_x = v_y, u_y = −v_x; f′ = u_x + i v_x. f = z² is entire with
    f′ = 2x + 2iy = 2z.
    Teacher explains: Suppose f = u + iv is differentiable at z₀ = x₀ + iy₀.
    The limit of the quotient must be the same along every path, so compute
    it along two. Along h real (h → 0):
       [f(z₀ + h) − f(z₀)]/h = [u(x₀ + h, y₀) − u]/h + i[v(x₀ + h, y₀) − v]/h
                             → u_x + i v_x
    Along h = ik (k real → 0), dividing by ik = multiplying by −i/k:
       [u(x₀, y₀ + k) − u]/(ik) + i[v(x₀, y₀ + k) − v]/(ik) → −i u_y + v_y
    Both equal f′(z₀), so equate real and imaginary parts:
       u_x = v_y        and        v_x = −u_y
    and f′ = u_x + i v_x = v_y − i u_y. SUFFICIENCY THEOREM: if the four
    partial derivatives exist in a neighbourhood of z₀, are continuous at
    z₀, and CR hold at z₀, then f′(z₀) exists. (Idea: continuous partials
    make u and v differentiable as real maps, so
    u(z₀ + h) − u(z₀) = u_x a + u_y b + o(|h|), h = a + ib; with CR the
    increment of f is (u_x + i v_x)(a + ib) + o(|h|).) For the example:
       u = x² − y²,  v = 2xy
       u_x = 2x,  v_y = 2x   ✓        u_y = −2y,  −v_x = −2y   ✓
    CR hold at every point and all partials are polynomials (continuous), so
    f is differentiable everywhere, i.e. ENTIRE, and f′ = u_x + i v_x =
    2x + 2iy = 2z. (Of course f = z².) Complex form: with ∂/∂z̄ =
    ½(∂/∂x + i ∂/∂y), CR ⇔ ∂f/∂z̄ = 0: an analytic function 'does not depend
    on z̄'. For z̄ itself ∂z̄/∂z̄ = 1 ≠ 0. Common mistakes: writing
    u_y = v_x (sign!); computing f′ as u_x + u_y. Now you try: show that
    f = eˣ(cos y + i sin y) satisfies CR and f′ = f. (u_x = eˣ cos y = v_y,
    u_y = −eˣ sin y = −v_x; f′ = u_x + i v_x = f.)

D4. Show that f(z) = √|xy| satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations at z = 0
    but is not differentiable there. What does the example teach?
    Answer: All four partials are 0 at the origin, so CR hold; the
    difference quotient is 0 along the real axis and 1/(1 + i) along the
    ray y = x (x > 0), so f′(0) does not exist.
    Teacher explains: Here u = √|xy| and v = 0. The partials at the origin
    come from the definition (not from a formula, which would divide by 0):
       u_x(0, 0) = lim [u(h, 0) − u(0, 0)]/h = lim (0 − 0)/h = 0
       u_y(0, 0) = 0 similarly,   v_x = v_y = 0
    so u_x = v_y (0 = 0) and u_y = −v_x (0 = 0): CR HOLD. Now the complex
    quotient f(h)/h. Along h = t real: f(h) = 0, quotient 0. Along
    h = t(1 + i), t > 0: |xy| = t², f(h) = t, and
       f(h)/h = t/(t(1 + i)) = 1/(1 + i) = (1 − i)/2 ≠ 0
    Different limits, so f is not differentiable at 0. What went wrong with
    the sufficiency theorem? Its hypotheses fail: for x, y > 0,
    u_x = √y/(2√x), which is unbounded near the origin, so the partials are
    not continuous at 0. LESSON: CR are NECESSARY; for SUFFICIENCY you need
    continuity of the partials (or real differentiability of u and v). A
    second classic example is f(z) = z⁵/|z|⁴ (f(0) = 0): again CR hold at 0,
    yet f(h)/h = h⁴/|h|⁴ is 1 along the real axis and −1 along y = x
    (h⁴ = t⁴(1 + i)⁴ = −4t⁴, |h|⁴ = 4t⁴). Common mistakes: 'CR hold at z₀,
    therefore f is analytic at z₀' — two errors at once: not even
    differentiable, and analyticity needs a whole disc. Now you try: for
    f = z⁵/|z|⁴, check u_x(0, 0) = 1. (u(h, 0) = h⁵/h⁴ = h, so the quotient
    is 1.)

D5. Decide where each function is differentiable and where it is analytic:
    (a) f(z) = eˣ(cos y + i sin y); (b) g(z) = x² + iy²;
    (c) h(z) = z³ + 1/(z − i); (d) k(z) = 2xy + i(y² − x²).
    Answer: (a) entire, f′ = f (this is eᶻ). (b) differentiable exactly on
    the line y = x, analytic nowhere. (c) analytic on C − {i}. (d) entire,
    k = −iz², k′ = −2iz.
    Teacher explains: The routine: (1) write u, v; (2) compute the four
    partials; (3) solve CR; (4) check continuity of partials; (5) the
    solution set is where f′ exists; f is analytic on the largest OPEN set
    contained in it.
    (a) u = eˣ cos y, v = eˣ sin y:
       u_x = eˣ cos y = v_y    u_y = −eˣ sin y = −v_x
    for all (x, y); partials continuous ⇒ entire; f′ = u_x + i v_x = f.
    (b) u = x², v = y²:
       u_x = 2x, v_y = 2y  ⇒  x = y;     u_y = 0 = −v_x  ✓
    So g′ exists exactly on the line y = x (g′ = u_x + i v_x = 2x there). A
    line contains no disc, so g is analytic NOWHERE. (c) No need for CR:
    sums, products, quotients and compositions of analytic functions are
    analytic where defined. z³ is entire and 1/(z − i) is analytic except
    at z = i, the only singular point. h′ = 3z² − 1/(z − i)². (d) u = 2xy,
    v = y² − x²:
       u_x = 2y = v_y ✓     u_y = 2x,  −v_x = 2x ✓
    Entire, k′ = u_x + i v_x = 2y − 2ix = −2i(x + iy) = −2iz, and guessing
    from k′ gives k = −iz² (check: −i(x² − y² + 2ixy) = 2xy + i(y² − x²)).
    Common mistakes: calling g 'analytic on y = x'; forgetting to ask where
    the formula is even defined in (c). Now you try: where is
    f(z) = x² + y² + 2ixy differentiable? (u_x = 2x = v_y ✓; u_y = 2y,
    −v_x = −2y ⇒ y = 0: on the real axis only; analytic nowhere.)

D6. Derive the Cauchy-Riemann equations in polar form and the polar formula
    for f′. Use them to show that Log z = ln r + iθ (r > 0, −π < θ < π) is
    analytic with derivative 1/z, and that zⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ)
    satisfies them.
    Answer: u_r = (1/r)v_θ, v_r = −(1/r)u_θ; f′(z) = e^(−iθ)(u_r + i v_r).
    (Log z)′ = 1/z; (zⁿ)′ = nzⁿ⁻¹.
    Teacher explains: With x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ the chain rule gives
       u_r = u_x cos θ + u_y sin θ
       u_θ = −u_x r sin θ + u_y r cos θ
    and the same for v. Substitute CR (v_x = −u_y, v_y = u_x):
       v_θ = −v_x r sin θ + v_y r cos θ = r(u_y sin θ + u_x cos θ) = r u_r
       v_r = v_x cos θ + v_y sin θ = −u_y cos θ + u_x sin θ = −(1/r) u_θ
    So u_r = (1/r)v_θ and v_r = −(1/r)u_θ. For the derivative:
       u_r + i v_r = (u_x + i v_x)cos θ + (u_y + i v_y) sin θ
    and u_y + i v_y = −v_x + i u_x = i(u_x + i v_x) = i f′, so
       u_r + i v_r = f′(cos θ + i sin θ) = f′e^(iθ),  f′ = e^(−iθ)(u_r + i v_r)
    (Conversely polar CR with continuous partials, r > 0, give
    differentiability.) Log z: u = ln r, v = θ:
       u_r = 1/r = (1/r)·1 = (1/r)v_θ ✓      v_r = 0 = −(1/r)·0 ✓
    continuous for r > 0, −π < θ < π (the cut along the negative real axis
    is where θ jumps by 2π). f′ = e^(−iθ)(1/r) = 1/(re^(iθ)) = 1/z.
    zⁿ: u = rⁿ cos nθ, v = rⁿ sin nθ:
       u_r = nrⁿ⁻¹ cos nθ = (1/r)(nrⁿ cos nθ) = (1/r)v_θ ✓
       v_r = nrⁿ⁻¹ sin nθ = −(1/r)(−nrⁿ sin nθ) = −(1/r)u_θ ✓
    f′ = e^(−iθ)·nrⁿ⁻¹e^(inθ) = nrⁿ⁻¹e^(i(n−1)θ) = nzⁿ⁻¹. Common mistakes:
    forgetting the factors 1/r; writing f′ = u_r + i v_r without e^(−iθ).
    Now you try: check that √z = √r e^(iθ/2) satisfies polar CR and that
    (√z)′ = 1/(2√z). (u_r = cos(θ/2)/(2√r) = (1/r)v_θ; f′ = e^(−iθ)
    ·e^(iθ/2)/(2√r) = 1/(2√r e^(iθ/2)).)

D7. Prove that the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are
    harmonic. Show that u = x³ − 3xy² + y is harmonic, find a harmonic
    conjugate v, and express u + iv as a function of z.
    Answer: v = 3x²y − y³ − x + C; f(z) = z³ − iz + iC.
    Teacher explains: Let f = u + iv be analytic. (It will be shown in 10.10
    that f′ is again analytic, so u and v have continuous partial derivatives
    of every order.) Differentiate CR:
       u_x = v_y  ⇒  u_xx = v_yx          u_y = −v_x  ⇒  u_yy = −v_xy
    Mixed partials are equal (continuous), so u_xx + u_yy = v_yx − v_xy = 0.
    Similarly Δv = 0. Now the example:
       u_x = 3x² − 3y²,  u_xx = 6x;   u_y = −6xy + 1,  u_yy = −6x
    Δu = 6x − 6x = 0: harmonic. Find v from CR, one equation at a time:
       v_y = u_x = 3x² − 3y²  ⇒  v = 3x²y − y³ + g(x)
       v_x = −u_y             ⇒  6xy + g′(x) = 6xy − 1  ⇒  g′(x) = −1
    so g = −x + C and v = 3x²y − y³ − x + C. Recognise f: x³ − 3xy² and
    3x²y − y³ are Re z³ and Im z³; y and −x are Re and Im of −iz
    (−i(x + iy) = y − ix). Hence f = z³ − iz + iC. Remarks: (1) the
    conjugate of v is −u, not u (i f = −v + iu). (2) u, v both harmonic does
    NOT make u + iv analytic: u = x, v = −y gives z̄. (3) On a domain with a
    hole a conjugate may fail to exist globally: u = ln|z| on C − {0} would
    need v = arg z, which is not single-valued. Common mistakes: integrating
    v_y = u_x and forgetting the '+ g(x)'; getting g′ with the wrong sign
    from v_x = −u_y. Now you try: find a harmonic conjugate of
    u = eˣ(x cos y − y sin y). (v = eˣ(x sin y + y cos y); f = zeᶻ.)

D8. Explain the Milne-Thomson method and use it to find the analytic
    function f = u + iv when (a) u = eˣ(x cos y − y sin y), f(0) = 0;
    (b) v = 2xy + 3y, f(0) = 0; (c) u − v = eˣ(cos y − sin y), f(0) = 1.
    Answer: (a) f = zeᶻ. (b) f = z² + 3z. (c) f = eᶻ.
    Teacher explains: From D3, f′ = u_x − i u_y (use CR v_x = −u_y). The
    right side is a function of x and y; since f′ is analytic its values on
    the real axis (y = 0) determine it, and on y = 0 we have x = z. So
    REPLACE x BY z AND y BY 0:
       f′(z) = u_x(z, 0) − i u_y(z, 0)        (u given)
       f′(z) = v_y(z, 0) + i v_x(z, 0)        (v given)
    then integrate. No harmonic conjugate needs to be found.
    (a) u_x = eˣ(x cos y − y sin y + cos y), u_y = eˣ(−x sin y − sin y −
    y cos y). At (z, 0): u_x = eᶻ(z + 1), u_y = 0. So
       f′(z) = (z + 1)eᶻ  ⇒  f(z) = zeᶻ + C        (d/dz(zeᶻ) = eᶻ + zeᶻ)
    f(0) = 0 gives C = 0. (b) v_y = 2x + 3 → 2z + 3; v_x = 2y → 0:
    f′ = 2z + 3, f = z² + 3z + C, C = 0. (c) If f = u + iv then
       (1 + i)f = (u − v) + i(u + v)
    so F = (1 + i)f is analytic with Re F = U = u − v = eˣ cos y − eˣ sin y:
       U_x(z, 0) = eᶻ,  U_y(z, 0) = [−eˣ sin y − eˣ cos y] at y = 0 = −eᶻ
       F′ = eᶻ − i(−eᶻ) = (1 + i)eᶻ  ⇒  F = (1 + i)eᶻ + C
    f = F/(1 + i) = eᶻ + C′; f(0) = 1 ⇒ C′ = 0. Why a condition is needed:
    u determines f only up to an imaginary constant (v up to a real one).
    Common mistakes: substituting y = 0 into u itself before
    differentiating; forgetting the minus in u_x − i u_y. Now you try: find
    f with Re f = x² − y² − 2y and f(0) = 0. (f′ = 2z − i(−2) = 2z + 2i,
    f = z² + 2iz.)

D9. Let f = u + iv be analytic on a domain D (open and connected). Prove:
    (a) if f′ ≡ 0 then f is constant; (b) if |f| is constant then f is
    constant; (c) where f′ ≠ 0 the curves u = c and v = d are orthogonal.
    Illustrate (c) with f = z².
    Answer: Proofs below; for z² the hyperbolas x² − y² = c and xy = d/2
    cut at right angles (except at 0, where f′ = 0).
    Teacher explains: (a) f′ = u_x + i v_x = v_y − i u_y = 0 gives
    u_x = u_y = v_x = v_y = 0, so u and v are constant along every segment
    parallel to an axis in D. A domain is polygonally connected with such
    segments, so u and v are constant. (Connectedness matters: on two
    disjoint discs f could be 0 on one, 1 on the other.) (b) Let u² + v² = c.
    If c = 0 then f ≡ 0. Otherwise differentiate:
       u u_x + v v_x = 0,    u u_y + v v_y = 0
    Replace v_x = −u_y, v_y = u_x:
       u u_x − v u_y = 0
       v u_x + u u_y = 0
    A linear system for (u_x, u_y) with determinant u² + v² = c ≠ 0, so
    u_x = u_y = 0, hence also v_x = v_y = 0: f′ ≡ 0 and f is constant by (a).
    (The same idea shows Re f constant ⇒ f constant: u_x = u_y = 0 gives
    f′ = u_x − i u_y = 0.) (c) Normals to the level curves are ∇u = (u_x, u_y)
    and ∇v = (v_x, v_y) = (−u_y, u_x), and
       ∇u · ∇v = −u_x u_y + u_y u_x = 0,   |∇u| = |∇v| = |f′| ≠ 0
    so the curves cross at 90°. For z²: u = x² − y², v = 2xy. At (2, 1):
    ∇u = (4, −2), ∇v = (2, 4), dot product 8 − 8 = 0 ✓. At the origin both
    gradients vanish, and indeed the curves x² = y² and xy = 0 meet at 45°
    there. Common mistakes: in (b) dividing by u or v, which may vanish
    somewhere; forgetting that (a) needs connectedness. Now you try: prove
    that if f and f̄ are both analytic on a domain, f is constant. (Then
    f + f̄ = 2u is analytic and real-valued, so constant; similarly v.)

D10. Define eᶻ, sin z and cos z. Prove that eᶻ has period 2πi and is never
     0, that sin z = sin x cosh y + i cos x sinh y and |sin z|² = sin²x +
     sinh²y, and deduce that sin z = 0 only for z = kπ. Solve cos z = 2.
     Answer: cos z = 2 ⇔ z = 2kπ ± i ln(2 + √3) ≈ 2kπ ± 1.3170i, k ∈ Z.
     Teacher explains: eᶻ = eˣ(cos y + i sin y). Then |eᶻ| = eˣ > 0, so
     eᶻ ≠ 0, and e^(z + 2πi) = eˣ(cos(y + 2π) + i sin(y + 2π)) = eᶻ. Also
     eᶻ = 1 ⇔ eˣ = 1 and cos y = 1, sin y = 0 ⇔ z = 2kπi: these are ALL the
     periods. Define
        sin z = (e^(iz) − e^(−iz))/(2i),   cos z = (e^(iz) + e^(−iz))/2
     These are entire, agree with the real functions for real z, and keep
     the identities sin² + cos² = 1, addition formulas, (sin z)′ = cos z.
     Using cos(iy) = cosh y and sin(iy) = i sinh y (put z = iy in the
     definitions):
        sin(x + iy) = sin x cos(iy) + cos x sin(iy)
                    = sin x cosh y + i cos x sinh y
        |sin z|² = sin²x cosh²y + cos²x sinh²y
                 = sin²x (1 + sinh²y) + (1 − sin²x) sinh²y = sin²x + sinh²y
     So sin z = 0 ⇔ sin x = 0 and sinh y = 0 ⇔ x = kπ, y = 0: no new zeros.
     But |sin(iy)| = |sinh y| → ∞: sin is unbounded on C. To solve cos z = 2
     put w = e^(iz):
        (w + 1/w)/2 = 2  ⇒  w² − 4w + 1 = 0  ⇒  w = 2 ± √3
        iz = ln(2 ± √3) + 2kπi  ⇒  z = 2kπ − i ln(2 ± √3)
     Since (2 − √3)(2 + √3) = 1, ln(2 − √3) = −ln(2 + √3), so
     z = 2kπ ± i ln(2 + √3), and ln(2 + √3) ≈ 1.3170. Check with the formula
     cos z = cos x cosh y − i sin x sinh y at z = i·1.3170: cosh 1.3170 = 2 ✓.
     Common mistakes: 'cos z = 2 has no solution' (true only for real z);
     losing the ± or the 2kπ. Now you try: solve sin z = 2.
     (z = π/2 + 2kπ ± i ln(2 + √3).)

D11. Define the complex logarithm and its principal value. Find all values
     of log(−1 + i), the principal values Log(−1 + i), i^i and (1 + i)^(1−i),
     and show by an example that Log(z₁z₂) ≠ Log z₁ + Log z₂ in general.
     Where is Log analytic?
     Answer: log(−1 + i) = ½ ln 2 + i(3π/4 + 2kπ); Log(−1 + i) = ½ ln 2 +
     3πi/4 ≈ 0.3466 + 2.3562i; i^i = e^(−π/2 − 2kπ), principal
     e^(−π/2) ≈ 0.2079; (1 + i)^(1−i) = √2 e^(π/4) e^(i(π/4 − ½ ln 2))
     ≈ 2.8079 + 1.3179i. Log(−1·−1) = 0 but Log(−1) + Log(−1) = 2πi. Log is
     analytic on C − (−∞, 0].
     Teacher explains: We want w with e^w = z (z ≠ 0). Writing w = a + ib,
     e^a e^(ib) = |z| e^(i arg z) gives a = ln|z|, b = arg z + 2kπ:
        log z = ln|z| + i arg z    (infinitely many values)
        Log z = ln|z| + i Arg z,   −π < Arg z ≤ π    (principal value)
     For −1 + i: |z| = √2, the point is in the second quadrant with angle
     3π/4, so log(−1 + i) = ln √2 + i(3π/4 + 2kπ) = ½ ln 2 + i(3π/4 + 2kπ).
     POWERS: z^c = e^(c log z). For i^i: log i = i(π/2 + 2kπ), so
        i^i = e^(i·i(π/2 + 2kπ)) = e^(−π/2 − 2kπ)
     — infinitely many REAL values; the principal one (k = 0) is
     e^(−π/2) ≈ 0.2079. For (1 + i)^(1−i) use Log(1 + i) = ½ ln 2 + iπ/4:
        (1 − i)(½ ln 2 + iπ/4) = ½ ln 2 + π/4 + i(π/4 − ½ ln 2)
        (1 + i)^(1−i) = √2 e^(π/4)[cos(0.43883) + i sin(0.43883)]
                     ≈ 3.1018 × (0.90526 + 0.42486i) ≈ 2.8079 + 1.3179i
     The law of logs breaks: (−1)(−1) = 1, Log 1 = 0, but Log(−1) + Log(−1)
     = iπ + iπ = 2πi. The multivalued statement log(z₁z₂) = log z₁ + log z₂
     holds as an equality of SETS. Analyticity: Arg z jumps from π to −π
     across the negative real axis, so Log is not even continuous there; on
     the cut plane C − (−∞, 0] it is analytic with (Log z)′ = 1/z (D6).
     Common mistakes: using arctan(y/x) = arctan(−1) = −π/4 for −1 + i
     (wrong quadrant); thinking i^i is complex. Now you try: find all values
     of (−8)^(1/3). (2e^(i(π + 2kπ)/3): 1 + √3 i, −2, 1 − √3 i.)

D12. State the radius-of-convergence theorem for power series and what it
     says about analyticity. Find the radius of convergence of
     (a) ∑ zⁿ/n!, (b) ∑ n! zⁿ, (c) ∑ (n/(n + 1))^(n²) zⁿ, (d) ∑ z^(2n)/4ⁿ,
     and describe the behaviour on |z| = 1 of ∑ zⁿ, ∑ zⁿ/n², ∑ zⁿ/n.
     Answer: (a) ∞ (b) 0 (c) e (d) 2. On |z| = 1: ∑ zⁿ diverges at every
     point; ∑ zⁿ/n² converges at every point; ∑ zⁿ/n converges at every
     point except z = 1.
     Teacher explains: For ∑ aₙ(z − a)ⁿ there is R ∈ [0, ∞] with
        1/R = limsup |aₙ|^(1/n)     (CAUCHY-HADAMARD; 1/0 = ∞, 1/∞ = 0)
     such that the series converges ABSOLUTELY for |z − a| < R (uniformly on
     every smaller closed disc) and DIVERGES for |z − a| > R. If
     |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| → R, that limit is the radius (ratio test). THEOREM: the sum
     S(z) is analytic in |z − a| < R, and S′(z) = ∑ n aₙ(z − a)ⁿ⁻¹ with the
     same R (since n^(1/n) → 1). Hence S has derivatives of all orders and
     aₙ = S⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n!. (a) |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| = (n + 1)!/n! = n + 1 → ∞: converges for
     all z (this is eᶻ). (b) |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| = 1/(n + 1) → 0: converges only at
     z = 0. (c) Root test: |aₙ|^(1/n) = (n/(n + 1))ⁿ = 1/(1 + 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e,
     so R = e. (d) Coefficients are 0 for odd powers, so treat it as a
     series in w = z²: ∑ (w/4)ⁿ converges ⇔ |w| < 4 ⇔ |z| < 2; R = 2
     (Cauchy-Hadamard agrees: |a₂ₙ|^(1/(2n)) = 4^(−1/2) = 1/2). On the circle:
        ∑ zⁿ, |z| = 1: terms have modulus 1, do not → 0: diverges everywhere.
        ∑ zⁿ/n²: ∑ |zⁿ/n²| = ∑ 1/n² < ∞: converges everywhere.
        ∑ zⁿ/n: at z = 1 harmonic series (diverges); at z = −1 alternating
        (converges); for z = e^(iθ) ≠ 1 it converges by Dirichlet's test
        (partial sums of zⁿ are bounded by 2/|1 − z|, 1/n ↓ 0).
     So all three series have R = 1 and totally different boundary
     behaviour. Common mistakes: 'the series converges on the circle of
     convergence'; applying the ratio test to (d) directly (every other
     ratio is 0/0). Now you try: find R for ∑ (2n)!/(n!)² zⁿ.
     ((2n + 2)(2n + 1)/(n + 1)² → 4, so R = 1/4.)

M6. Find a harmonic conjugate v (normalised by v(0, 0) = 0 unless stated)
    and the analytic function f = u + iv in terms of z.
    a) u = x² − y²                  b) u = xy
    c) u = 2x(1 − y)                d) u = x³ − 3xy²
    e) u = eˣ cos y                 f) u = e^(−y) cos x
    g) u = sinh x sin y             h) u = ln(x² + y²), x > 0, v(1, 0) = 0
    i) u = x/(x² + y²), z ≠ 0, v → 0 as |z| → ∞
    j) u = x² − y² + x              k) u = 3x²y − y³
    l) u = eˣ(x cos y − y sin y)    m) u = sin x cosh y
    n) u = cos x cosh y             o) u = x + y
    p) u = x⁴ − 6x²y² + y⁴          q) u = e^(x²−y²) cos 2xy
    r) u = y/(x² + y²), z ≠ 0, v → 0 as |z| → ∞
    Answers:
      a) v = 2xy; f = z²
      b) v = (y² − x²)/2; f = −iz²/2
      c) v = x² − y² + 2y; f = iz² + 2z
      d) v = 3x²y − y³; f = z³
      e) v = eˣ sin y; f = eᶻ
      f) v = e^(−y) sin x; f = e^(iz)
      g) v = 1 − cosh x cos y; f = i(1 − cosh z)
      h) v = 2 arctan(y/x); f = 2 Log z
      i) v = −y/(x² + y²); f = 1/z
      j) v = 2xy + y; f = z² + z
      k) v = 3xy² − x³; f = −iz³
      l) v = eˣ(x sin y + y cos y); f = zeᶻ
      m) v = cos x sinh y; f = sin z
      n) v = −sin x sinh y; f = cos z
      o) v = y − x; f = (1 − i)z
      p) v = 4x³y − 4xy³; f = z⁴
      q) v = e^(x²−y²) sin 2xy; f = e^(z²)
      r) v = x/(x² + y²); f = i/z

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: drill the passage z ↔ (x, y) until writing u and v is
  automatic, and make the student test every 'does the limit exist?'
  question along the real axis, the imaginary axis AND the line y = x.
  Insist on the five-step CR routine (u, v; four partials; solve; check
  continuity; interior = analytic) and on the sentence 'differentiable on
  a line is not analytic'. For conjugates, always integrate one equation,
  keep '+ g(x)', then use the other; for Milne-Thomson, differentiate
  first, then put y = 0. Draw the branch cut of Log and mark Arg = π on its
  upper edge. Harder: prove the sufficiency theorem with the mean value
  theorem; show that an analytic f with f(D) contained in a line is
  constant; prove that Re f and Im f cannot both be non-constant functions
  of x alone; find all entire f with |f(z)| = e^(Re z) (f = ce^z, |c| = 1,
  after 10.10); show that ∂/∂z = ½(∂x − i∂y) makes f′ = ∂f/∂z and
  Δ = 4∂²/∂z∂z̄; and prove Cauchy-Hadamard from the root test.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.10 — CAUCHY'S THEOREM AND INTEGRAL FORMULA; TAYLOR AND LAURENT
SERIES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - CONTOUR INTEGRAL: for a piecewise smooth path z(t), a ≤ t ≤ b,
    ∫_C f(z) dz = ∫ₐᵇ f(z(t)) z′(t) dt. Standard paths: segment
    z = z₀ + t(z₁ − z₀), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1; circle z = a + re^(it), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π
    (anticlockwise = POSITIVE orientation). Reversing the path changes the
    sign. In general the value DEPENDS ON THE PATH (∫ z̄ dz does).
  - KEY INTEGRAL: ∮_{|z−a|=r} (z − a)ⁿ dz = 2πi if n = −1, and 0 for every
    other integer n.
  - ML-INEQUALITY: |∫_C f dz| ≤ M·L, where |f| ≤ M on C and L = length of C.
    Used to bound integrals and to show arc integrals → 0.
  - FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM: if F′ = f on a domain containing C then
    ∫_C f dz = F(end) − F(start); the integral is PATH-INDEPENDENT and every
    closed integral is 0. 1/z has no antiderivative on C − {0}, which is why
    ∮ dz/z = 2πi ≠ 0.
  - CAUCHY'S THEOREM (CAUCHY-GOURSAT): if f is analytic on and inside a
    simple closed contour C (more generally, on a SIMPLY CONNECTED domain
    containing C) then ∮_C f dz = 0. Proof via Green's theorem when f′ is
    continuous: ∮ f dz = ∬(−v_x − u_y) dA + i∬(u_x − v_y) dA = 0 by CR.
  - DEFORMATION PRINCIPLE: a contour may be moved without changing the
    integral as long as it does not cross a singularity. If C encloses
    C₁, ..., Cₖ (all positive) and f is analytic between them,
    ∮_C f = ∮_{C₁} f + ... + ∮_{Cₖ} f.
  - CAUCHY'S INTEGRAL FORMULA: f analytic on and inside C, a inside C:
    f(a) = (1/2πi) ∮_C f(z)/(z − a) dz. GENERALISED:
    f⁽ⁿ⁾(a) = (n!/2πi) ∮_C f(z)/(z − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dz. So ∮ f/(z − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dz =
    2πi f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n!. An analytic function has derivatives of ALL orders.
    Several points inside: partial fractions or small circles round each.
  - CONSEQUENCES: CAUCHY'S ESTIMATE |f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)| ≤ n!M/rⁿ (|f| ≤ M on
    |z − a| = r); LIOUVILLE: a bounded entire function is constant;
    FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ALGEBRA: every non-constant polynomial has a
    root in C; MORERA: continuous f with ∮ f = 0 round every triangle is
    analytic; MEAN VALUE: f(a) = (1/2π)∫₀^(2π) f(a + re^(it)) dt; MAXIMUM
    MODULUS: a non-constant analytic f on a bounded domain attains max |f|
    on the BOUNDARY only.
  - TAYLOR'S THEOREM: f analytic in |z − a| < R ⇒ f(z) = ∑ aₙ(z − a)ⁿ there,
    aₙ = f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! = (1/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dz. The radius of convergence
    is the DISTANCE FROM a TO THE NEAREST SINGULARITY. Series are unique:
    obtain them from known series (geometric, eᶻ, sin, cos, Log(1 + z)) by
    substitution, multiplication, division, differentiation, integration.
  - ZEROS: f(a) = 0 has ORDER m if f(a) = ... = f⁽ᵐ⁻¹⁾(a) = 0 ≠ f⁽ᵐ⁾(a), i.e.
    f = (z − a)ᵐg with g(a) ≠ 0. Zeros of a non-zero analytic function are
    ISOLATED; IDENTITY THEOREM: if f = g on a set with a limit point in the
    domain, f ≡ g.
  - LAURENT'S THEOREM: f analytic in the ANNULUS r < |z − a| < R ⇒
    f(z) = ∑_{n=−∞}^{∞} cₙ(z − a)ⁿ, cₙ = (1/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dz. The
    negative-power part is the PRINCIPAL PART. The expansion depends on the
    annulus: 1/((z − 1)(z − 2)) has different series in |z| < 1,
    1 < |z| < 2 and |z| > 2. Method: partial fractions + geometric series
    in the small quantity (z/b if |z| < |b|, b/z if |z| > |b|).
  - ISOLATED SINGULARITIES (from the Laurent series in 0 < |z − a| < R):
    REMOVABLE (no negative powers; f bounded near a; e.g. sin z/z);
    POLE OF ORDER m (finitely many, lowest (z − a)^(−m); |f| → ∞; e.g.
    1/zᵐ); ESSENTIAL (infinitely many negative powers; e.g. e^(1/z);
    CASORATI-WEIERSTRASS: f comes arbitrarily close to every value). A
    zero of order m of g is a pole of order m of 1/g. c₋₁ is the RESIDUE.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Evaluate ∫_C z̄ dz and ∫_C z² dz from 0 to 1 + i along (i) the segment
    C₁ and (ii) the path C₂ from 0 to 1 then to 1 + i. Explain the
    difference.
    Answer: ∫ z̄ dz: 1 along C₁, 1 + i along C₂. ∫ z² dz = (−2 + 2i)/3 along
    both.
    Teacher explains: The recipe: parametrise, replace z and dz, integrate
    in t.
       C₁: z = t(1 + i), dz = (1 + i) dt, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1; z̄ = t(1 − i)
       ∫ z̄ dz = ∫₀¹ t(1 − i)(1 + i) dt = ∫₀¹ 2t dt = 1
    C₂ in two pieces: 0 → 1: z = t, dz = dt: ∫₀¹ t dt = 1/2. 1 → 1 + i:
    z = 1 + it, dz = i dt, z̄ = 1 − it:
       ∫₀¹ (1 − it) i dt = ∫₀¹ (i + t) dt = i + 1/2
    Total 1/2 + i + 1/2 = 1 + i. The two answers differ: the integral of z̄
    depends on the path. For z²:
       C₁: ∫₀¹ t²(1 + i)²(1 + i) dt = (1 + i)³/3 = (−2 + 2i)/3
       C₂: ∫₀¹ t² dt + ∫₀¹ (1 + it)² i dt = 1/3 + [(1 + it)³/3]₀¹
           = 1/3 + ((1 + i)³ − 1)/3 = (1 + i)³/3
    The same, because z² has the antiderivative z³/3: the value is
    F(1 + i) − F(0) whatever the path. z̄ is not analytic and has no
    antiderivative. Note also that the difference ∫_{C₂} − ∫_{C₁} = i is
    the integral round the closed triangle, which equals
    ∮ z̄ dz = 2i × (area) = 2i × 1/2 = i ✓ (Green: ∮ z̄ dz = 2i·Area).
    Common mistakes: forgetting the factor z′(t); integrating from 0 to 1
    along the second leg with z = 1 + t. Now you try: ∫ Re z dz along C₁
    and C₂. ((1 + i)/2 and 1/2 + i.)

D2. Prove that for an integer n and r > 0,
    ∮_{|z−a|=r} (z − a)ⁿ dz = 2πi (n = −1), 0 (n ≠ −1). Use it to evaluate
    ∮_{|z|=1} (z + 1/z)³ dz and ∮_{|z|=1} z̄ dz.
    Answer: 6πi and 2πi.
    Teacher explains: Parametrise z = a + re^(it), dz = ire^(it) dt,
    0 ≤ t ≤ 2π:
       ∮ (z − a)ⁿ dz = ∫₀^(2π) rⁿe^(int)·ire^(it) dt = irⁿ⁺¹ ∫₀^(2π) e^(i(n+1)t) dt
    If n = −1 the integrand is 1 and the value is i·2π = 2πi. If n ≠ −1,
    ∫₀^(2π) e^(ikt) dt = [e^(ikt)/(ik)]₀^(2π) = 0 (k = n + 1 ≠ 0). Another
    view: for n ≠ −1, (z − a)ⁿ has the antiderivative (z − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) on
    C − {a}, so its closed integrals vanish; (z − a)⁻¹ has only the
    multivalued 'antiderivative' log(z − a), which gains 2πi on one turn.
    Note the result does not depend on r. Examples: expand
       (z + 1/z)³ = z³ + 3z + 3/z + 1/z³
    Only 3/z survives: 3·2πi = 6πi. On |z| = 1 we have z z̄ = 1, so z̄ = 1/z
    ON THE CIRCLE and ∮ z̄ dz = ∮ dz/z = 2πi (this is allowed because only
    values on C matter; z̄ is still not analytic). Common mistakes: using
    the formula with a outside the circle (then every n gives 0, including
    n = −1: ∮_{|z|=1} dz/(z − 2) = 0); forgetting that clockwise
    orientation gives −2πi. Now you try: ∮_{|z|=1} (z² + 3/z − 4/z²) dz.
    (6πi)

D3. State and prove the ML-inequality. Use it to (a) bound
    |∮_{|z|=2} dz/(z² + 1)|, (b) show that ∫_{C_R} dz/(z² + 1) → 0 as
    R → ∞, where C_R is the upper semicircle |z| = R, and (c) bound
    |∫_C dz/z⁴| on the segment from i to 1.
    Answer: (a) ≤ 4π/3 (the true value is 0). (b) |∫| ≤ πR/(R² − 1) → 0.
    (c) ≤ 4√2.
    Teacher explains: For complex numbers |∫ₐᵇ g(t) dt| ≤ ∫ₐᵇ |g(t)| dt
    (write ∫ g = |∫ g|e^(iφ) and take the real part of e^(−iφ)∫ g). So
       |∫_C f dz| = |∫ f(z(t)) z′(t) dt| ≤ ∫ |f(z(t))||z′(t)| dt ≤ M ∫ |z′| dt
                                                               = M·L
    The work is always in finding M: an UPPER bound for |f|, i.e. a LOWER
    bound for the denominator, via |a + b| ≥ |a| − |b|.
    (a) On |z| = 2: |z² + 1| ≥ |z|² − 1 = 3, so |f| ≤ 1/3, L = 4π:
    |∫| ≤ 4π/3. (b) On |z| = R > 1: |z² + 1| ≥ R² − 1, L = πR:
       |∫_{C_R}| ≤ πR/(R² − 1) → 0     (degree of denominator exceeds that
                                         of numerator by 2)
    This is the step that makes the residue method for ∫ dx/(x² + 1) work
    (10.11). (c) The segment z = i + t(1 − i) has length √2. Its closest
    point to 0 is the midpoint (1 + i)/2, with |z| = 1/√2, so
    |1/z⁴| ≤ (√2)⁴ = 4 and |∫| ≤ 4√2. (Exact value: [−1/(3z³)] from i to 1
    = −1/3 + 1/(3i³) = −1/3 + i/3, modulus √2/3 — well inside the bound.)
    Common mistakes: using |z² + 1| ≤ |z|² + 1 (the wrong direction gives
    no bound); forgetting that L for a semicircle is πR. Now you try: show
    |∮_{|z|=3} eᶻ/(z² + 1) dz| ≤ 3πe³/4. (|eᶻ| = eˣ ≤ e³, |z² + 1| ≥ 8,
    L = 6π.)

D4. State Cauchy's theorem, prove it (assuming f′ continuous) using Green's
    theorem, and deduce the deformation principle. Hence evaluate
    ∮_S dz/(z − 1), S the square with vertices ±2 ± 2i, and
    ∮_{|z|=2} dz/(z² − 1).
    Answer: 2πi and 0.
    Teacher explains: THEOREM (Cauchy-Goursat): if f is analytic at all
    points on and inside a simple closed contour C, then ∮_C f dz = 0.
    PROOF (with f′ continuous): write f = u + iv and dz = dx + i dy:
       ∮ f dz = ∮ (u dx − v dy) + i ∮ (v dx + u dy)
    Green's theorem ∮ P dx + Q dy = ∬ (Q_x − P_y) dA gives
       ∮ f dz = ∬ (−v_x − u_y) dA + i ∬ (u_x − v_y) dA = 0 + i·0
    by the CR equations. (Goursat proved it without continuity of f′, by
    subdividing triangles; that is why analytic ⇒ f′ continuous can be
    PROVED afterwards.) DEFORMATION: let C enclose a small circle C₁ and f
    be analytic in the region between. Cut the ring by a segment; the
    closed path 'C, along the cut, C₁ backwards, back along the cut'
    encloses no singularity, so its integral is 0; the cut contributions
    cancel, leaving ∮_C f − ∮_{C₁} f = 0. For the square: 1/(z − 1) is
    analytic except at 1, which is inside S, so
       ∮_S dz/(z − 1) = ∮_{|z−1|=1} dz/(z − 1) = 2πi         (D2)
    — no need to parametrise four sides. For the circle use partial
    fractions: 1/(z² − 1) = ½[1/(z − 1) − 1/(z + 1)]. Both 1 and −1 are
    inside |z| = 2, each piece gives 2πi:
       ∮ = ½(2πi − 2πi) = 0
    It is 0 although the integrand is NOT analytic inside: Cauchy's
    theorem is sufficient, not necessary. Common mistakes: applying Cauchy
    when a singularity is inside ('the answer is 0 because it is a closed
    curve'); forgetting orientation. Now you try: ∮_{|z|=2} z dz/(z² − 1).
    (½[1/(z − 1) + 1/(z + 1)] gives 2πi.)

D5. State and prove Cauchy's integral formula. Evaluate
    (a) ∮_{|z|=2} eᶻ/(z − 1) dz, (b) ∮_{|z|=4} cos z/(z − π) dz,
    (c) ∮_{|z−i|=1} dz/(z² + 1), (d) ∮_{|z|=1} e^(2z)/(2z − 1) dz.
    Answer: (a) 2πie (b) −2πi (c) π (d) πie.
    Teacher explains: THEOREM: if f is analytic on and inside a simple
    closed positive contour C and a is inside C, then
       f(a) = (1/2πi) ∮_C f(z)/(z − a) dz.
    PROOF: by deformation replace C by the small circle C_ρ: |z − a| = ρ.
    Split:
       ∮ f(z)/(z − a) dz = f(a)∮ dz/(z − a) + ∮ [f(z) − f(a)]/(z − a) dz
                         = 2πi f(a) + I_ρ
    f is continuous at a: given ε, for small ρ, |f(z) − f(a)| < ε on C_ρ,
    so by ML |I_ρ| ≤ (ε/ρ)(2πρ) = 2πε. But the left side does not depend
    on ρ, so I_ρ = 0 exactly ∎. Remarkable: the values of f on C determine
    f everywhere inside. HOW TO USE: write the integrand as
    f(z)/(z − a) with f analytic inside C; the answer is 2πi f(a).
       (a) f = eᶻ, a = 1 inside |z| = 2:   2πi e
       (b) f = cos z, a = π inside |z| = 4:  2πi cos π = −2πi
       (c) 1/(z² + 1) = [1/(z + i)]/(z − i); −i is OUTSIDE |z − i| = 1
           (distance 2), so f = 1/(z + i) is analytic inside:
           2πi·1/(2i) = π
       (d) first make the coefficient of z equal to 1:
           e^(2z)/(2z − 1) = ½·e^(2z)/(z − ½), so ∮ = ½·2πi·e¹ = πie
    Common mistakes: in (d) forgetting the ½; in (c) keeping z + i in the
    'singular' part although only z − i vanishes inside. Now you try:
    ∮_{|z|=2} z eᶻ/(z + 1) dz. (2πi(−1)e⁻¹ = −2πi/e)

D6. Derive the generalised Cauchy integral formula and explain why an
    analytic function has derivatives of every order. Evaluate
    (a) ∮_{|z|=1} e^(2z)/z⁴ dz, (b) ∮_{|z|=2} sin z/(z − π/2)³ dz,
    (c) ∮_{|z|=2} z³/(z − 1)² dz, (d) ∮_{|z|=1} (z⁴ + 3z² + 1)/z³ dz.
    Answer: (a) 8πi/3 (b) −πi (c) 6πi (d) 6πi.
    Teacher explains: Differentiate f(a) = (1/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − a) dz with
    respect to a under the integral sign (justified because the integrand
    and its a-derivatives are continuous and z stays away from a):
       f′(a)  = (1/2πi) ∮ f(z)/(z − a)² dz
       f″(a)  = (2/2πi) ∮ f(z)/(z − a)³ dz
       f⁽ⁿ⁾(a) = (n!/2πi) ∮ f(z)/(z − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dz
    The right-hand sides exist for every n, so f′ is again differentiable,
    and so on: ANALYTIC ⇒ INFINITELY DIFFERENTIABLE (no real analogue:
    x|x| is differentiable once only). In particular u and v are C^∞ and
    the proof in 10.9 D7 that they are harmonic is complete. USE:
       ∮ f(z)/(z − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dz = 2πi f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n!
    (a) f = e^(2z), n = 3: f‴ = 8e^(2z), f‴(0) = 8: 2πi·8/3! = 8πi/3.
    (b) f = sin z, n = 2, a = π/2 (inside, as π/2 ≈ 1.57 < 2):
    f″(π/2) = −sin(π/2) = −1: 2πi(−1)/2! = −πi. (c) f = z³, n = 1:
    f′(1) = 3: 2πi·3 = 6πi. (d) Just divide: z + 3/z + 1/z³, and only 3/z
    contributes: 6πi. (Generalised CIF gives the same: f″(0)/2! = 3.)
    Common mistakes: using n instead of n + 1 in the power (for (z − a)⁴
    you need f‴, not f⁗); forgetting n!. Now you try: ∮_{|z|=1} cos z/z³ dz.
    (f″(0) = −1: 2πi(−1)/2 = −πi)

D7. Evaluate ∮_{|z|=3} eᶻ/(z(z − 2)) dz in two ways: (a) by partial
    fractions, (b) by splitting the contour into two circles. Then evaluate
    ∮_{|z|=1} eᶻ/(z(z − 2)) dz.
    Answer: πi(e² − 1) ≈ 20.07i; over |z| = 1: −πi.
    Teacher explains: Both singular points 0 and 2 are inside |z| = 3, so
    Cauchy's formula does not apply directly. (a) Partial fractions:
       1/(z(z − 2)) = ½[1/(z − 2) − 1/z]
       ∮ eᶻ/(z(z − 2)) dz = ½[2πi e² − 2πi e⁰] = πi(e² − 1)
    (b) By deformation, ∮_{|z|=3} = ∮_{C₀} + ∮_{C₂}, small circles round 0
    and 2. On C₀ write the integrand as [eᶻ/(z − 2)]/z, where eᶻ/(z − 2) is
    analytic inside C₀:
       ∮_{C₀} = 2πi·e⁰/(0 − 2) = −πi
    On C₂ write it as [eᶻ/z]/(z − 2):
       ∮_{C₂} = 2πi·e²/2 = πie²
    Sum πi(e² − 1) ✓ ≈ 3.1416 × 6.389 i ≈ 20.07i. Method (b) generalises:
    each singular point contributes 2πi × (a 'residue'), which is the
    residue theorem of 10.11. For |z| = 1 only 0 is inside: the answer is
    the C₀ part, −πi. Common mistakes: taking f = eᶻ/z and a = 2 on the big
    circle (f is not analytic inside because of z = 0); forgetting a point.
    Now you try: ∮_{|z|=3} z/((z − 1)(z − 2)) dz. (2πi[1/(1 − 2) + 2/(2 − 1)]
    = 2πi)

D8. Prove Cauchy's estimate |f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)| ≤ n!M/rⁿ, Liouville's theorem and the
    fundamental theorem of algebra. What can you say about an entire f with
    |f(z)| ≤ 3|z|² for all z?
    Answer: Proofs below; f(z) = cz² with |c| ≤ 3.
    Teacher explains: CAUCHY'S ESTIMATE: let f be analytic on and inside
    |z − a| = r with |f| ≤ M there. By the generalised CIF and ML:
       |f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)| = (n!/2π)|∮ f(z)/(z − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dz| ≤ (n!/2π)·(M/rⁿ⁺¹)·2πr
                = n!M/rⁿ
    LIOUVILLE: if f is entire and |f| ≤ M on all of C, take n = 1 and any
    r: |f′(a)| ≤ M/r → 0 as r → ∞. So f′ ≡ 0 and f is constant. (sin z is
    entire and non-constant, so it must be unbounded — as 10.9 found.)
    FTA: let p be a polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 with no root. Then 1/p is
    entire. Since |p(z)| ≥ |aₙ||z|ⁿ/2 for large |z|, 1/p → 0 at ∞, so 1/p is
    bounded (continuous on a big disc, small outside). Liouville: 1/p
    constant, so p constant: contradiction. Repeating (divide by z − z₁),
    p has exactly n roots counted with multiplicity. For |f| ≤ 3|z|²:
    Cauchy's estimate on |z| = r with M = 3r² gives
       |f⁽ⁿ⁾(0)| ≤ n!·3r²/rⁿ → 0 (r → ∞) for n ≥ 3
    So the Taylor series of f stops at z²: f = a + bz + cz². |f(0)| ≤ 0
    gives a = 0; then f(z)/z → b at 0 but |f(z)/z| ≤ 3|z| → 0, so b = 0;
    finally |c| = lim |f(z)/z²| ≤ 3. Common mistakes: applying Liouville to
    functions bounded only on R (sin x is bounded on R but not on C);
    forgetting that the estimate needs f analytic on the WHOLE closed disc.
    Now you try: f is analytic in |z| < 3 and |f| ≤ 10 on |z| = 2. Bound
    |f″(0)|. (2!·10/2² = 5)

D9. State Morera's theorem, the mean value property and the maximum
    modulus principle. (a) Evaluate (1/2π)∫₀^(2π) e^(e^(it)) dt. (b) Find
    the maximum of |z² − z| on |z| ≤ 1 and where it occurs. (c) Find the
    maximum of |eᶻ| on |z| ≤ 1.
    Answer: (a) 1. (b) 2, at z = −1. (c) e, at z = 1.
    Teacher explains: MORERA (converse of Cauchy): if f is continuous on a
    domain D and ∮_T f dz = 0 for every triangle T in D, then f is analytic
    in D. (Proof: F(z) = ∫_{z₀}^z f is well defined on discs and F′ = f; F
    is analytic, hence so is its derivative f by D6.) It is the tool for
    showing that limits of uniformly convergent sequences of analytic
    functions are analytic. MEAN VALUE: put z = a + re^(it) in CIF,
    dz = ire^(it) dt:
       f(a) = (1/2πi)∫₀^(2π) f(a + re^(it)) ire^(it)/(re^(it)) dt
            = (1/2π)∫₀^(2π) f(a + re^(it)) dt
    the value at the centre is the average over the circle. (a) With
    f = eᶻ, a = 0, r = 1: the average is e⁰ = 1. (Taking real parts:
    ∫₀^(2π) e^(cos t) cos(sin t) dt = 2π — a real integral done for free.)
    MAXIMUM MODULUS: if |f| had an interior maximum at a, the mean value
    gives |f(a)| ≤ average of |f| on every small circle ≤ |f(a)|, forcing
    |f| constant near a, hence f constant (10.9 D9). So on a closed bounded
    region max |f| occurs on the boundary. (b) On |z| = 1 write
    |z² − z| = |z||z − 1| = |z − 1|, the distance from z to 1, largest at
    z = −1 where it is 2. (c) |eᶻ| = e^(Re z) ≤ e¹ with equality at z = 1.
    (MINIMUM modulus: min |f| is also on the boundary provided f has no
    zeros inside; z² − z has zeros 0 and 1, so its minimum 0 is at z = 0.)
    Common mistakes: looking for critical points of |f| inside the disc;
    applying the minimum principle when f has zeros. Now you try: max of
    |z² + 1| on |z| ≤ 1. (2, at z = ±1)

D10. State Taylor's theorem, with the formula for the coefficients and the
     radius of convergence, and sketch its proof. Find the Taylor series of
     (a) 1/(3 − z) about z = 1, (b) Log z about z = 1, (c) 1/(1 + z²) about
     z = 0, stating the radius in each case, and explain why the real
     series of 1/(1 + x²) stops converging at |x| = 1.
     Answer: (a) ∑ (z − 1)ⁿ/2ⁿ⁺¹, R = 2. (b) ∑_{n≥1} (−1)ⁿ⁺¹(z − 1)ⁿ/n,
     R = 1. (c) ∑ (−1)ⁿz²ⁿ, R = 1 (singularities at ±i).
     Teacher explains: THEOREM: if f is analytic in the disc |z − a| < R,
     then for every z in it
        f(z) = ∑_{n≥0} aₙ(z − a)ⁿ,  aₙ = f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! = (1/2πi)∮ f(w)/(w − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dw
     PROOF sketch: fix z, take a circle C: |w − a| = ρ with
     |z − a| < ρ < R. Expand the Cauchy kernel as a geometric series
     (|(z − a)/(w − a)| < 1):
        1/(w − z) = 1/((w − a) − (z − a)) = ∑ (z − a)ⁿ/(w − a)ⁿ⁺¹
     converging uniformly on C; put it into f(z) = (1/2πi)∮ f(w)/(w − z) dw
     and integrate term by term. So the series converges in the BIGGEST
     disc about a free of singularities: R = distance to the nearest
     singularity. (a) Geometric series in the small quantity (z − 1)/2:
        1/(3 − z) = 1/(2 − (z − 1)) = ½·1/(1 − (z − 1)/2) = ∑ (z − 1)ⁿ/2ⁿ⁺¹
     valid for |z − 1| < 2: the singularity z = 3 is at distance 2. (b)
     Log z = Log(1 + (z − 1)), and Log(1 + w) = w − w²/2 + w³/3 − ... (the
     integral of 1/(1 + w) = ∑ (−w)ⁿ), valid for |z − 1| < 1: the branch point
     0 is at distance 1. (c) Put w = z² into 1/(1 + w) = ∑ (−w)ⁿ: R = 1. On
     the real line 1/(1 + x²) is perfectly smooth, yet its Maclaurin series
     diverges for |x| > 1. Real analysis cannot see why; complex analysis
     can: the poles ±i lie at distance 1 from 0. Common mistakes: reading
     the radius off the real graph; expanding 1/(3 − z) in powers of z when
     powers of z − 1 are asked. Now you try: find the Taylor series of eᶻ
     about z = 1 and its radius. (e∑(z − 1)ⁿ/n!, R = ∞)

D11. State Laurent's theorem. Find the Laurent series of
     f(z) = 1/((z − 1)(z − 2)) in (a) |z| < 1, (b) 1 < |z| < 2, (c) |z| > 2,
     (d) 0 < |z − 1| < 1.
     Answer: (a) ∑_{n≥0} (1 − 2^(−n−1))zⁿ. (b) −∑_{n≥1} z^(−n) −
     ∑_{n≥0} zⁿ/2ⁿ⁺¹. (c) ∑_{n≥2} (2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1)z^(−n) = 1/z² + 3/z³ + 7/z⁴ + ...
     (d) −1/(z − 1) − ∑_{n≥0} (z − 1)ⁿ.
     Teacher explains: THEOREM: if f is analytic in the annulus
     r < |z − a| < R, then
        f(z) = ∑_{n=−∞}^{∞} cₙ(z − a)ⁿ,  cₙ = (1/2πi)∮_C f(w)/(w − a)ⁿ⁺¹ dw
     (C any positive circle in the annulus); the expansion is UNIQUE, so any
     method that produces one gives THE Laurent series. (Proof: CIF on the
     annulus as the difference of two circles; expand 1/(w − z) in powers
     of (z − a)/(w − a) on the outer circle and of (w − a)/(z − a) on the
     inner.) Partial fractions first:
        f(z) = 1/(z − 2) − 1/(z − 1)
     RULE: for 1/(z − b) use b as the big number when |z| < |b|, and z when
     |z| > |b|:
        |z| < |b|:  1/(z − b) = −(1/b)·1/(1 − z/b) = −∑_{n≥0} zⁿ/bⁿ⁺¹
        |z| > |b|:  1/(z − b) = (1/z)·1/(1 − b/z) = ∑_{n≥1} bⁿ⁻¹/zⁿ
     (a) |z| < 1 < 2: −∑ zⁿ/2ⁿ⁺¹ + ∑ zⁿ = ∑ (1 − 2^(−n−1))zⁿ (a Taylor
     series: f is analytic there). (b) 1 < |z| < 2: 1/(z − 2) uses the first
     rule, −1/(z − 1) the second:
        f = −∑_{n≥0} zⁿ/2ⁿ⁺¹ − ∑_{n≥1} 1/zⁿ
     (c) |z| > 2: both use the second rule:
        f = ∑_{n≥1} (2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1)/zⁿ = 0/z + 1/z² + 3/z³ + 7/z⁴ + ...
     (d) Centre 1: put w = z − 1, f = 1/(w(w − 1)) = −(1/w)·1/(1 − w)
     = −(1/w)(1 + w + w² + ...) = −1/w − 1 − w − w² − ...  (0 < |w| < 1).
     The coefficient c₋₁ = −1 here is the residue of f at 1. Common
     mistakes: using one expansion outside its region (in (b) the series
     ∑ zⁿ diverges for |z| > 1); forgetting that in (c) the n = 1 terms
     cancel. Now you try: Laurent series of 1/(z(1 − z)) in |z| > 1.
     (−1/z² − 1/z³ − 1/z⁴ − ... )

D12. (a) Define the order of a zero and find the order of the zero of
     z − sin z at 0. (b) Classify the isolated singularities of sin z/z,
     (1 − cos z)/z⁴ and e^(1/z) at 0 using Laurent series. (c) Show that
     e^(1/z) takes the value i at points arbitrarily close to 0. (d) State
     the identity theorem and use it to find the entire f with
     f(1/n) = 1/n² (n ∈ N).
     Answer: (a) order 3. (b) removable; pole of order 2; essential.
     (c) z = 1/(i(π/2 + 2kπ)) → 0. (d) f(z) = z².
     Teacher explains: (a) If f(a) = 0 and f ≢ 0 near a, the Taylor series
     starts at some (z − a)ᵐ: f = (z − a)ᵐg, g(a) ≠ 0; m is the ORDER
     (= the first non-vanishing derivative). For z − sin z:
        z − (z − z³/6 + z⁵/120 − ...) = z³/6 − z⁵/120 + ...
     so the order is 3 (check: f(0) = f′(0) = f″(0) = 0, f‴(0) = cos 0 = 1).
     Since g(a) ≠ 0, g ≠ 0 near a: ZEROS ARE ISOLATED. (b) Laurent series in
     0 < |z| < ∞:
        sin z/z = 1 − z²/6 + ...                 no negative powers:
                                                 REMOVABLE (define f(0) = 1)
        (1 − cos z)/z⁴ = (z²/2 − z⁴/24 + ...)/z⁴ = 1/(2z²) − 1/24 + ...
                                                 POLE OF ORDER 2
        e^(1/z) = 1 + 1/z + 1/(2!z²) + 1/(3!z³) + ...
                                                 ESSENTIAL (infinitely many)
     Quick tests: removable ⇔ f bounded near a (RIEMANN); pole of order m
     ⇔ (z − a)ᵐf → non-zero limit; pole ⇔ |f| → ∞. (c) Solve e^(1/z) = i:
     1/z = log i = i(π/2 + 2kπ), so z = 1/(i(π/2 + 2kπ)) = −i/(π/2 + 2kπ),
     which → 0 as k → ∞. The same works for every w ≠ 0: in every
     neighbourhood of an essential singularity f takes every value except
     possibly one (Picard; Casorati-Weierstrass is the weaker 'comes
     arbitrarily close'). (d) IDENTITY THEOREM: if f and g are analytic on a
     domain D and f = g on a set with a limit point in D, then f ≡ g on D.
     Here f(z) and z² agree on {1/n}, which accumulates at 0 ∈ C, so
     f(z) = z². Common mistakes: calling (1 − cos z)/z⁴ a pole of order 4
     (count the zero of the numerator); calling Log z's singularity at 0
     'essential' (it is not isolated at all). Now you try: classify the
     singularity of (eᶻ − 1)/z² at 0. (1/z + 1/2 + ...: simple pole)

M4. Evaluate. First decide whether Cauchy's theorem alone gives 0.

M5. Cauchy's integral formula.
    a) ∮_{|z|=2} eᶻ/(z − 1) dz          b) ∮_{|z|=4} cos z/(z − π) dz
    c) ∮_{|z|=1} z²/(z − 1/2) dz        d) ∮_{|z|=2} sin z/(z − i) dz
    e) ∮_{|z|=2} dz/(z² + 1)            f) ∮_{|z−i|=1} dz/(z² + 1)
