TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: for every contour integral first draw the contour and mark
  the singular points, then classify: no singular point inside → 0 by
  Cauchy; one point, simple factor → CIF; power (z − a)ⁿ⁺¹ → generalised CIF
  with n!; several points → partial fractions or one small circle each.
  Make the student write 'f(z) = ..., analytic inside, a = ...' every time.
  For Laurent series always do partial fractions first and write, for each
  factor, which of |z| and |b| is bigger. Harder: prove Goursat's lemma for
  triangles; prove that the uniform limit of analytic functions is
  analytic (Morera) and apply it to ζ(s) = ∑ n^(−s) on Re s > 1; show that
  an entire f with |f(z)| ≤ A + B|z|ᵏ is a polynomial of degree ≤ k; derive
  the Laurent coefficients of e^((w/2)(z − 1/z)) as Bessel functions
  Jₙ(w) = (1/π)∫₀^π cos(nt − w sin t) dt; and prove the Schwarz lemma
  (|f(z)| ≤ |z| for f: D → D, f(0) = 0).


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.11 — RESIDUE THEOREM; EVALUATION OF REAL INTEGRALS; CONFORMAL
MAPPINGS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - RESIDUE: at an isolated singularity a, Res(f, a) = c₋₁, the coefficient
    of 1/(z − a) in the Laurent series in 0 < |z − a| < r. Equivalently
    Res(f, a) = (1/2πi)∮ f dz round a small circle. At a removable
    singularity the residue is 0.
  - FORMULAS: SIMPLE POLE: Res = lim (z→a) (z − a)f(z); if f = g/h with
    g(a) ≠ 0, h(a) = 0, h′(a) ≠ 0 then Res = g(a)/h′(a). POLE OF ORDER m:
    Res = [1/(m − 1)!] lim (z→a) dᵐ⁻¹/dzᵐ⁻¹ [(z − a)ᵐ f(z)]. ESSENTIAL
    singularity: read c₋₁ off the Laurent series (e.g. Res(e^(1/z), 0) = 1).
  - RESIDUE THEOREM: if f is analytic on and inside a simple closed positive
    contour C except at finitely many points a₁, ..., aₙ inside C, then
    ∮_C f dz = 2πi ∑ Res(f, aₖ). Points OUTSIDE C do not count.
  - RESIDUE AT INFINITY: Res(f, ∞) = −(coefficient of 1/z in the expansion
    for large |z|) = −Res(w⁻²f(1/w), 0). The sum of ALL residues, including
    ∞, is 0; so ∮_C f = −2πi Res(f, ∞) when every finite singularity is
    inside C. If f = O(1/z²) then Res(f, ∞) = 0.
  - TRIGONOMETRIC INTEGRALS ∫₀^(2π) R(cos θ, sin θ) dθ: put z = e^(iθ),
    cos θ = (z + 1/z)/2, sin θ = (z − 1/z)/(2i), dθ = dz/(iz); integrate over
    |z| = 1, keeping only poles INSIDE the unit circle. Key result:
    ∫₀^(2π) dθ/(a + b cos θ) = 2π/√(a² − b²) (a > |b|).
  - RATIONAL INTEGRALS ∫_{−∞}^{∞} P(x)/Q(x) dx, Q with no real zeros and
    deg Q ≥ deg P + 2: close with a large upper semicircle (its integral →
    0 by the ML-inequality); the answer is 2πi ∑ residues in the UPPER
    half-plane.
  - FOURIER-TYPE INTEGRALS ∫ R(x)e^(iax) dx (a > 0), deg Q ≥ deg P + 1: use
    e^(iaz) (not cos az, which blows up) and JORDAN'S LEMMA:
    |∫_{C_R} e^(iaz)g(z) dz| ≤ (π/a) max_{C_R} |g| → 0; then take real and
    imaginary parts: ∫ cos ax R dx = Re(...), ∫ sin ax R dx = Im(...).
  - INDENTED CONTOURS: for a simple pole ON the real axis, detour on a small
    semicircle; a small arc of angle α round a simple pole a contributes
    −iα Res(f, a) when traversed clockwise (α = π for a semicircle). The
    result is a PRINCIPAL VALUE: PV ∫ e^(ix)/x dx = iπ, ∫₀^∞ sin x/x dx = π/2.
  - BRANCH CUTS AND WEDGES: ∫₀^∞ x^(a−1)/(1 + x) dx = π/sin(πa) (0 < a < 1)
    from a KEYHOLE contour (on the lower edge z^(a−1) gains e^(2πi(a−1)));
    ∫₀^∞ dx/(1 + xⁿ) = (π/n)/sin(π/n) from a WEDGE of angle 2π/n.
  - ARGUMENT PRINCIPLE: (1/2πi)∮_C f′/f dz = Z − P (zeros minus poles
    inside C, with multiplicity) = number of times f(C) winds round 0.
    ROUCHÉ: if |g| < |f| on C then f and f + g have the same number of
    zeros inside C. Method: find the DOMINANT term on the circle.
  - CONFORMAL MAP: an analytic f with f′(z₀) ≠ 0 PRESERVES ANGLES (size and
    orientation) at z₀; it rotates by Arg f′(z₀) and magnifies lengths by
    |f′(z₀)| (areas by |f′|²). At a CRITICAL POINT (f′ = 0, zero of order
    m − 1 of f′) angles are multiplied by m. z̄ reverses orientation.
  - STANDARD MAPS: z² (first quadrant → upper half-plane; angles at 0
    doubled), e^z (strip 0 < Im z < π → upper half-plane; vertical lines →
    circles), Log z (inverse), 1/z (circles and lines → circles and lines),
    √z, sin z (half-strip → half-plane), JOUKOWSKI z + 1/z (circles
    |z| = r → ellipses, unit circle → [−2, 2]).
  - MÖBIUS TRANSFORMATIONS w = (az + b)/(cz + d), ad − bc ≠ 0: bijections
    of the extended plane; compositions of translations, rotation-
    dilations and inversion 1/z; they map CIRCLES/LINES to CIRCLES/LINES;
    exactly one sends three given points to three given points (solve via
    the CROSS RATIO (w − w₁)(w₂ − w₃)/((w − w₃)(w₂ − w₁)) = same in z).
    (z − i)/(z + i) maps the upper half-plane onto the unit disc;
    (z − a)/(1 − āz) (|a| < 1) maps the disc onto itself with a ↦ 0.
  - APPLICATIONS: harmonic ∘ analytic is harmonic, so Laplace problems
    (heat, electrostatics, flow) are solved by mapping the region onto a
    half-plane or disc, solving there (e.g. (1/π)Arg w), and mapping back.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Derive the residue formulas for simple poles and for poles of order m,
    and compute (a) Res(1/(z² + 1), i), (b) Res(cot z, 0), (c) Res(e^z/z⁴,
    0), (d) Res(1/(z² + 1)², i), (e) Res(z²e^(1/z), 0),
    (f) Res(1/(z − sin z), 0).
    Answer: (a) −i/2 (b) 1 (c) 1/6 (d) −i/4 (e) 1/6 (f) 3/10.
    Teacher explains: Near a pole of order m,
       f(z) = c₋ₘ/(z − a)ᵐ + ... + c₋₁/(z − a) + c₀ + c₁(z − a) + ...
    Multiply by (z − a)ᵐ:
       (z − a)ᵐf = c₋ₘ + ... + c₋₁(z − a)ᵐ⁻¹ + c₀(z − a)ᵐ + ...
    Differentiate m − 1 times and let z → a: only (m − 1)!c₋₁ survives, so
       Res(f, a) = [1/(m − 1)!] lim dᵐ⁻¹/dzᵐ⁻¹ [(z − a)ᵐ f(z)]
    For m = 1: Res = lim (z − a)f. If f = g/h with h(a) = 0 ≠ h′(a):
    (z − a)g/h = g/[(h(z) − h(a))/(z − a)] → g(a)/h′(a).
    (a) g/h′ = 1/(2z) at i = 1/(2i) = −i/2.
    (b) cot z = cos z/sin z, simple pole: cos 0/cos 0 = 1.
    (c) Pole of order 4: d³/dz³ eᶻ = eᶻ → 1, divided by 3! = 1/6. (Or read
        the z³ coefficient of eᶻ: 1/3!.)
    (d) (z − i)²f = 1/(z + i)², derivative −2/(z + i)³ at i = −2/(2i)³
        = −2/(−8i) = 1/(4i) = −i/4.
    (e) Essential: z²e^(1/z) = z² + z + 1/2! + 1/(3!z) + ...: c₋₁ = 1/6.
    (f) z − sin z = z³/6 − z⁵/120 + ... = (z³/6)(1 − z²/20 + ...), so
        1/(z − sin z) = (6/z³)(1 + z²/20 + ...) = 6/z³ + (6/20)/z + ...
        and the residue is 3/10. (Series division is much quicker than
        differentiating twice.)
    Common mistakes: using the simple-pole formula at a double pole;
    forgetting (m − 1)!; for (f) assuming 'order 3 pole, residue = 0'. Now
    you try: Res(1/(z⁴ + 1), e^(iπ/4)). (1/(4z³) = −z/4 = −e^(iπ/4)/4)

D2. State and prove the residue theorem. Evaluate
    (a) ∮_{|z|=2} (3z + 2)/(z(z − 1)(z + 3)) dz,
    (b) ∮_{|z|=2} eᶻ/(z(z − 1)²) dz, (c) ∮_{|z|=4} dz/sin z.
    Answer: (a) 7πi/6 (b) 2πi (c) −2πi.
    Teacher explains: THEOREM: f analytic on and inside the positive simple
    closed contour C except at a₁, ..., aₙ inside C ⇒
    ∮_C f dz = 2πi ∑ Res(f, aₖ). PROOF: surround each aₖ by a small circle
    Cₖ. By deformation (10.10 D4) ∮_C f = ∑ ∮_{Cₖ} f. On Cₖ use the Laurent
    series ∑ cₙ(z − aₖ)ⁿ, converging uniformly on Cₖ, and integrate term by
    term: every term gives 0 except c₋₁ ∮ dz/(z − aₖ) = 2πi c₋₁ ∎. RECIPE:
    (1) find all singular points; (2) keep those INSIDE C; (3) residue at
    each; (4) multiply the sum by 2πi.
    (a) Poles 0, 1, −3; −3 is outside |z| = 2.
       Res at 0: (3·0 + 2)/((0 − 1)(0 + 3)) = 2/(−3) = −2/3
       Res at 1: (3 + 2)/(1·4) = 5/4
       ∮ = 2πi(−2/3 + 5/4) = 2πi·7/12 = 7πi/6
    (b) Simple pole 0: e⁰/(0 − 1)² = 1. Double pole 1:
       d/dz (eᶻ/z) = eᶻ(z − 1)/z² → 0 at z = 1
       ∮ = 2πi(1 + 0) = 2πi
    (c) sin z = 0 at 0, ±π (|±π| ≈ 3.14 < 4), ±2π outside. Residues
    1/cos z: 1, −1, −1. ∮ = 2πi(−1) = −2πi. Common mistakes: including
    poles outside C; forgetting that a residue can be 0 although the pole
    is genuine. Now you try: ∮_{|z|=3} (z² + 1)/(z(z − 1)(z − 2)) dz.
    (Residues 1/2, −2, 5/2: 2πi)

D3. Define the residue at infinity and prove that the sum of all residues
    of a rational function (including ∞) is 0. Use it to evaluate
    (a) ∮_{|z|=3} z⁵/(z⁶ − 1) dz and (b) ∮_{|z|=2} dz/((z⁵ − 1)(z − 3)).
    Answer: (a) 2πi (b) −πi/121.
    Teacher explains: A large circle C_R containing all finite singularities
    'encloses ∞ from the other side'. DEFINE
       Res(f, ∞) = −(1/2πi)∮_{C_R} f dz = −c₋₁
    where c₋₁ is the coefficient of 1/z in the Laurent series valid for
    |z| > R. (Substituting z = 1/w: Res(f, ∞) = −Res(f(1/w)/w², 0).) By the
    residue theorem ∮_{C_R} f = 2πi ∑ (finite residues), so
       ∑ (finite residues) + Res(f, ∞) = 0
    for any f analytic except at finitely many points. (a) The six poles
    are the sixth roots of unity, all inside |z| = 3. Instead of six
    residues, expand for large |z|:
       z⁵/(z⁶ − 1) = (1/z)·1/(1 − z⁻⁶) = 1/z + 1/z⁷ + ...
    c₋₁ = 1, so the integral is 2πi·1 = 2πi. (b) Inside |z| = 2: the five
    fifth roots of unity; outside: z = 3 and ∞. Use the outside ones:
       Res at 3: 1/(3⁵ − 1) = 1/242
       Res at ∞: f ~ 1/z⁶ for large z, so c₋₁ = 0
       sum inside = −1/242,   ∮ = 2πi(−1/242) = −πi/121
    Common mistakes: forgetting the minus sign in Res(f, ∞); thinking
    Res(f, ∞) = 0 whenever f is analytic at ∞ (1/z is analytic at ∞ but
    Res(1/z, ∞) = −1). Now you try: ∮_{|z|=2} z³/(z⁴ − 1) dz. (z³/(z⁴ − 1) =
    1/z + ...: 2πi)

D4. Evaluate I = ∫₀^(2π) dθ/(2 + cos θ) by residues, and derive the general
    formula for ∫₀^(2π) dθ/(a + b cos θ), a > |b|.
    Answer: I = 2π/√3 ≈ 3.6276; in general 2π/√(a² − b²).
    Teacher explains: On the unit circle z = e^(iθ):
       cos θ = (z + 1/z)/2,  sin θ = (z − 1/z)/(2i),  dθ = dz/(iz)
    and as θ runs over [0, 2π], z runs once round |z| = 1. So
       I = ∮_{|z|=1} [1/(2 + (z + 1/z)/2)]·dz/(iz)
         = ∮ 2 dz/(i(z² + 4z + 1))
    The roots of z² + 4z + 1 are z = −2 ± √3: z₁ = −2 + √3 ≈ −0.268 is
    INSIDE, z₂ = −2 − √3 ≈ −3.73 is OUTSIDE (their product is 1, so exactly
    one is inside). Residue at z₁ (g/h′):
       2/(i(2z₁ + 4)) = 2/(i·2√3) = 1/(i√3)
       I = 2πi·1/(i√3) = 2π/√3
    General case: the same substitution gives ∮ 2 dz/(i(bz² + 2az + b)),
    roots (−a ± √(a² − b²))/b, the inside one z₁ having bz₁ + a = √(a² − b²),
    and the residue 2/(i(2bz₁ + 2a)) = 1/(i√(a² − b²)), so
    ∫ = 2π/√(a² − b²). Sanity check: b = 0 gives 2π/a ✓. For sin θ the answer
    is the same (shift θ). Common mistakes: forgetting the 1/(iz) from dθ;
    including the outside root; for integrals over [0, π] of an even
    function of cos θ, remember ∫₀^π = ½∫₀^(2π). Now you try:
    ∫₀^(2π) cos 2θ/(5 − 4cos θ) dθ. (Write cos 2θ = Re z²; answer π/6.)

D5. Evaluate ∫_{−∞}^{∞} dx/(x⁴ + 1), justifying every step, and state the
    general theorem for ∫ P(x)/Q(x) dx.
    Answer: π/√2 ≈ 2.2214.
    Teacher explains: THEOREM: if P, Q are polynomials, Q has no real zeros
    and deg Q ≥ deg P + 2, then
       ∫_{−∞}^{∞} P/Q dx = 2πi ∑ Res(P/Q) at the poles in the UPPER half-plane
    Proof: let Γ_R be the segment [−R, R] followed by the upper semicircle
    C_R. For R large Γ_R encloses all upper poles, so ∫_{−R}^{R} + ∫_{C_R}
    = 2πi ∑ Res. On C_R, |P/Q| ≤ K/R² for large R, so by ML
    |∫_{C_R}| ≤ (K/R²)·πR → 0; the improper integral converges because of
    the degree condition. For 1/(z⁴ + 1): z⁴ = −1 gives z = e^(iπ/4),
    e^(3iπ/4), e^(5iπ/4), e^(7iπ/4); the first two are in the upper half-
    plane. At a zero of z⁴ + 1, Res = 1/(4z³) = z/(4z⁴) = −z/4:
       Res at e^(iπ/4) + Res at e^(3iπ/4) = −(e^(iπ/4) + e^(3iπ/4))/4
                                          = −(1/4)(i√2) = −i√2/4
    (the real parts ±√2/2 cancel, the imaginary parts √2/2 add.)
       ∫ = 2πi·(−i√2/4) = π√2/2 = π/√2
    The answer is real and positive, as it must be — a quick check that
    catches sign slips. Common mistakes: taking poles from both half-planes;
    using the upper semicircle for a function that does not decay fast
    enough (∫ x dx/(x² + 1) diverges, although its 'residue answer' is πi).
    Now you try: ∫ dx/((x² + 1)(x² + 4)). (Residues at i and 2i:
    1/(2i·3) and 1/(−3·4i): 2πi(1/(6i) − 1/(12i)) = π/6)

D6. State Jordan's lemma and evaluate (a) ∫_{−∞}^{∞} cos x/(x² + a²) dx
    (a > 0) and (b) ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x sin x/(x² + 1) dx.
    Answer: (a) πe^(−a)/a. (b) π/e ≈ 1.1557.
    Teacher explains: Replacing cos x by cos z fails: cos(iy) = cosh y grows
    on the upper semicircle. Use e^(iz) = e^(ix)e^(−y), which is BOUNDED
    (|e^(iz)| = e^(−y) ≤ 1) in the upper half-plane, then take real or
    imaginary parts. JORDAN'S LEMMA: if |g| ≤ M_R on C_R (upper semicircle)
    and a > 0, then |∫_{C_R} e^(iaz)g(z) dz| ≤ (π/a)M_R. (Uses
    ∫₀^π e^(−R sin t) dt < π/R, from sin t ≥ 2t/π on [0, π/2].) So the arc
    integral → 0 whenever g → 0, even like 1/R only.
    (a) f(z) = e^(iz)/(z² + a²), upper pole ia:
       Res = e^(i·ia)/(2ia) = e^(−a)/(2ia)
       ∫ e^(ix)/(x² + a²) dx = 2πi·e^(−a)/(2ia) = πe^(−a)/a
    real already: the sine part vanishes (odd integrand), and
    ∫ cos x/(x² + a²) dx = πe^(−a)/a. For a = 1: π/e.
    (b) f(z) = ze^(iz)/(z² + 1): g = z/(z² + 1) ~ 1/R — the ML-inequality
    alone gives only πR·(1/R) = π, not → 0; Jordan is needed.
       Res at i: ie^(−1)/(2i) = 1/(2e)
       ∫ xe^(ix)/(x² + 1) dx = 2πi/(2e) = iπ/e
    Imaginary part: ∫ x sin x/(x² + 1) dx = π/e (the cosine part is 0 as
    x cos x/(x² + 1) is odd). Common mistakes: taking Re when Im is needed;
    closing in the lower half-plane with e^(iz) (there it blows up). Now you
    try: ∫ cos 2x/(x² + 1) dx. (πe^(−2) ≈ 0.4252)

D7. Using an indented contour, prove that ∫₀^∞ sin x/x dx = π/2. State the
    small-arc lemma used and find PV ∫_{−∞}^{∞} cos x/(x − 1) dx.
    Answer: π/2; PV ∫ cos x/(x − 1) dx = −π sin 1 ≈ −2.6436.
    Teacher explains: f(z) = e^(iz)/z has a simple pole AT 0, on the path.
    Contour: [−R, −ε], the small upper semicircle c_ε from −ε to ε
    (clockwise), [ε, R], then the big semicircle C_R. No poles inside, so
       ∫_{−R}^{−ε} + ∫_{c_ε} + ∫_ε^R + ∫_{C_R} = 0
    SMALL-ARC LEMMA: if a is a simple pole and c_ε an arc of angle α of
    |z − a| = ε traversed clockwise, then ∫_{c_ε} f → −iα Res(f, a). (Write
    f = c₋₁/(z − a) + analytic: the analytic part gives O(ε); c₋₁∫ dz/(z − a)
    = c₋₁·(−iα).) Here α = π, Res = 1, so ∫_{c_ε} → −iπ. By Jordan
    ∫_{C_R} → 0. Hence
       PV ∫_{−∞}^{∞} e^(ix)/x dx = iπ
    Imaginary part: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} sin x/x dx = π, and by evenness
    ∫₀^∞ sin x/x dx = π/2. (The real part says PV ∫ cos x/x dx = 0, which is
    clear from oddness; the integral of cos x/x itself diverges at 0.)
    For cos x/(x − 1): same method with the pole at 1:
       PV ∫ e^(ix)/(x − 1) dx = iπ·Res = iπe^i = iπ(cos 1 + i sin 1)
    Real part: −π sin 1 ≈ −2.6436; the imaginary part gives
    ∫ sin x/(x − 1) dx = π cos 1. Common mistakes: counting the pole on the
    axis as 'inside' (2πi) or 'outside' (0) — it contributes HALF, πi;
    forgetting that the answer is a principal value. Now you try:
    ∫₀^∞ (1 − cos x)/x² dx. (Integrate (1 − e^(iz))/z²; the small arc gives
    −iπ·(−i) and the answer is π/2.)

D8. (a) With a keyhole contour prove ∫₀^∞ x^(a−1)/(1 + x) dx = π/sin(πa) for
    0 < a < 1, and find ∫₀^∞ dx/(√x(1 + x)). (b) With a wedge contour find
    ∫₀^∞ dx/(1 + x³).
    Answer: (a) π/sin(πa); a = 1/2 gives π. (b) 2π/(3√3) ≈ 1.2092.
    Teacher explains: (a) Use z^(a−1) = e^((a−1) log z) with 0 < arg z < 2π
    (cut along the positive real axis). KEYHOLE: along the top of the cut
    from ε to R (arg ≈ 0), round |z| = R, back along the bottom from R to ε
    (arg ≈ 2π), round |z| = ε clockwise. On the bottom edge
    z^(a−1) = x^(a−1)e^(2πi(a−1)). The circles vanish: on |z| = R,
    |f| ≈ R^(a−2), times 2πR gives R^(a−1) → 0 (a < 1); on |z| = ε,
    ε^(a−1)·2πε = 2πε^a → 0 (a > 0). The only pole is z = −1 = e^(iπ):
       Res = (e^(iπ))^(a−1) = e^(iπ(a−1))
       (1 − e^(2πi(a−1)))·I = 2πi e^(iπ(a−1))
       I = 2πi/(e^(−iπ(a−1)) − e^(iπ(a−1))) = 2πi/(−2i sin(π(a − 1)))
         = −π/sin(πa − π) = π/sin(πa)
    With a = 1/2: ∫₀^∞ dx/(√x(1 + x)) = π/sin(π/2) = π (check: x = t² turns it
    into ∫₀^∞ 2dt/(1 + t²) = π ✓). (b) WEDGE: [0, R], the arc to Re^(2πi/3),
    and the ray back to 0. On the ray z = re^(2πi/3), z³ = r³, so that leg
    gives −e^(2πi/3)I. The arc is O(R/R³) → 0. Only z = e^(iπ/3) is inside:
       Res = 1/(3z²) = 1/(3e^(2πi/3))
       (1 − e^(2πi/3))I = 2πi/(3e^(2πi/3))
       I = 2πi/(3(e^(2πi/3) − e^(4πi/3))) = 2πi/(3·i√3) = 2π/(3√3)
    Common mistakes: using the principal branch (the cut must not cross the
    keyhole's interior); forgetting the factor e^(2πi(a−1)) on the lower
    edge. Now you try: ∫₀^∞ dx/(1 + x⁴) by a quarter-circle wedge.
    (π/(2√2) ≈ 1.1107)

D9. State the argument principle and Rouché's theorem. How many zeros does
    p(z) = z⁵ + 3z + 1 have in |z| < 1, in |z| < 2, and in 1 < |z| < 2?
    Evaluate ∮_{|z|=4} tan z dz by the argument principle.
    Answer: 1, 5, 4. ∮ tan z dz = −4πi.
    Teacher explains: ARGUMENT PRINCIPLE: if f is analytic inside and on C
    except for poles, and has no zeros or poles on C, then
       (1/2πi)∮_C f′(z)/f(z) dz = Z − P
    Proof: near a zero of order m, f = (z − a)ᵐg, f′/f = m/(z − a) + g′/g,
    residue m; near a pole of order m, residue −m; sum by the residue
    theorem. Since f′/f = (log f)′, the left side counts how many times
    f(z) winds round 0 as z goes round C. ROUCHÉ: if f, g are analytic
    inside and on C and |g| < |f| on C, then f and f + g have the same
    number of zeros inside C. (f + g = f(1 + g/f), and 1 + g/f stays in the
    disc |w − 1| < 1, which does not wind round 0.) Choose the DOMINANT
    term on the circle:
       |z| = 1:  f = 3z, |3z| = 3;  |z⁵ + 1| ≤ 2 < 3     → as 3z: 1 zero
       |z| = 2:  f = z⁵, |z⁵| = 32; |3z + 1| ≤ 7 < 32   → as z⁵: 5 zeros
    and no zero lies on |z| = 1 (there |p| ≥ 3 − 2 > 0), so 5 − 1 = 4 zeros
    in 1 < |z| < 2. For tan z = sin z/cos z = −f′/f with f = cos z:
       ∮ tan z dz = −2πi(Z − P) for cos z inside |z| = 4
    cos z has zeros ±π/2 inside (±3π/2 ≈ ±4.71 outside) and no poles, so
    the integral is −2πi·2 = −4πi (agrees with residues −1, −1). Rouché also
    proves the fundamental theorem of algebra: on a large circle zⁿ
    dominates the lower terms. Common mistakes: choosing a term that is
    not dominant (the inequality must be STRICT on the whole circle);
    forgetting zeros on the boundary circle. Now you try: zeros of
    z⁴ − 6z + 3 in |z| < 1 and in 1 < |z| < 2. (1 and 3)

D10. Prove that an analytic map preserves angles where f′ ≠ 0, and find the
     rotation and magnification of w = z² at z₀ = 1 + i. What happens at
     z = 0? Find the images under w = z² of the lines x = 1 and y = 1 and
     check that they meet at a right angle.
     Answer: rotation π/4, magnification 2√2 (areas ×8). At 0 angles are
     doubled. x = 1 → parabola u = 1 − v²/4; y = 1 → parabola
     u = v²/4 − 1; they meet at w = 2i at a right angle.
     Teacher explains: Let a smooth curve z(t) pass through z₀ = z(t₀) with
     tangent z′(t₀) ≠ 0. The image curve w(t) = f(z(t)) has tangent
        w′(t₀) = f′(z₀)z′(t₀)
     If f′(z₀) = ρe^(iφ) ≠ 0, EVERY tangent direction is rotated by the same
     angle φ = Arg f′(z₀) and every small length is multiplied by ρ = |f′(z₀)|.
     So the angle between two curves (difference of arguments of the
     tangents) is unchanged in size and sense: f is CONFORMAL at z₀. For
     w = z² at 1 + i: f′ = 2(1 + i) = 2√2 e^(iπ/4): rotation 45°, lengths
     ×2√2, areas ×|f′|² = 8. At z = 0, f′ = 0: the ray arg z = θ goes to the
     ray arg w = 2θ, so angles are DOUBLED (the first quadrant, angle π/2,
     opens into the upper half-plane, angle π). In general at a zero of
     order m − 1 of f′ angles are multiplied by m. Images: u = x² − y²,
     v = 2xy.
        x = 1: u = 1 − y², v = 2y ⇒ u = 1 − v²/4
        y = 1: u = x² − 1, v = 2x ⇒ u = v²/4 − 1
     Both pass through w = f(1 + i) = 2i, i.e. u = 0, v = 2. There
     du/dv = −v/2 = −1 on the first and du/dv = v/2 = 1 on the second, so
     the tangent vectors (du, dv) are (−1, 1) and (1, 1), with dot product
     −1 + 1 = 0 ✓. The grid lines x = 1, y = 1 were orthogonal and their
     images still are, as conformality predicts. Common mistakes:
     calling z² conformal at 0; forgetting that z̄ keeps the size of angles
     but reverses their sense (not conformal). Now you try: where is
     w = z + 1/z not conformal? (1 − 1/z² = 0: z = ±1)

D11. Explain why Möbius transformations map circles and lines to circles and
     lines. Find the Möbius map T with T(1) = 0, T(i) = 1, T(−1) = ∞, and
     show that it maps the unit disc onto the upper half-plane. Show that
     S(z) = (z − i)/(z + i) maps the upper half-plane onto the unit disc.
     Answer: T(z) = −i(z − 1)/(z + 1) = i(1 − z)/(1 + z); T(0) = i.
     Teacher explains: w = (az + b)/(cz + d), ad − bc ≠ 0. If c = 0 it is
     linear. If c ≠ 0,
        w = a/c + (bc − ad)/(c(cz + d))
     so T is a chain z ↦ cz + d ↦ 1/(·) ↦ scale, rotate ↦ translate.
     Translations, rotations and dilations obviously map circles to circles
     and lines to lines. For 1/z: every circle or line has the equation
     A(x² + y²) + Bx + Cy + D = 0 (A = 0 for a line). With z = 1/w,
     x = u/(u² + v²), y = −v/(u² + v²), x² + y² = 1/(u² + v²); substituting
     and multiplying by u² + v² gives D(u² + v²) + Bu − Cv + A = 0 — again a
     circle or line. So the whole chain maps 'circlines' to circlines.
     THREE POINTS: the cross ratio (z − z₁)(z₂ − z₃)/((z − z₃)(z₂ − z₁))
     sends z₁, z₂, z₃ to 0, 1, ∞. Here z₁ = 1, z₂ = i, z₃ = −1:
        T(z) = (z − 1)(i + 1)/((z + 1)(i − 1))
     and (1 + i)/(i − 1) = (1 + i)(−1 − i)/((−1 + i)(−1 − i)) = −2i/2 = −i, so
        T(z) = −i(z − 1)/(z + 1)
     Check T(i) = −i(i − 1)/(i + 1) = −i·i = 1 ✓. The unit circle passes
     through 1, i, −1, so its image is the circline through 0, 1, ∞: the
     real axis. The disc goes to one side of it; test one point:
     T(0) = −i(−1)/1 = i, in the upper half-plane. So T maps |z| < 1 onto
     Im w > 0. For S: a real x has |x − i| = |x + i| (equal distances), so
     |S(x)| = 1: the real axis goes to the unit circle, and S(i) = 0 shows
     the upper half-plane goes to the inside. Common mistakes: forgetting
     to test a point to decide which side; writing the cross ratio with
     indices in the wrong order (then the points go to 1, 0, ∞). Now you
     try: find the Möbius map with 0, 1, ∞ ↦ 1, i, −1. ((i − z)/(i + z))

D12. Find the steady temperature u in the upper half-plane with u = 1 on the
     negative real axis and u = 0 on the positive real axis. Then use a
     conformal map to find the harmonic u in the unit disc equal to 1 on the
     upper semicircle and 0 on the lower semicircle, and find u(0) and
     u(0, 1/2).
     Answer: Half-plane: u = (1/π)Arg w. Disc: u = 1/2 +
     (1/π)arctan(2y/(1 − x² − y²)); u(0) = 1/2, u(0, 1/2) = 1/2 +
     (1/π)arctan(4/3) ≈ 0.7952.
     Teacher explains: KEY FACT: if φ is harmonic in a region Ω′ and
     w = f(z) is analytic from Ω onto Ω′, then u = φ(f(z)) is harmonic in Ω
     (locally φ = Re F with F analytic, and F ∘ f is analytic). Boundary
     values travel with the boundary. Half-plane: Arg w is Im(Log w),
     harmonic, equal to 0 on the positive axis and π on the negative, so
     u = (1/π)Arg w solves it; level lines are rays from 0. Disc: map the
     disc onto the upper half-plane with T(z) = i(1 + z)/(1 − z) (this is
     the map of D11 applied to −z). For z = e^(it), 0 < t < π:
        (1 + e^(it))/(1 − e^(it)) = i cot(t/2),  T = i·i cot(t/2) = −cot(t/2) < 0
     so the upper semicircle goes to the NEGATIVE real axis (where the
     temperature is 1) and similarly the lower one to the positive axis;
     T(0) = i is in the upper half-plane ✓. Hence u(z) = (1/π)Arg T(z). To
     make it explicit, (1 + z)/(1 − z) = (1 − |z|² + 2iy)/|1 − z|², whose
     argument is arctan(2y/(1 − x² − y²)) (real part > 0 in the disc), and
     multiplying by i adds π/2:
        u = 1/2 + (1/π)arctan(2y/(1 − x² − y²))
     u(0) = 1/2, as the mean value property demands (half the boundary at
     1, half at 0). At (0, 1/2): 2y/(1 − 1/4) = 4/3, arctan(4/3) ≈ 0.9273,
     u ≈ 0.5 + 0.2952 = 0.7952: warmer, being nearer the hot arc. Common
     mistakes: mapping the boundary pieces to the wrong halves of the axis
     (always test one boundary point); forgetting that Arg w is measured
     from the POSITIVE axis. Now you try: find the harmonic u in the strip
     0 < y < π with u = 0 on y = 0 and u = 1 on y = π. (u = y/π; or via
     w = eᶻ: (1/π)Arg eᶻ = y/π.)

M3. Evaluate by the residue theorem (positive orientation).
    a) ∮_{|z|=2} (z + 1)/(z²(z − 1)) dz
    b) ∮_{|z|=2} eᶻ/(z² + 1) dz
    c) ∮_{|z|=3} tan z dz

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make a residue card — simple pole: g/h′; order m: formula
  with (m − 1)!; anything awkward: series division — and drill it before
  any contour work. For every real integral draw the contour, mark the
  poles, state which are inside and why each extra piece → 0 (ML for
  rational functions, Jordan for e^(iaz), small-arc lemma for poles on the
  axis). Check that the final answer is real and has the right sign. For
  conformal maps always test ONE point to decide which side of an image
  curve a region goes to. Harder: prove Jordan's lemma; derive
  π cot(πz) summation (∑ f(n) = −∑ Res(π cot(πz)f(z)) at the poles of f)
  and use it for ∑ 1/n²; prove Rouché from the argument principle; show
  that the only conformal automorphisms of the disc are e^(iφ)(z − a)/(1 − āz)
  (Schwarz lemma); state the Riemann mapping theorem and use the
  Schwarz-Christoffel formula to map the upper half-plane onto a strip or
  a triangle.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.12 — FOURIER SERIES AND FOURIER TRANSFORM
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - ORTHOGONALITY on [−π, π]: ∫ cos mx cos nx dx = ∫ sin mx sin nx dx = 0
    (m ≠ n) and = π (m = n ≥ 1); ∫ sin mx cos nx dx = 0 always; ∫ 1 dx = 2π.
    Complex form: ∫ e^(imx)e^(−inx) dx = 2π if m = n, 0 otherwise.
  - FOURIER SERIES of a 2π-periodic f: f(x) ~ a₀/2 + ∑ (aₙ cos nx + bₙ sin nx)
    with EULER'S FORMULAS aₙ = (1/π)∫_{−π}^{π} f(x) cos nx dx (n ≥ 0),
    bₙ = (1/π)∫_{−π}^{π} f(x) sin nx dx. Any interval of length 2π may be
    used. PERIOD 2L: replace nx by nπx/L and 1/π by 1/L.
  - PARITY: f EVEN ⇒ bₙ = 0 (COSINE series), aₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π f cos nx dx;
    f ODD ⇒ aₙ = 0 (SINE series), bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π f sin nx dx. Useful
    integrals: ∫₀^π x sin nx dx = π(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n, ∫₀^π x² cos nx dx = 2π(−1)ⁿ/n²,
    cos nπ = (−1)ⁿ, sin nπ = 0.
  - STANDARD SERIES on (−π, π): x = 2∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n;
    x² = π²/3 + 4∑ (−1)ⁿ cos nx/n²; |x| = π/2 − (4/π)∑_{n odd} cos nx/n²;
    square wave sgn x = (4/π)∑_{n odd} sin nx/n.
  - DIRICHLET'S THEOREM: if f is 2π-periodic and PIECEWISE SMOOTH, its
    Fourier series converges at every x to ½[f(x⁺) + f(x⁻)] — to f(x) at
    points of continuity, to the MIDPOINT of a jump. Convergence is uniform
    if f is continuous and piecewise smooth. Near a jump the partial sums
    overshoot by about 9% of the jump (GIBBS PHENOMENON), however many
    terms are taken.
  - HALF-RANGE SERIES: f given on (0, L) can be extended ODDLY (sine
    series, bₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f sin(nπx/L) dx) or EVENLY (cosine series,
    a₀ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f dx, aₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f cos(nπx/L) dx). Both equal f on
    (0, L); they differ outside and at the ends.
  - COMPLEX FORM: f ~ ∑_{n∈Z} cₙe^(inx), cₙ = (1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π} f(x)e^(−inx) dx;
    c₀ = a₀/2, cₙ = (aₙ − ibₙ)/2, c₋ₙ = (aₙ + ibₙ)/2 (real f: c₋ₙ = c̄ₙ);
    aₙ = cₙ + c₋ₙ, bₙ = i(cₙ − c₋ₙ).
  - PARSEVAL: (1/π)∫_{−π}^{π} f² dx = a₀²/2 + ∑ (aₙ² + bₙ²), or
    (1/2π)∫ |f|² = ∑ |cₙ|². BESSEL'S INEQUALITY (≤) holds for every square-
    integrable f; RIEMANN-LEBESGUE: aₙ, bₙ → 0. Substituting special x or
    using Parseval gives ∑ 1/n² = π²/6, ∑ 1/n⁴ = π⁴/90, 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ... =
    π/4, etc.
  - SMOOTHNESS vs DECAY: jump in f ⇒ coefficients ~ 1/n; f continuous with a
    corner ⇒ ~ 1/n²; f ∈ Cᵏ periodic ⇒ o(1/nᵏ); analytic ⇒ exponential
    decay. A Fourier series may always be INTEGRATED term by term; it may be
    DIFFERENTIATED term by term if f is continuous, periodic and piecewise
    smooth (the series of x may not be differentiated).
  - APPLICATION: separation of variables for u_t = ku_xx or u_tt = c²u_xx
    on (0, L) with u = 0 at the ends gives u = ∑ bₙ e^(−kn²π²t/L²) sin(nπx/L)
    (or cos/sin(nπct/L) for waves), bₙ = the sine coefficients of u(x, 0).
  - FOURIER TRANSFORM (convention used here): F(ω) = f̂(ω) =
    ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f(x)e^(−iωx) dx, inverse f(x) = (1/2π)∫_{−∞}^{∞} F(ω)e^(iωx) dω.
    (Other books put 1/√(2π) in both, or use e^(−2πiξx); constants in
    answers change accordingly.) At a jump the inversion integral gives the
    midpoint (FOURIER INTEGRAL THEOREM).
  - STANDARD PAIRS: 1_{|x|<a} ↔ 2 sin(aω)/ω; e^(−a|x|) ↔ 2a/(a² + ω²);
    e^(−ax)H(x) ↔ 1/(a + iω); e^(−ax²) ↔ √(π/a) e^(−ω²/(4a));
    1/(a² + x²) ↔ (π/a)e^(−a|ω|); δ(x) ↔ 1 (a > 0; H = Heaviside step).
  - PROPERTIES: f(x − a) ↔ e^(−iaω)F; e^(iax)f ↔ F(ω − a); f(ax) ↔
    (1/|a|)F(ω/a); f′ ↔ iωF; xf ↔ iF′(ω); f(−x) ↔ F(−ω); F(x) ↔ 2πf(−ω)
    (DUALITY); CONVOLUTION (f * g)(x) = ∫ f(s)g(x − s) ds ↔ F·G; PLANCHEREL
    ∫ |f|² dx = (1/2π)∫ |F|² dω. The transform turns derivatives into
    multiplication, so linear ODEs/PDEs with constant coefficients become
    algebra (heat kernel e^(−x²/(4t))/√(4πt)).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove the orthogonality relations for 1, cos nx, sin nx on [−π, π] and
    use them to derive Euler's formulas for aₙ and bₙ. What changes for
    period 2L?
    Answer: See the relations above; aₙ = (1/π)∫ f cos nx dx,
    bₙ = (1/π)∫ f sin nx dx; for period 2L: aₙ = (1/L)∫_{−L}^{L} f cos(nπx/L) dx,
    bₙ = (1/L)∫_{−L}^{L} f sin(nπx/L) dx.
    Teacher explains: Use the product-to-sum formulas:
       cos mx cos nx = ½[cos(m − n)x + cos(m + n)x]
       sin mx sin nx = ½[cos(m − n)x − cos(m + n)x]
       sin mx cos nx = ½[sin(m + n)x + sin(m − n)x]
    and ∫_{−π}^{π} cos kx dx = 0 for an integer k ≠ 0 (= 2π for k = 0),
    ∫_{−π}^{π} sin kx dx = 0 always. So for m ≠ n (m, n ≥ 0) both cos(m − n)x
    and cos(m + n)x integrate to 0, while for m = n ≥ 1 the first gives
    ½·2π = π. The sin·cos integrals vanish (odd integrand). Now suppose
       f(x) = a₀/2 + ∑ (aₖ cos kx + bₖ sin kx)
    and that we may integrate term by term (true if the series converges
    uniformly). Multiply by cos nx and integrate over [−π, π]: every term
    dies except k = n:
       ∫ f cos nx dx = aₙ·π   ⇒   aₙ = (1/π)∫ f(x) cos nx dx
    Multiplying by sin nx gives bₙ; integrating f itself gives
    ∫ f = (a₀/2)·2π, which is why the constant is written a₀/2: then the
    formula for aₙ holds for n = 0 too. For period 2L substitute
    x = πt/L: the functions become cos(nπt/L), sin(nπt/L), the integrals
    run over [−L, L] and the factor becomes 1/L. Geometric meaning: these
    functions are PERPENDICULAR vectors for the inner product
    ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫ fg, and aₙ, bₙ are the components of f along them.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the ½ in front of a₀; using 1/(2π) for aₙ.
    Now you try: compute ∫_{−π}^{π} sin 3x sin 5x dx and ∫_{−π}^{π} sin²4x dx.
    (0 and π)

D2. Find the Fourier series of f(x) = x on (−π, π), extended 2π-periodically.
    What does the series converge to at x = π/2 and at x = π? Deduce the sum
    of 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + ....
    Answer: x = 2∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n = 2(sin x − sin 2x/2 + sin 3x/3 − ...).
    At π/2 it converges to π/2; at π to 0. 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ... = π/4.
    Teacher explains: f is ODD, so aₙ = 0 for all n and
       bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x sin nx dx
    Integrate by parts (u = x, dv = sin nx dx):
       ∫₀^π x sin nx dx = [−x cos nx/n]₀^π + (1/n)∫₀^π cos nx dx
                        = −π cos nπ/n + 0 = π(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n
    so bₙ = 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n. The periodic extension is a SAWTOOTH with jumps of
    2π at x = ±π, ±3π, .... At x = π/2 (continuity) the series converges to
    π/2:
       π/2 = 2[sin(π/2) − 0 + sin(3π/2)/3 − 0 + sin(5π/2)/5 − ...]
           = 2[1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + ...]
    so 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ... = π/4 (LEIBNIZ). At x = π every term is
    sin nπ = 0: the series gives 0 = ½[f(π⁻) + f(π⁺)] = ½[π + (−π)], the
    midpoint of the jump, as Dirichlet predicts. The coefficients decay only
    like 1/n because of the jump, so convergence is slow and non-uniform.
    Common mistakes: writing bₙ = 2/n (losing (−1)ⁿ⁺¹); claiming the series
    equals π at x = π. Now you try: Fourier series of f(x) = x on (0, 2π)
    (period 2π). (π − 2∑ sin nx/n)

D3. Find the Fourier series of f(x) = x² on [−π, π] and deduce
    ∑ 1/n² = π²/6 and ∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n² = π²/12.
    Answer: x² = π²/3 + 4∑ (−1)ⁿ cos nx/n².
    Teacher explains: f is EVEN, so bₙ = 0 and
       a₀ = (2/π)∫₀^π x² dx = 2π²/3,  so a₀/2 = π²/3
       aₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x² cos nx dx
    By parts twice:
       ∫₀^π x² cos nx dx = [x² sin nx/n]₀^π − (2/n)∫₀^π x sin nx dx
                         = 0 − (2/n)·π(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n = 2π(−1)ⁿ/n²
    so aₙ = 4(−1)ⁿ/n². The periodic extension is CONTINUOUS (f(−π) = f(π) =
    π²) with corners, and the coefficients decay like 1/n²: the series
    converges uniformly to x² on [−π, π]. At x = π, cos nπ = (−1)ⁿ:
       π² = π²/3 + 4∑ (−1)ⁿ(−1)ⁿ/n² = π²/3 + 4∑ 1/n²
       ∑ 1/n² = (π² − π²/3)/4 = π²/6
    At x = 0:
       0 = π²/3 + 4∑ (−1)ⁿ/n²  ⇒  ∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n² = π²/12
    (and adding the two: 2∑_{n odd} 1/n² = π²/4, so ∑_{odd} 1/n² = π²/8).
    Common mistakes: forgetting to halve a₀; making a sign slip in the
    second integration by parts — check n = 1 directly:
    ∫₀^π x² cos x dx = [x² sin x + 2x cos x − 2 sin x]₀^π = −2π, so
    a₁ = (2/π)(−2π) = −4 ✓. Now you try: series of |x| on [−π, π] and
    deduce ∑_{odd} 1/n² = π²/8. (π/2 − (4/π)∑_{odd} cos nx/n²; put x = 0)

D4. State Dirichlet's theorem. Find the Fourier series of the square wave
    f(x) = −1 on (−π, 0), 1 on (0, π), give the value of the series at 0
    and at π/2, and describe the Gibbs phenomenon.
    Answer: f ~ (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x/3 + sin 5x/5 + ...); value 0 at x = 0,
    1 at π/2 (again π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + ...). The partial sums overshoot to
    about (2/π)Si(π) ≈ 1.179 near the jump, i.e. ~9% of the jump 2.
    Teacher explains: DIRICHLET: if f is 2π-periodic and piecewise smooth
    (finitely many pieces on which f and f′ are continuous with one-sided
    limits), then the Fourier series converges for every x to
       ½[f(x⁺) + f(x⁻)]
    f is odd, so aₙ = 0 and
       bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π sin nx dx = (2/π)(1 − cos nπ)/n
          = 4/(πn) for n odd,  0 for n even
    At x = 0 (a jump from −1 to 1) every sine vanishes: the sum 0 is the
    midpoint. At π/2 the series is (4/π)(1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ...) = 1, i.e.
    π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − .... GIBBS: the partial sum S_N(x) has its first
    maximum at x = π/(2N) or so, where
       S_N ≈ (2/π)∫₀^π sin t/t dt = (2/π)Si(π) ≈ 1.1790
    for every large N. The peak moves towards the jump but does not
    shrink: the overshoot is about 0.179 = 8.9% of the jump 2. So the
    convergence is pointwise but NOT uniform near the jump (a uniform limit
    of continuous functions would be continuous). Common mistakes: 'the
    series converges to f(0) = 1' (f(0) is not even defined; the series
    gives 0); thinking more terms remove the overshoot. Now you try: where
    does the series of f(x) = 0 on (−π, 0), 1 on (0, π) converge to at
    x = 0 and x = π? (1/2 at both)

D5. For f(x) = x on (0, 2), find (a) the half-range sine series and (b) the
    half-range cosine series. Sketch the extensions, state what each series
    converges to at x = 2, and compare the rates of decay.
    Answer: (a) (4/π)∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin(nπx/2)/n; at x = 2 it gives 0.
    (b) 1 − (8/π²)∑_{n odd} cos(nπx/2)/n²; at x = 2 it gives 2.
    Teacher explains: Here L = 2. (a) ODD extension to (−2, 2), then period
    4: a sawtooth with jumps at x = ±2, ±6, ....
       bₙ = (2/2)∫₀² x sin(nπx/2) dx
          = [−2x cos(nπx/2)/(nπ)]₀² + (2/(nπ))∫₀² cos(nπx/2) dx
          = −4 cos(nπ)/(nπ) + 0 = 4(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/(nπ)
    At x = 2 the extension jumps from 2 to −2: the series gives 0.
    (b) EVEN extension: |x| on (−2, 2), period 4: a continuous triangle wave.
       a₀ = (2/2)∫₀² x dx = 2,   so a₀/2 = 1
       aₙ = ∫₀² x cos(nπx/2) dx = [2x sin(nπx/2)/(nπ)]₀² − (2/(nπ))∫₀² sin(nπx/2) dx
          = 0 + (4/(n²π²))[cos(nπx/2)]₀² = 4((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(n²π²)
    which is −8/(n²π²) for n odd and 0 for n even. At x = 2 the even
    extension is continuous with value 2, so the series gives 2: check
    1 − (8/π²)∑_{odd} cos(nπ)/n² = 1 + (8/π²)(π²/8) = 2 ✓. The cosine
    coefficients decay like 1/n² (continuous extension), the sine
    coefficients only like 1/n (jumps): for approximation the cosine series
    is better here. Common mistakes: using 1/L = 1/2 instead of 2/L = 1 in
    half-range formulas; forgetting that the sine series must vanish at 0
    and L. Now you try: the half-range sine series of f(x) = 1 on (0, π).
    ((4/π)∑_{odd} sin nx/n)

D6. Derive the complex form of the Fourier series and find it for f(x) = eˣ
    on (−π, π). Use it to find ∑_{n≥1} 1/(1 + n²).
    Answer: eˣ = (sinh π/π)∑_{n∈Z} (−1)ⁿ e^(inx)/(1 − in);
    ∑_{n≥1} 1/(1 + n²) = (π coth π − 1)/2 ≈ 1.0767.
    Teacher explains: With cos nx = (e^(inx) + e^(−inx))/2 and
    sin nx = (e^(inx) − e^(−inx))/(2i):
       aₙ cos nx + bₙ sin nx = ½(aₙ − ibₙ)e^(inx) + ½(aₙ + ibₙ)e^(−inx)
    so f ~ ∑_{n∈Z} cₙe^(inx) with c₀ = a₀/2, cₙ = (aₙ − ibₙ)/2,
    c₋ₙ = (aₙ + ibₙ)/2, and directly (by orthogonality of e^(inx))
       cₙ = (1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π} f(x)e^(−inx) dx
    For eˣ this integral is easy (no integration by parts):
       cₙ = (1/2π)∫ e^((1−in)x) dx = (1/2π)[e^((1−in)x)/(1 − in)]_{−π}^{π}
          = (1/2π)(e^π e^(−inπ) − e^(−π)e^(inπ))/(1 − in)
          = (−1)ⁿ(e^π − e^(−π))/(2π(1 − in)) = (−1)ⁿ sinh π/(π(1 − in))
    At x = π the extension jumps from e^π to e^(−π); the series converges to
    the midpoint cosh π. With e^(inπ) = (−1)ⁿ:
       cosh π = (sinh π/π)∑ 1/(1 − in) = (sinh π/π)∑ (1 + in)/(1 + n²)
    The imaginary parts cancel in pairs (n and −n), so
       ∑_{n∈Z} 1/(1 + n²) = π cosh π/sinh π = π coth π
       ∑_{n≥1} 1/(1 + n²) = (π coth π − 1)/2 ≈ (3.1533 − 1)/2 ≈ 1.0767
    Common mistakes: forgetting (−1)ⁿ from e^(∓inπ); using 1/π instead of
    1/2π for cₙ. Now you try: cₙ for f(x) = x on (−π, π). (c₀ = 0,
    cₙ = i(−1)ⁿ/n)

D7. State and prove Parseval's identity (assuming uniform convergence) and
    use it with the series of x² to show ∑ 1/n⁴ = π⁴/90. State Bessel's
    inequality and the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma.
    Answer: (1/π)∫_{−π}^{π} f² dx = a₀²/2 + ∑ (aₙ² + bₙ²); ∑ 1/n⁴ = π⁴/90.
    Teacher explains: Multiply f = a₀/2 + ∑ (aₙ cos nx + bₙ sin nx) by f and
    integrate term by term; by Euler's formulas ∫ f cos nx = πaₙ etc.:
       ∫ f² dx = (a₀/2)(πa₀) + ∑ (aₙ·πaₙ + bₙ·πbₙ)
       (1/π)∫ f² dx = a₀²/2 + ∑ (aₙ² + bₙ²)
    It is 'Pythagoras' in the orthogonal system: length² = sum of squared
    components. (It holds for every square-integrable f, the series
    converging in the mean-square sense.) For x²: a₀ = 2π²/3, aₙ = 4(−1)ⁿ/n²:
       (1/π)∫_{−π}^{π} x⁴ dx = (1/π)(2π⁵/5) = 2π⁴/5
       a₀²/2 = (4π⁴/9)/2 = 2π⁴/9
       2π⁴/5 = 2π⁴/9 + 16∑ 1/n⁴  ⇒  16∑ 1/n⁴ = 8π⁴/45  ⇒  ∑ 1/n⁴ = π⁴/90
    With f = x (bₙ = 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n): (1/π)(2π³/3) = ∑ 4/n², again π²/6.
    BESSEL: for any N, 0 ≤ ∫ (f − S_N)² = ∫ f² − π[a₀²/2 + ∑_{n≤N}(aₙ² + bₙ²)],
    so a₀²/2 + ∑ (aₙ² + bₙ²) ≤ (1/π)∫ f² (S_N is the BEST mean-square
    approximation among trigonometric polynomials of degree N). Since the
    series of squares converges, aₙ → 0 and bₙ → 0: RIEMANN-LEBESGUE
    (true even for merely integrable f). Common mistakes: forgetting the ½
    on a₀² (it is a₀²/2, NOT a₀²/4 — (a₀/2)² times 2); applying Parseval to
    the series values instead of squares. Now you try: use Parseval with
    |x| to find ∑_{odd} 1/n⁴. (2π²/3 = π²/2 + (16/π²)∑_{odd} 1/n⁴ ⇒ π⁴/96)

D8. (a) Integrate the series x = 2∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n term by term to obtain
    the series of x². (b) Differentiate the series of x² term by term; is
    the result valid? (c) Differentiate the series of x; what goes wrong?
    (d) How fast do the coefficients of f(x) = x(π² − x²) on (−π, π)
    decay, and why?
    Answer: (a) x² = π²/3 + 4∑ (−1)ⁿ cos nx/n². (b) Yes: it gives
    2x = 4∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n. (c) 1 = 2∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ cos nx, a divergent series.
    (d) bₙ = 12(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n³, decay 1/n³ (extension is C¹ with jumps in f″).
    Teacher explains: INTEGRATION is always allowed (for piecewise
    continuous f), because integrating divides the coefficients by n and
    improves convergence. (a) ∫₀ˣ t dt = x²/2 and
       ∫₀ˣ 2∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nt/n dt = 2∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹(1 − cos nx)/n²
                                 = 2·π²/12 + 2∑ (−1)ⁿ cos nx/n²
    using ∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n² = π²/12. So x² = π²/3 + 4∑ (−1)ⁿ cos nx/n² ✓ (D3).
    DIFFERENTIATION is allowed when the periodic extension is CONTINUOUS and
    piecewise smooth. (b) x² extends continuously: differentiating
    −4n(−1)ⁿ sin nx/n² = 4(−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n gives exactly the series of 2x ✓.
    (c) x extends with jumps (sawtooth); the derived series
    2∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ cos nx has terms not tending to 0, so it diverges everywhere:
    the jumps would contribute delta functions. (d) Rule of thumb: each
    integration by parts produces a boundary term involving the jump of a
    derivative, divided by n. For f = π²x − x³: f(±π) = 0 (no jump),
    f′ = π² − 3x² has f′(π) = f′(−π) = −2π² (no jump), but f″ = −6x jumps
    from −6π to 6π, so the coefficients are ~ 1/n³: indeed
    bₙ = 12(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n³. Common mistakes: differentiating the sawtooth series;
    forgetting the constant of integration (it is fixed by the mean value
    a₀/2). Now you try: integrate the square-wave series from 0 to x to
    get the series of |x|. (|x| = (4/π)∑_{odd}(1 − cos nx)/n², and
    (4/π)(π²/8) = π/2 recovers π/2 − (4/π)∑_{odd} cos nx/n².)

D9. Solve the heat equation u_t = u_xx for 0 < x < π, t > 0, with
    u(0, t) = u(π, t) = 0 and u(x, 0) = x(π − x). Estimate u(π/2, 1).
    Answer: u = (8/π)∑_{n odd} e^(−n²t) sin nx/n³; u(π/2, 1) ≈ 0.9368.
    Teacher explains: SEPARATION of variables: u = X(x)T(t) gives
    X″/X = T′/T = −λ. The boundary conditions X(0) = X(π) = 0 force
    X = sin nx, λ = n² (n = 1, 2, ...), and then T = e^(−n²t). Superpose:
       u(x, t) = ∑ bₙ e^(−n²t) sin nx,  with ∑ bₙ sin nx = x(π − x)
    so bₙ are the HALF-RANGE SINE coefficients of x(π − x):
       bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π (πx − x²) sin nx dx
    Using ∫₀^π x sin nx = π(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n and ∫₀^π x² sin nx = π²(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n +
    2((−1)ⁿ − 1)/n³:
       bₙ = (2/π)[π²(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n − π²(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n − 2((−1)ⁿ − 1)/n³]
          = 4(1 − (−1)ⁿ)/(πn³) = 8/(πn³) for n odd, 0 for n even
    At x = π/2, t = 1: sin(nπ/2) = 1, −1, 1, ... for n = 1, 3, 5:
       u ≈ (8/π)[e⁻¹ − e⁻⁹/27 + ...] ≈ 2.5465 × 0.36788 ≈ 0.9368
    The first term dominates after a short time: higher modes die like
    e^(−n²t). (Initially u(π/2, 0) = π²/4 ≈ 2.467: the rod cools.) Common
    mistakes: using a full-range series; forgetting that the n-th mode
    decays with n², not n. Now you try: for the same rod with
    u(x, 0) = sin x + 3 sin 2x, find u. (e^(−t) sin x + 3e^(−4t) sin 2x)

D10. Define the Fourier transform and its inverse. Compute the transforms
     of (a) the box f(x) = 1 for |x| < a, 0 otherwise; (b) e^(−a|x|);
     (c) e^(−ax)H(x) (a > 0). Use the inversion theorem for (a) at x = 0 to
     evaluate ∫_{−∞}^{∞} sin ω/ω dω.
     Answer: (a) 2 sin(aω)/ω (value 2a at ω = 0). (b) 2a/(a² + ω²).
     (c) 1/(a + iω). ∫ sin ω/ω dω = π.
     Teacher explains: Think of a Fourier series on (−L, L) and let L → ∞:
     the frequencies nπ/L fill the line and the sum becomes an integral.
     With the convention
        F(ω) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f(x)e^(−iωx) dx,   f(x) = (1/2π)∫_{−∞}^{∞} F(ω)e^(iωx) dω
     (valid, e.g., for f absolutely integrable and piecewise smooth, with the
     midpoint value at jumps). (a)
        F = ∫_{−a}^{a} e^(−iωx) dx = [e^(−iωx)/(−iω)]_{−a}^{a}
          = (e^(iaω) − e^(−iaω))/(iω) = 2 sin(aω)/ω
     (b) Split at 0:
        ∫₀^∞ e^(−ax)e^(−iωx) dx = 1/(a + iω)
        ∫_{−∞}^0 e^(ax)e^(−iωx) dx = 1/(a − iω)
        F = 1/(a + iω) + 1/(a − iω) = 2a/(a² + ω²)
     (c) is the first half: 1/(a + iω). Note (b) is real and even because f
     is real and even; (c) is complex because f is not even. Inversion for
     (a) with a = 1 at x = 0 (a point of continuity, f = 1):
        1 = (1/2π)∫ 2 sin ω/ω dω   ⇒   ∫_{−∞}^{∞} sin ω/ω dω = π
     (the same answer as 10.11 D7). At x = 1 the inversion gives 1/2, the
     midpoint of the jump. Common mistakes: mixing conventions (with
     1/√(2π) in front, (b) becomes √(2/π)·a/(a² + ω²)); forgetting the value
     F(0) = ∫ f = 2a for the box. Now you try: transform the triangle
     f(x) = 1 − |x| for |x| < 1, 0 otherwise. (2(1 − cos ω)/ω²
     = 4 sin²(ω/2)/ω²)

D11. Prove the shift, modulation, scaling and derivative rules and the
     convolution theorem. Use the derivative rule to find the transform of
     e^(−x²), and then find the transforms of e^(−(x−1)²), x e^(−x²) and
     e^(−|x|) cos 3x.
     Answer: e^(−x²) ↔ √π e^(−ω²/4); e^(−(x−1)²) ↔ √π e^(−iω)e^(−ω²/4);
     xe^(−x²) ↔ −(iω/2)√π e^(−ω²/4); e^(−|x|)cos 3x ↔ 1/(1 + (ω − 3)²) +
     1/(1 + (ω + 3)²).
     Teacher explains: Each rule is one substitution:
        SHIFT:      ∫ f(x − a)e^(−iωx) dx  (x = s + a)  = e^(−iaω)F(ω)
        MODULATION: ∫ e^(iax)f e^(−iωx) dx = ∫ f e^(−i(ω−a)x) dx = F(ω − a)
        SCALING:    ∫ f(ax)e^(−iωx) dx (s = ax, a > 0) = (1/a)F(ω/a)
        DERIVATIVE: ∫ f′e^(−iωx) dx = [f e^(−iωx)] + iω∫ f e^(−iωx) = iωF
                    (f → 0 at ±∞)
        x·f:        dF/dω = ∫ (−ix)f e^(−iωx) dx, so xf ↔ iF′(ω)
     CONVOLUTION: ∫∫ f(s)g(x − s) ds e^(−iωx) dx; put x = s + t:
        = ∫ f(s)e^(−iωs) ds · ∫ g(t)e^(−iωt) dt = F(ω)G(ω)
     GAUSSIAN: f = e^(−x²) satisfies f′ = −2xf. Transform both sides:
        iωF = −2·iF′(ω)  ⇒  F′ = −(ω/2)F  ⇒  F = F(0)e^(−ω²/4)
     and F(0) = ∫ e^(−x²) dx = √π. So e^(−x²) ↔ √π e^(−ω²/4): a Gaussian
     transforms into a Gaussian (narrow in x ⇔ wide in ω). Then:
        e^(−(x−1)²):  shift by 1       → √π e^(−iω)e^(−ω²/4)
        x e^(−x²):    iF′              → i√π(−ω/2)e^(−ω²/4)
        e^(−|x|)cos 3x = ½(e^(3ix) + e^(−3ix))e^(−|x|): modulation of
                      2/(1 + ω²) → ½[2/(1 + (ω − 3)²) + 2/(1 + (ω + 3)²)]
     Common mistakes: shift sign (f(x − a) gives e^(−iaω), not e^(iaω));
     forgetting 1/|a| in scaling. Now you try: transform e^(−4x²).
     (Scaling with a = 2: ½√π e^(−ω²/16) = √(π/4)e^(−ω²/16).)

D12. State Plancherel's theorem and use it to evaluate
     ∫_{−∞}^{∞} sin²x/x² dx and ∫_{−∞}^{∞} dx/(1 + x²)². Then solve the heat
     equation u_t = u_xx on the whole line with u(x, 0) = e^(−x²).
     Answer: π; π/2; u(x, t) = e^(−x²/(1 + 4t))/√(1 + 4t).
     Teacher explains: PLANCHEREL: ∫ |f|² dx = (1/2π)∫ |F|² dω (more
     generally ∫ f ḡ = (1/2π)∫ F Ḡ). It follows from the convolution theorem
     applied to f(x) * conj f(−x) at x = 0. For the box of half-width 1:
        ∫ |f|² = 2,   F = 2 sin ω/ω
        2 = (1/2π)∫ 4 sin²ω/ω² dω   ⇒   ∫ sin²ω/ω² dω = π
     For f = e^(−|x|): ∫ e^(−2|x|) dx = 1 and F = 2/(1 + ω²):
        1 = (1/2π)∫ 4/(1 + ω²)² dω   ⇒   ∫ dω/(1 + ω²)² = π/2
     (the same as the residue computation of 10.11 M5 b)). HEAT EQUATION:
     transform in x (t is a parameter): U(ω, t) = ∫ u e^(−iωx) dx. Since
     u_xx ↔ (iω)²U = −ω²U:
        U_t = −ω²U  ⇒  U(ω, t) = U(ω, 0)e^(−ω²t) = √π e^(−ω²/4)e^(−ω²t)
                                          = √π e^(−ω²(1 + 4t)/4)
     Compare with e^(−ax²) ↔ √(π/a) e^(−ω²/(4a)) with a = 1/(1 + 4t):
     √(π/a) = √π·√(1 + 4t), so
        u(x, t) = e^(−x²/(1 + 4t))/√(1 + 4t)
     The bump spreads and flattens, keeping ∫ u dx = √π (heat is
     conserved). In general u = u₀ * K_t with the HEAT KERNEL
     K_t(x) = e^(−x²/(4t))/√(4πt), the inverse transform of e^(−ω²t).
     Common mistakes: forgetting the 1/2π in Plancherel; inverting
     e^(−ω²t) without the 1/√(4πt). Now you try: use Plancherel with the
     triangle (D10) to find ∫ sin⁴x/x⁴ dx. (∫ (1 − |x|)² = 2/3 =
     (1/2π)∫ 16 sin⁴(ω/2)/ω⁴ dω; with ω = 2s this gives 2π/3)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY

M1. Evaluate (m, n positive integers where they appear; ∫ means
    ∫_{−π}^{π} unless limits are shown).
    a) ∫ sin 3x sin 5x dx             b) ∫ sin²4x dx
    c) ∫ cos²2x dx                    d) ∫ sin 2x cos 3x dx
    e) ∫ cos 5x dx                    f) ∫ 1 dx
    g) ∫₀^π sin 2x sin 3x dx          h) ∫₀^π cos x sin 2x dx
    i) ∫₀^π sin x cos 2x dx           j) ∫_{−2}^{2} cos²(3πx/2) dx
    k) ∫₀^(2π) e^(3ix)e^(−5ix) dx     l) ∫₀^(2π) |e^(inx)|² dx
    m) ∫ x sin nx dx                  n) ∫ x² cos nx dx
    o) ∫₀^π x sin nx dx               p) ∫ eˣ cos nx dx
    q) ∫ |x| cos nx dx                r) ∫_{−1}^{1} x cos nπx dx
    Answers:
      a) 0                   b) π                   c) π
      d) 0                   e) 0                   f) 2π
      g) 0                   h) 4/3                 i) −2/3
      j) 2                   k) 0                   l) 2π
      m) 2π(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n         n) 4π(−1)ⁿ/n²          o) π(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n
      p) 2(−1)ⁿ sinh π/(1 + n²)                     q) 2((−1)ⁿ − 1)/n²
      r) 0

M2. Fourier series of the 2π-periodic function given on (−π, π) (or on the
    interval shown).
    a) x                            b) x²
    c) |x|                          d) −1 (x < 0), 1 (x > 0)
    e) 0 (x < 0), 1 (x > 0)         f) eˣ
    g) x + x²                       h) |sin x|
    i) 0 (x < 0), x (x > 0)         j) cos²x
    k) sin³x                        l) x³
    m) cosh x                       n) π − x on (0, 2π)
    o) x sin x
    Answers:
      a) 2∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n
      b) π²/3 + 4∑ (−1)ⁿ cos nx/n²
      c) π/2 − (4/π)∑_{n odd} cos nx/n²
      d) (4/π)∑_{n odd} sin nx/n
      e) 1/2 + (2/π)∑_{n odd} sin nx/n
      f) (sinh π/π)[1 + 2∑ (−1)ⁿ(cos nx − n sin nx)/(1 + n²)]
      g) π²/3 + ∑ [4(−1)ⁿ cos nx/n² + 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n]
      h) 2/π − (4/π)∑_{n≥1} cos 2nx/(4n² − 1)
      i) π/4 + ∑ [((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(πn²)] cos nx + ∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n
      j) 1/2 + (1/2)cos 2x
      k) (3/4)sin x − (1/4)sin 3x
      l) ∑ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹(2π²/n − 12/n³) sin nx
      m) (sinh π/π)[1 + 2∑ (−1)ⁿ cos nx/(1 + n²)]
      n) 2∑ sin nx/n
      o) 1 − (1/2)cos x + 2∑_{n≥2} (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ cos nx/(n² − 1)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: before computing anything, sketch the periodic extension:
  it shows the parity (which coefficients vanish), the jumps (where the
  series gives midpoints, decay 1/n) and continuity (decay 1/n²). Keep a
  card with ∫₀^π x sin nx, ∫₀^π x² cos nx, cos nπ = (−1)ⁿ, and insist on
  writing a₀/2. For transforms, fix ONE convention and check every answer
  at ω = 0 (F(0) = ∫ f). Harder: prove Dirichlet's theorem using the
  Dirichlet kernel Dₙ(t) = sin((n + ½)t)/(2 sin(t/2)) and Riemann-Lebesgue;
  prove Fejér's theorem (Cesàro means of the series of a continuous f
  converge uniformly) and deduce Weierstrass approximation; show that
  x ↦ e^(−x²/2) is an eigenfunction of the transform; prove the Poisson
  summation formula ∑ f(n) = ∑ F(2πk) and use it to show
  ∑ e^(−πn²t) = t^(−1/2)∑ e^(−πn²/t); and prove the Heisenberg uncertainty
  inequality, which in this convention reads
  (∫ x²|f|²)(∫ ω²|F|²) ≥ (π/2)(∫ |f|²)², with equality for Gaussians.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.13 — STURM-LIOUVILLE THEORY; SPECIAL FUNCTIONS (GAMMA, BETA,
LEGENDRE, BESSEL)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A STURM-LIOUVILLE (SL) EQUATION is (p(x)y′)′ + q(x)y + λw(x)y = 0 on
    [a, b], with p, p′, q, w continuous, p > 0 and WEIGHT w > 0. A REGULAR SL
    PROBLEM adds SEPARATED boundary conditions α₁y(a) + α₂y′(a) = 0,
    β₁y(b) + β₂y′(b) = 0 (not both α's zero, not both β's zero). PERIODIC
    conditions y(a) = y(b), y′(a) = y′(b) (with p(a) = p(b)) and SINGULAR
    problems (p = 0 at an end, or an infinite interval; then 'y bounded'
    replaces a boundary condition) behave in the same way.
  - Any a₂y″ + a₁y′ + (a₀ + λr)y = 0 (a₂ ≠ 0) becomes SL form with the
    INTEGRATING FACTOR p = exp(∫a₁/a₂ dx), then q = a₀p/a₂ and w = rp/a₂.
  - The operator Ly = (py′)′ + qy is SELF-ADJOINT: LAGRANGE'S IDENTITY
    uLv − vLu = [p(uv′ − vu′)]′ gives GREEN'S FORMULA
    ∫ₐᵇ (uLv − vLu) dx = [p(uv′ − vu′)]ₐᵇ, which is 0 for functions satisfying
    the boundary conditions.
  - THEOREMS for a regular SL problem: all EIGENVALUES are REAL; they are
    SIMPLE (one eigenfunction each, up to a constant) and form an infinite
    sequence λ₁ < λ₂ < λ₃ < ... → ∞; eigenfunctions of different
    eigenvalues are ORTHOGONAL with the weight: ∫ₐᵇ yₘyₙw dx = 0 (m ≠ n); the
    n-th eigenfunction has exactly n − 1 zeros in (a, b) (oscillation); the
    eigenfunctions are COMPLETE: f = ∑ cₙyₙ with cₙ = ∫ f yₙ w / ∫ yₙ² w, in
    the mean-square sense (uniformly if f is smooth and meets the boundary
    conditions). RAYLEIGH QUOTIENT: λ₁ ≤ (∫ p u′² − q u² dx − [p u u′]ₐᵇ)/∫ w u²
    for every admissible trial function u.
  - The model problem y″ + λy = 0 on [0, L]: y(0) = y(L) = 0 gives λₙ = (nπ/L)²,
    sin(nπx/L), n ≥ 1; y′(0) = y′(L) = 0 gives (nπ/L)², cos(nπx/L), n ≥ 0;
    y(0) = 0 = y′(L) gives ((2n − 1)π/(2L))²; periodic on [−L, L] gives
    (nπ/L)² with BOTH cos and sin (eigenvalues double for n ≥ 1). ROBIN
    conditions lead to transcendental equations such as tan k = −k (λ = k²).
  - GAMMA FUNCTION: Γ(x) = ∫₀^∞ t^(x−1) e^(−t) dt (x > 0). Γ(x + 1) = xΓ(x),
    Γ(1) = 1, Γ(n + 1) = n!, Γ(1/2) = √π, Γ(n + 1/2) = (2n)!√π/(4ⁿ n!).
    Extended to x < 0 by Γ(x) = Γ(x + 1)/x; POLES at 0, −1, −2, ... (residue
    (−1)ⁿ/n! at −n). REFLECTION Γ(x)Γ(1 − x) = π/sin πx; DUPLICATION
    Γ(x)Γ(x + 1/2) = 2^(1−2x) √π Γ(2x); STIRLING n! ~ √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ, with
    relative error about 1/(12n).
  - BETA FUNCTION: B(x, y) = ∫₀¹ t^(x−1)(1 − t)^(y−1) dt = Γ(x)Γ(y)/Γ(x + y)
    = 2∫₀^(π/2) sin^(2x−1)θ cos^(2y−1)θ dθ = ∫₀^∞ t^(x−1)/(1 + t)^(x+y) dt.
    Symmetric; B(m, n) = (m − 1)!(n − 1)!/(m + n − 1)! for integers.
  - LEGENDRE'S EQUATION (1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + n(n + 1)y = 0, SL form
    ((1 − x²)y′)′ + n(n + 1)y = 0 on [−1, 1] (singular, w = 1). The series
    solution terminates only for integer n, giving the LEGENDRE POLYNOMIAL
    Pₙ with Pₙ(1) = 1. RODRIGUES: Pₙ(x) = (1/(2ⁿn!)) dⁿ/dxⁿ (x² − 1)ⁿ.
    P₀ = 1, P₁ = x, P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2, P₃ = (5x³ − 3x)/2,
    P₄ = (35x⁴ − 30x² + 3)/8.
  - Legendre facts: GENERATING FUNCTION (1 − 2xt + t²)^(−1/2) = ∑ Pₙ(x)tⁿ;
    BONNET'S RECURRENCE (n + 1)Pₙ₊₁ = (2n + 1)xPₙ − nPₙ₋₁; Pₙ(−x) = (−1)ⁿPₙ(x);
    Pₙ′(1) = n(n + 1)/2; ORTHOGONALITY ∫₋₁¹ PₘPₙ dx = 2δₘₙ/(2n + 1);
    FOURIER-LEGENDRE SERIES f = ∑ cₙPₙ, cₙ = ((2n + 1)/2)∫₋₁¹ f Pₙ dx.
  - BESSEL'S EQUATION x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − ν²)y = 0 (ν ≥ 0). Frobenius gives
    Jᵥ(x) = ∑ₖ (−1)ᵏ/(k! Γ(k + ν + 1)) (x/2)^(2k+ν). General solution
    c₁Jᵥ + c₂J₋ᵥ (ν not an integer) or c₁Jₙ + c₂Yₙ (integer n; J₋ₙ = (−1)ⁿJₙ,
    Yₙ is unbounded at 0). J₁/₂ = √(2/(πx)) sin x, J₋₁/₂ = √(2/(πx)) cos x.
  - BESSEL RECURRENCES: (xᵛJᵥ)′ = xᵛJᵥ₋₁, (x^(−ν)Jᵥ)′ = −x^(−ν)Jᵥ₊₁,
    Jᵥ₋₁ + Jᵥ₊₁ = (2ν/x)Jᵥ, Jᵥ₋₁ − Jᵥ₊₁ = 2Jᵥ′; so J₀′ = −J₁ and
    ∫ xJ₀ dx = xJ₁. Generating function exp((x/2)(t − 1/t)) = ∑ Jₙ(x)tⁿ.
  - BESSEL AS SL: (xy′)′ + (λx − ν²/x)y = 0 on [0, a] has solutions Jᵥ(√λ x);
    y(a) = 0 gives λ = (αᵥₘ/a)² where αᵥₘ are the ZEROS of Jᵥ (J₀: 2.4048,
    5.5201, 8.6537; J₁: 3.8317, 7.0156, 10.1735). ORTHOGONALITY
    ∫₀ᵃ x Jᵥ(αₘx/a)Jᵥ(αₙx/a) dx = (a²/2)Jᵥ₊₁(αₙ)² δₘₙ, giving FOURIER-BESSEL
    series. Equations x²y″ + (1 − 2a)xy′ + (b²c²x^(2c) + a² − ν²c²)y = 0 have
    solutions y = xᵃ Zᵥ(bxᶜ) (Z = J or Y).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Put each equation into Sturm-Liouville form (py′)′ + qy + λwy = 0 and
    name p, q, w: (a) y″ + 2y′ + λy = 0; (b) Legendre
    (1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + λy = 0; (c) x²y″ + xy′ + (λx² − ν²)y = 0; (d) Hermite
    y″ − 2xy′ + λy = 0; (e) Chebyshev (1 − x²)y″ − xy′ + λy = 0.
    Answer: (a) (e^(2x)y′)′ + λe^(2x)y = 0: p = w = e^(2x), q = 0.
    (b) ((1 − x²)y′)′ + λy = 0: p = 1 − x², w = 1. (c) (xy′)′ − (ν²/x)y + λxy
    = 0: p = x, q = −ν²/x, w = x. (d) (e^(−x²)y′)′ + λe^(−x²)y = 0.
    (e) (√(1 − x²) y′)′ + λ(1/√(1 − x²))y = 0.
    Teacher explains: Write the equation as a₂y″ + a₁y′ + (a₀ + λr)y = 0 and
    multiply by an unknown p/a₂. We want the first two terms to become (py′)′
    = py″ + p′y′, so we need p′/p = a₁/a₂:
       p = exp(∫ a₁/a₂ dx),   q = a₀p/a₂,   w = rp/a₂.
    (a) a₂ = 1, a₁ = 2, r = 1: p = e^(2x); multiplying by e^(2x):
       e^(2x)y″ + 2e^(2x)y′ = (e^(2x)y′)′ ✓.
    (b) Already in form: (1 − x²)′ = −2x, so the first two terms ARE
    ((1 − x²)y′)′. (c) Divide by x (a₂ = x², a₁ = x): p = exp(∫ 1/x) = x,
    q = −ν²x/x² = −ν²/x, w = x²·x/x² = x. (d) p = exp(∫ −2x dx) = e^(−x²).
    (e) p = exp(∫ −x/(1 − x²) dx) = exp(½ ln(1 − x²)) = √(1 − x²) and
    w = p/a₂ = 1/√(1 − x²). Why bother: the weight w is exactly the one for
    which the eigenfunctions are orthogonal (Hermite polynomials with
    e^(−x²), Chebyshev polynomials with 1/√(1 − x²)). Common mistakes:
    forgetting to divide by a₂ before integrating a₁/a₂; taking w = r
    instead of rp/a₂. Now you try: Laguerre xy″ + (1 − x)y′ + λy = 0.
    ((xe^(−x)y′)′ + λe^(−x)y = 0: p = xe^(−x), w = e^(−x))

D2. Let L y = (py′)′ + qy. Prove Lagrange's identity and Green's formula,
    and deduce that for a regular SL problem with separated boundary
    conditions (a) every eigenvalue is real, (b) eigenfunctions of distinct
    eigenvalues are orthogonal with weight w, (c) each eigenvalue is simple.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: Lagrange: expand, the p′-terms and q-terms cancel:
       uLv − vLu = u(pv′)′ − v(pu′)′ = [p(uv′ − vu′)]′
    (differentiate the right side: p′(uv′ − vu′) + p(u′v′ + uv″ − v′u′ − vu″)
    = u(p′v′ + pv″) − v(p′u′ + pu″) ✓). Integrating gives Green's formula
       ∫ₐᵇ (uLv − vLu) dx = [p(uv′ − vu′)]ₐᵇ.
    At x = a both u and v satisfy α₁y + α₂y′ = 0 with (α₁, α₂) ≠ (0, 0), so
    the vectors (u(a), u′(a)) and (v(a), v′(a)) are both perpendicular to
    (α₁, α₂), hence parallel, and the WRONSKIAN uv′ − vu′ is 0 at a; same at
    b. So ∫(uLv − vLu) = 0: L is SELF-ADJOINT.
    (a) Let Ly = −λwy with y ≠ 0, possibly complex. The conjugate ȳ satisfies
    the same (p, q, w real): Lȳ = −λ̄wȳ. Green with u = ȳ, v = y:
       0 = ∫ (ȳLy − yLȳ) = (λ̄ − λ) ∫ w|y|² dx
    and ∫ w|y|² > 0, so λ̄ = λ: λ is real.
    (b) Lyₘ = −λₘwyₘ, Lyₙ = −λₙwyₙ; Green with u = yₘ, v = yₙ:
       0 = ∫ (yₘLyₙ − yₙLyₘ) = (λₘ − λₙ) ∫ yₘyₙw dx
    and λₘ ≠ λₙ gives ∫ₐᵇ yₘyₙw dx = 0.
    (c) If u, v are eigenfunctions for the same λ, their Wronskian is 0 at a
    (shown above). Since W(x) = C/p(x) (Abel), W ≡ 0 and u, v are dependent.
    Note (c) FAILS for periodic conditions: cos nx and sin nx share λ = n².
    Common mistakes: forgetting the boundary term; claiming orthogonality in
    the plain sense ∫ yₘyₙ = 0 when w ≢ 1. Now you try: why does Green's
    formula need no boundary condition for Legendre's equation on [−1, 1]?
    (p = 1 − x² is 0 at ±1, so the boundary term vanishes for bounded
    solutions.)

D3. Find all eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of y″ + λy = 0 on [0, L] with
    (a) y(0) = y(L) = 0; (b) y′(0) = y′(L) = 0; (c) y(0) = 0, y′(L) = 0.
    Answer: (a) λₙ = (nπ/L)², yₙ = sin(nπx/L), n = 1, 2, ... (b) λₙ = (nπ/L)²,
    yₙ = cos(nπx/L), n = 0, 1, 2, ... (λ₀ = 0, y₀ = 1). (c) λₙ =
    ((2n − 1)π/(2L))², yₙ = sin((2n − 1)πx/(2L)), n = 1, 2, ...
    Teacher explains: Always split into THREE cases.
       λ = −μ² < 0:  y = A cosh μx + B sinh μx
       λ = 0:        y = A + Bx
       λ = k² > 0:   y = A cos kx + B sin kx
    (a) λ < 0: y(0) = A = 0, y(L) = B sinh μL = 0 ⇒ B = 0 (sinh μL > 0).
    λ = 0: A = 0, BL = 0. No eigenvalues there. λ = k²: A = 0 and
    B sin kL = 0; for a NON-ZERO solution B ≠ 0, so sin kL = 0, kL = nπ,
       λₙ = n²π²/L²,   yₙ = sin(nπx/L),   n = 1, 2, 3, ...
    (n = 0 gives y ≡ 0 and negative n repeat the same functions.)
    (b) y′ = −Ak sin kx + Bk cos kx: y′(0) = Bk = 0 ⇒ B = 0; y′(L) =
    −Ak sin kL = 0 ⇒ kL = nπ. Now λ = 0 IS an eigenvalue: y = A + Bx,
    y′ = B = 0, so y = 1 works. λ < 0 gives only 0.
    (c) λ = k²: A = 0, y′(L) = Bk cos kL = 0 ⇒ kL = π/2, 3π/2, ...
    Check the SL theorems: eigenvalues real, increasing to ∞; sin(nπx/L) has
    n − 1 zeros inside (0, L); and ∫₀ᴸ sin(mπx/L) sin(nπx/L) dx = 0 (m ≠ n),
    = L/2 (m = n). These are exactly the Fourier sine and cosine series.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the case λ = 0 (vital in (b)); listing n = 0
    in (a). Now you try: y″ + λy = 0, y′(0) = 0, y(1) = 0. (λₙ =
    ((2n − 1)π/2)², yₙ = cos((2n − 1)πx/2))

D4. Solve y″ + λy = 0, y(0) = 0, y′(1) + y(1) = 0. Show there are no
    eigenvalues λ ≤ 0, find the equation for λ > 0, estimate λ₁ and λ₂,
    and give the large-n behaviour.
    Answer: λ = k² where tan k = −k; λ₁ ≈ 4.1159 (k ≈ 2.0288), λ₂ ≈ 24.139
    (k ≈ 4.9132); kₙ ≈ (2n − 1)π/2 for large n. Eigenfunctions sin(kₙx).
    Teacher explains: y(0) = 0 kills the cosh/cos/constant part.
       λ = −μ²: y = sinh μx; y′(1) + y(1) = μ cosh μ + sinh μ > 0 ⇒ none.
       λ = 0:   y = x;       y′(1) + y(1) = 1 + 1 = 2 ≠ 0 ⇒ none.
       λ = k²:  y = sin kx;  k cos k + sin k = 0 ⇔ tan k = −k.
    Graphically the line y = −k meets the branches of tan k once in each
    interval ((2n − 1)π/2, nπ): just to the right of π/2, 3π/2, ... Newton's
    method on f(k) = tan k + k from k₀ = 2:
       k₁ ≈ 2.028758,  λ₁ = k₁² ≈ 4.1159
       k₂ ≈ 4.913180,  λ₂ ≈ 24.139
    As n grows, −k is a steep negative value, so tan k must be near its pole:
    kₙ → (2n − 1)π/2 from above. A second way to see λ > 0 without cases is
    the RAYLEIGH QUOTIENT: multiply −y″ = λy by y and integrate by parts,
       λ∫₀¹ y² = ∫₀¹ y′² − [yy′]₀¹ = ∫₀¹ y′² + y(1)² > 0.
    Common mistakes: writing tan k = k (sign error); looking for the first
    root in (0, π/2) where tan k > 0 > −k is impossible. Now you try: for
    y(0) = 0, y′(1) = y(1) show λ = 0 is an eigenvalue. (y = x: y′(1) = 1 =
    y(1); the positive ones solve tan k = k, λ ≈ 20.19, 59.68)

D5. Solve the SL problem x²y″ + xy′ + λy = 0, y(1) = 0, y(e) = 0. Put it in
    SL form, check orthogonality of the eigenfunctions, and expand f(x) = 1
    on [1, e] in them.
    Answer: λₙ = n²π², yₙ = sin(nπ ln x), n ≥ 1; SL form (xy′)′ + (λ/x)y = 0,
    weight 1/x; 1 = (4/π) ∑ (n odd) sin(nπ ln x)/n.
    Teacher explains: It is a CAUCHY-EULER equation: try y = xʳ,
    r(r − 1) + r + λ = r² + λ = 0.
       λ < 0 (λ = −μ²): y = Ax^μ + Bx^(−μ); A + B = 0, Ae^μ + Be^(−μ) = 0 ⇒
                        A(e^μ − e^(−μ)) = 0 ⇒ A = B = 0.
       λ = 0:           y = A + B ln x; A = 0, B = 0.
       λ = k² > 0:      y = A cos(k ln x) + B sin(k ln x); A = 0, sin k = 0.
    So k = nπ. SL form: divide by x: xy″ + y′ = (xy′)′, giving
    (xy′)′ + λ(1/x)y = 0 with p = x, w = 1/x. Orthogonality with weight 1/x,
    substituting u = ln x (du = dx/x):
       ∫₁ᵉ sin(mπ ln x) sin(nπ ln x) dx/x = ∫₀¹ sin mπu sin nπu du = δₘₙ/2.
    The expansion coefficient of f = 1 is
       cₙ = ∫₁ᵉ yₙ (1/x) dx / ∫₁ᵉ yₙ² (1/x) dx = 2∫₀¹ sin nπu du
          = 2(1 − (−1)ⁿ)/(nπ) = 4/(nπ) (n odd), 0 (n even).
    So 1 = (4/π)[sin(π ln x) + sin(3π ln x)/3 + ...] for 1 < x < e (at the
    ends the series gives 0, the average of the odd extension). The weight is
    not decoration: without 1/x the functions are NOT orthogonal. Common
    mistakes: using ∫ yₘyₙ dx; forgetting the λ ≤ 0 cases. Now you try:
    expand f(x) = ln x on [1, e]. (cₙ = 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/(nπ), the sine series of u on
    [0, 1])

D6. Define Γ(x), show that the integral converges for x > 0, prove
    Γ(x + 1) = xΓ(x) and Γ(n + 1) = n!, prove Γ(1/2) = √π, and compute Γ(5/2),
    Γ(−1/2), Γ(−3/2).
    Answer: Γ(5/2) = 3√π/4 ≈ 1.3293; Γ(−1/2) = −2√π ≈ −3.5449;
    Γ(−3/2) = 4√π/3 ≈ 2.3633.
    Teacher explains: Γ(x) = ∫₀^∞ t^(x−1)e^(−t) dt. Two dangers. Near 0:
    t^(x−1)e^(−t) ≤ t^(x−1), and ∫₀¹ t^(x−1) dt = 1/x converges iff x > 0. Near ∞:
    t^(x−1)e^(−t) ≤ e^(−t/2) for large t (exponentials beat powers), which is
    integrable. Recursion by parts (u = tˣ, dv = e^(−t)dt):
       Γ(x + 1) = [−tˣe^(−t)]₀^∞ + x∫₀^∞ t^(x−1)e^(−t) dt = 0 + xΓ(x).
    Γ(1) = ∫₀^∞ e^(−t) dt = 1, so Γ(2) = 1, Γ(3) = 2·1, ..., Γ(n + 1) = n!.
    For Γ(1/2) substitute t = u² (dt = 2u du):
       Γ(1/2) = ∫₀^∞ t^(−1/2)e^(−t) dt = 2∫₀^∞ e^(−u²) du = 2I.
    Square I and use polar coordinates in the first quadrant:
       I² = ∫₀^∞∫₀^∞ e^(−(u²+v²)) du dv = ∫₀^(π/2)∫₀^∞ e^(−r²) r dr dθ
          = (π/2)(1/2) = π/4,   I = √π/2,   Γ(1/2) = √π.
    Now step with Γ(x + 1) = xΓ(x):
       Γ(3/2) = ½Γ(1/2) = √π/2,   Γ(5/2) = (3/2)Γ(3/2) = 3√π/4.
    For negative x use it backwards, Γ(x) = Γ(x + 1)/x, which DEFINES Γ there:
       Γ(−1/2) = Γ(1/2)/(−1/2) = −2√π,  Γ(−3/2) = Γ(−1/2)/(−3/2) = 4√π/3.
    At x = 0, −1, −2, ... this would divide by 0: Γ has POLES there, and
    1/Γ(x) = 0 at those points (used for Bessel functions). Common mistakes:
    Γ(n) = n! (it is (n − 1)!); forgetting the sign alternation for
    negative half-integers. Now you try: Γ(7/2) and Γ(−5/2). (15√π/8;
    −8√π/15)

D7. Prove B(x, y) = Γ(x)Γ(y)/Γ(x + y) and the trigonometric form, then
    evaluate (a) ∫₀¹ x⁴(1 − x)³ dx, (b) ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁴θ cos⁶θ dθ,
    (c) ∫₀^∞ dx/(1 + x⁴).
    Answer: (a) 1/280; (b) 3π/512 ≈ 0.018408; (c) π/(2√2) ≈ 1.1107.
    Teacher explains: TRIG FORM: put t = sin²θ in B(x, y) = ∫₀¹ t^(x−1)(1−t)^(y−1)
    dt; dt = 2 sin θ cos θ dθ, so
       B(x, y) = 2∫₀^(π/2) sin^(2x−1)θ cos^(2y−1)θ dθ.
    PRODUCT: in Γ(x) = 2∫₀^∞ u^(2x−1)e^(−u²) du (t = u²) and similarly Γ(y),
       Γ(x)Γ(y) = 4∫₀^∞∫₀^∞ u^(2x−1)v^(2y−1)e^(−(u²+v²)) du dv.
    Polar coordinates u = r cos θ, v = r sin θ, du dv = r dr dθ:
       = [2∫₀^∞ r^(2x+2y−1)e^(−r²) dr]·[2∫₀^(π/2) cos^(2x−1)θ sin^(2y−1)θ dθ]
       = Γ(x + y)·B(y, x) = Γ(x + y)B(x, y)       (B is symmetric).
    (a) exponents 4 = x − 1, 3 = y − 1:
       B(5, 4) = Γ(5)Γ(4)/Γ(9) = 24·6/40320 = 1/280.
    (b) 2x − 1 = 4, 2y − 1 = 6 ⇒ x = 5/2, y = 7/2:
       ½B(5/2, 7/2) = ½·(3√π/4)(15√π/8)/Γ(6) = ½·(45π/32)/120 = 3π/512.
    (c) Put t = x⁴, x = t^(1/4), dx = ¼t^(−3/4) dt:
       ∫₀^∞ dx/(1 + x⁴) = ¼∫₀^∞ t^(−3/4)/(1 + t) dt = ¼B(1/4, 3/4)
                       = ¼Γ(1/4)Γ(3/4) = ¼·π/sin(π/4) = π/(2√2)
    using the fourth form B(x, y) = ∫₀^∞ t^(x−1)/(1 + t)^(x+y) dt and the
    reflection formula (D8). Common mistakes: in (b) using the exponents
    themselves instead of solving 2x − 1 = 4; forgetting the factor ½.
    Now you try: ∫₀^(π/2) sin³θ cos²θ dθ. (½B(2, 3/2) = 2/15; check:
    ∫₀¹ (u² − u⁴) du = 1/3 − 1/5)

D8. State the reflection and duplication formulas and use them to find
    Γ(1/2), Γ(1/4)Γ(3/4) and Γ(1/3)Γ(2/3); check duplication at x = 1/4.
    Then explain Stirling's formula and test it on 10! (with and without the
    correction factor 1 + 1/(12n)).
    Answer: Γ(1/2)² = π; Γ(1/4)Γ(3/4) = π√2; Γ(1/3)Γ(2/3) = 2π/√3.
    Stirling: 10! ≈ 3 598 696 (true 3 628 800, error 0.83%); with the
    correction ≈ 3 628 685 (error 0.003%).
    Teacher explains: REFLECTION Γ(x)Γ(1 − x) = π/sin πx (0 < x < 1; proved
    from B(x, 1 − x) = ∫₀^∞ t^(x−1)/(1 + t) dt = π/sin πx by contour
    integration). Uses:
       x = 1/2:  Γ(1/2)² = π/1          ⇒ Γ(1/2) = √π (positive)
       x = 1/4:  Γ(1/4)Γ(3/4) = π/sin(π/4) = π√2
       x = 1/3:  Γ(1/3)Γ(2/3) = π/(√3/2) = 2π/√3
    DUPLICATION Γ(x)Γ(x + 1/2) = 2^(1−2x)√π Γ(2x). At x = 1/4 the right side is
    2^(1/2)√π Γ(1/2) = √2 π, agreeing with reflection ✓. STIRLING: write
       n! = Γ(n + 1) = ∫₀^∞ e^(n ln t − t) dt.
    The exponent φ(t) = n ln t − t is largest at t = n with φ(n) = n ln n − n
    and φ″(n) = −1/n. Near the peak φ(t) ≈ n ln n − n − (t − n)²/(2n), and the
    Gaussian integral gives
       n! ≈ e^(n ln n − n) ∫ e^(−(t−n)²/(2n)) dt = (n/e)ⁿ √(2πn)   (LAPLACE's
    method). For n = 10:
       √(20π) (10/e)¹⁰ ≈ 7.9267 × 453 999.3 ≈ 3 598 696
    Ratio 0.99170, i.e. 0.83% too small, close to 1/(12n) = 0.0083. Times
    (1 + 1/120) it becomes ≈ 3 628 685, only 115 short. Stirling is used for
    limits such as (n!)^(1/n)/n → 1/e and for ln n! ≈ n ln n − n. Common
    mistakes: forgetting the √(2πn) factor; using reflection outside its
    meaning at integers (sin πx = 0 matches the poles of Γ). Now you try:
    Stirling for 5!. (√(10π)(5/e)⁵ ≈ 118.02; with 1 + 1/60 ≈ 119.99)

D9. Solve Legendre's equation (1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + n(n + 1)y = 0 by power
    series, show that one solution is a polynomial when n is a non-negative
    integer, and obtain P₃ from the series, P₂ from Rodrigues' formula, and
    P₃ again from Bonnet's recurrence.
    Answer: aₖ₊₂ = −(n − k)(n + k + 1)aₖ/((k + 1)(k + 2)); P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2,
    P₃ = (5x³ − 3x)/2.
    Teacher explains: x = 0 is an ordinary point, so put y = ∑ aₖxᵏ. Collect
    the coefficient of xᵏ:
       (k + 2)(k + 1)aₖ₊₂ − k(k − 1)aₖ − 2kaₖ + n(n + 1)aₖ = 0
       aₖ₊₂ = [k(k + 1) − n(n + 1)]/((k + 1)(k + 2)) · aₖ
            = −(n − k)(n + k + 1)/((k + 1)(k + 2)) · aₖ.
    a₀ starts the even series, a₁ the odd one. At k = n the factor (n − k)
    is 0, so the series with the same parity as n STOPS: a polynomial of
    degree n. The other series is infinite and blows up at x = ±1 (it gives
    Qₙ, with a log singularity). n = 3, odd series, a₁ = 1:
       a₃ = −(3 − 1)(3 + 2)/(2·3) · 1 = −5/3,   a₅ = 0 (factor n − k = 0)
    y = x − 5x³/3, and y(1) = −2/3. Normalising to Pₙ(1) = 1 multiplies by
    −3/2: P₃ = (5x³ − 3x)/2. Rodrigues for n = 2:
       (x² − 1)² = x⁴ − 2x² + 1,  d²/dx² = 12x² − 4,  P₂ = (12x² − 4)/(2²·2!)
                 = (3x² − 1)/2.
    Bonnet with n = 2: 3P₃ = 5xP₂ − 2P₁ = (15x³ − 5x)/2 − 2x = (15x³ − 9x)/2,
    so P₃ = (5x³ − 3x)/2 again. Three methods, one answer. Common mistakes:
    forgetting to normalise Pₙ(1) = 1; using the wrong parity series.
    Now you try: build P₄ from the even series. (a₂ = −10a₀, a₄ = (35/3)a₀;
    1 − 10x² + 35x⁴/3 at x = 1 is 8/3; P₄ = (35x⁴ − 30x² + 3)/8)

D10. Prove ∫₋₁¹ PₘPₙ dx = 0 (m ≠ n) and ∫₋₁¹ Pₙ² dx = 2/(2n + 1). From the
     generating function find Pₙ(1) and Pₙ(−1). Then find the first three
     non-zero terms of the Fourier-Legendre series of f(x) = |x| and the best
     quadratic approximation to |x| on [−1, 1] in the mean-square sense.
     Answer: |x| = ½P₀ + (5/8)P₂ − (3/16)P₄ + ...; best quadratic
     (3 + 15x²)/16. Pₙ(1) = 1, Pₙ(−1) = (−1)ⁿ.
     Teacher explains: ORTHOGONALITY comes free from D2: Pₘ, Pₙ are
     eigenfunctions of ((1 − x²)y′)′ + λy = 0 with λ = m(m + 1) ≠ n(n + 1), and
     the boundary term p(uv′ − vu′) vanishes at ±1 because p = 1 − x² = 0.
     NORM via Rodrigues, writing Dⁿ = dⁿ/dxⁿ and integrating by parts n times
     (the boundary terms vanish since (x² − 1)ⁿ has n-fold zeros at ±1):
        ∫ Pₙ² = (1/(2ⁿn!))² ∫ Dⁿ(x²−1)ⁿ · Dⁿ(x²−1)ⁿ
              = (1/(2ⁿn!))² (−1)ⁿ ∫ (x² − 1)ⁿ D²ⁿ(x² − 1)ⁿ dx
              = (1/(2ⁿn!))² (2n)! ∫₋₁¹ (1 − x²)ⁿ dx.
     With x = 2t − 1 the last integral is 2²ⁿ⁺¹B(n + 1, n + 1) =
     2²ⁿ⁺¹(n!)²/(2n + 1)!, and everything cancels to 2/(2n + 1).
     GENERATING FUNCTION at x = 1: (1 − 2t + t²)^(−1/2) = 1/(1 − t) = ∑ tⁿ, so
     Pₙ(1) = 1; at x = −1: 1/(1 + t) = ∑ (−1)ⁿtⁿ. SERIES of |x|: it is even,
     so only even n appear; cₙ = ((2n + 1)/2)·2∫₀¹ x Pₙ dx:
        c₀ = ½·2·½ = 1/2
        c₂ = (5/2)·2∫₀¹ x(3x² − 1)/2 dx = 5·(3/4 − 1/2)/2 = 5/8
        c₄ = (9/2)·2∫₀¹ x(35x⁴ − 30x² + 3)/8 dx = 9(35/6 − 15/2 + 3/2)/8 = −3/16
     The partial sum c₀P₀ + c₂P₂ is the BEST mean-square approximation of
     degree ≤ 2 (orthogonal projection): ½ + (5/8)(3x² − 1)/2 = (3 + 15x²)/16.
     Common mistakes: forgetting the factor (2n + 1)/2; treating Pₙ as
     orthonormal. Now you try: write x³ in Legendre polynomials.
     (x³ = (3/5)P₁ + (2/5)P₃)

D11. Solve Bessel's equation x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − ν²)y = 0 by the Frobenius
     method, obtain Jᵥ, prove J₁/₂(x) = √(2/(πx)) sin x and J₋ₙ = (−1)ⁿJₙ,
     and state the general solution.
     Answer: Jᵥ(x) = ∑ₖ₌₀^∞ (−1)ᵏ(x/2)^(2k+ν)/(k!Γ(k + ν + 1)); general solution
     c₁Jᵥ + c₂J₋ᵥ (ν ∉ Z), c₁Jₙ + c₂Yₙ (ν = n ∈ Z).
     Teacher explains: x = 0 is a REGULAR SINGULAR point; put y = ∑ aₖx^(k+r),
     a₀ ≠ 0. Substituting, the coefficient of x^(k+r) is
        [(k + r)² − ν²]aₖ + aₖ₋₂ = 0     (a₋₁ = a₋₂ = 0).
     k = 0 gives the INDICIAL equation r² − ν² = 0, r = ±ν. Take r = ν. k = 1:
     ((1 + ν)² − ν²)a₁ = 0 ⇒ a₁ = 0, and so all odd a's vanish. Then
        a₂ₘ = −a₂ₘ₋₂/(2m(2m + 2ν)) = −a₂ₘ₋₂/(4m(m + ν))
        a₂ₘ = (−1)ᵐa₀/(4ᵐ m!(ν + 1)(ν + 2)...(ν + m)).
     Choosing a₀ = 1/(2ᵛΓ(ν + 1)) and using Γ(ν + m + 1) = (ν + m)...(ν + 1)Γ(ν + 1)
     gives the series for Jᵥ. For ν = 1/2 use Γ(k + 3/2) = (2k + 1)!√π/(2²ᵏ⁺¹k!):
        J₁/₂ = ∑ (−1)ᵏ(x/2)^(2k+1/2) 2²ᵏ⁺¹k!/(k!(2k + 1)!√π)
             = √(2/(πx)) ∑ (−1)ᵏx²ᵏ⁺¹/(2k + 1)! = √(2/(πx)) sin x.
     For ν = −n (integer) the terms k = 0, ..., n − 1 have 1/Γ(k − n + 1) = 0;
     shifting k = m + n,
        J₋ₙ = ∑ₘ (−1)ᵐ⁺ⁿ(x/2)^(2m+n)/((m + n)! m!) = (−1)ⁿJₙ,
     so for integer ν the two Frobenius solutions are dependent and a second
     solution Yₙ (Neumann/Weber, with a log x term, unbounded at 0) is needed.
     Common mistakes: forgetting a₁ = 0; using J₋ₙ as the second solution.
     Now you try: show J₋₁/₂(x) = √(2/(πx)) cos x. (the same computation with
     Γ(k + 1/2) = (2k)!√π/(4ᵏk!) gives the cosine series)

D12. Prove (xᵛJᵥ)′ = xᵛJᵥ₋₁ and (x^(−ν)Jᵥ)′ = −x^(−ν)Jᵥ₊₁, deduce the two
     standard recurrences, and use them to find J₀′, ∫ xJ₀ dx and J₂(1) (given
     J₀(1) ≈ 0.7652, J₁(1) ≈ 0.4401). Prove orthogonality of J₀(αₘx) on [0, 1]
     (αₘ zeros of J₀), and find the Fourier-Bessel series of f(x) = 1.
     Answer: J₀′ = −J₁; ∫ xJ₀ = xJ₁ + C; J₂(1) ≈ 0.1149;
     1 = ∑ 2J₀(αₙx)/(αₙJ₁(αₙ)) with coefficients ≈ 1.6020, −1.0648, 0.8514, ...
     Teacher explains: From the series,
        xᵛJᵥ = ∑ (−1)ᵏ x^(2k+2ν)/(2^(2k+ν)k!Γ(k + ν + 1)).
     Differentiate term by term; (2k + 2ν)/Γ(k + ν + 1) = 2/Γ(k + ν):
        (xᵛJᵥ)′ = ∑ (−1)ᵏ x^(2k+2ν−1)/(2^(2k+ν−1)k!Γ(k + ν)) = xᵛJᵥ₋₁.
     The second is similar (the k = 0 term is constant and drops out).
     Expanding the products: xJᵥ′ + νJᵥ = xJᵥ₋₁ and xJᵥ′ − νJᵥ = −xJᵥ₊₁. Add
     and subtract:
        Jᵥ₋₁ − Jᵥ₊₁ = 2Jᵥ′,        Jᵥ₋₁ + Jᵥ₊₁ = (2ν/x)Jᵥ.
     ν = 0 in the second identity: J₀′ = −J₁. ν = 1 in the first: (xJ₁)′ = xJ₀, so
     ∫ xJ₀ dx = xJ₁ + C. ν = 1 in the recurrence at x = 1:
        J₂(1) = 2J₁(1) − J₀(1) ≈ 0.8801 − 0.7652 = 0.1149.
     ORTHOGONALITY: u = J₀(αx), v = J₀(βx) satisfy (xu′)′ + α²xu = 0,
     (xv′)′ + β²xv = 0. Multiply crosswise and subtract (Lagrange):
        (β² − α²)∫₀¹ xuv dx = [x(uv′ − vu′)]₀¹ = 0   if J₀(α) = J₀(β) = 0.
     The norm is ∫₀¹ xJ₀(αₙx)² dx = J₁(αₙ)²/2. So for f = 1:
        cₙ = 2∫₀¹ xJ₀(αₙx) dx / J₁(αₙ)² = 2[xJ₁(αₙx)/αₙ]₀¹/J₁(αₙ)²
           = 2/(αₙJ₁(αₙ)).
     With α₁ = 2.4048, J₁(α₁) = 0.5191: c₁ ≈ 1.6020; α₂ = 5.5201,
     J₁(α₂) = −0.3403: c₂ ≈ −1.0648; α₃ = 8.6537, J₁ = 0.2715: c₃ ≈ 0.8514.
     This is how a circular drum or a cooling cylinder is solved: the modes
     are J₀(αₙr/a). Common mistakes: forgetting the weight x; dividing by
     J₀(αₙ)² (which is 0) instead of J₁(αₙ)². Now you try: ∫ x³J₀ dx.
     (By parts with u = x², dv = xJ₀ dx: x³J₁ − 2x²J₂ + C)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------

      g) −√(2/(πx)) (cos x/x + sin x)
      h) √(2/(πx)) ((3/x² − 1) sin x − (3/x) cos x)
      i) (2/x)J₁ − J₀                     j) (8/x² − 1)J₁ − (4/x)J₀
      k) −J₁                              l) J₀ − J₁/x
      m) (1 − 4/x²)J₁ + (2/x)J₀           n) −J₃
      o) 1 − 1/4 + 1/64 − 1/2304 ≈ 0.7652
      p) 0.4401      q) 0.1149      r) −J₃(2)      s) 1, 0
      t) 1 (put t = 1 in the generating function)
      u) J₀(x)

M10. Bessel integrals and equations reducible to Bessel's equation (general
     solution; Z denotes J or Y).
     a) ∫ xJ₀ dx                          b) ∫ J₁ dx
     c) ∫ x²J₁ dx                         d) ∫ x⁻¹J₂ dx
     e) ∫ x³J₀ dx                         f) ∫ J₃ dx
     g) ∫₀¹ xJ₀(x) dx (4 d.p.)            h) ∫₀^∞ J₀ dx
     i) x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − 9)y = 0        j) x²y″ + xy′ + (4x² − 1)y = 0
     k) x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − 1/4)y = 0      l) xy″ + y′ + xy = 0
     m) xy″ + y′ + 4xy = 0                n) xy″ + y′ + y = 0
     o) y″ + xy = 0                       p) x²y″ + 3xy′ + x²y = 0
     q) x²y″ − xy′ + x²y = 0              r) 4x²y″ + 4xy′ + (x² − 1)y = 0
     Answers:
       a) xJ₁ + C                         b) −J₀ + C
       c) x²J₂ + C                        d) −x⁻¹J₁ + C
       e) x³J₁ − 2x²J₂ + C (= (x³ − 4x)J₁ + 2x²J₀ + C)
       f) −J₀ − 2J₂ + C                   g) J₁(1) ≈ 0.4401
       h) 1
       i) c₁J₃(x) + c₂Y₃(x)               j) c₁J₁(2x) + c₂Y₁(2x)
       k) (c₁ sin x + c₂ cos x)/√x        l) c₁J₀(x) + c₂Y₀(x)
       m) c₁J₀(2x) + c₂Y₀(2x)             n) c₁J₀(2√x) + c₂Y₀(2√x)
       o) √x [c₁J₁/₃((2/3)x^(3/2)) + c₂J₋₁/₃((2/3)x^(3/2))]
       p) x⁻¹[c₁J₁(x) + c₂Y₁(x)]          q) x[c₁J₁(x) + c₂Y₁(x)]
       r) (c₁ sin(x/2) + c₂ cos(x/2))/√x

M11. Zeros, Bessel eigenvalue problems and Fourier-Bessel series (4 s.f.).
     a) first three positive zeros of J₀  b) first three positive zeros of J₁

     e) (xy′)′ + λxy = 0 on [0, 1], y(1) = 0, y bounded: λ₁, λ₂, λ₃

     j) Fourier-Bessel coefficients c₁, c₂, c₃ of f = 1 in J₀(αₙx) on [0, 1]

M12. Mixed Gamma-function applications.
     a) volume of the unit ball in R², R³, R⁴, R⁵ (Vₙ = π^(n/2)/Γ(n/2 + 1))
     b) surface area of the unit sphere in R⁴ (nVₙ)

       h) 1/x         i) 1/(6·B(4, 3)) = 60/6 = 10
       j) n = 1: Γ(3/2)/Γ(1) = √π/2 ≈ 0.886; n = 4: (105√π/16)/(6·2) ≈ 0.969
