TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: compute left and right cosets side by side in S₃ until
  'normal = left cosets equal right cosets' is felt; teach the relabelling
  rule for conjugation in Sₙ and the one-line kernel test (gng⁻¹ ∈ N); for a
  quotient, always write |G/N| first, then the orders of a few cosets,
  then match with the small groups list; for isomorphism questions, build
  a table of invariants (order, abelian, element-order counts, centre).
  Insist that every map out of Zₘ be checked for well-definedness
  (m·φ(1) = 0). Harder: prove that a subgroup of index p, the smallest prime
  dividing |G|, is normal; show that Aut(S₃) ≅ S₃ and Aut(Q₈) ≅ S₄; prove that
  G′ is normal and that G/G′ is the largest abelian quotient; prove the
  correspondence theorem in full; show that A₅ is simple from its class
  sizes 1, 12, 12, 15, 20; and prove that (Q, +) has no proper subgroup of
  finite index.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.17 — PERMUTATION GROUPS; GROUP ACTIONS; SYLOW THEOREMS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The SYMMETRIC GROUP Sₙ is the group of all bijections of {1, ..., n}
    under composition; |Sₙ| = n!. Convention used here: στ means 'first τ,
    then σ' (right to left). A permutation is written in TWO-LINE notation
    or in CYCLE notation: (a₁ a₂ ... aₖ) sends a₁ → a₂ → ... → aₖ → a₁ and
    fixes everything else (a k-CYCLE; a 2-cycle is a TRANSPOSITION).
  - Every permutation is a product of DISJOINT CYCLES, unique up to order of
    the cycles; disjoint cycles COMMUTE. The CYCLE TYPE is the list of cycle
    lengths (a PARTITION of n). The ORDER of σ is the LCM of its cycle
    lengths. A k-cycle raised to the power m splits into gcd(k, m) cycles of
    length k/gcd(k, m).
  - Every permutation is a product of TRANSPOSITIONS:
    (a₁ a₂ ... aₖ) = (a₁ aₖ)(a₁ aₖ₋₁)...(a₁ a₂), k − 1 of them. The parity of
    the number of transpositions is well defined: the SIGN
    sgn(σ) = (−1)^(n − c(σ)) = (−1)^(∑(length − 1)), where c(σ) counts cycles
    including fixed points. sgn : Sₙ → {±1} is a HOMOMORPHISM; a k-cycle has
    sign (−1)^(k−1). EVEN permutations form the ALTERNATING GROUP Aₙ = ker sgn,
    normal of index 2, |Aₙ| = n!/2 (n ≥ 2).
  - CONJUGATION RELABELS: τ(a₁ ... aₖ)τ⁻¹ = (τ(a₁) ... τ(aₖ)). Hence two
    permutations are CONJUGATE in Sₙ ⇔ they have the SAME CYCLE TYPE; the
    number of conjugacy classes of Sₙ is p(n), the number of partitions of
    n. The class of type 1^(m₁) 2^(m₂) ... has n!/∏(k^(mₖ)·mₖ!) elements.
    In Aₙ a class of Sₙ either stays one class or SPLITS into two of equal
    size (it splits exactly when the cycle lengths, counting fixed points
    as 1-cycles, are distinct and odd).
  - Facts to know: Sₙ is generated by (1 2) and (1 2 ... n); Aₙ (n ≥ 3) is
    generated by 3-cycles; A₄ (order 12) has NO subgroup of order 6; A₅ is
    SIMPLE (class sizes 1, 12, 12, 15, 20). CAYLEY'S THEOREM: every group of
    order n is isomorphic to a subgroup of Sₙ (left multiplication).
  - A (left) GROUP ACTION of G on a set X is a map G × X → X, (g, x) ↦ g·x,
    with e·x = x and g·(h·x) = (gh)·x. Equivalently a HOMOMORPHISM
    G → Sym(X); its kernel is the set of elements acting trivially
    (FAITHFUL if the kernel is {e}). Standard actions: Sₙ on {1, ..., n};
    G on itself by LEFT MULTIPLICATION or by CONJUGATION g·x = gxg⁻¹; G on
    the left cosets G/H; G on its subgroups by conjugation; symmetry groups
    on vertices, edges, faces.
  - ORBIT Orb(x) = G·x = {g·x : g ∈ G}; the orbits PARTITION X. STABILIZER
    Gₓ = {g : g·x = x}, a subgroup. ORBIT-STABILIZER THEOREM:
    |Orb(x)| = [G : Gₓ], so |G| = |Orb(x)|·|Gₓ| and orbit sizes divide |G|.
    Points in one orbit have conjugate stabilizers: G_{g·x} = gGₓg⁻¹.
    TRANSITIVE: one orbit. FIXED POINTS Fix(g) = {x : g·x = x}.
  - BURNSIDE'S (orbit-counting) LEMMA: number of orbits
    = (1/|G|) ∑_{g ∈ G} |Fix(g)|, the average number of fixed points. Used to
    count colourings (necklaces, cubes) up to symmetry: a colouring is fixed
    by g exactly when it is constant on each cycle of g, so
    |Fix(g)| = c^(number of cycles of g) for c colours.
  - CONJUGATION ACTION: orbits are CONJUGACY CLASSES, stabilizers are
    CENTRALIZERS C_G(x); so |class of x| = [G : C_G(x)]. CLASS EQUATION:
    |G| = |Z(G)| + ∑ [G : C_G(xᵢ)], summed over one xᵢ from each class of
    size > 1. On subgroups: the number of conjugates of H is [G : N_G(H)].
  - p-GROUPS (|G| = pⁿ): if a p-group acts on a finite X then
    |X| ≡ |Fix(G)| (mod p). A non-trivial p-group has NON-TRIVIAL CENTRE.
    If G/Z(G) is cyclic then G is abelian; hence every group of order p² is
    ABELIAN (≅ Z_{p²} or Z_p × Z_p).
  - CAUCHY'S THEOREM: if a prime p divides |G| then G has an element of order
    p. (Converse of Lagrange fails in general: A₄ has no subgroup of order 6.)
  - SYLOW THEOREMS. Let |G| = pᵃm with p prime, p ∤ m. A SYLOW p-SUBGROUP is
    a subgroup of order pᵃ; Syl_p(G) is the set of them, n_p = |Syl_p(G)|.
    (I) EXISTENCE: Sylow p-subgroups exist (and every p-subgroup lies in
    one). (II) CONJUGACY: any two Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate.
    (III) COUNTING: n_p ≡ 1 (mod p), n_p divides m, and n_p = [G : N_G(P)].
    Consequently n_p = 1 ⇔ the Sylow p-subgroup is NORMAL.
  - APPLICATIONS: (a) |G| = pq, p < q primes, p ∤ q − 1 ⇒ G is CYCLIC
    (orders 15, 33, 35, 51, 65, 77, 85, 91, ...). (b) PROVING A GROUP IS NOT
    SIMPLE: find some n_p forced to be 1; or COUNT ELEMENTS (distinct Sylow
    subgroups of prime order meet only in e, each giving p − 1 elements of
    order p); or let G act on the n_p Sylow subgroups (or on cosets of a
    subgroup of index k) to get G → S_k, which has a non-trivial kernel when
    |G| does not divide k!.
  - TRAPS: composing in the wrong order; reading the sign from the number of
    cycles instead of n − c(σ); thinking 'same order ⇒ conjugate'
    ((1 2)(3 4) and (1 2) in S₄ both have order 2); forgetting that Sylow
    numbers must divide m (not |G|); assuming the converse of Lagrange;
    claiming two Sylow p-subgroups of order p² meet trivially (only order p
    guarantees that).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Let σ ∈ S₈ be given in two-line notation by
       1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
       4 6 8 1 3 7 2 5
    and let τ = (1 2 3 4)(5 6). Write σ as a product of disjoint cycles, and
    find στ, τσ, σ⁻¹, the orders and signs of σ and τ, and σ¹⁰⁰.
    Answer: σ = (1 4)(2 6 7)(3 8 5); στ = (1 6 3)(2 8 5 7);
    τσ = (2 5 4)(3 8 6 7); σ⁻¹ = (1 4)(2 7 6)(3 5 8); ord σ = 6, sgn σ = −1;
    ord τ = 4, sgn τ = +1; σ¹⁰⁰ = (2 6 7)(3 8 5).
    Teacher explains: To find the cycles, start at the smallest unused number
    and follow the arrows until you come back:
       1 → 4 → 1                  gives (1 4)
       2 → 6 → 7 → 2              gives (2 6 7)
       3 → 8 → 5 → 3              gives (3 8 5)
    For στ read RIGHT TO LEFT: apply τ first, then σ. Track each number:
       1 →τ 2 →σ 6,   6 →τ 5 →σ 3,   3 →τ 4 →σ 1        (1 6 3)
       2 →τ 3 →σ 8,   8 →τ 8 →σ 5,   5 →τ 6 →σ 7,   7 →τ 7 →σ 2   (2 8 5 7)
       4 →τ 1 →σ 4                                       fixed
    Doing τσ the same way gives (2 5 4)(3 8 6 7) ≠ στ: Sₙ is not abelian
    (n ≥ 3). The INVERSE reverses every cycle: σ⁻¹ = (1 4)(2 7 6)(3 5 8).
    ORDER: the disjoint cycles commute, so σᵏ = (1 4)ᵏ(2 6 7)ᵏ(3 8 5)ᵏ is the
    identity exactly when 2 | k and 3 | k: ord σ = lcm(2, 3, 3) = 6. SIGN: a
    k-cycle is k − 1 transpositions, so sgn σ = (−1)^(1 + 2 + 2) = −1 (odd),
    and sgn τ = (−1)^(3 + 1) = +1 (even: a 4-cycle is ODD, a transposition is
    odd, odd × odd = even). Check: sgn(στ) = −1 and (1 6 3)(2 8 5 7) has
    2 + 3 = 5 transpositions ✓. POWER: 100 = 6·16 + 4, so σ¹⁰⁰ = σ⁴; now
    (1 4)⁴ = e and (2 6 7)⁴ = (2 6 7), so σ¹⁰⁰ = (2 6 7)(3 8 5). Common
    mistakes: composing left to right (some books do; always say which
    convention you use); saying a 4-cycle is even because 4 is even. Now you
    try: in S₅ compute (1 2 3)(3 4 5) and (3 4 5)(1 2 3). ((1 2 3 4 5) and
    (1 2 4 5 3): both 5-cycles, but different)

D2. Prove that the order of a permutation is the lcm of the lengths of its
    disjoint cycles, and that (1 2 ... k)ᵐ splits into gcd(k, m) cycles of
    length k/gcd(k, m). Find the largest order of an element of S₇ and of
    S₁₀, and the number of elements of order 6 in S₆.
    Answer: proofs below; max order 12 in S₇ (type 4 + 3) and 30 in S₁₀
    (type 5 + 3 + 2); S₆ has 240 elements of order 6.
    Teacher explains: A single k-cycle γ = (a₀ a₁ ... aₖ₋₁) sends aᵢ to
    a_{i+1} (indices mod k), so γᵐ sends aᵢ to a_{i+m}; this is the identity
    ⇔ k | m. Hence ord γ = k. If σ = γ₁γ₂...γᵣ (disjoint, so commuting), then
       σᵐ = γ₁ᵐγ₂ᵐ...γᵣᵐ,
    and the γᵢᵐ move disjoint sets of points, so σᵐ = e ⇔ every γᵢᵐ = e ⇔
    every length kᵢ divides m ⇔ lcm(k₁, ..., kᵣ) | m. So
    ord σ = lcm(k₁, ..., kᵣ). For the splitting: under γᵐ the point a₀ goes
    to a_m, a_{2m}, ...; it returns to a₀ first when jm ≡ 0 (mod k), i.e.
    after j = k/d steps, d = gcd(k, m). All cycles have this length, so there
    are k/(k/d) = d of them. Example: (1 2 3 4 5 6)² = (1 3 5)(2 4 6), two
    3-cycles since gcd(6, 2) = 2. LARGEST ORDER: split n into parts and
    maximise the lcm; use coprime parts:
       n = 7:   7 → 7,  6 + 1 → 6,  5 + 2 → 10,  4 + 3 → 12,  3 + 2 + 2 → 6
    so 12, e.g. (1 2 3 4)(5 6 7). For n = 10: 5 + 3 + 2 gives 30 (7 + 3 gives
    21, 6 + 4 gives 12). ORDER 6 in S₆: cycle types with lcm 6 are (6) and
    (3, 2, 1). Count: 6-cycles 6!/6 = 120; type (3, 2, 1): choose the 3-cycle
    C(6, 3)·2 = 40 ways, then the transposition C(3, 2) = 3 ways, 120. Total
    240. Common mistakes: 'order = product of lengths' ((1 2)(3 4) has order 2,
    not 4); forgetting type (3, 2, 1) or counting (1 2 3) and (2 3 1) as
    different. Now you try: how many elements of order 2 are in S₅? (type
    (2): 10, type (2, 2): 15; total 25)

D3. Define the sign of a permutation and prove that sgn : Sₙ → {±1} is a
    homomorphism with sgn(transposition) = −1. Deduce that Aₙ is a normal
    subgroup of order n!/2, list A₄, and prove that A₄ has no subgroup of
    order 6.
    Answer: proofs below; A₄ = {e, eight 3-cycles, (1 2)(3 4), (1 3)(2 4),
    (1 4)(2 3)}.
    Teacher explains: DEFINE sgn(σ) = ∏_{i<j} (σ(j) − σ(i))/(j − i). The
    numerator runs over the same pairs {σ(i), σ(j)} as the denominator, up to
    order, so the product is ±1: it is (−1)^(number of INVERSIONS, pairs i < j
    with σ(i) > σ(j)). HOMOMORPHISM: write
       sgn(στ) = ∏_{i<j} [σ(τj) − σ(τi)]/[τj − τi] · ∏_{i<j} [τj − τi]/[j − i]
    The second product is sgn τ. In the first, as {i, j} runs over all pairs
    so does {τi, τj}, and the factor (σ(b) − σ(a))/(b − a) does not change if
    a and b are swapped; so the first product is sgn σ. TRANSPOSITIONS: (1 2)
    has exactly one inversion (the pair 1, 2), so sgn(1 2) = −1. Any
    transposition (a b) = π(1 2)π⁻¹ for a suitable π, and sgn is multiplicative
    with values ±1, so sgn(a b) = sgn π · (−1) · sgn π = −1. Since a k-cycle
    is k − 1 transpositions, sgn(k-cycle) = (−1)^(k−1). Aₙ = ker sgn is a
    NORMAL subgroup; sgn is onto {±1} for n ≥ 2, so by the first isomorphism
    theorem [Sₙ : Aₙ] = 2 and |Aₙ| = n!/2. A₄ (order 12): the identity, the 8
    three-cycles (1 2 3), (1 3 2), (1 2 4), (1 4 2), (1 3 4), (1 4 3),
    (2 3 4), (2 4 3), and the 3 double transpositions. NO SUBGROUP OF ORDER 6:
    suppose |H| = 6. Then [A₄ : H] = 2, so H is normal and A₄/H has order 2;
    hence g² ∈ H for every g (as (gH)² = H). For a 3-cycle c, c = c⁴ = (c²)²
    ∈ H. So H contains all 8 three-cycles, more than 6 elements:
    contradiction. Common mistakes: counting the cycles to get the sign
    ((1 2 3) is one cycle but EVEN); assuming every divisor of |G| is the
    order of a subgroup. Now you try: is (1 2)(3 4 5 6)(7 8 9) even or odd?
    (1 + 3 + 2 = 6 transpositions: even)

D4. Prove that τ(a₁ a₂ ... aₖ)τ⁻¹ = (τ(a₁) τ(a₂) ... τ(aₖ)). Find τ ∈ S₅ with
    τ(1 2 3)(4 5)τ⁻¹ = (2 5 4)(1 3). List the conjugacy classes of S₅ with
    their sizes, find the classes of A₅, and prove that A₅ is simple.
    Answer: τ = (1 2 5 3 4) works. S₅: 1, 10, 15, 20, 20, 24, 30 (types e,
    (2), (2,2), (3), (3,2), (5), (4)). A₅: 1, 15, 20, 12, 12. A₅ is simple.
    Teacher explains: Put ρ = τ(a₁ ... aₖ)τ⁻¹ and apply it to τ(aᵢ):
       ρ(τ(aᵢ)) = τ((a₁ ... aₖ)(aᵢ)) = τ(aᵢ₊₁)
    (indices mod k). If b is not of the form τ(aᵢ), then τ⁻¹(b) is fixed by
    the cycle, so ρ(b) = b. That is exactly the cycle (τa₁ ... τaₖ). Applied
    to each cycle of a product: CONJUGATION = RELABELLING. So σ and ρ are
    conjugate ⇔ same cycle type, and to find τ write ρ UNDER σ and read off:
       σ = (1 2 3)(4 5)
       ρ = (2 5 4)(1 3)       τ: 1→2, 2→5, 3→4, 4→1, 5→3,  τ = (1 2 5 3 4)
    CLASSES of S₅ (use n!/∏ k^(mₖ)mₖ!):
       e 1;  (2) 10;  (2,2) 15;  (3) 20;  (3,2) 20;  (4) 30;  (5) 24
    Sum 120 ✓. The EVEN classes are e, (2,2), (3), (5): 1 + 15 + 20 + 24 = 60.
    In A₅ a class of S₅ splits in two when the centralizer C_{S₅}(σ) lies
    inside A₅ (then the A₅-class has size 60/|C| = half). For a 5-cycle σ,
    |C_{S₅}(σ)| = 120/24 = 5, so C = ⟨σ⟩ ⊆ A₅: the 24 splits as 12 + 12. For
    (1 2 3), C contains the odd (4 5): no split, 20. For (1 2)(3 4), C
    contains the odd (1 2): 15. So A₅: 1, 12, 12, 15, 20. SIMPLICITY: a normal
    subgroup N is a union of classes containing {e}, and |N| divides 60. The
    possible sums 1 + (some of 12, 12, 15, 20) are
       1, 13, 16, 21, 25, 28, 33, 36, 40, 45, 48, 60
    and only 1 and 60 divide 60. So N = {e} or A₅ ∎. Common mistakes:
    thinking (1 2 3 4 5) and (1 3 5 2 4) are conjugate in A₅ (they are in S₅,
    but σ² lies in the other A₅-class); forgetting that N must contain e.
    Now you try: find the class sizes of S₄. (1, 6, 3, 8, 6 for e, (2),
    (2,2), (3), (4); sum 24)

D5. Define a group action and show that it is the same thing as a
    homomorphism G → Sym(X). Prove Cayley's theorem. Show that if H ≤ G has
    index n and |G| does not divide n!, then H contains a non-trivial normal
    subgroup of G; deduce that a group of order 36 is not simple.
    Answer: proofs below (for |G| = 36 use a Sylow 3-subgroup of index 4:
    36 ∤ 4! = 24).
    Teacher explains: An ACTION is a map G × X → X with e·x = x and
    g·(h·x) = (gh)·x. For fixed g let φ_g(x) = g·x. Then φ_g ∘ φ_{g⁻¹} =
    φ_e = id and φ_{g⁻¹} ∘ φ_g = id, so φ_g ∈ Sym(X), and φ_{gh} = φ_g ∘ φ_h
    says g ↦ φ_g is a HOMOMORPHISM G → Sym(X). Conversely a homomorphism φ
    gives the action g·x = φ(g)(x). Examples:
       G on {1,...,n} (G ≤ Sₙ)   σ·i = σ(i)
       left multiplication       g·x = gx          (on X = G)
       conjugation               g·x = gxg⁻¹       (on X = G, or subgroups)
       cosets                    g·(aH) = gaH      (on X = G/H)
    CAYLEY: let G act on itself by left multiplication. The kernel is
    {g : gx = x ∀x} = {e}, so φ : G → Sym(G) ≅ Sₙ (n = |G|) is injective and
    G ≅ φ(G) ≤ Sₙ ∎. INDEX ARGUMENT: let G act on the n cosets G/H; we get
    φ : G → Sₙ. Its kernel K = ⋂ gHg⁻¹ is normal and lies in H (take g = e).
    If K = {e}, φ is injective and |G| divides |Sₙ| = n! by Lagrange; so if
    |G| ∤ n!, K ≠ {e}. And K ≠ G because the action is transitive (not
    trivial) when n > 1. ORDER 36 = 2²·3²: a Sylow 3-subgroup P (order 9,
    exists by Sylow I) has index 4, and 36 ∤ 24, so there is a normal K with
    {e} ≠ K ≤ P ≠ G: G is not simple. Common mistakes: forgetting to check
    the axiom (gh)·x = g·(h·x) (right multiplication g·x = xg FAILS it unless
    G is abelian; g·x = xg⁻¹ works); claiming the kernel is H. Now you try:
    show that a group of order 48 is not simple. (A Sylow 2-subgroup has index
    3 and 48 ∤ 3! = 6)

D6. State and prove the orbit-stabilizer theorem. Use it to find the order of
    the rotation group of a cube, and find the orbit and stabilizer of {1, 2}
    when S₄ acts on the 2-element subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4}.
    Answer: |Orb(x)| = [G : Gₓ]. Cube: 24. Orbit of {1, 2}: all 6 pairs;
    stabilizer {e, (1 2), (3 4), (1 2)(3 4)} of order 4 (6 × 4 = 24 ✓).
    Teacher explains: First Gₓ is a subgroup: e·x = x; if g, h fix x then
    (gh)·x = g·(h·x) = x and g⁻¹·x = g⁻¹·(g·x) = x. Now define
       Φ : G/Gₓ → Orb(x),   Φ(gGₓ) = g·x.
    WELL DEFINED and INJECTIVE together: gGₓ = hGₓ ⇔ h⁻¹g ∈ Gₓ ⇔
    h⁻¹g·x = x ⇔ g·x = h·x. SURJECTIVE: every point of the orbit is some g·x.
    So Φ is a bijection and |Orb(x)| = [G : Gₓ] = |G|/|Gₓ| (G finite) ∎. Also
    the orbits partition X, since 'y = g·x for some g' is an equivalence
    relation (reflexive by e, symmetric by g⁻¹, transitive by products).
    CUBE: rotations act TRANSITIVELY on the 6 faces; the stabilizer of the top
    face consists of the rotations about the vertical axis through its
    centre: 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 4 of them. So |G| = 6 × 4 = 24. Checks with
    other orbits: 8 vertices × 3 (rotations about a long diagonal) = 24;
    12 edges × 2 = 24. PAIRS: any pair {a, b} is π{1, 2} for a π with
    π(1) = a, π(2) = b, so the orbit is all C(4, 2) = 6 pairs. A permutation
    fixes the SET {1, 2} when it maps {1, 2} to itself and hence {3, 4} to
    itself: e, (1 2), (3 4), (1 2)(3 4). Common mistakes: taking the
    stabilizer of the pair to be the permutations fixing 1 AND 2 (that is
    only {e, (3 4)}); counting reflections in the rotation group. Now you
    try: find the order of the rotation group of a regular dodecahedron (12
    pentagonal faces). (12 × 5 = 60)

D7. Prove Burnside's lemma. How many different necklaces of 6 beads can be
    made with beads of 2 colours if (a) rotations only, (b) rotations and
    reflections are allowed? In how many ways can the faces of a cube be
    coloured with 3 colours, up to rotation?
    Answer: (a) 14, (b) 13; cube: 57.
    Teacher explains: Count the pairs S = {(g, x) : g·x = x} in two ways:
       ∑_{g} |Fix(g)|  =  |S|  =  ∑_{x} |Gₓ|  =  ∑_{x} |G|/|Orb(x)|
    Each orbit O contributes |O| terms |G|/|O|, i.e. |G| in total, so the
    right side is |G| × (number of orbits). Dividing:
       number of orbits = (1/|G|) ∑ |Fix(g)| ∎
    NECKLACES: the group C₆ of rotations acts on the 2⁶ = 64 colourings. A
    rotation by k places has gcd(6, k) cycles on the beads, and a fixed
    colouring is constant on each cycle, so |Fix| = 2^gcd(6, k):
       k = 0: 64   k = 1: 2   k = 2: 4   k = 3: 8   k = 4: 4   k = 5: 2
    Orbits = 84/6 = 14. With reflections (D₆, order 12) add 6 reflections:
    3 through opposite beads (2 fixed beads + 2 swapped pairs: 4 cycles,
    2⁴ = 16 each) and 3 through opposite edge midpoints (3 swapped pairs,
    2³ = 8 each): total 84 + 48 + 24 = 156, and 156/12 = 13. CUBE (24
    rotations acting on 6 faces), |Fix(g)| = 3^(cycles on faces):
       identity                      1     6 cycles     729
       ±90° about face axes          6     3 cycles     6 × 27 = 162
       180° about face axes          3     4 cycles     3 × 81 = 243
       ±120° about vertex axes       8     2 cycles     8 × 9 = 72
       180° about edge axes          6     3 cycles     6 × 27 = 162
    Sum 1368, and 1368/24 = 57. CHECK that the classes add to 24
    (1 + 6 + 3 + 8 + 6 ✓) and that the sum is divisible by |G|; if not,
    something is wrong. Common mistakes: dividing 64 by 6 (orbits have
    different sizes); forgetting the identity; using 3⁶/24. Now you try:
    necklaces of 5 beads in 3 colours up to rotation. ((243 + 4·3)/5 = 51)

D8. Derive the class equation. Prove that a group of order pⁿ (n ≥ 1) has
    non-trivial centre, that G/Z(G) cyclic implies G abelian, and that every
    group of order p² is abelian. Write the class equation of the dihedral
    group D₄ of order 8.
    Answer: |G| = |Z(G)| + ∑[G : C_G(xᵢ)]; D₄: 8 = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2.
    Teacher explains: G acts on itself by CONJUGATION. The orbit of x is its
    conjugacy class, the stabilizer is the centralizer C_G(x) = {g : gx = xg},
    so |class(x)| = [G : C_G(x)]. The class of x has size 1 ⇔ x ∈ Z(G).
    Collecting the one-element classes:
       |G| = |Z(G)| + ∑ᵢ [G : C_G(xᵢ)]     (sum over classes of size > 1)
    p-GROUPS: each term in the sum divides pⁿ and is > 1, so it is divisible
    by p. Then |Z(G)| = pⁿ − (multiple of p) is divisible by p; since e ∈ Z,
    |Z(G)| ≥ p. G/Z CYCLIC: suppose G/Z = ⟨gZ⟩. Every element is gⁱz with
    z ∈ Z; then (gⁱz)(gʲw) = g^(i+j)zw = (gʲw)(gⁱz), so G is abelian (and then
    G/Z is trivial). ORDER p²: |Z| is p or p². If |Z| = p then G/Z has order p
    and is cyclic, so G is abelian, so Z = G, contradiction; so |Z| = p² and G
    is abelian. D₄ = ⟨r, s : r⁴ = s² = e, srs⁻¹ = r⁻¹⟩. Z(D₄) = {e, r²}. The
    other classes: {r, r³}, {s, sr²}, {sr, sr³}; so
       8 = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2
    Each class size divides 8 ✓. Common mistakes: listing central elements
    as one class (each central element is its OWN class); thinking a group of
    order p³ must be abelian (D₄ and Q₈ have order 8 = 2³). Now you try:
    write the class equation of S₃ and of A₄. (6 = 1 + 2 + 3;
    12 = 1 + 3 + 4 + 4)

D9. Prove Cauchy's theorem: if a prime p divides |G|, then G has an element
    of order p. Show also that the number of elements of order p is ≡ −1
    (mod p), and check this in S₄ for p = 2 and p = 3.
    Answer: proof below (McKay's argument). S₄ has 9 elements of order 2
    (9 ≡ −1 mod 2) and 8 of order 3 (8 ≡ −1 mod 3).
    Teacher explains: Let n = |G| and
       X = {(g₁, g₂, ..., g_p) ∈ Gᵖ : g₁g₂...g_p = e}.
    The first p − 1 entries can be anything and g_p is then forced, so
    |X| = n^(p−1), which is divisible by p. The cyclic group Z_p acts on X by
    rotating the entries: if g₁g₂...g_p = e then g₂...g_pg₁ = g₁⁻¹(g₁...g_p)g₁
    = e, so the rotated tuple is again in X. Orbits have size 1 or p (they
    divide p). A tuple is FIXED by rotation ⇔ all entries are equal, (g, ..., g)
    with gᵖ = e. Since X is the union of orbits,
       |X| = (number of fixed tuples) + p·(number of orbits of size p)
    so p divides the number of fixed tuples. That number is at least 1
    (g = e), so it is at least p: there is g ≠ e with gᵖ = e, and as p is
    prime, ord g = p ∎. Moreover the fixed tuples correspond to
    {g : gᵖ = e} = {e} ∪ {elements of order p}; its size is ≡ 0, so the
    number of elements of order p is ≡ −1 (mod p). S₄: order 2 = 6
    transpositions + 3 double transpositions = 9; order 3 = 8 three-cycles.
    Common mistakes: using Lagrange backwards ('p divides |G| so there is a
    subgroup of order p' needs exactly this theorem); forgetting that p must
    be PRIME (a group of order 4 need not have an element of order 4).
    Now you try: prove directly that a group of even order has an element of
    order 2. (Pair each g with g⁻¹; the unpaired elements satisfy g = g⁻¹;
    e is one, and the total is even, so there is another)

D10. State Sylow's first theorem and prove it (Wielandt's argument). Find a
     Sylow 2-subgroup and a Sylow 3-subgroup of S₄.
     Answer: If |G| = pᵃm with p ∤ m, G has a subgroup of order pᵃ. In S₄
     (24 = 2³·3): D₄ = ⟨(1 2 3 4), (1 3)⟩ (order 8) and ⟨(1 2 3)⟩ (order 3).
     Teacher explains: Let Ω be the set of all SUBSETS of G of size pᵃ;
     |Ω| = C(pᵃm, pᵃ). STEP 1: p ∤ |Ω|. In F_p[x], (1 + x)ᵖ = 1 + xᵖ
     (binomial coefficients C(p, i) for 0 < i < p are divisible by p), so
        (1 + x)^(pᵃm) = (1 + x^(pᵃ))ᵐ   (mod p).
     Compare coefficients of x^(pᵃ): C(pᵃm, pᵃ) ≡ C(m, 1) = m ≢ 0 (mod p).
     STEP 2: G acts on Ω by left multiplication, g·S = gS. Ω is the union of
     orbits, and |Ω| is not divisible by p, so some orbit O has size not
     divisible by p. Pick S ∈ O and let H = G_S = {g : gS = S}. By
     orbit-stabilizer |O| = pᵃm/|H|; as p ∤ |O|, pᵃ divides |H|. STEP 3: fix
     s ∈ S. If h ∈ H then hs ∈ hS = S, so Hs ⊆ S and |H| = |Hs| ≤ |S| = pᵃ.
     Together |H| = pᵃ ∎. S₄: 24 = 8·3. The symmetries of a square with
     vertices 1, 2, 3, 4 in order form D₄ = {e, (1 2 3 4), (1 3)(2 4),
     (1 4 3 2), (1 3), (2 4), (1 2)(3 4), (1 4)(2 3)}, order 8, a Sylow
     2-subgroup; ⟨(1 2 3)⟩ is a Sylow 3-subgroup. (There are 3 Sylow
     2-subgroups, one for each way of arranging 1, 2, 3, 4 round a square up
     to symmetry, and 4 Sylow 3-subgroups.) Common mistakes: thinking Sylow I
     gives a subgroup of EVERY order dividing |G| (it gives prime-power
     orders only; in fact subgroups of every order pᵇ, b ≤ a, exist); taking
     pᵃ to be any power of p rather than the FULL power. Now you try: what is
     the order of a Sylow 2-subgroup of S₆? (720 = 2⁴·45, so 16)

D11. Prove Sylow's second and third theorems: all Sylow p-subgroups are
     conjugate, n_p = [G : N_G(P)] divides m, and n_p ≡ 1 (mod p). Check the
     theorems for A₄ and A₅.
     Answer: proofs below. A₄: n₂ = 1, n₃ = 4. A₅: n₂ = 5, n₃ = 10,
     n₅ = 6.
     Teacher explains: KEY LEMMA: if a p-group Q acts on a finite set Y then
     |Y| ≡ |Fix(Q)| (mod p), because every non-trivial orbit has size a
     power of p greater than 1. SYLOW II: let P, Q be Sylow p-subgroups. Q
     acts on the cosets G/P by left multiplication; |G/P| = m is not
     divisible by p, so by the lemma there is a fixed coset gP: QgP = gP for
     all q, i.e. g⁻¹qg ∈ P for all q ∈ Q. So g⁻¹Qg ⊆ P and both have order
     pᵃ: Q = gPg⁻¹ ∎ (the same argument with any p-subgroup Q shows it lies in
     a conjugate of P). SYLOW III: by II, G acts TRANSITIVELY by conjugation
     on Syl_p(G), and the stabilizer of P is the normalizer N_G(P). So
     n_p = [G : N_G(P)], which divides [G : P] = m because P ≤ N_G(P). For
     n_p ≡ 1: let P act on Syl_p(G) by conjugation. P fixes itself. If P fixes
     Q, then P ≤ N_G(Q); P and Q are Sylow p-subgroups of N_G(Q), so by II
     they are conjugate IN N_G(Q), where Q is normal: P = Q. So exactly one
     fixed point and n_p ≡ 1 (mod p) ∎. CHECKS: A₄, 12 = 4·3. The Sylow
     2-subgroup V = {e, (1 2)(3 4), (1 3)(2 4), (1 4)(2 3)} is normal, n₂ = 1
     (allowed: 1 | 3, 1 ≡ 1). The 8 three-cycles lie in 4 subgroups of order 3:
     n₃ = 4 (4 | 4, 4 ≡ 1 mod 3 ✓). A₅, 60 = 4·3·5: 24 five-cycles in groups
     of 4 non-identity elements give n₅ = 6 (6 | 12, 6 ≡ 1 mod 5 ✓); 20
     three-cycles in pairs give n₃ = 10 (10 | 20, ≡ 1 mod 3 ✓); the 15 double
     transpositions lie in 5 Klein groups (one fixing each point): n₂ = 5
     (5 | 15, ≡ 1 mod 2 ✓). Common mistakes: requiring n_p | |G| only (true
     but weaker); forgetting that N_G(P) ⊇ P. Now you try: find n₂ and n₃ in
     S₃. (n₂ = 3: ⟨(1 2)⟩, ⟨(1 3)⟩, ⟨(2 3)⟩; n₃ = 1: A₃)

D12. (a) Prove that every group of order 15 is cyclic, and more generally
     that a group of order pq (p < q primes, p ∤ q − 1) is cyclic. (b) Prove
     that no group of order 30 or 56 is simple.
     Answer: proofs below.
     Teacher explains: (a) |G| = 15 = 3·5. n₃ ≡ 1 (mod 3), n₃ | 5 ⇒ n₃ = 1;
     n₅ ≡ 1 (mod 5), n₅ | 3 ⇒ n₅ = 1. So P (order 3) and Q (order 5) are both
     normal; P ∩ Q = {e} (orders coprime). For x ∈ P, y ∈ Q the commutator
        xyx⁻¹y⁻¹ = (xyx⁻¹)y⁻¹ ∈ Q  and  = x(yx⁻¹y⁻¹) ∈ P,
     so it is e and xy = yx. Then PQ ≅ P × Q ≅ Z₃ × Z₅ ≅ Z₁₅ has 15 elements,
     so G ≅ Z₁₅. In general n_q | p and n_q ≡ 1 (mod q) with p < q force
     n_q = 1; n_p | q and n_p ≡ 1 (mod p): n_p = q would need p | q − 1, which
     is excluded, so n_p = 1, and the same argument gives G ≅ Z_{pq}.
     (b) ORDER 30 = 2·3·5: n₃ ∈ {1, 10}, n₅ ∈ {1, 6}. If both were > 1:
        10 Sylow 3-subgroups: 10 × 2 = 20 elements of order 3
         6 Sylow 5-subgroups:  6 × 4 = 24 elements of order 5
     (distinct subgroups of prime order meet only in e), 44 > 30,
     impossible. So n₃ = 1 or n₅ = 1: a normal Sylow subgroup, not simple.
     ORDER 56 = 2³·7: n₇ ∈ {1, 8}. If n₇ = 8 there are 8 × 6 = 48 elements of
     order 7, leaving 56 − 48 = 8 elements. A Sylow 2-subgroup has 8 elements,
     none of order 7, so it consists exactly of those 8: there is only one,
     n₂ = 1, normal. Either way G is not simple ∎. Common mistakes: in (a)
     stopping at 'P, Q normal' without showing G ≅ P × Q; counting elements in
     Sylow subgroups of order p² as if they met trivially. Now you try: show a
     group of order 12 is not simple. (n₃ ∈ {1, 4}; if 4, the 8 elements of
     order 3 leave 4 elements, which form the unique Sylow 2-subgroup)

      o) {1, 3, 5, 15}; {1, 4, 10}; {1, 6}
      p) {1, 3, 9}; {1, 4}              q) {1, 5}; {1, 16}
      r) {1, 7}; {1, 21}; {1, 15}
      s) {1, 3, 5, 15}; {1, 4, 10, 40}; {1, 6}
      t) {1, 3, 11, 33}; {1, 4, 22}; {1, 12}
      u) {1, 3, 7, 21}; {1, 4, 7, 28}; {1, 8}

M10. Find the actual Sylow numbers (D_n has order 2n).
    a) S₃: n₂, n₃                       b) Z₆: n₂, n₃

    q) elements of order 5 in A₅        r) elements of order 3 in A₄
    s) elements of order 7 in a group of order 56 with n₇ = 8

M11. Decide, with a short reason.
    Is every group of this order cyclic (Y/N)?
    a) 15             b) 21             c) 33              d) 35
    e) 39             f) 45             g) 51              h) 55
    i) 65             j) 77             k) 91              l) 255
    Can a group of this order be simple (Y/N)? (Non-abelian simple is meant;
    a group of prime order is simple.)
    m) 20             n) 30             o) 36              p) 40
    q) 42             r) 48             s) 56              t) 60
    u) 72             v) 105            w) 132             x) 200
    Answers:
      a) Y (3 ∤ 4)      b) N (3 | 6; a non-abelian group of order 21 exists)
      c) Y (3 ∤ 10)     d) Y (5 ∤ 6)
      e) N (3 | 12)     f) N (Z₃ × Z₁₅; every such group is abelian)
      g) Y (3 ∤ 16)     h) N (5 | 10)     i) Y (5 ∤ 12)      j) Y (7 ∤ 10)
      k) Y (7 ∤ 12)
      l) Y (n₁₇ = 1; G → Aut(Z₁₇) ≅ Z₁₆ is trivial as gcd(255, 16) = 1, so
         P₁₇ is central; G/P₁₇ (order 15) is cyclic, so G is abelian,
         ≅ Z₂₅₅)
      m) N (n₅ = 1)     n) N (counting, D12)
      o) N (index-4 argument, D5)       p) N (n₅ = 1)
      q) N (n₇ = 1)     r) N (index 3, 48 ∤ 6)
      s) N (counting, D12)              t) Y (A₅)
      u) N (n₃ ∈ {1, 4}; if 4, G → S₄ has a non-trivial kernel as 72 ∤ 24)
      v) N (n₅ = 21 and n₇ = 15 would give 84 + 90 > 105 elements)
      w) N (if n₁₁ = 12 and n₃ ≥ 4: 120 elements of order 11 and 8 of
         order 3; the 3 remaining non-identity elements with e form the
         unique Sylow 2-subgroup, so n₂ = 1)
      x) N (n₅ = 1)

M12. True (T) or false (F)?
    a) Sₙ is abelian for n ≥ 3.
    b) Disjoint cycles commute.
    c) Two permutations of the same order are conjugate in Sₙ.
    d) The product of two odd permutations is even.
    e) A 5-cycle is odd.
    f) Aₙ is normal in Sₙ.
    g) Every group of order 10 is isomorphic to a subgroup of S₁₀.
    h) The stabilizer of a point is a normal subgroup.
    i) Orbit sizes of a group action divide |G| (G finite).
    j) A group of order 16 acting on 7 points has a fixed point.
    k) Every group of order 25 is abelian.
    l) Every group of order 27 is abelian.
    m) A group of order 12 has an element of order 6.
    n) A group of order 12 has an element of order 3.
    o) If n_p = 1 then the Sylow p-subgroup is normal.
    p) Any two Sylow p-subgroups are isomorphic.
    q) A group of order 20 has a normal subgroup of order 5.
    r) A group of order 28 has a normal subgroup of order 7.
    s) Every subgroup of order 4 in S₄ is a Sylow 2-subgroup.
    t) A₄ has a subgroup of every order dividing 12.
    u) Every p-subgroup lies in some Sylow p-subgroup.
    v) A normal Sylow p-subgroup is the unique one.
    w) If |G| = p²q with distinct primes p, q, G may be simple.
    x) The number of elements of order 5 in any group is a multiple of 4.
    Answers:
      a) F   b) T   c) F ((1 2) and (1 2)(3 4))   d) T   e) F   f) T
      g) T (Cayley)   h) F (Stab(1) = ⟨(2 3)⟩ in S₃ is not normal)   i) T
      j) T (orbits have size 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 7 is odd)   k) T
      l) F (e.g. Heisenberg group mod 3)   m) F (A₄)   n) T (Cauchy)   o) T
      p) T (they are conjugate)   q) T (n₅ = 1)   r) T (n₇ = 1)
      s) F (orders 4 < 8)   t) F (no order 6)   u) T (Sylow II)   v) T
      w) F (never simple, a standard Sylow exercise)
      x) T (they come in groups of 4 inside the cyclic subgroups of order 5)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: practise the cycle-chasing routine aloud ('τ first, then σ;
  1 goes to 2, 2 goes to 6, ...') until it is automatic, and check every
  product by its sign (sgn is multiplicative). For actions draw pictures:
  label the vertices of a square or cube and move them physically; write
  down orbit and stabilizer before any formula, then check
  |orbit| × |stabilizer| = |G|. For Burnside make a table: type of symmetry,
  how many, cycles, fixed colourings; check the counts add to |G| and the
  total is divisible by |G|. For Sylow always write |G| = pᵃ·m first, then
  list the divisors of m that are ≡ 1 (mod p). Harder: prove that Sₙ is
  generated by (1 2) and (1 2 ... n); prove that Aₙ is simple for n ≥ 5;
  show that a group of order p²q is never simple; classify the groups of
  order 12 (five of them) and of order 8; prove that the number of
  subgroups of order pᵇ is ≡ 1 (mod p) (Frobenius); count necklaces with
  n beads in general using ∑ φ(d)c^(n/d)/n; and show that a simple group of
  order 60 must be isomorphic to A₅.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.18 — RINGS, IDEALS, QUOTIENT RINGS; INTEGRAL DOMAINS, PIDs, UFDs,
EUCLIDEAN DOMAINS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A RING (R, +, ·) is an abelian group under + with an associative
    multiplication distributing over + on both sides; here rings have an
    identity 1. COMMUTATIVE if ab = ba. Examples: Z, Q, R, C, Zₙ, R[x],
    Mₙ(R) (not commutative), Z[i] = {a + bi : a, b ∈ Z}, Z[√−5], C[0, 1],
    R × S (componentwise). A SUBRING contains 1 and is closed under −, ·.
    Consequences of the axioms: 0·a = 0, (−a)b = −(ab), (−1)(−1) = 1.
  - Special elements: UNIT (has a multiplicative inverse; the units form a
    group R×), ZERO DIVISOR (a ≠ 0 with ab = 0 for some b ≠ 0), NILPOTENT
    (aⁿ = 0), IDEMPOTENT (a² = a). In Zₙ: a is a unit ⇔ gcd(a, n) = 1,
    otherwise a (≠ 0) is a zero divisor; |Zₙ×| = φ(n). A FIELD is a
    commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 in which every non-zero element is a unit.
  - A RING HOMOMORPHISM satisfies f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b), f(ab) = f(a)f(b),
    f(1) = 1. Its KERNEL is an ideal and its image a subring. The
    CHARACTERISTIC of R is the least n > 0 with n·1 = 0 (0 if none): the
    kernel of Z → R is (char R).
  - An IDEAL I ⊆ R is an additive subgroup with ra ∈ I for all r ∈ R, a ∈ I
    (two-sided in the non-commutative case). (a) = aR is PRINCIPAL;
    (a₁, ..., aₖ) = {r₁a₁ + ... + rₖaₖ}. I + J, I ∩ J and IJ are ideals. An
    ideal containing a unit is all of R; a commutative ring is a field ⇔
    its only ideals are 0 and R. The ideals of Z are nZ, and
    (a, b) = (gcd(a, b)), (a) ∩ (b) = (lcm(a, b)).
  - QUOTIENT RING R/I: cosets a + I with (a + I)(b + I) = ab + I (well
    defined exactly because I is an ideal). FIRST ISOMORPHISM THEOREM:
    R/ker f ≅ im f. CORRESPONDENCE: ideals of R/I ↔ ideals of R containing
    I. Standard quotients: Z/nZ = Zₙ, R[x]/(x² + 1) ≅ C, Z[x]/(x² + 1) ≅ Z[i],
    Z[x]/(x) ≅ Z, Z[x]/(n, x) ≅ Zₙ, F[x]/(x − a) ≅ F (evaluation at a).
  - CHINESE REMAINDER THEOREM: if I + J = R (COPRIME ideals) then
    R/(I ∩ J) ≅ R/I × R/J, and I ∩ J = IJ (commutative R). In particular
    Z_{mn} ≅ Z_m × Z_n ⇔ gcd(m, n) = 1, and a system x ≡ aᵢ (mod nᵢ) with
    pairwise coprime nᵢ has a unique solution mod n₁n₂...nₖ.
  - PRIME ideal P ≠ R: ab ∈ P ⇒ a ∈ P or b ∈ P. MAXIMAL ideal M ≠ R: no ideal
    strictly between M and R. KEY FACTS (commutative R): R/P is an integral
    domain ⇔ P is prime; R/M is a field ⇔ M is maximal; so maximal ⇒ prime.
    In Z: (p) is maximal, (0) is prime but not maximal. In Z[x]: (x) is
    prime not maximal, (2, x) is maximal. Zorn: every proper ideal lies in a
    maximal ideal.
  - An INTEGRAL DOMAIN is a commutative ring, 1 ≠ 0, with no zero divisors
    (CANCELLATION: ab = ac, a ≠ 0 ⇒ b = c). Every field is a domain; a
    FINITE domain is a field; Zₙ is a domain ⇔ n is prime; char of a domain
    is 0 or a prime; R domain ⇒ R[x] domain with deg(fg) = deg f + deg g.
    Every domain embeds in its FIELD OF FRACTIONS (Frac Z = Q,
    Frac F[x] = F(x), Frac Z[i] = Q(i)).
  - DIVISIBILITY in a domain: a | b if b = ac; a, b are ASSOCIATES (a ~ b) if
    a = ub with u a unit (⇔ (a) = (b)). A non-zero non-unit p is IRREDUCIBLE
    if p = ab ⇒ a or b is a unit; PRIME if p | ab ⇒ p | a or p | b (⇔ (p) is a
    prime ideal). Always prime ⇒ irreducible; the converse FAILS in Z[√−5]:
    6 = 2·3 = (1 + √−5)(1 − √−5). NORMS: N(a + bi) = a² + b² on Z[i],
    N(a + b√−5) = a² + 5b², N(a + b√2) = a² − 2b²; N is multiplicative, units
    have norm ±1, and an element of prime norm (±p) is irreducible.
  - EUCLIDEAN DOMAIN (ED): a domain with a function d : R − {0} → N such
    that for all a and b ≠ 0 there are q, r with a = qb + r and r = 0 or
    d(r) < d(b). Examples: Z (d = |·|), F[x] for a field F (d = degree),
    Z[i] (d = N, divide in Q(i) and round), Z[√−2], Z[ω] (ω = e^(2πi/3)).
    The EUCLIDEAN ALGORITHM computes gcds and BÉZOUT coefficients.
  - PID: a domain in which every ideal is principal. ED ⇒ PID (generate by
    an element of least d). In a PID: gcd(a, b) exists and
    (a, b) = (gcd(a, b)) (Bézout); IRREDUCIBLE ⇔ PRIME; every non-zero prime
    ideal is MAXIMAL; so for irreducible p, R/(p) is a FIELD (e.g.
    Zₚ, F[x]/(f) with f irreducible).
  - UFD: a domain in which every non-zero non-unit is a product of
    irreducibles, uniquely up to order and associates (⇔ existence +
    'irreducible ⇒ prime'). PID ⇒ UFD. GAUSS: R UFD ⇒ R[x] UFD, so Z[x] and
    F[x, y] are UFDs, but NOT PIDs ((2, x) and (x, y) are not principal). In
    a UFD gcds exist (take the minimum exponents).
  - HIERARCHY: fields ⊂ EDs ⊂ PIDs ⊂ UFDs ⊂ integral domains, every
    inclusion STRICT: Z is an ED but not a field; Z[(1 + √−19)/2] is a PID
    but not an ED; Z[x] is a UFD but not a PID; Z[√−5] is a domain but not a
    UFD. GAUSSIAN PRIMES: 1 + i (above 2), p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (inert), and
    a ± bi with a² + b² = p for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) (FERMAT: p is a sum of two
    squares ⇔ p = 2 or p ≡ 1 mod 4).
  - TRAPS: forgetting to check r·a ∈ I for ALL r (Z is a subring of Q but
    not an ideal); saying 'x² + 1 is irreducible' without naming the field;
    (x) in Z[x] is prime but NOT maximal; irreducible ≠ prime outside UFDs;
    a subring of a PID need not be a PID (Z[√−3] ⊂ Z[ω]); in Z[i] gcds are
    defined only up to the units ±1, ±i.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. In Z₁₂ list the units, zero divisors, nilpotent and idempotent elements.
    Prove that in Zₙ every non-zero element is either a unit or a zero
    divisor, and that every finite integral domain is a field.
    Answer: units 1, 5, 7, 11; zero divisors 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10;
    nilpotents 0, 6; idempotents 0, 1, 4, 9. Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: Let a ∈ Zₙ, a ≠ 0, d = gcd(a, n). If d = 1, Bézout
    gives ax + ny = 1, so ax ≡ 1 and a is a UNIT. If d > 1 then
       a·(n/d) = (a/d)·n ≡ 0   with   n/d ≢ 0 (mod n),
    so a is a ZERO DIVISOR. For n = 12: gcd(a, 12) = 1 for a = 1, 5, 7, 11
    (inverses: each is its own inverse, e.g. 5·5 = 25 ≡ 1); the rest (≠ 0)
    are zero divisors, e.g. 4·3 = 12 ≡ 0, 8·3 ≡ 0, 9·4 ≡ 0, 10·6 ≡ 0.
    NILPOTENT: aᵏ ≡ 0 needs every prime of 12 (2 and 3) to divide a: only
    6 (6² = 36 ≡ 0). IDEMPOTENT: a² ≡ a ⇔ 12 | a(a − 1): a = 0, 1, 4
    (16 ≡ 4), 9 (81 ≡ 9). (By CRT, Z₁₂ ≅ Z₄ × Z₃ and the idempotents are the
    4 pairs of 0s and 1s.) FINITE DOMAIN: let a ≠ 0 and consider
    λₐ : R → R, x ↦ ax. If ax = ay then a(x − y) = 0, so x = y (no zero
    divisors): λₐ is injective, hence surjective as R is finite. So ax = 1
    for some x ∎. In particular Zₚ (p prime) is a field. Common mistakes:
    calling 0 a zero divisor (by the usual definition it is excluded);
    thinking that in any ring a non-unit is a zero divisor (in Z, 2 is
    neither). Now you try: list the units and nilpotents of Z₁₈.
    (units 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17; nilpotents 0, 6, 12)

D2. Prove that the kernel of a ring homomorphism is an ideal and that every
    ideal of Z is principal. Find a generator of (12, 18), (12) ∩ (18) and
    (12)(18) in Z. Show that (2, x) is a proper ideal of Z[x] that is not
    principal.
    Answer: (6), (36), (216). (2, x) = {polynomials with even constant
    term}, not principal.
    Teacher explains: KERNEL: f(0) = 0, so 0 ∈ ker f; if f(a) = f(b) = 0 then
    f(a − b) = 0; and for any r, f(ra) = f(r)f(a) = f(r)·0 = 0. So ker f is an
    additive subgroup ABSORBING multiplication: an ideal. IDEALS OF Z: let
    I ≠ 0 and n the least positive element (by well-ordering). For a ∈ I
    divide: a = qn + r, 0 ≤ r < n. Then r = a − qn ∈ I, and minimality forces
    r = 0: I = nZ. (The same proof with degree shows F[x] is a PID.)
       (12, 18) = (gcd) = (6)       since 6 = 18 − 12 ∈ I and 6 | 12, 18
       (12) ∩ (18) = (lcm) = (36)   common multiples
       (12)(18) = (216)              products
    Note (12) + (18) = (6) ⊋ (12)(18). (2, x): its elements are
    2f(x) + xg(x), exactly the polynomials with EVEN constant term; 1 is not
    one, so the ideal is proper. Suppose (2, x) = (h). Then h | 2, so h = ±1
    or ±2 (degree 0, since deg h ≤ deg 2); h = ±1 gives the whole ring, and
    h = ±2 does not divide x in Z[x]. Contradiction: Z[x] is NOT a PID.
    Common mistakes: 'the ideal generated by 2 and x is (gcd(2, x)) = (1)'
    (gcds only produce the ideal in a PID); forgetting to check absorption.
    Now you try: is the set of polynomials in Q[x] with f(1) = 0 an ideal?
    Find a generator. (Yes, the kernel of evaluation at 1: (x − 1))

D3. Prove the first isomorphism theorem for rings. Use it to show
    R[x]/(x² + 1) ≅ C, Z[x]/(x² + 1) ≅ Z[i] and Z[x]/(2, x) ≅ Z₂. In
    Q[x]/(x² − 2) find the inverse of 1 + x and of 3 + x.
    Answer: proof below; (1 + x)⁻¹ = −1 + x, (3 + x)⁻¹ = (3 − x)/7.
    Teacher explains: THEOREM: if f : R → S is a ring homomorphism with
    kernel K, then φ(a + K) = f(a) is an isomorphism R/K → f(R). WELL
    DEFINED and INJECTIVE: a + K = b + K ⇔ a − b ∈ K ⇔ f(a) = f(b). It
    respects + and · because f does: φ((a + K)(b + K)) = φ(ab + K) = f(ab)
    = f(a)f(b). It is onto f(R) by construction ∎. APPLICATIONS: use
    EVALUATION maps.
       R[x] → C,  f ↦ f(i):  onto (a + bx ↦ a + bi); kernel = polynomials
          with root i; real ones also have root −i, so are divisible by
          (x − i)(x + i) = x² + 1: kernel (x² + 1).
       Z[x] → Z[i], f ↦ f(i): same, dividing by the MONIC x² + 1 keeps
          integer coefficients.
       Z[x] → Z₂, f ↦ f(0) mod 2: kernel {even constant term} = (2, x).
    Computing in Q[x]/(x² − 2) means computing with x² = 2, i.e. in
    Q(√2). (1 + x)(a + bx) = a + (a + b)x + bx² = (a + 2b) + (a + b)x. Set
    this equal to 1: a + b = 0 and a + 2b = 1, so b = 1, a = −1:
       (1 + x)⁻¹ = −1 + x          check: (1 + √2)(√2 − 1) = 2 − 1 = 1 ✓
    For 3 + x use the 'conjugate': (3 + x)(3 − x) = 9 − x² = 9 − 2 = 7, so
    (3 + x)⁻¹ = (3 − x)/7. Common mistakes: forgetting to show the kernel is
    exactly (x² + 1) (both inclusions); inverting 1 + x as 1/(1 + x) in
    Q(x), which is not an element of the quotient. Now you try: in
    Z[x]/(x² + 1) compute (2 + 3x)(1 − x). (2 + x − 3x² ≡ 5 + x, i.e.
    (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 5 + i)

D4. State and prove the Chinese remainder theorem for rings. Solve
    x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7). Show that Q[x]/(x² − 1) is
    isomorphic to Q × Q, and find f with f ≡ 1 mod (x − 1), f ≡ 2 mod (x + 1).
    Answer: x ≡ 23 (mod 105); f = (3 − x)/2 (mod x² − 1).
    Teacher explains: Let I + J = R, so 1 = e + f with e ∈ I, f ∈ J. Map
       φ : R → R/I × R/J,   r ↦ (r + I, r + J).
    It is a homomorphism with kernel I ∩ J. ONTO: given (a + I, b + J) put
    r = af + be. Since f = 1 − e ≡ 1 (mod I) and e ≡ 0 (mod I), r ≡ a
    (mod I); similarly r ≡ b (mod J). By the first isomorphism theorem
    R/(I ∩ J) ≅ R/I × R/J ∎. NUMBERS: solve step by step. From x ≡ 2 (mod 3):
    x = 2 + 3k. Mod 5: 2 + 3k ≡ 3, 3k ≡ 1, k ≡ 2 (3·2 = 6 ≡ 1), so
    x = 8 + 15j. Mod 7: 8 + 15j ≡ 1 + j ≡ 2, j ≡ 1, x = 23. Check: 23 = 7·3 + 2,
    23 = 4·5 + 3, 23 = 3·7 + 2 ✓; unique mod 3·5·7 = 105. POLYNOMIALS: in
    Q[x], (x − 1) + (x + 1) contains (x + 1) − (x − 1) = 2, a unit, so they
    are coprime, and (x − 1) ∩ (x + 1) = (x² − 1). So
       Q[x]/(x² − 1) ≅ Q[x]/(x − 1) × Q[x]/(x + 1) ≅ Q × Q,
       f + (x² − 1) ↦ (f(1), f(−1)).
    Want f(1) = 1, f(−1) = 2 with f = a + bx: a + b = 1, a − b = 2, so
    a = 3/2, b = −1/2: f = (3 − x)/2. Common mistakes: applying CRT when the
    moduli are not coprime (Z₄ ≇ Z₂ × Z₂); checking only one congruence.
    Now you try: solve x ≡ 1 (mod 4), x ≡ 2 (mod 9). (x ≡ 29 mod 36)

D5. Prove that P is a prime ideal ⇔ R/P is an integral domain, and M is a
    maximal ideal ⇔ R/M is a field (R commutative). Classify (x), (2, x),
    (4, x) and (2) in Z[x], and (x² + 1) in R[x], C[x] and Z₂[x].
    Answer: (x) prime, not maximal; (2, x) maximal; (4, x) neither; (2)
    prime, not maximal; (x² + 1): maximal in R[x], neither in C[x] and
    Z₂[x].
    Teacher explains: PRIME: in R/P, (a + P)(b + P) = 0 means ab ∈ P, and
    'a + P = 0 or b + P = 0' means 'a ∈ P or b ∈ P'. So 'R/P has no zero
    divisors' is word for word 'P is prime' (and P ≠ R ⇔ R/P ≠ 0). MAXIMAL
    (⇒): let a ∉ M. Then M + (a) is an ideal strictly containing M, so it is
    R: 1 = m + ra, and (r + M)(a + M) = 1 + M: a + M is invertible. (⇐): if
    M ⊊ J ⊆ R, pick a ∈ J − M; a + M has an inverse r + M, so
    1 − ra ∈ M ⊆ J and ra ∈ J give 1 ∈ J, J = R. Since a field is a domain,
    MAXIMAL ⇒ PRIME. CLASSIFY by computing the quotient:
       Z[x]/(x)       ≅ Z          domain, not field    prime, not maximal
       Z[x]/(2, x)    ≅ Z₂         field                maximal
       Z[x]/(4, x)    ≅ Z₄         2·2 = 0              neither
       Z[x]/(2)       ≅ Z₂[x]      domain, not field    prime, not maximal
       R[x]/(x² + 1)  ≅ C          field                maximal
       C[x]/(x² + 1)  ≅ C × C      (x − i)(x + i) = 0   neither
       Z₂[x]/(x² + 1): x² + 1 = (x + 1)² in Z₂[x]; (x + 1)² = 0   neither
    Common mistakes: 'every prime ideal is maximal' (true in PIDs for P ≠ 0,
    false in Z[x]); forgetting the zero ideal (0) is prime in any domain.
    Now you try: is (3, x² + 1) maximal in Z[x]? (Yes: the quotient is
    Z₃[x]/(x² + 1), a field with 9 elements, since −1 is not a square mod 3)

D6. Prove that the characteristic of an integral domain is 0 or a prime,
    and that (a + b)ᵖ = aᵖ + bᵖ in a commutative ring of prime characteristic
    p. Describe the construction of the field of fractions and find
    Frac(Z[i]).
    Answer: proofs below; Frac(Z[i]) = Q(i) = {r + si : r, s ∈ Q}.
    Teacher explains: Let char R = n > 0 and suppose n = ab with
    1 < a, b < n. Then
       0 = n·1 = (a·1)(b·1),
    so a·1 = 0 or b·1 = 0 (domain), contradicting the minimality of n. So n
    is prime. FROBENIUS: by the binomial theorem (valid in any commutative
    ring) (a + b)ᵖ = ∑ C(p, k)aᵏbᵖ⁻ᵏ, and for 0 < k < p
       C(p, k) = p!/(k!(p − k)!)
    is divisible by p (p divides the numerator but not the denominator), so
    those terms vanish: (a + b)ᵖ = aᵖ + bᵖ. Example in Z₅: (1 + 2)⁵ = 3⁵ =
    243 ≡ 3 and 1⁵ + 2⁵ = 33 ≡ 3 ✓. FRACTIONS: for a domain R take pairs (a, b)
    with b ≠ 0, and declare (a, b) ~ (c, d) ⇔ ad = bc (transitivity uses
    cancellation, i.e. no zero divisors). Write a/b for the class and define
       a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/(bd),    (a/b)(c/d) = (ac)/(bd)
    (bd ≠ 0 because R is a domain). Every a/b ≠ 0 has inverse b/a, so this is
    a field, and a ↦ a/1 embeds R; it is the SMALLEST field containing R. For
    Z[i]: (a + bi)/(c + di) = (a + bi)(c − di)/(c² + d²) ∈ Q(i), and every
    r + si ∈ Q(i) is (m + ni)/k with a common denominator k. Common
    mistakes: thinking a ring of characteristic p must be finite (Z₂[x] has
    characteristic 2 and is infinite); using the fraction construction for
    rings with zero divisors. Now you try: find the
    characteristic of Z₃ × Z₅ and of Z₂[x]. (15, not a domain; 2)

D7. In R = Z[√−5] with N(a + b√−5) = a² + 5b², show that 2, 3, 1 + √−5 and
    1 − √−5 are irreducible, that 2 is not prime, and hence that R is not a
    UFD. Show also that in any domain a prime is irreducible.
    Answer: 6 = 2·3 = (1 + √−5)(1 − √−5) are two essentially different
    factorisations into irreducibles.
    Teacher explains: N is MULTIPLICATIVE (N(αβ) = |αβ|² = |α|²|β|²) with
    values in N. UNITS: αβ = 1 ⇒ N(α)N(β) = 1 ⇒ N(α) = 1 ⇒ a² + 5b² = 1 ⇒
    α = ±1. The norms are
       N(2) = 4,   N(3) = 9,   N(1 ± √−5) = 6.
    If 2 = αβ with non-units, N(α) = 2; but a² + 5b² = 2 has no integer
    solution (b = 0 gives a² = 2, b ≠ 0 gives ≥ 5). Similarly N = 3 is
    impossible, so 3 is irreducible, and 1 ± √−5 (norm 6 = 2·3) would need a
    factor of norm 2 or 3: irreducible too. The elements 2 and 1 ± √−5 are
    not associates (the only units are ±1). NOT PRIME: 2 divides
    6 = (1 + √−5)(1 − √−5), but 2 ∤ 1 ± √−5, since (1 ± √−5)/2 ∉ R. So
    factorisation is not unique and R is not a UFD. PRIME ⇒ IRREDUCIBLE in
    any domain: let p be prime and p = ab. Then p | ab, say p | a: a = pc.
    So p = pcb, and cancelling p (domain): cb = 1, b is a unit ∎. Common
    mistakes: concluding 'irreducible' from 'no obvious factor' instead of
    the norm argument; forgetting to check that the two factorisations are
    not related by units. Now you try: find another pair of factorisations
    of 21 in Z[√−5]. (21 = 3·7 = (1 + 2√−5)(1 − 2√−5) = (4 + √−5)(4 − √−5))

D8. Prove that Z[i] is a Euclidean domain with d(α) = N(α) = a² + b². Then
    divide 7 + 5i by 2 − i and compute gcd(11 + 3i, 1 + 8i) by the
    Euclidean algorithm.
    Answer: 7 + 5i = (2 + 3i)(2 − i) + i; gcd(11 + 3i, 1 + 8i) = 1 − 2i (up
    to units ±1, ±i).
    Teacher explains: Let α, β ∈ Z[i], β ≠ 0. In C, α/β = u + vi with
    u, v ∈ Q. Choose integers m, n with |u − m| ≤ 1/2, |v − n| ≤ 1/2 (round),
    and put q = m + ni, ρ = α − qβ ∈ Z[i]. Then
       N(ρ) = N(β)·|α/β − q|² ≤ N(β)(1/4 + 1/4) = N(β)/2 < N(β) ∎.
    DIVISION: (7 + 5i)/(2 − i) = (7 + 5i)(2 + i)/5 = (9 + 17i)/5
    = 1.8 + 3.4i, rounding to q = 2 + 3i. Then
       (2 + 3i)(2 − i) = 4 − 2i + 6i + 3 = 7 + 4i,   ρ = (7 + 5i) − (7 + 4i) = i
    and N(i) = 1 < N(2 − i) = 5 ✓. GCD: divide repeatedly.
       (11 + 3i)/(1 + 8i) = (35 − 85i)/65 ≈ 0.54 − 1.31i,  q = 1 − i
       11 + 3i = (1 − i)(1 + 8i) + (2 − 4i)
       (1 + 8i)/(2 − 4i) = (−30 + 20i)/20 = −1.5 + i,       q = −2 + i
       1 + 8i = (−2 + i)(2 − 4i) + (1 − 2i)
       2 − 4i = 2(1 − 2i) + 0
    The last non-zero remainder is 1 − 2i (N = 5). CHECK: 11 + 3i =
    (1 − 2i)(1 + 5i) and 1 + 8i = (1 − 2i)(−3 + 2i). Norms help too:
    N(11 + 3i) = 130 and N(1 + 8i) = 65 have gcd 65, but the gcd of the
    elements only has norm 5: norms give an upper bound, not the answer.
    Common mistakes: rounding wrongly (either choice at .5 is fine, but the
    norm must drop); stating the gcd as a unique number. Now you try: divide
    27 − 23i by 8 + i. (q = 3 − 3i, remainder −2i, norm 4 < 65)

D9. Prove that every Euclidean domain is a PID. In Q[x] find
    g = gcd(x³ − 1, x² − 1) and polynomials s, t with
    s(x³ − 1) + t(x² − 1) = g, and describe the ideal (x³ − 1, x² − 1).
    Answer: g = x − 1 = 1·(x³ − 1) + (−x)(x² − 1); the ideal is (x − 1).
    Teacher explains: Let I ≠ 0 be an ideal of the ED R. Choose b ∈ I − {0}
    with d(b) as small as possible. For a ∈ I write a = qb + r with r = 0 or
    d(r) < d(b). As r = a − qb ∈ I, minimality forces r = 0, so a ∈ (b):
    I = (b) ∎. (The zero ideal is (0).) The generator of (a, b) is a gcd,
    because (a, b) = (g) means g | a, g | b, and g = sa + tb is divisible by
    every common divisor. EUCLID in Q[x]:
       x³ − 1 = x·(x² − 1) + (x − 1)
       x² − 1 = (x + 1)(x − 1) + 0
    so g = x − 1, and from the first line x − 1 = (x³ − 1) − x(x² − 1): s = 1,
    t = −x. Check: x³ − 1 − x³ + x = x − 1 ✓. The ideal (x³ − 1, x² − 1) is
    (x − 1): all polynomials vanishing at 1. In a general Euclidean
    algorithm, back-substitute from the bottom line upwards. Common mistakes:
    forgetting to make the gcd monic (by convention in F[x]); stopping at a
    remainder that is a non-zero constant and not concluding gcd = 1. Now
    you try: find gcd(x⁴ + x³ + 2x² + x + 1, x³ + 2x² + 2x + 1) in Q[x].
    (x² + x + 1 = ½·first + ((1 − x)/2)·second)

D10. Prove that in a PID every irreducible element is prime and every
     non-zero prime ideal is maximal. Deduce that Z[x]/(3, x² + 1),
     Q[x]/(x³ − 2) and Z[i]/(3) are fields, and give their sizes where
     finite.
     Answer: proofs below; Z[x]/(3, x² + 1) ≅ Z[i]/(3) ≅ F₉ (9 elements);
     Q[x]/(x³ − 2) ≅ Q(∛2), an infinite field.
     Teacher explains: STEP 1: p irreducible ⇒ (p) MAXIMAL among principal
     ideals, hence among all ideals (PID). If (p) ⊆ (a) then p = ab; either
     a is a unit ((a) = R) or b is a unit ((a) = (p)). STEP 2: maximal ⇒
     prime ideal ⇒ p is prime. STEP 3: if (p) ≠ 0 is a prime ideal then p is
     prime, hence irreducible, hence (p) is maximal by step 1 ∎.
     APPLICATIONS: 3 is prime in Z[i] (a² + b² = 3 has no solution and N is
     multiplicative, so 3 is irreducible; Z[i] is a PID), so Z[i]/(3) is a
     field; its elements are a + bi with a, b ∈ {0, 1, 2}: 9 elements. Also
     Z[x]/(3, x² + 1) ≅ Z₃[x]/(x² + 1) ≅ Z[i]/(3): x² + 1 has no root in Z₃
     (0, 1, 2 give 1, 2, 2), so being of degree 2 it is irreducible in the PID
     Z₃[x]. x³ − 2 has no rational root (±1, ±2 fail), so it is irreducible
     over Q (degree 3), and Q[x]/(x³ − 2) is a field ≅ Q(∛2). Common mistakes:
     using 'no roots ⇒ irreducible' for degree ≥ 4 (x⁴ + 4 = (x² + 2x + 2)
     (x² − 2x + 2) has no rational root); applying the theorem in Z[x],
     which is not a PID ((x) is prime but not maximal). Now you try: is
     Z[i]/(5) a field? (No: 5 = (2 + i)(2 − i), so (2 + i)(2 − i) = 0 there;
     Z[i]/(5) ≅ Z₅ × Z₅)

D11. Factor 2, 3, 5, 13, 65 and 3 + 4i into Gaussian primes, and prove that
     a prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) is a sum of two squares while a prime p ≡ 3
     (mod 4) stays prime in Z[i].
     Answer: 2 = −i(1 + i)²; 3 prime; 5 = (2 + i)(2 − i);
     13 = (3 + 2i)(3 − 2i); 65 = (2 + i)(2 − i)(3 + 2i)(3 − 2i);
     3 + 4i = (2 + i)².
     Teacher explains: Z[i] is a Euclidean domain, hence a PID, hence a UFD,
     so the factorisation is unique up to units ±1, ±i and order. An element
     of PRIME norm is irreducible. Look for a² + b² = p:
        2 = 1 + 1:  (1 + i)(1 − i) = 2 and 1 − i = −i(1 + i), so
                    2 = −i(1 + i)²
        5 = 4 + 1:  (2 + i)(2 − i),      13 = 9 + 4: (3 + 2i)(3 − 2i)
        3:          a² + b² = 3 impossible, so 3 is irreducible (prime)
     For 3 + 4i: N = 25, so it is a product of two norm-5 primes; try
     (2 + i)² = 4 + 4i − 1 = 3 + 4i ✓. p ≡ 3 (mod 4): squares are 0 or 1 mod 4,
     so a² + b² ≠ p; if p = αβ with non-units then N(α) = p, impossible. So p
     is irreducible, hence prime. p ≡ 1 (mod 4): −1 is a square mod p (e.g.
     n = ((p − 1)/2)! satisfies n² ≡ −1 by Wilson's theorem; for p = 13,
     n = 5 works: 26 = 2·13). Then p | n² + 1 = (n + i)(n − i), but p divides
     neither factor ((n ± i)/p ∉ Z[i]). So p is NOT prime in Z[i], hence not
     irreducible (UFD): p = αβ with N(α) = N(β) = p, i.e. p = a² + b² ∎.
     Common mistakes: listing 2 + i and 1 + 2i as different primes (1 + 2i =
     i(2 − i), an associate of 2 − i, not of 2 + i!); forgetting the unit −i in
     the factorisation of 2. Now you try: factor 7 + i. (N = 50;
     7 + i = −i(1 + i)(2 + i)²)

D12. For each ring decide whether it is a field, ED, PID, UFD, integral
     domain: Q, Z, Q[x], Z[i], Z[x], Q[x, y], Z[√−5], Z₆. Justify the
     separating examples. Prove that in a UFD an irreducible element is
     prime.
     Answer: Q field (hence all); Z, Q[x], Z[i] ED (hence PID, UFD, domain);
     Z[x], Q[x, y] UFD not PID; Z[√−5] domain not UFD; Z₆ not a domain.
     Teacher explains: Go down the chain field ⇒ ED ⇒ PID ⇒ UFD ⇒ domain and
     stop at the first property that holds.
        ring        field  ED   PID  UFD  domain   reason
        Q           yes    yes  yes  yes  yes      all non-zero invertible
        Z           no     yes  yes  yes  yes      |·|, 2 not a unit
        Q[x]        no     yes  yes  yes  yes      degree, x not a unit
        Z[i]        no     yes  yes  yes  yes      norm (D8)
        Z[x]        no     no   no   yes  yes      (2, x) not principal
        Q[x, y]     no     no   no   yes  yes      (x, y) not principal
        Z[√−5]      no     no   no   no   yes      6 = 2·3 = (1+√−5)(1−√−5)
        Z₆          no     no   no   no   no       2·3 = 0
     UFD for Z[x], Q[x, y]: GAUSS'S LEMMA (topic 10.19) gives R UFD ⇒ R[x]
     UFD. (x, y) is not principal: a generator h would divide x and y, so h
     is a non-zero constant (a unit), but 1 ∉ (x, y) (every element has
     zero constant term). IRREDUCIBLE ⇒ PRIME in a UFD: let p be irreducible
     and p | ab, say ab = pc. Factor a, b, c into irreducibles; by
     uniqueness the irreducible p is an associate of one of the irreducible
     factors of a or of b, so p | a or p | b ∎. (Z[√−5] fails exactly this.)
     Common mistakes: calling Z[x] a PID because Z is one (PID-ness does not
     pass to R[x]: R[x] is a PID ⇔ R is a field); forgetting that every
     field is trivially a UFD. Now you try: is Z[√−3] a UFD? (No:
     4 = 2·2 = (1 + √−3)(1 − √−3) with all factors irreducible of norm 4,
     since a² + 3b² = 2 is impossible)

M2. True (T) or false (F)?
    a) Z is a subring of Q.             b) Z is an ideal of Q.
    c) 2Z is a subring of Z (with 1).   d) 2Z is an ideal of Z.
    e) {(a, 0)} is an ideal of Z × Z.   f) {(a, a)} is an ideal of Z × Z.
    g) The polynomials with f(0) = 0 form an ideal of R[x].
    h) The polynomials of degree ≤ 3 form an ideal of R[x].
    i) The continuous f on [0, 1] with f(1/2) = 0 form an ideal of C[0, 1].
    j) The upper triangular matrices form an ideal of M₂(R).
    k) Z[√2] = {a + b√2} is a subring of R.
    l) {a + b∛2 : a, b ∈ Z} is a subring of R.
    m) The union of two ideals is an ideal.
    n) The intersection of two ideals is an ideal.
    o) f : Z → Z, f(n) = 2n is a ring homomorphism.
    p) f : Z₆ → Z₃, n ↦ n mod 3 is a ring homomorphism.
    q) f : Z₃ → Z₆, n ↦ 4n is additive and multiplicative.
    r) f : C → C, z ↦ z̄ is a ring homomorphism.
    s) f : Mₙ(R) → R, A ↦ det A is a ring homomorphism.
    t) A field has exactly two ideals.
    u) M₂(R) has no two-sided ideals other than 0 and itself.
    v) The image of an ideal under a surjective homomorphism is an ideal.
    Answers:
      a) T   b) F (½·1 ∉ Z)   c) F (1 ∉ 2Z)   d) T   e) T
      f) F ((1, 0)(1, 1) = (1, 0))   g) T (kernel of f ↦ f(0))   h) F
      i) T   j) F   k) T   l) F ((∛2)² = ∛4 is not of that form)
      m) F ((2) ∪ (3) ∌ 5)   n) T   o) F (f(1) = 2 ≠ 1; f(1·1) ≠ f(1)f(1))
      p) T   q) T (4·4 = 16 ≡ 4 in Z₆; but f(1) = 4 ≠ 1, so not unital)
      r) T   s) F (det(A + B) ≠ det A + det B)   t) T   u) T   v) T

M6. Prime, maximal (hence also prime), or neither?
    a) (6) in Z             b) (7) in Z             c) (0) in Z
    d) (x) in Z[x]          e) (2, x) in Z[x]       f) (4, x) in Z[x]
    g) (2) in Z[x]          h) (3, x) in Z[x]       i) (x² + 1) in R[x]
    j) (x² + 1) in C[x]     k) (x² + 1) in Z₂[x]    l) (x² + 1) in Z₃[x]
    m) (x² + 1) in Q[x]     n) (x² − 2) in Q[x]     o) (x² − 2) in R[x]
    p) (x) in Q[x, y]       q) (x, y) in Q[x, y]    r) (2) in Z[i]
    s) (3) in Z[i]          t) (5) in Z[i]          u) (1 + i) in Z[i]
    v) (x² + x + 1) in Z₂[x]                        w) (x² + x + 1) in Z₃[x]
    x) (2), (3), (4) in Z₁₂
    Answers:
      a) neither            b) maximal            c) prime, not maximal
      d) prime, not maximal e) maximal            f) neither
      g) prime, not maximal h) maximal            i) maximal
      j) neither            k) neither ((x + 1)²) l) maximal
      m) maximal            n) maximal            o) neither
      p) prime, not maximal q) maximal            r) neither ((1 + i)²)
      s) maximal            t) neither            u) maximal
      v) maximal            w) neither ((x − 1)²)
      x) maximal, maximal, neither

    a) Z₇                   b) Z₈                   c) Z × Z
