M12. Classify and decide.
    Name the strongest of: field, ED, PID, UFD, domain, none.
    a) Q(√2)                b) Z                  c) R[x]
    d) Z[i]                 e) Z[x]               f) R[x, y]
    g) Z[√−5]               h) Z₁₅                i) Z₁₃
    j) Z[√−2]               k) Z[ω], ω = e^(2πi/3) l) Z[√−3]
    m) Z₂[x]                n) Z[(1 + √−19)/2]
    True (T) or false (F)?
    o) Every PID is a UFD.              p) Every UFD is a PID.
    q) In any domain, prime ⇒ irreducible.
    r) In any domain, irreducible ⇒ prime.
    s) A subring of a field is an integral domain.
    t) If R is a PID then so is R[x].   u) F[x] is a PID for every field F.
    v) Every non-zero prime ideal of Z[x] is maximal.
    w) In a PID, gcd(a, b) is a combination sa + tb.
    x) A quotient of a PID by a prime ideal is a field.
    Answers:
      a) field     b) ED        c) ED        d) ED        e) UFD
      f) UFD       g) domain    h) none      i) field     j) ED
      k) ED        l) domain    m) ED        n) PID
      o) T   p) F (Z[x])   q) T   r) F (2 in Z[√−5])   s) T
      t) F (Z[x]; true only if R is a field)   u) T
      v) F ((x) and (2))   w) T   x) F (R/(0) = R when P = (0); true for
      P ≠ 0)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make the student test every ideal claim with 'absorbs
  multiplication by EVERYTHING'; always identify a quotient ring by
  building a surjective homomorphism and finding its kernel; for prime and
  maximal ideals, compute R/I and ask 'domain? field?'. Keep one table of
  examples (Z, Zₙ, Q[x], Z[x], Z[i], Z[√−5]) and place every new fact in
  it. For Gaussian integers always compute the norm first. Harder: prove
  that a PID satisfies the ascending chain condition and deduce PID ⇒ UFD;
  prove that Z[√−2] and Z[ω] are Euclidean; show that R[x] is a PID only
  when R is a field; prove that the ideal (2, 1 + √−5) of Z[√−5] is not
  principal but its square is (2); show that Z[(1 + √−19)/2] is not
  Euclidean (it has no 'universal side divisor'); prove that the number of
  representations of n as a² + b² is 4(d₁(n) − d₃(n)), counting divisors
  ≡ 1 and ≡ 3 mod 4, and check it for n = 25 (12 ways).


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.19 — POLYNOMIAL RINGS; IRREDUCIBILITY CRITERIA (EISENSTEIN)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - R[x] is the ring of polynomials f = aₙxⁿ + ... + a₁x + a₀ with aᵢ ∈ R;
    for aₙ ≠ 0, n = deg f is the DEGREE and aₙ the LEADING COEFFICIENT
    (MONIC if aₙ = 1); deg 0 = −∞. Always deg(f + g) ≤ max(deg f, deg g) and
    deg(fg) ≤ deg f + deg g, with EQUALITY when R is an integral domain.
    Then R[x] is a domain and (R[x])× = R× (in Z₄[x], (1 + 2x)² = 1 shows
    this fails without the domain hypothesis). R[x, y] = R[x][y].
  - DIVISION ALGORITHM: if g has a UNIT leading coefficient (e.g. g monic,
    or any g ≠ 0 over a field) then f = qg + r with deg r < deg g, q and r
    unique. REMAINDER THEOREM: the remainder of f on division by x − a is
    f(a). FACTOR THEOREM: (x − a) | f ⇔ f(a) = 0.
  - ROOTS: over an integral domain a non-zero polynomial of degree n has at
    most n roots (FALSE in Z₈: x² − 1 has roots 1, 3, 5, 7). A polynomial is
    not the same as a function: x^p − x ≠ 0 in Zₚ[x] but vanishes at every
    point of Zₚ. LAGRANGE INTERPOLATION: over a field, through n points with
    distinct x-values there is exactly one polynomial of degree < n.
  - F[x] (F a field) is a EUCLIDEAN DOMAIN (d = degree), hence a PID and a
    UFD: every polynomial is a unit times a product of MONIC IRREDUCIBLES,
    uniquely. gcds are computed by the Euclidean algorithm (made monic) and
    satisfy Bézout. f IRREDUCIBLE ⇔ (f) MAXIMAL ⇔ F[x]/(f) is a FIELD (of
    size qⁿ if |F| = q and deg f = n).
  - MULTIPLE ROOTS: formal derivative (∑aₖxᵏ)′ = ∑kaₖxᵏ⁻¹ obeys the sum and
    product rules. a is a repeated root ⇔ f(a) = f′(a) = 0. f has a repeated
    irreducible factor ⇔ gcd(f, f′) ≠ 1. Over Q (char 0) an irreducible f
    has no repeated roots in C. In char p, f′ can be 0 (x⁴ + 1 over F₂).
  - LOW DEGREE: every degree-1 polynomial is irreducible; a polynomial of
    DEGREE 2 OR 3 over a field is irreducible ⇔ it has NO ROOT in the field.
    For degree ≥ 4 'no roots' is NOT enough (x⁴ + 4 = (x² + 2x + 2)
    (x² − 2x + 2)); also rule out quadratic factors (undetermined
    coefficients).
  - OVER C: irreducibles are linear (FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ALGEBRA). OVER R:
    linear and quadratics ax² + bx + c with b² − 4ac < 0; real polynomials
    of odd degree have a real root. OVER Q: irreducibles of every degree
    (xⁿ − 2).
  - RATIONAL ROOT TEST: if p/q (lowest terms) is a root of
    aₙxⁿ + ... + a₀ ∈ Z[x], then p | a₀ and q | aₙ. A MONIC integer
    polynomial has only INTEGER rational roots.
  - GAUSS'S LEMMA: the CONTENT c(f) is the gcd of the coefficients; f is
    PRIMITIVE if c(f) = 1. The product of primitive polynomials is
    primitive, so c(fg) = c(f)c(g). If f ∈ Z[x] factors in Q[x] into factors
    of degrees m and n, it factors in Z[x] with the same degrees. A primitive
    f is irreducible in Z[x] ⇔ irreducible in Q[x]. Z[x] (more generally
    R[x] for a UFD R) is a UFD.
  - EISENSTEIN'S CRITERION: f = aₙxⁿ + ... + a₀ ∈ Z[x] and a prime p with
    p ∤ aₙ, p | aᵢ for all i < n, and p² ∤ a₀ ⇒ f is IRREDUCIBLE over Q.
    Examples: xⁿ − p, xⁿ − 6 (p = 2 or 3), x⁵ − 6x + 3 (p = 3). It gives only
    irreducibility; when it fails nothing is proved.
  - SHIFTING: f(x) is irreducible ⇔ f(x + a) is irreducible. The CYCLOTOMIC
    polynomial Φₚ(x) = xᵖ⁻¹ + ... + x + 1 = (xᵖ − 1)/(x − 1) becomes
    Eisenstein at p after x ↦ x + 1; so does x⁴ + 1 at 2.
  - REDUCTION MOD p: if p ∤ aₙ and the reduction f̄ ∈ Zₚ[x] is irreducible
    (with the same degree), then f is irreducible over Q. The converse fails:
    x⁴ + 1 is irreducible over Q but reducible mod EVERY prime.
  - OVER FINITE FIELDS: monic irreducibles over F₂: degree 2: x² + x + 1;
    degree 3: x³ + x + 1, x³ + x² + 1; degree 4: x⁴ + x + 1, x⁴ + x³ + 1,
    x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1. The number of monic irreducibles of degree n over
    F_q is (1/n)∑_{d|n} μ(d)q^(n/d) (e.g. (q² − q)/2 for n = 2), and
    x^(qⁿ) − x is the product of all monic irreducibles of degree dividing n.
  - CYCLOTOMIC POLYNOMIALS: xⁿ − 1 = ∏_{d|n} Φ_d(x), deg Φₙ = φ(n),
    Φₙ ∈ Z[x] monic and irreducible over Q. Φ₁ = x − 1, Φ₂ = x + 1,
    Φ₃ = x² + x + 1, Φ₄ = x² + 1, Φ₆ = x² − x + 1, Φ₈ = x⁴ + 1,
    Φ₁₂ = x⁴ − x² + 1.
  - TRAPS: 'no rational roots ⇒ irreducible' for degree ≥ 4; applying
    Eisenstein with p² | a₀ or p | aₙ; saying 'irreducible' without naming
    the ring (x² + 1 over R vs C); in Z[x] the constant 2 in 2x + 4 = 2(x + 2)
    is NOT a unit, so 2x + 4 is reducible in Z[x] but irreducible in Q[x];
    reducing mod p when p divides the leading coefficient.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove the division algorithm in R[x] for a monic divisor g. Divide
    f = x⁴ + 3x³ − 2x + 5 by g = x² + x − 1. Prove the remainder theorem and
    find the remainder of x¹⁰⁰ on division by (x − 1)(x − 2).
    Answer: q = x² + 2x − 1, r = x + 4; remainder of x¹⁰⁰ is
    (2¹⁰⁰ − 1)x + (2 − 2¹⁰⁰).
    Teacher explains: Let deg g = m. EXISTENCE by induction on deg f. If
    deg f < m take q = 0, r = f. Otherwise f = aₙxⁿ + ... with n ≥ m, and
       f₁ = f − aₙxⁿ⁻ᵐg
    has degree < n (the leading terms cancel because g is MONIC). By
    induction f₁ = q₁g + r, so f = (aₙxⁿ⁻ᵐ + q₁)g + r. UNIQUENESS: if
    qg + r = q′g + r′ then (q − q′)g = r′ − r; the right side has degree < m,
    while a non-zero left side has degree ≥ m (g monic): so q = q′, r = r′.
    LONG DIVISION:
       x⁴ + 3x³ + 0x² − 2x + 5
       − x²·g = x⁴ + x³ − x²            leaves  2x³ + x² − 2x + 5
       − 2x·g = 2x³ + 2x² − 2x          leaves  −x² + 0x + 5
       − (−1)·g = −x² − x + 1           leaves  x + 4
    so q = x² + 2x − 1, r = x + 4. CHECK: (x² + x − 1)(x² + 2x − 1) + x + 4 =
    x⁴ + 3x³ − 3x + 1 + x + 4 ✓. REMAINDER THEOREM: divide by x − a:
    f = q(x − a) + r with r constant; put x = a: r = f(a). For a divisor of
    degree 2 the remainder is r = ax + b; put in the roots of the divisor:
       x = 1:  1 = a + b         x = 2:  2¹⁰⁰ = 2a + b
    so a = 2¹⁰⁰ − 1, b = 2 − 2¹⁰⁰. Common mistakes: dividing by a non-monic g
    in Z[x] (2x + 1 does not divide into x with integer quotient);
    forgetting the zero coefficient of x² in the long division. Now you try:
    the remainder of x¹⁰⁰ on division by (x − 1)². (Differentiate
    x¹⁰⁰ = q(x − 1)² + ax + b and put x = 1: a = 100, b = −99: 100x − 99)

D2. Prove that a non-zero polynomial of degree n over an integral domain has
    at most n roots, and show that this fails in Z₈[x]. Find the polynomial
    of degree ≤ 2 over Q through (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 6), and over Z₅ through
    (0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 0).
    Answer: proof below; in Z₈, x² − 1 has 4 roots; x² − 2x + 3;
    3x² + x + 1 over Z₅.
    Teacher explains: Induction on n. n = 0: a non-zero constant has no
    roots. If deg f = n ≥ 1 and f(a) = 0, the factor theorem gives
    f = (x − a)g with deg g = n − 1 (degrees add in a domain). If b ≠ a is
    another root, 0 = f(b) = (b − a)g(b), and b − a ≠ 0, so g(b) = 0 (NO ZERO
    DIVISORS used here!). So the roots of f are a and roots of g: at most
    1 + (n − 1) = n ∎. In Z₈: 1² = 1, 3² = 9 ≡ 1, 5² = 25 ≡ 1, 7² = 49 ≡ 1,
    and indeed x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1) = (x − 3)(x + 3) in Z₈[x]: unique
    factorisation fails too. LAGRANGE: the polynomial
       f(x) = ∑ yᵢ ∏_{j≠i} (x − xⱼ)/(xᵢ − xⱼ)
    passes through the points; uniqueness: the difference of two such has
    degree < n and n roots, so is 0. For (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 6) solve
    a + b + c = 2, 4a + 2b + c = 3, 9a + 3b + c = 6: subtracting gives
    3a + b = 1, 5a + b = 3, so a = 1, b = −2, c = 3: f = x² − 2x + 3. Over
    Z₅: f = c(x − 1)(x − 2) has the two zeros; f(0) = 2c = 1 gives c = 3
    (2·3 = 6 ≡ 1): f = 3(x² − 3x + 2) = 3x² + x + 1 (mod 5). Check f(1) = 5 ≡ 0,
    f(2) = 15 ≡ 0 ✓. Common mistakes: treating equal functions as equal
    polynomials over finite fields (x⁵ and x agree on Z₅); forgetting that
    the domain hypothesis is essential. Now you try: how many roots has
    x³ − x in Z₆? (All six: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, since n³ − n is always
    divisible by 6)

D3. Prove that for a field F and f ∈ F[x], F[x]/(f) is a field ⇔ f is
    irreducible. Construct the field F₈ = F₂[x]/(x³ + x + 1), find the
    inverse of α² + 1 (α the class of x) by the extended Euclidean
    algorithm, and list the powers of α.
    Answer: (α² + 1)⁻¹ = α; α has order 7: α, α², α + 1, α² + α,
    α² + α + 1, α² + 1, 1.
    Teacher explains: F[x] is a PID. If f = gh with 0 < deg g < deg f then
    ḡh̄ = 0 in F[x]/(f) with ḡ, h̄ ≠ 0: not even a domain. If f is
    irreducible and g ∉ (f), then gcd(f, g) = 1 (the only divisors of f are
    units and associates of f), so Bézout gives sf + tg = 1, i.e. t̄ḡ = 1: ḡ
    is invertible ∎. F₈: x³ + x + 1 has no root in F₂ (f(0) = 1, f(1) = 1),
    degree 3, so it is irreducible. Elements a + bα + cα², a, b, c ∈ F₂:
    2³ = 8 of them, computed with α³ = α + 1. INVERSE of α² + 1: Euclid
       x³ + x + 1 = x·(x² + 1) + 1         (x·(x² + 1) = x³ + x)
    so 1 = (x³ + x + 1) − x(x² + 1) = (x³ + x + 1) + x(x² + 1) (in F₂, − = +).
    Reduce mod x³ + x + 1: α(α² + 1) = 1. Check: α³ + α = (α + 1) + α = 1 ✓.
    POWERS: α³ = α + 1, α⁴ = α² + α, α⁵ = α³ + α² = α² + α + 1,
    α⁶ = α³ + α² + α = α² + 1, α⁷ = α³ + α = 1. All 7 non-zero elements
    appear: F₈× is cyclic generated by α. Common mistakes: forgetting
    1 + 1 = 0 in F₂; building a 'field' from a reducible polynomial
    (F₂[x]/(x³ + 1) has x + 1 as a zero divisor). Now you try: in
    F₂[x]/(x² + x + 1) find the inverse of x. (x + 1: x(x + 1) = x² + x = 1)

D4. Prove that a is a repeated root of f ⇔ f(a) = f′(a) = 0. Find
    gcd(f, f′) for f = x³ − 3x + 2 and use it to factor f. For which a does
    x³ − 3x + a have a repeated root? Why does an irreducible polynomial
    over Q have no repeated roots in C?
    Answer: gcd = x − 1, f = (x − 1)²(x + 2); a = ±2.
    Teacher explains: The formal derivative satisfies (fg)′ = f′g + fg′ (check
    on monomials and extend by linearity). (⇒) If f = (x − a)²g then
    f′ = 2(x − a)g + (x − a)²g′ vanishes at a. (⇐) Write f = (x − a)h (factor
    theorem). Then f′ = h + (x − a)h′, so 0 = f′(a) = h(a) and (x − a) | h:
    (x − a)² | f ∎. For f = x³ − 3x + 2: f′ = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1). Euclid:
       f = (x/3)·f′ + (−2x + 2)
       f′ = (−(3/2)x − 3/2)·(−2x + 2) + 0
    so gcd(f, f′) = x − 1 (monic). So 1 is a repeated root; dividing,
    f = (x − 1)²(x + 2) ✓. PARAMETER: a repeated root is a root of
    f′ = 3x² − 3, i.e. x = ±1; f(1) = a − 2 = 0 gives a = 2 and f(−1) = a + 2 = 0
    gives a = −2. IRREDUCIBLE OVER Q: gcd(f, f′) is computed in Q[x] and
    divides the irreducible f, so it is 1 or f. It is not f, because f′ ≠ 0
    (char 0) has smaller degree. So gcd = 1 = sf + tf′, and a common root in
    C would give 0 = 1 ∎. Common mistakes: using d/dx as a limit over finite
    fields (it is purely formal there); in characteristic p forgetting that
    f′ may be 0 (x⁴ + 1 over F₂ has f′ = 4x³ = 0 and equals (x + 1)⁴). Now
    you try: find the multiplicity of the root 1 of x⁵ − 5x + 4. (f(1) = 0,
    f′(1) = 5 − 5 = 0, f″(1) = 20 ≠ 0: multiplicity 2;
    f = (x − 1)²(x³ + 2x² + 3x + 4))

D5. Prove that a polynomial of degree 2 or 3 over a field is irreducible iff
    it has no root. Show that x⁴ + 4 has no rational root but is reducible,
    while x⁴ + 1 is irreducible over Q; factor x⁴ + 1 over R.
    Answer: x⁴ + 4 = (x² + 2x + 2)(x² − 2x + 2); x⁴ + 1 irreducible over Q,
    = (x² + √2x + 1)(x² − √2x + 1) over R.
    Teacher explains: If f of degree 2 or 3 is reducible, f = gh with
    degrees adding to 2 or 3 and both ≥ 1, so one factor has degree 1,
    ax + b with a ≠ 0, giving the root −b/a. Conversely a root gives the
    factor x − a. For degree 4 a factorisation could be 2 + 2 with no root:
       x⁴ + 4 = x⁴ + 4x² + 4 − 4x² = (x² + 2)² − (2x)²
             = (x² + 2x + 2)(x² − 2x + 2)
    (SOPHIE GERMAIN's trick), while by the rational root test only
    ±1, ±2, ±4 could be roots and all give positive values. x⁴ + 1: no rational
    roots (±1 give 2). A quadratic splitting may be taken with INTEGER monic
    factors by Gauss's lemma:
       x⁴ + 1 = (x² + ax + b)(x² + cx + d)
    Compare: x³: a + c = 0; x⁰: bd = 1, so b = d = ±1; x²: ac + b + d = 0 gives
    −a² ± 2 = 0, a² = ±2: impossible in Z. x¹: ad + bc = 0 is then automatic.
    So x⁴ + 1 is irreducible over Q. Over R, a² = 2 is fine: a = √2, b = d = 1:
       x⁴ + 1 = (x² + √2x + 1)(x² − √2x + 1)
    (the same trick: (x² + 1)² − 2x²). Common mistakes: 'no rational roots so
    irreducible' for quartics; forgetting that over R every polynomial of
    degree ≥ 3 is reducible. Now you try: is x⁴ + x² + 1 irreducible over Q?
    (No: (x² + 1)² − x² = (x² + x + 1)(x² − x + 1))

D6. Prove the rational root test. Find all rational roots of
    2x³ − 3x² − 3x + 2 and factor it. Show that x³ − 3x − 1 is irreducible
    over Q, and explain what this says about 2cos 20°.
    Answer: roots 2, −1, 1/2; 2x³ − 3x² − 3x + 2 = (x − 2)(x + 1)(2x − 1).
    x³ − 3x − 1 is irreducible; 2cos 20° is one of its roots, so it has
    degree 3 over Q.
    Teacher explains: Let p/q be a root, gcd(p, q) = 1, of
    aₙxⁿ + ... + a₀. Multiply by qⁿ:
       aₙpⁿ + aₙ₋₁pⁿ⁻¹q + ... + a₁pqⁿ⁻¹ + a₀qⁿ = 0.
    All terms but the last contain p, so p | a₀qⁿ; as gcd(p, q) = 1, p | a₀.
    All terms but the first contain q, so q | aₙpⁿ, hence q | aₙ ∎.
    CANDIDATES for 2x³ − 3x² − 3x + 2: p ∈ {±1, ±2}, q ∈ {1, 2}: ±1, ±2, ±1/2.
       f(1) = −2,  f(−1) = 0 ✓,  f(2) = 16 − 12 − 6 + 2 = 0 ✓,
       f(1/2) = 1/4 − 3/4 − 3/2 + 2 = 0 ✓
    Three roots of a cubic: f = 2(x − 2)(x + 1)(x − 1/2) = (x − 2)(x + 1)(2x − 1).
    x³ − 3x − 1: candidates ±1: f(1) = −3, f(−1) = 1. No root, degree 3:
    IRREDUCIBLE (D5). TRIGONOMETRY: cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3cos θ; with y = 2cos θ,
    y³ − 3y = 2cos 3θ. For θ = 20°, 2cos 60° = 1: y³ − 3y − 1 = 0. So
    2cos 20° has minimal polynomial of degree 3, which (topic 10.21) shows
    that a 60° angle cannot be trisected with ruler and compass. Common
    mistakes: forgetting the negative candidates or the fractions p/q with
    q | aₙ; stopping after one root instead of dividing out. Now you try:
    find the rational roots of 6x³ − 11x² + 6x − 1. (1, 1/2, 1/3;
    6x³ − 11x² + 6x − 1 = (x − 1)(2x − 1)(3x − 1))

D7. Define content and primitive polynomial and prove Gauss's lemma: the
    product of primitive polynomials is primitive. Deduce that if f ∈ Z[x]
    factors in Q[x], it factors in Z[x] with the same degrees. Illustrate
    with 2x² + 7x + 3 = (x + 1/2)(2x + 6).
    Answer: proof below; 2x² + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3) in Z[x].
    Teacher explains: c(f) = gcd of the coefficients; f = c(f)·f₀ with f₀
    PRIMITIVE. LEMMA: suppose f, g are primitive but a prime p divides every
    coefficient of fg. Reduce mod p: f̄ḡ = 0 in Zₚ[x]. But Zₚ[x] is an
    INTEGRAL DOMAIN, so f̄ = 0 or ḡ = 0, i.e. p divides all coefficients of f
    or of g: contradiction ∎. Hence c(fg) = c(f)c(g). COROLLARY: let
    f = gh with g, h ∈ Q[x]. Clear denominators: write g = (a/b)g₀,
    h = (c/d)h₀ with g₀, h₀ ∈ Z[x] primitive. Then f = (ac/bd)g₀h₀, and g₀h₀
    is primitive; since f has integer coefficients, comparing contents gives
    ac/bd = ±c(f) ∈ Z. So f = (±c(f)g₀)·h₀ in Z[x], same degrees ∎. EXAMPLE:
    (x + 1/2)(2x + 6) = (1/2)(2x + 1)·2(x + 3) = (2x + 1)(x + 3); the
    fractions cancel as the lemma promises. CONSEQUENCE: a PRIMITIVE f ∈ Z[x]
    is irreducible in Z[x] ⇔ irreducible in Q[x]. The word primitive matters:
    2x + 4 = 2(x + 2) is reducible in Z[x] (2 is not a unit there) but
    irreducible in Q[x]. Common mistakes: assuming a factorisation over Q
    must already have integer coefficients (it can be rescaled, not used as
    it stands); forgetting constants when talking about irreducibility in
    Z[x]. Now you try: find c(f) and the primitive part of 6x³ + 9x − 12.
    (c = 3, f₀ = 2x³ + 3x − 4)

D8. State and prove Eisenstein's criterion. Use it to prove that x⁵ − 6x + 3,
    3x⁴ + 14x² + 7 and xⁿ − 2 (every n ≥ 1) are irreducible over Q. What can
    be said about x⁴ − 4 and x³ + 2x + 12?
    Answer: primes 3, 7, 2 respectively. x⁴ − 4 = (x² − 2)(x² + 2) and
    x³ + 2x + 12 = (x + 2)(x² − 2x + 6): Eisenstein does not apply to them
    (no suitable prime) and they are in fact reducible.
    Teacher explains: Let f = aₙxⁿ + ... + a₀, p ∤ aₙ, p | aᵢ (i < n), p² ∤ a₀.
    By Gauss's lemma it is enough to rule out f = gh in Z[x] with
    g = bᵣxʳ + ... + b₀, h = cₛxˢ + ... + c₀, r, s ≥ 1. Reduce mod p:
       f̄ = āₙxⁿ   (all other coefficients vanish)
    In the UFD Zₚ[x] this forces ḡ = b̄ᵣxʳ and h̄ = c̄ₛxˢ (up to units), with
    r, s ≥ 1 (p ∤ aₙ = bᵣcₛ keeps the degrees). So p | b₀ and p | c₀, and then
    p² | b₀c₀ = a₀: contradiction ∎. (If a factor is a constant it must be
    ±1 when f is primitive.) EXAMPLES:
       x⁵ − 6x + 3:     p = 3: 3 ∤ 1, 3 | 0, 0, 0, −6, 3 and 9 ∤ 3     ✓
       3x⁴ + 14x² + 7:  p = 7: 7 ∤ 3, 7 | 0, 14, 0, 7 and 49 ∤ 7       ✓
       xⁿ − 2:          p = 2: 4 ∤ 2                                ✓
    So Q has irreducible polynomials of EVERY degree, and ⁿ√2 is irrational
    of degree n. x⁴ − 4: the only candidate is p = 2 but 4 | 4. x³ + 2x + 12:
    p = 2 fails (4 | 12), p = 3 fails (3 ∤ 2). And in fact −2 is a root.
    Failure of Eisenstein proves NOTHING by itself (x² + 1 is irreducible
    and no prime works). Common mistakes: checking p | aₙ instead of p ∤ aₙ;
    forgetting zero coefficients (they are divisible by every p); using
    Eisenstein to 'prove' reducibility. Now you try: which prime works for
    2x⁵ − 6x³ + 9x² − 15? (p = 3: 3 ∤ 2, 3 | 6, 9, 15 and 9 ∤ 15)

D9. Prove that Φₚ(x) = xᵖ⁻¹ + xᵖ⁻² + ... + x + 1 is irreducible over Q for
    every prime p, and that x⁴ + 1 and x⁴ + 4x³ + 6x² + 4x + 4 are
    irreducible over Q.
    Answer: substitute x ↦ x + 1 (for the last one x ↦ x − 1) and apply
    Eisenstein at p, 2 and 3 respectively.
    Teacher explains: If f(x) = g(x)h(x) then f(x + a) = g(x + a)h(x + a)
    with the same degrees; so f(x) is irreducible ⇔ f(x + a) is. For Φₚ use
    Φₚ(x) = (xᵖ − 1)/(x − 1):
       Φₚ(x + 1) = ((x + 1)ᵖ − 1)/x = xᵖ⁻¹ + C(p, 1)xᵖ⁻² + ... + C(p, p − 1).
    The leading coefficient is 1, every C(p, k) with 0 < k < p is divisible by
    p, and the constant term C(p, p − 1) = p is not divisible by p²: EISENSTEIN
    at p ∎. For p = 5: Φ₅(x + 1) = x⁴ + 5x³ + 10x² + 10x + 5 ✓. For x⁴ + 1:
       (x + 1)⁴ + 1 = x⁴ + 4x³ + 6x² + 4x + 2          Eisenstein at 2 ✓
    (This gives a second proof of D5.) For g = x⁴ + 4x³ + 6x² + 4x + 4 notice
    the binomial coefficients: g = (x + 1)⁴ + 3, so g(x − 1) = x⁴ + 3,
    Eisenstein at 3 ✓. HOW TO FIND THE SHIFT: look for binomial patterns, or
    try x ↦ x ± 1, x ± 2 and inspect the new coefficients; the aim is a
    polynomial in which a prime divides everything but the leading term.
    Common mistakes: forgetting that the shift must be applied to the whole
    polynomial; thinking Φₙ is 1 + x + ... + xⁿ⁻¹ for composite n
    (Φ₄ = x² + 1, not x³ + x² + x + 1). Now you try: prove x² − 2x − 1 and
    x³ − 3x² + 3x + 1 irreducible by shifting. (x ↦ x + 1 gives x² − 2 and
    x³ + 2, both Eisenstein at 2)

D10. Prove the mod p criterion: if p ∤ aₙ and f̄ is irreducible in Zₚ[x],
     then f is irreducible over Q (f primitive). Show that
     x⁴ + 3x³ + 7x² + 9x + 1 and x⁵ − x − 1 are irreducible, and explain why
     the test can never work for x⁴ + 1.
     Answer: mod 2 and mod 5 respectively; x⁴ + 1 is reducible modulo every
     prime although irreducible over Q.
     Teacher explains: Suppose f = gh in Z[x] (Gauss) with deg g, deg h ≥ 1.
     The leading coefficients multiply to aₙ, which p does not divide, so
     reduction mod p keeps both degrees: f̄ = ḡh̄ with deg ḡ = deg g ≥ 1 and
     deg h̄ = deg h ≥ 1. That contradicts irreducibility of f̄ ∎. (If p | aₙ
     the degree could drop and the argument breaks.) f = x⁴ + 3x³ + 7x² + 9x + 1
     mod 2 is x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1. It has no root in F₂ (values 1, 1), and
     the only irreducible quadratic over F₂ is x² + x + 1, with
     (x² + x + 1)² = x⁴ + x² + 1 ≠ f̄. So f̄ is irreducible and so is f. (Mod 3,
     f̄ = (x + 1)²(x − 1)² tells us nothing: one good prime suffices.)
     x⁵ − x − 1 mod 5: for every a ∈ F₅, a⁵ = a, so f̄(a) = −1 ≠ 0 and there
     is no linear factor; a finer argument (or computer) shows no quadratic
     factor either, so f̄ is irreducible; mod 2 it factors as
     (x² + x + 1)(x³ + x² + 1), which again says nothing. x⁴ + 1 mod p: for
     p = 2 it is (x + 1)⁴. For odd p, one of −1, 2, −2 is a square in Fₚ
     (their product is 4, a square, and Fₚ× modulo squares has order 2):
        −1 = a²:  x⁴ + 1 = (x² − a)(x² + a)
         2 = b²:  x⁴ + 1 = (x² + bx + 1)(x² − bx + 1)
        −2 = c²:  x⁴ + 1 = (x² + cx − 1)(x² − cx − 1)
     So the mod p test is sufficient but not necessary. Common mistakes:
     reducing mod a prime dividing the leading coefficient; concluding
     reducibility over Q from reducibility mod p. Now you try: show
     x³ − 9x + 7 is irreducible over Q. (Mod 2: x³ + x + 1, no root in F₂)

D11. List the monic irreducible polynomials of degree 1 to 4 over F₂,
     and check the count with the formula. Factor x⁸ − x and x¹⁶ − x over F₂
     into irreducibles, and count the monic irreducible quadratics over F₃.
     Answer: degree 1: x, x + 1; 2: x² + x + 1; 3: x³ + x + 1, x³ + x² + 1;
     4: x⁴ + x + 1, x⁴ + x³ + 1, x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1. x⁸ − x = x(x + 1)
     (x³ + x + 1)(x³ + x² + 1); x¹⁶ − x is the product of the 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 6
     irreducibles of degrees 1, 2, 4 (x, x + 1, x² + x + 1 and the three
     quartics). F₃: 3 quadratics: x² + 1, x² + x + 2, x² + 2x + 2.
     Teacher explains: DEGREE 2 AND 3: irreducible ⇔ no root ⇔ f(0) = 1 and
     f(1) = 1, i.e. constant term 1 and an ODD number of terms. Quadratics
     x² + bx + 1: only x² + x + 1. Cubics x³ + bx² + cx + 1 with b + c = 1:
     x³ + x + 1 and x³ + x² + 1. QUARTICS: no root (constant 1, odd number of
     terms): x⁴ + x + 1, x⁴ + x² + 1, x⁴ + x³ + 1, x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1; remove
     the square of the only irreducible quadratic, (x² + x + 1)² = x⁴ + x² + 1.
     Three remain. FORMULA N(n) = (1/n)∑μ(d)2^(n/d):
        N(2) = (4 − 2)/2 = 1,  N(3) = (8 − 2)/3 = 2,  N(4) = (16 − 4)/4 = 3
     all ✓. THE PRODUCT FORMULA: x^(2ⁿ) − x is the product of all monic
     irreducibles of degree d | n (topic 10.20). Degree check for n = 3:
     1 + 1 + 3 + 3 = 8 ✓; for n = 4: 1 + 1 + 2 + 4·3 = 16 ✓. OVER F₃ monic
     quadratics x² + bx + c number 9; the reducible ones (x − a)(x − b) with
     {a, b} a multiset from F₃ number 3 + 3 = 6; so 3 are irreducible,
     matching (9 − 3)/2. They are those with no root: x² + 1, x² + x + 2,
     x² + 2x + 2. Common mistakes: listing x⁴ + x² + 1 as irreducible (no
     roots but a square); forgetting that over F₂ the only coefficients are 0
     and 1. Now you try: how many monic irreducible polynomials of degree 5
     are there over F₂? ((32 − 2)/5 = 6)

D12. Define the cyclotomic polynomials by xⁿ − 1 = ∏_{d|n} Φ_d(x). Compute
     Φ₁, ..., Φ₆, Φ₈, Φ₉ and Φ₁₂, and factor x⁶ − 1, x⁸ − 1 and x¹² − 1 into
     irreducibles over Q. Summarise a strategy for irreducibility over Q.
     Answer: Φ₁ = x − 1, Φ₂ = x + 1, Φ₃ = x² + x + 1, Φ₄ = x² + 1,
     Φ₅ = x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1, Φ₆ = x² − x + 1, Φ₈ = x⁴ + 1,
     Φ₉ = x⁶ + x³ + 1, Φ₁₂ = x⁴ − x² + 1. x⁶ − 1 = Φ₁Φ₂Φ₃Φ₆,
     x⁸ − 1 = Φ₁Φ₂Φ₄Φ₈, x¹² − 1 = Φ₁Φ₂Φ₃Φ₄Φ₆Φ₁₂.
     Teacher explains: Φₙ(x) = ∏(x − ζ) over the PRIMITIVE n-th roots of unity
     ζ = e^(2πik/n), gcd(k, n) = 1, so deg Φₙ = φ(n). Every n-th root of unity
     is a primitive d-th root for exactly one d | n, giving the product
     formula. Compute recursively by division:
        Φ₁ = x − 1;  Φ₂ = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) = x + 1;  Φₚ = (xᵖ − 1)/(x − 1)
        Φ₄ = (x⁴ − 1)/((x − 1)(x + 1)) = x² + 1
        Φ₆ = (x⁶ − 1)/(Φ₁Φ₂Φ₃) = (x³ + 1)/(x + 1) = x² − x + 1
        Φ₈ = (x⁸ − 1)/(x⁴ − 1) = x⁴ + 1
        Φ₉ = (x⁹ − 1)/(x³ − 1) = x⁶ + x³ + 1
        Φ₁₂ = (x¹² − 1)/((x⁶ − 1)(x² + 1)) = (x⁶ + 1)/(x² + 1) = x⁴ − x² + 1
     Degrees check: φ(6) = 2, φ(8) = 4, φ(9) = 6, φ(12) = 4 ✓. Division by
     monic integer polynomials keeps integer coefficients, so Φₙ ∈ Z[x]; each
     Φₙ is irreducible over Q (for primes by D9; in general a harder theorem),
     so these are the complete factorisations. STRATEGY for f ∈ Q[x]:
        1. clear denominators, take out the content;
        2. degree ≤ 3: rational root test decides;
        3. try Eisenstein, then Eisenstein after x ↦ x ± 1, x ± 2;
        4. reduce mod a small prime not dividing the leading coefficient;
        5. otherwise look for factorisations with undetermined coefficients
           (Gauss lets you work in Z[x]) or spot patterns (differences of
           squares, cyclotomic factors).
     Common mistakes: writing Φ₆ = x² + x + 1 (that is Φ₃); thinking xⁿ − 1
     has only the factors x − 1 and 1 + x + ... + xⁿ⁻¹. Now you try: factor
     x¹⁰ − 1 over Q. (Φ₁Φ₂Φ₅Φ₁₀ = (x − 1)(x + 1)(x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1)
     (x⁴ − x³ + x² − x + 1))

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY

M1. Arithmetic in polynomial rings.
    a) (2x + 1)(3x + 2) in Z₆[x]        b) (2x + 1)² in Z₄[x]
    c) (3x² + 2)(2x + 3) in Z₆[x]       d) (2x² + 1)(2x + 3) in Z₄[x]
    e) (x + 1)⁵ in Z₅[x]                f) (x + 1)⁴ in Z₂[x]
    g) (x + 2)³ in Z₃[x]                h) f(2) for f = x³ + 2x + 1 in Z₅[x]
    i) is 1 + 3x a unit in Z₉[x]? inverse?
    j) units of Z[x], Q[x], Z₄[x] (examples)
    k) number of polynomials of degree ≤ 3 over Z₅; of monic cubics
    l) number of monic quadratics over F₃; how many are reducible?
    m) deg(fg) and deg(f + g) if deg f = 3, deg g = 5 over a domain
    n) is x⁵ − x the zero polynomial in Z₅[x]? the zero function on Z₅?
    o) x² + x as a function on Z₂
    p) coefficient of x⁵ in (1 + x)⁸ in Z[x] and in Z₂[x]
    q) (x + y)³ in Z₃[x, y]             r) (x − 1)(x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1)
    Answers:
      a) x + 2 (degree 1: 6x² = 0)      b) 1
      c) 3x² + 4x                       d) 2x² + 2x + 3 (degree 2, not 3)
      e) x⁵ + 1                         f) x⁴ + 1
      g) x³ + 2                         h) 3
      i) yes, (1 + 3x)(1 + 6x) = 1 + 9x + 18x² = 1: inverse 1 + 6x
      j) ±1; non-zero constants; e.g. 1, 3, 1 + 2x, 3 + 2x, 1 + 2x²
      k) 625, 125                       l) 9, 6
      m) 8, 5                           n) no; yes
      o) the zero function (0 ↦ 0, 1 ↦ 0) q) x³ + y³
      p) 56; 0 ((1 + x)⁸ = 1 + x⁸)      r) x⁵ − 1

M2. Remainders and divisibility (use the remainder theorem where possible).
    a) x¹⁰⁰ ÷ (x − 1)                   b) x¹⁰⁰ ÷ (x + 1)
    c) x¹⁰⁰ ÷ (x² − 1)                  d) x¹⁰⁰ ÷ (x² + 1)
    e) x¹⁰⁰ ÷ (x² + x + 1)              f) x¹⁰⁰ ÷ (x − 1)(x − 2)
    g) x¹⁰⁰ ÷ (x³ − x)                  h) x¹⁰⁰ ÷ (x − 1)²
    i) x¹⁰⁰ ÷ (x³ − 1)                  j) x¹⁰¹ ÷ (x² − 1)
    k) (x⁵⁰ + x²⁵ + 1) ÷ (x² + 1)       l) (x⁷ + 3x² + 1) ÷ (x − 2)
    m) (2x⁴ − 3x + 5) ÷ (x + 1)         n) x²⁰²³ ÷ (x² + x + 1)
    o) k such that x − 2 divides x³ + kx² − 2x + 4
    p) a, b such that x² − 3x + 2 divides x⁴ + ax² + b
    q) f(1) = 3, f(−1) = 5: remainder of f ÷ (x² − 1)
    r) quotient and remainder of x⁴ + 3x³ − 2x + 5 ÷ (x² + x − 1)
    Answers:
      a) 1              b) 1              c) 1               d) 1
      e) x              f) (2¹⁰⁰ − 1)x + 2 − 2¹⁰⁰             g) x²
      h) 100x − 99      i) x              j) x               k) x
      l) 141            m) 10             n) x               o) −2
      p) a = −5, b = 4  q) −x + 4         r) x² + 2x − 1, x + 4

M3. Roots and interpolation.
    Find all roots in the given ring:
    a) x² + 1 in Z₅                     b) x² + 1 in Z₇
    c) x² + 1 in Z₁₃                    d) x³ − 2 in Z₇
    e) x³ − 2 in Z₅                     f) x² + x + 1 in Z₇
    g) x⁵ − x in Z₅                     h) x⁴ − 1 in Z₅
    i) x² − 1 in Z₈                     j) x² − 1 in Z₁₅
    k) x² in Z₄                         l) x² + 3x + 2 in Z₆
    m) x³ + x² + x + 1 in Z₅            n) x⁴ + 1 in Z₁₇
    o) x² − 2 in Z₇                     p) x³ − x in Z₆
    Interpolate (lowest degree):
    q) (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 7) over Q    r) (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 6) over Q
    s) (0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 0) over Z₅   t) (−1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (2, 3)
                                           over Q
    Answers:
      a) 2, 3           b) none           c) 5, 8            d) none
      e) 3              f) 2, 4           g) 0, 1, 2, 3, 4   h) 1, 2, 3, 4
      i) 1, 3, 5, 7     j) 1, 4, 11, 14   k) 0, 2            l) 1, 2, 4, 5
      m) 2, 3, 4        n) 2, 8, 9, 15    o) 3, 4            p) 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
      q) x² + x + 1     r) x² − 2x + 3    s) 3x² + x + 1
      t) x³ − x² − x + 1 (write f = 1 − x² + c·x(x² − 1); f(2) = 3 gives
         c = 1)

       roots.

    l) A monic integer polynomial with no integer root has no rational

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: drill long division until the columns line up (write the
  zero coefficients!), and always check q·g + r = f. For irreducibility give
  the student a fixed checklist: degree ≤ 3 → roots; otherwise Eisenstein,
  shifted Eisenstein, reduction mod 2 or 3, undetermined coefficients. Make
  them say over WHICH field each time. Build tables of the small irreducible
  polynomials over F₂ and F₃ by hand, since they appear everywhere
  (topic 10.20). Harder: prove that Φₙ is irreducible over Q for all n;
  prove that x^(qⁿ) − x is the product of all monic irreducibles over F_q of
  degree dividing n and derive the Möbius counting formula; prove that
  x⁵ − x − 1 is irreducible over F₅ (Artin-Schreier: xᵖ − x − a is
  irreducible over Fₚ for a ≠ 0); show that R[x] is a UFD for every UFD R;
  and prove Perron's criterion (xⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + ... + a₀ with
  |aₙ₋₁| > 1 + |aₙ₋₂| + ... + |a₀|, a₀ ≠ 0, is irreducible).


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.20 — FIELDS AND FIELD EXTENSIONS; FINITE FIELDS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A FIELD is a commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 in which every non-zero element
    has an inverse. Its CHARACTERISTIC is 0 or a prime p. The PRIME SUBFIELD
    (smallest subfield) is Q (char 0) or Fₚ = Zₚ (char p). In char p,
    pa = 0 for all a and (a + b)ᵖ = aᵖ + bᵖ (FROBENIUS). Every homomorphism of
    fields is injective (its kernel is an ideal ≠ the whole field).
  - A FIELD EXTENSION L/K is a field L containing K as a subfield. L is a
    VECTOR SPACE over K; its dimension [L : K] is the DEGREE. FINITE if
    [L : K] < ∞. [L : K] = 1 ⇔ L = K. Examples: [C : R] = 2,
    [Q(√2) : Q] = 2, [R : Q] = ∞.
  - TOWER LAW: for K ⊆ L ⊆ M, [M : K] = [M : L][L : K]; if {aᵢ} is a basis of
    L/K and {bⱼ} of M/L then {aᵢbⱼ} is a basis of M/K. CONSEQUENCES: the
    degree of any intermediate field or element divides [M : K]; an
    extension of prime degree has no intermediate fields; if [K(α) : K] and
    [K(β) : K] are coprime then [K(α, β) : K] is their product.
  - α ∈ L is ALGEBRAIC over K if f(α) = 0 for some non-zero f ∈ K[x];
    otherwise TRANSCENDENTAL (π, e over Q: Lindemann 1882, Hermite 1873).
    The MINIMAL POLYNOMIAL m_α is the unique MONIC polynomial of least degree
    with m_α(α) = 0; it is IRREDUCIBLE, it divides every f with f(α) = 0, and
    it generates the kernel of evaluation K[x] → L. A monic irreducible
    polynomial with root α IS the minimal polynomial.
  - SIMPLE EXTENSIONS: for α algebraic of degree n,
    K(α) = K[α] ≅ K[x]/(m_α), with K-basis 1, α, ..., αⁿ⁻¹; so
    [K(α) : K] = deg m_α. Inverses in K(α) are found by the extended
    Euclidean algorithm, by 'rationalising' (conjugates, a³ − b³ identities)
    or by solving linear equations. For α transcendental K(α) ≅ K(x).
  - FINITE ⇒ ALGEBRAIC (1, α, ..., αⁿ are dependent). K(α₁, ..., αₖ) with
    all αᵢ algebraic is finite. The ALGEBRAIC elements of L form a subfield
    (α ± β, αβ, α/β are algebraic); the ALGEBRAIC NUMBERS Q̄ are a
    countable field, so almost all real numbers are transcendental. Q̄/Q is
    algebraic but not finite.
  - PRIMITIVE ELEMENT THEOREM: a finite extension of a field of
    characteristic 0 (or of a finite field) is simple: L = K(θ). Example:
    Q(√2, √3) = Q(√2 + √3), degree 4, minimal polynomial x⁴ − 10x² + 1.
  - KRONECKER: every non-constant f ∈ K[x] has a root in some extension:
    take L = K[x]/(p) for an irreducible factor p; then x̄ is a root. A
    SPLITTING FIELD of f is an extension generated by the roots over which f
    splits into linear factors; it exists, is unique up to isomorphism, and
    has degree ≤ n! (n = deg f). Examples over Q: x³ − 2 → Q(∛2, ω), degree 6;
    x⁴ − 2 → Q(⁴√2, i), degree 8; x⁴ + 1 → Q(√2, i), degree 4.
  - ALGEBRAICALLY CLOSED: every non-constant polynomial has a root (so
    splits). C is algebraically closed (FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ALGEBRA); Q̄
    is the algebraic closure of Q. An algebraically closed field is
    infinite.
  - FINITE FIELDS: a finite field F has char p and |F| = pⁿ (n = [F : Fₚ]).
    For every prime power q = pⁿ there is EXACTLY ONE field F_q (= GF(q)) up
    to isomorphism: the splitting field of x^q − x over Fₚ, whose q roots are
    exactly the elements (a^q = a for all a ∈ F_q). Concretely
    F_q = Fₚ[x]/(f) for any irreducible f of degree n. F_q is NOT Z_q
    when n > 1.
  - The MULTIPLICATIVE GROUP F_q× is CYCLIC of order q − 1; a generator is a
    PRIMITIVE ELEMENT; there are φ(q − 1) of them, and for d | q − 1 there
    are φ(d) elements of order d. The ADDITIVE group is (Z_p)ⁿ, not cyclic
    for n > 1. A PRIMITIVE POLYNOMIAL is the minimal polynomial of a
    primitive element (x⁴ + x + 1 over F₂).
  - SUBFIELDS: F_{pᵐ} ⊆ F_{pⁿ} ⇔ m | n, and each such subfield is unique:
    F_{pᵐ} = {a : a^(pᵐ) = a}. The FROBENIUS σ(a) = aᵖ is an automorphism of
    F_{pⁿ} of order n; Aut(F_{pⁿ}) = Gal(F_{pⁿ}/Fₚ) = ⟨σ⟩ ≅ Zₙ. The
    CONJUGATES of α over Fₚ are α, αᵖ, α^(p²), ..., and its minimal polynomial
    is ∏(x − conjugates). x^(pⁿ) − x = product of all monic irreducibles over
    Fₚ of degree dividing n.
  - TRAPS: confusing [L : K] with |L|; thinking K(α, β) has degree
    [K(α) : K]·[K(β) : K] always (Q(√2, √8) = Q(√2)); taking a reducible
    polynomial as a minimal polynomial; writing F₄ = Z₄ (Z₄ has the zero
    divisor 2); thinking F₈ ⊆ F₁₆ (3 ∤ 4); forgetting that Q(∛2) and Q(ω∛2)
    are different subfields of C though isomorphic.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that the prime subfield of a field F is Q or Fₚ, and that a finite
    field has pⁿ elements. Explain why Z₄ is not a field, and write the
    addition and multiplication tables of the field F₄ = F₂[x]/(x² + x + 1).
    Answer: F₄ = {0, 1, ω, ω + 1} with ω² = ω + 1; tables below.
    Teacher explains: Map φ : Z → F, n ↦ n·1. Its kernel is (char F). If
    char F = p then φ(Z) ≅ Z/pZ = Fₚ, a subfield. If char F = 0, φ is
    injective, and since F is a field it contains all quotients m/n: a copy
    of Q (its field of fractions). Any subfield contains 1, hence these, so
    this is the SMALLEST subfield. FINITE F: char 0 is impossible (Q is
    infinite), so char F = p and F is a vector space over Fₚ of some finite
    dimension n; choosing a basis e₁, ..., eₙ, the elements are
    c₁e₁ + ... + cₙeₙ with cᵢ ∈ Fₚ: exactly pⁿ of them ∎. Z₄ is not a field:
    2·2 = 0, so 2 has no inverse. F₄: x² + x + 1 has no root in F₂ (f(0) = 1,
    f(1) = 1), so the quotient is a field with elements a + bω, and ω² = ω + 1
    (since −1 = +1):
          +  |  0     1     ω     ω+1          ·  |  1     ω     ω+1
         ----+------------------------        ----+------------------
          0  |  0     1     ω     ω+1          1  |  1     ω     ω+1
          1  |  1     0     ω+1   ω            ω  |  ω     ω+1   1
          ω  |  ω     ω+1   0     1          ω+1  |  ω+1   1     ω
         ω+1 |  ω+1   ω     1     0
    Check: ω(ω + 1) = ω² + ω = 2ω + 1 = 1, and ω³ = 1: F₄× = {1, ω, ω²} is
    cyclic of order 3, while (F₄, +) ≅ Z₂ × Z₂. Common mistakes: 'a field with
    4 elements is Z₄'; adding 1 + 1 = 2 in characteristic 2. Now you try: can
    there be a field with 6 or with 12 elements? (No: neither is a prime
    power)

D2. Prove the tower law. Deduce that √2 ∉ Q(∛2), find [Q(√2, ∛2) : Q], and
    show that if [L : K] is prime there is no field strictly between K
    and L.
    Answer: proof below; [Q(√2, ∛2) : Q] = 6.
    Teacher explains: Let K ⊆ L ⊆ M, {a₁, ..., aₘ} a basis of L over K and
    {b₁, ..., bₙ} a basis of M over L. CLAIM: {aᵢbⱼ} is a basis of M over K.
    SPANNING: any z ∈ M is ∑ⱼ λⱼbⱼ with λⱼ ∈ L, and each λⱼ = ∑ᵢ μᵢⱼaᵢ with
    μᵢⱼ ∈ K, so z = ∑ μᵢⱼaᵢbⱼ. INDEPENDENCE: if ∑ μᵢⱼaᵢbⱼ = 0 then
    ∑ⱼ(∑ᵢ μᵢⱼaᵢ)bⱼ = 0 with coefficients in L; the bⱼ are independent over L,
    so each ∑ᵢ μᵢⱼaᵢ = 0, and the aᵢ are independent over K, so all μᵢⱼ = 0.
    Hence [M : K] = mn ∎ (the infinite case works the same way).
    CONSEQUENCES: x³ − 2 is irreducible (Eisenstein at 2), so
    [Q(∛2) : Q] = 3. If √2 ∈ Q(∛2) then Q ⊆ Q(√2) ⊆ Q(∛2) and
    2 = [Q(√2) : Q] would divide 3: impossible. For Q(√2, ∛2): both 2 and 3
    divide its degree (towers through Q(√2) and Q(∛2)), so 6 divides it; and
    [Q(√2, ∛2) : Q(∛2)] ≤ 2 (√2 is a root of x² − 2), so the degree is ≤ 6.
    Hence 6. PRIME DEGREE: an intermediate E has [E : K] dividing p, so it is
    1 (E = K) or p (E = L). Common mistakes: adding degrees instead of
    multiplying; concluding [Q(α, β) : Q] = 6 from degrees 2 and 3 without
    the divisibility argument. Now you try: is ∛2 ∈ Q(√2, √3)? (No:
    [Q(√2, √3) : Q] = 4 and 3 ∤ 4)

D3. Prove that the minimal polynomial of an algebraic element is
    irreducible and divides every polynomial vanishing at α, and that
    K(α) ≅ K[x]/(m_α) with basis 1, α, ..., αⁿ⁻¹. Find the minimal polynomial
    of √2 + √3 over Q and over Q(√2).
    Answer: over Q: x⁴ − 10x² + 1; over Q(√2): x² − 2√2x − 1.
    Teacher explains: The evaluation map ev : K[x] → L, f ↦ f(α), is a ring
    homomorphism; its kernel is a non-zero ideal (α is algebraic), hence
    principal: (m) with m monic of least degree: that is m_α. So f(α) = 0 ⇔
    m_α | f. IRREDUCIBLE: if m_α = gh with smaller degrees, then g(α)h(α) = 0
    in the field L, so g(α) = 0 or h(α) = 0, contradicting minimality. The
    image of ev is K[α] ≅ K[x]/(m_α) (first isomorphism theorem), a FIELD
    because m_α is irreducible (so (m_α) is maximal); hence K[α] = K(α).
    BASIS: every f(α) reduces, by division by m_α, to r(α) with deg r < n, so
    1, ..., αⁿ⁻¹ span; a dependence would be a polynomial of degree < n
    vanishing at α. EXAMPLE θ = √2 + √3:
       θ − √2 = √3 ⇒ θ² − 2√2θ + 2 = 3 ⇒ θ² − 1 = 2√2θ
                   ⇒ (θ² − 1)² = 8θ² ⇒ θ⁴ − 10θ² + 1 = 0.
    Degree: [Q(√2, √3) : Q] = 4 (D5) and θ generates it, so the monic quartic
    is the minimal polynomial. Over Q(√2) the second line already gives
    x² − 2√2x − 1, a quadratic with coefficients in Q(√2), irreducible there
    because √3 ∉ Q(√2). Check via the tower: 4 = 2·2 ✓. Common mistakes:
    naming x⁴ − 10x² + 1 without justifying irreducibility (it has no
    rational roots, but a quartic needs more — the degree argument settles
    it); forgetting that the minimal polynomial depends on the base field.
    Now you try: minimal polynomial of √(1 + √2) over Q. (x² = 1 + √2 ⇒
    (x² − 1)² = 2: x⁴ − 2x² − 1. Irreducible: no rational roots, and
    (x² + ax + b)(x² − ax + c) = x⁴ − 2x² − 1 in Z[x] needs bc = −1, so
    b + c = 0 and then −a² = −2, impossible)

D4. Let α = ∛2. Express (1 + α + α²)⁻¹ and (1 + α)⁻¹ in the basis 1, α, α² of
    Q(α) over Q, and find the minimal polynomials of 1 + α and of
    β = 1 + α + α².
    Answer: (1 + α + α²)⁻¹ = α − 1; (1 + α)⁻¹ = (1 − α + α²)/3; m of 1 + α:
    x³ − 3x² + 3x − 3; m of β: x³ − 3x² − 3x − 1.
    Teacher explains: FIRST INVERSE: use a³ − 1 = (a − 1)(a² + a + 1):
       (α − 1)(α² + α + 1) = α³ − 1 = 2 − 1 = 1,
    so (1 + α + α²)⁻¹ = α − 1. SECOND: a³ + 1 = (a + 1)(a² − a + 1):
       (1 + α)(1 − α + α²) = 1 + α³ = 3,
    so (1 + α)⁻¹ = (1 − α + α²)/3. General method (always works): write
    (1 + α)(a + bα + cα²) = 1, expand with α³ = 2:
       a + 2c = 1,   a + b = 0,   b + c = 0    ⇒ a = 1/3, b = −1/3, c = 1/3 ✓
    MINIMAL POLYNOMIALS: γ = 1 + α gives (γ − 1)³ = 2, i.e.
    γ³ − 3γ² + 3γ − 3 = 0; this is Eisenstein at 3, so irreducible: it is m_γ.
    For β: since β(α − 1) = 1, α = 1 + 1/β. Then α³ = 2 gives
       (β + 1)³ = 2β³ ⇒ β³ + 3β² + 3β + 1 = 2β³ ⇒ β³ − 3β² − 3β − 1 = 0.
    Its degree 3 equals [Q(β) : Q] (β ∉ Q and 3 is prime), so it is m_β. A
    matrix view: multiplication by β is a Q-linear map of Q(α) with matrix
    [[1, 2, 2], [1, 1, 2], [1, 1, 1]] in the basis 1, α, α²; its
    characteristic polynomial is x³ − 3x² − 3x − 1 (trace 3, determinant 1 =
    the norm of β). Common mistakes: leaving α⁴ unreduced (α⁴ = 2α); inverting
    'conjugate style' with √-type conjugates, which do not work for cube
    roots. Now you try: in Q(√2) write (3 + 2√2)⁻¹ and (1 + √2)⁵ in the form
    a + b√2. (3 − 2√2; 41 + 29√2)

D5. Prove that [Q(√2, √3) : Q] = 4 with basis 1, √2, √3, √6, and that
    Q(√2, √3) = Q(√2 + √3). Explain the primitive element theorem.
    Answer: proofs below; √2 = (θ³ − 9θ)/2 and √3 = (11θ − θ³)/2 for
    θ = √2 + √3.
    Teacher explains: STEP 1: √3 ∉ Q(√2). If √3 = a + b√2 (a, b ∈ Q) then
    3 = a² + 2b² + 2ab√2, so ab = 0 (√2 is irrational). b = 0 makes √3
    rational; a = 0 gives 3 = 2b², b² = 3/2, impossible in Q. So x² − 3 stays
    irreducible over Q(√2) and [Q(√2, √3) : Q(√2)] = 2. TOWER:
    [Q(√2, √3) : Q] = 2·2 = 4, basis {1, √2}·{1, √3} = {1, √2, √3, √6}.
    STEP 2: θ = √2 + √3 ∈ Q(√2, √3), so Q(θ) ⊆ Q(√2, √3). Conversely
       θ³ = 2√2 + 6√3 + 9√2 + 3√3 = 11√2 + 9√3,
       θ³ − 9θ = 2√2   ⇒  √2 = (θ³ − 9θ)/2 ∈ Q(θ),  √3 = θ − √2 = (11θ − θ³)/2.
    So Q(θ) = Q(√2, √3) and θ has degree 4, minimal polynomial x⁴ − 10x² + 1
    (D3). THEOREM (primitive element): a finite extension L/K with K of
    characteristic 0, or K finite, is simple, L = K(θ). For K infinite the
    proof shows that K(α, β) = K(α + cβ) for all but finitely many c ∈ K;
    for finite fields take θ a generator of L× (D9). Common mistakes:
    'proving' √3 ∉ Q(√2) by saying 'obviously'; assuming Q(α + β) is always
    smaller than Q(α, β). Now you try: find [Q(√2, √3, √5) : Q]. (8: √5 ∉
    Q(√2, √3), whose quadratic subfields are Q(√2), Q(√3), Q(√6))

D6. Prove that a finite extension is algebraic and that if α, β are
    algebraic over K so are α + β and αβ. Find the degree and minimal
    polynomial of √2 + ∛3 over Q, and explain why transcendental numbers
    exist.
    Answer: √2 + ∛3 has degree 6, minimal polynomial
    x⁶ − 6x⁴ − 6x³ + 12x² − 36x + 1.
    Teacher explains: If [L : K] = n and α ∈ L, the n + 1 elements
    1, α, ..., αⁿ are linearly DEPENDENT over K: c₀ + c₁α + ... + cₙαⁿ = 0
    with some cᵢ ≠ 0, a non-zero polynomial vanishing at α ∎. If α, β are
    algebraic of degrees m, n, then [K(α, β) : K] = [K(α, β) : K(α)][K(α) : K]
    ≤ nm (β still satisfies its polynomial over K(α)). So K(α, β) is finite,
    hence all its elements, including α + β, αβ, α − β and α/β, are
    algebraic ∎. EXAMPLE: x = √2 + ∛3. Then (x − √2)³ = 3:
       x³ − 3√2x² + 6x − 2√2 = 3  ⇒  x³ + 6x − 3 = √2(3x² + 2)
       square: x⁶ + 12x⁴ − 6x³ + 36x² − 36x + 9 = 2(9x⁴ + 12x² + 4)
       ⇒ x⁶ − 6x⁴ − 6x³ + 12x² − 36x + 1 = 0.
    DEGREE: Q(√2, ∛3) has degree 6 (2 and 3 coprime, as in D2), and
    Q(x) contains ∛3 = x − √2 once it contains √2; indeed from the first line
    √2 = (x³ + 6x − 3)/(3x² + 2) ∈ Q(x). So Q(x) = Q(√2, ∛3), degree 6, and
    the sextic is the minimal polynomial. TRANSCENDENTALS: Q[x] is
    countable and each polynomial has finitely many roots, so Q̄ is
    countable; R is uncountable (Cantor), so most reals are transcendental.
    Explicit examples: Liouville's ∑10^(−k!), e (Hermite), π (Lindemann).
    Common mistakes: believing the sum of two algebraic numbers needs an
    explicit polynomial to be algebraic; forgetting to check that the
    polynomial found is irreducible. Now you try: is π + e or πe
    transcendental? (At least one is: if both were algebraic, π and e would
    be roots of x² − (π + e)x + πe with algebraic coefficients, hence
    algebraic)

D7. Find the splitting fields over Q, and their degrees, of x³ − 2,
    x⁴ − 2 and x⁴ + 1. Why is the degree of a splitting field of a
    polynomial of degree n at most n!?
    Answer: Q(∛2, ω), degree 6; Q(⁴√2, i), degree 8; Q(√2, i) = Q(ζ₈),
    degree 4.
    Teacher explains: x³ − 2: roots ∛2, ∛2ω, ∛2ω² with ω = e^(2πi/3),
    ω² + ω + 1 = 0. The splitting field contains ∛2 and ω = (∛2ω)/∛2, and
    conversely: it is Q(∛2, ω). Degrees: [Q(∛2) : Q] = 3, and Q(∛2) ⊆ R does
    not contain ω, which has degree 2 (x² + x + 1): 3·2 = 6. x⁴ − 2: roots
    ±⁴√2, ±i⁴√2, so the field is Q(⁴√2, i): [Q(⁴√2) : Q] = 4 (Eisenstein), the
    field Q(⁴√2) is real, so i has degree 2 over it: 8. x⁴ + 1: roots
    ζ, ζ³, ζ⁵, ζ⁷ with ζ = e^(iπ/4) = (1 + i)/√2. ζ² = i and ζ + ζ⁷ = √2, so
    the field is Q(√2, i), of degree 4 (i ∉ R ⊇ Q(√2)); one root already
    generates everything: Q(ζ) has degree 4 = deg(x⁴ + 1). BOUND n!: adjoin
    one root α₁ of f: degree ≤ n. Over K(α₁), f = (x − α₁)g with deg g = n − 1;
    adjoin a root of g: degree ≤ n − 1; and so on. The tower law gives
    ≤ n(n − 1)...1 = n!. x³ − 2 attains 3! = 6. Common mistakes: saying the
    splitting field of x³ − 2 is Q(∛2) (the other two roots are not real);
    counting [Q(⁴√2, i) : Q] as 4 + 2. Now you try: find the splitting
    field of x⁴ − 5x² + 6 and its degree. ((x² − 2)(x² − 3): Q(√2, √3),
    degree 4)

D8. State Kronecker's theorem and prove it. Use it to build F₉ = F₃[x]/(x² + 1),
    find the inverse of 1 + i and show that 1 + i generates F₉×. Show that
    an algebraically closed field is infinite.
    Answer: (1 + i)⁻¹ = 2 + i; 1 + i has order 8.
    Teacher explains: KRONECKER: let f ∈ K[x] be non-constant and p an
    irreducible factor. Then L = K[x]/(p) is a FIELD ((p) is maximal in the
    PID K[x]); K embeds as the constants, and the class x̄ satisfies
    p(x̄) = p(x) + (p) = 0, so f(x̄) = 0: f has a root in L, and
    [L : K] = deg p ∎. Repeating gives a splitting field. F₉: x² + 1 has no
    root in F₃ (0, 1, 2 give 1, 2, 2), so F₃[x]/(x² + 1) is a field with 9
    elements a + bi, a, b ∈ F₃, i² = −1 = 2. INVERSE: (1 + i)(a + bi) =
    (a − b) + (a + b)i = 1 gives a + b = 0, a − b = 1, so a = 2, b = 1 (mod 3):
       (1 + i)(2 + i) = 2 + i + 2i + i² = 2 + 3i − 1 = 1 ✓.
    POWERS of g = 1 + i:
       g² = 1 + 2i + i² = 2i,   g⁴ = (2i)² = 4i² = −4 = 2,   g⁸ = 4 = 1
    The order divides 8 but g⁴ = 2 ≠ 1, so ord g = 8: g generates the 8
    non-zero elements. (By contrast i has order 4.) ALGEBRAICALLY CLOSED ⇒
    INFINITE: if F = {a₁, ..., aₙ} were finite, the polynomial
    (x − a₁)(x − a₂)...(x − aₙ) + 1 would take the value 1 at every element:
    no root ∎. So the algebraic closure of Fₚ is infinite (the union of all
    F_{pⁿ}). Common mistakes: taking a reducible p (F₃[x]/(x² + 2) is not a
    field: x² + 2 = (x − 1)(x + 1)); computing with i² = 1. Now you try: in F₉
    compute (2 + i)(1 + 2i). (2 + 4i + i + 2i² = 5i = 2i)

D9. Prove that the multiplicative group of a finite field is cyclic. How
    many generators has F₁₃×, and which are they? How many elements of
    order 3 has F₁₆×?
    Answer: F₁₃× has φ(12) = 4 generators: 2, 6, 7, 11. F₁₆× has φ(3) = 2
    elements of order 3.
    Teacher explains: Let |F| = q, G = F×, n = q − 1. For d | n let ψ(d) be
    the number of elements of order d. CLAIM: ψ(d) = 0 or φ(d). If a has
    order d, the d elements 1, a, ..., a^(d−1) are distinct roots of x^d − 1,
    which has at most d roots in the field F. So EVERY element of order d lies
    in the cyclic group ⟨a⟩, which contains exactly φ(d) elements of order d.
    Now every element has some order d | n, so
       n = ∑_{d|n} ψ(d) ≤ ∑_{d|n} φ(d) = n
    (the last identity: count the elements of Zₙ by their orders). Equality
    forces ψ(d) = φ(d) for every d | n; in particular ψ(n) = φ(n) ≥ 1: G has
    an element of order n and is cyclic ∎. F₁₃: try 2:
       2¹ = 2, 2² = 4, 2³ = 8, 2⁴ = 3, 2⁶ = 12 = −1
    so ord 2 is not 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6 (2⁶ = −1 ≠ 1): it is 12. The generators
    are 2ᵏ with gcd(k, 12) = 1: 2¹ = 2, 2⁵ = 32 ≡ 6, 2⁷ = 128 ≡ 11,
    2¹¹ = 2⁻¹ = 7 (2·7 = 14 ≡ 1). F₁₆×: cyclic of order 15; elements of order 3
    number φ(3) = 2 (they are ω, ω² of F₄ ⊆ F₁₆). Common mistakes: checking
    only that aⁿ = 1 (true for every element); thinking the additive group
    is cyclic too (F₁₆ under + is (Z₂)⁴). Now you try: is 2 a generator of
    F₇×? of F₁₁×? (No: 2³ = 8 ≡ 1 in F₇; yes: 2⁵ = 32 ≡ −1 and 2² ≠ 1 in F₁₁,
    so ord 2 = 10)

D10. Prove that for every prime power q = pⁿ there is a field with q
     elements, unique up to isomorphism, namely the splitting field of
     x^q − x over Fₚ. Check it for F₄.
     Answer: proof below; x⁴ − x = x(x + 1)(x² + x + 1) over F₂, whose roots
     0, 1, ω, ω² form F₄.
     Teacher explains: EXISTENCE: let L be a splitting field of f = x^q − x
     over Fₚ and R ⊆ L its set of roots. (i) The roots are DISTINCT:
     f′ = qx^(q−1) − 1 = −1 (q = 0 in char p), so gcd(f, f′) = 1: |R| = q.
     (ii) R is a SUBFIELD: the map a ↦ a^q is the n-th power of Frobenius,
     hence a ring homomorphism, so if a^q = a and b^q = b then
     (a ± b)^q = a^q ± b^q = a ± b, (ab)^q = ab and (a⁻¹)^q = a⁻¹. So R is a
     field with q elements (and in fact R = L). UNIQUENESS: let F be any field
     with q elements. F× has order q − 1, so a^(q−1) = 1 for a ≠ 0 (Lagrange)
     and a^q = a for ALL a ∈ F (including 0). So the q elements of F are q
     distinct roots of x^q − x: it splits in F, and F is generated by its
     roots, i.e. F is a splitting field of x^q − x over Fₚ. Splitting fields
     are unique up to isomorphism, so F ≅ R ∎. CHECK q = 4:
        x⁴ − x = x(x³ − 1) = x(x − 1)(x² + x + 1)   over F₂
     roots 0, 1 and the two roots ω, ω² = ω + 1 of x² + x + 1: exactly F₄ ✓.
     In general x^(pⁿ) − x is the product of all monic irreducibles over Fₚ of
     degree d | n; for q = 8: x(x + 1)(x³ + x + 1)(x³ + x² + 1). Common
     mistakes: forgetting to check that the roots are distinct; saying 'F_q
     = Z_q'. Now you try: why is x⁹ − x = x(x − 1)(x + 1)(x² + 1)(x² + x + 2)
     (x² + 2x + 2) over F₃? (Its roots are all of F₉: the elements of F₃ give
     the linear factors, and each of the 6 others has a quadratic minimal
     polynomial; these are the 3 irreducible quadratics over F₃)

D11. Prove that F_{pᵐ} is (isomorphic to) a subfield of F_{pⁿ} if and only
     if m | n. List the subfields of F₆₄ and of F_{2¹²}. Show that the
     Frobenius σ(a) = aᵖ is an automorphism of F_{pⁿ} of order n and find
     the fixed field of σᵏ.
     Answer: F₆₄: F₂, F₄, F₈, F₆₄. F_{2¹²}: F₂, F₄, F₈, F₁₆, F₆₄, F₄₀₉₆.
     Fixed field of σᵏ: F_{p^gcd(k, n)}.
     Teacher explains: (⇒) If F_{pᵐ} ⊆ F_{pⁿ}, then F_{pⁿ} is a vector space
     over F_{pᵐ} of some dimension d, so pⁿ = (pᵐ)ᵈ and n = md. (⇐) If m | n
     then pᵐ − 1 divides pⁿ − 1 (write n = md: xᵈ − 1 is divisible by x − 1
     with x = pᵐ). So the cyclic group F_{pⁿ}× of order pⁿ − 1 has a UNIQUE
     subgroup of order pᵐ − 1; together with 0 it is
     {a : a^(pᵐ) = a}, which is closed under +, · (Frobenius) — a field with
     pᵐ elements. It is the only one (any such subfield consists of roots of
     x^(pᵐ) − x) ∎. So subfields correspond to divisors of n:
        n = 6:   1, 2, 3, 6      → F₂, F₄, F₈, F₆₄
        n = 12:  1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 → F₂, F₄, F₈, F₁₆, F₆₄, F₄₀₉₆
     Note F₈ ⊄ F₁₆ (3 ∤ 4) and F₁₆ ⊄ F₆₄ (4 ∤ 6). FROBENIUS: σ is a ring
     homomorphism ((ab)ᵖ = aᵖbᵖ, (a + b)ᵖ = aᵖ + bᵖ), injective (field), hence
     bijective (finite). σᵏ(a) = a^(pᵏ) and σⁿ = id (a^(pⁿ) = a), while for
     k < n the polynomial x^(pᵏ) − x has fewer than pⁿ roots, so σᵏ ≠ id:
     ord σ = n. The fixed set of σᵏ is {a : a^(pᵏ) = a} ∩ F_{pⁿ} = F_{p^gcd(k, n)}
     (the unique subfield of degree gcd(k, n)). Moreover every automorphism
     fixes Fₚ, and there are at most n of them, so Aut(F_{pⁿ}) = ⟨σ⟩ ≅ Zₙ.
     Common mistakes: thinking F_{pᵐ} ⊆ F_{pⁿ} when m < n (it needs m | n);
     treating σ as the identity because aᵖ = a on Fₚ. Now you try: in F₆₄
     what is the fixed field of a ↦ a⁴? (σ², gcd(2, 6) = 2: F₄)

D12. Construct F₁₆ as F₂[x]/(x⁴ + x + 1) with α the class of x. Show that α
     is a primitive element, tabulate its powers, and find the minimal
     polynomials over F₂ of α³, α⁵ and α⁷. Factor x¹⁶ − x over F₂.
     Answer: α has order 15 (x⁴ + x + 1 is primitive). m(α³) = x⁴ + x³ + x² +
     x + 1, m(α⁵) = x² + x + 1, m(α⁷) = x⁴ + x³ + 1.
     x¹⁶ − x = x(x + 1)(x² + x + 1)(x⁴ + x + 1)(x⁴ + x³ + 1)(x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1).
     Teacher explains: x⁴ + x + 1 is irreducible over F₂ (no root; not
     (x² + x + 1)² = x⁴ + x² + 1), so F₁₆ = {a + bα + cα² + dα³}. Use
     α⁴ = α + 1:
        α⁴ = α + 1            α⁵ = α² + α           α⁶ = α³ + α²
        α⁷ = α³ + α + 1       α⁸ = α² + 1           α⁹ = α³ + α
        α¹⁰ = α² + α + 1      α¹¹ = α³ + α² + α     α¹² = α³ + α² + α + 1
        α¹³ = α³ + α² + 1     α¹⁴ = α³ + 1          α¹⁵ = 1
    Since ord α divides 15 and α³ ≠ 1, α⁵ ≠ 1, ord α = 15: PRIMITIVE; the
    table is a 'logarithm table' (multiply by adding exponents mod 15, e.g.
    (α² + 1)(α³ + α) = α⁸·α⁹ = α¹⁷ = α²). MINIMAL POLYNOMIALS: the conjugates
    of β are β, β², β⁴, β⁸ (Frobenius), so the exponents split into
    CYCLOTOMIC COSETS mod 15 under doubling:
       {0}, {1, 2, 4, 8}, {3, 6, 12, 9}, {5, 10}, {7, 14, 13, 11}.
    α³ has order 5, so it is a root of x⁵ − 1 = (x + 1)(x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1)
    and not of x + 1: m = x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1. α⁵ has order 3: m = x² + x + 1.
    α⁷ = α⁻⁸ is the 'reciprocal' of α⁸, a root of x⁴ + x + 1, so it is a root
    of the reversed polynomial x⁴(x⁻⁴ + x⁻¹ + 1) = x⁴ + x³ + 1. Every element of
    F₁₆ is a root of x¹⁶ − x, and grouping by cosets gives the factorisation
    above: degrees 1 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 ✓. Number of primitive elements:
    φ(15) = 8 (the cosets {1, 2, 4, 8} and {7, 14, 13, 11}), so exactly two of
    the three quartics are primitive polynomials. Common mistakes: reducing
    only once when high powers appear (reduce repeatedly, or use the
    table); assuming every irreducible quartic is primitive
    (x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1 is not: its roots have order 5). Now you
    try: compute α⁶·α¹³ and (α⁵)⁻¹. (α¹⁹ = α⁴ = α + 1; α¹⁰ = α² + α + 1)
