TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: do every factorisation on 2 × 2 examples first and multiply
  the factors back together every single time; keep a table 'which
  decomposition for which job' (LU: square systems; Cholesky: SPD; QR:
  least squares; SVD: rank, norms, pseudoinverse, compression, PCA). Draw
  least squares as 'drop a perpendicular from b to the plane of the
  columns', and draw the SVD as 'rotate, stretch along axes, rotate'. In
  PCA insist on the four-step routine: centre, covariance, eigenvectors,
  proportions. Harder: prove that LU without pivoting exists iff the
  leading minors are non-zero and that it is unique; show the growth factor
  of partial pivoting can be 2ⁿ⁻¹; prove modified Gram-Schmidt equals
  classical in exact arithmetic but not in floating point (try the Läuchli
  matrix); prove the Frobenius-norm Eckart-Young theorem; derive the
  pseudoinverse's four Penrose conditions; implement PCA in Python via
  numpy.linalg.svd on a real data set (e.g. the iris data) and compare with
  the covariance-eigenvector route; show that ridge regression
  (AᵀA + αI)⁻¹Aᵀb shrinks the SVD components by σᵢ/(σᵢ² + α).


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.25 — POINT-SET TOPOLOGY: TOPOLOGICAL SPACES, CONTINUITY, BASES,
PRODUCT AND QUOTIENT TOPOLOGIES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A TOPOLOGY on a set X is a family τ of subsets (the OPEN SETS) with
    (T1) ∅, X ∈ τ; (T2) any UNION of members of τ is in τ; (T3) any FINITE
    INTERSECTION of members of τ is in τ. (X, τ) is a TOPOLOGICAL SPACE.
    Infinite intersections of open sets need NOT be open:
    ⋂ (−1/n, 1/n) = {0} in R.
  - STANDARD EXAMPLES: DISCRETE (every set open), INDISCRETE (only ∅, X),
    COFINITE (∅ and sets with finite complement), COCOUNTABLE, the METRIC
    topology (U open ⇔ every point of U has a ball B(x, r) ⊆ U), the
    LOWER-LIMIT (Sorgenfrey) line R_ℓ with basis [a, b), the SIERPIŃSKI
    space {0, 1} with open sets ∅, {1}, {0, 1}, the PARTICULAR POINT topology.
    There are 1, 4, 29, 355 topologies on sets of 1, 2, 3, 4 points (1, 3,
    9, 33 up to homeomorphism). τ₂ is FINER than τ₁ when τ₁ ⊆ τ₂.
  - CLOSED sets are complements of open sets: ∅, X closed; finite unions and
    arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed. A set can be both
    (CLOPEN) or neither. INTERIOR int A = largest open set inside A; CLOSURE
    cl A = smallest closed set containing A; BOUNDARY ∂A = cl A ∩ cl(X − A).
    x ∈ cl A ⇔ EVERY open set containing x meets A. cl A = A ∪ A′, where A′
    is the set of LIMIT POINTS (every neighbourhood of x meets A − {x}).
    A is DENSE if cl A = X. int A = X − cl(X − A).
  - A sequence xₙ → x when every open U ∋ x contains all but finitely many
    xₙ. Limits need not be unique (indiscrete space: every sequence converges
    to every point; cofinite R: xₙ = n converges to every point).
  - BASIS: a family B of subsets with (B1) the members cover X and (B2) if
    x ∈ B₁ ∩ B₂ there is B₃ ∈ B with x ∈ B₃ ⊆ B₁ ∩ B₂. The topology generated
    by B = all unions of members of B (U open ⇔ ∀x ∈ U ∃B ∈ B, x ∈ B ⊆ U).
    COMPARISON: τ_B′ ⊇ τ_B ⇔ for every B ∋ x there is B′ ∋ x with B′ ⊆ B.
    A SUBBASIS S is any cover; finite intersections of its members form a
    basis. Open intervals (with rational endpoints: a COUNTABLE basis) give
    the standard R; open rectangles or open discs give R².
  - SUBSPACE topology on Y ⊆ X: τ_Y = {Y ∩ U : U ∈ τ}. C is closed in Y ⇔
    C = Y ∩ F with F closed in X. [0, 1/2) is open in [0, 1] but not in R.
    An open set of an open subspace is open in X (same for closed).
  - CONTINUITY: f : X → Y is continuous ⇔ f⁻¹(V) is open for every open V ⇔
    f⁻¹(C) is closed for every closed C ⇔ f(cl A) ⊆ cl f(A) for all A ⇔
    f⁻¹(B) is open for every basic (or subbasic) B. For metric spaces this is
    the ε-δ definition. Composites of continuous maps are continuous;
    constant maps, inclusions, maps FROM discrete and INTO indiscrete spaces
    are always continuous.
  - PASTING LEMMA: if X = A ∪ B with A, B both CLOSED (or both open), and
    f|A, f|B are continuous and agree on A ∩ B, then f is continuous.
  - HOMEOMORPHISM: a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. Examples
    (−1, 1) ≅ R (x ↦ x/(1 − |x|)), S¹ − {pt} ≅ R, S² − {pt} ≅ R²
    (stereographic projection). A continuous BIJECTION need NOT be a
    homeomorphism: t ↦ (cos 2πt, sin 2πt) from [0, 1) onto S¹. A TOPOLOGICAL
    PROPERTY is one kept by homeomorphisms (compactness, connectedness,
    number of components after removing a point); boundedness is NOT one.
  - PRODUCT TOPOLOGY on X × Y: basis {U × V : U, V open}. Projections
    π₁, π₂ are continuous and OPEN (not closed). UNIVERSAL PROPERTY:
    f = (f₁, f₂) : Z → X × Y is continuous ⇔ f₁ and f₂ are continuous.
    cl(A × B) = cl A × cl B. R × R = R² (standard). For infinite products
    ∏ X_α the PRODUCT topology has basic sets ∏ U_α with U_α = X_α for all
    but finitely many α (the universal property holds, and convergence is
    coordinatewise); the BOX topology allows all ∏ U_α and is strictly finer.
  - QUOTIENT TOPOLOGY: for a surjection q : X → Y, V ⊆ Y is open ⇔ q⁻¹(V) is
    open in X. Open sets of Y ↔ open SATURATED sets of X. UNIVERSAL
    PROPERTY: if g : X → Z is constant on each fibre q⁻¹(y), the induced
    ḡ : Y → Z is continuous ⇔ g is. A continuous surjection which is OPEN or
    CLOSED is a quotient map. Standard quotients: [0, 1]/(0 ~ 1) ≅ R/Z ≅ S¹;
    square → cylinder, Möbius band, torus (aba⁻¹b⁻¹), Klein bottle
    (abab⁻¹), RP² (abab); D²/S¹ ≅ S². A quotient of a Hausdorff space need
    NOT be Hausdorff (R/Q is indiscrete; the line with two origins).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Let X = {a, b, c}. Decide which of the following are topologies on X:
    τ₁ = {∅, {a}, {b}, X}, τ₂ = {∅, {a}, {a, b}, X}, τ₃ = {∅, {a, b}, {b, c},
    X}, τ₄ = {∅, {a}, {b, c}, X}. List all topologies on a 2-point set, and
    show that an infinite intersection of open sets in R need not be open.
    Answer: τ₂ and τ₄ are topologies; τ₁ fails (T2: {a} ∪ {b} = {a, b} is
    missing); τ₃ fails (T3: {a, b} ∩ {b, c} = {b} is missing). On {p, q}
    there are 4 topologies: {∅, X}, {∅, {p}, X}, {∅, {q}, X}, P(X).
    ⋂ (−1/n, 1/n) = {0} is not open.
    Teacher explains: Check the three axioms in order. (T1) is easy: every
    list contains ∅ and X. For a finite X it is enough to check PAIRS for
    (T2) and (T3), because a union or intersection of several sets can be
    built two at a time.
       τ₁: {a} ∪ {b} = {a, b} ∉ τ₁                    ✗ (not closed under ∪)
       τ₂: {a} ⊆ {a, b} ⊆ X: a chain, so unions and
           intersections are just the larger/smaller set ✓
       τ₃: {a, b} ∩ {b, c} = {b} ∉ τ₃                  ✗ (not closed under ∩)
       τ₄: {a} ∪ {b, c} = X, {a} ∩ {b, c} = ∅          ✓
    τ₄ is really the 'discrete topology on two blobs' {a} and {b, c}. On
    {p, q} every family must contain ∅ and X, and the only freedom is whether
    {p} and {q} are in; all 2² = 4 choices work, since {p} ∪ {q} = X and
    {p} ∩ {q} = ∅. {∅, {p}, X} and {∅, {q}, X} are homeomorphic (swap p and
    q), so there are 3 topologies UP TO HOMEOMORPHISM (the Sierpiński space
    is the middle one). Finally 0 ∈ (−1/n, 1/n) for every n and, for x ≠ 0,
    choosing n with 1/n < |x| shows x is not in every set, so the
    intersection is {0}; {0} contains no open interval around 0, so it is not
    open. This is why (T3) says FINITE. Common mistakes: forgetting to check
    that X and ∅ belong; checking only unions. Now you try: is {∅, {a},
    {a, b}, {a, c}, X} a topology on {a, b, c}? (Yes: {a, b} ∪ {a, c} = X and
    {a, b} ∩ {a, c} = {a}.)

D2. On an infinite set X let τ_f consist of ∅ together with all U ⊆ X whose
    complement X − U is finite (the COFINITE topology). Prove τ_f is a
    topology. Show that in (R, τ_f) any two non-empty open sets meet, that
    the closed sets are the finite sets and R, and that the sequence xₙ = n
    converges to every real number.
    Answer: Proofs below; limits are not unique in (R, τ_f).
    Teacher explains: Work with complements, where the conditions become
    statements about finite sets.
       (T1) ∅ ∈ τ_f by definition; X − X = ∅ is finite, so X ∈ τ_f.
       (T2) Let Uᵢ ∈ τ_f, not all empty (empty ones add nothing). Pick
            U_j ≠ ∅. Then X − ⋃Uᵢ = ⋂(X − Uᵢ) ⊆ X − U_j, a finite set, so
            the complement of the union is finite.
       (T3) X − (U ∩ V) = (X − U) ∪ (X − V), a union of two finite sets; if
            U or V is ∅ the intersection is ∅ ∈ τ_f anyway.
    If U, V are non-empty open sets and U ∩ V = ∅, then
    X = (X − U) ∪ (X − V) would be finite: impossible, as X is infinite. So
    non-empty open sets always meet; in particular the space is NOT
    Hausdorff. Closed sets are complements of open ones: the finite sets and
    X itself. For the sequence xₙ = n take any x ∈ R and any open U ∋ x.
    X − U is finite, so it contains only finitely many of the (distinct)
    terms 1, 2, 3, ...; hence all but finitely many xₙ lie in U, and xₙ → x.
    Every real is a limit. Compare R with its usual topology: (−1, 1) is open
    there but not cofinite, while every cofinite set R − {a₁, ..., aₖ} is a
    union of open intervals; the standard topology is strictly FINER. Common
    mistakes: 'the union of cofinite sets has finite complement because the
    complements are finite' (the complements INTERSECT, which is even
    better); forgetting ∅, which has infinite complement but is included by
    hand. Now you try: in the cocountable topology on R, which sequences
    converge? (Only those that are eventually constant: if xₙ ≠ x infinitely
    often, U = R − {xₙ : xₙ ≠ x} is an open set containing x missing
    infinitely many terms.)

D3. Define interior, closure, boundary and limit point. Prove that x ∈ cl A
    if and only if every open set containing x meets A. Compute int, cl and ∂
    of A = [0, 1) ∪ {2} and of Q in the standard R, and of A = (0, 1) in the
    lower-limit line R_ℓ.
    Answer: Standard R: int A = (0, 1), cl A = [0, 1] ∪ {2}, ∂A = {0, 1, 2};
    int Q = ∅, cl Q = R, ∂Q = R. In R_ℓ: int (0, 1) = (0, 1),
    cl (0, 1) = [0, 1), ∂(0, 1) = {0}.
    Teacher explains: int A is the union of all open sets inside A; cl A is
    the intersection of all closed sets containing A; ∂A = cl A ∩ cl(X − A)
    = cl A − int A. Proof of the criterion, both directions by
    contrapositive. (⇒) Suppose some open U ∋ x has U ∩ A = ∅. Then X − U is
    closed and contains A, so cl A ⊆ X − U, and x ∉ cl A. (⇐) Suppose
    x ∉ cl A. Then U = X − cl A is open, contains x and misses A. □
    For A = [0, 1) ∪ {2} in R:
       int: points with an interval around them inside A → (0, 1)
            (0 fails: (−ε, ε) contains negatives; 2 fails: isolated)
       cl:  every interval around 1 meets A, around 3 it does not
            → [0, 1] ∪ {2}
       ∂ = cl − int = {0, 1, 2}
    For Q: every interval contains rationals and irrationals, so no
    interval fits inside Q (int Q = ∅) and every point is a limit (cl Q = R),
    giving ∂Q = R. In R_ℓ the basic neighbourhoods of x are [x, x + ε). The
    point 1: [1, 1 + ε) misses (0, 1), so 1 ∉ cl(0, 1) — unlike in R. The
    point 0: [0, ε) meets (0, 1), so 0 ∈ cl. Hence cl (0, 1) = [0, 1), and
    since (0, 1) = ⋃ [1/n, 1) is already open, ∂ = [0, 1) − (0, 1) = {0}.
    Note [0, 1) is CLOPEN in R_ℓ. Common mistakes: thinking closure and
    boundary are the same in every topology; forgetting isolated points
    (2 is in ∂A but not a limit point of A). Now you try: find the limit
    points and closure of A = {1/n : n ∈ N} in R. (A′ = {0}; cl A = A ∪ {0};
    int A = ∅, so ∂A = A ∪ {0}.)

D4. In a metric space (X, d) call U open if for every x ∈ U some ball
    B(x, r) = {y : d(x, y) < r} ⊆ U. Prove that open balls are open sets and
    that this defines a topology. Then show that d₁, d₂ (Euclidean) and d∞
    give the same topology on R², and that d and d′ = min(d, 1) give the
    same topology.
    Answer: Proofs below; the key inequalities are d∞ ≤ d₂ ≤ d₁ ≤ 2d∞.
    Teacher explains: BALLS ARE OPEN: let y ∈ B(x, r) and put
    s = r − d(x, y) > 0. If d(y, z) < s then by the triangle inequality
       d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) < d(x, y) + s = r,
    so B(y, s) ⊆ B(x, r). TOPOLOGY: ∅ (vacuously) and X are open; a union
    of open sets is open (the ball for x inside one of them lies in the
    union); for U ∩ V take r = min(r₁, r₂) — this is where FINITE matters,
    since a minimum of infinitely many radii may be 0. For R² with
    d₁ = |Δx| + |Δy|, d₂ = √(Δx² + Δy²), d∞ = max(|Δx|, |Δy|):
       d∞ ≤ d₂ ≤ d₁ ≤ 2 d∞
    (d₂² = Δx² + Δy² ≤ (|Δx| + |Δy|)², and each of |Δx|, |Δy| is ≤ d∞). In
    terms of balls about the same centre:
       B∞(x, r/2) ⊆ B₁(x, r) ⊆ B₂(x, r) ⊆ B∞(x, r)
    (open diamond ⊆ open disc ⊆ open square). So every ball of one metric
    contains a ball of each other metric with the same centre, and the three
    families of open sets coincide. For d′ = min(d, 1): balls of radius
    r < 1 are the same for d and d′, and only small balls matter for
    openness. So d′ is BOUNDED but gives the same topology: boundedness is
    not a topological property. Common mistakes: thinking equal topologies
    need equal balls; using the triangle inequality the wrong way round.
    Now you try: show that the discrete metric (d = 1 for x ≠ y) gives the
    discrete topology. (B(x, 1/2) = {x}, so every singleton is open.)

D5. State and prove the basis criterion: if B satisfies (B1) and (B2), the
    family τ_B of all unions of members of B is a topology. Show that
    B = {[a, b) : a < b} is a basis, and that the topology it generates
    (the lower-limit line R_ℓ) is strictly finer than the standard topology.
    Show that intervals with rational endpoints form a countable basis of R.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: Equivalently, U ∈ τ_B ⇔ for every x ∈ U there is
    B ∈ B with x ∈ B ⊆ U. (T1): ∅ is the empty union; X = ⋃B by (B1).
    (T2): a union of unions of basis sets is a union of basis sets. (T3): let
    x ∈ U ∩ V; pick B₁, B₂ ∈ B with x ∈ B₁ ⊆ U and x ∈ B₂ ⊆ V; by (B2) there
    is B₃ with x ∈ B₃ ⊆ B₁ ∩ B₂ ⊆ U ∩ V. So U ∩ V is the union of such B₃'s. □
    For [a, b): (B1) x ∈ [x, x + 1). (B2) [a, b) ∩ [c, d) = [max(a, c),
    min(b, d)), which is itself in B (or empty). Comparison: an open
    interval is a union of half-open ones,
       (a, b) = ⋃ (n large) [a + 1/n, b),
    so every standard-open set is open in R_ℓ. But [0, 1) is not open in R:
    no interval (−ε, ε) around 0 fits inside it. So R_ℓ is STRICTLY FINER.
    Rational endpoints: given x ∈ (a, b) choose rationals p, q with
    a < p < x < q < b (Q is dense); then x ∈ (p, q) ⊆ (a, b). So these
    countably many intervals form a basis (R is SECOND COUNTABLE). The same
    trick fails for R_ℓ: [x, q) with q rational needs its left end exactly x,
    and in fact R_ℓ has no countable basis. Common mistakes: forgetting to
    check (B2) (the family {[a, b] : a < b} fails it: [0, 1] ∩ [1, 2] = {1}
    contains no member); confusing 'basis' with 'all open sets'. Now you try:
    show that S = {(−∞, a)} ∪ {(b, ∞)} is not a basis but is a subbasis of
    the standard topology. ((−∞, 2) ∩ (0, ∞) = (0, 2) contains no ray; finite
    intersections give all (b, a), a basis.)

D6. Define the subspace topology on Y ⊆ X and prove it is a topology. Let
    Y = [0, 1] ∪ [2, 3] ⊆ R. Which of [0, 1/2), [0, 1], (1/2, 1] ∪ [2, 3] are
    open in Y, and which are closed in Y? Prove: C is closed in Y ⇔ C = Y ∩ F
    for a closed F ⊆ X; and if Y is open in X, a set open in Y is open in X.
    Answer: All three are open in Y; [0, 1] is also closed in Y (clopen);
    [0, 1/2) is not closed in Y; (1/2, 1] ∪ [2, 3] is not closed in Y.
    Teacher explains: τ_Y = {Y ∩ U : U open in X}. Axioms: ∅ = Y ∩ ∅,
    Y = Y ∩ X; ⋃(Y ∩ Uᵢ) = Y ∩ ⋃Uᵢ; (Y ∩ U) ∩ (Y ∩ V) = Y ∩ (U ∩ V). Now
    exhibit the open sets of R:
       [0, 1/2) = Y ∩ (−1, 1/2)                      open in Y
       [0, 1] = Y ∩ (−1, 3/2)                        open in Y
       (1/2, 1] ∪ [2, 3] = Y ∩ (1/2, 4)              open in Y
    [0, 1] = Y ∩ [0, 1] is also closed; so Y is disconnected (see 10.26).
    [0, 1/2) is not closed in Y: 1/2 is a limit point in Y outside it. The
    third set's complement in Y is [0, 1/2], which is not open in Y (every
    Y-neighbourhood of 1/2 meets (1/2, 1]), so the third set is not closed.
    Closed sets: C closed in Y ⇔ Y − C = Y ∩ U with U open ⇔
    C = Y ∩ (X − U), and X − U is an arbitrary closed set. Open in open: if
    V = Y ∩ U with U and Y open in X, then V is an intersection of two open
    sets of X, hence open in X. (It fails without Y open: [0, 1/2) is open in
    [0, 1] but not in R.) Common mistakes: saying '[0, 1/2) is half-open, so
    neither'; 'open' always means 'open in which space?'. Now you try: in
    Y = Q, show A = {q ∈ Q : q² < 2} is clopen. (A = Q ∩ (−√2, √2)
    = Q ∩ [−√2, √2], since ±√2 ∉ Q.)

D7. Prove that for f : X → Y the following are equivalent: (1) f⁻¹(V) is
    open for every open V; (2) f⁻¹(C) is closed for every closed C;
    (3) f(cl A) ⊆ cl f(A) for every A ⊆ X; (4) f⁻¹(B) is open for every B in
    a basis of Y. Use (3) to show the floor function is not continuous.
    Answer: Proofs below; with A = [0, 1): f(cl A) = {0, 1} ⊄ {0} = cl f(A).
    Teacher explains: (1) ⇔ (2): preimages respect complements,
    f⁻¹(Y − C) = X − f⁻¹(C), so 'preimage of open is open' and 'preimage of
    closed is closed' say the same thing. (2) ⇒ (3): the set f⁻¹(cl f(A)) is
    closed by (2) and contains A (since f(A) ⊆ cl f(A)); a closed set
    containing A contains cl A. Hence f(cl A) ⊆ cl f(A). (3) ⇒ (2): let C be
    closed and A = f⁻¹(C). Then
       f(cl A) ⊆ cl f(A) ⊆ cl C = C,   so cl A ⊆ f⁻¹(C) = A,
    and A is closed. (1) ⇔ (4): (1) ⇒ (4) since basis sets are open;
    conversely every open V is a union ⋃Bᵢ, and f⁻¹(⋃Bᵢ) = ⋃f⁻¹(Bᵢ) is a union
    of open sets. (A subbasis also suffices, as preimages respect finite
    intersections too.) Floor: A = [0, 1) has cl A = [0, 1] and
       f(cl A) = {⌊0⌋, ⌊1⌋, ...} = {0, 1},   cl f(A) = cl{0} = {0}.
    Condition (3) fails, so ⌊·⌋ is not continuous (the point 1 'jumps out').
    Intuition for (3): a continuous map sends points close to A to points
    close to f(A). Common mistakes: 'images of open sets are open' (that is
    an OPEN MAP, a different notion: x ↦ x² sends (−1, 1) to [0, 1));
    forgetting the topology on the target. Now you try: show f(cl A) may be
    strictly smaller than cl f(A) for continuous f. (f(x) = eˣ, A = R:
    f(R) = (0, ∞), cl f(A) = [0, ∞).)

D8. (a) Prove the pasting lemma for two closed sets and use it to show that
    f(x) = x for x ≤ 0, f(x) = x/2 for x ≥ 0 is continuous. Show by example
    that 'closed' cannot be dropped. (b) Show that for metric spaces
    topological continuity is the ε-δ definition. (c) For the identity map
    of R, decide continuity between the discrete, standard, cofinite and
    indiscrete topologies.
    Answer: (a), (b) below. (c) id : (R, τ) → (R, σ) is continuous exactly
    when σ ⊆ τ: discrete → anything, standard → cofinite/indiscrete,
    cofinite → indiscrete are continuous; the reverse directions are not.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let X = A ∪ B, A and B closed, g = f|A and h = f|B
    continuous. For C closed in Y,
       f⁻¹(C) = g⁻¹(C) ∪ h⁻¹(C).
    g⁻¹(C) is closed in A, i.e. A ∩ F for a closed F, which is closed in X
    because A is; same for h⁻¹(C). A union of two closed sets is closed. □
    Here A = (−∞, 0], B = [0, ∞), both pieces are continuous and agree at 0
    (both give 0). Without closedness: A = (−∞, 0), B = [0, ∞), f = 0 on A
    and 1 on B; each piece is continuous, but f jumps. (b) In a metric space
    the balls form a basis. If f⁻¹ of open sets is open, then f⁻¹(B(f(x), ε))
    is open and contains x, so contains some B(x, δ): that is 'd(x, y) < δ ⇒
    d(f(x), f(y)) < ε'. Conversely, given ε-δ and V open, for x ∈ f⁻¹(V) take
    ε with B(f(x), ε) ⊆ V and the corresponding δ; then B(x, δ) ⊆ f⁻¹(V).
    (c) id⁻¹(V) = V, so id is continuous ⇔ every σ-open set is τ-open:
       discrete  ⊇  standard  ⊇  cofinite  ⊇  indiscrete
    Continuity goes 'from finer to coarser'. id from standard to discrete
    fails: {0} is open in the target but not in the source. Common mistakes:
    thinking continuity is a property of the formula alone; forgetting that
    the pasting sets must be closed (or both open). Now you try: is
    id : (R, standard) → R_ℓ continuous? (No: [0, 1) is open in R_ℓ but not
    in R. The other direction is continuous.)

D9. Prove that (−1, 1) and R are homeomorphic, and that S¹ − {(0, 1)} ≅ R by
    stereographic projection. Show that f : [0, 1) → S¹,
    f(t) = (cos 2πt, sin 2πt) is a continuous bijection but not a
    homeomorphism. Show that 'bounded' is not a topological property.
    Answer: h(x) = x/(1 − |x|), h⁻¹(y) = y/(1 + |y|); σ(x, y) = x/(1 − y),
    σ⁻¹(u) = (2u, u² − 1)/(u² + 1); f⁻¹ is discontinuous at (1, 0).
    Teacher explains: A homeomorphism needs four checks: well-defined,
    bijective, continuous, inverse continuous. For h: if |x| < 1 then
    1 − |x| > 0, h is continuous and increasing, and solving y = x/(1 − |x|)
    (x, y have the same sign) gives x = y/(1 + |y|) with |x| < 1; both
    formulas are continuous and are inverse to each other:
       h(h⁻¹(y)) = (y/(1 + |y|)) / (1 − |y|/(1 + |y|)) = y.
    Stereographic projection from N = (0, 1): the line through N and
    (x, y) ∈ S¹ meets the x-axis at u = x/(1 − y). Inverse: substitute
    x = u(1 − y) into x² + y² = 1: u²(1 − y)² = (1 − y)(1 + y), so
    u²(1 − y) = 1 + y, y = (u² − 1)/(u² + 1), x = 2u/(u² + 1). Check u = 1:
    (x, y) = (1, 0) and 1/(1 − 0) = 1 ✓. For f: it is continuous (components
    are) and bijective [0, 1) → S¹. But the image of the open set [0, 1/2) is
    the upper arc from angle 0 (included) to angle π (excluded); every
    neighbourhood of (1, 0) = f(0) in S¹ contains points just below the axis
    (angles near 2π) that are not in the image. So f([0, 1/2)) is not open,
    i.e. (f⁻¹)⁻¹([0, 1/2)) is not open: f⁻¹ is not continuous. Points
    f(1 − 1/n) → (1, 0) but f⁻¹ sends them to 1 − 1/n → 1 ≠ 0.
    (−1, 1) is bounded and R is not, yet they are homeomorphic: boundedness
    depends on the metric, not on the topology. Common mistakes: forgetting
    to check the inverse; claiming [0, 1) ≅ S¹ (removing a point from S¹
    leaves it connected, removing 1/2 from [0, 1) does not). Now you try:
    give a homeomorphism (0, 1) → (0, ∞). (x ↦ x/(1 − x), inverse
    y ↦ y/(1 + y).)

D10. For spaces X, Y show that B = {U × V : U open in X, V open in Y} is a
     basis, that the projections are continuous and open, and prove the
     universal property: f = (f₁, f₂) : Z → X × Y is continuous iff f₁, f₂
     are. Show that the product topology on R × R is the standard topology
     of R², that cl(A × B) = cl A × cl B, and find cl((0, 1) × Q).
     Answer: Proofs below; cl((0, 1) × Q) = [0, 1] × R.
     Teacher explains: (B1): X × Y ∈ B. (B2): the intersection of two basic
     sets is basic:
        (U₁ × V₁) ∩ (U₂ × V₂) = (U₁ ∩ U₂) × (V₁ ∩ V₂).
     π₁⁻¹(U) = U × Y is basic, so π₁ is continuous; π₁ of a basic set is U,
     and images respect unions, so π₁ is OPEN. It is NOT closed:
     {(x, y) : xy = 1} is closed in R² but π₁ of it is R − {0}. UNIVERSAL
     PROPERTY: (⇒) f₁ = π₁ ∘ f is a composite of continuous maps. (⇐) By D7(4)
     it suffices to test basic sets:
        f⁻¹(U × V) = f₁⁻¹(U) ∩ f₂⁻¹(V),
     an intersection of two open sets. R × R versus R²: every open disc
     around p contains an open rectangle around p and vice versa (D4 with d∞
     and d₂), so the topologies agree. Closure: (x, y) ∈ cl(A × B) ⇔ every
     basic U × V ∋ (x, y) meets A × B ⇔ every U ∋ x meets A and every
     V ∋ y meets B (take V = Y or U = X for one direction) ⇔ x ∈ cl A and
     y ∈ cl B. Hence
        cl((0, 1) × Q) = cl(0, 1) × cl Q = [0, 1] × R.
     Common mistakes: thinking every open set of X × Y is a product U × V (an
     open disc is not); 'projections are closed maps'. Now you try: is
     t ↦ (t², sin t) continuous R → R²? Find int([0, 1] × Q). (Yes, by the
     universal property; int = (0, 1) × ∅ = ∅.)

D11. Let X = R^N = ∏ R (sequences). Describe the product and box topologies.
     Show that f(t) = (t, t, t, ...) is continuous into the product topology
     but not into the box topology, and decide whether xⁿ = (1/n, 1/n, ...)
     and eⁿ = (0, ..., 0, 1, 0, ...) (1 in place n) converge to 0 in each.
     Answer: f is product-continuous, not box-continuous. xⁿ → 0 in the
     product topology but not in the box topology; eⁿ → 0 in the product
     topology, not in the box topology.
     Teacher explains: PRODUCT topology: basic sets ∏ Uₖ with each Uₖ open
     and Uₖ = R for all but finitely many k; equivalently it is generated by
     the subbasis πₖ⁻¹(U). BOX topology: all ∏ Uₖ. Box ⊇ product. f: each
     component t ↦ t is continuous, so f is continuous for the product
     topology (the universal property, proved as in D10 using finitely many
     coordinates at a time). In the box topology take
        W = (−1, 1) × (−1/2, 1/2) × (−1/3, 1/3) × ...
     Then f⁻¹(W) = {t : |t| < 1/k for all k} = {0}, not open in R. So f is
     not box-continuous: the universal property FAILS for the box topology.
     Convergence in the product topology is COORDINATEWISE (a basic set
     restricts only finitely many coordinates). xⁿ: coordinate k is 1/n → 0,
     so xⁿ → 0 in the product topology; but W above contains no xⁿ (the k-th
     coordinate 1/n fails |·| < 1/k once k > n), so no box-convergence.
     eⁿ: each coordinate is eventually 0, so eⁿ → 0 in the product topology;
     the box set ∏(−1/2, 1/2) contains no eⁿ. Common mistakes: 'the product
     topology is the box topology' (true only for finitely many factors);
     assuming metric intuition. Now you try: does (1, 1/2, 1/3, ...)·(1/n)
     → 0 in the box topology? (No: take W = ∏(−1/k², 1/k²); coordinate k of
     the n-th term is 1/(kn), which fails for k ≥ n.)

D12. Define the quotient topology and prove its universal property. Use it
     to show [0, 1]/(0 ~ 1) ≅ S¹. Describe the quotients of the unit square
     for the words aba⁻¹b⁻¹, abab⁻¹, abab. Show that R/Q (x ~ y ⇔ x − y ∈ Q)
     has the indiscrete topology, and describe the line with two origins.
     Answer: Proofs below; torus, Klein bottle, RP²; R/Q is indiscrete; the
     line with two origins is not Hausdorff.
     Teacher explains: For a surjection q : X → Y put V open ⇔ q⁻¹(V) open;
     this is the FINEST topology making q continuous. UNIVERSAL PROPERTY: if
     g : X → Z is constant on fibres, ḡ(q(x)) = g(x) is well defined, and for
     W ⊆ Z open
        q⁻¹(ḡ⁻¹(W)) = g⁻¹(W),
     so ḡ⁻¹(W) is open in Y ⇔ g⁻¹(W) is open in X. Hence ḡ continuous ⇔ g
     continuous. Circle: g(t) = (cos 2πt, sin 2πt) is continuous on [0, 1],
     identifies exactly 0 and 1, so ḡ : [0, 1]/~ → S¹ is a continuous
     bijection. [0, 1]/~ is compact (image of a compact set) and S¹ is
     Hausdorff, so ḡ is a homeomorphism (a continuous bijection from compact
     to Hausdorff is closed; see 10.26). Square words: read the boundary
     anticlockwise; equal letters are glued in the direction of the arrows.
        aba⁻¹b⁻¹  both pairs of sides glued straight      TORUS
        abab⁻¹    one pair straight, one pair flipped     KLEIN BOTTLE
        abab      both pairs flipped (antipodal)          RP²
     (One pair only: straight gives a CYLINDER, flipped a MÖBIUS BAND.)
     R/Q: let V ≠ ∅ be open. q⁻¹(V) is open, non-empty and SATURATED: with x
     it contains x + Q. It contains an interval (a, b), and every real y lies
     in some a < y + r < b with r ∈ Q, so y ∈ q⁻¹(V): q⁻¹(V) = R, V = R/Q.
     Two origins: glue two copies of R by (x, 1) ~ (x, 2) for x ≠ 0. The two
     origins 0₁, 0₂ are distinct, but every neighbourhood of each contains
     (−ε, ε) − {0}, so they cannot be separated: a quotient of a Hausdorff
     space need not be Hausdorff (yet every point has a neighbourhood ≅ R).
     Common mistakes: gluing a Möbius band as a cylinder (check the arrows);
     forgetting that open sets of Y correspond only to SATURATED open sets of
     X. Now you try: show D²/S¹ ≅ S². (Map rx ↦ point at angle πr from the
     north pole along the direction x: the whole boundary r = 1 goes to the
     south pole; continuous bijection compact → Hausdorff.)

M4. Find the closure and interior in the stated topology on R (or X).
    a) (0, 1), discrete                b) (0, 1), indiscrete
    c) (0, 1), cofinite                d) {1, 2, 3}, cofinite
    e) Z, cofinite                     f) (0, 1), cocountable
    g) Q, cocountable                  h) R − Q, cocountable
    i) (0, 1), lower-limit R_ℓ         j) [0, 1], R_ℓ
    k) (0, 1], R_ℓ                     l) {1/n : n ∈ N}, R_ℓ
    m) {−1/n : n ∈ N}, R_ℓ             n) {0} and {1} in Sierpiński {0, 1}
                                          (open: ∅, {1}, {0, 1})
    o) {5}, particular point topology (open: ∅ and sets containing 0)
    p) {0}, particular point topology

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep three pictures in mind — R with intervals, a 3-point set
  drawn as dots with blobs, and the cofinite line — and test every new
  definition on all three. Insist that 'open' is always 'open IN WHICH
  SPACE'. For closures, use the criterion 'every neighbourhood meets A', and
  for continuity use preimages, never images; draw the arrow and pull sets
  back. For products draw rectangles, for quotients draw the arrows on the
  square and physically glue a strip of paper for the cylinder and the
  Möbius band. Harder: show R_ℓ is first countable, separable but not
  second countable (for a basis B pick Bₓ with x = min Bₓ); show that
  {(x, −x)} is a closed discrete uncountable subspace of R_ℓ²; prove that a
  map into a product is continuous iff each component is, for arbitrary
  products, and find a counterexample for the box topology; prove Kuratowski's
  14-set theorem on closure and complement; and show that the quotient of a
  compact Hausdorff space X by a closed equivalence relation is Hausdorff.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.26 — COMPACTNESS, CONNECTEDNESS, SEPARATION AXIOMS, URYSOHN,
TYCHONOFF
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - COMPACT: every OPEN COVER of X has a FINITE SUBCOVER. Equivalently
    (FINITE INTERSECTION PROPERTY): every family of closed sets in which any
    finitely many members meet has non-empty total intersection. A subset K
    is compact when it is compact as a subspace (covers by open sets of X
    suffice). Finite sets, [a, b], {0} ∪ {1/n}, any cofinite or indiscrete
    space are compact; (0, 1), R, Z, an infinite discrete space are not.
  - BASIC THEOREMS: a CLOSED subset of a compact space is compact; a compact
    subset of a HAUSDORFF space is closed; the continuous image of a compact
    space is compact; hence the EXTREME VALUE THEOREM (a continuous
    f : K → R on compact K ≠ ∅ attains its max and min); a continuous
    BIJECTION from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a HOMEOMORPHISM.
  - HEINE-BOREL: K ⊆ Rⁿ is compact ⇔ K is closed and bounded. In a METRIC
    space: compact ⇔ SEQUENTIALLY compact (every sequence has a convergent
    subsequence) ⇔ COMPLETE and TOTALLY BOUNDED; compact ⇒ closed and
    bounded, but not conversely (closed unit ball of ℓ²). LEBESGUE NUMBER
    LEMMA: for an open cover of a compact metric space there is δ > 0 such
    that every set of diameter < δ lies in one member; so continuous maps on
    compact metric spaces are UNIFORMLY continuous.
  - PRODUCTS: TUBE LEMMA (if Y is compact and {x} × Y ⊆ N open, then
    W × Y ⊆ N for some open W ∋ x), so a finite product of compact spaces is
    compact. TYCHONOFF'S THEOREM: an ARBITRARY product of compact spaces is
    compact in the PRODUCT topology (it is equivalent to the axiom of
    choice; it fails for the box topology). Examples: the Cantor space
    {0, 1}^N, the Hilbert cube [0, 1]^N, tori.
  - LOCALLY COMPACT Hausdorff spaces have a ONE-POINT COMPACTIFICATION
    X* = X ∪ {∞} (neighbourhoods of ∞ are complements of compact sets):
    R* ≅ S¹, (Rⁿ)* ≅ Sⁿ, N* ≅ {0} ∪ {1/n}.
  - CONNECTED: X is not the union of two disjoint non-empty open sets
    (a SEPARATION) ⇔ the only CLOPEN sets are ∅ and X ⇔ every continuous
    map X → {0, 1} (discrete) is constant. The connected subsets of R are
    exactly the INTERVALS. Continuous images of connected spaces are
    connected ⇒ INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM.
  - BUILDING connected sets: a union of connected sets with a common point
    is connected; if A is connected and A ⊆ B ⊆ cl A then B is connected;
    finite and arbitrary products of connected spaces are connected.
    COMPONENTS (maximal connected subsets) partition X into closed sets. Q
    and the Cantor set are TOTALLY DISCONNECTED (components are points).
  - PATH-CONNECTED (any two points joined by a continuous path
    γ : [0, 1] → X) ⇒ connected; the converse FAILS: the TOPOLOGIST'S SINE
    CURVE {(x, sin(1/x)) : 0 < x ≤ 1} ∪ ({0} × [−1, 1]) is connected but not
    path-connected. An OPEN connected subset of Rⁿ is path-connected.
    Connectedness invariants: number of components, CUT POINTS (R − {p} is
    disconnected but R² − {p} is not, so R ≇ R²).
  - SEPARATION AXIOMS: T0 (points are topologically distinguishable); T1
    (points are CLOSED; ⇔ for x ≠ y some open set contains x but not y);
    T2 = HAUSDORFF (distinct points have disjoint neighbourhoods; ⇒ limits
    of sequences are unique; ⇔ the diagonal is closed in X × X); REGULAR
    (a point and a closed set not containing it have disjoint
    neighbourhoods); NORMAL (two disjoint closed sets have disjoint
    neighbourhoods). T3 = T1 + regular, T4 = T1 + normal, and
    T4 ⇒ T3 ⇒ T2 ⇒ T1 ⇒ T0. Metric spaces and compact Hausdorff spaces are
    normal. Counterexamples: Sierpiński (T0 not T1), cofinite R (T1 not T2),
    K-topology R_K (T2 not T3), Sorgenfrey plane R_ℓ² (T3 not T4).
  - URYSOHN'S LEMMA: X is normal ⇔ for disjoint closed A, B there is a
    continuous f : X → [0, 1] with f = 0 on A and f = 1 on B. In a metric
    space f(x) = d(x, A)/(d(x, A) + d(x, B)). TIETZE EXTENSION: on a normal
    space every continuous f : A → [a, b] (or R) on a closed set A extends
    to X. URYSOHN METRISATION: a second countable T3 space is metrisable.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Define compactness. Show that (0, 1) and R are not compact, prove that
    [0, 1] is compact, and show that every space with the cofinite topology
    is compact while an infinite discrete space is not.
    Answer: {(1/n, 1) : n ≥ 2} and {(−n, n)} have no finite subcovers;
    [0, 1] by the 'supremum' argument; proofs below.
    Teacher explains: To show NOT compact, produce one open cover with no
    finite subcover. (0, 1) = ⋃ (n ≥ 2) (1/n, 1), and finitely many of these
    sets have union (1/N, 1), missing 1/(2N). R = ⋃ (−n, n), and a finite
    subfamily has union (−N, N), missing N. To show compact you must handle
    EVERY cover. For [0, 1] let U be an open cover and
       S = {x ∈ [0, 1] : [0, x] is covered by finitely many members of U}.
    0 ∈ S, S is bounded by 1; let s = sup S. Now s lies in some U ∈ U, and U
    contains [0, 1] ∩ (s − ε, s + ε) for some ε > 0. Pick x ∈ S with
    x > s − ε: finitely many sets cover [0, x], and adding U covers
    [0, min(s + ε/2, 1)]. So s ∈ S, and if s < 1 then s + ε/2 ∈ S (or a
    point beyond s), contradicting s = sup S. Hence s = 1 ∈ S. □ (This uses
    the COMPLETENESS of R: in Q the interval [0, 2] ∩ Q is not compact.)
    Cofinite: let U cover X; pick one non-empty U₀ ∈ U. X − U₀ is finite,
    say {x₁, ..., xₖ}; choose Uᵢ ∋ xᵢ. Then U₀, U₁, ..., Uₖ is a finite
    subcover. Infinite discrete X: the cover by singletons {x} has no finite
    subcover (each set covers one point). Common mistakes: 'every finite
    cover has a subcover' (the definition starts from an ARBITRARY open
    cover); taking one particular cover and showing it has a finite
    subcover. Now you try: prove directly that K = {0} ∪ {1/n : n ∈ N} is
    compact. (The member U₀ ∋ 0 contains (−ε, ε), hence all 1/n with
    n > 1/ε; cover the finitely many others one at a time.)

D2. Prove: (a) a closed subset of a compact space is compact; (b) a compact
    subset of a Hausdorff space is closed; (c) in a Hausdorff space two
    disjoint compact sets have disjoint neighbourhoods. Give an example of a
    compact subset that is not closed.
    Answer: Proofs below. Example: in Sierpiński space {0, 1} (open sets ∅,
    {1}, X) the set {1} is compact but not closed.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let C ⊆ X be closed, X compact, and {Uᵢ} a cover
    of C by open sets of X. Add the open set X − C: now we have a cover of
    X, so finitely many sets U₁, ..., Uₙ, X − C cover X; then U₁, ..., Uₙ
    cover C. (b) Let K be compact in Hausdorff X and x ∉ K. For each y ∈ K
    choose disjoint open U_y ∋ x and V_y ∋ y. The V_y cover K; take a
    finite subcover V_(y₁), ..., V_(yₙ). Then
       U = U_(y₁) ∩ ... ∩ U_(yₙ)
    is open (FINITE intersection — this is where compactness is used),
    contains x and misses V_(y₁) ∪ ... ∪ V_(yₙ) ⊇ K. So X − K is open. (c)
    The proof of (b) separates a point from a compact set; repeat it with
    the point replaced by a compact set L, covering L by the resulting
    neighbourhoods. Example: {1} is finite, hence compact, but its
    complement {0} is not open, so {1} is not closed; Sierpiński space is
    not Hausdorff. Consequence for R: compact sets are closed (by (b)) and
    bounded (the cover {(−n, n)}). Common mistakes: using infinitely many
    Uᵢ in (b) (an infinite intersection need not be open); applying (b) in
    a non-Hausdorff space. Now you try: in R with the cofinite topology,
    which subsets are compact? (All of them: every subspace of a cofinite
    space is cofinite; so (0, 1) is compact but not closed.)

D3. Prove that a continuous image of a compact space is compact and deduce
    the extreme value theorem. Prove that a continuous bijection from a
    compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism. Find the maximum
    and minimum of f(x, y) = x² + 2y² − x on the closed unit disc.
    Answer: max 9/4 at (−1/2, ±√3/2); min −1/4 at (1/2, 0).
    Teacher explains: Let f : X → Y be continuous and X compact. Given an
    open cover {Vᵢ} of f(X), the sets f⁻¹(Vᵢ) are open and cover X; finitely
    many do, and the corresponding Vᵢ cover f(X). EVT: for f : K → R, f(K)
    is compact in R, so closed and bounded, so it contains sup f(K) and
    inf f(K). Homeomorphism: let f : X → Y be a continuous bijection, X
    compact, Y Hausdorff. It suffices that f is CLOSED (then
    (f⁻¹)⁻¹(C) = f(C) is closed). C closed in X ⇒ C compact (D2(a)) ⇒ f(C)
    compact ⇒ f(C) closed in Y (D2(b)). □ The disc D is compact
    (Heine-Borel), so the extremes exist; find them by checking candidates.
       interior: fₓ = 2x − 1 = 0, f_y = 4y = 0  ⇒  (1/2, 0), f = −1/4
       boundary: y² = 1 − x², f = x² + 2 − 2x² − x = 2 − x − x²,
                 x ∈ [−1, 1]; derivative −1 − 2x = 0 at x = −1/2:
                 f = 2 + 1/2 − 1/4 = 9/4; ends x = 1: 0, x = −1: 2
    Compare: max 9/4 at (−1/2, ±√3/2), min −1/4 at (1/2, 0). Common
    mistakes: forgetting the boundary; claiming a max exists on an open
    disc (f(x) = x has no max on x² + y² < 1). Now you try: the
    continuous bijection id : (R, discrete) → (R, std) is not a
    homeomorphism. Which hypothesis fails? (The domain is not compact.)

D4. Prove Heine-Borel: K ⊆ Rⁿ is compact iff closed and bounded. Show that
    in a metric space compact ⇒ sequentially compact, and that the closed
    unit ball of ℓ² is closed and bounded but not compact. Decide which of
    A = [0, 1] ∩ Q, B = {(x, y) : x² + 4y² ≤ 4}, C = {(x, y) : xy = 1} are
    compact.
    Answer: Only B is compact.
    Teacher explains: (⇒) Rⁿ is Hausdorff, so compact K is closed; the
    open balls B(0, m) cover K, and a finite subcover shows K ⊆ B(0, M).
    (⇐) If K is bounded then K ⊆ [−M, M]ⁿ, a product of compact intervals,
    compact by the tube lemma (D5). K is closed in it, so compact (D2(a)).
    Sequential compactness: let (xₖ) be a sequence in compact metric K with
    no convergent subsequence. Then every point p ∈ K has a ball B(p, r_p)
    containing xₖ for only finitely many k (otherwise one could extract a
    subsequence converging to p). Finitely many such balls cover K, so
    only finitely many indices k occur: contradiction. In ℓ² let
    eₙ = (0, ..., 0, 1, 0, ...). ‖eₙ‖ = 1, but
       ‖eₙ − eₘ‖ = √(1 + 1) = √2   (n ≠ m),
    so no subsequence is Cauchy, let alone convergent: the closed unit ball
    is closed and bounded but not (sequentially) compact. Heine-Borel is a
    fact about Rⁿ, not about metric spaces in general. The three sets:
       A: bounded, not closed (√2/2 is a limit point outside A)   not compact
       B: ellipse x²/4 + y² ≤ 1: closed (≤) and |x| ≤ 2, |y| ≤ 1    compact
       C: closed but unbounded ((n, 1/n) ∈ C)                    not compact
    Common mistakes: applying 'closed and bounded' in ℓ², in Q or in a
    discrete metric space (Z is closed and bounded for d = min(1, |x − y|)
    but not compact). Now you try: is the set of 2 × 2 orthogonal matrices
    compact in R⁴? (Yes: closed, since given by polynomial equations
    AᵀA = I, and bounded, since each column has length 1.)

D5. State and prove the tube lemma, and deduce that X × Y is compact when X
    and Y are. State Tychonoff's theorem and explain why {0, 1}^N and the
    Hilbert cube [0, 1]^N are compact in the product topology but not in the
    box topology.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: TUBE LEMMA: let Y be compact, x ∈ X, and N open in
    X × Y with {x} × Y ⊆ N. For each y ∈ Y choose a basic set
    Uᵧ × Vᵧ ∋ (x, y) inside N. The Vᵧ cover the compact Y, so finitely many
    V_(y₁), ..., V_(yₙ) do. Put W = U_(y₁) ∩ ... ∩ U_(yₙ), open and
    containing x. Every (x′, y) ∈ W × Y has y ∈ some V_(yᵢ) and
    x′ ∈ U_(yᵢ), so it lies in N: W × Y ⊆ N. PRODUCT: let U cover X × Y.
    For each x the 'slice' {x} × Y is compact (≅ Y), so finitely many
    members of U cover it; their union N_x contains a tube W_x × Y. The W_x
    cover X; finitely many W_(x₁), ..., W_(xₘ) do; the finitely many
    members of U used for these tubes cover X × Y. □ TYCHONOFF: any product
    ∏ Xα of compact spaces is compact in the product topology. Sketch: use
    the FIP form; extend a family of closed sets with the FIP to a MAXIMAL
    one (Zorn's lemma); its projections to each Xα have the FIP, so by
    compactness of Xα have a common point pα; the point p = (pα) lies in the
    closure of every member. (Kelley: Tychonoff ⇔ axiom of choice.) So
    {0, 1}^N (≅ the Cantor set) and [0, 1]^N are compact. In the BOX
    topology {0, 1}^N is DISCRETE: {x} = ∏ {xₖ} is a product of open sets.
    An infinite discrete space is not compact, and {0, 1}^N is closed in
    box [0, 1]^N, which is therefore not compact either. Common mistakes:
    thinking Tychonoff is 'obvious' from the finite case (induction only
    gives finite products); using the box topology. Now you try: is R × [0, 1]
    compact? Is S¹ × S¹? (No: its projection R is not compact. Yes: a
    product of two compact spaces.)

D6. Prove that X is compact iff every family of closed sets with the finite
    intersection property has non-empty intersection. State the Lebesgue
    number lemma, find the largest Lebesgue number of the cover
    {(−1, 1/2), (1/3, 2)} of [0, 1], and use the lemma to show that a
    continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous.
    Answer: FIP proof below; Lebesgue number 1/6.
    Teacher explains: Complements turn covers into intersections: {Uᵢ}
    covers X ⇔ ⋂ (X − Uᵢ) = ∅. So 'every open cover has a finite subcover'
    reads, for Cᵢ = X − Uᵢ: 'if ⋂ Cᵢ = ∅ then some finite ⋂ Cᵢ is empty',
    whose contrapositive is: 'if every finite intersection is non-empty
    (FIP), then ⋂ Cᵢ ≠ ∅'. Example: in R the closed sets [n, ∞) have the FIP
    but empty intersection, confirming R is not compact; in [0, 1] the
    nested sets [0, 1/n] meet in {0}. LEBESGUE: for any open cover of a
    compact metric space there is δ > 0 such that each subset of diameter
    < δ lies in a single member. For the given cover the overlap is
    (1/3, 1/2), of length 1/6. If A ⊆ [0, 1] has diameter < 1/6 and is not
    inside (−1, 1/2), it contains a point ≥ 1/2, so all its points are
    > 1/2 − 1/6 = 1/3, and A ⊆ (1/3, 2). So δ = 1/6 works; no larger δ does,
    since [1/3, 1/2] has diameter 1/6 < δ and lies in neither set. Uniform
    continuity: given ε > 0, the sets f⁻¹(B(f(p), ε/2)) form an open cover;
    let δ be a Lebesgue number. If d(x, y) < δ then {x, y} (diameter < δ)
    lies in one f⁻¹(B(f(p), ε/2)), so |f(x) − f(y)| < ε. Common mistakes:
    forgetting that the δ must work for ALL small sets at once; using the
    FIP with open sets ((0, 1/n) has the FIP and empty intersection even
    in compact [0, 1]). Now you try: find the largest Lebesgue number of
    {[0, 0.6), (0.4, 1]} for [0, 1]. (0.2)

D7. Define connectedness and prove that the three definitions (no
    separation; no proper non-empty clopen set; every continuous map to the
    discrete {0, 1} is constant) are equivalent. Prove that [0, 1] is
    connected and that a subset of R is connected iff it is an interval.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: A SEPARATION is X = U ∪ V with U, V open, disjoint and
    non-empty. Then U = X − V is also closed: a proper clopen set. Conversely
    a proper non-empty clopen U gives the separation U, X − U. And a
    continuous onto map f : X → {0, 1} gives the separation f⁻¹(0), f⁻¹(1);
    a separation gives f = 0 on U, 1 on V. [0, 1] IS CONNECTED: suppose
    [0, 1] = U ∪ V is a separation with 0 ∈ U. Let s = sup{x : [0, x] ⊆ U}.
       If s ∈ U: U is open in [0, 1], so [0, s + ε) ⊆ U (if s < 1),
                 contradicting the sup; if s = 1 then V = ∅.
       If s ∈ V: V is open, so (s − ε, s] ⊆ V, but points just below s
                 are in U: contradiction.
    INTERVALS: a set I ⊆ R is an interval ⇔ a, b ∈ I, a < c < b ⇒ c ∈ I. If
    I is not an interval, some c ∉ I lies between two points of I, and
    I ∩ (−∞, c), I ∩ (c, ∞) separate I. If I is an interval, the argument
    for [0, 1] works for every closed subinterval, and a union of such
    intervals containing a common point is connected (D9). So Q, R − {0},
    [0, 1] ∪ [2, 3] are disconnected; R, (0, 1], (−∞, 5) are connected.
    Common mistakes: separating with sets that are not open in the SUBSPACE
    (for Q use Q ∩ (−∞, √2) and Q ∩ (√2, ∞)); thinking a closed set cannot
    be open. Now you try: show that (R, cofinite) is connected. (Any two
    non-empty open sets meet, so no separation exists.)

D8. Prove that a continuous image of a connected space is connected and
    deduce the intermediate value theorem. Use connectedness to show:
    (a) every continuous f : [0, 1] → [0, 1] has a fixed point; (b) R and R²
    are not homeomorphic; (c) x⁵ − 3x + 1 = 0 has exactly three real roots;
    (d) if f : [0, 1] → R is continuous with f(0) = f(1), then
    f(x + 1/2) = f(x) for some x ∈ [0, 1/2].
    Answer: Proofs below; in (c) the roots lie in (−2, −1), (0, 1), (1, 2).
    Teacher explains: If f(X) = U ∪ V were a separation, then f⁻¹(U), f⁻¹(V)
    would separate X. IVT: f : [a, b] → R continuous, f(a) < y < f(b); f([a, b])
    is a connected subset of R, i.e. an interval, containing f(a) and f(b),
    hence y. (a) g(x) = f(x) − x has g(0) = f(0) ≥ 0 and g(1) = f(1) − 1 ≤ 0;
    by the IVT g(c) = 0, i.e. f(c) = c. (b) If h : R → R² were a
    homeomorphism, it would restrict to a homeomorphism R − {0} →
    R² − {h(0)}. The first is disconnected, the second connected
    (path-connected: go around the hole). (c) Values:
       x      −2     −1     0     1     2
       f(x)   −25     3     1    −1    27
    Three sign changes give at least three roots; f′(x) = 5x⁴ − 3 has only
    two real zeros, so by Rolle f has at most three roots. Exactly three.
    (d) g(x) = f(x + 1/2) − f(x) on [0, 1/2]:
       g(0) + g(1/2) = f(1/2) − f(0) + f(1) − f(1/2) = f(1) − f(0) = 0,
    so g(0), g(1/2) have opposite signs (or one is 0), and the IVT gives a
    zero. Common mistakes: applying the IVT to a discontinuous function or
    on a disconnected domain; counting sign changes and forgetting to bound
    the number of roots from above. Now you try: show that every continuous
    f : S¹ → R takes equal values at some pair of antipodal points.
    (g(z) = f(z) − f(−z) satisfies g(−z) = −g(z); S¹ is connected, so g = 0
    somewhere.)

D9. Prove: (a) a union of connected sets with a common point is connected;
    (b) if A is connected and A ⊆ B ⊆ cl A, then B is connected; (c) X × Y
    is connected when X and Y are; (d) path-connected ⇒ connected. Find the
    components of Q, of R − Z and of GL(2, R).
    Answer: Proofs below. Q: the single points. R − Z: the open intervals
    (n, n + 1). GL(2, R): {det > 0} and {det < 0}.
    Teacher explains: The workhorse: if C is connected and C ⊆ U ∪ V is a
    separation of the big space, then C lies entirely in U or entirely in V
    (otherwise C ∩ U, C ∩ V separate C). (a) Let p be common to all Aᵢ and
    let U ∪ V separate ⋃Aᵢ with p ∈ U. Each Aᵢ ∋ p lies in U, so V = ∅.
    (b) If U ∪ V separates B, then A lies in U, say; V is open in B and
    meets B ⊆ cl A, so V meets A: contradiction. (c) Fix (a, b). For each
    x the set ({x} × Y) ∪ (X × {b}) is a union of a copy of Y and a copy of
    X meeting at (x, b), connected by (a); all these contain (a, b), and
    their union is X × Y, connected by (a) again. (d) If X = U ∪ V were a
    separation, take x ∈ U, y ∈ V and a path γ from x to y; then γ([0, 1])
    is connected and meets both U and V: impossible. Components: in Q any
    set with two points a < b is separated by an irrational c between them,
    so components are singletons (TOTALLY DISCONNECTED) — yet Q is not
    discrete. R − Z: each (n, n + 1) is connected and clopen in R − Z. For
    GL(2, R), det is continuous onto R − {0}, which is disconnected, so
    GL(2, R) is disconnected; each of {det > 0}, {det < 0} is
    path-connected (a harder fact), giving exactly 2 components. Common
    mistakes: 'the intersection of connected sets is connected' (two arcs
    of a circle can meet in two points); forgetting that (b) needs B ⊆ cl A.
    Now you try: how many components has R² − (x-axis ∪ y-axis)? (4, the
    open quadrants.)

D10. Let S = {(x, sin(1/x)) : 0 < x ≤ 1} and T = S ∪ ({0} × [−1, 1]) (the
     topologist's sine curve). Prove that T is connected but not
     path-connected. Then prove that an open connected subset of Rⁿ is
     path-connected.
     Answer: Proofs below.
     Teacher explains: S is the image of (0, 1] under the continuous map
     x ↦ (x, sin(1/x)), so S is connected (even path-connected). Every point
     (0, y) with |y| ≤ 1 is a limit of points of S: choose xₖ → 0 with
     sin(1/xₖ) = y (e.g. 1/xₖ = arcsin y + 2πk). So S ⊆ T ⊆ cl S and T is
     connected by D9(b). NOT PATH-CONNECTED: suppose γ : [0, 1] → T is a path
     from (0, 0) to a point of S. Let t₀ = sup{t : γ(t) ∈ {0} × [−1, 1]};
     the segment is closed, so γ(t₀) = (0, y₀), and γ(t) ∈ S for t > t₀. Write
     γ(t) = (x(t), y(t)). As t ↓ t₀, x(t) → 0 through positive values, so on
     every interval (t₀, t₀ + δ) the continuous x(t) takes all values in
     some (0, η), in particular the values 1/(π/2 + 2πk) and
     1/(3π/2 + 2πk) for large k, where y = 1 and y = −1. So y(t) does not
     converge as t ↓ t₀, contradicting continuity of γ at t₀. OPEN
     CONNECTED U ⊆ Rⁿ: fix p ∈ U and let A = {q ∈ U : q is joined to p by a
     path in U}. A is open: if q ∈ A and B(q, r) ⊆ U, every point of the
     ball is joined to q by a segment. U − A is open for the same reason (a
     ball around a point not in A contains no point of A). A ≠ ∅ (p ∈ A),
     so by connectedness A = U. Common mistakes: 'the curve reaches the
     segment' — it never does, it only accumulates; forgetting the openness
     hypothesis (T itself is connected, not open, and not path-connected).
     Now you try: how many path components does T have? (Two: S and the
     segment {0} × [−1, 1].)

D11. Define T0, T1, T2 (Hausdorff), regular and normal. Show: Sierpiński
     space is T0 but not T1; cofinite R is T1 but not T2; in a Hausdorff
     space limits are unique; metric spaces are normal; compact Hausdorff
     spaces are normal; the K-topology on R is Hausdorff but not regular.
     Answer: Proofs below.
     Teacher explains: T1 means every singleton is closed. Sierpiński
     {0, 1}: open sets ∅, {1}, X. The points are distinguished by {1} (T0),
     but no open set contains 0 without 1, so {1} is not closed: not T1.
     Cofinite R: singletons are closed (T1), but non-empty open sets always
     meet (10.25 D2): not T2. Unique limits in Hausdorff X: if
     xₙ → a and xₙ → b ≠ a, take disjoint U ∋ a, V ∋ b; eventually xₙ lies in
     both. METRIC ⇒ NORMAL: for disjoint closed A, B put
        U = {x : d(x, A) < d(x, B)},   V = {x : d(x, B) < d(x, A)}.
     Both are open (x ↦ d(x, A) is continuous), disjoint, and A ⊆ U because
     d(a, A) = 0 < d(a, B) (B closed, a ∉ B). COMPACT HAUSDORFF ⇒ NORMAL:
     closed sets are compact, and D2(c) separates disjoint compact sets. The
     K-topology R_K: basis all (a, b) and all (a, b) − K, K = {1/n : n ∈ N}.
     It is finer than the standard topology, so Hausdorff. K is closed in
     R_K, since R − K = ((−2, 2) − K) ∪ (−∞, −1) ∪ (1, ∞) is open; 0 ∉ K.
     Any open U ∋ 0 contains (−ε, ε) − K, and any open V ⊇ K contains an
     interval around each 1/n; for 1/n < ε that interval meets (−ε, ε) − K.
     So 0 and K cannot be separated: not regular. Common mistakes:
     forgetting that 'regular' is usually required together with T1 (the
     indiscrete space is vacuously regular); believing Hausdorff ⇒ normal.
     Now you try: prove that X is Hausdorff iff the diagonal Δ = {(x, x)} is
     closed in X × X. ((x, y) ∉ Δ has a basic U × V missing Δ ⇔ U ∋ x and
     V ∋ y are disjoint.)

D12. State Urysohn's lemma and the Tietze extension theorem. For A = {0} and
     B = [2, ∞) in R write down an Urysohn function and evaluate it at
     x = 1, 3, −3. Sketch the proof of Urysohn's lemma for a normal space,
     and state the Urysohn metrisation theorem.
     Answer: f(x) = d(x, A)/(d(x, A) + d(x, B)) = |x|/(|x| + d(x, B)):
     f(1) = 1/2, f(3) = 1, f(−3) = 3/8.
     Teacher explains: URYSOHN: X normal, A, B disjoint closed ⇒ there is a
     continuous f : X → [0, 1] with f|A = 0, f|B = 1. (Conversely such an f
     gives the disjoint open sets f⁻¹[0, 1/2) and f⁻¹(1/2, 1], so this
     CHARACTERISES normality.) In a metric space the formula works because
     the denominator is never 0 (a point cannot be at distance 0 from both
     closed disjoint sets). Here d(x, A) = |x| and
     d(x, B) = max(2 − x, 0):
        x = 1:   1/(1 + 1) = 1/2
        x = 3:   3/(3 + 0) = 1               (3 ∈ B)
        x = −3:  3/(3 + 5) = 3/8
     PROOF SKETCH for normal X: normality is equivalent to 'if closed C ⊆ U
     open, there is open V with C ⊆ V ⊆ cl V ⊆ U'. Put U₁ = X − B and choose
     U₀ with A ⊆ U₀ ⊆ cl U₀ ⊆ U₁. Insert U_(1/2) between U₀ and U₁, then U_(1/4),
     U_(3/4), ..., one for every dyadic rational r, with cl Uᵣ ⊆ Uₛ for
     r < s. Define f(x) = inf{r : x ∈ Uᵣ} (and 1 if x is in none). Then
     f = 0 on A, 1 on B, and f⁻¹([0, α)) = ⋃(r < α) Uᵣ and
     f⁻¹((α, 1]) = ⋃(s > α) (X − cl Uₛ) are open, so f is continuous.
     TIETZE: on normal X, every continuous f : A → [a, b] on a closed A
     extends to a continuous F : X → [a, b] (also for R-valued f). On R this
     is just 'join the dots': f(0) = 1, f(1) = −1, f(3) = 2 on A = {0, 1, 3}
     extends piecewise-linearly with F(2) = −1 + (1/2)·3 = 1/2. Closedness
     matters: sin(1/x) on (0, 1] has no continuous extension to [0, 1].
     URYSOHN METRISATION: a second countable T3 space is metrisable (it
     embeds in the Hilbert cube via countably many Urysohn functions).
     Common mistakes: using Urysohn in a space that is not normal; forgetting
     that the sets must be disjoint and CLOSED. Now you try: find the Urysohn
     function for A = x-axis, B = {y = 2} in R² and evaluate it at (5, 1/2).
     (f = |y|/(|y| + |y − 2|); f(5, 1/2) = (1/2)/2 = 1/4)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY

M1. Compact (C) or not (N)? (standard topologies)
    a) [0, 1]                          b) (0, 1]
    c) [0, ∞)                          d) {0} ∪ {1/n : n ∈ N}
    e) {1/n : n ∈ N}                   f) Z
    g) {1, 2, ..., 100}                h) [0, 1] ∩ Q
    i) the Cantor set                  j) [0, 1] ∪ [2, 3]
    k) closed unit disc                l) open unit disc
    m) S¹                              n) S¹ ∪ {(0, 0)}
    o) {xy = 1}                        p) {x² + 4y² ≤ 4}
    q) {x² − y² ≤ 1}                   r) {(x, sin(1/x)) : 0 < x ≤ 1}
    s) its closure in R²               t) {|x| + |y| ≤ 1}
    u) O(2) ⊆ R⁴                       v) SL(2, R) ⊆ R⁴
    w) closed unit ball of ℓ²          x) {x ∈ R³ : x₁² + x₂² + x₃² = 1,
                                          x₃ ≥ 0}
    Answers: a) C   b) N   c) N   d) C   e) N   f) N   g) C   h) N   i) C
             j) C   k) C   l) N   m) C   n) C   o) N   p) C   q) N   r) N
             s) C   t) C   u) C   v) N   w) N   x) C

M2. Compact (C) or not (N)?
    a) R, cofinite topology            b) R, cocountable topology
    c) R, discrete                     d) a finite discrete space
    e) any indiscrete space            f) [0, 1] in R_ℓ
    g) R, right-ray topology {∅, R, (a, ∞)}
    h) [0, 5] in the right-ray topology
    i) R, particular point topology (open: ∅ and sets containing 0)
    j) R, excluded point topology (open: R and sets not containing 0)
    k) {0} ∪ {1/n} with the discrete topology
    l) Sierpiński space                m) Z, cofinite topology
    n) N with open sets ∅, N, {1, ..., n}
    o) the one-point compactification N ∪ {∞}
    p) (0, 1) in the cofinite topology on R
    Answers: a) C   b) N   c) N   d) C   e) C   f) N   g) N   h) C   i) N
             j) C (a cover must contain R itself)   k) N   l) C   m) C
             n) N   o) C   p) C

M3. Does f attain a maximum and a minimum on the set? Give the values (or
    the sup/inf when not attained).
    a) x² on [−1, 2]                   b) x² on (−1, 2)
    c) 1/x on (0, 1]                   d) x³ − 3x on [−2, 2]
    e) sin x on [0, π]                 f) x e^(−x) on [0, ∞)
    g) arctan x on R                   h) x + y on x² + y² ≤ 1
    i) xy on x² + y² ≤ 1               j) x² + y² on [−1, 1]²
    k) x² − y² on x² + y² ≤ 1          l) x on Q ∩ [0, √2]
    m) distance to (3, 4) on S¹        n) (x² − 1)/(x² + 1) on R
    o) x² + 2y² − x on x² + y² ≤ 1     p) e^(−x²) on R

M12. True (T) or false (F)?

    q) Every subspace of a normal space is normal.

    u) If limits of sequences are unique then X is Hausdorff.
