TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: drill the two directions separately — to show NOT compact,
  build one bad cover (usually growing intervals or balls); to show compact,
  quote a theorem (closed and bounded in Rⁿ, closed in compact, image of
  compact, Tychonoff). For connectedness use the 'continuous map to {0, 1}'
  test and the fact that connected pieces never straddle a separation. Keep a
  counterexample card: Sierpiński, cofinite R, R_K, Sorgenfrey plane, the
  topologist's sine curve, the line with two origins, the ℓ² ball. Harder:
  prove the Lebesgue number lemma via sequential compactness; show that
  compact ⇔ every net has a convergent subnet; prove Tychonoff with the
  Alexander subbase lemma; show the Cantor set is homeomorphic to {0, 1}^N
  and that every compact metric space is a continuous image of it; prove
  Urysohn's lemma in full and deduce Tietze by successive approximation with
  the series ∑ (2/3)ⁿ; and show that the Sorgenfrey plane is not normal by
  Jones' lemma (a separable normal space has no closed discrete subset of
  size 2^ℵ₀, but the antidiagonal of R_ℓ² is one, and Q × Q is dense).


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.27 — DIFFERENTIAL GEOMETRY OF CURVES AND SURFACES: CURVATURE,
TORSION, FRENET-SERRET, FIRST AND SECOND FUNDAMENTAL FORMS, GAUSS'S
THEOREMA EGREGIUM, GAUSS-BONNET
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A parametrised curve r(t) is REGULAR if r′(t) ≠ 0. ARC LENGTH
    s(t) = ∫ |r′(u)| du (from t₀ to t) does not depend on the
    parametrisation; a regular curve can be reparametrised BY ARC LENGTH
    (|dr/ds| = 1). Speed v = |r′| = ds/dt. Example: the helix
    (3 cos t, 3 sin t, 4t) has v = 5, s = 5t.
  - CURVATURE: T = r′/|r′| is the unit TANGENT, κ = |dT/ds|. Formulas:
    κ = |r′ × r″|/|r′|³ (space); for a plane curve the SIGNED curvature is
    k = (x′y″ − y′x″)/(x′² + y′²)^(3/2) = dθ/ds (θ = angle of T); for a graph
    y = f(x), κ = |f″|/(1 + f′²)^(3/2); in polar form
    κ = |r² + 2r′² − rr″|/(r² + r′²)^(3/2). RADIUS of curvature ρ = 1/κ; the
    OSCULATING circle has centre r + ρN. Line: κ = 0; circle of radius R:
    κ = 1/R.
  - FRENET FRAME (κ > 0): N = (dT/ds)/κ (principal NORMAL), B = T × N
    (BINORMAL). TORSION τ is defined by dB/ds = −τN;
    τ = (r′ × r″)·r‴/|r′ × r″|². Osculating plane ⟂ B, normal plane ⟂ T,
    rectifying plane ⟂ N. HELIX (a cos t, a sin t, bt): κ = a/(a² + b²),
    τ = b/(a² + b²).
  - FRENET-SERRET: T′ = κN, N′ = −κT + τB, B′ = −τN (′ = d/ds); the matrix
    [[0, κ, 0], [−κ, 0, τ], [0, −τ, 0]] is SKEW-symmetric. With respect to
    t multiply each right side by v. DARBOUX vector ω = τT + κB (each
    frame vector X satisfies X′ = ω × X). Consequences: τ ≡ 0 ⇔ the curve is
    PLANAR; κ constant, τ = 0 ⇒ circle; κ, τ constant ⇒ circular helix.
    FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM: κ(s) > 0 and τ(s) determine the curve up to a rigid
    motion (a plane curve is determined by k(s) alone).
  - SURFACES: a regular patch x(u, v) has x_u × x_v ≠ 0; unit normal
    n = x_u × x_v/|x_u × x_v|. FIRST FUNDAMENTAL FORM
    I = E du² + 2F du dv + G dv², E = x_u·x_u, F = x_u·x_v, G = x_v·x_v. It
    gives LENGTH ∫ √(Eu′² + 2Fu′v′ + Gv′²) dt, ANGLES (cos α = F/√(EG)
    between coordinate curves) and AREA dA = √(EG − F²) du dv. A map that
    preserves I is an ISOMETRY (plane → cylinder locally).
  - SECOND FUNDAMENTAL FORM II = e du² + 2f du dv + g dv², e = x_uu·n,
    f = x_uv·n, g = x_vv·n. NORMAL CURVATURE in direction (du : dv):
    kₙ = II/I. SHAPE OPERATOR (Weingarten map) S = −dn has matrix
    [[E, F], [F, G]]⁻¹[[e, f], [f, g]]; its eigenvalues are the PRINCIPAL
    CURVATURES k₁, k₂ (max and min of kₙ), eigenvectors the principal
    directions. EULER: kₙ = k₁cos²θ + k₂sin²θ.
  - GAUSSIAN CURVATURE K = k₁k₂ = (eg − f²)/(EG − F²); MEAN CURVATURE
    H = (k₁ + k₂)/2 = (eG − 2fF + gE)/(2(EG − F²)). Points: ELLIPTIC K > 0,
    HYPERBOLIC K < 0, PARABOLIC K = 0 but II ≠ 0, PLANAR II = 0; UMBILIC
    k₁ = k₂. Graph z = h(x, y) with p, q, r, s, t = hₓ, h_y, hₓₓ, hₓᵧ, h_yy:
    K = (rt − s²)/(1 + p² + q²)², H = ((1 + q²)r − 2pqs + (1 + p²)t)/
    (2(1 + p² + q²)^(3/2)). MINIMAL surfaces have H = 0.
  - STANDARD VALUES: plane K = H = 0; sphere of radius R: K = 1/R², |H| = 1/R
    (all points umbilic); cylinder of radius R: K = 0, |H| = 1/(2R); torus
    ((R + r cos v) cos u, (R + r cos v) sin u, r sin v):
    K = cos v/(r(R + r cos v)); catenoid K = −1/cosh⁴v, H = 0; helicoid
    (v cos u, v sin u, cu) K = −c²/(c² + v²)², H = 0; pseudosphere K = −1.
  - THEOREMA EGREGIUM (Gauss): K depends only on E, F, G and their
    derivatives, so it is preserved by ISOMETRIES (bending without
    stretching). For F = 0: K = −(1/(2√(EG)))[(E_v/√(EG))_v + (G_u/√(EG))_u];
    for I = du² + G dv²: K = −(√G)_uu/√G; for I = λ(du² + dv²):
    K = −Δ(ln λ)/(2λ). Hence no map of a sphere to a plane preserves
    distances, but paper can be rolled into a cylinder or cone (K = 0).
  - GEODESICS and GAUSS-BONNET: the curvature vector of a curve on a surface
    splits as κ² = κ_g² + κₙ² (GEODESIC and normal curvature); GEODESICS have
    κ_g = 0 (great circles on a sphere, straight lines on a plane). LOCAL
    GAUSS-BONNET for a region D bounded by a piecewise smooth simple closed
    curve with exterior angles θᵢ: ∬_D K dA + ∮ κ_g ds + ∑θᵢ = 2π. For a
    geodesic triangle with interior angles α, β, γ: ∬ K dA = α + β + γ − π.
    GLOBAL: for a compact surface ∬_S K dA = 2πχ(S), χ = V − E + F
    = 2 − 2g (genus g): sphere 4π, torus 0.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. For the helix r(t) = (3 cos t, 3 sin t, 4t) find the arc length from t = 0
    to t, the length of one turn, and the arc-length parametrisation. Find
    the length of y = cosh x from x = 0 to x = a, and decide whether
    r(t) = (t², t³) is regular.
    Answer: s = 5t; one turn 10π ≈ 31.42; r(s) = (3 cos(s/5), 3 sin(s/5),
    4s/5); length sinh a; (t², t³) is not regular at t = 0.
    Teacher explains: Differentiate, take the length, integrate.
       r′(t) = (−3 sin t, 3 cos t, 4)
       |r′(t)| = √(9 sin²t + 9 cos²t + 16) = √25 = 5
       s(t) = ∫₀ᵗ 5 du = 5t
    One turn is t ∈ [0, 2π], length 10π. Invert s = 5t, t = s/5, and
    substitute: r(s) = (3 cos(s/5), 3 sin(s/5), 4s/5). Check:
    |dr/ds| = √(9/25 + 16/25) = 1 ✓. For the catenary, as a graph
    r(x) = (x, cosh x):
       |r′| = √(1 + sinh²x) = cosh x,   L = ∫₀ᵃ cosh x dx = sinh a.
    Regularity: r′(t) = (2t, 3t²) = (0, 0) at t = 0, and the curve y² = x³
    has a CUSP there; the tangent is not defined. The arc length does not
    depend on the parametrisation (by the chain rule
    |dr/du| du = |dr/dt| |dt/du| du = |dr/dt| dt), so it is a geometric
    quantity. Common mistakes: forgetting the square root; integrating the
    speed squared; parametrising by arc length a curve whose speed integral
    cannot be inverted in closed form (then keep s abstract). Now you try:
    find the length of the cycloid (t − sin t, 1 − cos t), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π.
    (|r′| = √(2 − 2 cos t) = 2 sin(t/2); L = ∫₀^(2π) 2 sin(t/2) dt = 8)

D2. Derive the curvature formula for a plane curve and for a graph y = f(x).
    For y = x² at (1, 1) find the curvature, the radius and centre of
    curvature and the osculating circle. Find the curvature of the ellipse
    (3 cos t, 2 sin t) at its vertices.
    Answer: κ = 2/5^(3/2) = 2√5/25 ≈ 0.179; ρ = 5√5/2 ≈ 5.59; centre
    (−4, 7/2); circle (x + 4)² + (y − 7/2)² = 125/4. Ellipse: 3/4 at (±3, 0),
    2/9 at (0, ±2).
    Teacher explains: Let θ be the angle of the tangent, tan θ = y′/x′ (′ =
    d/dt). Differentiating, sec²θ · θ′ = (x′y″ − y′x″)/x′², and
    sec²θ = (x′² + y′²)/x′², so θ′ = (x′y″ − y′x″)/(x′² + y′²). The signed
    curvature is k = dθ/ds = θ′/v with v = √(x′² + y′²):
       k = (x′y″ − y′x″)/(x′² + y′²)^(3/2).
    For a graph x = t, y = f(t): k = f″/(1 + f′²)^(3/2). For y = x² at x = 1:
    f′ = 2, f″ = 2, so
       κ = 2/(1 + 4)^(3/2) = 2/(5√5),    ρ = 1/κ = 5√5/2.
    The centre lies at distance ρ along the unit normal towards the concave
    side. T ∝ (1, 2), so N = (−2, 1)/√5 (pointing up and to the left, into
    the cup):
       centre = (1, 1) + (5√5/2)(−2, 1)/√5 = (1, 1) + (−5, 5/2) = (−4, 7/2).
    In general the centre is (x − f′(1 + f′²)/f″, y + (1 + f′²)/f″). The
    osculating circle is (x + 4)² + (y − 7/2)² = 125/4; it matches the curve
    to second order. Ellipse: x′ = −3 sin t, y′ = 2 cos t, x″ = −3 cos t,
    y″ = −2 sin t, x′y″ − y′x″ = 6, so k = 6/(9 sin²t + 4 cos²t)^(3/2). At
    t = 0: 6/8 = 3/4; at t = π/2: 6/27 = 2/9. (In general
    k = ab/(a²sin²t + b²cos²t)^(3/2): a/b² at (a, 0), b/a² at (0, b).) The
    sharp ends have the larger curvature.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the power 3/2; putting the centre on the
    convex side. Now you try: curvature and centre of curvature of y = eˣ
    at (0, 1). (κ = 1/(2√2) = √2/4; centre (−2, 3))

D3. For a regular space curve r(t) prove κ = |r′ × r″|/|r′|³ and
    τ = (r′ × r″)·r‴/|r′ × r″|². Apply them to the helix
    r(t) = (a cos t, a sin t, bt) (a > 0) and find T, N, B.
    Answer: κ = a/(a² + b²), τ = b/(a² + b²); T = (−a sin t, a cos t, b)/c,
    N = (−cos t, −sin t, 0), B = (b sin t, −b cos t, a)/c, c = √(a² + b²).
    Teacher explains: Write v = |r′|. Then r′ = vT. Differentiate using
    dT/dt = v dT/ds = vκN:
       r″ = v′T + v²κN
       r′ × r″ = vT × (v′T + v²κN) = v³κ (T × N) = v³κB
    so |r′ × r″| = v³κ, the first formula. Differentiate again; we only need
    the B-component of r‴. From dN/dt = v(−κT + τB),
       r‴ = (...)T + (...)N + v²κ · vτB = (...)T + (...)N + v³κτB,
    hence (r′ × r″)·r‴ = v³κ · v³κτ = v⁶κ²τ = |r′ × r″|² τ. For the helix,
    with c² = a² + b²:
       r′ = (−a sin t, a cos t, b),  |r′| = c
       r″ = (−a cos t, −a sin t, 0)
       r‴ = (a sin t, −a cos t, 0)
       r′ × r″ = (ab sin t, −ab cos t, a²),  |r′ × r″| = ac
       κ = ac/c³ = a/c²,   τ = (a²b sin²t + a²b cos²t)/(a²c²) = b/c²
    T = r′/c; N is the unit vector of dT/dt = r″/c, i.e. (−cos t, −sin t, 0),
    pointing horizontally towards the axis; B = T × N as stated (check
    B · T = 0 ✓). Both κ and τ are CONSTANT; b < 0 (left-handed helix) gives
    τ < 0. Common mistakes: dividing by |r′ × r″| instead of its square in
    τ; forgetting that N points to the concave side (towards the axis). Now
    you try: find κ and τ of (cos t, sin t, t). (1/2 and 1/2)

D4. Derive the Frenet-Serret equations. Prove: (a) a curve with κ > 0 and
    τ ≡ 0 lies in a plane; (b) a plane curve with constant curvature κ > 0
    is part of a circle of radius 1/κ; (c) state the fundamental theorem of
    space curves and identify the curves with κ = 3/25, τ = 4/25 and with
    κ = 1/3, τ = 0.
    Answer: T′ = κN, N′ = −κT + τB, B′ = −τN. The curves are the helix
    (3 cos t, 3 sin t, 4t) (up to rigid motion) and a circle of radius 3.
    Teacher explains: T′ = κN is the definition of N. B = T × N gives
       B′ = T′ × N + T × N′ = κN × N + T × N′ = T × N′,
    so B′ ⟂ T; also B′ ⟂ B (since B·B = 1). So B′ is a multiple of N,
    written −τN. Finally N = B × T gives
       N′ = B′ × T + B × T′ = −τN × T + κB × N = τB − κT.
    In matrix form (T, N, B)′ = (T, N, B) times a skew-symmetric matrix: this
    is forced, because the frame stays orthonormal. (a) τ = 0 ⇒ B′ = 0 ⇒ B
    is a constant vector B₀. Then (r · B₀)′ = T · B₀ = 0, so r · B₀ is
    constant: the curve lies in a plane perpendicular to B₀. (b) Let
    c = r + N/κ (the would-be centre). Then c′ = T + (−κT + τB)/κ = 0 (τ = 0 for
    a plane curve), so c is fixed and |r − c| = |N/κ| = 1/κ. (c) FUNDAMENTAL
    THEOREM: given smooth κ(s) > 0 and τ(s), there is a curve with these
    functions, unique up to a rotation and translation (solve the linear
    ODE system for the frame, then integrate T). For constant κ, τ the helix
    has a = κ/(κ² + τ²), b = τ/(κ² + τ²):
       κ = 3/25, τ = 4/25:  κ² + τ² = 25/625 = 1/25,  a = 3, b = 4.
    κ = 1/3, τ = 0 is a circle of radius 3. Common mistakes: sign
    conventions (some books write B′ = τN; then helix torsions change sign);
    forgetting that N is only defined where κ > 0. Now you try: which curve
    has κ = τ = 1/2? (The helix (cos t, sin t, t): a = b = 1.)

D5. For the twisted cubic r(t) = (t, t², t³) find κ and τ at t = 0 and at
    t = 1, the general torsion, the Frenet frame at t = 1, and the
    osculating and normal planes at t = 1.
    Answer: t = 0: κ = 2, τ = 3. t = 1: κ = √266/98 ≈ 0.166, τ = 3/19.
    τ(t) = 3/(9t⁴ + 9t² + 1). At t = 1: T = (1, 2, 3)/√14,
    N = (−11, −8, 9)/√266, B = (3, −3, 1)/√19; osculating plane
    3x − 3y + z = 1; normal plane x + 2y + 3z = 6.
    Teacher explains: Compute the three derivatives once:
       r′ = (1, 2t, 3t²),  r″ = (0, 2, 6t),  r‴ = (0, 0, 6)
       r′ × r″ = (2t·6t − 3t²·2, 3t²·0 − 1·6t, 1·2 − 2t·0) = (6t², −6t, 2)
       |r′ × r″|² = 36t⁴ + 36t² + 4,   (r′ × r″)·r‴ = 12
    So τ = 12/(36t⁴ + 36t² + 4) = 3/(9t⁴ + 9t² + 1), never 0: the curve is
    nowhere planar. At t = 0: r′ = (1, 0, 0), r′ × r″ = (0, 0, 2), κ = 2/1 = 2,
    τ = 3. At t = 1:
       r′ = (1, 2, 3), |r′| = √14;  r′ × r″ = (6, −6, 2), |·| = √76 = 2√19
       κ = 2√19/(14√14) = √19/(7√14) = √266/98 ≈ 0.1664,   τ = 12/76 = 3/19
    B is the unit vector of r′ × r″: (3, −3, 1)/√19. N = B × T:
       (3, −3, 1) × (1, 2, 3) = (−9 − 2, 1 − 9, 6 + 3) = (−11, −8, 9),
    with |(−11, −8, 9)| = √266 = √19·√14, so N = (−11, −8, 9)/√266. Checks:
    N·T = −11 − 16 + 27 = 0, N·B ∝ −33 + 24 + 9 = 0, and N·r″ = 38 > 0, so N
    points to the side the curve bends ✓. Planes through r(1) = (1, 1, 1):
       osculating (normal vector B):  3(x − 1) − 3(y − 1) + (z − 1) = 0
                                      ⇔ 3x − 3y + z = 1
       normal (normal vector T):      (x − 1) + 2(y − 1) + 3(z − 1) = 0
                                      ⇔ x + 2y + 3z = 6
    Common mistakes: cross product sign errors (check with a dot product);
    using |r′| instead of |r′|³. Now you try: find κ and τ of
    (t, t²/2, t³/3) at t = 1. (r′ × r″ = (1, −2, 1), |r′| = √3: κ = √6/3^(3/2)
    = √2/3, τ = 2/6 = 1/3)

D6. Show that the signed curvature of a plane curve satisfies k = dθ/ds, and
    use it to reconstruct the unit-speed plane curve with k(s) = 1/(1 + s²),
    starting at the origin heading along the x-axis. Explain the total
    curvature of a closed curve (rotation index).
    Answer: x(s) = arsinh s, y(s) = √(1 + s²) − 1, i.e. the catenary
    y = cosh x − 1. For a simple closed curve ∮ k ds = ±2π.
    Teacher explains: For a unit-speed curve T = (cos θ, sin θ), so
    dT/ds = θ′(−sin θ, cos θ): the length of dT/ds is |θ′| and the signed
    curvature is k = θ′ (positive when turning left). This gives the
    FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM FOR PLANE CURVES: θ(s) = θ₀ + ∫ k, then
       x(s) = x₀ + ∫ cos θ ds,   y(s) = y₀ + ∫ sin θ ds.
    Here θ(s) = ∫₀ˢ du/(1 + u²) = arctan s, so
       cos θ = 1/√(1 + s²),   sin θ = s/√(1 + s²)
       x(s) = ∫₀ˢ du/√(1 + u²) = arsinh s
       y(s) = ∫₀ˢ u du/√(1 + u²) = √(1 + s²) − 1
    Eliminating s = sinh x: y = √(1 + sinh²x) − 1 = cosh x − 1. Check: for
    y = cosh x, arc length from 0 is sinh x = s and κ = cosh x/cosh³x
    = 1/cosh²x = 1/(1 + s²) ✓. Total curvature: for a closed curve of
    length L, ∫₀ᴸ k ds = θ(L) − θ(0) = 2π × (number of turns of T), the
    ROTATION INDEX. Hopf's Umlaufsatz: a SIMPLE closed curve has index ±1,
    e.g. the ellipse gives 2π; a figure eight has index 0. Constant k ≠ 0
    gives θ linear and the curve is a circle. Common mistakes: losing the
    sign of k; integrating k to get the curve directly (integrate TWICE:
    first θ, then position). Now you try: which unit-speed curve has k = 2,
    starting at the origin heading along the x-axis? (Circle of radius 1/2
    centred at (0, 1/2): (sin 2s/2, (1 − cos 2s)/2))

D7. For the sphere x(u, v) = (R cos v cos u, R cos v sin u, R sin v) (u =
    longitude, v = latitude) compute the first fundamental form, the area of
    the sphere, the length of the parallel v = v₀ and the area of the zone
    0 ≤ v ≤ π/6. Show that the plane and the cylinder of radius 1 are
    locally isometric, and find the area of the torus.
    Answer: I = R²cos²v du² + R² dv²; area 4πR²; parallel 2πR cos v₀; zone
    πR². Cylinder (cos u, sin u, v) has I = du² + dv², like the plane. Torus
    area 4π²Rr.
    Teacher explains:
       x_u = (−R cos v sin u, R cos v cos u, 0)
       x_v = (−R sin v cos u, −R sin v sin u, R cos v)
       E = x_u·x_u = R²cos²v,  F = x_u·x_v = 0,  G = x_v·x_v = R²
    F = 0 means the meridians and parallels meet at right angles. Area
    element √(EG − F²) = R² cos v, so
       area = ∫₀^(2π) ∫_(−π/2)^(π/2) R² cos v dv du = 2π R² · 2 = 4πR².
    The parallel v = v₀ is u = t, v = v₀: length ∫₀^(2π) √E dt = 2πR cos v₀.
    Zone: 2πR² ∫₀^(π/6) cos v dv = 2πR² sin(π/6) = πR² (Archimedes: a zone
    of height h has area 2πRh; here h = R/2). Cylinder x = (cos u, sin u, v):
    x_u = (−sin u, cos u, 0), x_v = (0, 0, 1), E = 1, F = 0, G = 1: the same
    I as the plane with coordinates (u, v). So the map (u, v) ↦ (cos u,
    sin u, v) preserves all lengths and angles locally — rolling paper.
    Torus: E = (R + r cos v)², F = 0, G = r², dA = r(R + r cos v) du dv,
       area = ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀^(2π) r(R + r cos v) dv du = 2π · r · 2πR = 4π²Rr.
    Common mistakes: forgetting the square root in dA; using the colatitude
    formulas with latitude limits. Now you try: find I for the cone
    (v cos u, v sin u, v) and its lateral area for 0 ≤ v ≤ h. (E = v², F = 0,
    G = 2; area ∫∫ √2 v du dv = √2 πh²)

D8. Define the second fundamental form, normal curvature and shape operator.
    For the cylinder x = (R cos u, R sin u, v) with inward normal compute II,
    the principal curvatures, K and H, and the normal curvature in the
    direction making angle θ with the circle. Do the same for the sphere of
    radius R, and prove Euler's formula.
    Answer: Cylinder: II = R du², k₁ = 1/R, k₂ = 0, K = 0, H = 1/(2R),
    kₙ = cos²θ/R. Sphere: kₙ = 1/R in every direction, K = 1/R², H = 1/R.
    Teacher explains: For a unit-speed curve on the surface, r″ = κN has a
    component along the surface normal n; that component is the NORMAL
    CURVATURE kₙ = r″·n. Since r′ = x_u u′ + x_v v′ and r′·n = 0,
       kₙ = r″·n = e u′² + 2f u′v′ + g v′² = II(r′)
    (with I(r′) = 1); for a non-unit direction kₙ = II/I. Cylinder:
       x_u = (−R sin u, R cos u, 0), x_v = (0, 0, 1), n = (−cos u, −sin u, 0)
       x_uu = (−R cos u, −R sin u, 0), x_uv = x_vv = 0
       E = R², F = 0, G = 1;  e = R, f = 0, g = 0
    Shape operator [[E, F], [F, G]]⁻¹[[e, f], [f, g]] = [[1/R, 0], [0, 0]], so
    k₁ = 1/R (around the circle), k₂ = 0 (along the ruling),
    K = 0, H = 1/(2R). A unit direction at angle θ to the circle is
    (du, dv) = (cos θ/R, sin θ), giving kₙ = R cos²θ/R² = cos²θ/R. EULER'S
    FORMULA in general: the shape operator is self-adjoint with respect to
    I, so it has orthonormal eigenvectors e₁, e₂ with eigenvalues k₁, k₂;
    for w = cos θ e₁ + sin θ e₂, kₙ(w) = II(w, w) = k₁cos²θ + k₂sin²θ. So k₁,
    k₂ are the max and min of kₙ. Sphere (inward normal): n = −x/R gives
    II = I/R, so kₙ = 1/R for every direction: every point is UMBILIC,
    K = 1/R², H = 1/R. Common mistakes: sign of II depends on the choice of
    n (K does not); computing e with x_u instead of x_uu. Now you try: on the
    cylinder of radius 2, what is the normal curvature at 60° to the
    circle? (cos²60°/2 = 1/8)

D9. Derive K and H for a graph z = h(x, y). Compute K, H and the principal
    curvatures of z = x² + y² at (1, 0, 1), K and H of z = xy at (1, 1, 1),
    and classify the origin for z = x² + y², x² − y², x² and x³ − 3xy².
    Answer: z = x² + y² at (1, 0): K = 4/25, H = 6√5/25, k = 2√5/25 and 2√5/5.
    z = xy at (1, 1): K = −1/9, H = −√3/9 (upward normal). Origin: elliptic
    (umbilic, K = 4), hyperbolic (K = −4), parabolic (K = 0, H = 1), planar
    (monkey saddle).
    Teacher explains: With x = (u, v, h(u, v)) and p = h_u, q = h_v, r = h_uu,
    s = h_uv, t = h_vv:
       x_u = (1, 0, p),  x_v = (0, 1, q),  n = (−p, −q, 1)/W,  W = √(1 + p² + q²)
       E = 1 + p², F = pq, G = 1 + q²,  EG − F² = W²
       e = r/W, f = s/W, g = t/W
       K = (rt − s²)/W⁴,  H = ((1 + q²)r − 2pqs + (1 + p²)t)/(2W³)
    z = x² + y² at (1, 0): p = 2, q = 0, r = t = 2, s = 0, W² = 5.
       K = 4/25;  H = (1·2 + 5·2)/(2·5√5) = 12/(10√5) = 6√5/25
    Here F = 0, so the principal curvatures are e/E = (2/√5)/5 = 2√5/25
    (radial) and g/G = 2/√5 = 2√5/5 (around); product 4/25 ✓. z = xy at
    (1, 1): p = q = 1, r = t = 0, s = 1, W² = 3:
       K = −1/9,   H = −2·1·1·1/(2·3√3) = −1/(3√3) = −√3/9.
    At a critical point (p = q = 0) the formulas reduce to the Hessian:
    K = det, H = trace/2:
       x² + y²:   Hessian diag(2, 2)    K = 4,  H = 2    elliptic, umbilic
       x² − y²:   diag(2, −2)           K = −4, H = 0    hyperbolic
       x²:        diag(2, 0)            K = 0,  H = 1    parabolic
       x³ − 3xy²: zero matrix           K = 0,  H = 0    planar
    Common mistakes: forgetting W at non-critical points; using K = rt − s²
    away from critical points. Now you try: K and H of z = x² + xy + y² at the
    origin, and its principal curvatures. (Hessian [[2, 1], [1, 2]]: K = 3,
    H = 2, k = 1 and 3)

D10. For the torus x(u, v) = ((R + r cos v) cos u, (R + r cos v) sin u,
     r sin v), 0 < r < R, compute I, II (inward normal), K and H. Where is K
     positive, negative, zero? Compute ∬ K dA over the whole torus and over
     the outer half (cos v ≥ 0).
     Answer: I = (R + r cos v)² du² + r² dv²; II = (R + r cos v) cos v du²
     + r dv²; K = cos v/(r(R + r cos v)); H = (R + 2r cos v)/(2r(R + r cos v)).
     K > 0 on the outer half, < 0 on the inner half, 0 on the top and bottom
     circles. Total curvature 0; outer half 4π (inner half −4π).
     Teacher explains:
        x_u = (R + r cos v)(−sin u, cos u, 0)
        x_v = r(−sin v cos u, −sin v sin u, cos v)
        E = (R + r cos v)²,  F = 0,  G = r²
     The inward normal is n = −(cos v cos u, cos v sin u, sin v) (pointing to
     the centre of the tube). Then
        x_uu = −(R + r cos v)(cos u, sin u, 0)    e = (R + r cos v) cos v
        x_uv = r sin v (sin u, −cos u, 0)         f = 0
        x_vv = −r(cos v cos u, cos v sin u, sin v)  g = r
     K = eg/(EG) = r(R + r cos v)cos v/(r²(R + r cos v)²) = cos v/(r(R + r cos v))
     and H = (eG + gE)/(2EG) = (R + 2r cos v)/(2r(R + r cos v)). Outer
     equator v = 0: K = 1/(r(R + r)) > 0 (dome-like); inner equator v = π:
     K = −1/(r(R − r)) < 0 (saddle-like); v = ±π/2: K = 0 (parabolic). With
     dA = r(R + r cos v) du dv the awkward factor cancels:
        ∬ K dA = ∫₀^(2π) ∫ cos v dv du.
     Over v ∈ [0, 2π]: 0 = 2πχ(torus). Over v ∈ [−π/2, π/2]: 2π · 2 = 4π, the
     same as a whole sphere (the Gauss map of the outer half covers the
     sphere once). Common mistakes: sign of the normal (flips e, g and H but
     not K); integrating K without the area element. Now you try: for R = 2,
     r = 1 find K at v = 0, v = π/2, v = π. (1/3, 0, −1)

D11. State the Theorema Egregium and explain why it is 'remarkable'. Using
     the formula for orthogonal coordinates compute K for: (a) the sphere
     I = R²(dφ² + sin²φ dθ²); (b) the metric (dx² + dy²)/y² on y > 0;
     (c) the catenoid I = cosh²v (du² + dv²). Deduce that no map from a
     region of the sphere to the plane preserves distances, and that the
     catenoid and helicoid can be locally isometric.
     Answer: (a) 1/R²; (b) −1; (c) −1/cosh⁴v.
     Teacher explains: K was defined with the normal n, i.e. by how the
     surface sits in space. Gauss proved (via the Gauss equations, which
     express x_uu, x_uv, x_vv in terms of the Christoffel symbols of I and the
     coefficients of II, and the compatibility (x_uu)_v = (x_uv)_u) that
        eg − f² = (a formula in E, F, G and their first and second
                  derivatives only)   (BRIOSCHI's formula).
     So K is INTRINSIC: an ant measuring lengths on the surface can compute
     it. For F = 0:
        K = −(1/(2√(EG)))[(E_v/√(EG))_v + (G_u/√(EG))_u].
     (a) With u = φ, E = R², G = R²sin²φ, √(EG) = R² sin φ. E_v = 0 and
        G_u/√(EG) = 2R² sin φ cos φ/(R² sin φ) = 2 cos φ,  derivative −2 sin φ,
        K = −(−2 sin φ)/(2R² sin φ) = 1/R².
     (Shortcut for I = du² + G dv²: K = −(√G)_uu/√G; with u = Rφ,
     √G = R sin(u/R), K = 1/R².) (b) Conformal λ = 1/y²: K = −Δ(ln λ)/(2λ)
     = −(y²/2)·Δ(−2 ln y) = −(y²/2)(2/y²) = −1. (c) λ = cosh²v:
     ln λ = 2 ln cosh v, Δ = 2 sech²v, K = −2 sech²v/(2 cosh²v)
     = −1/cosh⁴v. Consequences: an isometry preserves K; the sphere has
     K = 1/R² ≠ 0 = K(plane), so every flat map of the Earth distorts
     distances. The catenoid and helicoid (c = 1) have the same K at
     corresponding points and indeed there is a local isometry: the helicoid
     can be bent into the catenoid. Equal K alone is not always enough, but
     different K always prevents an isometry. Common mistakes: 'K = 0 ⇒ flat
     plane' (a cylinder is curved in space but intrinsically flat); mixing
     up E and G in the formula. Now you try: K for I = du² + e^(2u) dv².
     (√G = eᵘ, K = −eᵘ/eᵘ = −1)

D12. State the local and global Gauss-Bonnet theorems. Verify the global
     theorem for the sphere and the torus, and the local theorem for a
     spherical cap of angular radius φ₀ on the unit sphere. Find the area of
     a geodesic triangle on the unit sphere with three right angles, and on
     a sphere of radius 2. What is the angle sum of a geodesic triangle of
     area π/2 on a surface of constant curvature −1?
     Answer: Sphere ∬K = 4π = 2π·2; torus 0 = 2π·0; cap: 2π(1 − cos φ₀)
     + 2π cos φ₀ = 2π. Triangle area π/2 (unit sphere), 2π (radius 2).
     Hyperbolic triangle: angle sum π − π/2 = π/2.
     Teacher explains: LOCAL: for a simply connected region D whose boundary
     is a piecewise smooth curve with exterior angles θᵢ at the corners,
        ∬_D K dA + ∮_∂D κ_g ds + ∑ θᵢ = 2π.
     For a GEODESIC polygon κ_g = 0, and with interior angles αᵢ = π − θᵢ a
     geodesic triangle gives ∬ K dA = α + β + γ − π (the ANGLE EXCESS). GLOBAL:
     for a compact orientable surface ∬_S K dA = 2πχ(S), χ = V − E + F of any
     triangulation = 2 − 2g. Checks: unit sphere K = 1, area 4π, χ = 2 ✓;
     sphere of any radius R: (1/R²)·4πR² = 4π ✓; torus: ∬ K dA = 0 by D10,
     χ = 0 ✓. Spherical cap φ ≤ φ₀ on the unit sphere:
        ∬ K dA = area = 2π(1 − cos φ₀)
        boundary: circle of radius sin φ₀, curvature 1/sin φ₀; its normal
        curvature on the unit sphere is 1, so κ_g = √(1/sin²φ₀ − 1) = cot φ₀
        ∮ κ_g ds = cot φ₀ · 2π sin φ₀ = 2π cos φ₀
     and the sum is 2π with no corners ✓ (χ(disc) = 1). The octant triangle
     (vertices on the three axes) has α = β = γ = π/2: area = 3π/2 − π = π/2,
     one eighth of 4π ✓. On radius 2, K = 1/4 and ∬K dA = π/2, so the area is
     2π. For K = −1: −π/2 = α + β + γ − π gives α + β + γ = π/2. Geodesics
     themselves: curves with κ_g = 0, i.e. whose acceleration is normal to the
     surface (great circles). Common mistakes: using interior instead of
     exterior angles in the local formula; forgetting that χ is a topological
     invariant: ANY metric on a torus has total curvature 0. Now you try: the
     total curvature of an ellipsoid, and of a genus-2 surface. (4π; −4π)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always compute r′, r″, r‴ (or x_u, x_v, x_uu, x_uv, x_vv, n)
  first in a neat column, then plug into the formulas; check every cross
  product with a dot product (the result must be perpendicular to both
  factors) and every frame by T·N = N·B = 0. Test each formula on the circle,
  the helix, the sphere and the cylinder, where the answers are known. Draw
  the normal and ask 'which way does the surface bend?' to get signs right.
  Harder: prove that a curve with all normal lines through a fixed point is
  a circle; prove that a curve on a sphere satisfies
  (1/κ)² + ((1/κ)′/τ)² = R²; derive the Gauss equations and prove the
  Theorema Egregium via the Christoffel symbols; show that a compact surface
  in R³ has an elliptic point; prove Gauss-Bonnet for a geodesic triangle
  using geodesic polar coordinates (K = −(√G)_rr/√G); and use it to show
  that on a surface with K < 0 two geodesics from a point cannot meet again
  bounding a disc.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.28 — INTRODUCTION TO ALGEBRAIC TOPOLOGY: HOMOTOPY, FUNDAMENTAL
GROUP, COVERING SPACES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - HOMOTOPY: continuous maps f, g : X → Y are HOMOTOPIC (f ≃ g) if there is
    a continuous H : X × [0, 1] → Y with H(x, 0) = f(x), H(x, 1) = g(x). It
    is an equivalence relation. Into a CONVEX set any two maps are homotopic
    by the STRAIGHT-LINE homotopy H = (1 − t)f + tg. f is NULL-HOMOTOPIC if
    it is homotopic to a constant. A map S¹ → S¹ that is not onto is
    null-homotopic.
  - HOMOTOPY EQUIVALENCE: f : X → Y and g : Y → X with g ∘ f ≃ id_X and
    f ∘ g ≃ id_Y (X ≃ Y). A DEFORMATION RETRACTION of X onto A ⊆ X is a
    homotopy from id_X to a retraction r : X → A fixing A. CONTRACTIBLE
    means ≃ a point (Rⁿ, discs, convex and star-shaped sets, trees).
    Examples: R² − {0} ≃ annulus ≃ cylinder ≃ Möbius band ≃ S¹;
    R² − {2 points} ≃ S¹ ∨ S¹ (figure eight); Rⁿ − {0} ≃ Sⁿ⁻¹.
  - PATHS: a path f : [0, 1] → X from x₀ to x₁; PATH HOMOTOPY (f ≃ₚ g) keeps
    the endpoints fixed during the homotopy. PRODUCT f·g (first f, then g,
    each at double speed: f(2s) for s ≤ 1/2, g(2s − 1) for s ≥ 1/2), INVERSE
    f̄(s) = f(1 − s). On path classes the product is associative, has
    identities (constant paths) and inverses [f][f̄] = [e] (a GROUPOID);
    reparametrisations f ∘ φ (φ(0) = 0, φ(1) = 1) are path homotopic to f.
  - FUNDAMENTAL GROUP π₁(X, x₀) = path-homotopy classes of LOOPS at x₀ with
    [f][g] = [f·g]. A path β from x₀ to x₁ gives an ISOMORPHISM
    β̂[f] = [β̄·f·β] : π₁(X, x₀) → π₁(X, x₁), so for path-connected X the
    group is independent of the base point up to isomorphism. SIMPLY
    CONNECTED = path-connected with trivial π₁. Contractible ⇒ simply
    connected (not conversely: S²).
  - FUNCTORIALITY: h : (X, x₀) → (Y, y₀) induces h_*[f] = [h ∘ f], a
    homomorphism with (k ∘ h)_* = k_* ∘ h_* and (id)_* = id. Homeomorphisms
    and HOMOTOPY EQUIVALENCES induce isomorphisms. If A is a RETRACT of X
    (r ∘ i = id_A) then i_* is injective and r_* is surjective.
  - COVERING MAP p : E → B: continuous, surjective, and every b ∈ B has an
    open EVENLY COVERED neighbourhood U: p⁻¹(U) is a disjoint union of open
    SHEETS each mapped homeomorphically onto U. Fibres have constant size
    (the number of SHEETS) over a connected base. Examples: R → S¹,
    t ↦ e^(2πit) (∞ sheets); S¹ → S¹, z ↦ zⁿ (n sheets); R² → T²;
    Sⁿ → RPⁿ (2 sheets); exp : C → C − {0}. A surjective local
    homeomorphism need NOT be a covering ((0, 3) → S¹).
  - LIFTING: PATH LIFTING — for each path γ in B and e₀ ∈ p⁻¹(γ(0)) there is
    a UNIQUE lift γ̃ with p ∘ γ̃ = γ, γ̃(0) = e₀. HOMOTOPY LIFTING — path
    homotopies lift, so path-homotopic paths have lifts with the same
    endpoint. LIFTING CRITERION: f : (Y, y₀) → (B, b₀) with Y connected and
    locally path-connected lifts to (E, e₀) ⇔ f_*π₁(Y) ⊆ p_*π₁(E).
  - π₁(S¹) ≅ Z: [f] ↦ f̃(1) (the endpoint of the lift through R → S¹ starting
    at 0), the DEGREE or WINDING NUMBER; the loop t ↦ e^(2πint) has degree n.
    Consequences: no RETRACTION D² → S¹; BROUWER'S fixed point theorem in
    dimension 2; the FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF ALGEBRA; Borsuk-Ulam for S².
  - COMPUTING π₁: π₁(X × Y) ≅ π₁(X) × π₁(Y) (torus Z², Tⁿ Zⁿ); Sⁿ is simply
    connected for n ≥ 2; π₁(RPⁿ) ≅ Z/2 (n ≥ 2). SEIFERT-VAN KAMPEN: if
    X = U ∪ V with U, V, U ∩ V open and path-connected (base point in U ∩ V),
    then π₁(X) ≅ π₁(U) *_(π₁(U ∩ V)) π₁(V); with U ∩ V simply connected it is
    the FREE PRODUCT. Wedge of n circles: free group Fₙ; a graph with V
    vertices and E edges: F_(E − V + 1); attaching a 2-cell along a loop w
    adds the RELATION w: torus ⟨a, b | aba⁻¹b⁻¹⟩, Klein bottle
    ⟨a, b | abab⁻¹⟩, RP² ⟨a | a²⟩, genus g ⟨a₁, b₁, ..., a_g, b_g |
    [a₁, b₁]...[a_g, b_g]⟩.
  - CLASSIFICATION: p_* : π₁(E, e₀) → π₁(B, b₀) is INJECTIVE and the number of
    sheets equals the INDEX [π₁(B) : p_*π₁(E)] (E connected). For nice B,
    connected covers (up to isomorphism) ↔ CONJUGACY classes of subgroups of
    π₁(B). DECK transformations (homeomorphisms φ of E with p ∘ φ = p) form
    Deck(E/B) ≅ N(H)/H, H = p_*π₁(E); the cover is REGULAR (normal) when H
    is normal, then Deck ≅ π₁(B)/H. The UNIVERSAL cover (simply connected
    E) has Deck ≅ π₁(B): R → S¹ (Z), R² → T² (Z²), S² → RP² (Z/2), the
    4-valent tree → figure eight (F₂).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Define homotopy of maps and prove that ≃ is an equivalence relation.
    Show that any two maps X → C (C ⊆ Rⁿ convex) are homotopic, that
    z ↦ z and z ↦ −z on S¹ are homotopic, and that a map f : X → S¹ that is
    not surjective is null-homotopic.
    Answer: Proofs below; H(z, t) = e^(iπt)z joins z ↦ z to z ↦ −z.
    Teacher explains: Think of t as time: H(·, t) is a film of maps from f
    to g. REFLEXIVE: H(x, t) = f(x). SYMMETRIC: run the film backwards,
    H′(x, t) = H(x, 1 − t). TRANSITIVE: if H goes from f to g and K from g to
    k, play them one after the other at double speed:
       L(x, t) = H(x, 2t)          for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1/2
       L(x, t) = K(x, 2t − 1)      for 1/2 ≤ t ≤ 1
    The pieces agree at t = 1/2 (both give g(x)) and are defined on closed
    sets X × [0, 1/2], X × [1/2, 1], so L is continuous by the PASTING LEMMA.
    CONVEX C: H(x, t) = (1 − t)f(x) + t g(x) stays in C because C contains
    the segment between f(x) and g(x). In particular every map into Rⁿ or a
    disc is null-homotopic. ROTATION: H(z, t) = e^(iπt) z is continuous,
    stays on S¹ (|e^(iπt)| = 1), and H(z, 0) = z, H(z, 1) = −z. NOT
    SURJECTIVE: if f misses p ∈ S¹, then f maps into S¹ − {p}, which is
    homeomorphic to an open interval via stereographic projection σ; the
    map σ ∘ f is homotopic to a constant in R by a straight line, and σ⁻¹ of
    that homotopy is a null-homotopy of f. Common mistakes: using the
    straight line in a non-convex set (in S¹ or R² − {0} the segment may leave
    the space); forgetting to check continuity at t = 1/2. Now you try: show
    that any two maps D² → S¹ are homotopic. (D² is contractible:
    f(x) ≃ f(0) by H(x, t) = f((1 − t)x), and any two constant maps to the
    path-connected S¹ are homotopic along a path.)

D2. Define homotopy equivalence and deformation retraction. Show that
    R² − {0} deformation retracts onto S¹, that the Möbius band ≃ S¹, and that
    Rⁿ is contractible. Sort the capital letters A, B, C, O, P, X (drawn as
    graphs) by homotopy type.
    Answer: H(x, t) = (1 − t)x + t x/|x|; Möbius band retracts to its core
    circle; H(x, t) = (1 − t)x. Letters: C, X ≃ point; A, O, P ≃ S¹; B ≃
    S¹ ∨ S¹.
    Teacher explains: X ≃ Y if there are maps f : X → Y, g : Y → X whose
    composites are homotopic to the identities. If A ⊆ X, a deformation
    retraction is H : X × I → X with H(x, 0) = x, H(x, 1) ∈ A and H(a, t) = a;
    then the inclusion i : A → X and r = H(·, 1) are inverse homotopy
    equivalences. For R² − {0}: r(x) = x/|x|, and
       H(x, t) = (1 − t)x + t x/|x| = x((1 − t) + t/|x|)
    is a positive multiple of x, so never 0: it stays in R² − {0} ✓. It
    fixes S¹ (|x| = 1). Möbius band M = [0, 1] × [−1, 1]/((0, y) ~ (1, −y)):
    H((s, y), t) = (s, (1 − t)y) respects the identification ((0, y) and
    (1, −y) go to (0, (1 − t)y) and (1, −(1 − t)y), still identified), and at
    t = 1 squashes M onto the core circle y = 0. Rⁿ: H(x, t) = (1 − t)x
    deforms everything to 0. For letters: a graph is ≃ a wedge of k circles,
    k = E − V + 1 (the number of independent loops). Shrinking a tree
    inside a graph to a point does not change the homotopy type:
       C, X: trees                                    ≃ point
       A (triangle with two legs), O, P (loop + tail)  ≃ S¹
       B (two loops)                                  ≃ S¹ ∨ S¹
    Homotopy equivalence is much coarser than homeomorphism: X and C are
    not homeomorphic (cut points) but both are contractible. Common mistakes:
    'a deformation retraction must be a retraction at every time' (only at
    t = 1); confusing ≃ with ≅. Now you try: show R³ − {0} ≃ S². (Same
    formula: H(x, t) = (1 − t)x + t x/|x|.)

D3. Define the product of paths and show that the path-homotopy classes of
    loops at x₀ form a group π₁(X, x₀). In particular prove the
    reparametrisation lemma, and show f·f̄ ≃ₚ e_(x₀). Deduce that π₁ of a convex
    set is trivial.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: (f·g)(s) = f(2s) (0 ≤ s ≤ 1/2), g(2s − 1) (1/2 ≤ s ≤ 1),
    defined when f(1) = g(0). WELL DEFINED on classes: if F : f ≃ₚ f′ and
    G : g ≃ₚ g′ then F·G (put side by side) is a path homotopy f·g ≃ₚ f′·g′.
    REPARAMETRISATION LEMMA: if φ : [0, 1] → [0, 1] is continuous with
    φ(0) = 0, φ(1) = 1, then
       H(s, t) = f((1 − t)φ(s) + ts)
    is a path homotopy from f ∘ φ to f (endpoints: s = 0 gives f(0), s = 1
    gives f(1) for all t) — straight line in the convex [0, 1]. ASSOCIATIVITY:
    (f·g)·h runs f on [0, 1/4], g on [1/4, 1/2], h on [1/2, 1], while
    f·(g·h) uses [0, 1/2], [1/2, 3/4], [3/4, 1]. One is the other composed
    with a piecewise-linear φ fixing 0 and 1, so they are path homotopic.
    IDENTITY: e·f = f ∘ φ with φ = 0 on [0, 1/2], 2s − 1 after. INVERSE:
       H(s, t) = f(2s(1 − t))            for s ≤ 1/2
       H(s, t) = f((2 − 2s)(1 − t))      for s ≥ 1/2
    At t = 0 this is f·f̄ (go out along f and back); at time t we only go as
    far as f(1 − t) and return; at t = 1 it is constant at f(0). Endpoints
    stay at x₀ ✓. So π₁(X, x₀) is a group. CONVEX C: any loop f at x₀ is
    path homotopic to the constant loop by H(s, t) = (1 − t)f(s) + tx₀
    (endpoints stay at x₀), so π₁(C, x₀) = 1. Common mistakes: forgetting
    that homotopies of paths must fix the endpoints (without this every path
    is homotopic to a constant, since [0, 1] is contractible); believing f·g
    and g·f are always equal (they are not even both defined unless both are
    loops). Now you try: in R² let f(s) = (s, 0), g(s) = (1, s). Find
    (f·g)(1/4) and (f·g)(3/4). ((1/2, 0) and (1, 1/2))

D4. (a) Show that a path β from x₀ to x₁ induces an isomorphism
    β̂ : π₁(X, x₀) → π₁(X, x₁). (b) Define h_* and prove (k ∘ h)_* = k_* ∘ h_*.
    (c) Prove: if r : X → A is a retraction then i_* : π₁(A) → π₁(X) is
    injective. (d) Show homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental
    groups, and state homotopy invariance.
    Answer: β̂[f] = [β̄·f·β], inverse (β̄)^; proofs below.
    Teacher explains: (a) β̄·f·β is a loop at x₁: go back along β to x₀, do
    f, return along β. β̂ is a homomorphism:
       β̂[f]β̂[g] = [β̄·f·β·β̄·g·β] = [β̄·f·g·β] = β̂([f][g])
    since β·β̄ ≃ₚ constant. The map for β̄ is the inverse. If π₁ is not
    abelian β̂ depends on the class of β (another path changes it by a
    conjugation), so the isomorphism is not canonical. (b) h_*[f] = [h ∘ f];
    well defined because h ∘ F is a path homotopy when F is; a homomorphism
    because h ∘ (f·g) = (h ∘ f)·(h ∘ g). Functoriality:
    (k ∘ h)_*[f] = [k ∘ h ∘ f] = k_*(h_*[f]). (c) r ∘ i = id_A, so
    r_* ∘ i_* = (id_A)_* = id; a map with a left inverse is injective (and
    r_* is surjective). (d) If h is a homeomorphism, h_* and (h⁻¹)_* are
    inverse isomorphisms by (b). HOMOTOPY INVARIANCE: if f ≃ g by H, then
    g_* = β̂ ∘ f_*, where β(t) = H(x₀, t) is the track of the base point;
    hence a homotopy equivalence induces an isomorphism on π₁. Example of
    (c) in action: S¹ is a retract of R² − {0} (x ↦ x/|x|), so i_* is
    injective there — consistent with π₁(R² − {0}) ≅ Z. But S¹ is NOT a
    retract of D², since i_* : Z → 1 cannot be injective (D8). Common
    mistakes: forgetting base points when a homotopy moves them; assuming
    h injective ⇒ h_* injective (the inclusion S¹ → D² is injective, but
    i_* = 0). Now you try: what is i_* for the inclusion of S¹ as the
    equator of S²? (The zero map Z → 1, since π₁(S²) = 1.)

D5. Define a covering map. Verify that p : R → S¹, p(t) = e^(2πit) is a
    covering, and that q : S¹ → S¹, q(z) = z³ is a 3-sheeted covering. Show
    that p restricted to (0, 3) is a surjective local homeomorphism but not
    a covering. List four more coverings.
    Answer: Proofs below; e.g. R² → T², S² → RP², exp : C → C − {0},
    T² → Klein bottle.
    Teacher explains: p : E → B is a COVERING if each b ∈ B has an open
    U ∋ b with p⁻¹(U) = ⊔ Vα (disjoint open sheets), p : Vα → U a
    homeomorphism for each α. For p(t) = e^(2πit) and b = 1 take
    U = S¹ − {−1}:
       p⁻¹(U) = ⋃ₙ (n − 1/2, n + 1/2)   (disjoint open intervals)
    and on each interval p is a continuous bijection onto U whose inverse
    is a branch of (1/2π)·arg (+ n), continuous: a homeomorphism. For other
    b rotate the picture. The fibre p⁻¹(1) = Z: infinitely many sheets. For
    q(z) = z³, U = S¹ − {−1} has preimage three open arcs (arguments in
    (−π/3, π/3), (π/3, π), (π, 5π/3)), each mapped homeomorphically by
    tripling the angle: 3 sheets. (0, 3): the map is still a local
    homeomorphism and onto, but look at b = 1 = p(1) = p(2). Every small
    arc U around 1 has preimage (1 − ε, 1 + ε) ∪ (2 − ε, 2 + ε) ∪ (0, ε) ∪
    (3 − ε, 3): the pieces (0, ε) and (3 − ε, 3) are mapped onto only HALF of
    U, not homeomorphically onto U. So 1 is not evenly covered. (Fibres have
    3 points over some b and 2 over others — another giveaway.) More
    coverings: R² → T², (x, y) ↦ (e^(2πix), e^(2πiy)); S² → RP², x ↦ {±x};
    exp : C → C − {0}; T² → Klein bottle (2 sheets); S¹ × R → T². Common
    mistakes: thinking 'local homeomorphism + surjective' suffices; not
    checking that sheets are DISJOINT and OPEN. Now you try: is
    R → R, x ↦ x³ a covering? Is C → C, z ↦ z²? (Yes: a homeomorphism,
    1 sheet. No: at 0 the map is not a local homeomorphism.)

D6. State and prove the path lifting lemma for p : R → S¹ (in fact for any
    covering), including uniqueness. State the homotopy lifting lemma and
    explain why path-homotopic loops have lifts ending at the same point.
    Lift γ(s) = e^(2πi·3s²) and γ(s) = e^(πis) from 0.
    Answer: Proofs below. Lifts: 3s² (endpoint 3); s/2 (endpoint 1/2).
    Teacher explains: EXISTENCE: cover S¹ by evenly covered open sets U;
    the sets γ⁻¹(U) cover the compact [0, 1], so by the LEBESGUE NUMBER
    LEMMA there is a partition 0 = s₀ < s₁ < ... < sₙ = 1 with each
    γ([sᵢ, sᵢ₊₁]) inside one evenly covered Uᵢ. Lift step by step: having
    γ̃(sᵢ), it lies in exactly one sheet V over Uᵢ; define
    γ̃ = (p|V)⁻¹ ∘ γ on [sᵢ, sᵢ₊₁]. The pieces join continuously. UNIQUENESS:
    if γ̃, γ̂ are two lifts with the same start, the set where they agree is
    closed (Hausdorff target) and open (near a point where they agree both
    lie in the same sheet, on which p is injective); [0, 1] is connected,
    so they agree everywhere. HOMOTOPY LIFTING: a map F : [0, 1]² → B with a
    chosen lift of F(0, 0) lifts uniquely to F̃ (same proof with a grid of
    small squares). If F is a path homotopy from f to g, the sides s = 0 and
    s = 1 of F̃ are lifts of constant paths, hence constant; so f̃(1) = g̃(1).
    Examples through p(t) = e^(2πit): we need p(γ̃(s)) = γ(s), i.e.
    γ̃(s) ≡ exponent/2π modulo integers, continuous, starting at 0:
       e^(2πi·3s²):  γ̃(s) = 3s², ends at 3 (the loop winds 3 times)
       e^(πis):      γ̃(s) = s/2, ends at 1/2 (half a turn, not a loop)
    Starting the second lift at 5 instead gives 5 + s/2: lifts are unique
    ONCE the starting point is chosen. Common mistakes: lifting without
    choosing a starting point; claiming the lift of a loop is a loop (it
    need not be: that failure is exactly what π₁ measures). Now you try:
    lift γ(s) = e^(2πi(s + sin 2πs)) from 0 and find its endpoint.
    (γ̃(s) = s + sin 2πs; endpoint 1)

D7. Prove that π₁(S¹, 1) ≅ Z. Define the degree of a map S¹ → S¹, and find the
    degrees of z ↦ zⁿ, z ↦ z̄ and z ↦ −z.
    Answer: Φ[f] = f̃(1) is an isomorphism; degrees n, −1, 1.
    Teacher explains: Let p(t) = e^(2πit). For a loop f at 1 let f̃ be its
    lift starting at 0; f̃(1) ∈ p⁻¹(1) = Z. Define Φ[f] = f̃(1).
       WELL DEFINED: path-homotopic loops have lifts with the same endpoint
         (homotopy lifting, D6).
       HOMOMORPHISM: if f̃(1) = m, then the lift of f·g is f̃ followed by
         m + g̃ (translation by m is also a lift of g, since p(m + t) = p(t)),
         which ends at m + n. So Φ([f][g]) = m + n.
       SURJECTIVE: γₙ(s) = e^(2πins) lifts to ns, ending at n.
       INJECTIVE: if f̃(1) = 0, f̃ is a loop in R; R is convex, so f̃ ≃ₚ
         constant by a straight-line homotopy F̃, and p ∘ F̃ is a path
         homotopy from f to the constant loop.
    Hence π₁(S¹) ≅ Z, generated by the loop once around. DEGREE: for
    h : S¹ → S¹, deg h = Φ of the loop s ↦ h(e^(2πis)) (after rotating so that
    h(1) = 1; rotations do not change the class). For h(z) = zⁿ the loop is
    e^(2πins): degree n, and h_* is multiplication by n on Z. z̄: the loop
    e^(−2πis) lifts to −s: degree −1. −z: the loop −e^(2πis) = e^(2πi(s + 1/2))
    has lift s + 1/2, which increases by 1: degree 1 (it is a rotation).
    Degrees multiply under composition. Common mistakes: using the 'angle'
    arg as if it were continuous on S¹ (it is not: that is why we lift);
    thinking the lift of a loop must be a loop. Now you try: the degree of
    h(z) = z²z̄³ on S¹. (z̄ = z⁻¹ on S¹, so h(z) = z⁻¹: degree −1)

D8. Prove: (a) there is no retraction D² → S¹; (b) Brouwer: every continuous
    f : D² → D² has a fixed point; (c) the fundamental theorem of algebra:
    every non-constant complex polynomial has a root.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: (a) If r : D² → S¹ were a retraction, then
    r ∘ i = id_(S¹) would give r_* ∘ i_* = id on π₁(S¹) ≅ Z. But i_* maps into
    π₁(D²) = 1, so r_* ∘ i_* = 0 ≠ id. (b) Suppose f(x) ≠ x for all x. Draw the
    ray from f(x) through x and let r(x) be where it leaves the disc. r is
    continuous (solve a quadratic with continuous coefficients for the
    positive root), and if x ∈ S¹ then r(x) = x. So r is a retraction
    D² → S¹, contradicting (a). (c) WLOG p(z) = zⁿ + a_(n−1)z^(n−1) + ... + a₀,
    n ≥ 1, and suppose p has no root. For r ≥ 0 consider the loop
       f_r(s) = [p(re^(2πis))/|p(re^(2πis))|] / [p(r)/|p(r)|],
    a loop in S¹ starting at 1. As r varies from 0 to R this is
    a homotopy from the constant loop (r = 0) to f_R, so deg f_R = 0. But for
    R > max(1, |a₀| + ... + |a_(n−1)|), on |z| = R we have
       |a_(n−1)z^(n−1) + ... + a₀| ≤ (|a_(n−1)| + ... + |a₀|)R^(n−1) < Rⁿ = |zⁿ|,
    so pₜ(z) = zⁿ + t(a_(n−1)z^(n−1) + ... + a₀) never vanishes on |z| = R for
    t ∈ [0, 1]: this homotopes f_R to the loop of zⁿ, which has degree n ≠ 0.
    Contradiction. Common mistakes: in (b) drawing the ray from x through
    f(x) (then r(x) = x fails on the boundary); in (c) forgetting to
    normalise to a loop in S¹. Now you try: why does the Brouwer argument
    fail for the open disc, and is it true there? (No retraction lemma needs
    compactness of D²; the statement is false: x ↦ (x + a)/2 with |a| = 1
    maps the open disc into itself, and its only possible fixed point a is
    not in the open disc.)

D9. Prove that π₁(X × Y, (x₀, y₀)) ≅ π₁(X, x₀) × π₁(Y, y₀) and compute π₁ of
    the torus. Prove that Sⁿ is simply connected for n ≥ 2. Deduce that
    R² is not homeomorphic to Rⁿ for n ≥ 3, and that S² ≇ T².
    Answer: π₁(T²) ≅ Z × Z; proofs below.
    Teacher explains: A loop in X × Y is a pair of loops, f = (f₁, f₂)
    (universal property of the product topology), and a path homotopy is a
    pair of path homotopies. So
       [f] ↦ ([f₁], [f₂])
    is a well-defined bijection; it is a homomorphism because products are
    formed coordinatewise. TORUS: T² = S¹ × S¹, so π₁ ≅ Z × Z, generated by
    a = (loop around the first factor, constant) and b; ab = ba, since
    a·b and b·a are both path homotopic to the 'diagonal' loop
    (e^(2πis), e^(2πis)). Sⁿ, n ≥ 2: write Sⁿ = U ∪ V with U = Sⁿ − {N},
    V = Sⁿ − {S}, both ≅ Rⁿ (stereographic projection), so simply connected,
    and U ∩ V ≅ Rⁿ − {0} ≃ Sⁿ⁻¹, which is path-connected when n ≥ 2. By a
    Lebesgue-number argument any loop at a point of U ∩ V is a product of
    loops lying in U or in V (joined to the base point inside U ∩ V), each
    null-homotopic; so π₁(Sⁿ) = 1. (The tempting argument 'a loop misses a
    point' fails: there are space-filling loops!) R² vs Rⁿ: a homeomorphism
    would give R² − {0} ≅ Rⁿ − {p}, but π₁ = Z versus π₁(Sⁿ⁻¹) = 1 (n ≥ 3).
    S² vs T²: π₁ = 1 versus Z². Common mistakes: forgetting path-
    connectedness of U ∩ V (for n = 1 it fails: S¹ − {N, S} has two pieces,
    and S¹ is not simply connected). Now you try: π₁ of S¹ × S² and of the
    solid torus S¹ × D². (Z × 1 ≅ Z; Z × 1 ≅ Z)

D10. State the Seifert-van Kampen theorem. Use it to find π₁ of the figure
     eight, of R² minus two points, of the torus (from the square with word
     aba⁻¹b⁻¹), of RP² and of the Klein bottle, and of a graph.
     Answer: F₂ = ⟨a, b⟩; F₂; ⟨a, b | aba⁻¹b⁻¹⟩ ≅ Z²; ⟨a | a²⟩ ≅ Z/2;
     ⟨a, b | abab⁻¹⟩; a graph with V vertices, E edges (connected): F_(E−V+1).
     Teacher explains: VAN KAMPEN: if X = U ∪ V, U, V open, U, V and U ∩ V
     path-connected, x₀ ∈ U ∩ V, then π₁(X) is generated by the images of
     π₁(U) and π₁(V), with the relations i₁(c) = i₂(c) for c ∈ π₁(U ∩ V):
        π₁(X) ≅ π₁(U) *_(π₁(U ∩ V)) π₁(V)   (AMALGAMATED FREE PRODUCT).
     FIGURE EIGHT: U = one circle plus a small open arc of the other (≃ S¹),
     V likewise, U ∩ V = a small cross around the wedge point (contractible),
     so π₁ ≅ Z * Z = F₂, free on a, b; ab ≠ ba (the lifts to the universal
     cover end at different vertices of the tree). R² minus two points
     deformation retracts onto a figure eight: F₂. ATTACHING A 2-CELL: if
     X = A ∪_w D² (disc glued along a loop w in A), take U = X − {centre}
     (≃ A) and V = open disc; U ∩ V ≃ S¹ whose generator maps to w in A and
     to 1 in V. So π₁(X) = π₁(A)/⟨⟨w⟩⟩: add the relation w = 1. The square
     with all corners identified has a 1-skeleton = wedge of circles, one per
     edge letter:
        torus         a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹    ⟨a, b | aba⁻¹b⁻¹⟩ = Z²
        Klein bottle  a b a b⁻¹      ⟨a, b | abab⁻¹⟩, abelianised Z ⊕ Z/2
        RP² (disc with antipodal boundary)  a a   ⟨a | a²⟩ = Z/2
     GRAPH: contract a spanning tree (V − 1 edges) to a point: what remains
     is a wedge of E − (V − 1) circles. Common mistakes: applying van Kampen
     with a disconnected intersection; thinking π₁ of the figure eight is Z²
     (that would be the torus, which has the extra 2-cell). Now you try:
     π₁ of the theta graph (two vertices, three edges) and of the complete
     graph K₄. (F₂; F₃)

D11. Let p : (E, e₀) → (B, b₀) be a covering with E path-connected. Prove
     that p_* is injective and that the number of sheets equals the index
     [π₁(B, b₀) : p_*π₁(E, e₀)]. Use this to show π₁(RP²) ≅ Z/2 and to find the
     connected 2-sheeted covers of the figure eight.
     Answer: Proofs below; π₁(RP²) has order 2; there are 3 connected
     2-sheeted covers of S¹ ∨ S¹.
     Teacher explains: INJECTIVE: if p ∘ f̃ is null-homotopic in B, lift the
     null-homotopy (homotopy lifting) starting at e₀: it is a null-homotopy
     of f̃ in E. SHEETS: define Ψ : π₁(B, b₀) → p⁻¹(b₀) by Ψ[γ] = γ̃(1), the
     end of the lift of γ from e₀. Ψ is onto: E path-connected, so any
     e ∈ p⁻¹(b₀) is joined to e₀ by a path α̃, and γ = p ∘ α̃ is a loop with
     Ψ[γ] = e. With H = p_*π₁(E, e₀): Ψ[γ] = Ψ[δ] ⇔ γ̃·(δ̃)‾ is a loop in E ⇔
     [γ][δ]⁻¹ ∈ H ⇔ H[γ] = H[δ]. So Ψ induces a bijection from the right
     cosets of H onto the fibre: #sheets = [π₁(B) : H]. RP²: S² → RP² is a
     2-sheeted covering with S² simply connected, so H = 1 and
     |π₁(RP²)| = 2: π₁(RP²) ≅ Z/2. (The nontrivial loop lifts to a path
     from x to −x.) FIGURE EIGHT: connected 2-sheeted covers ↔ index-2
     subgroups of F₂ (all normal) ↔ surjections F₂ → Z/2, determined by
     where a, b go:
        (a, b) ↦ (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)      → 3 covers
     Each is a graph with 2 vertices and 4 edges; for (1, 1) both loops swap
     the two vertices (two vertices joined by four edges, two labelled a
     and two labelled b). Rank of the covering group: E − V + 1 = 3, matching
     the Schreier formula n(k − 1) + 1 = 2·1 + 1. Common mistakes: counting
     disconnected covers; thinking p_* is surjective (it is onto only for
     1-sheeted covers). Now you try: how many connected 3-sheeted covers has
     S¹, and what is H? (One, z ↦ z³, H = 3Z.)

D12. Define deck transformations, regular covers and the universal cover.
     State the Galois correspondence. Find Deck(E/B) for R → S¹, z ↦ zⁿ,
     R² → T², S² → RP², and explain why a non-regular 3-sheeted cover of the
     figure eight has trivial deck group. How many connected 3-sheeted covers
     does the figure eight have, and how many are regular?
     Answer: Z, Z/n, Z², Z/2; N(H) = H gives Deck = 1. There are 7 connected
     3-sheeted covers up to isomorphism (13 index-3 subgroups), 4 of them
     regular.
     Teacher explains: A DECK transformation is a homeomorphism φ : E → E
     with p ∘ φ = p; they form a group acting on each fibre, and a deck
     transformation is determined by the image of one point (uniqueness of
     lifts). With H = p_*π₁(E, e₀):
        Deck(E/B) ≅ N(H)/H,
     and the cover is REGULAR (deck group transitive on fibres) ⇔ H is
     NORMAL, then Deck ≅ π₁(B)/H. The UNIVERSAL cover is the simply connected
     one (H = 1), so Deck ≅ π₁(B) — another way to compute π₁. GALOIS
     CORRESPONDENCE (B connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply
     connected): connected covers ↔ conjugacy classes of subgroups; the
     covers with base points ↔ subgroups; bigger subgroups ↔ fewer sheets.
     Examples: R → S¹, deck = translations t ↦ t + n: Z. z ↦ zⁿ: rotations by
     n-th roots of unity: Z/n. R² → T²: translations by Z². S² → RP²:
     {id, antipodal}: Z/2. All four are regular (abelian π₁, or index 2).
     A non-normal H of index 3 in F₂: N(H) contains H, and [F₂ : N(H)]
     divides 3 and is not 1 (H is not normal), so N(H) = H and Deck = 1.
     COUNT: connected 3-sheeted covers ↔ transitive actions of F₂ = ⟨a, b⟩
     on {1, 2, 3} (a pair of permutations generating a transitive group), up
     to relabelling. There are 13 subgroups of index 3; they fall into 7
     conjugacy classes. The regular ones correspond to normal subgroups with
     quotient Z/3, i.e. surjections F₂ → Z/3 up to sign: (3² − 1)/2 = 4. So 4
     regular and 3 non-regular (quotient S₃ acting on 3 letters). Common
     mistakes: confusing the number of subgroups (base-pointed covers) with
     the number of covers up to isomorphism; thinking every cover is
     regular. Now you try: the universal cover of the Klein bottle and its
     deck group. (R², with the group ⟨a, b | abab⁻¹⟩ of glide reflections
     and translations acting on it.)

M12. True (T) or false (F)?
