TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw everything — homotopies as films, loops as strings on a
  surface, lifts as paths climbing the helix above the circle. Compute every
  degree by following the lift ('how many times does the string go
  around?'). Keep a table of π₁ for the standard spaces and use homotopy
  equivalences to reduce new spaces to it (deformation retract first, then
  products or van Kampen). For covers, always check 'evenly covered' with a
  picture of the sheets. Harder: prove that the universal cover of a graph
  is a tree and deduce the Nielsen-Schreier theorem with the rank formula
  n(k − 1) + 1; prove Borsuk-Ulam for S² (an odd map S¹ → S¹ has odd degree)
  and deduce the ham-sandwich theorem; classify all covers of T²
  (subgroups of Z²: σ(n) of index n); compute π₁ of the complement of the
  trefoil knot (⟨x, y | x² = y³⟩); and construct the universal cover of
  S¹ ∨ S¹ as the Cayley graph of F₂.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.29 — PROJECTIVE AND NON-EUCLIDEAN GEOMETRY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The REAL PROJECTIVE PLANE RP² is the set of lines through 0 in R³. A point
    is written in HOMOGENEOUS COORDINATES [x : y : z], (x, y, z) ≠ (0, 0, 0),
    with [x : y : z] = [λx : λy : λz] for every λ ≠ 0. The affine point (x, y)
    is [x : y : 1]; the points [x : y : 0] are POINTS AT INFINITY (one for each
    direction) and together form the LINE AT INFINITY z = 0. RPⁿ is defined in
    the same way; over a finite field Fq, PG(n, q) has (qⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(q − 1) points.
  - A LINE is ax + by + cz = 0, written [a : b : c]. Point p lies on line ℓ
    ⇔ ℓ·p = 0. The line through points p, q is p × q; the meeting point of
    lines ℓ, m is ℓ × m. Any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point
    (parallel lines meet at infinity). Three points are COLLINEAR (three lines
    CONCURRENT) ⇔ the 3 × 3 determinant of their coordinates is 0.
  - PRINCIPLE OF DUALITY: interchanging 'point' and 'line', 'lies on' and
    'passes through', 'collinear' and 'concurrent' turns every theorem of
    projective plane geometry into another theorem (Pascal ↔ Brianchon).
  - A PROJECTIVE TRANSFORMATION (collineation, homography) of RPⁿ is
    [v] ↦ [Av] with A invertible (n + 1) × (n + 1); A and λA give the same map,
    so the group is PGL(n + 1, R) of dimension n² + 2n. FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM:
    any n + 2 points in GENERAL POSITION (no n + 1 in a hyperplane) can be sent
    to any other such n + 2 points by exactly one projective transformation.
    On the line RP¹ these are the Möbius maps x ↦ (ax + b)/(cx + d), ad ≠ bc.
  - CROSS-RATIO of four points on a line: (a, b; c, d) =
    (c − a)(d − b)/((c − b)(d − a)); ∞ is handled by cancelling it. It is
    PROJECTIVELY INVARIANT; distances, ratios and midpoints are not. Under the
    24 permutations it takes the six values λ, 1/λ, 1 − λ, 1/(1 − λ),
    (λ − 1)/λ, λ/(λ − 1). (a, b; c, d) = −1 means c, d are HARMONIC CONJUGATES
    with respect to a, b; the midpoint of ab and the point at infinity are
    harmonic.
  - DESARGUES: two triangles in PERSPECTIVE from a point are in perspective
    from a line (and conversely). PAPPUS: if A, B, C lie on one line and
    A′, B′, C′ on another, the points AB′ ∩ A′B, AC′ ∩ A′C, BC′ ∩ B′C are
    collinear. PASCAL: the three meeting points of opposite sides of a hexagon
    inscribed in a conic are collinear.
  - A CONIC is xᵀCx = 0 with C a symmetric 3 × 3 matrix; NON-DEGENERATE ⇔
    det C ≠ 0. The TANGENT at a point p of the conic is the line Cp; for any p
    the line Cp is the POLAR of p (p is its POLE). All non-degenerate real
    conics with real points are projectively equivalent to x² + y² = z². The
    affine type is decided by the line at infinity: ELLIPSE (0 real points at
    infinity, B² − 4AC < 0), PARABOLA (1, tangent to it, B² − 4AC = 0),
    HYPERBOLA (2, B² − 4AC > 0).
  - EUCLID'S FIFTH (PARALLEL) POSTULATE ⇔ PLAYFAIR: through a point not on a
    line there is exactly one parallel. It is independent of the other axioms.
    NEUTRAL geometry (no parallel axiom) gives angle sum ≤ π
    (Saccheri–Legendre). Three constant-curvature geometries: EUCLIDEAN (K = 0,
    one parallel, angle sum π), HYPERBOLIC (K = −1, infinitely many parallels,
    angle sum < π), ELLIPTIC/SPHERICAL (K = +1, no parallels, angle sum > π).
  - UPPER HALF-PLANE H = {z : Im z > 0}, ds = |dz|/y. GEODESICS: vertical
    half-lines and semicircles centred on the real axis. DISTANCE:
    cosh d(z, w) = 1 + |z − w|²/(2 Im z Im w); d(ai, bi) = |ln(b/a)|.
    ISOMETRIES: z ↦ (az + b)/(cz + d) with a, b, c, d real, ad − bc = 1
    (the group PSL(2, R)), plus reflections such as z ↦ −z̄.
  - POINCARÉ DISC D = {|z| < 1}, ds = 2|dz|/(1 − |z|²): geodesics are diameters
    and circular arcs meeting the unit circle at right angles;
    d(0, r) = ln((1 + r)/(1 − r)) = 2 artanh r; cosh d(z, w) =
    1 + 2|z − w|²/((1 − |z|²)(1 − |w|²)). The CAYLEY map z ↦ (z − i)/(z + i)
    is an isometry H → D. Both models are CONFORMAL (true angles). The KLEIN
    model (geodesics = straight chords) is not conformal; the HYPERBOLOID model
    x² + y² − t² = −1 has cosh d = t₁t₂ − x₁x₂ − y₁y₂.
  - HYPERBOLIC TRIGONOMETRY (K = −1): area of a triangle = π − (α + β + γ)
    (GAUSS–BONNET), so every triangle has area < π and an IDEAL triangle
    (all vertices at infinity) has area π. Law of cosines
    cosh c = cosh a cosh b − sinh a sinh b cos γ; right angle at C:
    cosh c = cosh a cosh b, sin A = sinh a/sinh c, cos A = tanh b/tanh c.
    Circle of radius R: circumference 2π sinh R, area 2π(cosh R − 1). AAA
    determines a triangle up to congruence (no similar non-congruent
    triangles). ANGLE OF PARALLELISM: tan(Π(d)/2) = e^(−d).
  - SPHERICAL geometry on the unit sphere: lines are GREAT CIRCLES, distance is
    the central angle. GIRARD: area = α + β + γ − π (× R² on radius R), a LUNE
    of angle θ has area 2θ. Law of cosines cos c = cos a cos b +
    sin a sin b cos γ; right angle: cos c = cos a cos b. Circle of radius r:
    circumference 2π sin r, area 2π(1 − cos r). ELLIPTIC geometry = sphere with
    antipodal points identified = RP² (area 2π, any two lines meet once).
  - ISOMETRIES of H (≠ id) are classified by |trace| of the normalised matrix
    (ad − bc = 1): ELLIPTIC |tr| < 2 (one fixed point inside, a rotation by θ
    with |tr| = 2cos(θ/2)); PARABOLIC |tr| = 2 (one fixed point on the
    boundary); HYPERBOLIC |tr| > 2 (two fixed boundary points, translation
    along the axis joining them by ℓ with |tr| = 2cosh(ℓ/2)).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Using homogeneous coordinates find (a) the line through the points (1, 2)
    and (3, 1); (b) the common point of the parallel lines x + 2y = 3 and
    x + 2y = 5; (c) the common point of x + 2y = 5 and x − y = −1. Explain
    what a point at infinity is.
    Answer: (a) [1 : 2 : −5], i.e. x + 2y = 5. (b) [2 : −1 : 0], the point at
    infinity in the direction (2, −1). (c) [1 : 2 : 1], i.e. (1, 2).
    Teacher explains: Put z = 1 to lift an affine point: (1, 2) ↦ (1, 2, 1),
    (3, 1) ↦ (3, 1, 1). A line [a : b : c] means ax + by + cz = 0, and p lies on
    it when the dot product is 0. The line through p and q must be orthogonal
    (in R³) to both, so it is the CROSS PRODUCT:
       (1, 2, 1) × (3, 1, 1) = (2·1 − 1·1, 1·3 − 1·1, 1·1 − 2·3) = (1, 2, −5)
    giving x + 2y − 5z = 0; with z = 1, x + 2y = 5. Check: 1 + 4 = 5 ✓,
    3 + 2 = 5 ✓. (b) By duality the meeting point of two lines is the cross
    product of the lines:
       (1, 2, −3) × (1, 2, −5) = (2·(−5) − (−3)·2, (−3)·1 − 1·(−5), 1·2 − 2·1)
                               = (−4, 2, 0) ~ [2 : −1 : 0]
    The third coordinate is 0: there is no affine point, but a point at
    infinity. [2 : −1 : 0] is the limit of [2t : −t : 1] as t → ∞, i.e. of
    points running off along the common DIRECTION (2, −1) of both lines. All
    lines with that direction pass through it, so 'parallel' in the affine
    plane becomes 'meeting at infinity' in RP². (c) (1, 2, −5) × (1, −1, 1) =
    (2 − 5, −5 − 1, −1 − 2) = (−3, −6, −3) ~ [1 : 2 : 1], the point (1, 2);
    check 1 − 2 = −1 ✓. So in RP² every two distinct lines meet in exactly
    one point, with no exceptions — the first gain of the projective plane.
    The points at infinity fill the line z = 0, the LINE AT INFINITY
    [0 : 0 : 1]. Common mistakes: dividing by z when z = 0; treating
    [2 : −1 : 0] and [−2 : 1 : 0] as different points (they are equal:
    λ = −1). Now you try: where do y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x − 4 meet? ([1 : 3 : 0])

D2. State the principle of duality and dualise 'two distinct points lie on
    exactly one line'. Decide whether the points (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 5) are
    collinear and whether the lines x + y = 1, 2x − y = 2, x − 2y = 1 are
    concurrent. Describe the Fano plane.
    Answer: Dual: 'two distinct lines pass through exactly one point'. The
    points are collinear (det = 0, line y = 2x − 1); the lines are concurrent
    (det = 0, at (1, 0)). The Fano plane PG(2, 2) has 7 points, 7 lines, 3
    points on each line and 3 lines through each point.
    Teacher explains: In RP² points and lines are both 'non-zero vectors of
    R³ up to scale', and incidence ℓ·p = 0 is symmetric in ℓ and p. So any
    statement about incidence stays true when we swap the words:
       point ↔ line,  lies on ↔ passes through,
       collinear ↔ concurrent,  join of two points ↔ meet of two lines.
    Three vectors are linearly dependent ⇔ determinant 0; for points this says
    they lie on one line, for lines that they pass through one point:
       | 1 1 1 |                       | 1  1 −1 |
       | 2 3 1 | = 0 (collinear)        | 2 −1 −2 | = 0 (concurrent)
       | 3 5 1 |                       | 1 −2 −1 |
    (expand: 1(3 − 5) − 1(2 − 3) + 1(10 − 9) = −2 + 1 + 1 = 0 and
    1(1 − 4) − 1(−2 + 2) − 1(−4 + 1) = −3 − 0 + 3 = 0.) The line through the
    points is y = 2x − 1; the lines meet at (1, 0) (1 + 0 = 1, 2 − 0 = 2,
    1 − 0 = 1 ✓). The FANO PLANE is RP² over F₂ = {0, 1}: the non-zero vectors
    of F₂³ number 2³ − 1 = 7, and λ can only be 1, so there are 7 points; by
    duality 7 lines. Each line x + y = 0 etc. has 2² − 1 = 3 non-zero
    solutions, so 3 points per line. Example: [1:1:0], [0:1:1], [1:0:1] are
    collinear over F₂ (det = 2 ≡ 0) but not over R (det = 2 ≠ 0). In general
    PG(2, q) has q² + q + 1 points and lines, q + 1 on each. Common mistakes:
    thinking 'collinear' needs slopes (vertical lines and points at infinity
    are handled by the determinant); forgetting to dualise every word. Now you
    try: are the lines x = 0, x = 1 and z = 0 concurrent? (Yes, at [0 : 1 : 0])

D3. Find the projective transformation of the plane that fixes (0, 0), (1, 0),
    (0, 1) and sends (1, 1) to (2, 2). Where do (1/2, 0) and (2, 0) go? Which
    line goes to infinity? Show the cross-ratio of 0, 1/2, 1, 2 on the x-axis
    is preserved although distances are not.
    Answer: A = [[2, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [−1, −1, 3]], i.e.
    (x, y) ↦ (2x, 2y)/(3 − x − y). (1/2, 0) ↦ (2/5, 0), (2, 0) ↦ (4, 0). The
    line x + y = 3 goes to the line at infinity. Cross-ratio −1/2 before and
    after.
    Teacher explains: FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM: four points of RP², no three
    collinear, can be sent to any four such points by exactly one projective
    map. Method: find the map from the STANDARD FRAME e₁, e₂, e₃, (1, 1, 1) to
    each quadrilateral and compose. For the target [0:0:1], [1:0:1], [0:1:1],
    [2:2:1] solve λ₁(0, 0, 1) + λ₂(1, 0, 1) + λ₃(0, 1, 1) = (2, 2, 1):
    λ₂ = 2, λ₃ = 2, λ₁ = 1 − 4 = −3, so B has columns −3(0,0,1), 2(1,0,1),
    2(0,1,1). For the source (target (1,1,1)) λ = (−1, 1, 1) and A₀ has
    columns −(0,0,1), (1,0,1), (0,1,1). Then the map is B A₀⁻¹. A quicker
    route here: fixing (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1) forces the form
       (x, y) ↦ (ax, ay)/(px + qy + r)
    (1, 0) fixed: a = p + r; (0, 1) fixed: a = q + r; (1, 1) ↦ (2, 2):
    a = 2(p + q + r). With a = 2: p = q = 2 − r and 2 = 2(4 − r) ⇒ r = 3,
    p = q = −1. So
       A = [[2, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [−1, −1, 3]],  (x, y) ↦ (2x, 2y)/(3 − x − y).
    Check (1, 1): (2, 2)/1 ✓. The denominator vanishes on x + y = 3: that line
    goes to infinity (the image of the line at infinity is x + y = −2). On the
    x-axis: 0 ↦ 0, 1/2 ↦ 1/(5/2) = 2/5, 1 ↦ 1, 2 ↦ 4/1 = 4. The midpoint 1/2 of
    [0, 1] went to 2/5: midpoints are not projective. But
       (0, 1; 1/2, 2) = (1/2)(1)/((−1/2)(2)) = −1/2
       (0, 1; 2/5, 4) = (2/5)(3)/((−3/5)(4)) = −1/2   ✓
    Why n + 2 points: A has 9 entries up to scale = 8 unknowns; each point
    gives 2 equations; 4 points give 8. Common mistakes: using three points
    only (then a one-parameter family remains); forgetting that A is only
    defined up to scale. Now you try: where does (1, 2) go? (Denominator 0:
    to the point at infinity [2 : 4 : 0] = [1 : 2 : 0].)

D4. Define the cross-ratio, prove it is invariant under x ↦ (ax + b)/(cx + d),
    compute (1, 2; 3, 4) and its six values under permutation, and find the
    harmonic conjugate of 0 with respect to 1 and 3.
    Answer: (1, 2; 3, 4) = 4/3; six values 4/3, 3/4, −1/3, −3, 1/4, 4. The
    harmonic conjugate is 3/2.
    Teacher explains: (a, b; c, d) = (c − a)(d − b)/((c − b)(d − a)). Write
    the map as f(x) = (αx + β)/(γx + δ) with Δ = αδ − βγ ≠ 0. Then
       f(x) − f(y) = [(αx + β)(γy + δ) − (αy + β)(γx + δ)]/((γx + δ)(γy + δ))
                   = Δ(x − y)/((γx + δ)(γy + δ)).
    In the cross-ratio every point occurs once in the numerator and once in
    the denominator, so each factor (γx + δ) and each Δ cancels:
    (f(a), f(b); f(c), f(d)) = (a, b; c, d) ∎. (Points at ∞ follow by
    continuity.) Every projective map of a line is of this form, and central
    projection from one line to another is projective, so four concurrent
    lines cut every transversal in the same cross-ratio. Now
       (1, 2; 3, 4) = (3 − 1)(4 − 2)/((3 − 2)(4 − 1)) = 4/3.
    Swapping a ↔ b or c ↔ d gives 1/λ; swapping b ↔ c gives 1 − λ; hence six
    values
       λ = 4/3, 1/λ = 3/4, 1 − λ = −1/3, 1/(1 − λ) = −3,
       (λ − 1)/λ = 1/4, λ/(λ − 1) = 4.
    Harmonic conjugate: solve (1, 3; 0, d) = −1:
       (0 − 1)(d − 3)/((0 − 3)(d − 1)) = −1 ⇒ (d − 3) = −3(d − 1) ⇒ d = 3/2.
    Check with the rule 'midpoint ↔ ∞': (−1, 1; 0, ∞) = (1)(1)/((−1)(1)) = −1
    (cancel ∞/∞). Geometric construction (no measuring!): the complete
    quadrilateral — harmonic conjugates are built with a ruler alone.
    Common mistakes: mixing conventions (some books define (a, b; c, d) with
    another order — the six values are the same set); forgetting that
    λ = 0, 1, ∞ only occur when two points coincide. Now you try: (0, 2; 1, 4).
    (−1/2)

D5. State and prove Desargues' theorem in RP². State Pappus' theorem and
    explain its relation to Pascal's theorem.
    Answer: Proof below by vectors.
    Teacher explains: DESARGUES: let ABC and A′B′C′ be triangles such that
    the lines AA′, BB′, CC′ meet at a point O (perspective from a POINT). Then
    P = AB ∩ A′B′, Q = BC ∩ B′C′, R = CA ∩ C′A′ are collinear (perspective from
    a LINE). Proof: write a, a′, ... for representing vectors in R³. O lies on
    line AA′, so o = αa + α′a′; rescale the representatives (allowed!) so that
       o = a + a′ = b + b′ = c + c′.
    Then a − b = b′ − a′. The left side is a combination of a and b, so it is
    on line AB; the right side is on A′B′; hence
       p = a − b,   q = b − c,   r = c − a
    represent P, Q, R (they are non-zero because the triangles are genuine).
    And p + q + r = 0: three linearly dependent vectors, so P, Q, R lie on one
    line ∎. The converse is the dual statement, so it needs no new proof.
    Desargues holds in every projective plane coming from a field (even a
    skew field) but FAILS in some abstract projective planes (Moulton plane):
    it is a real axiom about coordinates. PAPPUS: A, B, C on a line ℓ and
    A′, B′, C′ on a line m; then X = AB′ ∩ A′B, Y = AC′ ∩ A′C, Z = BC′ ∩ B′C
    are collinear. It holds exactly when the coordinates commute (a field), and
    Pappus ⇒ Desargues (Hessenberg). PASCAL: for six points on a
    non-degenerate conic the opposite sides of the hexagon meet in three
    collinear points; Pappus is Pascal for the DEGENERATE conic ℓ ∪ m. The dual
    of Pascal is BRIANCHON: the diagonals of a hexagon circumscribed about a
    conic are concurrent. Common mistakes: forgetting to rescale (then a − b
    is not on A′B′); drawing a figure where two sides are parallel and
    concluding the theorem fails (the point is at infinity). Now you try:
    dualise Desargues. (If two triangles are perspective from a line they are
    perspective from a point — the converse.)

D6. For the conic x² + 4xy + y² = 1 find its matrix, check it is
    non-degenerate, decide its affine type, find its points at infinity and
    the tangent at (1, 0). Also find the polar of (2, 0) with respect to
    x² + y² = 1 and interpret it.
    Answer: C = [[1, 2, 0], [2, 1, 0], [0, 0, −1]], det C = 3 ≠ 0; a
    hyperbola with points at infinity [−2 ± √3 : 1 : 0]; tangent x + 2y = 1.
    Polar of (2, 0): x = 1/2, the chord of contact of the two tangents from
    (2, 0).
    Teacher explains: Homogenise with z: x² + 4xy + y² − z² = 0, i.e. xᵀCx = 0
    where the cross term 4xy is split as 2 + 2 off the diagonal:
       C = [[1, 2, 0], [2, 1, 0], [0, 0, −1]],  det C = −(1 − 4) = 3 ≠ 0.
    Points at infinity: put z = 0: x² + 4xy + y² = 0 ⇒ x/y = −2 ± √3, two real
    points ⇒ HYPERBOLA (equivalently B² − 4AC = 16 − 4 = 12 > 0). These two
    points are the directions of the asymptotes. Tangent at p = (1, 0, 1):
       Cp = (1, 2, −1) ⇒ x + 2y − 1 = 0.
    Check by substitution x = 1 − 2y: (1 − 2y)² + 4(1 − 2y)y + y² = 1 − 3y² = 1
    gives y² = 0, a DOUBLE root — the line touches. Why Cp works: if pᵀCp = 0
    and pᵀCx = 0 then (p + tx)ᵀC(p + tx) = t²xᵀCx, a double root at t = 0, so
    the line meets the conic only at p. For x² + y² − z² the matrix is
    diag(1, 1, −1), so the polar of (2, 0, 1) is (2, 0, −1): 2x − 1 = 0,
    x = 1/2. It meets the circle at (1/2, ±√3/2), and the tangent there,
    x/2 ± (√3/2)y = 1, passes through (2, 0) ✓ — the polar of an outside point
    is its chord of contact. CLASSIFICATION: over R every non-degenerate conic
    with a real point can be brought to x² + y² = z²; ellipse, parabola and
    hyperbola differ only in how the line at infinity meets it (0, 1 tangent,
    2 points): projectively they are the same curve. Common mistakes: putting
    4 instead of 2 off the diagonal; calling x² + y² + 1 = 0 an ellipse (no
    real points). Now you try: tangent to xy = 1 at (2, 1/2). (x + 4y = 4)

D7. Explain Euclid's parallel postulate, Playfair's axiom and some statements
    equivalent to it, the Saccheri–Legendre theorem, and how models show the
    postulate is independent. Compare the three classical geometries.
    Answer: See the table and explanation below.
    Teacher explains: Euclid's fifth postulate: if a line crossing two lines
    makes interior angles on one side summing to less than two right angles,
    the two lines meet on that side. With the other axioms (incidence,
    betweenness, congruence, continuity = NEUTRAL geometry) it is equivalent
    to each of:
       Playfair: through P ∉ ℓ there is EXACTLY ONE line parallel to ℓ;
       the angle sum of every (or of one) triangle is π;
       a rectangle exists; similar non-congruent triangles exist;
       Pythagoras' theorem; parallel lines are equidistant.
    SACCHERI–LEGENDRE: in neutral geometry every triangle has angle sum ≤ π.
    (Idea: repeatedly replace the triangle by one with the same angle sum and
    one angle at most half as large; if the sum were π + ε, eventually an
    angle < ε remains while the other two exceed π, contradicting the
    exterior angle theorem.) For 2000 years people tried to prove the fifth
    postulate from the others. Gauss, Bolyai and Lobachevsky found a
    consistent geometry in which it fails; Beltrami, Klein and Poincaré built
    MODELS of it inside Euclidean geometry. A model makes all the neutral
    axioms true and the parallel postulate false, so if Euclidean geometry is
    consistent, so is hyperbolic geometry, and the postulate cannot be a
    theorem.
                      Euclidean     hyperbolic         elliptic
       curvature K    0             −1                 +1
       parallels      exactly 1     infinitely many    none
       angle sum      = π           < π                > π
       triangle area  any           π − Σ < π          Σ − π (Σ = angle sum)
       circumference  2πr           2π sinh r          2π sin r
       AAA ⇒ ≅        no            yes                yes
    (Elliptic geometry also drops the axiom that lines are infinite, since
    great circles are closed.) Common mistakes: saying 'hyperbolic geometry
    has no parallels' (it has too many); thinking the sphere satisfies all
    neutral axioms (two points need not determine a unique great circle unless
    antipodes are identified). Now you try: in hyperbolic geometry, can the
    angle sum of a quadrilateral be 2π? (No: cut it into two triangles, each
    < π, so the sum < 2π — no rectangles.)

D8. In the upper half-plane H with ds = |dz|/y: derive d(ai, bi) = ln(b/a);
    find the geodesic through i and 2 + i and the distance between them, and
    compare with the length of the horizontal segment.
    Answer: d(ai, bi) = ln(b/a) for b > a; geodesic (x − 1)² + y² = 2;
    d(i, 2 + i) = arccosh 3 = ln(3 + 2√2) ≈ 1.7627; the horizontal segment has
    length 2.
    Teacher explains: LENGTH of a path γ(t) = x(t) + iy(t) is
    ∫ √(x′² + y′²)/y dt. For a path from ai to bi, √(x′² + y′²) ≥ |y′|, so
       L ≥ ∫ |y′|/y dt ≥ ∫ₐᵇ dy/y = ln(b/a),
    with equality exactly for the vertical segment: it is the GEODESIC.
    Isometries: z ↦ z + t, z ↦ kz (k > 0) and z ↦ −1/z preserve ds (for the
    last, Im(−1/z) = y/|z|² and |d(−1/z)| = |dz|/|z|²). They map vertical lines
    to vertical lines or semicircles orthogonal to R, so ALL geodesics are
    vertical half-lines and semicircles centred on the real axis. Using the
    isometries one proves
       cosh d(z, w) = 1 + |z − w|²/(2 Im z · Im w).
    (Check on ai, bi: 1 + (b − a)²/(2ab) = (a² + b²)/(2ab) = cosh ln(b/a) ✓.)
    Geodesic through i and 2 + i: centre c on R with |i − c| = |2 + i − c|,
    i.e. c² + 1 = (2 − c)² + 1, c = 1, radius √2: (x − 1)² + y² = 2, with
    endpoints 1 ± √2 on the boundary. Distance:
       cosh d = 1 + 4/(2·1·1) = 3,  d = arccosh 3 = ln(3 + √8) = ln(3 + 2√2)
                                    ≈ 1.7627.
    The horizontal segment from i to 2 + i has length ∫₀² dx/1 = 2 > 1.7627:
    the geodesic bulges UPWARDS where the metric is cheaper (large y). Points
    near the boundary are very far apart: d(0.01i, 1 + 0.01i) ≈ 9.2. Common
    mistakes: using Euclidean straight segments; forgetting the 2 in
    2 Im z Im w. Now you try: d(i, 1 + i). (arccosh(3/2) = ln((3 + √5)/2)
    ≈ 0.9624)

D9. In the Poincaré disc with ds = 2|dz|/(1 − |z|²): show d(0, r) =
    ln((1 + r)/(1 − r)); compute d(0, 1/2), d(1/2, −1/2) and d(1/2, i/2); show
    that the hyperbolic circle of radius R about 0 has circumference 2π sinh R;
    and relate the disc to H.
    Answer: d(0, 1/2) = ln 3 ≈ 1.0986, d(1/2, −1/2) = ln 9 ≈ 2.1972,
    d(1/2, i/2) = arccosh(25/9) = ln((25 + 4√34)/9) ≈ 1.6807.
    Teacher explains: Rotations z ↦ e^(iθ)z preserve the metric, and the
    diameter is the shortest path from 0 to r (the same argument as in D8):
       d(0, r) = ∫₀ʳ 2 dt/(1 − t²) = ∫₀ʳ (1/(1 − t) + 1/(1 + t)) dt
               = ln((1 + r)/(1 − r)) = 2 artanh r.
    So d(0, 1/2) = ln((3/2)/(1/2)) = ln 3; as r → 1 the distance → ∞: the
    boundary circle is infinitely far away. Along a diameter distances add:
    d(1/2, −1/2) = ln 3 + ln 3 = ln 9. General formula:
       cosh d(z, w) = 1 + 2|z − w|²/((1 − |z|²)(1 − |w|²)).
    Check: z = 1/2, w = −1/2: 1 + 2·1/((3/4)(3/4)) = 1 + 32/9 = 41/9, and
    cosh(ln 9) = (9 + 1/9)/2 = 41/9 ✓. For z = 1/2, w = i/2: |z − w|² = 1/2, so
    cosh d = 1 + 1/(9/16) = 25/9, d = ln(25/9 + √(625/81 − 1)) =
    ln((25 + √544)/9) = ln((25 + 4√34)/9) ≈ 1.6807. Circle: the hyperbolic
    circle of radius R about 0 is the Euclidean circle of radius
    ρ = tanh(R/2); its hyperbolic length is 2πρ·2/(1 − ρ²) = 2π sinh R (since
    2 tanh u/(1 − tanh² u) = sinh 2u). This grows like πe^R — exponentially,
    compared with 2πR. The CAYLEY map φ(z) = (z − i)/(z + i) sends H onto D,
    i ↦ 0, 2i ↦ i/(3i) = 1/3, and is an isometry: d(i, 2i) = ln 2 =
    ln((4/3)/(2/3)) = d(0, 1/3) ✓. Geodesics of D are the images of those of
    H: diameters and arcs of circles ORTHOGONAL to the unit circle. Common
    mistakes: forgetting the factor 2 in ds (then all distances halve);
    adding distances along a non-geodesic path. Now you try: d(0, 3/5).
    (ln 4)

D10. Prove that an ideal triangle has area π and state the Gauss–Bonnet
     formula for a hyperbolic triangle. For the right-angled triangle with legs
     a = b = arccosh 2 find the hypotenuse, the other two angles and the area.
     Answer: Area = π − (α + β + γ). Hypotenuse c = arccosh 4 ≈ 2.0634;
     A = B = arctan(1/2) ≈ 26.57°; area = π/2 − 2 arctan(1/2) = arctan(3/4)
     ≈ 0.6435.
     Teacher explains: In H the area element is dA = dx dy/y². Take the ideal
     triangle with vertices −1, 1, ∞: it lies above the semicircle
     x² + y² = 1 between x = −1 and x = 1:
        Area = ∫₋₁¹ ∫_(√(1 − x²))^∞ dy/y² dx = ∫₋₁¹ dx/√(1 − x²) = π.
     All ideal triangles are congruent (PSL(2, R) moves any three boundary
     points to any three), so every ideal triangle has area π. A triangle with
     vertices ∞, −1 and e^(iα) has angle α at e^(iα), and the same integral
     from −1 to cos α gives π − α; a general triangle with angles α, β, γ is an
     ideal triangle minus three such pieces, giving
        Area = π − (α + β + γ)          (Gauss–Bonnet with K = −1).
     So angle sums are < π, the 'defect' is the area, and no triangle has
     area ≥ π. Now the example: right angle at C, a = b = arccosh 2, so
     cosh a = cosh b = 2, sinh a = sinh b = √3.
        cosh c = cosh a cosh b = 4,  c = arccosh 4 ≈ 2.0634
     (Euclidean with legs 1.3170 would give 1.8625: hyperbolic triangles are
     'thin'.) sinh c = √15, tanh b = √3/2, tanh c = √15/4:
        sin A = sinh a/sinh c = √3/√15 = 1/√5,
        cos A = tanh b/tanh c = (√3/2)(4/√15) = 2/√5 ⇒ tan A = 1/2,
     A = B = arctan(1/2) ≈ 26.57°. Angle sum ≈ 143.13° < 180°, and
        Area = π − π/2 − 2 arctan(1/2) = arctan(3/4) ≈ 0.6435
     (since 2 arctan(1/2) = arctan(4/3)). Common mistakes: using cos c =
     cos a cos b (the spherical rule); computing area with Heron's formula.
     Now you try: area of a triangle with angles π/2, π/3, π/7. (π/42)

D11. On the unit sphere prove Girard's theorem Area = α + β + γ − π. Two
     points A, B lie at latitude 45° N with longitudes 0° and 90° E; find
     their great-circle distance on the Earth (R = 6371 km), compare it with
     the path along the parallel, and find the angles and area of triangle NAB
     (N = north pole). What is the elliptic plane?
     Answer: AB = π/3 → ≈ 6672 km (along the parallel ≈ 7076 km). Angles:
     N = 90°, A = B = arccos(1/√3) ≈ 54.74°; excess ≈ 19.47° = 0.3398 rad;
     area ≈ 1.379 × 10⁷ km².
     Teacher explains: GIRARD. A LUNE of angle θ (region between two half
     great circles) has area (θ/2π)·4π = 2θ. The three great circles through
     the sides of the triangle make, at each vertex, a pair of antipodal lunes
     containing the triangle Δ or its antipode Δ′. The six lunes cover the
     sphere, covering Δ and Δ′ three times each and every other point once:
        2(2α + 2β + 2γ) = 4π + 4·Area  ⇒  Area = α + β + γ − π.
     On radius R multiply by R². Spherical law of cosines (from dot products of
     position vectors): cos c = cos a cos b + sin a sin b cos γ. For A, B use
     the pole N: NA = NB = 45° = π/4, angle at N = 90°:
        cos AB = cos²(π/4) + sin²(π/4)·0 = 1/2 ⇒ AB = π/3,
        distance = 6371·π/3 ≈ 6671.7 km.
     Along the parallel (a small circle of radius R cos 45°): (π/2)·R/√2
     ≈ 7076.4 km — longer, since only great circles are geodesics. Angle at A
     (opposite side NB = π/4, adjacent sides π/4 and π/3):
        cos(π/4) = cos(π/4)cos(π/3) + sin(π/4)sin(π/3) cos A
        ⇒ (√2/2)(1/2) = (√2/2)(√3/2) cos A ⇒ cos A = 1/√3, A ≈ 54.7356°.
     Excess = 90° + 2(54.7356°) − 180° ≈ 19.4712° ≈ 0.339837 rad; area
     ≈ 0.339837 × 6371² ≈ 1.3794 × 10⁷ km². For small triangles the excess is
     tiny and the geometry looks Euclidean. ELLIPTIC PLANE: identify each
     point with its antipode; the result is RP² with the round metric; two
     lines (great circles) now meet in exactly ONE point, there are no
     parallels, total area 2π, largest distance π/2, and it is
     non-orientable. Common mistakes: measuring the angle in degrees inside
     Girard's formula; taking the parallel of latitude as the shortest route.
     Now you try: a triangle with three right angles on the unit sphere — area?
     (π/2, one eighth of 4π)

D12. Classify the orientation-preserving isometries of H. Classify
     f(z) = (2z + 1)/(z + 1), g(z) = −1/(z + 1) and h(z) = z + 1, with fixed
     points, translation length or rotation angle. Describe the Klein and
     hyperboloid models.
     Answer: f hyperbolic, fixed (1 ± √5)/2, translation length
     2 ln((3 + √5)/2) ≈ 1.9248; g elliptic of order 3, fixed (−1 + i√3)/2,
     rotation 2π/3; h parabolic, fixed ∞.
     Teacher explains: Isom⁺(H) = PSL(2, R) = SL(2, R)/{±I}: normalise the
     matrix to determinant 1, then t = |a + d| decides the type. Fixed points
     solve cz² + (d − a)z − b = 0, discriminant (a + d)² − 4:
        t < 2   two complex conjugate roots: one fixed point in H, ELLIPTIC
                (a rotation about it by θ with t = 2cos(θ/2));
        t = 2   a double real root: PARABOLIC (like z ↦ z + 1);
        t > 2   two real roots: HYPERBOLIC, translation by ℓ along the
                geodesic joining them, t = 2cosh(ℓ/2).
     f: [[2, 1], [1, 1]], det 1, t = 3 > 2. Fixed: z(z + 1) = 2z + 1 ⇒
     z² − z − 1 = 0 ⇒ z = (1 ± √5)/2; axis the semicircle centre 1/2, radius
     √5/2. cosh(ℓ/2) = 3/2 ⇒ ℓ = 2 arccosh(3/2) = 2 ln((3 + √5)/2) ≈ 1.9248.
     (Conjugated to z ↦ kz, k = ((3 + √5)/2)², and d(i, ki) = ln k.)
     g: [[0, −1], [1, 1]], det 1, t = 1 < 2: elliptic, 1 = 2cos(θ/2) ⇒
     θ = 2π/3. Fixed: z² + z + 1 = 0 ⇒ z = (−1 + i√3)/2 (the root in H).
     g³ = id: g²(z) = −(z + 1)/z, g³(z) = z. h: t = 2, parabolic, fixed only ∞.
     Orientation-REVERSING isometries are z ↦ (az̄ + b)/(cz̄ + d) with
     ad − bc = −1, e.g. the reflection z ↦ −z̄ in the imaginary axis. KLEIN
     MODEL: the unit disc with geodesics the straight CHORDS; the point r of
     the Poincaré disc corresponds to 2r/(1 + r²); distance
     d = ½ ln((AQ·BP)/(AP·BQ)) with A, P, Q, B in order on the chord (a
     cross-ratio!), so it is projective geometry of a conic — but angles are
     distorted. HYPERBOLOID MODEL: the sheet x² + y² − t² = −1, t > 0, with
     the Minkowski form; cosh d = t₁t₂ − x₁x₂ − y₁y₂; isometries are the
     Lorentz group SO⁺(2, 1). Common mistakes: using the trace before
     normalising det = 1 (for 9z + 2 the matrix [[9, 2], [0, 1]] has det 9, so
     t = 10/3, not 10); forgetting that the elliptic fixed point must be the
     root in the upper half-plane. Now you try: classify z ↦ (5z − 3)/(2z − 1).
     (t = 4: hyperbolic, fixed (3 ± √3)/2, ℓ = 2 ln(2 + √3) ≈ 2.6339)

M8. Poincaré disc D and the Cayley map φ(z) = (z − i)/(z + i).

M11. Isometries of H. Normalise to det 1 and classify as elliptic (E),
     parabolic (P) or hyperbolic (Hy); give fixed points and the rotation angle
     θ (|tr| = 2cos(θ/2)) or translation length ℓ (|tr| = 2cosh(ℓ/2)).
     a) z + 1                        b) 4z
     c) −1/z                         d) (2z + 1)/(z + 1)
     e) (z + 1)/(−z + 1)             f) z/(z + 1)
     g) (3z − 1)/(z + 1)             h) (5z − 3)/(2z − 1)
     i) −1/(z + 1)                   j) 9z + 2
     k) (z − 1)/(z + 3)              l) (z cos(π/6) + sin(π/6))/
                                        (−z sin(π/6) + cos(π/6))
     m) 2z + 3                       n) −z̄

M12. True (T) or false (F)? E = Euclidean, H = hyperbolic, S = spherical/elliptic.
     a) In H every triangle has angle sum < π.
     b) In H two triangles with the same angles are congruent.
     c) In E similar triangles are congruent.
     d) In H, through a point off a line pass infinitely many non-meeting
        lines.
     e) In the elliptic plane any two lines meet.
     f) On the sphere two distinct great circles meet in exactly one point.
     g) In H there are triangles of arbitrarily large area.
     h) In H a quadrilateral with four right angles exists.
     i) In H a circle of radius r has circumference > 2πr.
     j) On the unit sphere a circle of radius r has circumference 2π sin r.
     k) The Klein model is conformal.
     l) The Poincaré disc model is conformal.
     m) Geodesics of the Klein model are Euclidean chords.
     n) The parallel postulate follows from Euclid's other axioms.
     o) Cross-ratio is preserved by affine maps.
     p) Ratios of lengths on a line are preserved by projective maps.
     q) Desargues' theorem holds in every projective plane.
     r) Pappus' theorem implies Desargues' theorem.
     s) All non-degenerate real conics with real points are projectively
        equivalent.
     t) The midpoint of a segment is a projective notion.
     u) A parabola is tangent to the line at infinity.
     v) The complete hyperbolic plane embeds isometrically as a smooth surface
        in R³.
     w) Every orientation-preserving isometry of H is a Möbius map with real
        coefficients.
     x) In S the angle sum of a triangle can exceed 2π.
     Answers:
       a) T   b) T   c) F   d) T   e) T   f) F (two antipodal points)
       g) F (< π)   h) F   i) T (2π sinh r)   j) T   k) F   l) T   m) T
       n) F   o) T   p) F   q) F (Moulton plane)   r) T (Hessenberg)   s) T
       t) F   u) T   v) F (Hilbert's theorem)   w) T
       x) T (the sum lies in (π, 3π); angles 3π/4 each give 9π/4, area 5π/4)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: make the student compute EVERY join and meet as a cross product
  and check with a dot product — this removes all special cases, and parallel
  lines simply give a third coordinate 0. Draw a railway track vanishing on
  the horizon to motivate points at infinity. For cross-ratio, fix one
  convention, write it on the board, and always test with (−1, 1; 0, ∞) = −1.
  In hyperbolic geometry keep one formula card: cosh d in H and in D,
  area = π − angle sum, the right-angle rules, and draw every geodesic as a
  semicircle meeting the boundary at right angles. Compare each hyperbolic
  answer with the Euclidean and spherical ones (2πr, 2π sinh r, 2π sin r).
  Harder: prove the formula for cosh d in H by moving z to i and w to the
  imaginary axis with an isometry; derive the hyperbolic law of cosines from
  the hyperboloid model; prove that the angle of parallelism satisfies
  tan(Π/2) = e^(−d); show that PSL(2, Z) acts on H with fundamental domain
  |z| ≥ 1, |Re z| ≤ 1/2 of area π/3; and construct a genus-2 surface by gluing
  the sides of a regular octagon with angles π/4 (area 4π = −2πχ, χ = −2).


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.30 — TENSOR ANALYSIS AND INDEX NOTATION
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - INDEX NOTATION: a vector is aᵢ (i = 1, 2, 3), a matrix Aᵢⱼ. SUMMATION
    CONVENTION (Einstein): an index repeated ONCE in a term is summed over its
    range (a DUMMY index, may be renamed); an index appearing once is FREE and
    must appear once in every term of the equation. No index may occur more
    than twice in a term. So a·b = aᵢbᵢ, (Ax)ᵢ = Aᵢⱼxⱼ, (AB)ᵢⱼ = AᵢₖBₖⱼ,
    tr A = Aᵢᵢ, xᵀAx = Aᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ.
  - KRONECKER DELTA δᵢⱼ (1 if i = j, else 0): δᵢᵢ = 3 (n in n dimensions),
    δᵢⱼaⱼ = aᵢ (SUBSTITUTION rule), δᵢⱼδⱼₖ = δᵢₖ, ∂ᵢxⱼ = δᵢⱼ.
  - LEVI-CIVITA SYMBOL εᵢⱼₖ: +1 for (1,2,3), (2,3,1), (3,1,2); −1 for odd
    permutations; 0 if an index repeats. (a × b)ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖaⱼbₖ,
    a·(b × c) = εᵢⱼₖaᵢbⱼcₖ, det A = εᵢⱼₖA₁ᵢA₂ⱼA₃ₖ, εᵢⱼₖAᵢₗAⱼₘAₖₙ = (det A)εₗₘₙ.
  - The ε–δ IDENTITY εᵢⱼₖεᵢₗₘ = δⱼₗδₖₘ − δⱼₘδₖₗ, with contractions
    εᵢⱼₖεᵢⱼₘ = 2δₖₘ and εᵢⱼₖεᵢⱼₖ = 6. It gives a × (b × c) = b(a·c) − c(a·b),
    (a × b)·(c × d) = (a·c)(b·d) − (a·d)(b·c), and, with ∂ᵢ = ∂/∂xᵢ, all the
    vector-calculus identities: ∇ × ∇φ = 0, ∇·(∇ × a) = 0,
    ∇ × (∇ × a) = ∇(∇·a) − ∇²a, ∇·(a × b) = b·(∇ × a) − a·(∇ × b).
  - CARTESIAN TENSORS: under a rotation of axes x′ᵢ = Lᵢⱼxⱼ with L orthogonal
    (LᵢₖLⱼₖ = δᵢⱼ), a TENSOR OF RANK n obeys T′ᵢⱼ... = LᵢₚLⱼₘ...Tₚₘ... (one L per
    index). Rank 0 = scalar, rank 1 = vector, rank 2: T′ = LTLᵀ. δᵢⱼ is a
    tensor; εᵢⱼₖ is a tensor under rotations (det L = 1) but a PSEUDOTENSOR
    under reflections, so a × b is an AXIAL (pseudo) vector.
  - TENSOR ALGEBRA: sums of tensors of the same rank, OUTER products
    (aᵢbⱼ, rank adds), CONTRACTION (set two indices equal and sum, rank drops
    by 2: Tᵢᵢ is a scalar). QUOTIENT THEOREM: if Tᵢⱼvⱼ is a vector for every
    vector v then Tᵢⱼ is a rank-2 tensor.
  - SYMMETRY: Tᵢⱼ = Sᵢⱼ + Aᵢⱼ with S = ½(T + Tᵀ), A = ½(T − Tᵀ); in n
    dimensions S has n(n + 1)/2 and A has n(n − 1)/2 independent components.
    SᵢⱼAᵢⱼ = 0 always. In 3D an antisymmetric tensor is a vector in disguise:
    Aⱼₖ = εⱼₖᵢωᵢ ⇔ ωᵢ = ½εᵢⱼₖAⱼₖ.
  - INVARIANTS and PRINCIPAL AXES of a symmetric rank-2 tensor: real
    eigenvalues (PRINCIPAL VALUES), orthogonal eigenvectors (PRINCIPAL AXES);
    invariants I₁ = Tᵢᵢ, I₂ = ½(TᵢᵢTⱼⱼ − TᵢⱼTⱼᵢ), I₃ = det T. Examples: the
    INERTIA tensor Iᵢⱼ = ∑ m(r²δᵢⱼ − xᵢxⱼ) (moment about unit axis n is
    Iᵢⱼnᵢnⱼ, kinetic energy ½Iᵢⱼωᵢωⱼ), the STRESS and STRAIN tensors.
  - ISOTROPIC tensors (same components in every rotated frame): rank 0 any
    scalar; rank 1 only 0; rank 2 λδᵢⱼ; rank 3 λεᵢⱼₖ; rank 4
    λδᵢⱼδₖₗ + μδᵢₖδⱼₗ + νδᵢₗδⱼₖ. They evaluate symmetric integrals:
    ∫(ball r ≤ a) xᵢxⱼ dV = (4πa⁵/15)δᵢⱼ, average of nᵢnⱼ over the sphere
    = δᵢⱼ/3, of nᵢnⱼnₖnₗ = (δᵢⱼδₖₗ + δᵢₖδⱼₗ + δᵢₗδⱼₖ)/15.
  - GENERAL COORDINATES xⁱ ↦ x′ⁱ: a CONTRAVARIANT vector (upper index, like
    dxⁱ, velocity) transforms V′ⁱ = (∂x′ⁱ/∂xʲ)Vʲ; a COVARIANT vector (lower
    index, like ∂φ/∂xⁱ) transforms W′ᵢ = (∂xʲ/∂x′ⁱ)Wⱼ; mixed tensors take one
    factor per index. VᵢWⁱ is a scalar. Summation now pairs one upper with one
    lower index.
  - METRIC TENSOR: ds² = gᵢⱼdxⁱdxʲ (gᵢⱼ symmetric, gᵢⱼ = eᵢ·eⱼ); gⁱʲ is the
    inverse matrix, gⁱʲgⱼₖ = δⁱₖ. Lowering Vᵢ = gᵢⱼVʲ, raising Wⁱ = gⁱʲWⱼ,
    |V|² = gᵢⱼVⁱVʲ, volume element √g dx¹...dxⁿ (g = det gᵢⱼ). Polar:
    diag(1, r²); cylindrical: diag(1, r², 1); spherical: diag(1, r², r² sin²θ),
    √g = r² sin θ.
  - CHRISTOFFEL SYMBOLS Γⁱⱼₖ = ½gⁱˡ(∂ⱼgₗₖ + ∂ₖgₗⱼ − ∂ₗgⱼₖ), symmetric in j, k,
    NOT a tensor, zero in Cartesian coordinates. Polar: Γ^r_θθ = −r,
    Γ^θ_rθ = Γ^θ_θr = 1/r. COVARIANT DERIVATIVE ∇ⱼVⁱ = ∂ⱼVⁱ + ΓⁱⱼₖVᵏ,
    ∇ⱼWᵢ = ∂ⱼWᵢ − ΓᵏⱼᵢWₖ (a tensor); ∇ₖgᵢⱼ = 0. DIVERGENCE
    ∇ᵢVⁱ = (1/√g)∂ᵢ(√g Vⁱ); LAPLACIAN ∇²φ = (1/√g)∂ᵢ(√g gⁱʲ∂ⱼφ).
  - GEODESICS: ẍⁱ + Γⁱⱼₖẋʲẋᵏ = 0. RIEMANN TENSOR
    Rⁱⱼₖₗ = ∂ₖΓⁱₗⱼ − ∂ₗΓⁱₖⱼ + ΓⁱₖₘΓᵐₗⱼ − ΓⁱₗₘΓᵐₖⱼ; RICCI Rⱼₗ = Rⁱⱼᵢₗ, scalar
    R = gʲˡRⱼₗ. A metric is flat ⇔ Riemann = 0 (polar coordinates have Γ ≠ 0
    but R = 0). In 2D everything is fixed by the GAUSSIAN CURVATURE
    K = R₁₂₁₂/det g (R = 2K); for dr² + G(r)²dθ², K = −G″/G.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. State the rules of the summation convention. Evaluate δᵢᵢ, δᵢⱼδⱼᵢ and
    δᵢⱼaᵢbⱼ, decide which of aᵢbᵢcᵢ, aᵢ = bⱼcⱼdᵢ, Tᵢⱼ = aᵢbₖ are valid, and write
    (AB)ᵢⱼ, tr(AB), xᵀAx and ABᵀ in index notation.
    Answer: δᵢᵢ = 3, δᵢⱼδⱼᵢ = 3, δᵢⱼaᵢbⱼ = a·b. aᵢbᵢcᵢ is invalid; aᵢ = bⱼcⱼdᵢ is
    valid (a = (b·c)d); Tᵢⱼ = aᵢbₖ is invalid. (AB)ᵢⱼ = AᵢₖBₖⱼ,
    tr(AB) = AᵢⱼBⱼᵢ, xᵀAx = Aᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ, (ABᵀ)ᵢⱼ = AᵢₖBⱼₖ.
    Teacher explains: Three rules.
       1. An index occurring TWICE in a term is summed from 1 to n (dummy).
       2. An index occurring ONCE is free; each term must have the SAME free
          indices (the equation holds for each value of them).
       3. No index occurs three or more times in one term.
    δᵢᵢ = δ₁₁ + δ₂₂ + δ₃₃ = 3. For δᵢⱼδⱼᵢ first sum over j with the substitution
    rule (δⱼᵢ replaces j by i in δᵢⱼ): δᵢⱼδⱼᵢ = δᵢᵢ = 3. Similarly
    δᵢⱼaᵢbⱼ = aⱼbⱼ = a·b: 'δ eats a sum and renames'. Validity: in aᵢbᵢcᵢ the
    index i appears three times — you cannot tell which pair is summed, so it
    is meaningless (a·b times c would be written (aⱼbⱼ)cᵢ). aᵢ = bⱼcⱼdᵢ: j is
    dummy, i free on both sides ✓. Tᵢⱼ = aᵢbₖ: left free {i, j}, right free
    {i, k} ✗. Matrices: the product sums over the 'inner' index,
       (AB)ᵢⱼ = AᵢₖBₖⱼ,   tr(AB) = (AB)ᵢᵢ = AᵢₖBₖᵢ,
       xᵀAx = xᵢAᵢⱼxⱼ,     (ABᵀ)ᵢⱼ = AᵢₖBⱼₖ.
    Because index expressions are just numbers, their ORDER does not matter
    (AᵢₖBₖⱼ = BₖⱼAᵢₖ): what matters is WHICH indices are paired. So
    tr(AB) = AᵢₖBₖᵢ = BₖᵢAᵢₖ = tr(BA) is a one-line proof. With
    A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], B = [[2, 1], [0, 3]]: AᵢⱼBⱼᵢ = 2 + 0 + 3 + 12 = 17
    = tr(AB), while AᵢⱼBᵢⱼ = 2 + 2 + 0 + 12 = 16. Common mistakes: re-using a
    dummy letter already used ((a·b)(c·d) must be aᵢbᵢcⱼdⱼ, not aᵢbᵢcᵢdᵢ);
    'cancelling' an index. Now you try: simplify δᵢⱼδⱼₖδₖᵢ. (δᵢᵢ = 3)

D2. Define εᵢⱼₖ and use it to compute a × b for a = (1, 2, 3), b = (4, 5, 6),
    prove that a·(b × c) is unchanged by cyclic permutation, and evaluate
    det [[2, 1, 3], [0, 4, 1], [5, 2, 6]] with the ε-formula.
    Answer: a × b = (−3, 6, −3); cyclic invariance follows from
    εᵢⱼₖ = εⱼₖᵢ; det = −11.
    Teacher explains: εᵢⱼₖ = +1 if (i, j, k) is an even permutation of
    (1, 2, 3), −1 if odd, 0 if two indices are equal. Only 6 of the 27
    components are non-zero. (a × b)ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖaⱼbₖ; for i = 1 only (j, k) = (2, 3)
    and (3, 2) survive:
       (a × b)₁ = ε₁₂₃a₂b₃ + ε₁₃₂a₃b₂ = a₂b₃ − a₃b₂ = 12 − 15 = −3
       (a × b)₂ = a₃b₁ − a₁b₃ = 12 − 6 = 6
       (a × b)₃ = a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 5 − 8 = −3
    Triple product: a·(b × c) = aᵢεᵢⱼₖbⱼcₖ = εᵢⱼₖaᵢbⱼcₖ. A cyclic shift of
    (i, j, k) is two transpositions, so εᵢⱼₖ = εⱼₖᵢ; renaming dummies,
       b·(c × a) = εᵢⱼₖbᵢcⱼaₖ = εⱼₖᵢbⱼcₖaᵢ = εᵢⱼₖaᵢbⱼcₖ = a·(b × c) ∎,
    while a swap changes the sign: a·(c × b) = −a·(b × c). Also
    a × a = 0 because εᵢⱼₖ is antisymmetric in j, k and aⱼaₖ symmetric.
    Determinant: det A = εᵢⱼₖA₁ᵢA₂ⱼA₃ₖ is the sum over the 6 permutations:
       det = 2(4·6 − 1·2) − 1(0·6 − 1·5) + 3(0·2 − 4·5)
           = 44 + 5 − 60 = −11.
    Common mistakes: ε₁₃₂ = +1 (it is −1); forgetting that ε with a repeated
    index is 0. Now you try: compute a·(b × c) with c = (1, 0, 2). (−9)

D3. Prove the ε–δ identity εᵢⱼₖεᵢₗₘ = δⱼₗδₖₘ − δⱼₘδₖₗ and deduce εᵢⱼₖεᵢⱼₘ = 2δₖₘ,
    εᵢⱼₖεᵢⱼₖ = 6 and a × (b × c) = b(a·c) − c(a·b). Check the last with
    a = (1, 2, 3), b = (4, 5, 6), c = (1, 0, 2).
    Answer: a × (b × c) = (−4, 35, −22).
    Teacher explains: Proof by cases. Both sides are antisymmetric in (j, k)
    and in (l, m), so both vanish if j = k or l = m; assume j ≠ k, l ≠ m. On
    the left, the sum over i has at most one non-zero term: i must be the
    third number different from j, k, AND the third different from l, m. So
    the left side is non-zero only if {l, m} = {j, k}:
       l = j, m = k:  εᵢⱼₖεᵢⱼₖ = (±1)² = 1;  right side δⱼⱼδₖₖ − δⱼₖδₖⱼ = 1 − 0
       l = k, m = j:  εᵢⱼₖεᵢₖⱼ = −1;          right side 0 − 1 = −1
    and if {l, m} ≠ {j, k} both sides are 0. (Here j, k are fixed, not
    summed.) ∎ Contract l = j:
       εᵢⱼₖεᵢⱼₘ = δⱼⱼδₖₘ − δⱼₘδₖⱼ = 3δₖₘ − δₖₘ = 2δₖₘ,
    and then k = m: 2δₖₖ = 6 (the number of non-zero ε's). Triple cross
    product:
       [a × (b × c)]ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖaⱼ(εₖₗₘbₗcₘ) = εₖᵢⱼεₖₗₘ aⱼbₗcₘ
                      = (δᵢₗδⱼₘ − δᵢₘδⱼₗ)aⱼbₗcₘ = bᵢ(aⱼcⱼ) − cᵢ(aⱼbⱼ).
    (εᵢⱼₖ = εₖᵢⱼ, cyclic, puts the repeated index first.) Check:
       b × c = (5·2 − 6·0, 6·1 − 4·2, 4·0 − 5·1) = (10, −2, −5)
       a × (b × c) = (2(−5) − 3(−2), 3·10 − 1(−5), 1(−2) − 2·10)
                   = (−4, 35, −22)
       a·c = 7, a·b = 32: 7(4, 5, 6) − 32(1, 0, 2) = (−4, 35, −22) ✓
    Memory aid 'BAC − CAB'. Common mistakes: using εᵢⱼₖεₗₘᵢ without first
    rotating indices so the SUMMED index is in the same place; sign errors in
    the δδ − δδ. Now you try: show (a × b)·(c × d) = (a·c)(b·d) − (a·d)(b·c).
    (εᵢⱼₖεᵢₗₘaⱼbₖcₗdₘ = (δⱼₗδₖₘ − δⱼₘδₖₗ)aⱼbₖcₗdₘ)

D4. Using index notation prove ∇ × (∇ × a) = ∇(∇·a) − ∇²a and
    ∇·(a × b) = b·(∇ × a) − a·(∇ × b). With x the position vector and
    r = |x| show ∂ᵢr = xᵢ/r and ∇²(rⁿ) = n(n + 1)rⁿ⁻², and deduce ∇²(1/r) = 0.
    Answer: Proofs below; ∇²rⁿ = n(n + 1)rⁿ⁻², zero for n = −1 (and n = 0).
    Teacher explains: Write ∂ᵢ for ∂/∂xᵢ; (∇ × a)ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖ∂ⱼaₖ. Then
       [∇ × (∇ × a)]ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖ∂ⱼ(εₖₗₘ∂ₗaₘ) = εₖᵢⱼεₖₗₘ∂ⱼ∂ₗaₘ
                      = (δᵢₗδⱼₘ − δᵢₘδⱼₗ)∂ⱼ∂ₗaₘ = ∂ᵢ(∂ₘaₘ) − ∂ⱼ∂ⱼaᵢ,
    i.e. ∇(∇·a) − ∇²a (ε is constant, so it passes through ∂). Next, by the
    product rule
       ∂ᵢ(εᵢⱼₖaⱼbₖ) = εᵢⱼₖ(∂ᵢaⱼ)bₖ + εᵢⱼₖaⱼ(∂ᵢbₖ)
                    = bₖ(εₖᵢⱼ∂ᵢaⱼ) − aⱼ(εⱼᵢₖ∂ᵢbₖ) = b·(∇ × a) − a·(∇ × b)
    (εᵢⱼₖ = εₖᵢⱼ and εᵢⱼₖ = −εⱼᵢₖ). Two quick zeros: ∇·(∇ × a) = εᵢⱼₖ∂ᵢ∂ⱼaₖ = 0
    and (∇ × ∇φ)ᵢ = εᵢⱼₖ∂ⱼ∂ₖφ = 0, since ε is antisymmetric in the pair and
    mixed partials are symmetric. Now r² = xⱼxⱼ, ∂ᵢxⱼ = δᵢⱼ:
       2r ∂ᵢr = 2xⱼδᵢⱼ = 2xᵢ ⇒ ∂ᵢr = xᵢ/r,
       ∂ᵢ(rⁿ) = nrⁿ⁻¹xᵢ/r = nrⁿ⁻²xᵢ,
       ∂ᵢ∂ᵢ(rⁿ) = n[(n − 2)rⁿ⁻⁴xᵢxᵢ + rⁿ⁻²δᵢᵢ] = n[(n − 2) + 3]rⁿ⁻²
                = n(n + 1)rⁿ⁻².
    For n = −1 this is 0: 1/r is harmonic away from the origin (the Newton /
    Coulomb potential). Also ∇²r = 2/r and ∇²r² = 6. Common mistakes:
    ∂ᵢxᵢ = 1 (it is δᵢᵢ = 3); dropping the product rule on xᵢ. Now you try:
    ∇·(rⁿx). (∂ᵢ(rⁿxᵢ) = nrⁿ⁻²xᵢxᵢ + 3rⁿ = (n + 3)rⁿ, zero for n = −3)

D5. Define a Cartesian tensor. Show δᵢⱼ is isotropic and that εᵢⱼₖ is
    isotropic under rotations but changes sign under reflections. Rotate the
    axes by 90° about the z-axis (x′ = y, y′ = −x, z′ = z) and find the new
    components of T = [[1, 2, 0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 4]]; check the trace.
    Answer: T′ = [[3, 0, 0], [−2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 4]]; tr T′ = tr T = 8.
    Teacher explains: New axes e′ᵢ = Lᵢⱼeⱼ with L orthogonal; a fixed vector
    has components v′ᵢ = Lᵢⱼvⱼ. A Cartesian tensor of rank 2 is a set of 9
    numbers transforming like the products vᵢwⱼ:
       T′ᵢⱼ = LᵢₚLⱼₘTₚₘ,   i.e. T′ = LTLᵀ.
    δᵢⱼ: δ′ᵢⱼ = LᵢₚLⱼₘδₚₘ = LᵢₚLⱼₚ = (LLᵀ)ᵢⱼ = δᵢⱼ — same in every frame
    (ISOTROPIC). εᵢⱼₖ: LᵢₚLⱼₘLₖₙεₚₘₙ = (det L)εᵢⱼₖ (the determinant formula
    with rows i, j, k). For rotations det L = 1: isotropic; for a reflection
    det L = −1 and the sign flips, so ε is a PSEUDOTENSOR and a × b is an
    AXIAL vector: under x ↦ −x, a and b flip but a × b does not. Here
       L = [[0, 1, 0], [−1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]].
    Compute T′ = LTLᵀ. LT = [[0, 3, 0], [−1, −2, 0], [0, 0, 4]]; then
       T′ = (LT)Lᵀ = [[3, 0, 0], [−2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 4]].
    Check one entry by the index formula: T′₂₁ = L₂ₚL₁ₘTₚₘ = L₂₁L₁₂T₁₂
    = (−1)(1)(2) = −2 ✓. The trace Tᵢᵢ is a contraction, hence a scalar:
    1 + 3 + 4 = 8 = 3 + 1 + 4 ✓; so is det (12 = 12). Being a tensor is a
    statement about how components CHANGE, not about a single array of
    numbers. Common mistakes: T′ = LᵀTL (that is the inverse change); using
    one L for a rank-2 tensor. Now you try: rotate v = (1, 2, 3) by the same
    L. ((2, −1, 3))

D6. Explain outer products and contraction, and prove that contracting a
    rank-2 tensor gives a scalar and that Tᵢⱼⱼ (rank 3 contracted) is a
    vector. State and prove the quotient theorem for rank 2.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: If aᵢ and bⱼ are vectors, Tᵢⱼ = aᵢbⱼ is a rank-2 tensor
    (the OUTER or tensor product a ⊗ b):
       T′ᵢⱼ = a′ᵢb′ⱼ = (Lᵢₚaₚ)(Lⱼₘbₘ) = LᵢₚLⱼₘTₚₘ ✓.
    In general rank(S ⊗ T) = rank S + rank T. CONTRACTION: set two indices
    equal and sum.
       T′ᵢᵢ = LᵢₚLᵢₘTₚₘ = δₚₘTₚₘ = Tₚₚ          (scalar)
       T′ᵢⱼⱼ = LᵢₚLⱼₘLⱼₙTₚₘₙ = LᵢₚδₘₙTₚₘₙ = LᵢₚTₚₘₘ (vector)
    — the key fact LⱼₘLⱼₙ = δₘₙ (orthogonality) kills the two contracted L's.
    So a·b = aᵢbᵢ is the contraction of a ⊗ b, and tr is the contraction of
    a matrix. QUOTIENT THEOREM: suppose that for EVERY vector v the numbers
    uᵢ = Tᵢⱼvⱼ are the components of a vector. Then u′ᵢ = Lᵢₚuₚ, i.e.
       T′ᵢⱼv′ⱼ = LᵢₚTₚₘvₘ = LᵢₚTₚₘLⱼₘv′ⱼ     (vₘ = Lⱼₘv′ⱼ).
    So (T′ᵢⱼ − LᵢₚLⱼₘTₚₘ)v′ⱼ = 0 for all v′, and choosing v′ = e₁, e₂, e₃ gives
    T′ᵢⱼ = LᵢₚLⱼₘTₚₘ ∎. Use: the stress σᵢⱼ is a tensor because σᵢⱼnⱼ is the
    force vector on any surface with normal n; the inertia tensor because
    Iᵢⱼωⱼ is the angular momentum for every ω. Warning: it must hold for ALL
    v; one v says nothing. Common mistakes: thinking any 3 × 3 array is a
    tensor (e.g. Tᵢⱼ = 1 for all i, j is not: it is not preserved by
    rotations); forgetting that contraction needs two indices of the SAME
    tensor product. Now you try: show that Aᵢⱼbᵢcⱼ is a scalar when A is a
    tensor and b, c vectors. (It is the double contraction of A ⊗ b ⊗ c.)

D7. Split T = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]] into symmetric and
    antisymmetric parts, find the axial vector of the antisymmetric part and
    prove SᵢⱼAᵢⱼ = 0. How many independent components do symmetric and
    antisymmetric rank-2 tensors have in n dimensions?
    Answer: S = [[1, 3, 5], [3, 5, 7], [5, 7, 9]],
    A = [[0, −1, −2], [1, 0, −1], [2, 1, 0]], ω = (−1, 2, −1);
    n(n + 1)/2 and n(n − 1)/2.
    Teacher explains: Tᵢⱼ = ½(Tᵢⱼ + Tⱼᵢ) + ½(Tᵢⱼ − Tⱼᵢ) = Sᵢⱼ + Aᵢⱼ. Both parts
    are tensors (Tⱼᵢ is a tensor) and symmetry survives rotation, so the
    split is frame-independent. S₁₂ = (2 + 4)/2 = 3, A₁₂ = (2 − 4)/2 = −1, etc.
    PROOF of SᵢⱼAᵢⱼ = 0: rename the dummies i ↔ j:
       SᵢⱼAᵢⱼ = SⱼᵢAⱼᵢ = Sᵢⱼ(−Aᵢⱼ) ⇒ 2SᵢⱼAᵢⱼ = 0.
    (The same argument gives εᵢⱼₖaⱼaₖ = 0 and εᵢⱼₖ∂ⱼ∂ₖφ = 0.) Consequence:
    xᵀTx = Tᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ only sees the symmetric part. AXIAL VECTOR: in 3D an
    antisymmetric A has 3 independent entries and ωᵢ = ½εᵢⱼₖAⱼₖ:
       ω₁ = ½(A₂₃ − A₃₂) = ½(−1 − 1) = −1
       ω₂ = ½(A₃₁ − A₁₃) = ½(2 + 2) = 2
       ω₃ = ½(A₁₂ − A₂₁) = ½(−1 − 1) = −1
    Conversely Aⱼₖ = εⱼₖᵢωᵢ (check A₁₂ = ε₁₂₃ω₃ = −1 ✓), and then
    (Ax)ⱼ = εⱼₖᵢxₖωᵢ = (x × ω)ⱼ. This is why angular velocity, a rotation-rate
    matrix, is 'a vector' — only in 3D. Counting: a symmetric n × n matrix is
    fixed by the diagonal and the upper triangle, n + n(n − 1)/2 = n(n + 1)/2;
    antisymmetric: diagonal zero, n(n − 1)/2. In 3D: 6 and 3 (9 = 6 + 3);
    in 4D: 10 and 6 (the electromagnetic field tensor Fμν has 6 = E and B).
    Common mistakes: forgetting the ½ in ωᵢ = ½εᵢⱼₖAⱼₖ (without it you get
    2ω); thinking the diagonal of A may be non-zero. Now you try: the
    antisymmetric matrix of ω = (1, 2, 3) with Aⱼₖ = εⱼₖᵢωᵢ.
    ([[0, 3, −2], [−3, 0, 1], [2, −1, 0]])

D8. Three unit point masses sit at (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (1, 1, 0). Find the
    inertia tensor about the origin, its invariants, its principal moments and
    axes, the moment about the axis (1, 1, 1)/√3, and the kinetic energy for
    ω = (1, 1, 0).
    Answer: I = [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 2, 0], [0, 0, 4]]; I₁ = 8, I₂ = 19, I₃ = 12;
    principal moments 1, 3, 4 about (1, 1, 0)/√2, (1, −1, 0)/√2, (0, 0, 1);
    moment 2; kinetic energy 1.
    Teacher explains: Iᵢⱼ = ∑ m(r²δᵢⱼ − xᵢxⱼ), one term per mass:
       (1, 0, 0): r² = 1  →  diag(1, 1, 1) − diag(1, 0, 0) = diag(0, 1, 1)
       (0, 1, 0): r² = 1  →  diag(1, 0, 1)
       (1, 1, 0): r² = 2  →  [[2 − 1, −1, 0], [−1, 2 − 1, 0], [0, 0, 2]]
    Sum: I = [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 2, 0], [0, 0, 4]]. Diagonal entries are moments
    about the axes (I₃₃ = ∑m(x² + y²) = 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 ✓), off-diagonal are
    minus the PRODUCTS OF INERTIA. Invariants: I₁ = tr = 8;
    I₂ = sum of principal 2 × 2 minors = (4 − 1) + 8 + 8 = 19; I₃ = det
    = 4(4 − 1) = 12. Eigenvalues: the z-block gives 4; the 2 × 2 block
    [[2, −1], [−1, 2]] has λ = 2 ∓ 1 = 1, 3 with eigenvectors (1, 1), (1, −1).
    Check: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8, 1·3 + 3·4 + 1·4 = 19, 1·3·4 = 12 ✓. Being symmetric,
    I has real eigenvalues and orthogonal principal axes; in that frame it is
    diagonal and L = Iω becomes Lᵢ = Iᵢωᵢ (no sum). Moment about unit n:
       Iᵢⱼnᵢnⱼ = (1/3)(2 + 2 + 4 − 1 − 1) = 2.
    Kinetic energy ½Iᵢⱼωᵢωⱼ with ω = (1, 1, 0): ½(2 − 1 − 1 + 2) = 1. (ω is
    along the principal axis with moment 1: ½·1·|ω|² = ½·2 = 1 ✓.) Common
    mistakes: +xᵢxⱼ instead of −xᵢxⱼ; forgetting δᵢⱼr² on the diagonal. Now
    you try: inertia tensor of a mass m at (1, 1, 1).
    (m[[2, −1, −1], [−1, 2, −1], [−1, −1, 2]])

D9. In plane polar coordinates (r, θ) find the contravariant components of the
    vector field V = (−y, x) and the covariant components of ∇φ for φ = xy.
    Verify the transformation laws and that Vⁱ∂ᵢφ is the same in both
    systems.
    Answer: (Vʳ, V^θ) = (0, 1), i.e. V = ∂/∂θ; (∂ᵣφ, ∂_θφ) = (r sin 2θ,
    r² cos 2θ); Vⁱ∂ᵢφ = x² − y² = r² cos 2θ in both.
    Teacher explains: For a general change xⁱ ↦ x′ⁱ, differentials obey the
    chain rule dx′ⁱ = (∂x′ⁱ/∂xʲ)dxʲ: anything transforming like dxⁱ is
    CONTRAVARIANT (upper index). Partial derivatives obey
    ∂φ/∂x′ⁱ = (∂xʲ/∂x′ⁱ)∂φ/∂xʲ: COVARIANT (lower index). The two matrices are
    inverse to each other, so VⁱWᵢ is invariant. Here x = r cos θ,
    y = r sin θ, r² = x² + y², θ = arctan(y/x):
       ∂r/∂x = x/r, ∂r/∂y = y/r, ∂θ/∂x = −y/r², ∂θ/∂y = x/r².
    Contravariant:
       Vʳ = (x/r)(−y) + (y/r)(x) = 0,   V^θ = (−y/r²)(−y) + (x/r²)(x) = 1.
    So the rotation field is simply ∂/∂θ. Covariant: with ∂x/∂r = cos θ,
    ∂y/∂r = sin θ, ∂x/∂θ = −r sin θ, ∂y/∂θ = r cos θ and ∇φ = (y, x):
       W_r = cos θ·y + sin θ·x = 2r sin θ cos θ = r sin 2θ
       W_θ = −r sin θ·y + r cos θ·x = r²(cos²θ − sin²θ) = r² cos 2θ
    Directly: φ = r² sin θ cos θ = ½r² sin 2θ gives ∂ᵣφ = r sin 2θ,
    ∂_θφ = r² cos 2θ ✓. Invariant: Cartesian (−y)(y) + x(x) = x² − y²;
    polar 0·W_r + 1·W_θ = r² cos 2θ = x² − y² ✓. Note W_θ is NOT the
    'physical' component along the unit vector e_θ (that is W_θ/r); tensor
    components refer to coordinate basis vectors ∂/∂xⁱ, whose lengths √gᵢᵢ
    vary. Common mistakes: using the same matrix for both laws; confusing
    coordinate and physical components. Now you try: the polar components of
    V = (x, y). ((Vʳ, V^θ) = (r, 0))

D10. Derive the metric tensor of spherical coordinates, its inverse and √g,
     and use ∇²φ = (1/√g)∂ᵢ(√g gⁱʲ∂ⱼφ) to write the Laplacian. Check it on
     φ = z² = r² cos²θ. Explain raising and lowering indices.
     Answer: gᵢⱼ = diag(1, r², r² sin²θ), gⁱʲ = diag(1, 1/r², 1/(r² sin²θ)),
     √g = r² sin θ; ∇²φ = (1/r²)∂ᵣ(r²∂ᵣφ) + (1/(r² sin θ))∂_θ(sin θ ∂_θφ)
     + (1/(r² sin²θ))∂²φ/∂φ²; ∇²(z²) = 2.
     Teacher explains: x = r sin θ cos φ, y = r sin θ sin φ, z = r cos θ. The
     coordinate basis vectors are the partial derivatives of the position:
        e_r = (sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, cos θ),            |e_r|² = 1
        e_θ = (r cos θ cos φ, r cos θ sin φ, −r sin θ),     |e_θ|² = r²
        e_φ = (−r sin θ sin φ, r sin θ cos φ, 0),           |e_φ|² = r² sin²θ
     and they are mutually orthogonal, so gᵢⱼ = eᵢ·eⱼ = diag(1, r², r² sin²θ):
        ds² = dr² + r²dθ² + r² sin²θ dφ².
     Inverse: reciprocal diagonal; det g = r⁴ sin²θ, √g = r² sin θ (the
     volume element). Laplacian: for a diagonal metric √g gⁱⁱ = r² sin θ,
     sin θ, 1/sin θ, giving the formula in the answer. Check on
     φ = r² cos²θ (= z², whose Cartesian Laplacian is 2):
        radial:  (1/r²)∂ᵣ(r²·2r cos²θ) = 6 cos²θ
        angular: (1/(r² sin θ))∂_θ(sin θ·(−2r² cos θ sin θ))
                 = (1/sin θ)(−4 sin θ cos²θ + 2 sin³θ) = −4cos²θ + 2sin²θ
        total:   2cos²θ + 2sin²θ = 2 ✓
     RAISING and LOWERING: Vᵢ = gᵢⱼVʲ, Wⁱ = gⁱʲWⱼ. In polar coordinates at
     r = 2, the vector (Vʳ, V^θ) = (3, 2) has V_θ = r²V^θ = 8, and
     |V|² = VᵢVⁱ = 3·3 + 8·2 = 25, |V| = 5 (= √(9 + 4·4)). In Cartesian
     coordinates g = I and upper = lower, which is why the distinction never
     appeared before. Common mistakes: writing √g = r sin θ; forgetting the
     inverse metric gⁱʲ in the Laplacian. Now you try: the metric of
     cylindrical coordinates. (diag(1, r², 1), √g = r)

D11. Compute the Christoffel symbols of the plane in polar coordinates, show
     that ∇ⱼVⁱ = ∂ⱼVⁱ + ΓⁱⱼₖVᵏ gives the divergence (1/r)∂ᵣ(rVʳ) + ∂_θV^θ, check
     it on V = (x, y), and show the geodesic equations have the straight line
     r cos θ = 1 as a solution.
     Answer: Γ^r_θθ = −r, Γ^θ_rθ = Γ^θ_θr = 1/r, all others 0; ∇·V = 2 for
     V = (x, y).
     Teacher explains: g = diag(1, r²), gⁱʲ = diag(1, 1/r²); the only
     non-constant entry is g_θθ = r², with ∂ᵣg_θθ = 2r. From
     Γⁱⱼₖ = ½gⁱˡ(∂ⱼgₗₖ + ∂ₖgₗⱼ − ∂ₗgⱼₖ):
        Γ^r_θθ = ½g^rr(0 + 0 − ∂ᵣg_θθ) = ½(−2r) = −r
        Γ^θ_rθ = ½g^θθ(∂ᵣg_θθ + 0 − 0) = ½(1/r²)(2r) = 1/r
     and Γ^r_rr = Γ^r_rθ = Γ^θ_rr = Γ^θ_θθ = 0. Meaning: as you move in θ the
     basis vector e_θ turns and grows, ∂_θe_θ = −r e_r, ∂ᵣe_θ = (1/r)e_θ. The
     covariant derivative adds these basis changes, so ∇ⱼVⁱ is a tensor while
     ∂ⱼVⁱ is not. Divergence = contraction ∇ᵢVⁱ:
        ∇ᵢVⁱ = ∂ᵣVʳ + ∂_θV^θ + ΓⁱᵢₖVᵏ,  Γⁱᵢᵣ = Γ^r_rr + Γ^θ_θr = 1/r, Γⁱᵢθ = 0,
        ∇ᵢVⁱ = ∂ᵣVʳ + Vʳ/r + ∂_θV^θ = (1/r)∂ᵣ(rVʳ) + ∂_θV^θ,
     the case √g = r of (1/√g)∂ᵢ(√gVⁱ) (because Γⁱᵢⱼ = ∂ⱼ ln √g). For
     V = (x, y): Vʳ = r, V^θ = 0, so ∇·V = (1/r)∂ᵣ(r²) = 2 = ∂ₓx + ∂ᵧy ✓.
     Geodesics ẍⁱ + Γⁱⱼₖẋʲẋᵏ = 0:
        r̈ − rθ̇² = 0,   θ̈ + (2/r)ṙθ̇ = 0 (⇔ d(r²θ̇)/dt = 0).
     The line x = 1 traversed as x = 1, y = t: r = √(1 + t²), θ = arctan t,
     r²θ̇ = (1 + t²)/(1 + t²) = 1 constant ✓; ṙ = t/r, r̈ = 1/r³, rθ̇² = r/r⁴
     = 1/r³ ✓. So Γ ≠ 0 does not mean curvature — it only reflects curved
     coordinates. Common mistakes: forgetting the factor 2 (both Γ^θ_rθ and
     Γ^θ_θr) in the θ-equation; treating Γ as a tensor (it is zero in
     Cartesian coordinates but not in polar ones, which is impossible for a
     tensor). Now you try: divergence of Vʳ = 1/r, V^θ = 0. (0 for r ≠ 0)

D12. For the sphere of radius a with ds² = a²(dθ² + sin²θ dφ²) find the
     Christoffel symbols, the geodesic equations, R^θ_φθφ, R_θφθφ, the Gaussian
     curvature and the Ricci scalar. Is a circle of latitude a geodesic?
     Answer: Γ^θ_φφ = −sin θ cos θ, Γ^φ_θφ = cot θ; R^θ_φθφ = sin²θ,
     R_θφθφ = a² sin²θ, K = 1/a², R = 2/a². Only the equator θ = π/2.
     Teacher explains: g = diag(a², a² sin²θ), only g_φφ depends on θ:
     ∂_θg_φφ = 2a² sin θ cos θ. Then
        Γ^θ_φφ = ½(1/a²)(−2a² sin θ cos θ) = −sin θ cos θ,
        Γ^φ_θφ = ½(1/(a² sin²θ))(2a² sin θ cos θ) = cot θ,
     others 0. Geodesics:
        θ̈ − sin θ cos θ φ̇² = 0,   φ̈ + 2 cot θ θ̇φ̇ = 0.
     A latitude circle θ = θ₀, φ = t has θ̈ = 0 but sin θ₀ cos θ₀ ≠ 0 unless
     θ₀ = π/2: only the EQUATOR (a great circle) is a geodesic. Curvature,
     with Rⁱⱼₖₗ = ∂ₖΓⁱₗⱼ − ∂ₗΓⁱₖⱼ + ΓⁱₖₘΓᵐₗⱼ − ΓⁱₗₘΓᵐₖⱼ:
        R^θ_φθφ = ∂_θΓ^θ_φφ − ∂_φΓ^θ_θφ + Γ^θ_θₘΓᵐ_φφ − Γ^θ_φₘΓᵐ_θφ
                = −(cos²θ − sin²θ) − 0 + 0 − (−sin θ cos θ)(cot θ)
                = −cos²θ + sin²θ + cos²θ = sin²θ.
     Lower: R_θφθφ = g_θθ R^θ_φθφ = a² sin²θ, and
        K = R_θφθφ/det g = a² sin²θ/(a⁴ sin²θ) = 1/a².
     In 2D the Riemann tensor has only this one independent component, the
     Ricci tensor is Rᵢⱼ = K gᵢⱼ and the scalar R = 2K = 2/a². Unlike polar
     coordinates of the plane (Γ ≠ 0 but R = 0), no change of coordinates can
     make the sphere flat, because a tensor that is non-zero in one system is
     non-zero in all — this is Gauss's Theorema Egregium in tensor language.
     For metrics dr² + G(r)²dθ² the same computation gives K = −G″/G:
     G = r (plane) 0, G = sin r (unit sphere) 1, G = sinh r (hyperbolic)
     −1. Common mistakes: sign conventions for R differ between books — check
     with the sphere (K > 0); forgetting the Γ·Γ terms. Now you try: K for
     (dx² + dy²)/y². (−1)
