       o) −1                          p) −1
       q) 1                           r) −1
       s) cos θ/(b(R + b cos θ)) (positive outside, negative inside)
       t) 0 (a cone is flat away from its tip)
       u) a² sin²θ; 2/a²

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: before every manipulation, underline free indices and circle
  dummy ones; check that every term has the same free indices. Drill the
  substitution rule for δ and the 'δδ − δδ' identity until automatic (say it
  as 'same-same minus different-different'). Always rotate an ε so the summed
  index comes first before using the identity. For rank-2 tensors translate
  back into matrix language (T′ = LTLᵀ, eigenvalues, trace) and check
  invariants numerically. In curvilinear coordinates write the metric first;
  everything (Γ, divergence, Laplacian) follows from it. Harder: prove the
  general formula εᵢⱼₖεₗₘₙ = det[δ's], show every isotropic rank-2 tensor is
  λδᵢⱼ by using rotations through 90°, derive Γⁱᵢⱼ = ∂ⱼ ln √g and hence the
  divergence formula, prove ∇g = 0 and that ∇ commutes with raising indices,
  and verify the Bianchi identity for the sphere; then compute the curvature
  of the Schwarzschild metric's (t, r) part as a first step towards general
  relativity.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.31 — FRACTALS AND DIMENSION (INTRODUCTION)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A FRACTAL is a set with detail at every scale: typically SELF-SIMILAR
    (made of scaled copies of itself), too irregular for classical geometry,
    defined by a simple recursive rule, and with a FRACTAL DIMENSION larger
    than its topological dimension (often not an integer). Not every fractal
    is exactly self-similar.
  - The (middle-third) CANTOR SET C = ⋂ Cₙ, where C₀ = [0, 1] and Cₙ₊₁ removes
    the open middle third of each interval of Cₙ. Cₙ has 2ⁿ intervals of
    length 3⁻ⁿ, total length (2/3)ⁿ → 0; the removed lengths add up to 1. C is
    the set of x ∈ [0, 1] with a TERNARY expansion using only digits 0 and 2:
    it is compact, uncountable, PERFECT, TOTALLY DISCONNECTED, NOWHERE DENSE,
    of LEBESGUE MEASURE 0, and contains points like 1/4 = 0.0202...₃ that are
    not endpoints. The CANTOR FUNCTION (devil's staircase) is continuous,
    increasing, constant on each removed interval, maps C onto [0, 1].
  - KOCH CURVE: replace the middle third of each segment by two sides of an
    equilateral triangle. After n steps: 4ⁿ segments of length 3⁻ⁿ, length
    (4/3)ⁿ → ∞. The KOCH SNOWFLAKE has infinite perimeter but finite area
    (8/5)A₀ (A₀ = area of the starting triangle). The limit curve is
    continuous and nowhere differentiable.
  - SIERPINSKI TRIANGLE (3 copies, ratio 1/2), SIERPINSKI CARPET (8, 1/3),
    MENGER SPONGE (20, 1/3), VICSEK fractal (5, 1/3), CANTOR DUST C × C
    (4, 1/3): all have zero area/volume in their ambient space.
  - SIMILARITY DIMENSION: a set made of N copies of itself scaled by r has
    dimension s with N rˢ = 1, s = ln N/ln(1/r). With different ratios
    r₁, ..., r_m the MORAN EQUATION ∑ rᵢˢ = 1 has a unique solution s. Reason:
    scaling a set by λ multiplies its s-dimensional 'size' by λˢ. Values:
    Cantor ln 2/ln 3 ≈ 0.6309, Koch ln 4/ln 3 ≈ 1.2619, Sierpinski
    ln 3/ln 2 ≈ 1.5850, carpet ln 8/ln 3 ≈ 1.8928, sponge ln 20/ln 3 ≈ 2.7268.
  - BOX-COUNTING DIMENSION: with N_δ(F) the least number of sets of diameter
    ≤ δ (or of δ-grid boxes) meeting F, dim_B F = lim (δ → 0)
    ln N_δ(F)/(−ln δ) when the limit exists (otherwise upper and lower box
    dimensions). N_δ ≈ Cδ^(−s): the slope of ln N against ln(1/δ). Box
    dimension equals that of the closure, so dim_B(Q ∩ [0, 1]) = 1 and
    dim_B{1/n : n ∈ N} = 1/2: it is NOT countably stable.
  - HAUSDORFF MEASURE: Hˢ_δ(F) = inf{∑|Uᵢ|ˢ : F ⊆ ⋃Uᵢ, |Uᵢ| ≤ δ},
    Hˢ(F) = lim (δ → 0) Hˢ_δ(F). As s increases Hˢ(F) jumps from ∞ to 0 at
    one value, the HAUSDORFF DIMENSION dim_H F. H⁰ counts points, H¹ is length
    on curves, Hⁿ is a multiple of Lebesgue measure in Rⁿ; Hˢ(λF) = λˢHˢ(F).
  - PROPERTIES of dim_H: MONOTONE (E ⊆ F ⇒ dim E ≤ dim F), COUNTABLY STABLE
    (dim ⋃Fᵢ = sup dim Fᵢ, so countable sets have dimension 0), LIPSCHITZ maps
    do not increase it and BI-LIPSCHITZ maps preserve it; open sets of Rⁿ have
    dimension n, smooth curves 1, smooth surfaces 2. Always
    dim_T F ≤ dim_H F ≤ lower dim_B F ≤ upper dim_B F (dim_T = topological).
    For self-similar sets with the OPEN SET CONDITION (pieces do not overlap
    too much) all these equal the similarity dimension.
  - ITERATED FUNCTION SYSTEMS (IFS): contractions f₁, ..., f_m of a complete
    metric space. The HUTCHINSON operator F(A) = f₁(A) ∪ ... ∪ f_m(A) is a
    contraction of the compact sets in the HAUSDORFF METRIC
    d_H(A, B) = max(sup(a ∈ A) d(a, B), sup(b ∈ B) d(b, A)); by the BANACH
    fixed point theorem there is a unique non-empty compact ATTRACTOR K with
    F(K) = K, and Fⁿ(A) → K from any start A, with d_H(Fⁿ(A), K)
    ≤ rⁿ d_H(A, K). The CHAOS GAME draws K by random iteration.
  - JULIA and MANDELBROT sets for f_c(z) = z² + c: the FILLED JULIA SET K_c =
    {z : orbit bounded}, the JULIA SET J_c = ∂K_c. ESCAPE CRITERION: if
    |z| > 2 and |z| ≥ |c| the orbit tends to ∞. The MANDELBROT SET
    M = {c : orbit of 0 bounded} ⊆ {|c| ≤ 2}; M ∩ R = [−2, 1/4]; M is
    connected; J_c is connected ⇔ c ∈ M and is a Cantor set (dust) if c ∉ M.
    J₀ = unit circle, J₋₂ = [−2, 2].
  - The MAIN CARDIOID of M (attracting fixed point, |2z| < 1) is
    c = μ/2 − μ²/4, |μ| < 1; the PERIOD-2 BULB (attracting 2-cycle) is the disc
    |c + 1| < 1/4. Period doubling along R accumulates at the Feigenbaum point
    c ≈ −1.4012.
  - MEASURING dimension in practice: log-log plots of box counts, of measured
    length L(δ) ∝ δ^(1 − D) (Richardson's coastlines, D ≈ 1.25 for the west
    coast of Britain) or of mass M(r) ∝ r^D; the slope estimates D.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Construct the Cantor set C. Show the removed intervals have total length 1,
    that C consists of the numbers with a ternary expansion using only 0 and 2,
    that C is uncountable, and that 1/4 ∈ C although 1/4 is not an endpoint.
    Answer: Removed length ∑ 2ⁿ⁻¹/3ⁿ = 1; C ↔ {0, 2}^N ↔ binary sequences, so
    |C| = |R|; 1/4 = 0.020202...₃.
    Teacher explains: C₀ = [0, 1]; C₁ = [0, 1/3] ∪ [2/3, 1]; C₂ = [0, 1/9] ∪
    [2/9, 1/3] ∪ [2/3, 7/9] ∪ [8/9, 1]; in general Cₙ is 2ⁿ closed intervals of
    length 3⁻ⁿ, and C = ⋂ Cₙ. At step n we remove 2ⁿ⁻¹ open intervals of length
    3⁻ⁿ, so the total removed is
       ∑ (n ≥ 1) 2ⁿ⁻¹/3ⁿ = (1/3)·1/(1 − 2/3) = 1.
    So C has length 0, yet it is far from empty. TERNARY picture: removing
    (1/3, 2/3) removes exactly the numbers whose first ternary digit must be
    1; removing the middle thirds at step n removes those whose n-th digit
    must be 1. (Endpoints have two expansions: 1/3 = 0.1₃ = 0.0222...₃ — use
    the one without 1s.) Hence
       C = {∑ aₖ3⁻ᵏ : aₖ ∈ {0, 2}}.
    The map 0.a₁a₂a₃...₃ ↦ 0.(a₁/2)(a₂/2)...₂ is a surjection from C onto
    [0, 1] (every binary sequence occurs), so C is UNCOUNTABLE — as big as R.
    For 1/4: multiply by 3 repeatedly and take integer parts:
       1/4 → 3/4 (digit 0) → 9/4 = 2 + 1/4 (digit 2) → repeat
    so 1/4 = 0.020202...₃ ∈ C. The endpoints of C all have expansions ending
    in constant 0s or 2s, so 1/4 is not one: C contains far more than the
    endpoints (which are only countably many). Common mistakes: thinking C
    consists only of endpoints; saying 1/3 ∉ C because its expansion 0.1₃ has
    a 1. Now you try: is 1/10 in C? (Yes: 1/10 = 0.00220022...₃)

D2. Prove that C is compact, nowhere dense, perfect and totally disconnected.
    Define the Cantor function F and compute F(1/4), F(1/10), F(1/2) and
    F(2/9). Why is F remarkable?
    Answer: F(1/4) = 1/3, F(1/10) = 1/5, F(1/2) = 1/2, F(2/9) = 1/4. F is
    continuous, increasing, onto [0, 1], with F′ = 0 on the complement of C
    (a set of full measure).
    Teacher explains: COMPACT: each Cₙ is closed, so C = ⋂Cₙ is closed, and
    bounded ⊆ [0, 1] (Heine–Borel). TOTALLY DISCONNECTED: if x < y in C,
    choose n with 3⁻ⁿ < y − x; x and y lie in different intervals of Cₙ, and a
    removed gap between them splits C into two relatively open pieces; so the
    only connected subsets are points. NOWHERE DENSE: C is closed and contains
    no interval (any interval has positive length, C has length 0).
    PERFECT (no isolated points): for x ∈ C and n, the interval of Cₙ
    containing x has an endpoint ≠ x within 3⁻ⁿ, and endpoints lie in C. The
    CANTOR FUNCTION: for x = 0.a₁a₂...₃ ∈ C put
       F(x) = 0.(a₁/2)(a₂/2)(a₃/2)...₂ ;
    on a removed interval F is constant, equal to its value at the ends. So
       F(1/4) = F(0.0202...₃) = 0.0101...₂ = 1/3,
       F(1/10) = F(0.00220022...₃) = 0.00110011...₂ = 3/15 = 1/5,
       F(1/2): 1/2 ∈ (1/3, 2/3), where F = F(1/3) = F(0.0222...₃)
               = 0.0111...₂ = 1/2,
       F(2/9) = F(0.02₃) = 0.01₂ = 1/4.
    F is increasing and continuous (points within 3⁻ⁿ agree in n ternary
    digits, so their images agree in n binary digits: |F(x) − F(y)| ≤ 2⁻ⁿ).
    F is constant on each removed interval, so F′ = 0 on a set of total
    length 1, and still F rises from 0 to 1: the fundamental theorem
    F(1) − F(0) = ∫F′ fails, because F is not absolutely continuous. It is
    even Hölder continuous with exponent ln 2/ln 3 — the Cantor dimension.
    Common mistakes: reading a ternary digit 2 as binary 2 (it becomes 1);
    evaluating F on a gap without converting the left end to 0/2 digits.
    Now you try: F(7/9). (7/9 = 0.21₃ lies in the gap (7/9, 8/9) at its left
    end: 7/9 = 0.2022...₃ ↦ 0.1011...₂ = 3/4)

D3. Starting from an equilateral triangle of side 1, build the Koch snowflake.
    Find the number of sides, the perimeter and the area after n steps, the
    limiting area, and the similarity dimension of the Koch curve.
    Answer: sides 3·4ⁿ, perimeter 3(4/3)ⁿ → ∞, area
    Aₙ = A₀[1 + (3/5)(1 − (4/9)ⁿ)] → (8/5)A₀ = 2√3/5 ≈ 0.6928; dimension
    ln 4/ln 3 ≈ 1.2619.
    Teacher explains: Each step replaces every segment by 4 segments of one
    third its length:
       sides Sₙ = 3·4ⁿ,  side length 3⁻ⁿ,  perimeter Pₙ = 3·(4/3)ⁿ → ∞.
    AREA: at step n + 1 a new small triangle is added on every side, of side
    3⁻⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ and area A₀/9ⁿ⁺¹ (area scales with the square), where
    A₀ = √3/4. So
       Aₙ₊₁ = Aₙ + 3·4ⁿ·A₀/9ⁿ⁺¹ = Aₙ + (A₀/3)(4/9)ⁿ,
       Aₙ = A₀[1 + (1/3)∑ (k = 0 to n − 1)(4/9)ᵏ] = A₀[1 + (3/5)(1 − (4/9)ⁿ)].
    Check: A₁ = (4/3)A₀ (three triangles of area A₀/9), A₂ = (40/27)A₀. The
    limit is A₀(1 + 3/5) = (8/5)A₀ = 8√3/20 = 2√3/5 ≈ 0.6928. The snowflake
    fits in a disc, so the area had to be finite; the boundary is infinitely
    long because it wiggles at every scale. DIMENSION: the Koch curve is 4
    copies of itself at ratio 1/3, so 4(1/3)ˢ = 1, s = ln 4/ln 3 ≈ 1.2619:
    bigger than a curve (1), smaller than a region (2). Its 1-dimensional
    measure (length) is ∞ and its 2-dimensional measure (area) is 0; only in
    dimension 1.2619 is its 'size' finite and positive. Common mistakes:
    adding 3·4ⁿ triangles at step n instead of step n + 1; using ratio 1/4.
    Now you try: the QUADRATIC Koch curve replaces each segment by 8 segments
    of one quarter its length. Its dimension? (ln 8/ln 4 = 3/2)

D4. For the Sierpinski triangle, the Sierpinski carpet and the Menger sponge
    find the number of pieces and the remaining area/volume after n steps, and
    their similarity dimensions. Explain why the dimension lies between the
    topological dimension and that of the space.
    Answer: triangle 3ⁿ pieces, area (3/4)ⁿA₀, s = ln 3/ln 2 ≈ 1.5850; carpet
    8ⁿ, (8/9)ⁿ, s = ln 8/ln 3 ≈ 1.8928; sponge 20ⁿ, (20/27)ⁿ,
    s = ln 20/ln 3 ≈ 2.7268. All measures → 0.
    Teacher explains: SIERPINSKI TRIANGLE: join the midpoints of the sides and
    remove the middle triangle; 3 triangles of half size remain. After n
    steps: 3ⁿ triangles each of area A₀/4ⁿ, total (3/4)ⁿA₀ → 0. Yet the total
    length of the edges, 3ⁿ·3·2⁻ⁿ = 3(3/2)ⁿ, → ∞. Dimension 3(1/2)ˢ = 1,
    s = ln 3/ln 2 ≈ 1.5850. CARPET: divide a square into 9, remove the centre:
    8 pieces at ratio 1/3, area (8/9)ⁿ → 0, s = ln 8/ln 3 ≈ 1.8928. MENGER
    SPONGE: divide a cube into 27, remove the centre cube and the 6 face
    centres (7 cubes): 20 remain, volume (20/27)ⁿ → 0, s = ln 20/ln 3 ≈
    2.7268, while the surface area → ∞. Why between: a self-similar set of
    N pieces at ratio r inside Rᵈ that does not fill space must have N < r⁻ᵈ
    (the pieces fit into the r⁻ᵈ sub-cubes), so s = ln N/ln(1/r) < d. It
    contains curves (the carpet contains the sides of every removed square,
    the Sierpinski triangle all its edges), so s ≥ 1 = topological dimension
    of those sets. The carpet is universal: every compact 1-dimensional plane
    curve embeds in it; the sponge is universal for curves in space. Common
    mistakes: removing 6 cubes instead of 7 from the sponge (the centre also
    goes); computing (8/9)ⁿ as the area removed instead of remaining. Now you
    try: the Vicsek fractal keeps the centre and the 4 corner squares of a
    3 × 3 grid. Its dimension? (ln 5/ln 3 ≈ 1.4650)

D5. Explain why the similarity dimension is defined by N rˢ = 1, and solve the
    Moran equation ∑ rᵢˢ = 1 for a Cantor-like set built from [0, 1] by keeping
    [0, 1/2] and [3/4, 1] at each step. Also for pieces of ratios 1/2, 1/2, 1/4.
    Answer: s = ln((1 + √5)/2)/ln 2 ≈ 0.6942; s = ln(1 + √2)/ln 2 ≈ 1.2716.
    Teacher explains: For a sensible s-dimensional 'size' μ_s (length for
    s = 1, area for s = 2), scaling by λ multiplies μ_s by λˢ: a square scaled
    by 3 has 9 = 3² times the area. If F is the union of N non-overlapping
    copies of itself scaled by r, then μ_s(F) = N rˢ μ_s(F). For
    0 < μ_s(F) < ∞ we need N rˢ = 1, s = ln N/ln(1/r) — for a square
    (N = 4, r = 1/2) this gives 2, as it should. With ratios r₁, ..., r_m the
    same argument gives the MORAN equation ∑ rᵢˢ = 1; the left side decreases
    strictly from m (s = 0) to 0 (s → ∞), so there is exactly one solution.
    First set: keep [0, 1/2] (ratio 1/2) and [3/4, 1] (ratio 1/4):
       (1/2)ˢ + (1/4)ˢ = 1.  Put x = 2⁻ˢ: x + x² = 1,
       x = (√5 − 1)/2,  s = −ln x/ln 2 = ln((1 + √5)/2)/ln 2 ≈ 0.6942.
    (The golden ratio appears; indeed this set is related to binary sequences
    without two consecutive 1s.) Second: 2(1/2)ˢ + (1/4)ˢ = 1, i.e.
    2x + x² = 1, x = √2 − 1, s = ln(1 + √2)/ln 2 ≈ 1.2716 (a planar set). When
    no substitution works, solve numerically: (1/2)ˢ + (1/3)ˢ = 1 gives
    s ≈ 0.7879 (try s = 0.8: 0.5743 + 0.4152 = 0.9895 < 1, so s < 0.8).
    Warning: the formula needs the pieces to be essentially disjoint (OPEN SET
    CONDITION); with heavy overlaps the true dimension is smaller. Common
    mistakes: averaging the ratios (r = 3/8 gives the wrong value 0.7067);
    forgetting a piece. Now you try: ratios 1/3, 1/3, 1/9. (x = 3⁻ˢ:
    2x + x² = 1, s = ln(1 + √2)/ln 3 ≈ 0.8023)

D6. Define box-counting dimension. Compute it for the Cantor set, for
    F = {1/n : n ∈ N} ∪ {0} and for Q ∩ [0, 1], and explain what the last two
    show.
    Answer: ln 2/ln 3; 1/2; 1. Box dimension is not countably stable and does
    not see the difference between a set and its closure.
    Teacher explains: dim_B F = lim ln N_δ(F)/(−ln δ): if about Cδ^(−s) boxes
    of size δ are needed, then ln N_δ = ln C + s ln(1/δ) and the ratio tends to
    s. It suffices to use δ = δₖ → 0 with δₖ₊₁ ≥ cδₖ. CANTOR: with δ = 3⁻ᵏ the
    2ᵏ intervals of Cₖ cover C, and a set of diameter ≤ 3⁻ᵏ meets at most 2
    of them (the gaps are ≥ 3⁻ᵏ), so 2ᵏ⁻¹ ≤ N_δ ≤ 2ᵏ, and
       ln N_δ/(−ln δ) → k ln 2/(k ln 3) = ln 2/ln 3 ≈ 0.6309.
    F = {1/n} ∪ {0}: the gap between 1/n and 1/(n + 1) is 1/(n(n + 1)) ≈ 1/n².
    Given δ, let k ≈ δ^(−1/2) (where the gap equals δ). The points 1/1, ...,
    1/k are more than δ apart: they need k boxes. The rest lies in [0, 1/k],
    covered by (1/k)/δ ≈ δ^(−1/2) boxes. So N_δ ≈ 2δ^(−1/2) and
       dim_B F = 1/2,
    although F is countable! Q ∩ [0, 1] is dense, so every δ-box of [0, 1]
    meets it: N_δ ≈ 1/δ, dim_B = 1. Each single point has box dimension 0, so
    box dimension fails COUNTABLE STABILITY, and dim_B E = dim_B (closure of
    E). Hausdorff dimension repairs both (countable sets have dim_H = 0), at
    the cost of being harder to compute. In practice (computer, data) box
    counting is what one measures. Common mistakes: counting only the points
    1/n and forgetting that near 0 they are packed closer than δ; taking one
    value of δ instead of a limit. Now you try: dim_B {1/n² : n ∈ N}.
    (Gap ≈ 2/n³, k ≈ δ^(−1/3), N_δ ≈ δ^(−1/3): 1/3)

D7. Define the s-dimensional Hausdorff measure and the Hausdorff dimension.
    Show that for the Cantor set Hˢ(C) ≤ 1 when s = ln 2/ln 3 and Hᵗ(C) = 0 for
    t > s, and explain why Hˢ(F) jumps from ∞ to 0.
    Answer: dim_H C = ln 2/ln 3 (in fact Hˢ(C) = 1).
    Teacher explains: For δ > 0,
       Hˢ_δ(F) = inf{∑ |Uᵢ|ˢ : F ⊆ ⋃Uᵢ, diam Uᵢ ≤ δ}   (countable covers),
    and Hˢ(F) = lim (δ → 0) Hˢ_δ(F) (it increases as δ decreases, since fewer
    covers are allowed). Unlike box counting, the covering sets may have
    DIFFERENT sizes — this is what makes countable sets negligible. JUMP: if
    t > s and the Uᵢ have diameter ≤ δ, then ∑|Uᵢ|ᵗ ≤ δ^(t − s)∑|Uᵢ|ˢ, so
    Hᵗ_δ(F) ≤ δ^(t − s)Hˢ_δ(F). If Hˢ(F) < ∞, letting δ → 0 gives Hᵗ(F) = 0.
    Hence there is a critical value
       dim_H F = inf{s : Hˢ(F) = 0} = sup{s : Hˢ(F) = ∞},
    at which Hˢ may be 0, finite, or ∞. CANTOR: cover C by the 2ᵏ intervals
    of Cₖ, each of diameter 3⁻ᵏ:
       ∑|Uᵢ|ˢ = 2ᵏ·3^(−ks) = (2·3⁻ˢ)ᵏ = 1   when 3ˢ = 2.
    So Hˢ_δ(C) ≤ 1 for δ = 3⁻ᵏ, and Hˢ(C) ≤ 1; thus dim_H C ≤ s. For t > s,
    ∑ = (2·3⁻ᵗ)ᵏ → 0, giving Hᵗ(C) = 0 directly. The lower bound needs an
    argument that NO cover does better: spread a unit mass evenly over C
    (mass 2⁻ᵏ on each interval of Cₖ) and show that every set U carries mass
    at most a constant times |U|ˢ (the MASS DISTRIBUTION PRINCIPLE). This
    gives Hˢ(C) ≥ 1/2 > 0, so dim_H C = ln 2/ln 3 exactly. In general upper
    bounds come from clever covers, lower bounds from measures spread over
    the set. Common mistakes:
    thinking one cover gives the value (it only gives an upper bound);
    forgetting the limit δ → 0. Now you try: why is H⁰(F) the number of
    points of F? (∑|Uᵢ|⁰ counts the covering sets, and for small δ each point
    needs its own set.)

D8. Using the properties of Hausdorff dimension find dim_H of: Q; the
    irrationals in [0, 1]; C ∪ [2, 3]; C × C; C × [0, 1]; the image of C under
    x ↦ 5x + 1; the graph of a C¹ function on [0, 1]; the unit sphere in R³.
    Answer: 0; 1; 1; 2 ln 2/ln 3 ≈ 1.2619; 1 + ln 2/ln 3 ≈ 1.6309;
    ln 2/ln 3; 1; 2.
    Teacher explains: The toolbox:
       monotone:            E ⊆ F ⇒ dim E ≤ dim F
       countably stable:    dim ⋃Fᵢ = sup dim Fᵢ
       Lipschitz f:         dim f(F) ≤ dim F; bi-Lipschitz: equal
       open sets of Rⁿ:     dimension n
    Q is a countable union of points (dimension 0 each): dim Q = 0. [0, 1]
    = (Q ∩ [0, 1]) ∪ irrationals, so 1 = max(0, dim irrationals): dim = 1.
    C ∪ [2, 3]: max(0.6309, 1) = 1. x ↦ 5x + 1 is a similarity (bi-Lipschitz):
    dimension unchanged, although H^s is multiplied by 5ˢ. The graph of a C¹
    function g is the image of [0, 1] under x ↦ (x, g(x)), which is
    bi-Lipschitz (constants 1 and √(1 + max g′²)): dimension 1. The sphere is
    locally a bi-Lipschitz image of a disc: 2. PRODUCTS: C × C (Cantor dust)
    is self-similar with 4 pieces at ratio 1/3: ln 4/ln 3 = 2 ln 2/ln 3 ≈
    1.2619 = dim C + dim C; C × [0, 1] is 1 + ln 2/ln 3 ≈ 1.6309. (For general
    sets only dim(E × F) ≥ dim E + dim F holds; equality needs regularity,
    e.g. equal Hausdorff and box dimension for one factor.) Contrast with
    TOPOLOGICAL dimension: C and C × C both have dim_T = 0 (totally
    disconnected), and dim_T ≤ dim_H always; Mandelbrot's definition of a
    fractal was dim_H > dim_T. Common mistakes: adding dimensions for unions
    (take the maximum); thinking a dimension-0 set must be countable (there are
    uncountable sets of dimension 0, e.g. the Liouville numbers). Now you try:
    dim_H of the set of x ∈ [0, 1] whose decimal expansion has no digit 7.
    (Self-similar with 9 pieces of ratio 1/10: ln 9/ln 10 ≈ 0.9542)

D9. Define the Hausdorff metric and the Hutchinson operator of an IFS, and
    prove that the operator is a contraction. For the IFS f₁(x) = x/3,
    f₂(x) = x/3 + 2/3 starting from [0, 1], find d_H(Fⁿ[0, 1], C). Give an IFS
    for the Sierpinski triangle and describe the chaos game.
    Answer: d_H(Cₙ, C) = 1/(2·3ⁿ⁺¹) = (1/3)ⁿ·(1/6); Sierpinski:
    fᵢ(x) = (x + vᵢ)/2 for the three vertices vᵢ.
    Teacher explains: For non-empty compact A, B,
       d_H(A, B) = max{ sup(a ∈ A) d(a, B), sup(b ∈ B) d(b, A) }
    = the least ε such that each set lies in the ε-neighbourhood of the other.
    E.g. d_H({0}, [0, 1]) = 1, d_H({0, 1}, [0, 1]) = 1/2. The compact sets with
    d_H form a complete metric space. If each fᵢ is a contraction with ratio
    rᵢ, and r = max rᵢ < 1, then for F(A) = ⋃fᵢ(A):
       d_H(F(A), F(B)) ≤ max d_H(fᵢ(A), fᵢ(B)) ≤ max rᵢ d_H(A, B) = r d_H(A, B)
    (a point fᵢ(a) of F(A) is within rᵢ d_H(A, B) of fᵢ(B) ⊆ F(B), and
    symmetrically). BANACH: there is a unique compact K ≠ ∅ with F(K) = K, and
    d_H(Fⁿ(A), K) ≤ rⁿ d_H(A, K). For the Cantor IFS, Fⁿ([0, 1]) = Cₙ and
    K = C (it satisfies C = C/3 ∪ (C/3 + 2/3)). d_H([0, 1], C) = 1/6: the worst
    point is 1/2, at distance 1/6 from 1/3 and 2/3. So
       d_H(Cₙ, C) ≤ (1/3)ⁿ/6 = 1/(2·3ⁿ⁺¹),
    and equality holds: the centre of a removed interval of length 3⁻⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ is
    that far from C. SIERPINSKI: with vertices v₁ = (0, 0), v₂ = (1, 0),
    v₃ = (0, 1), fᵢ(x) = (x + vᵢ)/2 (move halfway to vᵢ). CHAOS GAME: start
    anywhere, repeatedly pick i at random and apply fᵢ; after a few steps
    every point lies within tiny distance of K, and the orbit fills K
    densely — the 'random' dots draw the Sierpinski triangle. An IFS is a
    tiny program for a complicated picture (Barnsley's fern uses 4 affine
    maps). Common mistakes: taking d_H as the smallest distance between the
    sets (d_H({0}, [0, 1]) is 1, not 0); forgetting that the attractor does not
    depend on the starting set. Now you try: the attractor of x/2 and
    x/2 + 1/2 on R. ([0, 1])

D10. For fc(z) = z² + c prove the escape criterion: if |z| > 2 and |z| ≥ |c|
     then |fcⁿ(z)| → ∞. Deduce M ⊆ {|c| ≤ 2}. Decide which of c = 1, −1, −2, i,
     1/4, 0.3 lie in the Mandelbrot set.
     Answer: 1 ∉ M, −1 ∈ M, −2 ∈ M, i ∈ M, 1/4 ∈ M, 0.3 ∉ M.
     Teacher explains: Let |z| = 2 + ε with ε > 0 and |c| ≤ |z|. Then
        |z² + c| ≥ |z|² − |c| ≥ |z|² − |z| = |z|(|z| − 1) = (1 + ε)|z|.
     The new point again satisfies |z| > 2 ≥ ... and |z| ≥ |c| (it only grew),
     so by induction |fcⁿ(z)| ≥ (1 + ε)ⁿ|z| → ∞. If |c| > 2 the orbit of 0 is
     0, c, ..., and z₁ = c already satisfies the criterion: c ∉ M. For
     |c| ≤ 2 the criterion becomes simply: once |zₙ| > 2, the orbit escapes.
     That is how computer pictures are made. Orbits of 0:
        c = 1:   0, 1, 2, 5, 26, ...            escapes    1 ∉ M
        c = −1:  0, −1, 0, −1, ...              period 2   ∈ M
        c = −2:  0, −2, 2, 2, 2, ...            fixed      ∈ M
        c = i:   0, i, −1 + i, −i, −1 + i, ...  period 2 after one step ∈ M
        c = 1/4: 0, 0.25, 0.3125, 0.3477, ... increases to 1/2 (the fixed
                 point of z² + 1/4, z = 1/2 double)                ∈ M
        c = 0.3: 0, 0.3, 0.39, 0.4521, 0.5044, ... no fixed point (z² − z +
                 0.3 = 0 has no real root), exceeds 2 at step 12     ∉ M
     For real c the orbit of 0 is bounded exactly for −2 ≤ c ≤ 1/4:
     M ∩ R = [−2, 1/4]. c = 1/4 is the CUSP of the main cardioid. Common
     mistakes: iterating from z₀ = c and z₀ = 0 inconsistently (either is fine
     — it only shifts the count by one); thinking the orbit must converge
     (bounded is enough). Now you try: is c = 1 + i in M? (0, 1 + i, 1 + 3i:
     |1 + 3i| = √10 > 2: no)

D11. Find the region of c for which z² + c has an attracting fixed point (the
     main cardioid) and the region with an attracting 2-cycle. Classify
     c = −1/2, −3/4, −1.2, −1.3, 1/4, 1/4 + i/2. Describe J_c for c = 0 and
     c = −2.
     Answer: cardioid c = μ/2 − μ²/4, |μ| < 1; 2-cycle disc |c + 1| < 1/4.
     −1/2: attracting fixed point; −3/4: on the boundary between cardioid and
     disc; −1.2: attracting 2-cycle; −1.3: neither (period 4 region);
     1/4: cusp, neutral fixed point; 1/4 + i/2: boundary of the cardioid
     (μ = i). J₀ = unit circle, J₋₂ = [−2, 2].
     Teacher explains: A fixed point z* = z*² + c is ATTRACTING when
     |f′(z*)| = |2z*| < 1. Write μ = 2z* (the multiplier); then z* = μ/2 and
        c = z* − z*² = μ/2 − μ²/4,   |μ| < 1.
     As μ = e^(iθ) runs round the unit circle this traces a CARDIOID with cusp
     at c = 1/4 (μ = 1) and leftmost point −3/4 (μ = −1). Period 2: the points
     with fc(fc(z)) = z but fc(z) ≠ z satisfy
        (z⁴ + 2cz² + c² + c − z)/(z² − z + c) = z² + z + c + 1 = 0,
     so z₁ + z₂ = −1, z₁z₂ = c + 1, and the multiplier of the cycle is
     f′(z₁)f′(z₂) = 4z₁z₂ = 4(c + 1): attracting ⇔ |c + 1| < 1/4, a disc of
     radius 1/4 touching the cardioid at −3/4. Now:
        c = −1/2:  z² − z − 1/2 = 0, z* = (1 − √3)/2, μ = 1 − √3 ≈ −0.732,
                   |μ| < 1: attracting fixed point.
        c = −3/4:  μ = −1 and also |c + 1| = 1/4: the meeting point.
        c = −1.2:  |c + 1| = 0.2 < 1/4: attracting 2-cycle.
        c = −1.3:  |c + 1| = 0.3 > 1/4: the 2-cycle repels (period doubling at
                   c = −5/4); here a 4-cycle attracts.
        c = 1/4 + i/2: μ = i gives c = i/2 − i²/4 = 1/4 + i/2, |μ| = 1.
     Julia sets: c = 0, z ↦ z²: |z| < 1 goes to 0, |z| > 1 to ∞, so K₀ is the
     closed disc and J₀ the unit circle (dimension 1, a smooth curve). For
     c = −2, the substitution z = 2 cos θ gives z² − 2 = 2 cos 2θ, so [−2, 2]
     is invariant and J₋₂ = [−2, 2]. For other c, J_c is a genuine fractal
     (e.g. c = i: a dendrite; c = −1: the 'basilica'). Common mistakes:
     using |z*| < 1 instead of |2z*| < 1; forgetting to discard the fixed
     points when looking for 2-cycles. Now you try: the multiplier of the
     2-cycle when c = −1. (4(−1 + 1) = 0: superattracting; the cycle is 0, −1)

D12. A coastline is measured with rulers of length δ = 100, 50, 25, 12.5 km
     giving lengths L = 1600, 1903, 2263, 2691 km. Estimate its fractal
     dimension. Also, box counts for a set in the plane give N(1/3) = 8 and
     N(1/27) = 512: estimate its dimension. Explain the methods.
     Answer: D ≈ 1.25; D = ln 64/ln 9 = ln 8/ln 3 ≈ 1.8928.
     Teacher explains: RICHARDSON'S LAW: for a curve of dimension D the number
     of rulers of length δ needed is N(δ) ≈ Cδ^(−D), so the measured length is
        L(δ) = δN(δ) ≈ Cδ^(1 − D).
     On a log-log plot, ln L against ln δ is a line of slope 1 − D. Here each
     halving of δ multiplies L by
        1903/1600 ≈ 2263/1903 ≈ 2691/2263 ≈ 1.189 = 2^0.25,
     so L ∝ δ^(−0.25), 1 − D = −0.25, D ≈ 1.25 — Richardson's value for the
     west coast of Britain. A smooth coast would give constant L (D = 1). The
     'length of a coastline' has no meaning without the scale. BOX COUNTING:
     the slope between two scales,
        D ≈ ln(N₂/N₁)/ln(δ₁/δ₂) = ln(512/8)/ln(27/3) = ln 64/ln 9 = ln 8/ln 3
          ≈ 1.8928,
     the carpet's value. With real data use many scales and a least-squares
     line, and ignore the smallest and largest scales, where resolution and
     finite size spoil the power law. MASS–RADIUS: count points M(r) within
     radius r of a point of the set; M ∝ r^D (for diffusion-limited
     aggregation in the plane D ≈ 1.7). Common mistakes: using the slope of L
     directly as D (it is 1 − D); fitting one scale only. Now you try: box
     counts N(0.1) = 40, N(0.01) = 800. (D ≈ ln 20/ln 10 ≈ 1.3010)

       g) 4(c + 1)
       h) {0, −1}; 0 (superattracting)
       i) yes (|c + 1| = 0.2 < 1/4)
       j) no (|c + 1| = 0.3 > 1/4)
       k) −5/4 and −3/4
       l) [−2, 1/4]
       m) the unit circle; [−2, 2]
       n) 3 (= max(2, |c|))
       o) yes (c ∈ M, a dendrite); no (c ∉ M, a Cantor set)
       p) c ≈ −1.4012; δ ≈ 4.6692

M11. Dimension from data and scaling.
     a) N(1/2) = 3, N(1/4) = 9
     b) N(1/3) = 4, N(1/9) = 16
     c) N(0.1) = 40, N(0.01) = 800
     d) N(1/3) = 8, N(1/27) = 512
     e) coastline: L(1 km) = 1000 km, L(0.1 km) = 1500 km
     f) coastline: L(δ) ∝ δ^(−0.26)
     g) coastline data L = 1600, 1903, 2263, 2691 at δ = 100, 50, 25, 12.5
     h) mass–radius: M(1) = 100, M(10) = 5000
     i) mass–radius: M(r) ∝ r^1.71 — dimension?
     j) factor by which the s-measure of the Koch curve grows when scaled by 3
     k) same for the Sierpinski triangle scaled by 2
     l) same for the Menger sponge scaled by 3
     m) factor for the Cantor set scaled by 9
     n) number of copies at ratio 1/5 for a self-similar set with D = 1.5
     o) ruler length needed to measure 3× the length of δ = 1 for D = 1.25
     Answers:
       a) ln 3/ln 2 ≈ 1.5850      b) ln 4/ln 3 ≈ 1.2619
       c) ln 20/ln 10 ≈ 1.3010    d) ln 8/ln 3 ≈ 1.8928
       e) 1 + log₁₀ 1.5 ≈ 1.1761  f) 1.26
       g) 1.25                    h) log₁₀ 50 ≈ 1.6990
       i) 1.71                    j) 4
       k) 3                       l) 20
       m) 4                       n) 5^1.5 ≈ 11.18 (not an integer: no exact
                                     construction with equal pieces)
       o) δ = 3^(−4) = 1/81 (L ∝ δ^(−1/4))

M12. True (T) or false (F)?
     a) The Cantor set is uncountable.
     b) The Cantor set contains an interval.
     c) The Cantor set has Lebesgue measure 0.
     d) The Koch snowflake has finite area and infinite perimeter.
     e) Every fractal is exactly self-similar.
     f) Box-counting dimension is countably stable.
     g) Hausdorff dimension is countably stable.
     h) dim_H F ≤ lower box dimension of F.
     i) Every set of Hausdorff dimension 0 is countable.
     j) Lipschitz maps cannot increase Hausdorff dimension.
     k) dim_T F ≤ dim_H F.
     l) The Mandelbrot set is connected.
     m) The boundary of the Mandelbrot set has Hausdorff dimension 2.
     n) J_c is connected if and only if c ∈ M.
     o) For c ∉ M, J_c is totally disconnected.
     p) The Cantor function has derivative 0 almost everywhere.
     q) C + C = {x + y : x, y ∈ C} = [0, 2].
     r) The Sierpinski triangle has zero area.
     s) The Menger sponge has zero volume and infinite surface area.
     t) C is homeomorphic to C × C.
     u) Similarity dimension always equals Hausdorff dimension.
     v) A self-similar set in R² made of N copies of ratio r with N r² > 1
        cannot satisfy the open set condition.
     Answers:
       a) T   b) F   c) T   d) T   e) F   f) F   g) T   h) T
       i) F (Liouville numbers)   j) T   k) T   l) T
       m) T (Shishikura)   n) T   o) T   p) T   q) T   r) T   s) T
       t) T   u) F (needs the open set condition)   v) T

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build the first three stages of every fractal by hand (Cantor
  on a ruler, Koch and Sierpinski on squared paper) and tabulate pieces,
  scale and length/area in columns — the pattern Nrˢ = 1 then appears by
  itself. Practise ternary expansions (multiply by 3, take integer parts)
  before any Cantor-set question. For box counting draw the grid and count;
  then plot ln N against ln(1/δ) and read the slope. For Mandelbrot questions
  compute the first five iterates in a table and stop as soon as |z| > 2.
  Harder: prove Hˢ(C) ≥ 1/2 with the mass distribution principle; show
  C + C = [0, 2]; prove the Hutchinson operator is a contraction and that
  the attractor of a similarity IFS with the open set condition has
  dim_H = similarity dimension; show that the Cantor function is Hölder with
  exponent ln 2/ln 3 but not better; prove that J_c is a Cantor set for
  |c| > 2; and program the chaos game and a Mandelbrot plot, estimating the
  box dimension of the Julia set of z² − 1 from the output.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.32 — PARTIAL DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS: HEAT, WAVE, LAPLACE EQUATIONS;
SEPARATION OF VARIABLES; METHOD OF CHARACTERISTICS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A PDE relates a function of several variables to its partial derivatives.
    ORDER = highest derivative. LINEAR (u and its derivatives appear linearly,
    coefficients depend only on the variables), SEMILINEAR, QUASILINEAR
    (linear in the highest derivatives, e.g. u_t + uu_x = 0) or fully
    NONLINEAR. For linear HOMOGENEOUS equations SUPERPOSITION holds. A problem
    is WELL-POSED (Hadamard) if a solution exists, is unique and depends
    continuously on the data.
  - CLASSIFICATION of Au_xx + Bu_xy + Cu_yy + (lower order) = 0 by the
    DISCRIMINANT B² − 4AC: > 0 HYPERBOLIC (wave, canonical u_ξη = ...),
    = 0 PARABOLIC (heat), < 0 ELLIPTIC (Laplace). CHARACTERISTICS solve
    A(dy/dx)² − B(dy/dx) + C = 0; the type can change from region to region
    (Tricomi yu_xx + u_yy = 0).
  - HEAT (diffusion) EQUATION u_t = ku_xx. On 0 < x < L with u(0, t) =
    u(L, t) = 0, u(x, 0) = f(x):
       u = ∑ bₙ e^(−k(nπ/L)²t) sin(nπx/L),   bₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx.
    High modes die fastest; u → 0. Insulated ends (u_x = 0) give a cosine
    series and u → the MEAN a₀/2 of f. Non-zero boundary values: subtract the
    STEADY STATE (a straight line for constant end temperatures).
  - HEAT properties: MAXIMUM PRINCIPLE (max of u on the closed rectangle is
    attained at t = 0 or on the ends), hence uniqueness; ENERGY ∫u² decreases;
    on R, u = (4πkt)^(−1/2)∫ e^(−(x−y)²/(4kt)) f(y) dy (HEAT KERNEL,
    Gaussian of variance 2kt): infinitely smooth for t > 0, infinite speed of
    propagation; the BACKWARD heat equation is ill-posed.
  - WAVE EQUATION u_tt = c²u_xx. On R, D'ALEMBERT:
       u = ½[f(x − ct) + f(x + ct)] + (1/(2c))∫ (x−ct to x+ct) g(s) ds
    (u(x, 0) = f, u_t(x, 0) = g): two waves travelling at speed c. DOMAIN OF
    DEPENDENCE of (x, t) is [x − ct, x + ct]; finite speed; singularities
    travel along characteristics x ± ct = const. Energy
    E = ½∫(u_t² + c²u_x²) dx is conserved.
  - STRING with fixed ends u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0:
       u = ∑ [aₙ cos(nπct/L) + bₙ sin(nπct/L)] sin(nπx/L),
       aₙ = (2/L)∫ f sin(nπx/L), bₙ = (2/(nπc))∫ g sin(nπx/L).
    NORMAL MODES with frequencies nc/(2L) (fundamental c/(2L)), nodes at
    x = mL/n; the motion is periodic with period 2L/c. Equivalent to
    d'Alembert with the ODD 2L-periodic extension of f and g.
  - LAPLACE EQUATION ∇²u = 0 (harmonic functions; steady heat, potentials).
    MEAN VALUE PROPERTY (u(centre) = average over any circle), MAXIMUM
    PRINCIPLE (max and min on the boundary), uniqueness of the DIRICHLET
    problem; the NEUMANN problem needs ∮ ∂u/∂n ds = 0 and fixes u up to a
    constant. Rectangle: products sin(nπx/a) sinh(nπy/a). Disc of radius a:
       u = a₀/2 + ∑ (r/a)ⁿ(aₙ cos nθ + bₙ sin nθ)
    with aₙ, bₙ the Fourier coefficients of the boundary data (POISSON integral).
  - SEPARATION OF VARIABLES: try u = X(x)T(t); the PDE splits into ODEs linked
    by a SEPARATION CONSTANT −λ; the boundary conditions give a STURM–LIOUVILLE
    eigenvalue problem X″ + λX = 0:
       X(0) = X(L) = 0:     λ = (nπ/L)², sin(nπx/L), n ≥ 1
       X′(0) = X′(L) = 0:   λ = (nπ/L)², cos(nπx/L), n ≥ 0 (λ = 0 allowed)
       X(0) = X′(L) = 0:    λ = ((2n − 1)π/(2L))², sin((2n − 1)πx/(2L))
       periodic, period 2π: λ = n², cos nx and sin nx.
    Eigenfunctions are ORTHOGONAL; expand the data in them (FOURIER SERIES)
    and superpose. In polar coordinates Θ″ + n²Θ = 0 and the EULER equation
    r²R″ + rR′ − n²R = 0 (R = rⁿ, r⁻ⁿ; 1, ln r if n = 0).
  - FOURIER SERIES facts: on (0, π), 1 = (4/π)∑(odd n) sin nx/n,
    x = 2∑(−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n, x(π − x) = (8/π)∑(odd n) sin nx/n³; on (−π, π),
    x² = π²/3 + 4∑(−1)ⁿ cos nx/n². At a jump the series converges to the
    average (GIBBS overshoot ≈ 9% of the jump).
  - METHOD OF CHARACTERISTICS for a(x, y)u_x + b(x, y)u_y = c(x, y, u):
    along curves with dx/ds = a, dy/ds = b the PDE becomes the ODE
    du/ds = c. Transport u_t + cu_x = 0: u = f(x − ct). u_t + xu_x = 0:
    u = f(xe^(−t)). The general solution contains an arbitrary function of the
    characteristic constant; the data curve must cross each characteristic
    once (not be characteristic).
  - QUASILINEAR / BURGERS u_t + uu_x = 0, u(x, 0) = f(x): u is constant on the
    straight characteristics x = x₀ + f(x₀)t, so u = f(x − ut) implicitly.
    Characteristics cross (a SHOCK forms) at the BREAKING TIME
    t* = −1/min f′ (if f′ < 0 somewhere). Shocks move with the
    RANKINE–HUGONIOT speed s = [F(u)]/[u] = (u_L + u_R)/2 (for flux u²/2) and
    are admissible only if u_L > u_R; for u_L < u_R a RAREFACTION FAN
    u = x/t fills the gap.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Classify u_xx + 4u_xy + 3u_yy = 0, find its characteristics, reduce it to
    canonical form and find the general solution. Then classify the Tricomi
    equation yu_xx + u_yy = 0.
    Answer: hyperbolic; characteristics y − x = const, y − 3x = const;
    u_ξη = 0 with ξ = y − x, η = y − 3x; u = F(y − x) + G(y − 3x). Tricomi:
    elliptic for y > 0, parabolic on y = 0, hyperbolic for y < 0.
    Teacher explains: A = 1, B = 4, C = 3: B² − 4AC = 16 − 12 = 4 > 0, so
    HYPERBOLIC (like the wave equation). Characteristic slopes solve
       (dy/dx)² − 4(dy/dx) + 3 = 0  ⇒  dy/dx = 1 or 3,
    so the characteristics are the lines y − x = const and y − 3x = const. Take
    them as new coordinates ξ = y − x, η = y − 3x. By the chain rule
    ∂ₓ = −∂_ξ − 3∂_η, ∂ᵧ = ∂_ξ + ∂_η, and
       u_xx = u_ξξ + 6u_ξη + 9u_ηη,  u_xy = −u_ξξ − 4u_ξη − 3u_ηη,
       u_yy = u_ξξ + 2u_ξη + u_ηη.
    In u_xx + 4u_xy + 3u_yy collect the coefficients:
       u_ξξ: 1 − 4 + 3 = 0;  u_ηη: 9 − 12 + 3 = 0;  u_ξη: 6 − 16 + 6 = −4,
    so the equation becomes −4u_ξη = 0, i.e. u_ξη = 0: integrate in η then ξ:
       u = F(ξ) + G(η) = F(y − x) + G(y − 3x)
    with F, G arbitrary (twice differentiable). Check G(y − 3x): u_xx = 9G″,
    u_xy = −3G″, u_yy = G″: 9 − 12 + 3 = 0 ✓. The wave equation is the case
    u = F(x − ct) + G(x + ct). Tricomi: A = y, B = 0, C = 1, B² − 4AC = −4y:
    the type depends on the region — it models transonic flow (subsonic =
    elliptic, supersonic = hyperbolic). Common mistakes: using B² − AC (that is
    the rule when the middle term is written 2Bu_xy); forgetting the
    coefficient 4 is the full B. Now you try: classify
    u_xx − 6u_xy + 10u_yy = 0. (36 − 40 = −4 < 0: elliptic)

D2. Solve the eigenvalue problem X″ + λX = 0, X(0) = X(L) = 0, showing that
    λ ≤ 0 gives nothing. List the eigenvalues for Neumann, mixed and periodic
    conditions, prove orthogonality of sin(nπx/L), and write the formula for
    Fourier sine coefficients. Find the sine series of f(x) = 1 on (0, π).
    Answer: λₙ = (nπ/L)², Xₙ = sin(nπx/L); 1 = (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x/3 +
    sin 5x/5 + ...).
    Teacher explains: Three cases for the sign of λ.
       λ = −μ² < 0: X = A cosh μx + B sinh μx; X(0) = 0 ⇒ A = 0;
                    X(L) = B sinh μL = 0 ⇒ B = 0 (sinh μL ≠ 0).
       λ = 0:       X = A + Bx; X(0) = X(L) = 0 ⇒ A = B = 0.
       λ = μ² > 0:  X = A cos μx + B sin μx; A = 0; B sin μL = 0 with B ≠ 0
                    ⇒ μL = nπ.
    So λₙ = (nπ/L)², Xₙ = sin(nπx/L), n = 1, 2, 3, .... With X′(0) = X′(L) = 0
    one gets cos(nπx/L), n = 0, 1, 2, ... (λ = 0, X = 1 now survives); with
    X(0) = 0, X′(L) = 0: cos μL = 0, μ = (2n − 1)π/(2L); periodic on
    (−π, π): λ = n², both cos nx and sin nx. ORTHOGONALITY: for m ≠ n
       ∫₀ᴸ sin(mπx/L) sin(nπx/L) dx = ½∫₀ᴸ [cos((m − n)πx/L)
                                     − cos((m + n)πx/L)] dx = 0,
    while ∫₀ᴸ sin²(nπx/L) dx = L/2. (General reason: X″ + λX = 0 with these
    conditions is self-adjoint.) So if f = ∑ bₙ sin(nπx/L), multiply by
    sin(mπx/L) and integrate: bₘ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f sin(mπx/L) dx. For f = 1,
    L = π:
       bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π sin nx dx = (2/π)(1 − cos nπ)/n = 4/(nπ) (n odd), 0 (even).
    At x = π/2 this gives 1 = (4/π)(1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ...), Leibniz's
    π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − .... At x = 0 and π the series gives 0 (the odd
    extension jumps there), and near the jumps partial sums overshoot to
    ≈ 1.179 (GIBBS). Common mistakes: forgetting λ = 0 in the Neumann case;
    using (1/L) instead of (2/L). Now you try: the sine series of x on
    (0, π). (2(sin x − sin 2x/2 + sin 3x/3 − ...))

D3. Solve u_t = u_xx on 0 < x < π with u(0, t) = u(π, t) = 0 and (a)
    u(x, 0) = 3 sin x − sin 4x, (b) u(x, 0) = 1. In (b) find u(π/2, 1) and
    describe the long-time behaviour.
    Answer: (a) u = 3e^(−t) sin x − e^(−16t) sin 4x. (b) u = (4/π)∑(n odd)
    e^(−n²t) sin nx/n; u(π/2, 1) ≈ 0.4683; u ≈ (4/π)e^(−t) sin x for large t.
    Teacher explains: SEPARATE: u = X(x)T(t) gives XT′ = X″T, so
       T′/T = X″/X = −λ   (a constant: the left side depends on t only, the
                          middle on x only).
    X″ + λX = 0 with X(0) = X(π) = 0 gives λ = n², X = sin nx (D2), and
    T′ = −n²T gives T = e^(−n²t). Every uₙ = e^(−n²t) sin nx solves the PDE and
    the boundary conditions, so by superposition
       u = ∑ bₙ e^(−n²t) sin nx,   with ∑ bₙ sin nx = u(x, 0).
    (a) The data is already a sine series: b₁ = 3, b₄ = −1, so
       u = 3e^(−t) sin x − e^(−16t) sin 4x.
    Check: u_t = −3e^(−t) sin x + 16e^(−16t) sin 4x = u_xx ✓. (b) bₙ = 4/(nπ) for
    odd n (D2):
       u(x, t) = (4/π)[e^(−t) sin x + e^(−9t) sin 3x/3 + e^(−25t) sin 5x/5 + ...]
       u(π/2, 1) = (4/π)[e^(−1) − e^(−9)/3 + e^(−25)/5 − ...]
                 ≈ (4/π)(0.367879 − 0.000041) ≈ 0.4683.
    For t > 0 the series converges extremely fast (e^(−n²t)), so u is smooth
    even though the data jumps at the ends: DIFFUSION SMOOTHS. After a short
    time only the first mode matters, u ≈ (4/π)e^(−t) sin x, decaying at rate
    λ₁ = 1 (in general kπ²/L²: a rod twice as long cools four times slower).
    Common mistakes: writing e^(−nt) instead of e^(−n²t); dropping the factor
    1/n from bₙ. Now you try: u(x, 0) = sin³x = (3 sin x − sin 3x)/4.
    (u = (3e^(−t) sin x − e^(−9t) sin 3x)/4)

D4. (a) Solve u_t = u_xx, 0 < x < 1, u(0, t) = 0, u(1, t) = 10, u(x, 0) = 0.
    (b) Solve u_t = u_xx, 0 < x < π, with insulated ends u_x(0, t) = u_x(π, t)
    = 0 and u(x, 0) = x, and show the mean temperature is conserved.
    Answer: (a) u = 10x + ∑ (20(−1)ⁿ/(nπ)) e^(−n²π²t) sin nπx → 10x.
    (b) u = π/2 − (4/π)∑(n odd) e^(−n²t) cos nx/n² → π/2.
    Teacher explains: (a) Separation needs HOMOGENEOUS boundary conditions, so
    first remove the boundary values with the STEADY STATE w(x): w″ = 0,
    w(0) = 0, w(1) = 10 ⇒ w = 10x. Put v = u − w. Then v_t = v_xx,
    v(0, t) = v(1, t) = 0 and v(x, 0) = −10x. Sine coefficients on (0, 1):
       bₙ = 2∫₀¹ (−10x) sin nπx dx = −20·(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/(nπ) = 20(−1)ⁿ/(nπ)
    (∫₀¹ x sin nπx dx = (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/(nπ)). So
       u = 10x − (20/π)[e^(−π²t) sin πx − e^(−4π²t) sin 2πx/2 + ...],
    b₁ ≈ −6.366, b₂ ≈ 3.183, b₃ ≈ −2.122. As t → ∞, u → 10x: heat flows in
    at x = 1 and the profile straightens. (b) Separation with X′(0) = X′(π)
    = 0 gives cos nx, n ≥ 0, and u = a₀/2 + ∑ aₙ e^(−n²t) cos nx with the
    cosine coefficients of x:
       a₀ = (2/π)∫₀^π x dx = π,  aₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x cos nx dx
          = 2((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(πn²) = −4/(πn²) (n odd), 0 (n even).
    So u → a₀/2 = π/2, the AVERAGE of the initial temperature. Directly:
       d/dt ∫₀^π u dx = ∫₀^π u_xx dx = u_x(π, t) − u_x(0, t) = 0
    — no heat crosses the insulated ends, so the total heat is constant.
    Common mistakes: applying separation straight to non-zero boundary data;
    in (b) using a sine series (it does not satisfy u_x = 0); forgetting the
    constant term a₀/2. Now you try: steady state for u(0) = 20, u(π) = 50.
    (w = 20 + 30x/π)

D5. Prove the maximum principle for u_t = ku_xx on [0, L] × [0, T] and deduce
    uniqueness; give the energy proof of uniqueness too. Solve the heat
    equation on R with u(x, 0) = e^(−x²) and comment on the properties of the
    heat kernel.
    Answer: u = (1 + 4kt)^(−1/2) exp(−x²/(1 + 4kt)).
    Teacher explains: MAXIMUM PRINCIPLE: the maximum of u over the closed
    rectangle is attained on the 'parabolic boundary' (t = 0, x = 0 or
    x = L). Proof: let v = u + εx² (ε > 0), so v_t − kv_xx = −2kε < 0. If v had
    its max at an interior point or on the top t = T, there v_t ≥ 0 and
    v_xx ≤ 0, so v_t − kv_xx ≥ 0: contradiction. Hence
    max u ≤ max v ≤ M + εL², where M is the max of u on the parabolic
    boundary; let ε → 0. UNIQUENESS: if u₁, u₂ have the same data, w = u₁ − u₂
    has zero data, so max w ≤ 0 and (applied to −w) min w ≥ 0: w = 0.
    ENERGY: for Dirichlet conditions put E(t) = ∫₀ᴸ w² dx; then
       E′ = 2∫ w w_t = 2k∫ w w_xx = −2k∫ w_x² ≤ 0   (integrate by parts),
    and E(0) = 0, E ≥ 0 force E ≡ 0. On R the solution is the convolution
    with the HEAT KERNEL
       Φ(x, t) = (4πkt)^(−1/2) e^(−x²/(4kt)),  ∫Φ dx = 1, variance 2kt.
    For f = e^(−x²) (a Gaussian of variance 1/2) the variances add:
    1/2 + 2kt = (1 + 4kt)/2, and mass ∫f = √π is conserved, so
       u = (1 + 4kt)^(−1/2) exp(−x²/(1 + 4kt)).
    Check: at t = 0 it is e^(−x²) ✓; u(0, t) = (1 + 4kt)^(−1/2) decays like
    t^(−1/2). Properties: for t > 0 u is C^∞ even for rough f; u(x, t) > 0 for
    ALL x as soon as t > 0 if f ≥ 0, f ≢ 0 (INFINITE SPEED); running time
    backwards is ILL-POSED: sin(nx)/n is small data, but u = e^(n²t) sin(nx)/n
    solves u_t = −u_xx and explodes. Common mistakes: in the max principle
    forgetting the top side t = T (there v_t ≥ 0, not v_t = 0); forgetting the
    normalising factor of the kernel. Now you try: u(x, 0) = x²
    on R. (u = x² + 2kt)

D6. Derive d'Alembert's formula for u_tt = c²u_xx on R. Solve it for (a)
    f = e^(−x²), g = 0, c = 2; (b) f = 0, g = cos x; (c) f = 1 for |x| < 1 and
    0 otherwise, g = 0, c = 1, and find u(0, 1/2), u(1.5, 1), u(0, 2). Explain
    the domain of dependence.
    Answer: (a) u = ½[e^(−(x−2t)²) + e^(−(x+2t)²)]. (b) u = cos x sin(ct)/c.
    (c) u(0, 1/2) = 1, u(1.5, 1) = 1/2, u(0, 2) = 0.
    Teacher explains: FACTORISE: (∂_t − c∂_x)(∂_t + c∂_x)u = 0. In the
    characteristic variables ξ = x − ct, η = x + ct the equation becomes
    u_ξη = 0 (as in D1), so u = F(x − ct) + G(x + ct): a right-moving and a
    left-moving wave, both unchanged in shape. Fit the data:
       F + G = f,   −cF′ + cG′ = g ⇒ −F + G = (1/c)∫₀ˣ g + const.
    Solve and add:
       u(x, t) = ½[f(x − ct) + f(x + ct)] + (1/(2c))∫ (x−ct to x+ct) g(s) ds.
    (a) u = ½[e^(−(x − 2t)²) + e^(−(x + 2t)²)]: the bump splits into two halves
    moving apart at speed 2. (b) u = (1/(2c))[sin(x + ct) − sin(x − ct)]
    = (1/c) cos x sin ct (a standing wave). (c) Use ½[f(x − t) + f(x + t)]:
       u(0, 1/2) = ½[f(−1/2) + f(1/2)] = ½(1 + 1) = 1
       u(1.5, 1) = ½[f(0.5) + f(2.5)] = ½(1 + 0) = 1/2
       u(0, 2)   = ½[f(−2) + f(2)] = 0   (both halves have passed)
    The corners of the box never smooth out: discontinuities travel along the
    characteristics x ± t = ±1 — unlike the heat equation. DOMAIN OF
    DEPENDENCE: u(x₀, t₀) depends only on the data in [x₀ − ct₀, x₀ + ct₀]
    (the base of the backward characteristic triangle); the RANGE OF INFLUENCE
    of a point x₁ is the forward cone |x − x₁| ≤ ct. Signals travel at speed
    exactly c. Common mistakes: forgetting the ½; integrating g over
    [x − t, x + t] when c ≠ 1. Now you try: f = x², g = 0. (u = x² + c²t²)

D7. Solve the string problem u_tt = 4u_xx, 0 < x < π, u(0, t) = u(π, t) = 0,
    u(x, 0) = sin x + ½ sin 3x, u_t(x, 0) = sin 2x. Find the frequencies of
    the modes and prove that the energy E = ½∫₀^π (u_t² + 4u_x²) dx is
    constant; evaluate it.
    Answer: u = sin x cos 2t + ¼ sin 2x sin 4t + ½ sin 3x cos 6t;
    angular frequencies 2n (period π); E = 7π/2.
    Teacher explains: Separate u = X(x)T(t): X″/X = T″/(4T) = −λ, X(0) = X(π)
    = 0 ⇒ λ = n², X = sin nx, and T″ + 4n²T = 0 ⇒ T = aₙ cos 2nt + bₙ sin 2nt.
       u = ∑ (aₙ cos 2nt + bₙ sin 2nt) sin nx.
    At t = 0: ∑ aₙ sin nx = sin x + ½ sin 3x ⇒ a₁ = 1, a₃ = ½. Differentiating:
    u_t(x, 0) = ∑ 2n bₙ sin nx = sin 2x ⇒ 4b₂ = 1, b₂ = ¼. So
       u = sin x cos 2t + ¼ sin 2x sin 4t + ½ sin 3x cos 6t.
    Mode n oscillates with angular frequency nc = 2n (for a string of length L,
    frequency nc/(2L) cycles per unit time); all are multiples of the
    fundamental, so u is periodic with period 2π/2 = π — musical HARMONICS.
    ENERGY: E′ = ∫(u_t u_tt + 4u_x u_xt) dx = ∫(4u_t u_xx + 4u_x u_xt) dx
    = 4[u_x u_t]₀^π = 0, since u_t = 0 at fixed ends. At t = 0:
       E = ½∫₀^π [sin²2x + 4(cos x + (3/2) cos 3x)²] dx
         = ½[π/2 + 4(π/2 + (9/4)(π/2))] = ½[π/2 + 13π/2] = 7π/2.
    (Cross terms vanish by orthogonality; by modes: π + π/4 + 9π/4 = 7π/2.)
    Common mistakes: bₙ = coefficient of g (it must be divided by nc);
    frequencies n instead of nc. Now you try: f = 0, g = sin 3x, c = 1, L = π.
    (u = (1/3) sin 3x sin 3t)

D8. A string of length π (c = 1) is plucked at its midpoint: u(x, 0) = x for
    0 ≤ x ≤ π/2, π − x for π/2 ≤ x ≤ π, u_t(x, 0) = 0. Find the Fourier series
    solution, and use the reflection (d'Alembert) method to find
    u(π/2, π/4), u(π/2, π/2) and u(π/2, π).
    Answer: u = (4/π)∑ sin(nπ/2) sin nx cos nt/n²
    = (4/π)[sin x cos t − sin 3x cos 3t/9 + sin 5x cos 5t/25 − ...];
    u(π/2, π/4) = π/4, u(π/2, π/2) = 0, u(π/2, π) = −π/2.
    Teacher explains: aₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π f sin nx dx. By symmetry about π/2 only
    odd n survive, and integration by parts on each half gives
       aₙ = (2/π)·2∫₀^(π/2) x sin nx dx (n odd) = 4 sin(nπ/2)/(πn²).
    (Coefficients fall like 1/n²: the kink makes the upper harmonics weak.
    Plucking near the end would give a brighter sound.) Series:
       u = (4/π)[sin x cos t − (1/9) sin 3x cos 3t + (1/25) sin 5x cos 5t − ...].
    REFLECTION: extend f to F, ODD about x = 0 and 2π-periodic (odd about π
    as well). Then u = ½[F(x − t) + F(x + t)] satisfies the PDE and u = 0 at
    the ends (because F is odd about 0 and π). So
       u(π/2, π/4) = ½[F(π/4) + F(3π/4)] = ½(π/4 + π/4) = π/4
       u(π/2, π/2) = ½[F(0) + F(π)] = 0
       u(π/2, π) = ½[F(−π/2) + F(3π/2)] = ½(−π/2 − π/2) = −π/2
    — at t = π the string is the initial shape upside down, and at t = 2π it
    is back. The shape at every time is a trapezoid (two corners moving
    apart), not a sine curve. Check the series at t = 0, x = π/2:
    (4/π)(1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + ...) = (4/π)(π²/8) = π/2 ✓. Common mistakes:
    using the even extension (it does not keep the ends fixed); forgetting
    sin(nπ/2) = 0 for even n. Now you try: the value u(π/4, π/4).
    (½[F(0) + F(π/2)] = π/4)

D9. Solve Laplace's equation in the square 0 < x < π, 0 < y < π with u = 0 on
    x = 0, x = π, y = 0 and u(x, π) = f(x). Do it for f = sin x (value at the
    centre), and for f = 1 (show the centre value is 1/4 without the series).
    Answer: u = ∑ cₙ sin nx sinh ny with cₙ sinh nπ = bₙ(f);
    f = sin x: u = sin x sinh y/sinh π, u(π/2, π/2) = sinh(π/2)/sinh π
    ≈ 0.1993; f = 1: u(π/2, π/2) = 1/4.
    Teacher explains: u = X(x)Y(y): X″/X = −Y″/Y = −λ. The homogeneous
    conditions in x give X = sin nx, λ = n²; then Y″ = n²Y with Y(0) = 0 gives
    Y = sinh ny (not sin: in x oscillation, in y growth — the signs are
    forced). Superpose:
       u = ∑ cₙ sin nx sinh ny,   u(x, π) = ∑ cₙ sinh(nπ) sin nx = f(x),
    so cₙ = bₙ/sinh nπ with bₙ the sine coefficients of f. For f = sin x:
       u = sin x sinh y/sinh π,  u(π/2, π/2) = sinh(π/2)/sinh π
         = 2.3013/11.5487 ≈ 0.1993
    (= 1/(2 cosh(π/2)) ≈ 0.1993 since sinh 2a = 2 sinh a cosh a). For f = 1,
    bₙ = 4/(nπ) (n odd) and
       u = (4/π)∑(n odd) sin nx sinh ny/(n sinh nπ).
    At the centre use SYMMETRY instead: let u₁, ..., u₄ be the solutions with
    value 1 on one side and 0 on the others. Their sum has value 1 on the
    whole boundary, so it is ≡ 1 (uniqueness). By rotating the square they all
    have the same value at the centre, so each is 1/4 there. (Summing the
    series numerically indeed gives 0.2500.) If several sides carry data,
    solve one side at a time and add. Common mistakes: taking sin ny in y
    (it cannot vanish at y = 0 and grow to meet the data); forgetting to
    divide by sinh nπ. Now you try: u(x, 0) = sin x, u = 0 on the other sides.
    (u = sin x sinh(π − y)/sinh π)

D10. Solve Laplace's equation in the unit disc with (a) u(1, θ) = cos²θ,
     (b) u(1, θ) = sin³θ, by separation in polar coordinates. Verify the mean
     value property in (a) and state the Poisson integral formula and the
     compatibility condition for the Neumann problem.
     Answer: (a) u = ½ + ½r² cos 2θ = ½ + ½(x² − y²), u(0) = ½.
     (b) u = (3r sin θ − r³ sin 3θ)/4.
     Teacher explains: In polar form ∇²u = u_rr + u_r/r + u_θθ/r² = 0. With
     u = R(r)Θ(θ): r²R″/R + rR′/R = −Θ″/Θ = n². Θ must be 2π-periodic:
     Θ = cos nθ, sin nθ, n = 0, 1, 2, .... R solves the EULER equation
     r²R″ + rR′ − n²R = 0: R = rⁿ or r⁻ⁿ (n ≥ 1), 1 or ln r (n = 0). Bounded at
     r = 0 keeps rⁿ and 1:
        u = a₀/2 + ∑ rⁿ(aₙ cos nθ + bₙ sin nθ),
     where aₙ, bₙ are the Fourier coefficients of the boundary data. (a)
     cos²θ = ½ + ½ cos 2θ, so u = ½ + ½r² cos 2θ; in Cartesian form
     r² cos 2θ = x² − y², u = ½ + ½(x² − y²), clearly harmonic. MEAN VALUE:
     (1/2π)∫cos²θ dθ = ½ = u(0) ✓. (b) sin³θ = (3 sin θ − sin 3θ)/4, so
     u = (3r sin θ − r³ sin 3θ)/4. By the maximum principle
     |u| ≤ max|sin³θ| = 1 in the disc. POISSON: summing the series,
        u(r, θ) = (1/2π)∫₀^(2π) (1 − r²)/(1 − 2r cos(θ − φ) + r²) h(φ) dφ;
     at r = 0 the kernel is 1: the mean value property again. NEUMANN: data
     ∂u/∂r = h(θ) on r = 1 requires ∫₀^(2π) h dθ = 0 (the divergence theorem:
     ∮ ∂u/∂n = ∫∫ ∇²u = 0), and then u is unique up to a constant; h = 1 has
     no solution. For the EXTERIOR r > 1 keep r⁻ⁿ: data cos θ gives cos θ/r.
     Common mistakes: keeping r⁻ⁿ inside the disc (singular at 0); using
     cos²θ as a single mode instead of expanding it. Now you try: disc of
     radius 2 with u(2, θ) = sin 2θ. (u = (r²/4) sin 2θ = xy/2)

D11. Use the method of characteristics to solve (a) u_t + 2u_x = 0,
     u(x, 0) = e^(−x²); (b) u_t + u_x = −u, u(x, 0) = f(x); (c) u_t + xu_x = u,
     u(x, 0) = x²; (d) 2u_x + 3u_y = 0, u(0, y) = y.
     Answer: (a) e^(−(x − 2t)²); (b) e^(−t)f(x − t); (c) x²e^(−t);
     (d) y − 3x/2.
     Teacher explains: For a u_x + b u_t = c, the left side is the derivative
     of u along the curves with dx/ds = a, dt/ds = b. So: (1) find the
     CHARACTERISTIC curves, (2) solve the ODE for u along each, (3) use the
     data where each curve starts. (a) dx/dt = 2: x = x₀ + 2t, and du/dt = 0:
     u is constant, = e^(−x₀²) = e^(−(x − 2t)²). The profile moves right at
     speed 2 without changing shape (TRANSPORT). (b) Same lines x = x₀ + t;
     du/dt = −u ⇒ u = f(x₀)e^(−t) = e^(−t)f(x − t): transport with decay.
     (c) dx/dt = x ⇒ x = x₀eᵗ (curves fanning out); du/dt = u ⇒
     u = u(x₀, 0)eᵗ = x₀²eᵗ = (xe^(−t))²eᵗ = x²e^(−t). Check: u_t = −x²e^(−t),
     xu_x = 2x²e^(−t), sum x²e^(−t) = u ✓. (d) dy/dx = 3/2: 3x − 2y = const is
     characteristic, u constant along it: u = G(3x − 2y). Data at x = 0:
     G(−2y) = y ⇒ G(s) = −s/2, so u = −(3x − 2y)/2 = y − 3x/2 ✓
     (2(−3/2) + 3(1) = 0). WARNING: data given on a characteristic curve is
     either inconsistent or insufficient: for u_t + 2u_x = 0 data on the line
     x = 2t cannot determine u elsewhere. Common mistakes: solving for x₀ with
     the wrong sign (x₀ = x − 2t, not x + 2t); forgetting the source term on
     the right. Now you try: yu_x − xu_y = 0. (Characteristics x² + y² = const;
     u = F(x² + y²))

D12. For Burgers' equation u_t + uu_x = 0: (a) show u = f(x − ut) and solve
     with f(x) = −x; (b) find the breaking time for f(x) = e^(−x²); (c) solve the
     Riemann problems u_L = 1, u_R = 0 and u_L = 0, u_R = 1.
     Answer: (a) u = −x/(1 − t), blows up at t = 1; (b) t* = √(e/2) ≈ 1.1658;
     (c) a shock x = t/2; a rarefaction u = 0 (x < 0), x/t (0 ≤ x ≤ t),
     1 (x > t).
     Teacher explains: Along dx/dt = u we have du/dt = u_t + uu_x = 0, so u is
     constant on each characteristic, and therefore dx/dt is constant: the
     characteristics are STRAIGHT LINES x = x₀ + f(x₀)t. Hence
     u(x, t) = f(x₀) with x₀ = x − ut: u = f(x − ut), implicitly. (a)
     u = −(x − ut) ⇒ u(1 − t) = −x ⇒ u = −x/(1 − t). All characteristics
     x = x₀(1 − t) meet at x = 0 when t = 1: the slope becomes infinite.
     (b) u_x = f′(x₀)/(1 + f′(x₀)t) blows up first when 1 + f′(x₀)t = 0, i.e.
     at t* = −1/min f′. For f = e^(−x²), f′ = −2xe^(−x²) is most negative at
     x = 1/√2: min f′ = −√2 e^(−1/2) = −√(2/e), so t* = √(e/2) ≈ 1.1658. Faster
     fluid behind catches up with slower fluid ahead — a SHOCK. (c) Write the
     equation as a CONSERVATION LAW u_t + (u²/2)_x = 0. Across a jump the
     RANKINE–HUGONIOT condition gives the speed
        s = [u²/2]/[u] = (u_L + u_R)/2.
     For u_L = 1 > u_R = 0 the characteristics collide: shock x = t/2 with u = 1
     behind, 0 ahead. For u_L = 0 < u_R = 1 they diverge, leaving an empty
     wedge 0 < x < t filled by the RAREFACTION FAN u = x/t (itself a solution:
     u_t + uu_x = −x/t² + (x/t)(1/t) = 0). A shock there would also satisfy RH
     but violates the ENTROPY condition u_L > u_R (characteristics must run
     INTO shocks). This models traffic jams and gas dynamics. Common mistakes:
     using the characteristic speed u instead of the average for the shock;
     taking min |f′| instead of min f′. Now you try: shock speed for u_L = 3,
     u_R = 1. (2)

M1. Classify: order; linear (L), semilinear (S), quasilinear (Q) or nonlinear
    (N); and for second-order equations the type (E, P, H).
    a) u_xx + u_yy = 0              b) u_t = u_xx
    c) u_tt = u_xx                  d) u_xx + 4u_xy + 3u_yy = 0
    e) u_xx + 2u_xy + u_yy = 0      f) u_xx + u_xy + u_yy = 0

M6. Heat equation on R and general properties.

    l) bound for u if 0 ≤ f ≤ 3 and the boundary values are in [0, 3]

      c) 1               d) x               e) x² + 2kt
      f) e^(−kt) cos x   g) e^(x + kt)      h) 1; 2kt
      i) 1/2 (u = ½(1 + erf(x/√(4kt))))    j) 1/(2√π) ≈ 0.2821
      k) 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071; 1/2                l) 0 ≤ u ≤ 3
      m) ≤ 0 (E′ = −2k∫u_x²)
