TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: let the student run every method on a calculator or in a few
  lines of Python and PRINT the error column: seeing the error halve
  (bisection, Euler), square (Newton) or fall by 16 (Simpson, RK4 when h is
  halved) makes the idea of 'order' concrete. Always compare with an exact
  answer before trusting a method. Keep a card with the error formulas:
  trapezoid h²f″/12, Simpson h⁴f⁗/180, interpolation f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾w/(n + 1)!,
  Euler global O(h). Stress the difference between a badly conditioned
  PROBLEM and an unstable ALGORITHM, with the quadratic formula and the
  matrix [[1, 1], [1, 1.0001]] as the two standard examples. Harder: prove
  that Simpson's rule is exact for cubics and derive its error by Peano
  kernels; prove that the secant order is the golden ratio; show that
  Gauss nodes are the roots of Legendre polynomials; derive the stability
  region of RK4 in the complex plane; implement Gaussian elimination with
  partial pivoting and measure its growth factor; prove that Gauss-Seidel
  converges for symmetric positive definite matrices; and compare QR with
  the normal equations for an ill-conditioned least squares problem.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.35 — PROBABILITY THEORY II: JOINT DISTRIBUTIONS, MOMENT GENERATING
FUNCTIONS, LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS, CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - JOINT DISTRIBUTIONS: discrete (X, Y) has a JOINT PMF p(x, y) =
    P(X = x, Y = y) ≥ 0, ∑∑p = 1; continuous (X, Y) a JOINT PDF f(x, y) ≥ 0
    with ∬f = 1 and P((X, Y) ∈ A) = ∬_A f dx dy. JOINT CDF F(x, y) =
    P(X ≤ x, Y ≤ y), f = ∂²F/∂x∂y. MARGINALS: p_X(x) = ∑_y p(x, y),
    f_X(x) = ∫f(x, y) dy (integrate out the other variable, with the right
    limits when the support is not a rectangle).
  - INDEPENDENCE: X, Y independent ⇔ p(x, y) = p_X(x)p_Y(y) (f = f_X f_Y) for
    all x, y ⇔ F factorises. Quick test: f(x, y) = g(x)h(y) on a PRODUCT
    (rectangle) support. A triangular support (e.g. 0 < x < y < 1) always
    means DEPENDENT. Functions of independent variables are independent.
  - CONDITIONAL distributions: p_{Y|X}(y|x) = p(x, y)/p_X(x), f_{Y|X}(y|x) =
    f(x, y)/f_X(x). CONDITIONAL EXPECTATION E[Y|X] is a random variable;
    TOWER LAW E[E[Y|X]] = E[Y]; LAW OF TOTAL VARIANCE Var Y = E[Var(Y|X)] +
    Var(E[Y|X]). Random sums S = X₁ + ... + X_N: E S = E N·E X,
    Var S = E N·Var X + Var N·(E X)².
  - EXPECTATION: E[g(X, Y)] = ∬g f; E is LINEAR always; E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] if
    independent. COVARIANCE Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y], bilinear;
    Var(aX + bY) = a²Var X + b²Var Y + 2ab Cov(X, Y). CORRELATION
    ρ = Cov/(σ_Xσ_Y), −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1 (Cauchy-Schwarz), |ρ| = 1 ⇔ Y = aX + b.
    Independent ⇒ uncorrelated, NOT conversely (X uniform on {−1, 0, 1},
    Y = X²). INDICATOR method: E(count) = ∑ P(events).
  - TRANSFORMATIONS: for (U, V) = T(X, Y) one-to-one,
    f_{U,V}(u, v) = f_{X,Y}(x(u, v), y(u, v))·|∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)|. SUMS:
    f_{X+Y}(z) = ∫f_X(x)f_Y(z − x) dx (CONVOLUTION) for independent X, Y.
    MIN/MAX of iid: P(max ≤ z) = F(z)ⁿ, P(min > z) = (1 − F(z))ⁿ; the min of
    independent Exp(λᵢ) is Exp(∑λᵢ).
  - BIVARIATE NORMAL (μ_X, μ_Y, σ_X, σ_Y, ρ): marginals normal; every aX + bY
    normal; Y | X = x ~ N(μ_Y + ρ(σ_Y/σ_X)(x − μ_X), σ_Y²(1 − ρ²)) (the
    REGRESSION LINE); for jointly normal variables uncorrelated ⇔
    independent. Multivariate: X ~ N(μ, Σ) ⇒ AX + b ~ N(Aμ + b, AΣAᵀ).
  - MOMENT GENERATING FUNCTION M_X(t) = E[e^(tX)] (finite near 0):
    M^(k)(0) = E[Xᵏ]; M_{aX+b}(t) = e^(bt)M_X(at); for INDEPENDENT X, Y,
    M_{X+Y} = M_X M_Y. UNIQUENESS: equal MGFs on an interval around 0 ⇒ equal
    distributions. PGF G(s) = E[s^X] for integer X (P(X = k) = G⁽ᵏ⁾(0)/k!);
    CHARACTERISTIC FUNCTION φ(t) = E[e^(itX)] always exists.
  - MGF TABLE: Bernoulli 1 − p + peᵗ; Binomial (1 − p + peᵗ)ⁿ; Poisson
    e^(λ(eᵗ − 1)); Geometric (on 1, 2, ...) peᵗ/(1 − (1 − p)eᵗ); Exponential
    λ/(λ − t); Gamma(α, λ) (λ/(λ − t))^α; χ²ₖ (1 − 2t)^(−k/2); Normal
    e^(μt + σ²t²/2); Uniform(a, b) (e^(bt) − e^(at))/(t(b − a)). Hence sums of
    independent Poissons are Poisson, of normals normal, of n Exp(λ) Gamma(n, λ),
    of Bin(nᵢ, p) Bin(∑nᵢ, p).
  - INEQUALITIES: MARKOV P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a (X ≥ 0, a > 0); CHEBYSHEV
    P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k²; CHERNOFF P(X ≥ a) ≤ min_t e^(−ta)M(t).
  - MODES OF CONVERGENCE: ALMOST SURELY (P(Xₙ → X) = 1) ⇒ IN PROBABILITY
    (∀ε P(|Xₙ − X| > ε) → 0) ⇒ IN DISTRIBUTION (Fₙ(x) → F(x) at continuity
    points of F); convergence in distribution to a CONSTANT implies in
    probability. Convergence in probability does not imply E Xₙ → E X.
  - LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS for iid X₁, X₂, ... with mean μ: X̄ₙ → μ; WEAK law in
    probability (easy proof by Chebyshev when σ² < ∞), STRONG law almost
    surely (needs only E|X| < ∞). Also (1/n)∑g(Xᵢ) → E g(X) (MONTE CARLO,
    error ≈ σ/√n). Fails for the Cauchy distribution (no mean).
  - CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM: iid with mean μ and variance 0 < σ² < ∞:
    (X̄ₙ − μ)/(σ/√n) = (Sₙ − nμ)/(σ√n) → N(0, 1) in distribution. So
    Sₙ ≈ N(nμ, nσ²), X̄ₙ ≈ N(μ, σ²/n). NORMAL APPROXIMATION to Bin(n, p)
    (np, n(1 − p) ≥ 10, say) and Poisson(λ) (λ large) with CONTINUITY
    CORRECTION ±0.5. Proof idea: MGF of the standardised sum
    → e^(t²/2). DELTA METHOD: √n(g(X̄ₙ) − g(μ)) → N(0, g′(μ)²σ²).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A fair coin is tossed three times. X = number of heads in the first two
    tosses, Y = total number of heads. Find the joint pmf, the marginals,
    E[X], E[Y], Cov(X, Y), ρ, the conditional pmf of X given Y = 2, and decide
    whether X and Y are independent.
    Answer: p(0, 0) = p(0, 1) = 1/8, p(1, 1) = p(1, 2) = 1/4, p(2, 2) =
    p(2, 3) = 1/8. E X = 1, E Y = 3/2, Cov = 1/2, ρ = √(2/3) ≈ 0.816. Given
    Y = 2: X = 1 w.p. 2/3, X = 2 w.p. 1/3 (E[X|Y = 2] = 4/3). Dependent.
    Teacher explains: Write Y = X + T with T the third toss, independent of X.
    P(X = 0, 1, 2) = 1/4, 1/2, 1/4 and Y = X or X + 1 with probability 1/2
    each:
                Y = 0   Y = 1   Y = 2   Y = 3  |  p_X
       X = 0     1/8     1/8      0       0    |  1/4
       X = 1      0      1/4     1/4      0    |  1/2
       X = 2      0       0      1/8     1/8   |  1/4
       p_Y       1/8     3/8     3/8     1/8   |   1
    Marginals are row and column sums. E X = 1, E Y = 3/2,
       E[XY] = 1·1·(1/4) + 1·2·(1/4) + 2·2·(1/8) + 2·3·(1/8) = 2
       Cov = 2 − 1·(3/2) = 1/2
    (check: Cov(X, X + T) = Var X + Cov(X, T) = 1/2 + 0). Var X = 1/2,
    Var Y = 3/4, so ρ = (1/2)/√(3/8) = √(2/3) ≈ 0.816. Conditional: divide the
    column Y = 2 by p_Y(2) = 3/8: (1/4)/(3/8) = 2/3 and (1/8)/(3/8) = 1/3, so
    E[X | Y = 2] = 1·(2/3) + 2·(1/3) = 4/3. Independence fails: p(0, 2) = 0 but
    p_X(0)p_Y(2) = 3/32 ≠ 0 (one zero cell with nonzero marginals is enough).
    Common mistakes: using the conditional table without renormalising;
    thinking Cov > 0 needs a causal link. Now you try: E[X | Y = y] for each
    y. (0, 1/3, 4/3, 2, i.e. 2y/3)

D2. Let f(x, y) = c(x + y) for 0 ≤ x, y ≤ 1. Find c, the marginals,
    P(X + Y ≤ 1), P(X > 1/2), E[X], Var X, Cov(X, Y) and ρ. Are X, Y
    independent?
    Answer: c = 1; f_X(x) = x + 1/2; P(X + Y ≤ 1) = 1/3; P(X > 1/2) = 5/8;
    E X = 7/12, Var X = 11/144, Cov = −1/144, ρ = −1/11. Not independent.
    Teacher explains: Normalise:
       ∫₀¹∫₀¹ (x + y) dy dx = ∫₀¹ (x + 1/2) dx = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1,  so c = 1
    Marginal: f_X(x) = ∫₀¹ (x + y) dy = x + 1/2, and by symmetry f_Y(y) = y + 1/2.
    f_X f_Y = (x + 1/2)(y + 1/2) ≠ x + y (try x = y = 0): DEPENDENT. For the
    triangle x + y ≤ 1 let y run from 0 to 1 − x:
       ∫₀¹ ∫₀^{1−x} (x + y) dy dx = ∫₀¹ [x(1 − x) + (1 − x)²/2] dx
                                 = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3
    P(X > 1/2) = ∫_{1/2}^1 (x + 1/2) dx = [x²/2 + x/2] from 1/2 to 1 = 1 − 3/8
    = 5/8. Moments:
       E X = ∫ x(x + 1/2) dx = 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12
       E X² = ∫ x²(x + 1/2) dx = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12,  Var X = 5/12 − 49/144 = 11/144
       E[XY] = ∬ xy(x + y) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3,  Cov = 1/3 − 49/144 = −1/144
       ρ = (−1/144)/(11/144) = −1/11
    Common mistakes: forgetting to use the limits of the region in
    P(X + Y ≤ 1); declaring independence because the formula 'looks
    separable'. Now you try: f(x, y) = 4xy on the unit square. (c = 4;
    f_X = 2x; independent; P(X + Y ≤ 1) = 1/6)

D3. (X, Y) is uniform on the triangle 0 < x < y < 1. Find f(x, y), both
    marginals, f_{Y|X}, E[Y | X], and verify the tower law and the law of
    total variance for Y.
    Answer: f = 2; f_X(x) = 2(1 − x), f_Y(y) = 2y; Y | X = x ~ U(x, 1),
    E[Y|X] = (1 + X)/2; E Y = 2/3 both ways; Var Y = 1/24 + 1/72 = 1/18.
    Teacher explains: Area 1/2, so f = 2 on the triangle. Integrate out with
    the correct limits (draw the triangle!):
       f_X(x) = ∫_x^1 2 dy = 2(1 − x),   f_Y(y) = ∫₀^y 2 dx = 2y
    Conditional: f_{Y|X}(y|x) = 2/(2(1 − x)) = 1/(1 − x) on x < y < 1: uniform on
    (x, 1). Hence E[Y | X = x] = (1 + x)/2 and Var(Y | X = x) = (1 − x)²/12.
    TOWER: E X = ∫ 2x(1 − x) dx = 1/3, so E[E[Y|X]] = (1 + 1/3)/2 = 2/3, and
    directly E Y = ∫ 2y² dy = 2/3 ✓. TOTAL VARIANCE:
       E[Var(Y|X)] = E[(1 − X)²]/12 = (∫ 2(1 − x)³ dx)/12 = (1/2)/12 = 1/24
       Var(E[Y|X]) = Var X/4;  E X² = 1/6, Var X = 1/6 − 1/9 = 1/18;  → 1/72
       sum = 1/24 + 1/72 = 1/18
    Directly: E Y² = ∫ 2y³ dy = 1/2, Var Y = 1/2 − 4/9 = 1/18 ✓. The support
    is not a rectangle, so X and Y are dependent (f_X f_Y = 4y(1 − x) ≠ 2).
    Common mistakes: integrating over [0, 1] for both variables; forgetting
    that E[Y|X] is a function of X. Now you try: N ~ Poisson(3) customers,
    each spends X ~ Exp with mean 2 independently; mean and variance of the
    total. (E S = 3·2 = 6; Var S = 3·4 + 3·4 = 24)

D4. Prove that |ρ(X, Y)| ≤ 1 with equality iff Y is a linear function of X,
    and derive Var(aX + bY). Show that uncorrelated does not imply
    independent. Compute Var(2X − 3Y + 1) when Var X = 4, Var Y = 1,
    Cov(X, Y) = −1.
    Answer: proof below; Var(2X − 3Y + 1) = 37.
    Teacher explains: Bilinearity: Cov(aX + bY, Z) = a Cov(X, Z) + b Cov(Y, Z)
    and Cov(X, X) = Var X, so
       Var(aX + bY + c) = a²Var X + b²Var Y + 2ab Cov(X, Y)
    (constants do not change variance). Here
       4·4 + 9·1 + 2·2·(−3)·(−1) = 16 + 9 + 12 = 37
    CAUCHY-SCHWARZ: with centred X₀ = X − μ_X, Y₀ = Y − μ_Y, the quadratic
       q(t) = E[(Y₀ − tX₀)²] = Var Y − 2t Cov + t² Var X ≥ 0 for all t
    has discriminant ≤ 0: 4Cov² − 4Var X Var Y ≤ 0, i.e. ρ² ≤ 1. Equality
    means q(t₀) = 0 for some t₀, so Y₀ = t₀X₀ with probability 1: Y = aX + b
    (ρ = +1 if a > 0, −1 if a < 0). COUNTEREXAMPLE: X uniform on {−1, 0, 1},
    Y = X². E X = 0, E[XY] = E X³ = 0, so Cov = 0; but P(X = 0, Y = 1) = 0 ≠
    (1/3)(2/3): dependent. Correlation measures only LINEAR association.
    Common mistakes: Var(X − Y) = Var X − Var Y (the variances ADD);
    forgetting the factor 2 on the covariance. Now you try: Var X = 4,
    Var Y = 9, Cov = 2: Var(X + Y), Var(X − Y), ρ. (17, 9, 1/3)

D5. X, Y are independent Exp(1). Find the joint density of U = X + Y and
    V = X/(X + Y), and deduce their distributions. State the Jacobian method.
    Answer: f_{U,V}(u, v) = u e^(−u) for u > 0, 0 < v < 1: U ~ Gamma(2, 1),
    V ~ U(0, 1), and U, V are independent.
    Teacher explains: METHOD: if (u, v) = T(x, y) is one-to-one and smooth
    with inverse x(u, v), y(u, v), then
       f_{U,V}(u, v) = f_{X,Y}(x(u, v), y(u, v)) · |J|,  J = det ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)
    Invert: x = uv, y = u(1 − v). Jacobian:
       J = det [[∂x/∂u, ∂x/∂v], [∂y/∂u, ∂y/∂v]] = det [[v, u], [1 − v, −u]]
         = −uv − u(1 − v) = −u,    |J| = u
    f_{X,Y} = e^(−x−y) = e^(−u). New region: x, y > 0 ⇔ u > 0, 0 < v < 1. So
       f_{U,V}(u, v) = u e^(−u) · 1   on (0, ∞) × (0, 1)
    It factorises on a rectangle: U has density u e^(−u) (Gamma(2, 1)), V is
    uniform on (0, 1), and they are independent. Meaning: given the total
    waiting time of two Poisson arrivals, the first arrival is uniformly
    placed. The same method with polar coordinates proves the Box-Muller
    method: R = √(−2 ln U₁), Θ = 2πU₂ give independent N(0, 1) variables
    R cos Θ, R sin Θ. Common mistakes: using the Jacobian of the forward map
    ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) (you need its reciprocal); forgetting to transform the
    region. Now you try: U = X + Y, V = X − Y for iid N(0, 1). (|J| = 1/2;
    U, V independent N(0, 2))

D6. (a) Find the density of the sum of two independent U(0, 1) variables by
    convolution. (b) Three bulbs have independent Exp lifetimes with mean
    1000 h. Find the distribution of the first failure time, P(all survive
    500 h), and the expected time until all have failed.
    Answer: (a) f(z) = z on [0, 1], 2 − z on [1, 2] (triangular). (b) min ~
    Exp with rate 0.003 (mean 333.3 h); P = e^(−1.5) ≈ 0.2231; E max =
    1000(1 + 1/2 + 1/3) ≈ 1833.3 h.
    Teacher explains: (a) f_{X+Y}(z) = ∫ f_X(x)f_Y(z − x) dx; the integrand is 1
    exactly when 0 < x < 1 and 0 < z − x < 1, i.e. max(0, z − 1) < x < min(1, z):
       0 ≤ z ≤ 1:  ∫₀^z 1 dx = z;       1 ≤ z ≤ 2:  ∫_{z−1}^1 1 dx = 2 − z
    A triangle: the sum of two flat distributions is already peaked (the
    first hint of the CLT). (b) MIN: min > t ⇔ all three > t:
       P(min > t) = (e^(−t/1000))³ = e^(−0.003t)
    so min ~ Exp(0.003), mean 1000/3 ≈ 333.3 h, and P(min > 500) = e^(−1.5) ≈
    0.2231. MAX: P(max ≤ t) = (1 − e^(−t/1000))³. For the mean use
    memorylessness: wait for the first of 3 failures (mean 1000/3), then the
    first of 2 (1000/2), then the last (1000):
       E max = 1000(1/3 + 1/2 + 1) = 1833.3 h
    Common mistakes: 'the sum of uniforms is uniform on [0, 2]'; writing
    P(min ≤ t) = F(t)³. Now you try: max M of n iid U(0, 1): density and
    mean. (nzⁿ⁻¹ on (0, 1); n/(n + 1))

D7. Heights of fathers X and sons Y are bivariate normal with means 170 cm,
    standard deviations 10 cm and ρ = 0.5. Find the distribution of Y given
    X = 190, P(Y > 190 | X = 190), and the distribution of X + Y. Explain
    'regression to the mean'.
    Answer: Y | X = 190 ~ N(180, 75) (sd ≈ 8.66); P ≈ 0.124; X + Y ~ N(340, 300).
    Teacher explains: For the bivariate normal
       E[Y | X = x] = μ_Y + ρ(σ_Y/σ_X)(x − μ_X),  Var(Y | X = x) = σ_Y²(1 − ρ²)
    Here E[Y | X = 190] = 170 + 0.5·1·20 = 180 and Var = 100·0.75 = 75, sd
    = √75 ≈ 8.660. Then
       P(Y > 190 | X = 190) = P(Z > 10/8.660) = P(Z > 1.155) ≈ 0.124
    The conditional variance does not depend on x, and the conditional mean
    is the REGRESSION LINE y = 170 + 0.5(x − 170). A father 20 cm above average
    has a son on average only 10 cm above: REGRESSION TO THE MEAN (|ρ| < 1),
    not a biological 'pull'. Sums of jointly normal variables are normal:
       E(X + Y) = 340,  Var = 100 + 100 + 2·0.5·10·10 = 300
    Derivation sketch of the conditional law: write Y = μ_Y + ρ(σ_Y/σ_X)(X −
    μ_X) + W where W is normal, uncorrelated with X, hence (jointly normal)
    independent of X, with Var W = σ_Y²(1 − ρ²). Common mistakes: using σ_Y
    instead of the conditional sd; forgetting 2Cov in Var(X + Y). Now you
    try: μ_X = 1, μ_Y = 2, σ_X = 2, σ_Y = 3, ρ = 0.5: E[Y | X = 3] and
    Var(Y | X = 3). (3.5; 6.75)

D8. Define the MGF, prove M^(k)(0) = E[Xᵏ], and find the MGFs of Exp(λ) and
    N(μ, σ²); use them to get the means and variances. State the uniqueness
    theorem and use it to show that aX + b is normal when X is normal.
    Answer: M_Exp(t) = λ/(λ − t) (t < λ), mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ².
    M_N(t) = e^(μt + σ²t²/2), mean μ, variance σ².
    Teacher explains: M(t) = E[e^(tX)] = E[∑ tᵏXᵏ/k!] = ∑ E[Xᵏ]tᵏ/k! (allowed
    when M is finite near 0), so the k-th derivative at 0 picks out E[Xᵏ]:
    the MGF 'generates' the moments. Exponential:
       M(t) = ∫₀^∞ e^(tx)λe^(−λx) dx = λ/(λ − t)     (converges only for t < λ)
       M′(t) = λ/(λ − t)²  ⇒ E X = 1/λ
       M″(t) = 2λ/(λ − t)³ ⇒ E X² = 2/λ²,  Var X = 2/λ² − 1/λ² = 1/λ²
    Standard normal: complete the square,
       E e^(tZ) = ∫ e^(tz)e^(−z²/2)/√(2π) dz = e^(t²/2)∫ e^(−(z − t)²/2)/√(2π) dz
               = e^(t²/2)
    and X = μ + σZ gives M_X(t) = e^(μt)M_Z(σt) = e^(μt + σ²t²/2). Then
    M′(0) = μ and M″(0) = μ² + σ², Var = σ². UNIQUENESS: if M_X = M_Y on an
    open interval around 0 then X and Y have the same distribution. For
    Y = aX + b: M_Y(t) = e^(bt)e^(μat + σ²a²t²/2), the MGF of N(aμ + b, a²σ²),
    so Y is normal. Common mistakes: forgetting the domain t < λ;
    differentiating and evaluating at t = 1 instead of 0. Now you try: the
    MGF of Poisson(λ) and its mean and variance. (e^(λ(eᵗ − 1)); M′(0) = λ,
    M″(0) = λ + λ², variance λ)

D9. Use MGFs to find the distribution of a sum of independent (a) Poisson
    variables, (b) normal variables, (c) n iid Exp(λ). Calls arrive at a
    centre from two independent sources at Poisson rates 3 and 5 per hour;
    find P(no calls in an hour) and P(at most 2 calls). Identify the
    distribution with MGF (0.3 + 0.7eᵗ)¹⁰ and with (1 − 2t)⁻³.
    Answer: (a) Poisson(∑λᵢ); (b) N(∑μᵢ, ∑σᵢ²); (c) Gamma(n, λ).
    P(0) = e⁻⁸ ≈ 0.000335; P(≤ 2) = 41e⁻⁸ ≈ 0.013754. Bin(10, 0.7); χ²₆.
    Teacher explains: For independent X, Y, E[e^(t(X+Y))] = E[e^(tX)]E[e^(tY)],
    so MGFs MULTIPLY; then uniqueness identifies the product.
       (a) e^(λ₁(eᵗ − 1))·e^(λ₂(eᵗ − 1)) = e^((λ₁ + λ₂)(eᵗ − 1))
       (b) e^(μ₁t + σ₁²t²/2)·e^(μ₂t + σ₂²t²/2) = e^((μ₁ + μ₂)t + (σ₁² + σ₂²)t²/2)
       (c) (λ/(λ − t))ⁿ = MGF of Gamma(n, λ), density λⁿzⁿ⁻¹e^(−λz)/(n − 1)!
    Calls: total ~ Poisson(8), so
       P(0) = e⁻⁸ ≈ 0.000335,  P(≤ 2) = e⁻⁸(1 + 8 + 32) = 41e⁻⁸ ≈ 0.013754
    IDENTIFY by matching the table: (0.3 + 0.7eᵗ)¹⁰ is (1 − p + peᵗ)ⁿ with
    n = 10, p = 0.7; (1 − 2t)⁻³ = (1 − 2t)^(−6/2), the χ²₆ (= Gamma(3, 1/2))
    MGF. Warning: MGFs multiply only for INDEPENDENT summands; and a sum of
    independent uniforms or exponentials with different rates is NOT of the
    same family. Common mistakes: adding standard deviations instead of
    variances; multiplying MGFs of dependent variables. Now you try: X ~
    Bin(5, 0.3), Y ~ Bin(7, 0.3) independent: distribution of X + Y.
    (Bin(12, 0.3))

D10. Prove Markov's and Chebyshev's inequalities. For X ~ Exp(1) compare the
     bounds for P(X ≥ 3) with the exact value. How many tosses of a coin
     guarantee (by Chebyshev) that the proportion of heads is within 0.05 of
     p with probability at least 0.95? Compare with the CLT answer.
     Answer: Markov 1/3, Chebyshev 1/4, exact e⁻³ ≈ 0.0498. Chebyshev:
     n ≥ 2000; CLT: n ≥ 385.
     Teacher explains: MARKOV: for X ≥ 0 and a > 0, X ≥ a·1{X ≥ a}; take
     expectations: E X ≥ a P(X ≥ a). CHEBYSHEV: apply Markov to (X − μ)² with
     a = k²σ²:
        P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) = P((X − μ)² ≥ k²σ²) ≤ σ²/(k²σ²) = 1/k²
     Exp(1) has μ = σ = 1:
        Markov:     P(X ≥ 3) ≤ 1/3
        Chebyshev:  P(X ≥ 3) ≤ P(|X − 1| ≥ 2) ≤ 1/4
        exact:      e⁻³ ≈ 0.0498
     The bounds are crude because they hold for EVERY distribution with that
     mean (and variance). Coin: p̂ has mean p and variance p(1 − p)/n ≤ 1/(4n):
        P(|p̂ − p| ≥ 0.05) ≤ (1/(4n))/0.0025 = 100/n ≤ 0.05  ⇔  n ≥ 2000
     CLT: p̂ ≈ N(p, p(1 − p)/n); need 1.96·√(0.25/n) ≤ 0.05, n ≥ (1.96/0.1)² =
     384.16, so n = 385. Chebyshev is guaranteed but wasteful; the CLT is
     approximate but realistic. Common mistakes: using Markov for a
     variable that can be negative; forgetting that Chebyshev bounds a
     TWO-sided event. Now you try: E X = 5, Var X = 4: bound P(|X − 5| ≥ 4)
     and P(1 < X < 9) from below. (≤ 1/4; ≥ 3/4)

D11. State and prove the weak law of large numbers (finite variance). Define
     convergence almost surely, in probability and in distribution, and give
     an example that converges in probability but whose means do not
     converge. Estimate π by Monte Carlo with 10 000 random points and give
     the standard error.
     Answer: P(|X̄ₙ − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ²/(nε²) → 0. Example: Xₙ = n with
     probability 1/n, else 0. π̂ = 4 × (fraction inside the quarter circle),
     standard error ≈ 0.0164.
     Teacher explains: WLLN: X₁, X₂, ... iid, mean μ, variance σ². Then
     E X̄ₙ = μ and Var X̄ₙ = σ²/n (independence makes the variances add:
     n σ²/n²). Chebyshev:
        P(|X̄ₙ − μ| ≥ ε) ≤ σ²/(nε²) → 0   for every ε > 0   ∎
     MODES: Xₙ → X ALMOST SURELY if P(lim Xₙ = X) = 1; IN PROBABILITY if
     P(|Xₙ − X| > ε) → 0 for each ε; IN DISTRIBUTION if Fₙ(x) → F(x) at the
     continuity points. a.s. ⇒ probability ⇒ distribution. The STRONG law
     says X̄ₙ → μ almost surely (only E|X| < ∞ needed). Example: Xₙ = n with
     probability 1/n, 0 otherwise: P(|Xₙ| > ε) = 1/n → 0, so Xₙ → 0 in
     probability, yet E Xₙ = 1 for all n. MONTE CARLO: throw n uniform points
     in the unit square; Iᵢ = 1 if inside the quarter disc, P = π/4. By the
     LLN 4Ī → π. Standard error:
        4√(p(1 − p)/n) = 4√(0.7854·0.2146/10000) ≈ 4(0.004105) ≈ 0.0164
     so about two correct decimals: Monte Carlo error decreases only like
     1/√n. The LLN FAILS for the Cauchy distribution: X̄ₙ is again Cauchy for
     every n. Common mistakes: 'the LLN says Sₙ − nμ → 0' (it is Sₙ/n − μ → 0;
     Sₙ − nμ is of size √n); 'the LLN makes the next toss compensate'. Now
     you try: iid Xᵢ ~ N(0, 4): limit of (1/n)∑Xᵢ². (E X² = 4)

D12. State the central limit theorem and sketch its proof with MGFs. Use it
     with a continuity correction for P(X ≥ 60) when X ~ Bin(100, 0.5), and
     for P(S ≤ 330) when S is the total of 100 fair dice.
     Answer: (Sₙ − nμ)/(σ√n) → N(0, 1). P(X ≥ 60) ≈ P(Z ≥ 1.9) ≈ 0.0287
     (exact 0.0284). P(S ≤ 330) ≈ Φ(−1.142) ≈ 0.127.
     Teacher explains: THEOREM: iid, mean μ, variance σ² ∈ (0, ∞); then
     Zₙ = (Sₙ − nμ)/(σ√n) → N(0, 1) in distribution, whatever the shape of the
     original distribution. PROOF SKETCH (MGF exists): let Yᵢ = (Xᵢ − μ)/σ,
     mean 0, variance 1, M_Y(s) = 1 + s²/2 + o(s²). Then
        M_{Zₙ}(t) = [M_Y(t/√n)]ⁿ = [1 + t²/(2n) + o(1/n)]ⁿ → e^(t²/2)
     the N(0, 1) MGF; a continuity theorem turns MGF convergence into
     convergence in distribution. BINOMIAL: X = sum of 100 Bernoulli(0.5),
     μ = 50, σ = 5. X is integer valued, so P(X ≥ 60) = P(X > 59.5):
        P(Z ≥ (59.5 − 50)/5) = P(Z ≥ 1.9) = 0.0287      (exact 0.0284)
     Without the correction, P(Z ≥ 2) = 0.0228, noticeably worse. DICE: one
     die has μ = 3.5, σ² = 35/12; for 100 dice E S = 350, Var S = 291.67,
     sd 17.078:
        P(S ≤ 330) ≈ Φ((330.5 − 350)/17.078) = Φ(−1.142) ≈ 0.127
     Common mistakes: dividing by σ instead of σ√n (or σ/√n for a mean);
     applying the continuity correction in the wrong direction; using the
     CLT for n = 3 with a skewed distribution. Now you try: sum of 100 iid
     Exp(1): P(S > 110). (μ = 100, σ = 10: P(Z > 1) ≈ 0.1587)

M10. Laws of large numbers and convergence. Give the limit (or say 'no
     limit') and the type of convergence where asked.
     a) X̄ₙ for iid with mean 3
     b) (1/n)∑Xᵢ², Xᵢ iid N(0, 4)

     e) Xₙ ~ N(0, 1/n)
     f) Xₙ ~ N(0, n): converges in distribution?
     g) Xₙ uniform on {1/n, 2/n, ..., 1}
     h) Mₙ = max of n iid U(0, 1); also n(1 − Mₙ)
     i) Monte Carlo ∫₀¹ eˣ dx by (1/n)∑e^(Uᵢ): variance of one term; standard
        error for n = 10 000
     j) proportion of heads in Bernoulli(0.3) trials
     k) (U₁U₂···Uₙ)^(1/n), Uᵢ iid U(0, 1)
     l) sample variance sₙ² of iid data with variance σ²
     m) (1/n)∑XᵢYᵢ for iid pairs
     n) which implications hold among a.s., in probability, in distribution?
     o) proportion of sixes in die rolls
     Answers:
       a) 3 (in probability and a.s.)   b) 4      c) no limit (X̄ₙ is Cauchy)
       d) → 0 in probability; E Xₙ = 1 for all n
       e) → 0 (in probability)          f) no (mass escapes to ±∞)
       g) U(0, 1) in distribution       h) 1 in probability; Exp(1) in
                                           distribution
       i) (e² − 1)/2 − (e − 1)² ≈ 0.2420; ≈ 0.00492
       j) 0.3        k) e⁻¹ ≈ 0.3679 (E ln U = −1)      l) σ²
       m) E[XY]
       n) a.s. ⇒ probability ⇒ distribution; distribution to a constant ⇒
          probability
       o) 1/6

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always DRAW the support before integrating a joint density,
  shade the event, and write the limits from the picture; build joint pmf
  tables with row and column totals. Keep a one-page MGF table and practise
  'multiply and recognise'. For the CLT, drill the single recipe:
  mean nμ, variance nσ², standardise, continuity correction if integer,
  read Φ. Simulate: histograms of sums of 1, 2, 5, 30 dice show the CLT
  emerging; running averages of coin tosses show the LLN (and that the
  deviation Sₙ − n/2 does NOT shrink). Harder: prove the tower law from the
  definition; derive the bivariate normal conditional density by completing
  the square; show that the sum of independent Gamma(αᵢ, λ) is
  Gamma(∑αᵢ, λ); prove the SLLN under a finite fourth moment using
  Borel-Cantelli; prove Lyapunov's or Lindeberg's CLT; find the limit law of
  the maximum of n iid Exp(1) minus ln n (Gumbel); and show by a Cauchy
  example why the CLT needs a finite variance.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.36 — MATHEMATICAL STATISTICS: ESTIMATION, MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD,
HYPOTHESIS TESTING, CONFIDENCE INTERVALS, REGRESSION
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A RANDOM SAMPLE X₁, ..., Xₙ is iid from a model f(x; θ). A STATISTIC is a
    function of the data only; an ESTIMATOR θ̂ is a statistic used to guess θ.
    Its SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION describes how θ̂ varies from sample to sample;
    its standard deviation is the STANDARD ERROR (SE).
  - PROPERTIES: BIAS b(θ̂) = E θ̂ − θ (UNBIASED if 0); MSE = E(θ̂ − θ)² =
    Var θ̂ + b²; CONSISTENT if θ̂ₙ → θ in probability (enough: bias → 0 and
    variance → 0). X̄ is unbiased for μ; S² = ∑(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n − 1) is unbiased
    for σ² (the 1/n version has bias −σ²/n); S is biased for σ. A biased
    estimator can have smaller MSE. RELATIVE EFFICIENCY = ratio of variances.
  - METHOD OF MOMENTS: equate sample moments (1/n)∑Xᵢᵏ to population moments
    E[Xᵏ](θ) and solve (as many equations as parameters).
  - MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD: L(θ) = ∏f(xᵢ; θ), ℓ = ln L; solve the SCORE equation
    ℓ′(θ) = 0 and check it is a maximum; if the support depends on θ (U(0, θ))
    maximise directly (θ̂ = max xᵢ). INVARIANCE: the MLE of g(θ) is g(θ̂).
    Standard MLEs: Bernoulli/Poisson X̄, Exp(λ) 1/X̄, Normal μ̂ = X̄,
    σ̂² = (1/n)∑(xᵢ − x̄)².
  - FISHER INFORMATION I(θ) = E[(∂ ln f/∂θ)²] = −E[∂² ln f/∂θ²] (one
    observation). CRAMÉR-RAO: any unbiased θ̂ has Var θ̂ ≥ 1/(nI(θ)); an
    estimator attaining it is EFFICIENT. Under regularity the MLE is
    consistent and ASYMPTOTICALLY NORMAL: θ̂ ≈ N(θ, 1/(nI(θ))), giving
    SE ≈ 1/√(nI(θ̂)). SUFFICIENCY (FACTORISATION): T is sufficient iff
    L(θ) = g(T(x), θ)h(x); e.g. ∑Xᵢ for Poisson, Bernoulli, Exp; max Xᵢ for
    U(0, θ); (∑Xᵢ, ∑Xᵢ²) for the normal.
  - NORMAL SAMPLING THEORY: X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n); (n − 1)S²/σ² ~ χ²ₙ₋₁; X̄ and S²
    INDEPENDENT; T = (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) ~ tₙ₋₁; S₁²/S₂² ~ F(n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1) when
    σ₁ = σ₂. χ²ₖ has mean k, variance 2k; tₖ → N(0, 1) as k → ∞; tₖ² = F(1, k).
  - CONFIDENCE INTERVALS from a PIVOT: 95% z-interval x̄ ± 1.96σ/√n;
    t-interval x̄ ± t_{n−1, 0.025}s/√n; variance ((n − 1)s²/χ²_{upper},
    (n − 1)s²/χ²_{lower}); proportion p̂ ± z√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n); difference of
    means (pooled or not) and of proportions; PAIRED data: work with the
    differences. MEANING: the procedure covers the true θ in 95% of repeated
    samples (θ is fixed, the interval is random). Width ∝ 1/√n; SAMPLE SIZE
    n = (zσ/E)² (for proportions (z/E)²p(1 − p) ≤ (z/E)²/4).
  - HYPOTHESIS TESTS: null H₀ and alternative H₁ (one- or two-sided); TEST
    STATISTIC; REJECTION REGION; TYPE I error (reject a true H₀, probability
    α = SIGNIFICANCE LEVEL); TYPE II error (accept a false H₀, probability β);
    POWER = 1 − β; P-VALUE = probability, under H₀, of a result at least as
    extreme as observed; reject when p ≤ α. A two-sided level-α test rejects
    θ₀ exactly when θ₀ is outside the 100(1 − α)% interval (DUALITY).
    'Not rejected' is not 'proved true'.
  - NEYMAN-PEARSON LEMMA: for simple H₀: θ = θ₀ vs H₁: θ = θ₁ the most
    powerful level-α test rejects when L(θ₁)/L(θ₀) > k. LIKELIHOOD RATIO TEST
    Λ = sup_{H₀}L/sup L; WILKS: −2 ln Λ ≈ χ² with df = number of restrictions.
  - STANDARD TESTS: z-test (σ known or large n); one-sample, PAIRED and
    TWO-SAMPLE (pooled s_p² = ((n₁ − 1)s₁² + (n₂ − 1)s₂²)/(n₁ + n₂ − 2), or
    Welch) t-tests; tests for proportions; χ² test for σ²; F-test for σ₁²/σ₂²;
    PEARSON χ² = ∑(O − E)²/E for GOODNESS OF FIT (df = k − 1 − #estimated
    parameters) and INDEPENDENCE in an r × c table (E = row total × column
    total/n, df = (r − 1)(c − 1)); expected counts should be ≥ 5.
  - SIMPLE LINEAR REGRESSION Yᵢ = β₀ + β₁xᵢ + εᵢ, εᵢ iid N(0, σ²). LEAST
    SQUARES (= MLE under normal errors): β̂₁ = S_xy/S_xx, β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄, with
    S_xx = ∑(xᵢ − x̄)², S_xy = ∑(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ). Residuals eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ sum to
    0; SSE = ∑eᵢ², s² = SSE/(n − 2) unbiased for σ²; SST = SSR + SSE,
    R² = SSR/SST = r² (r = S_xy/√(S_xx S_yy)).
  - REGRESSION INFERENCE: SE(β̂₁) = s/√S_xx, (β̂₁ − β₁)/SE ~ tₙ₋₂;
    SE(β̂₀) = s√(1/n + x̄²/S_xx); mean response at x₀: ŷ₀ ± t·s√(1/n +
    (x₀ − x̄)²/S_xx); PREDICTION interval: ŷ₀ ± t·s√(1 + 1/n + (x₀ − x̄)²/S_xx).
    ANOVA F = MSR/MSE = t². MATRIX FORM y = Xβ + ε: β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy,
    Cov β̂ = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹; GAUSS-MARKOV: least squares is the BEST LINEAR
    UNBIASED ESTIMATOR (BLUE). Residual df = n − (number of β's).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove that S² is unbiased for σ² and that MSE = Var + bias². For a sample
    of n from U(0, θ) compare T₁ = 2X̄, T₂ = max Xᵢ and T₃ = ((n + 1)/n)max Xᵢ
    (bias, MSE, consistency); give the numbers for n = 10.
    Answer: E S² = σ². T₁: unbiased, MSE θ²/(3n); T₂: bias −θ/(n + 1), MSE
    2θ²/((n + 1)(n + 2)); T₃: unbiased, MSE θ²/(n(n + 2)). For n = 10:
    θ²/30 ≈ 0.0333θ², θ²/66 ≈ 0.0152θ², θ²/120 ≈ 0.0083θ². All consistent;
    T₃ is best.
    Teacher explains: S²: use ∑(Xᵢ − X̄)² = ∑Xᵢ² − nX̄² and E X² = σ² + μ²,
    E X̄² = σ²/n + μ²:
       E∑(Xᵢ − X̄)² = n(σ² + μ²) − n(σ²/n + μ²) = (n − 1)σ²
    so dividing by n − 1 gives E S² = σ². (We lose one degree of freedom
    because X̄ was estimated from the same data.) MSE:
       E(θ̂ − θ)² = E(θ̂ − Eθ̂ + Eθ̂ − θ)² = Var θ̂ + b² (cross term has mean 0)
    U(0, θ): Var X = θ²/12, so Var(2X̄) = 4θ²/(12n) = θ²/(3n). For M = max,
    P(M ≤ m) = (m/θ)ⁿ, density nmⁿ⁻¹/θⁿ, so
       E M = nθ/(n + 1),   E M² = nθ²/(n + 2),   Var M = nθ²/((n + 1)²(n + 2))
       MSE(M) = Var M + θ²/(n + 1)² = 2θ²/((n + 1)(n + 2))
       T₃ = ((n + 1)/n)M: Var = (n + 1)²/n² · Var M = θ²/(n(n + 2))
    n = 10: 0.0333θ², 0.0152θ², 0.0083θ². T₂ is biased yet beats the
    unbiased T₁; T₃ removes the bias and is best (its MSE falls like 1/n²,
    not 1/n). All MSEs → 0, so all three are CONSISTENT. Common mistakes:
    thinking 'unbiased' means 'good'; forgetting the bias term in the MSE.
    Now you try: is T = (X₁ + 2X₂)/3 unbiased for μ, and what is its
    variance? (yes; 5σ²/9, worse than X̄ = σ²/2 for n = 2)

D2. Find method-of-moments estimators for (a) U(0, θ), (b) Gamma(α, λ) and
    (c) f(x; θ) = θx^(θ−1) on (0, 1); evaluate (b) when n = 50, x̄ = 4 and
    (1/n)∑(xᵢ − x̄)² = 8, and (c) for data 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, 0.9. Then state
    the factorisation theorem and find sufficient statistics for the
    Poisson and normal models.
    Answer: (a) 2X̄; (b) α̂ = X̄²/σ̂², λ̂ = X̄/σ̂² → α̂ = 2, λ̂ = 0.5;
    (c) θ̂ = X̄/(1 − X̄) = 0.62/0.38 ≈ 1.632. Poisson: ∑Xᵢ; normal:
    (∑Xᵢ, ∑Xᵢ²).
    Teacher explains: METHOD: write E X (and E X² if needed) in terms of the
    parameters, set them equal to the sample versions, and solve.
       (a) E X = θ/2 = X̄ ⇒ θ̂ = 2X̄
       (b) E X = α/λ, Var X = α/λ²: dividing, λ = E X/Var X, α = (E X)²/Var X
           ⇒ λ̂ = 4/8 = 0.5, α̂ = 16/8 = 2
       (c) E X = ∫₀¹ θxᶿ dx = θ/(θ + 1) = X̄ ⇒ θ̂ = X̄/(1 − X̄)
    For the data in (c), x̄ = 3.1/5 = 0.62, so θ̂ = 1.632. Moment estimators
    are easy but can be silly: in (a) 2X̄ may be SMALLER than the largest
    observation (data 1.2, 3.4, 0.6, 2.8: 2x̄ = 4.0 fine, but 0.1, 0.1, 3 give
    2x̄ = 2.13 < 3). FACTORISATION: T(X) is SUFFICIENT for θ (contains all
    the information about θ) iff L(θ; x) = g(T(x), θ)·h(x). Poisson:
       L = ∏ e^(−λ)λ^(xᵢ)/xᵢ! = [e^(−nλ)λ^(∑xᵢ)]·[1/∏xᵢ!]
    so T = ∑Xᵢ. Normal: L = (2πσ²)^(−n/2) exp(−(∑xᵢ² − 2μ∑xᵢ + nμ²)/(2σ²))
    depends on the data only through (∑xᵢ, ∑xᵢ²). Common mistakes: using
    the (n − 1) variance in moment equations (the method uses 1/n); mixing
    up rate and scale for the Gamma. Now you try: method of moments for
    Poisson(λ) and for Geometric(p) on {1, 2, ...}. (λ̂ = X̄; p̂ = 1/X̄)

D3. Find the MLEs for (a) Exp(λ), (b) N(μ, σ²) with both unknown, (c) U(0, θ),
    and (d) f(x; θ) = θx^(θ−1). Evaluate (a) and the MLE of P(X > 1) for data
    2, 3, 1, 4, 5, and (d) for the data of D2.
    Answer: (a) λ̂ = 1/X̄ = 1/3, P̂(X > 1) = e^(−1/3) ≈ 0.7165; (b) μ̂ = X̄,
    σ̂² = (1/n)∑(Xᵢ − X̄)²; (c) θ̂ = max Xᵢ; (d) θ̂ = −n/∑ln xᵢ ≈ 1.827.
    Teacher explains: RECIPE: likelihood → log → differentiate → solve →
    check maximum.
       (a) ℓ(λ) = n ln λ − λ∑xᵢ,  ℓ′ = n/λ − ∑xᵢ = 0 ⇒ λ̂ = 1/x̄;
           ℓ″ = −n/λ² < 0 ✓
    Data: x̄ = 3, λ̂ = 1/3. By INVARIANCE the MLE of P(X > 1) = e^(−λ) is
    e^(−1/3) ≈ 0.7165 (no new maximisation needed).
       (b) ℓ = −(n/2)ln(2πσ²) − ∑(xᵢ − μ)²/(2σ²)
           ∂ℓ/∂μ = ∑(xᵢ − μ)/σ² = 0 ⇒ μ̂ = x̄
           ∂ℓ/∂σ² = −n/(2σ²) + ∑(xᵢ − μ)²/(2σ⁴) = 0 ⇒ σ̂² = (1/n)∑(xᵢ − x̄)²
    (biased: the MLE need not be unbiased.) (c) L(θ) = θ⁻ⁿ if θ ≥ all xᵢ,
    and 0 otherwise. θ⁻ⁿ DEcreases in θ, so take θ as small as allowed:
    θ̂ = max xᵢ. Calculus fails here (ℓ′ = −n/θ ≠ 0): the support depends on
    θ. (d) ℓ = n ln θ + (θ − 1)∑ln xᵢ, ℓ′ = n/θ + ∑ln xᵢ = 0:
       θ̂ = −n/∑ln xᵢ = −5/(−1.20397 − 0.69315 − 0.51083 − 0.22314 − 0.10536)
          = 5/2.73645 ≈ 1.827
    different from the moment estimate 1.632 of D2. Common mistakes: setting
    the derivative of L (not ln L) with products; differentiating with
    respect to σ instead of σ² and then mixing them (both give the same
    σ̂², but be consistent). Now you try: MLE of λ for Poisson counts
    3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2 and of P(X = 0). (x̄ = 25/7 ≈ 3.571; e^(−25/7) ≈ 0.0281)

D4. Define Fisher information and state the Cramér-Rao bound. Compute I for
    Bernoulli(p) and Poisson(λ), show that X̄ attains the bound for the
    Poisson mean, and use the asymptotic normality of the MLE to give an
    approximate 95% interval for p when 30 successes occur in 100 trials.
    Answer: I(p) = 1/(p(1 − p)), I(λ) = 1/λ; Var X̄ = λ/n = CRLB. p̂ = 0.3,
    SE ≈ 0.0458, interval ≈ (0.210, 0.390).
    Teacher explains: For one observation, I(θ) = E[(∂ ln f/∂θ)²] =
    −E[∂² ln f/∂θ²]: the expected curvature of the log-likelihood (sharper
    peak = more information). Bernoulli: ln f = x ln p + (1 − x)ln(1 − p),
       ∂²/∂p² = −x/p² − (1 − x)/(1 − p)²,
       I(p) = 1/p + 1/(1 − p) = 1/(p(1 − p))
    Poisson: ln f = −λ + x ln λ − ln x!, ∂²/∂λ² = −x/λ², I(λ) = E X/λ² = 1/λ.
    CRAMÉR-RAO: for unbiased θ̂ based on n iid observations,
    Var θ̂ ≥ 1/(nI(θ)). (Proof idea: Cov(θ̂, score) = 1 and Cauchy-Schwarz.)
    For Poisson the bound is λ/n and Var X̄ = λ/n: X̄ is EFFICIENT (no
    unbiased estimator does better). ASYMPTOTICS: the MLE satisfies
    θ̂ ≈ N(θ, 1/(nI(θ))) for large n. With 30/100, p̂ = 0.3 and
       SE = √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) = √(0.21/100) = 0.0458
       95%:  0.3 ± 1.96 × 0.0458 = 0.3 ± 0.0898 = (0.210, 0.390)
    This is the WALD interval. Common mistakes: forgetting the factor n in
    the bound; using the CRLB for biased estimators without adjustment.
    Now you try: I(λ) for Exp(λ) and the approximate SE of λ̂ = 1/X̄ when
    n = 50, x̄ = 2. (1/λ²; λ̂/√n = 0.5/√50 ≈ 0.0707)

D5. State the sampling theorem for normal samples, derive the t-interval,
    and compute a 95% interval for μ from the 10 measurements 12.1, 11.8,
    12.5, 12.0, 11.6, 12.3, 12.2, 11.9, 12.4, 12.2.
    Answer: x̄ = 12.1, s ≈ 0.2789, SE ≈ 0.0882, t₉ = 2.262; interval
    12.1 ± 0.1995 = (11.90, 12.30).
    Teacher explains: THEOREM: for iid N(μ, σ²), X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n),
    (n − 1)S²/σ² ~ χ²ₙ₋₁, and X̄, S² are independent. Hence
       T = (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) = [(X̄ − μ)/(σ/√n)] / √[((n − 1)S²/σ²)/(n − 1)]
    is N(0, 1)/√(χ²ₙ₋₁/(n − 1)) with independent parts: the t distribution with
    n − 1 degrees of freedom, whatever μ and σ are (a PIVOT). So
       P(−t_{n−1,0.025} ≤ T ≤ t_{n−1,0.025}) = 0.95
    and rearranging for μ: X̄ ± t_{n−1,0.025}S/√n. Numbers: ∑x = 121,
    x̄ = 12.1; deviations 0, −0.3, 0.4, −0.1, −0.5, 0.2, 0.1, −0.2, 0.3, 0.1,
    sum of squares 0.70, s² = 0.70/9 = 0.07778, s = 0.2789, SE = 0.2789/√10
    = 0.0882, t₉,0.025 = 2.262:
       12.1 ± 2.262 × 0.0882 = 12.1 ± 0.1995 = (11.90, 12.30)
    MEANING: if we repeated the experiment many times, 95% of such intervals
    would contain μ; we do not say 'μ is in (11.90, 12.30) with probability
    0.95' (μ is not random). The t-quantile (2.262) is larger than 1.96
    because s is itself uncertain; for large n they agree. Common mistakes:
    using 1.96 with s and small n; dividing by √(n − 1); using s² instead of
    s. Now you try: x̄ = 20, s = 4, n = 10, 95% interval. (20 ± 2.262·1.265
    = 20 ± 2.861 = (17.14, 22.86))

D6. (a) A poll finds 520 of 1000 in favour: give a 95% interval for p and
    decide how large n must be for a margin of 0.03. (b) A sample of 10 from
    a normal population has s² = 4: 95% interval for σ² and σ. (c) Explain
    how the width of an interval depends on n and on the confidence level.
    Answer: (a) 0.52 ± 0.031 = (0.489, 0.551); n ≥ 1068. (b) σ²: (1.892,
    13.33); σ: (1.376, 3.651). (c) width ∝ z/√n: ×4 in n halves it; 99%
    instead of 95% multiplies it by 1.314.
    Teacher explains: (a) By the CLT p̂ ≈ N(p, p(1 − p)/n):
       SE = √(0.52 × 0.48/1000) = 0.0158,   0.52 ± 1.96 × 0.0158 = 0.52 ± 0.031
    The interval contains 0.5, so a 5% two-sided test would NOT reject
    p = 0.5 (duality). Sample size: z√(p(1 − p)/n) ≤ E with the worst case
    p(1 − p) ≤ 1/4:
       n ≥ (1.96/0.03)² × 0.25 = 1067.1  ⇒  n = 1068
    (b) Pivot (n − 1)S²/σ² ~ χ²₉. With χ²₉ quantiles 2.700 (2.5%) and 19.023
    (97.5%):
       2.700 ≤ 9 × 4/σ² ≤ 19.023  ⇔  36/19.023 ≤ σ² ≤ 36/2.700
       σ² ∈ (1.892, 13.33),   σ ∈ (1.376, 3.651)   (take square roots)
    The interval is NOT symmetric about s² = 4 (the χ² is skewed), and it
    is wide: 10 observations say little about a variance. (c) Half-width
    z·σ/√n: quadrupling n halves the width; going from 95% to 99% changes
    z from 1.960 to 2.576, factor 1.314. More confidence costs width.
    Common mistakes: swapping the χ² quantiles (the larger quantile gives
    the LOWER limit); rounding n down. Now you try: 30 successes in 100,
    99% interval. (0.3 ± 2.576 × 0.0458 = (0.182, 0.418))

D7. A machine should fill packets with mean 500 g; σ = 10 g is known. A sample
    of 25 has x̄ = 496. Test H₀: μ = 500 against H₁: μ ≠ 500 at the 5% level,
    give the p-value, and compute the power of the test when μ = 495. How
    large should n be for power 0.90 at μ = 495? Explain type I and II errors.
    Answer: z = −2, p ≈ 0.0455 < 0.05: reject H₀ (not at 1%). Power at 495
    ≈ 0.705 (β ≈ 0.295). n ≈ 43.
    Teacher explains: TEST STATISTIC under H₀: Z = (X̄ − 500)/(σ/√n) ~ N(0, 1).
       z = (496 − 500)/(10/5) = −2
    Rejection region at 5% two-sided: |z| > 1.96, so reject. P-VALUE:
    P(|Z| ≥ 2) = 2(0.02275) = 0.0455: the chance of a result this extreme if
    H₀ were true. Since 0.01 < p < 0.05, reject at 5% but not at 1%. TYPE I
    error = rejecting a true H₀ (probability α = 0.05 by design); TYPE II
    error = failing to reject a false H₀ (probability β). POWER at μ = 495:
    now X̄ ~ N(495, 2²), and we reject if X̄ < 500 − 3.92 = 496.08 or
    X̄ > 503.92:
       P(X̄ < 496.08) = Φ((496.08 − 495)/2) = Φ(0.54) = 0.7054
       P(X̄ > 503.92) = 1 − Φ(4.46) ≈ 0
    power ≈ 0.705, β ≈ 0.295. SAMPLE SIZE for power 0.9 (ignoring the far
    tail): need √n·5/10 ≥ 1.96 + 1.2816, i.e.
       n ≥ ((1.96 + 1.2816) × 10/5)² = 42.03  ⇒  n = 43
    Common mistakes: 'p = 0.0455 is the probability that H₀ is true' (it is
    not); forgetting to double the one-tail probability for a two-sided
    test; 'accepting' H₀ when not rejecting. Now you try: power of the same
    test at μ = 496. (Φ(0.04) ≈ 0.516)

D8. Carry out (a) a paired t-test on blood pressure before 140, 135, 150, 145,
    160, 138 and after 132, 130, 148, 140, 151, 136 treatment, and (b) a pooled
    two-sample t-test for group A (n = 8, x̄ = 25.3, s = 2.1) against group B
    (n = 10, x̄ = 23.1, s = 2.5), both at the 5% level, two-sided. Why is the
    paired design better when it is possible?
    Answer: (a) d = 8, 5, 2, 5, 9, 2; d̄ ≈ 5.167, s_d ≈ 2.927, t ≈ 4.32 > 2.571
    (df 5, p ≈ 0.0075): reject, the treatment lowers pressure. (b) s_p² =
    5.445, SE ≈ 1.107, t ≈ 1.99 < 2.120 (df 16, p ≈ 0.064): do not reject.
    Teacher explains: (a) PAIRED: the same people are measured twice, so the
    two samples are dependent. Reduce to one sample of differences:
       d = 8, 5, 2, 5, 9, 2;  d̄ = 31/6 = 5.167;  s_d = 2.927;  SE = 2.927/√6
         = 1.195
       t = 5.167/1.195 = 4.32,  df = 5,  t₅,0.025 = 2.571  ⇒ reject H₀: μ_d = 0
    A 95% interval for the mean drop: 5.167 ± 2.571 × 1.195 = (2.10, 8.24).
    (b) TWO INDEPENDENT SAMPLES with equal variances assumed:
       s_p² = (7 × 2.1² + 9 × 2.5²)/16 = (30.87 + 56.25)/16 = 5.445
       SE = √(5.445(1/8 + 1/10)) = 1.107
       t = (25.3 − 23.1)/1.107 = 1.99,  df = 16,  t₁₆,0.025 = 2.120
    so we do not reject (p ≈ 0.064). An F-test (F = 2.5²/2.1² = 1.42, far
    below its 5% two-sided critical value 4.82 for (9, 7) df) supports the
    equal-variance assumption; Welch's test gives t ≈ 2.03 with ≈ 15.9 df, the
    same conclusion. Pairing removes the large person-to-person variation
    from the comparison, so the SE is smaller and the test more powerful.
    Common mistakes: analysing paired data as two independent samples;
    using n₁ + n₂ − 1 degrees of freedom. Now you try: one-sample t-test of
    μ = 12.5 with the data of D5. (t = (12.1 − 12.5)/0.0882 ≈ −4.54, df 9:
    reject, p ≈ 0.0014)

D9. State and prove the Neyman-Pearson lemma (continuous case). Use it to
    find the most powerful 5% test of H₀: μ = 0 against H₁: μ = 1 for a
    sample of n = 9 from N(μ, 1), and compute its power. What is a
    likelihood ratio test and what does Wilks' theorem say?
    Answer: reject when x̄ > 1.645/3 ≈ 0.548; power = Φ(3 − 1.645) = Φ(1.355)
    ≈ 0.912. LRT: reject for small Λ = sup_{H₀}L/sup L; −2 ln Λ ≈ χ²_r.
    Teacher explains: LEMMA: among all tests with P₀(reject) ≤ α, the test φ*
    that rejects when L₁(x)/L₀(x) > k (k chosen so P₀(reject) = α) has the
    largest power. PROOF: for any other level-α test φ,
       ∫ (φ* − φ)(L₁ − kL₀) dx ≥ 0
    because where L₁ > kL₀, φ* = 1 ≥ φ, and where L₁ < kL₀, φ* = 0 ≤ φ. So
    P₁(φ*) − P₁(φ) ≥ k[P₀(φ*) − P₀(φ)] ≥ 0. ∎  Normal example:
       L₁/L₀ = exp(−∑(xᵢ − 1)²/2 + ∑xᵢ²/2) = exp(∑xᵢ − n/2)
    which increases with x̄: 'ratio large' ⇔ 'x̄ large'. Under H₀,
    X̄ ~ N(0, 1/9), so reject when x̄ > 1.645/3 = 0.5483. Power: under H₁,
    X̄ ~ N(1, 1/9):
       P(X̄ > 0.5483) = P(Z > (0.5483 − 1) × 3) = P(Z > −1.355) = 0.912
    The same region is most powerful for EVERY μ₁ > 0: a UNIFORMLY MOST
    POWERFUL one-sided test. LRT for composite hypotheses: Λ =
    sup_{θ∈H₀}L(θ)/sup_θ L(θ) ∈ [0, 1]; reject when Λ is small. WILKS: under H₀,
    −2 ln Λ → χ² with df = number of parameters fixed by H₀. The t-test and
    the χ² tests are LRTs (or approximations). Common mistakes: putting the
    rejection region on the wrong side; forgetting that the constant k is
    fixed by α, not chosen freely. Now you try: coin, 60 heads in 100:
    compute −2 ln Λ for H₀: p = 1/2. (2[60 ln 1.2 + 40 ln 0.8] ≈ 4.03 > 3.841:
    reject at 5%)

D10. (a) A die is rolled 120 times with counts 15, 25, 18, 22, 16, 24. Is it
     fair (5% level)? (b) In a trial, 60 of 100 patients on a drug improve
     against 45 of 100 on placebo. Test independence of treatment and
     outcome with a χ² test and relate it to the two-proportion z-test.
     Answer: (a) χ² = 4.5 < 11.07 (df 5, p ≈ 0.48): no evidence of bias.
     (b) χ² ≈ 4.511 > 3.841 (df 1, p ≈ 0.034): reject independence; z ≈ 2.124
     and z² = χ².
     Teacher explains: (a) Under H₀ each face has expected count 120/6 = 20.
        χ² = ∑(O − E)²/E = (25 + 25 + 4 + 4 + 16 + 16)/20 = 90/20 = 4.5
     df = 6 − 1 = 5 (one constraint: the counts add to 120). Critical value
     χ²₅,0.05 = 11.07. Not significant: deviations of this size happen about
     half the time with a fair die. (b) Table with totals:
                 improved  not   total
        drug        60      40    100
        placebo     45      55    100
        total      105      95    200
     Expected counts E = row total × column total/n: 52.5, 47.5 in each row.
        χ² = 7.5²(1/52.5 + 1/47.5 + 1/52.5 + 1/47.5) = 56.25 × 0.0802 = 4.511
     df = (2 − 1)(2 − 1) = 1, critical 3.841: reject independence (p ≈ 0.034).
     Same data as proportions: p̂₁ = 0.60, p̂₂ = 0.45, pooled p̂ = 0.525,
        z = 0.15/√(0.525 × 0.475 × (1/100 + 1/100)) = 0.15/0.0706 = 2.124
     and 2.124² = 4.511: for 2 × 2 tables the χ² test is the two-sided
     two-proportion test. (Yates' continuity correction gives 3.93, still
     significant.) Common mistakes: using percentages instead of counts;
     wrong df; applying χ² with expected counts below 5. Now you try:
     counts 315, 108, 101, 32 against Mendel's 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. (E = 312.75,
     104.25, 104.25, 34.75; χ² ≈ 0.470, df 3: an excellent fit)

D11. Derive the least-squares estimates for the line y = β₀ + β₁x and fit it
     to (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5). Find the fitted values,
     residuals, SSE, R² and r, and explain why least squares is also the MLE
     under normal errors.
     Answer: β̂₁ = 0.6, β̂₀ = 2.2; ŷ = 2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6, 5.2; residuals −0.8,
     0.6, 1.0, −0.6, −0.2; SSE = 2.4; SST = 6; R² = 0.6; r ≈ 0.775.
     Teacher explains: Minimise Q(β₀, β₁) = ∑(yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ)². Setting the
     partial derivatives to 0 gives the NORMAL EQUATIONS
        ∑(yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ) = 0,     ∑xᵢ(yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ) = 0
     The first gives β₀ = ȳ − β₁x̄ (the line passes through (x̄, ȳ)); putting
     it in the second gives β₁ = S_xy/S_xx. Data: x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4,
        x − x̄:  −2, −1, 0, 1, 2       y − ȳ:  −2, 0, 1, 0, 1
        S_xx = 10,  S_xy = 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 6,  S_yy = 6
        β̂₁ = 0.6,  β̂₀ = 4 − 0.6 × 3 = 2.2
     Fitted ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6x: 2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6, 5.2; residuals −0.8, 0.6, 1.0,
     −0.6, −0.2 (they sum to 0, and ∑xᵢeᵢ = 0: the normal equations).
        SSE = 0.64 + 0.36 + 1 + 0.36 + 0.04 = 2.4,  SSR = β̂₁S_xy = 3.6
        R² = SSR/SST = 3.6/6 = 0.6,  r = 6/√(10 × 6) = 0.775 (r² = R²)
     60% of the variation of y is explained by x. MLE: with εᵢ ~ N(0, σ²),
     ℓ = −(n/2)ln(2πσ²) − Q(β₀, β₁)/(2σ²), so maximising ℓ over β is
     minimising Q; and σ̂²_MLE = SSE/n (biased; SSE/(n − 2) is unbiased).
     Common mistakes: β̂₁ = S_xy/S_yy (that is the regression of x on y);
     reading R² as 'the slope is 0.6'. Now you try: n = 10, ∑x = 50,
     ∑y = 100, ∑x² = 300, ∑xy = 560: the line. (S_xx = 50, S_xy = 60,
     β̂₁ = 1.2, β̂₀ = 4)

D12. For the data of D11, test H₀: β₁ = 0 at 5%, give a 95% interval for β₁,
     a 95% interval for the mean response at x₀ = 4 and a 95% prediction
     interval for a new observation there. Write the model in matrix form and
     recover β̂. State the Gauss-Markov theorem.
     Answer: s² = 0.8, SE(β̂₁) ≈ 0.283, t ≈ 2.12 < 3.182 (df 3, p ≈ 0.124):
     do not reject. β₁ ∈ (−0.300, 1.500). Mean at 4: 4.6 ± 1.559 =
     (3.04, 6.16); prediction 4.6 ± 3.245 = (1.35, 7.85). β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy
     = (2.2, 0.6).
     Teacher explains: s² = SSE/(n − 2) = 2.4/3 = 0.8 (two parameters were
     estimated). SE(β̂₁) = s/√S_xx = √(0.8/10) = 0.2828, and
     (β̂₁ − β₁)/SE ~ t₃:
        t = 0.6/0.2828 = 2.12 < t₃,0.025 = 3.182     not significant
        interval 0.6 ± 3.182 × 0.2828 = 0.6 ± 0.900 = (−0.300, 1.500)
     (it contains 0: duality again). With only 5 points a moderate R² is not
     convincing. At x₀ = 4, ŷ₀ = 4.6 and
        mean response:  SE = s√(1/5 + (4 − 3)²/10) = √(0.8 × 0.3) = 0.4899
                        4.6 ± 3.182 × 0.4899 = 4.6 ± 1.559
        new observation: SE = s√(1 + 0.3) = 1.0198,  4.6 ± 3.245
     The prediction interval is wider: it must also cover the new ε. Both
     widen as x₀ moves from x̄. MATRIX FORM: y = Xβ + ε with rows (1, xᵢ):
        XᵀX = [[5, 15], [15, 55]],  Xᵀy = (20, 66),
        (XᵀX)⁻¹ = (1/50)[[55, −15], [−15, 5]] = [[1.1, −0.3], [−0.3, 0.1]]
        β̂ = (1.1·20 − 0.3·66, −0.3·20 + 0.1·66) = (2.2, 0.6) ✓
     and Cov β̂ = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹ gives Var β̂₁ = 0.1σ² ≈ 0.08 ✓. GAUSS-MARKOV: if
     E ε = 0 and Cov ε = σ²I (no normality needed), β̂ has the smallest
     variance among all LINEAR UNBIASED estimators (BLUE). Common mistakes:
     using n − 1 df; confusing the confidence interval for the mean response
     with the prediction interval; extrapolating far outside the data. Now
     you try: the ANOVA F statistic for the fit. (F = (3.6/1)/(2.4/3) = 4.5
     = t²)

    l) Poisson: is (1 − 1/n)^(∑Xᵢ) unbiased for e^(−λ)?

       weights and the resulting variance

    Answers:

M6. Confidence intervals for means and variances (95% unless stated).
    a) x̄ = 50, σ = 10, n = 25 (z)
    b) a) at 99%                    c) a) at 90%
    d) x̄ = 20, s = 4, n = 10 (t)
    e) x̄ = 12.1, s = 0.3, n = 16 (t)
    f) data 4, 6, 5, 7, 3 (t)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: insist on the same three lines for every problem: MODEL (what
  is random, which parameter), PIVOT or TEST STATISTIC with its
  distribution under H₀, and CONCLUSION in words. Simulate 100 confidence
  intervals on a screen and count how many miss the true mean; simulate a
  test many times under H₀ to see that it rejects about 5% of the time.
  Keep a small table of z, t and χ² values and practise reading it. For MLE
  always write ln L before differentiating and check the support. For
  regression, compute S_xx, S_xy, S_yy in a table and draw the scatter plot
  first. Harder: prove the independence of X̄ and S² for normal samples
  (Helmert transformation or Basu's theorem); prove the Cramér-Rao bound
  and the Rao-Blackwell theorem; show that the LRT for a normal mean is the
  t-test; derive Wilks' theorem in one dimension by Taylor expansion; prove
  Gauss-Markov in matrix form; and explore multiple testing (Bonferroni) and
  Bayesian credible intervals as alternatives to the frequentist ideas.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.37 — BAYESIAN STATISTICS; REGRESSION AND LINEAR MODELS; TIME SERIES
(INTRODUCTION)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - BAYESIAN VIEW: the parameter θ is treated as random. A PRIOR density π(θ)
    expresses belief before the data; the LIKELIHOOD L(θ; x) = f(x | θ) comes
    from the model; BAYES' THEOREM gives the POSTERIOR
       π(θ | x) = f(x | θ)π(θ) / m(x)  ∝  likelihood × prior,
    where m(x) = ∫ f(x | θ)π(θ) dθ is the MARGINAL LIKELIHOOD (evidence). Work
    'up to proportionality' and recognise the kernel of a known density.
  - CONJUGATE PRIORS (posterior in the same family as the prior):
       Binomial(n, θ), prior Beta(a, b)  → Beta(a + k, b + n − k)
       Poisson(λ) sample, prior Gamma(α, β) → Gamma(α + ∑xᵢ, β + n)
       Exponential(λ) sample, prior Gamma(α, β) → Gamma(α + n, β + ∑xᵢ)
       N(μ, σ²), σ² known, prior N(μ₀, τ₀²) → N(μₙ, τₙ²) with
       1/τₙ² = 1/τ₀² + n/σ² (PRECISIONS ADD) and μₙ = τₙ²(μ₀/τ₀² + nx̄/σ²),
       a precision-weighted average of prior mean and sample mean.
    (Gamma(α, β) uses the RATE β: mean α/β, variance α/β².) Beta(a, b) has mean
    a/(a + b), mode (a − 1)/(a + b − 2) for a, b > 1, variance
    ab/((a + b)²(a + b + 1)).
  - POINT ESTIMATES are BAYES RULES for a loss: POSTERIOR MEAN (squared loss),
    POSTERIOR MEDIAN (absolute loss), POSTERIOR MODE = MAP (0-1 loss). A
    100(1 − α)% CREDIBLE INTERVAL C has P(θ ∈ C | x) = 1 − α (equal-tailed, or
    HPD = highest posterior density, the shortest). The POSTERIOR PREDICTIVE
    is f(y | x) = ∫ f(y | θ)π(θ | x) dθ (Beta-binomial: P(next success) =
    posterior mean). A FLAT or JEFFREYS prior π(θ) ∝ √I(θ) may be IMPROPER;
    Jeffreys gives Beta(½, ½) for a binomial θ, λ^(−1/2) for a Poisson mean.
  - BAYESIAN TESTING: POSTERIOR ODDS = BAYES FACTOR × PRIOR ODDS, with
    B₀₁ = m₀(x)/m₁(x). For simple hypotheses B₀₁ is the likelihood ratio.
    Bayes factors and p-values can disagree strongly (LINDLEY's paradox: a
    vague prior under H₁ favours H₀). As n → ∞ the posterior concentrates at
    the true θ and the prior's influence vanishes.
  - LINEAR MODEL: Y = Xβ + ε, X an n × p DESIGN MATRIX of full rank p,
    E(ε) = 0, Var(ε) = σ²I. LEAST SQUARES minimises ‖Y − Xβ‖²; the NORMAL
    EQUATIONS XᵀXβ̂ = XᵀY give β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY. Then E(β̂) = β,
    Var(β̂) = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹, fitted values Ŷ = HY with the HAT MATRIX
    H = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ (symmetric, idempotent, trace p), residuals e = (I − H)Y,
    Xᵀe = 0, and s² = RSS/(n − p) is unbiased for σ².
  - GAUSS-MARKOV THEOREM: under these assumptions (no normality needed) β̂ is
    BLUE: every linear unbiased estimator of cᵀβ has variance ≥ that of cᵀβ̂.
  - SIMPLE LINEAR REGRESSION y = α + βx + ε: b = Sxy/Sxx, a = ȳ − bx̄, with
    Sxx = ∑(xᵢ − x̄)², Sxy = ∑(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ), Syy = ∑(yᵢ − ȳ)²;
    RSS = Syy − bSxy; Var(b) = σ²/Sxx; Var(a) = σ²(1/n + x̄²/Sxx). The line
    passes through (x̄, ȳ).
  - ANOVA: TSS = ESS + RSS (∑(yᵢ − ȳ)² = ∑(ŷᵢ − ȳ)² + ∑(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²);
    R² = ESS/TSS = 1 − RSS/TSS (= r² in simple regression); ADJUSTED
    R̄² = 1 − (RSS/(n − p))/(TSS/(n − 1)). With NORMAL errors:
    t = (b − β₀)/SE(b) ~ t(n − 2); overall F = (ESS/(p − 1))/(RSS/(n − p));
    NESTED F = ((RSS_red − RSS_full)/q)/(RSS_full/(n − p)) ~ F(q, n − p); in
    simple regression F = t². CONFIDENCE interval for the mean response at x₀:
    ŷ₀ ± t·s√(1/n + (x₀ − x̄)²/Sxx); PREDICTION interval for a new y:
    ŷ₀ ± t·s√(1 + 1/n + (x₀ − x̄)²/Sxx) (always wider).
  - MODELLING: a factor with k levels needs k − 1 DUMMY variables (k dummies
    plus an intercept = DUMMY TRAP, XᵀX singular); polynomial regression is
    still LINEAR (in β); LEVERAGE hᵢᵢ = 1/n + (xᵢ − x̄)²/Sxx; check residual
    plots for curvature, non-constant variance, outliers; MULTICOLLINEARITY
    inflates Var(β̂).
  - TIME SERIES: (Xₜ) is WEAKLY STATIONARY if E Xₜ = μ and
    Cov(Xₜ, Xₜ₊ₖ) = γ(k) do not depend on t. AUTOCORRELATION ρ(k) = γ(k)/γ(0).
    WHITE NOISE εₜ: mean 0, variance σ², uncorrelated. RANDOM WALK
    Xₜ = Xₜ₋₁ + εₜ is NOT stationary (Var Xₜ = tσ²).
  - MA(q): Xₜ = εₜ + θ₁εₜ₋₁ + ... + θqεₜ₋q, always stationary, ACF CUTS OFF
    after lag q; MA(1): ρ(1) = θ/(1 + θ²), |ρ(1)| ≤ ½; INVERTIBLE iff the roots
    of 1 + θ₁z + ... + θqz^q lie outside the unit circle. AR(p):
    Xₜ = φ₁Xₜ₋₁ + ... + φpXₜ₋p + εₜ, STATIONARY iff the roots of
    1 − φ₁z − ... − φpz^p lie outside |z| = 1; AR(1): |φ| < 1,
    γ(0) = σ²/(1 − φ²), ρ(k) = φᵏ; AR(2) region: φ₁ + φ₂ < 1, φ₂ − φ₁ < 1,
    |φ₂| < 1. YULE-WALKER: ρ(k) = φ₁ρ(k − 1) + ... + φpρ(k − p). The PACF
    cuts off after lag p for AR(p); the ACF of AR decays geometrically.
  - NONSTATIONARITY and FORECASTING: a trend or seasonality is removed by
    DIFFERENCING ∇Xₜ = Xₜ − Xₜ₋₁ (∇^d kills a polynomial trend of degree d;
    seasonal ∇ₛXₜ = Xₜ − Xₜ₋ₛ); ARIMA(p, d, q) = ARMA(p, q) for ∇^dXₜ. AR(1)
    forecast: X̂ₙ₊ₕ = μ + φʰ(xₙ − μ), error variance σ²(1 + φ² + ... +
    φ^(2(h−1))). SAMPLE ACF rₖ = ∑(xₜ − x̄)(xₜ₊ₖ − x̄)/∑(xₜ − x̄)²; for white
    noise rₖ ≈ N(0, 1/n) (bands ±2/√n); portmanteau Q = n∑rₖ² (Box-Pierce).
    SIMPLE EXPONENTIAL SMOOTHING: ℓₜ = αxₜ + (1 − α)ℓₜ₋₁, forecast ℓₙ.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A coin with unknown head-probability θ has prior Beta(2, 2). In 10 tosses
    it shows 7 heads. Derive the posterior, and find the posterior mean, mode
    and variance, the MLE, and the probability that the next toss is a head.
    Answer: θ | x ~ Beta(9, 5). Mean 9/14 ≈ 0.643, mode 2/3 ≈ 0.667, variance
    3/196 ≈ 0.0153; MLE 0.7; P(next head | data) = 9/14 ≈ 0.643.
    Teacher explains: Write prior and likelihood, dropping constants that do
    not involve θ:
       prior       π(θ) ∝ θ^(2−1)(1 − θ)^(2−1) = θ(1 − θ)
       likelihood  f(x | θ) = C(10, 7)θ⁷(1 − θ)³ ∝ θ⁷(1 − θ)³
       posterior   π(θ | x) ∝ θ⁸(1 − θ)⁴
    θ⁸(1 − θ)⁴ is the kernel of Beta(9, 5), so the constant must be 1/B(9, 5);
    no integration is needed. In general Beta(a, b) → Beta(a + k, b + n − k):
    'a counts prior heads, b prior tails'. Summaries of Beta(9, 5):
       mean = 9/14 ≈ 0.643       mode = (9 − 1)/(9 + 5 − 2) = 8/12 = 2/3
       variance = 9·5/(14²·15) = 45/2940 = 3/196 ≈ 0.0153 (sd ≈ 0.124)
    The MLE k/n = 0.7 ignores the prior; the posterior mean
       9/14 = (4/14)·(1/2) + (10/14)·(0.7)
    is a weighted average of prior mean ½ and MLE 0.7 with weights prior
    'sample size' a + b = 4 and data size n = 10: the SHRINKAGE towards the
    prior. Predictive: P(head | x) = ∫ θ π(θ | x) dθ = E(θ | x) = 9/14. Note
    the mode with a FLAT prior Beta(1, 1) would equal the MLE 0.7. Common
    mistakes: adding k to b; forgetting that Beta(a, b) has exponents a − 1,
    b − 1; quoting the mode when the question asks for the Bayes estimate
    under squared loss (the mean). Now you try: prior Beta(1, 1), 3 successes
    in 5 trials. Posterior and its mean? (Beta(4, 3), mean 4/7 ≈ 0.571)

D2. X₁, ..., Xₙ ~ N(μ, σ²) with σ² known, prior μ ~ N(μ₀, τ₀²). Show that the
    posterior is normal with precision 1/τ₀² + n/σ². Then take μ₀ = 50,
    τ₀² = 4, σ² = 16, n = 4, x̄ = 56 and find the posterior and a 95% credible
    interval for μ. Compare with the classical 95% confidence interval.
    Answer: μ | x ~ N(53, 2); 95% credible interval 53 ± 1.96√2 ≈
    (50.23, 55.77); classical interval 56 ± 3.92 = (52.08, 59.92).
    Teacher explains: Only the μ-dependent parts matter. The likelihood in μ is
    ∝ exp(−n(x̄ − μ)²/(2σ²)) (x̄ is sufficient), so
       π(μ | x) ∝ exp(−(μ − μ₀)²/(2τ₀²) − n(μ − x̄)²/(2σ²))
    The exponent is a quadratic in μ with coefficient of −μ²/2 equal to
       1/τ₀² + n/σ²  =  1/τₙ²    (posterior PRECISION = sum of precisions)
    and completing the square gives the centre
       μₙ = (μ₀/τ₀² + nx̄/σ²) / (1/τ₀² + n/σ²).
    A density ∝ exp(−(μ − μₙ)²/(2τₙ²)) is N(μₙ, τₙ²). Numbers:
       prior precision 1/4 = 0.25,  data precision n/σ² = 4/16 = 0.25
       posterior precision 0.5, so τₙ² = 2
       μₙ = (50·0.25 + 56·0.25)/0.5 = 53
    Equal precisions give equal weights: the posterior mean is halfway
    between 50 and 56. Credible interval: 53 ± 1.96·√2 = 53 ± 2.772, i.e.
    (50.23, 55.77); it MEANS 'P(50.23 < μ < 55.77 | data) = 0.95', a
    statement the frequentist interval x̄ ± 1.96σ/√n = 56 ± 1.96·2 cannot
    make. With a flat prior (τ₀² → ∞) the two intervals coincide. Common
    mistakes: averaging variances instead of precisions; using σ² instead of
    σ²/n for the data. Now you try: μ₀ = 10, τ₀² = 4, σ² = 4, n = 4, x̄ = 13.
    (precision 1/4 + 1 = 5/4, τₙ² = 0.8, μₙ = (2.5 + 13)/1.25 = 12.4)

D3. Counts of accidents per week are Poisson(λ). The prior is Gamma(3, 1)
    (shape 3, rate 1). Five weeks give 2, 4, 3, 5, 1. Find the posterior, its
    mean, mode and variance, and the posterior predictive probability of no
    accident next week. Which estimate minimises expected squared error, and
    which absolute error?
    Answer: λ | x ~ Gamma(18, 6); mean 3, mode 17/6 ≈ 2.833, variance 1/2;
    P(Y = 0 | x) = (6/7)¹⁸ ≈ 0.0624. Squared loss: the posterior mean 3;
    absolute loss: the posterior median (≈ 2.94).
    Teacher explains:
       prior        π(λ) ∝ λ^(3−1) e^(−λ)
       likelihood   ∏ e^(−λ)λ^(xᵢ)/xᵢ! ∝ λ^(∑xᵢ) e^(−nλ) = λ¹⁵ e^(−5λ)
       posterior    ∝ λ^(17) e^(−6λ)  → Gamma(α + ∑xᵢ, β + n) = Gamma(18, 6)
    so the prior acts like β = 1 extra week with α = 3 extra accidents.
       mean α/β = 18/6 = 3,  mode (α − 1)/β = 17/6,  variance α/β² = 18/36
    Predictive for next week: P(Y = 0 | x) = E(e^(−λ) | x)
       = ∫ e^(−λ) · 6¹⁸λ¹⁷e^(−6λ)/Γ(18) dλ = 6¹⁸/7¹⁸ = (6/7)¹⁸ ≈ 0.0624
    (the Gamma integral with rate 7). Compare the 'plug-in' answer e^(−3) ≈
    0.0498: the predictive is larger because it allows for uncertainty in λ
    (the predictive is NEGATIVE BINOMIAL, more spread than Poisson). Why mean
    for squared loss: E((λ − d)² | x) = Var(λ | x) + (E(λ | x) − d)², least at
    d = E(λ | x). For absolute loss the derivative of E|λ − d| is
    P(λ < d) − P(λ > d), zero at the median. Common mistakes: using the
    SCALE parametrisation (then mean = αθ) without saying so; adding the
    number of observations to α. Now you try: prior Gamma(2, 1), data 0, 1,
    0, 2. (Gamma(5, 5), posterior mean 1)

D4. A coin is tossed 12 times and shows 9 heads. Compare H₀ : θ = ½ with
    H₁ : θ ~ U(0, 1) by a Bayes factor, find P(H₀ | x) when P(H₀) = ½, and
    compare with the two-sided p-value.
    Answer: B₀₁ = 2860/4096 ≈ 0.698; P(H₀ | x) = 2860/6956 ≈ 0.411; p-value
    ≈ 0.146. The data favour H₁ only weakly.
    Teacher explains: The Bayes factor compares how well each hypothesis
    PREDICTED the data:
       m₀(x) = C(12, 9)(½)¹² = 220/4096 ≈ 0.0537
       m₁(x) = ∫₀¹ C(12, 9)θ⁹(1 − θ)³ dθ = C(12, 9)·B(10, 4)
             = 220 · 9!3!/13! = 1/13 ≈ 0.0769
    (in general ∫ C(n, k)θᵏ(1 − θ)ⁿ⁻ᵏ dθ = 1/(n + 1): under a uniform prior
    every k is equally likely). So
       B₀₁ = m₀/m₁ = (220/4096)·13 = 2860/4096 ≈ 0.698,  B₁₀ ≈ 1.43
    Posterior odds = B₀₁ × prior odds = 0.698 × 1, so
       P(H₀ | x) = 0.698/(1 + 0.698) = 2860/6956 ≈ 0.411.
    The p-value: P(X ≥ 9) + P(X ≤ 3) = 2(220 + 66 + 12 + 1)/4096 = 598/4096
    ≈ 0.146. Here both say 'not much evidence', but in large samples a
    p-value of 0.05 can go with P(H₀ | x) > ½ (Lindley's paradox): the
    p-value measures surprise under H₀ alone, the Bayes factor weighs H₀
    against a specific H₁. Rough scale (Jeffreys/Kass-Raftery): B₁₀ of 1-3
    'barely worth mentioning', 3-20 positive, 20-150 strong, > 150 very
    strong. Common mistakes: reading the p-value as P(H₀ | x); using an
    improper prior under H₁ (the Bayes factor is then undefined). Now you
    try: 5 heads in 10 tosses, same hypotheses. (B₀₁ = 252·11/1024 ≈ 2.71,
    favouring H₀)

D5. Derive the least squares estimates for y = α + βx + ε and fit the line to
    x: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5;  y: 2, 4, 5, 4, 5. Give fitted values, residuals, RSS
    and R², and check that the residuals sum to zero.
    Answer: ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6x; fitted 2.8, 3.4, 4.0, 4.6, 5.2; residuals −0.8,
    0.6, 1.0, −0.6, −0.2 (sum 0); RSS = 2.4; R² = 0.6.
    Teacher explains: Minimise S(α, β) = ∑(yᵢ − α − βxᵢ)². Set the partial
    derivatives to zero:
       ∂S/∂α = −2∑(yᵢ − α − βxᵢ) = 0   ⇒  ȳ = α + βx̄
       ∂S/∂β = −2∑xᵢ(yᵢ − α − βxᵢ) = 0
    Substituting α = ȳ − βx̄ into the second gives ∑xᵢ(yᵢ − ȳ) = β∑xᵢ(xᵢ − x̄),
    i.e. b = Sxy/Sxx and a = ȳ − bx̄. (S is a convex quadratic, so this
    stationary point is the minimum.) The first equation says the residuals
    sum to 0 and the line passes through (x̄, ȳ); the second says
    ∑xᵢeᵢ = 0. Table (x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4):
       x − x̄ : −2  −1   0   1   2        Sxx = 10
       y − ȳ : −2   0   1   0   1        Syy = 6
       products 4   0   0   0   2        Sxy = 6
    b = 6/10 = 0.6, a = 4 − 0.6·3 = 2.2. Residuals eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ:
       2 − 2.8 = −0.8, 4 − 3.4 = 0.6, 5 − 4 = 1, 4 − 4.6 = −0.6, 5 − 5.2 = −0.2
    Sum 0 ✓. RSS = 0.64 + 0.36 + 1 + 0.36 + 0.04 = 2.4 = Syy − bSxy
    = 6 − 3.6 ✓. R² = 1 − 2.4/6 = 0.6: 60% of the variation in y is explained
    by x; r = Sxy/√(SxxSyy) = 6/√60 ≈ 0.775 and r² = 0.6 ✓. Common mistakes:
    b = Sxy/Syy (regressing x on y); forgetting a = ȳ − bx̄ uses the SAME b.
    Now you try: x: 1, 2, 3, 4; y: 2, 3, 5, 6. (b = 7/5 = 1.4, a = 0.5,
    R² = 0.98)

D6. For the data of D5 assume normal errors. Estimate σ², test H₀ : β = 0 at
    the 5% level, give a 95% CI for β, the ANOVA table, a 95% confidence
    interval for the mean response and a 95% prediction interval at x₀ = 6.
    (t₃,₀.₉₇₅ = 3.182, F₁,₃,₀.₉₅ = 10.13.)
    Answer: s² = 0.8; SE(b) ≈ 0.283, t ≈ 2.12 < 3.182, do not reject; CI for
    β: (−0.300, 1.500); F = 4.5 = t²; at x₀ = 6: ŷ₀ = 5.8, mean CI
    5.8 ± 2.985 ≈ (2.82, 8.78), prediction interval 5.8 ± 4.124 ≈ (1.68, 9.92).
    Teacher explains: Two parameters were estimated, so the residual degrees
    of freedom are n − 2 = 3:
       s² = RSS/(n − 2) = 2.4/3 = 0.8
       SE(b) = s/√Sxx = √(0.8/10) = √0.08 ≈ 0.2828
       t = b/SE(b) = 0.6/0.2828 ≈ 2.121
    |t| < 3.182: no significant evidence of a slope (only 5 points!). The CI
    is b ± 3.182·0.2828 = 0.6 ± 0.900, containing 0, consistent with the
    test. ANOVA:
       source       SS    df   MS     F
       regression   3.6    1   3.6    4.5
       residual     2.4    3   0.8
       total        6.0    4
    (ESS = bSxy = 3.6.) F = 4.5 = 2.121² = t² and 10.13 = 3.182²: the F-test
    and the two-sided t-test are the same test. At x₀ = 6 (outside the data:
    extrapolation, be careful): ŷ₀ = 2.2 + 3.6 = 5.8 and
       mean response: s√(1/5 + 9/10) = √(0.8·1.1) = √0.88 ≈ 0.938,
                      5.8 ± 3.182·0.938 = 5.8 ± 2.985
       new value:     s√(1 + 1/5 + 9/10) = √1.68 ≈ 1.296,
                      5.8 ± 3.182·1.296 = 5.8 ± 4.124
    The prediction interval adds the variance σ² of the new observation's own
    error; it never shrinks to zero as n grows, while the mean CI does.
    Common mistakes: n − 1 degrees of freedom; forgetting the (x₀ − x̄)²
    term, which makes intervals widen away from x̄. Now you try: at x₀ = 3
    (= x̄), the mean CI half-width? (3.182·√(0.8/5) = 3.182·0.4 ≈ 1.273)

D7. For Y = Xβ + ε with X of full rank p, E ε = 0, Var ε = σ²I: derive the
    normal equations; prove E β̂ = β and Var β̂ = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹; show that the hat
    matrix H is symmetric and idempotent with trace p, and that
    E(RSS) = (n − p)σ². Illustrate with x = 1, 2, 3, y = 1, 3, 4.
    Answer: β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY, unbiased, Var = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹, tr H = p,
    E(RSS) = (n − p)σ². Example: XᵀX = [[3, 6], [6, 14]], Xᵀy = (8, 19),
    β̂ = (−1/3, 3/2).
    Teacher explains: S(β) = (Y − Xβ)ᵀ(Y − Xβ) = YᵀY − 2βᵀXᵀY + βᵀXᵀXβ. Its
    gradient −2XᵀY + 2XᵀXβ vanishes at XᵀXβ̂ = XᵀY. Full rank makes XᵀX
    positive definite, hence invertible, and S strictly convex, so
    β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY is the unique minimiser. Write β̂ = AY with
    A = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ. Then
       E β̂ = A·E Y = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀXβ = β
       Var β̂ = A(σ²I)Aᵀ = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀX(XᵀX)⁻¹ = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹
    H = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ: Hᵀ = H since XᵀX is symmetric, and
       H² = X(XᵀX)⁻¹(XᵀX)(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ = H
    tr H = tr((XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀX) = tr Iₚ = p (cyclic property of trace). H projects
    orthogonally onto the column space of X. Residuals e = (I − H)Y =
    (I − H)ε since (I − H)X = 0, so
       E(RSS) = E(εᵀ(I − H)ε) = σ² tr(I − H) = σ²(n − p),
    using E(εᵀMε) = tr(M·σ²I). Hence s² = RSS/(n − p) is unbiased. Example:
       X = [[1, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3]],  XᵀX = [[3, 6], [6, 14]], det = 6
       (XᵀX)⁻¹ = (1/6)[[14, −6], [−6, 3]],  Xᵀy = (1 + 3 + 4, 1 + 6 + 12) = (8, 19)
       β̂ = (1/6)(14·8 − 6·19, −6·8 + 3·19) = (1/6)(−2, 9) = (−1/3, 3/2)
    Check with b = Sxy/Sxx = 3/2, a = 8/3 − 3 = −1/3 ✓. Common mistakes:
    writing (XᵀX)⁻¹ = X⁻¹(Xᵀ)⁻¹ (X is not square); forgetting the column of
    1s for the intercept. Now you try: tr(I − H) for n = 30 observations and
    5 columns? (25, the residual degrees of freedom)

D8. Prove the Gauss-Markov theorem. Then, for a regression with n = 20
    observations, the full model with p = 4 parameters has RSS = 30 and a
    reduced model with 2 parameters has RSS = 45. Test the reduced model at
    5% (F₂,₁₆,₀.₉₅ = 3.63). Also explain the dummy variable trap.
    Answer: β̂ is BLUE (proof below). F = 4.0 > 3.63: reject the reduced
    model; the two dropped variables matter.
    Teacher explains: Let β̃ = CY be any LINEAR UNBIASED estimator. Write
    C = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ + D. Unbiasedness for every β:
       E β̃ = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀXβ + DXβ = β + DXβ = β for all β  ⇒  DX = 0
    Then
       Var β̃ = σ²CCᵀ = σ²[(XᵀX)⁻¹ + (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀDᵀ + DX(XᵀX)⁻¹ + DDᵀ]
             = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹ + σ²DDᵀ = Var β̂ + σ²DDᵀ
    since DX = 0 kills the cross terms. DDᵀ is positive semidefinite, so
    Var(cᵀβ̃) − Var(cᵀβ̂) = σ²‖Dᵀc‖² ≥ 0 for every c, with equality iff
    Dᵀc = 0. ∎ No normality was used: only mean zero, equal variances and
    no correlation. (With normal errors β̂ is even best among ALL unbiased
    estimators.) Nested F-test: q = 4 − 2 = 2 restrictions,
       F = ((45 − 30)/2) / (30/(20 − 4)) = 7.5/1.875 = 4.0 > 3.63.
    Dummy trap: a factor with levels A, B, C and an intercept needs only two
    dummies (say D_B, D_C; A is the baseline). If all three are included,
    D_A + D_B + D_C = 1 = the intercept column, so the columns of X are
    linearly dependent, XᵀX is singular and β is not identifiable.
    Coefficients then mean 'difference from the baseline level'. Common
    mistakes: in the F-test dividing by RSS_red; using n − 2 as the
    denominator df. Now you try: with n = 25, p = 5 (full), RSS_full = 40,
    RSS_red = 52 for p = 3, find F. (((52 − 40)/2)/(40/20) = 6/2 = 3)

D9. Define weak stationarity. Compute the mean, autocovariance and
    autocorrelation of (a) the MA(1) process Xₜ = εₜ + θεₜ₋₁ and (b) the
    stationary AR(1) process Xₜ = φXₜ₋₁ + εₜ, |φ| < 1. (c) Show the random
    walk is not stationary. Give numbers for θ = 0.5 and φ = 0.8.
    Answer: (a) γ(0) = σ²(1 + θ²), γ(1) = θσ², γ(k) = 0 (k ≥ 2);
    ρ(1) = θ/(1 + θ²) = 0.4 for θ = 0.5. (b) γ(0) = σ²/(1 − φ²), ρ(k) = φ^|k|;
    for φ = 0.8: γ(0) ≈ 2.778σ², ρ = 0.8, 0.64, 0.512, ... (c) Var Xₜ = tσ².
    Teacher explains: Weakly stationary: constant mean, finite variance, and
    Cov(Xₜ, Xₜ₊ₖ) depending only on the lag k. (a) E Xₜ = 0. Expand using
    the fact that different ε's are uncorrelated:
       γ(0) = Var(εₜ + θεₜ₋₁) = σ² + θ²σ²
       γ(1) = Cov(εₜ + θεₜ₋₁, εₜ₊₁ + θεₜ) = θσ²     (only εₜ is shared)
       γ(k) = 0 for k ≥ 2                           (nothing shared)
    ρ(1) = θ/(1 + θ²): for θ = 0.5, 0.5/1.25 = 0.4. Because
    (1 − θ)² ≥ 0 ⇔ 1 + θ² ≥ 2θ, |ρ(1)| ≤ ½ always. θ and 1/θ give the same ρ
    (θ = 2: 2/5 = 0.4): we choose the INVERTIBLE one, |θ| < 1. (b) Iterating,
    Xₜ = ∑ φʲεₜ₋ⱼ (converges since |φ| < 1), so E Xₜ = 0 and
       γ(0) = σ²∑φ^(2j) = σ²/(1 − φ²)
    Multiply Xₜ = φXₜ₋₁ + εₜ by Xₜ₋ₖ (k ≥ 1) and take expectations; εₜ is
    uncorrelated with the past: γ(k) = φγ(k − 1), so ρ(k) = φᵏ. For φ = 0.8,
    γ(0) = σ²/0.36 ≈ 2.778σ²; the ACF decays GEOMETRICALLY, never cutting
    off, in contrast to MA(1). (c) Xₜ = X₀ + ε₁ + ... + εₜ, so with X₀ = 0
    Var Xₜ = tσ², growing with t: not stationary, although ∇Xₜ = εₜ is.
    Common mistakes: γ(1) = θσ²(1 + θ²); saying AR(1) with φ = 1 is
    stationary. Now you try: ρ(1) for θ = −0.8? (−0.8/1.64 ≈ −0.488)

D10. For the AR(2) process Xₜ = 0.5Xₜ₋₁ + 0.3Xₜ₋₂ + εₜ check stationarity, use
     the Yule-Walker equations to find ρ(1), ρ(2), ρ(3), and give the partial
     autocorrelations. Then estimate an AR(2) model from sample
     autocorrelations r₁ = 0.6, r₂ = 0.5.
     Answer: stationary (roots ≈ 1.174 and −2.840, both outside |z| = 1);
     ρ(1) = 5/7 ≈ 0.714, ρ(2) = 23/35 ≈ 0.657, ρ(3) = 19/35 ≈ 0.543;
     PACF φ₁₁ = 5/7, φ₂₂ = 0.3, φₖₖ = 0 for k ≥ 3. Estimates φ̂₁ = 0.46875,
     φ̂₂ = 0.21875.
     Teacher explains: The characteristic polynomial is
     1 − 0.5z − 0.3z² = 0 ⇔ 0.3z² + 0.5z − 1 = 0, so
        z = (−0.5 ± √(0.25 + 1.2))/0.6 = (−0.5 ± 1.2042)/0.6
          ≈ 1.1736 or −2.8403.
     Both outside the unit circle ⇒ stationary. The quick triangle check
     agrees: φ₁ + φ₂ = 0.8 < 1, φ₂ − φ₁ = −0.2 < 1, |φ₂| = 0.3 < 1. Yule-Walker:
     multiply by Xₜ₋ₖ, take expectations, divide by γ(0):
        ρ(k) = 0.5ρ(k − 1) + 0.3ρ(k − 2),   ρ(0) = 1, ρ(−1) = ρ(1)
        k = 1:  ρ(1) = 0.5 + 0.3ρ(1)  ⇒  ρ(1) = 0.5/0.7 = 5/7
        k = 2:  ρ(2) = 0.5·5/7 + 0.3 = 2.5/7 + 2.1/7 = 23/35
        k = 3:  ρ(3) = 0.5·23/35 + 0.3·5/7 = 11.5/35 + 7.5/35 = 19/35
     The PACF at lag k is the last coefficient of the best AR(k) fit: φ₁₁ =
     ρ(1), φ₂₂ = φ₂ = 0.3, and zero beyond lag 2 — this CUT-OFF identifies the
     order of an AR model. Estimation: solve the sample equations
        r₁ = φ₁ + φ₂r₁,  r₂ = φ₁r₁ + φ₂
     giving φ̂₁ = r₁(1 − r₂)/(1 − r₁²) = 0.6·0.5/0.64 = 0.46875 and
     φ̂₂ = (r₂ − r₁²)/(1 − r₁²) = (0.5 − 0.36)/0.64 = 0.21875. Common mistakes:
     using ρ(−1) = −ρ(1) (ρ is EVEN); requiring roots INSIDE the circle (that
     is the condition for the reciprocal polynomial). Now you try: Xₜ =
     Xₜ₋₁ − 0.5Xₜ₋₂ + εₜ: ρ(1), ρ(2)? (ρ(1) = 1/1.5 = 2/3, ρ(2) = 2/3 − 1/2 = 1/6)

D11. An AR(1) model Xₜ − 10 = 0.6(Xₜ₋₁ − 10) + εₜ, σ² = 4, has last value
     xₙ = 15. Find the forecasts for h = 1, 2, 3, their error variances, a 95%
     prediction interval for h = 1, and the limits as h → ∞.
     Answer: 13, 11.8, 11.08; variances 4, 5.44, 5.9584; interval
     13 ± 3.92 = (9.08, 16.92); forecasts → 10 (the mean), variance → 6.25
     (the process variance).
     Teacher explains: The best (minimum mean square error) forecast is the
     conditional expectation. Future ε's have mean 0:
        X̂ₙ₊₁ = 10 + 0.6·5 = 13
        X̂ₙ₊₂ = 10 + 0.6²·5 = 11.8
        X̂ₙ₊₃ = 10 + 0.6³·5 = 11.08
     General X̂ₙ₊ₕ = μ + φʰ(xₙ − μ): forecasts decay towards the mean. The
     error: Xₙ₊ₕ − X̂ₙ₊ₕ = εₙ₊ₕ + φεₙ₊ₕ₋₁ + ... + φ^(h−1)εₙ₊₁, so
        Var = σ²(1 + φ² + ... + φ^(2(h−1)))
        h = 1: 4;  h = 2: 4(1 + 0.36) = 5.44;  h = 3: 4(1.36 + 0.1296) = 5.9584
     95% interval for h = 1 (normal errors): 13 ± 1.96·2 = (9.08, 16.92). As
     h → ∞ the variance → σ²/(1 − φ²) = 4/0.64 = 6.25, the unconditional
     variance: far-ahead forecasts are no better than knowing the mean. For
     a RANDOM WALK (φ = 1) the forecast stays xₙ and the variance hσ² grows
     without bound. Common mistakes: forgetting to subtract the mean before
     multiplying by φ (0.6·15 = 9 is wrong); using σ² for every horizon. Now
     you try: μ = 0, φ = 0.5, xₙ = 8, σ² = 1: forecasts and variances for
     h = 1, 2. (4, 2; 1, 1.25)

D12. (a) Show that differencing removes a linear trend and that ∇² removes a
     quadratic one; difference 3, 5, 8, 12, 17. (b) Explain ARIMA(p, d, q) and
     seasonal differencing. (c) Apply simple exponential smoothing with
     α = 0.3, ℓ₀ = 10 to 10, 12, 11, 13, 15 and give the forecast. (d)
     Compute r₁ and r₂ for the series 1, 3, 5, 4, 2.
     Answer: (a) ∇: 2, 3, 4, 5; ∇²: 1, 1, 1 (quadratic trend). (c) levels
     10, 10.6, 10.72, 11.404, 12.4828; forecast ≈ 12.48 for all future t.
     (d) r₁ = 0.1, r₂ = −0.6.
     Teacher explains: (a) If Xₜ = a + bt + Yₜ with Yₜ stationary,
        ∇Xₜ = Xₜ − Xₜ₋₁ = b + Yₜ − Yₜ₋₁,
     stationary with mean b. A quadratic ct² gives ∇(ct²) = c(2t − 1), linear,
     so one more difference makes it constant (2c). For 3, 5, 8, 12, 17:
        ∇: 2, 3, 4, 5      ∇²: 1, 1, 1
     (b) Xₜ is ARIMA(p, d, q) if ∇^dXₜ is a stationary, invertible
     ARMA(p, q): φ(B)(1 − B)^dXₜ = θ(B)εₜ with B the BACKSHIFT (BXₜ = Xₜ₋₁).
     A random walk is ARIMA(0, 1, 0). Monthly data with a yearly pattern use
     ∇₁₂Xₜ = Xₜ − Xₜ₋₁₂. Identification: difference until the ACF dies out
     quickly, then read p from the PACF cut-off and q from the ACF cut-off.
     (c) ℓₜ = 0.3xₜ + 0.7ℓₜ₋₁:
        ℓ₁ = 3 + 7 = 10;  ℓ₂ = 3.6 + 7 = 10.6;  ℓ₃ = 3.3 + 7.42 = 10.72
        ℓ₄ = 3.9 + 7.504 = 11.404;  ℓ₅ = 4.5 + 7.9828 = 12.4828
     Unrolled, ℓₜ = α∑(1 − α)ʲxₜ₋ⱼ + ...: weights decay geometrically. It is
     optimal for an ARIMA(0, 1, 1) model; it lags behind a trend (Holt's
     method adds a slope). (d) x̄ = 3, deviations −2, 0, 2, 1, −1, sum of
     squares 10:
        r₁ = [(−2)(0) + (0)(2) + (2)(1) + (1)(−1)]/10 = 1/10 = 0.1
        r₂ = [(−2)(2) + (0)(1) + (2)(−1)]/10 = −6/10 = −0.6
     Always divide by the FULL sum of squares (n terms), not by the number of
     products. With n = 5 the white-noise bands ±2/√5 ≈ ±0.89 are so wide
     that nothing is significant. Common mistakes: forgetting ℓ₀; dividing
     rₖ by n − k products. Now you try: 3-point moving averages of 3, 5, 7,
     6, 8, 10. (5, 6, 7, 8)

M1. Beta prior, binomial data (k successes in n trials). Give the posterior,
    its mean and its mode.
    a) Beta(1, 1), k = 3, n = 5            b) Beta(2, 2), k = 7, n = 10
    c) Beta(1, 1), k = 0, n = 4            d) Beta(3, 7), k = 4, n = 10
    e) Beta(5, 5), k = 10, n = 20          f) Beta(2, 8), k = 12, n = 20
    g) Beta(10, 10), k = 30, n = 40        h) Beta(½, ½), k = 1, n = 4
    i) Beta(4, 1), k = 0, n = 6            j) Beta(1, 1), k = 9, n = 9
    k) Beta(3, 3), k = 15, n = 25          l) Beta(20, 30), k = 50, n = 100
    m) Beta(1, 1), then S, S, F observed one at a time (posterior after each)
    n) posterior variance in b)
    o) P(next trial succeeds) in d)
    Answers:
      a) Beta(4, 3), 4/7, 3/5            b) Beta(9, 5), 9/14, 2/3
      c) Beta(1, 5), 1/6, 0              d) Beta(7, 13), 7/20, 1/3
      e) Beta(15, 15), 1/2, 1/2          f) Beta(14, 16), 7/15, 13/28
      g) Beta(40, 20), 2/3, 39/58        h) Beta(3/2, 7/2), 3/10, 1/6
      i) Beta(4, 7), 4/11, 1/3           j) Beta(10, 1), 10/11, 1
      k) Beta(18, 13), 18/31, 17/29      l) Beta(70, 80), 7/15, 69/148
      m) Beta(2, 1), Beta(3, 1), Beta(3, 2) (same as all at once)
      n) 3/196 ≈ 0.0153                  o) 7/20

M2. Other conjugate pairs. Give the posterior and its mean (Gamma(α, β) has
    rate β).
