TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: for Bayesian problems always write three lines — prior ∝ ...,
  likelihood ∝ ..., posterior ∝ ... — dropping every constant, then name the
  family by its kernel; a table 'prior + data = posterior' for the parameters
  (a + k, b + n − k; α + ∑x, β + n) settles most questions. For regression,
  build the Sxx, Sxy, Syy table by hand before touching formulas and draw the
  scatter plot; remember the line passes through (x̄, ȳ) and the residuals
  sum to 0 as checks. For time series draw the ACF and PACF as bar charts and
  learn the two-row rule: 'AR: ACF decays, PACF cuts off; MA: ACF cuts off,
  PACF decays'. Harder: show that the posterior mean of a normal mean is a
  shrinkage estimator and compute its mean squared error; derive the ridge
  estimator (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹XᵀY as a posterior mode with a normal prior on β;
  prove Cochran's theorem for RSS/σ² ~ χ²(n − p) under normal errors; find
  the ACF of a general ARMA(1, 1); show that exponential smoothing is the
  optimal forecast for ARIMA(0, 1, 1) with θ = α − 1; and simulate an AR(1)
  with φ = 0.95 to see how slowly the sample mean settles.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.38 — OPTIMISATION: LINEAR PROGRAMMING (SIMPLEX, DUALITY), CONVEX
OPTIMISATION BASICS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A LINEAR PROGRAMME (LP) optimises a linear OBJECTIVE cᵀx subject to linear
    equality/inequality CONSTRAINTS. FORMULATION: name the decision variables,
    write the objective, every constraint, and the sign conditions x ≥ 0.
    STANDARD (equality) FORM: max cᵀx, Ax = b, x ≥ 0, b ≥ 0, obtained with
    SLACK variables (≤), SURPLUS variables (≥), x = x⁺ − x⁻ for a FREE
    variable, and min cᵀx = −max(−cᵀx).
  - The FEASIBLE REGION {x : Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0} is a convex POLYHEDRON; its corner
    points are VERTICES (extreme points). FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM: if an LP has an
    optimal solution it has one at a vertex; an LP is either INFEASIBLE,
    UNBOUNDED, or has an optimum. In two variables solve GRAPHICALLY: draw the
    region, then slide the objective line (or evaluate every vertex).
  - With A of size m × n and rank m, a BASIC SOLUTION sets n − m NONBASIC
    variables to 0 and solves for the m BASIC ones; a BASIC FEASIBLE SOLUTION
    (BFS: all ≥ 0) is exactly a vertex. There are at most C(n, m) of them. A
    DEGENERATE BFS has a basic variable equal to 0.
  - SIMPLEX METHOD (maximisation tableau, objective row z − cᵀx = 0): (1) if
    all objective-row entries are ≥ 0, STOP: optimal; (2) otherwise the
    ENTERING variable has the most negative entry; (3) RATIO TEST: among rows
    with positive entry in that column, the smallest rhs/entry picks the
    LEAVING variable (if no entry is positive the LP is UNBOUNDED); (4)
    PIVOT: make the pivot 1 and clear its column; repeat. A zero reduced cost
    for a nonbasic variable at the optimum signals MULTIPLE OPTIMA.
    Degeneracy can cause CYCLING; BLAND'S RULE (smallest index) prevents it.
  - ARTIFICIAL VARIABLES for ≥ and = rows: TWO-PHASE method (Phase I
    minimises the sum of artificials; positive minimum ⇒ INFEASIBLE; zero ⇒
    start Phase II from that BFS) or BIG-M (penalty −M·aᵢ in the objective).
  - DUALITY: the dual of (P) max cᵀx, Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0 is (D) min bᵀy, Aᵀy ≥ c,
    y ≥ 0. Rules for a max primal: constraint ≤ / ≥ / = ↔ dual variable
    ≥ 0 / ≤ 0 / free; variable ≥ 0 / ≤ 0 / free ↔ dual constraint ≥ / ≤ / =.
    The dual of the dual is the primal.
  - WEAK DUALITY: cᵀx ≤ bᵀy for all feasible x, y (so equal values prove
    both optimal). STRONG DUALITY: if either has a finite optimum, both do
    and max cᵀx = min bᵀy. If (P) is unbounded then (D) is infeasible.
    COMPLEMENTARY SLACKNESS: feasible x, y are optimal iff
    yᵢ(b − Ax)ᵢ = 0 for all i and xⱼ(Aᵀy − c)ⱼ = 0 for all j.
  - SENSITIVITY: the optimal dual values are SHADOW PRICES: the increase in
    the optimum per unit increase in bᵢ, valid while the optimal basis stays
    feasible (a RANGE for bᵢ). They are read from the objective row under the
    slack columns of the final tableau. A new activity with column a and
    profit c is worth introducing iff its REDUCED COST yᵀa − c < 0.
  - CONVEX SET: λx + (1 − λ)y ∈ C for x, y ∈ C, λ ∈ [0, 1]. Half-spaces,
    balls, polyhedra, cones of PSD matrices are convex; intersections of
    convex sets are convex; unions usually are not. CONVEX FUNCTION:
    f(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y) (JENSEN); STRICTLY convex with <
    for x ≠ y; f concave iff −f convex.
  - TESTS: f differentiable is convex iff f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x) (lies
    above its tangent planes); f twice differentiable is convex iff the
    HESSIAN ∇²f(x) is positive SEMIDEFINITE everywhere (PD ⇒ strictly
    convex). Convexity is preserved by nonnegative sums, composition with
    affine maps, and pointwise MAXIMA. Sublevel sets {f ≤ c} of convex f are
    convex.
  - CONVEX PROGRAMME: minimise a convex f over a convex set. Every LOCAL
    minimum is GLOBAL; the set of minimisers is convex; strict convexity ⇒ at
    most one minimiser. Unconstrained differentiable case: x* is optimal ⇔
    ∇f(x*) = 0.
  - ALGORITHMS: GRADIENT DESCENT xₖ₊₁ = xₖ − α∇f(xₖ) converges for
    0 < α < 2/L when ∇f is L-Lipschitz (for a quadratic L = largest Hessian
    eigenvalue); its speed depends on the CONDITION NUMBER. EXACT LINE SEARCH
    on ½xᵀQx: α = gᵀg/(gᵀQg). NEWTON'S METHOD xₖ₊₁ = xₖ − [∇²f]⁻¹∇f minimises
    a quadratic in one step and converges quadratically near a nondegenerate
    minimum.
  - KKT CONDITIONS for min f(x) s.t. gᵢ(x) ≤ 0, hⱼ(x) = 0: STATIONARITY
    ∇f + ∑λᵢ∇gᵢ + ∑νⱼ∇hⱼ = 0, PRIMAL feasibility, DUAL feasibility λᵢ ≥ 0,
    COMPLEMENTARY SLACKNESS λᵢgᵢ(x) = 0. For convex problems (f, gᵢ convex,
    hⱼ affine) KKT points are global minima; with SLATER's condition (a
    strictly feasible point) KKT is also necessary.
  - LAGRANGIAN DUALITY: L(x, λ, ν) = f + ∑λᵢgᵢ + ∑νⱼhⱼ; DUAL FUNCTION
    g(λ, ν) = infₓ L is always CONCAVE; WEAK DUALITY g(λ, ν) ≤ p* for λ ≥ 0;
    STRONG DUALITY d* = p* holds for convex problems under Slater (and always
    for feasible LPs). LP duality is the special case f = cᵀx.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A firm makes doors (x) and windows (y). Profit is 3 per door and 5 per
    window (thousands). Plant 1 has 4 hours: a door needs 1 h. Plant 2 has 12
    hours: a window needs 2 h. Plant 3 has 18 hours: a door needs 3 h, a
    window 2 h. Formulate the LP and solve it graphically.
    Answer: max z = 3x + 5y s.t. x ≤ 4, 2y ≤ 12, 3x + 2y ≤ 18, x, y ≥ 0.
    Optimum x = 2, y = 6, z = 36.
    Teacher explains: Step 1, variables: x doors, y windows per week. Step 2,
    objective: profit 3x + 5y. Step 3, one constraint per resource, and
    x, y ≥ 0 because negative production is meaningless. Draw the lines
    x = 4, y = 6, 3x + 2y = 18 (through (6, 0) and (0, 9)); the feasible
    region is the pentagon with vertices
       (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 3), (2, 6), (0, 6)
    ((4, 3): x = 4 in 3x + 2y = 18; (2, 6): y = 6 in 3x + 2y = 18). Evaluate:
       z(0, 0) = 0,  z(4, 0) = 12,  z(4, 3) = 27,  z(2, 6) = 36,  z(0, 6) = 30
    The best is 36 at (2, 6). Equivalently slide the ISO-PROFIT line
    3x + 5y = k (slope −3/5) upward: the last point it touches is (2, 6),
    where the lines y = 6 (slope 0) and 3x + 2y = 18 (slope −3/2) meet; −3/5
    lies between them, confirming the vertex. At the optimum plants 2 and 3
    are fully used (BINDING constraints) and plant 1 has 2 hours spare
    (SLACK 2). Common mistakes: forgetting x, y ≥ 0; checking only the
    intercepts; reading off a point that is not feasible. Now you try: max
    x + y s.t. x + 2y ≤ 4, 3x + y ≤ 6, x, y ≥ 0. (x = 8/5, y = 6/5, z = 14/5)

D2. (a) Put in standard form: min 2x₁ − x₂ s.t. x₁ + x₂ ≥ 2, x₁ − x₂ ≤ 3,
    x₁ ≥ 0, x₂ free. (b) Prove that if a linear objective attains a maximum
    over a bounded polyhedron, it attains it at a vertex. (c) Give
    two-variable examples of an infeasible LP, an unbounded LP, and an LP with
    multiple optima.
    Answer: (a) max −2x₁ + x₂⁺ − x₂⁻ s.t. x₁ + x₂⁺ − x₂⁻ − e₁ = 2,
    x₁ − x₂⁺ + x₂⁻ + s₁ = 3, all variables ≥ 0. (b) Proof below. (c) See
    below.
    Teacher explains: (a) Four moves: min → max by negating the objective;
    free x₂ = x₂⁺ − x₂⁻ with both parts ≥ 0; ≥ gets a SURPLUS e₁ subtracted;
    ≤ gets a SLACK s₁ added. The optimal value of the original problem is
    MINUS the maximum found. (b) A bounded polyhedron P is the convex hull of
    its finitely many vertices v₁, ..., vₖ (Minkowski). Any x ∈ P is
    x = ∑λᵢvᵢ with λᵢ ≥ 0, ∑λᵢ = 1. Then
       cᵀx = ∑λᵢcᵀvᵢ ≤ ∑λᵢ·maxⱼ cᵀvⱼ = maxⱼ cᵀvⱼ.
    So no point beats the best vertex. ∎ (For unbounded polyhedra the same
    idea uses vertices plus extreme rays; this is why the simplex method may
    move only between vertices.) (c) INFEASIBLE: x + y ≤ 2 and x + y ≥ 3.
    UNBOUNDED: max x + y s.t. x − y ≤ 1, x, y ≥ 0 (take x = y = t → ∞).
    MULTIPLE OPTIMA: max 2x + 4y s.t. x + 2y ≤ 5, x + y ≤ 4, x, y ≥ 0: the
    objective is parallel to x + 2y = 5 and every point of the segment from
    (0, 5/2) to (3, 1) gives 10. Note an unbounded REGION does not mean an
    unbounded LP: min x + y over the same region has optimum 0 at (0, 0).
    Common mistakes: writing x₂ = −x₂′ for a free variable (that only
    allows x₂ ≤ 0); forgetting to change the sign of the final answer after
    min → max. Now you try: how many basic solutions can
    x₁ + x₂ + s₁ = 4, x₁ + 3x₂ + s₂ = 6 have, and how many are feasible?
    (C(4, 2) = 6; 4 feasible: (0, 0), (4, 0), (3, 1), (0, 2) in (x₁, x₂))

D3. Solve the LP of D1 by the simplex method, showing every tableau, and read
    off the optimal dual values.
    Answer: two pivots (x₂ enters/s₂ leaves, then x₁ enters/s₃ leaves);
    x₁ = 2, x₂ = 6, s₁ = 2, z = 36; dual values y = (0, 3/2, 1).
    Teacher explains: Add slacks: x₁ + s₁ = 4, 2x₂ + s₂ = 12,
    3x₁ + 2x₂ + s₃ = 18, and write z − 3x₁ − 5x₂ = 0 as the bottom row.
       basis   x₁    x₂    s₁    s₂    s₃  | rhs
       s₁       1     0     1     0     0  |   4
       s₂       0     2     0     1     0  |  12
       s₃       3     2     0     0     1  |  18
       z       −3    −5     0     0     0  |   0
    Start: BFS x = 0, z = 0. Most negative: −5, so x₂ ENTERS. Ratios:
    s₁ row has 0 (skip), s₂: 12/2 = 6, s₃: 18/2 = 9. Smallest 6: s₂ LEAVES;
    the pivot is 2. Divide row 2 by 2, then clear the x₂ column:
       s₁       1     0     1     0     0  |   4
       x₂       0     1     0    1/2    0  |   6
       s₃       3     0     0    −1     1  |   6
       z       −3     0     0    5/2    0  |  30
    Now x₁ enters (−3). Ratios: s₁: 4/1 = 4, s₃: 6/3 = 2, so s₃ leaves,
    pivot 3:
       s₁       0     0     1    1/3  −1/3 |   2
       x₂       0     1     0    1/2    0  |   6
       x₁       1     0     0   −1/3   1/3 |   2
       z        0     0     0    3/2    1  |  36
    No negative entries remain: optimal, x₁ = 2, x₂ = 6, z = 36 (the vertex
    found in D1; the path was (0, 0) → (0, 6) → (2, 6)). The entries under
    the slacks, (0, 3/2, 1), are the DUAL VALUES: 4·0 + 12·3/2 + 18·1 = 36 ✓.
    Why the ratio test: x₁ may increase only until the first basic variable
    hits 0; the smallest ratio is that point. Common mistakes: choosing the
    leaving row by the largest ratio or including rows with 0 or negative
    entries; forgetting to update the z-row. Now you try: max 2x₁ + 3x₂ s.t.
    x₁ + x₂ ≤ 4, x₁ + 3x₂ ≤ 6, x₁ ≤ 3. (x₂ in/s₂ out, x₁ in/s₁ out;
    x = (3, 1), z = 9)

D4. Use the two-phase method to solve min z = 2x₁ + 3x₂ s.t. x₁ + x₂ ≥ 4,
    x₁ + 3x₂ ≥ 6, x₁, x₂ ≥ 0.
    Answer: Phase I reaches w = 0 at x = (3, 1); Phase II confirms it is
    optimal: min z = 9 at (3, 1).
    Teacher explains: The origin is infeasible, so there is no obvious
    starting BFS. Subtract surpluses and add ARTIFICIALS:
       x₁ + x₂ − e₁ + a₁ = 4,    x₁ + 3x₂ − e₂ + a₂ = 6
    Phase I: minimise w = a₁ + a₂, i.e. maximise −w. Expressing w in the
    nonbasic variables, w = 10 − 2x₁ − 4x₂ + e₁ + e₂, gives the bottom row:
       basis   x₁    x₂    e₁    e₂    a₁    a₂  | rhs
       a₁       1     1    −1     0     1     0  |   4
       a₂       1     3     0    −1     0     1  |   6
       −w      −2    −4     1     1     0     0  | −10
    x₂ enters; ratios 4/1 = 4, 6/3 = 2: a₂ leaves.
       a₁      2/3    0    −1    1/3    1   −1/3 |   2
       x₂      1/3    1     0   −1/3    0    1/3 |   2
       −w     −2/3    0     1   −1/3    0    4/3 |  −2
    x₁ enters; ratios 2/(2/3) = 3, 2/(1/3) = 6: a₁ leaves.
       x₁       1     0   −3/2   1/2   3/2  −1/2 |   3
       x₂       0     1    1/2  −1/2  −1/2   1/2 |   1
       −w       0     0     0     0     1     1  |   0
    w = 0: a feasible BFS x = (3, 1) exists. Phase II: delete the artificial
    columns, restore the real objective max −z = −2x₁ − 3x₂ (row 2, 3, 0, 0),
    and price out the basic columns (subtract 2 × row x₁ and 3 × row x₂):
       −z       0     0    3/2   1/2  |  −9
    All entries ≥ 0, so the BFS is optimal: min z = 9. The entries 3/2, 1/2
    under the surplus columns are the dual values (see D6). If Phase I had
    ended with w > 0, the LP would be INFEASIBLE. Common mistakes: forgetting
    to express w in terms of the nonbasic variables (the bottom row must have
    zeros under basic columns); using a surplus as a starting basic variable
    (it would be −4 < 0). Now you try: min x₁ + x₂ s.t. 2x₁ + x₂ ≥ 4,
    x₁ + 2x₂ ≥ 4. (x = (4/3, 4/3), z = 8/3)

D5. Show how the simplex method detects (a) unboundedness, using max x₁ + x₂
    s.t. x₁ − x₂ ≤ 1, −x₁ + x₂ ≤ 2; (b) multiple optima; (c) degeneracy, using
    max 3x₁ + 2x₂ s.t. x₁ + x₂ ≤ 4, 2x₁ + x₂ ≤ 8, x₁ ≤ 4. Explain cycling and
    Bland's rule.
    Answer: (a) after one pivot x₂ has reduced cost −2 but no positive entry
    in its column: unbounded along x = (1 + t, t). (b) a nonbasic variable
    with reduced cost 0 at the optimum. (c) three-way tie in the ratio test;
    the new BFS x = (4, 0) has basic variables equal to 0; optimum z = 12.
    Teacher explains: (a) Tableau with slacks s₁, s₂; x₁ enters (tie −1, −1,
    take the lower index); the only positive entry in its column is in row
    s₁ (ratio 1). After the pivot:
       x₁       1    −1     1     0  |   1
       s₂       0     0     1     1  |   3
       z        0    −2     1     0  |   1
    x₂ should enter (−2), but its column (−1, 0) has no positive entry: no
    constraint stops x₂ growing. Setting x₂ = t keeps x₁ = 1 + t, s₂ = 3,
    and z = 1 + 2t → ∞. (b) At an optimal tableau, if a NONBASIC variable
    has reduced cost 0, pivoting it in changes the vertex but not z: for
    max 2x + 4y in D2(c) the optimum (0, 5/2) has a zero entry for x, and
    entering x leads to (3, 1). (c) For x₁ the ratios are 4/1, 8/2, 4/1: a
    TIE. Whichever row leaves, the other two basic variables become 0:
    x = (4, 0) is a DEGENERATE vertex, where three constraint lines meet.
    Here z = 12 is already optimal (x₂ has reduced cost +1). In general a
    degenerate pivot can leave z unchanged (a step of length 0), and a
    sequence of such pivots can return to an earlier basis: CYCLING.
    BLAND'S RULE (enter the lowest-index improving variable, break ratio
    ties by lowest index) provably prevents cycling. Common mistakes:
    declaring unboundedness when the entering column has a positive entry
    somewhere; thinking degeneracy means infeasibility. Now you try: max
    x₁ + 3x₂ s.t. −x₁ + x₂ ≤ 2, x₁ − 2x₂ ≤ 4. (x₂ enters, s₁ leaves; then
    x₁ has reduced cost −4 with column (−1, −1): unbounded)

D6. State the rules for writing the dual, prove weak duality for
    (P) max cᵀx, Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0 and (D) min bᵀy, Aᵀy ≥ c, y ≥ 0, and solve the
    dual of D4 graphically, checking that the optimal values agree.
    Answer: dual of D4: max 4y₁ + 6y₂ s.t. y₁ + y₂ ≤ 2, y₁ + 3y₂ ≤ 3,
    y ≥ 0; optimum y = (3/2, 1/2), value 9 = min of D4.
    Teacher explains: Each primal constraint gets a dual variable (a price);
    each primal variable gives a dual constraint. Transpose A, swap b and c,
    swap max and min; the signs follow the table
       max problem          min problem
       constraint ≤    ↔    variable ≥ 0
       constraint ≥    ↔    variable ≤ 0
       constraint =    ↔    variable free
       variable ≥ 0    ↔    constraint ≥
       variable free   ↔    constraint =
    Weak duality: for x feasible in (P) and y feasible in (D),
       cᵀx ≤ (Aᵀy)ᵀx = yᵀAx ≤ yᵀb
    — the first step uses c ≤ Aᵀy and x ≥ 0, the second Ax ≤ b and y ≥ 0.
    ∎ Consequences: any dual feasible y gives an UPPER bound for (P); if
    cᵀx = bᵀy, both are optimal. D4 is a min with ≥ constraints; its dual is
    a max with ≤ constraints and y ≥ 0:
       max 4y₁ + 6y₂  s.t.  y₁ + y₂ ≤ 2,  y₁ + 3y₂ ≤ 3,  y ≥ 0
    Vertices: (0, 0): 0; (2, 0): 8; (0, 1): 6; intersection of the two lines:
    subtract, 2y₂ = 1, y₂ = 1/2, y₁ = 3/2: 6 + 3 = 9. Max 9 = min of D4 ✓,
    and y = (3/2, 1/2) are exactly the numbers under e₁, e₂ in D4's final
    tableau. Interpretation: if the constraints are nutrient requirements
    and x amounts of foods, y are the prices a pill-maker can charge per unit
    nutrient. Common mistakes: forgetting to transpose A; mixing up the sign
    rules for ≥ constraints in a max problem. Now you try: write the dual of
    max 3x₁ + 5x₂ s.t. x₁ ≤ 4, 2x₂ ≤ 12, 3x₁ + 2x₂ ≤ 18, x ≥ 0.
    (min 4y₁ + 12y₂ + 18y₃ s.t. y₁ + 3y₃ ≥ 3, 2y₂ + 2y₃ ≥ 5, y ≥ 0)

D7. State the strong duality theorem and prove complementary slackness. Use
    it to verify that x = (5/2, 3/2, 0) is optimal for max 3x₁ + 2x₂ + 4x₃
    s.t. x₁ + x₂ + 2x₃ ≤ 4, 2x₁ + 3x₃ ≤ 5, 2x₁ + x₂ + 3x₃ ≤ 7, x ≥ 0.
    Answer: optimal, with dual y = (2, 1/2, 0) and common value 21/2.
    Teacher explains: STRONG DUALITY: if (P) has an optimal solution then so
    does (D) and the values are equal (proof: the final simplex tableau
    supplies y = c_Bᵀ B⁻¹, which is dual feasible because all reduced costs
    are ≥ 0, and bᵀy = c_BᵀB⁻¹b = cᵀx; or via Farkas' lemma). COMPLEMENTARY
    SLACKNESS: for feasible x, y the proof of weak duality gives
       bᵀy − cᵀx = yᵀ(b − Ax) + xᵀ(Aᵀy − c),
    a sum of products of nonnegative numbers. Both are optimal ⇔ the gap is
    0 ⇔ every product yᵢ(b − Ax)ᵢ and xⱼ(Aᵀy − c)ⱼ is 0: a positive price
    only on a fully used resource, a positive activity only if it breaks
    even. ∎ Check the given x: feasible? Row 1: 5/2 + 3/2 = 4 (tight); row 2:
    5 (tight); row 3: 5 + 3/2 = 13/2 < 7 (slack), so y₃ = 0. x₁, x₂ > 0, so
    the first two dual constraints are tight:
       y₁ + 2y₂ + 2y₃ = 3,   y₁ + y₃ = 2   ⇒  y₁ = 2, y₂ = 1/2
    Check the third dual constraint: 2y₁ + 3y₂ + 3y₃ = 4 + 3/2 = 11/2 ≥ 4 ✓,
    and y ≥ 0 ✓. Values: cᵀx = 15/2 + 3 = 21/2; bᵀy = 8 + 5/2 = 21/2 ✓. Both
    optimal. If the forced y had failed feasibility, x would NOT be optimal.
    Common mistakes: setting yᵢ = 0 for a TIGHT constraint (only slack
    constraints force yᵢ = 0); forgetting to check dual feasibility. Now you
    try: in D1, is x = (4, 3) optimal? (Row 2 is slack ⇒ y₂ = 0; tight dual
    constraints give y₃ = 5/2, y₁ = 3 − 15/2 < 0: not dual feasible, so no)

D8. For the LP of D1 interpret the shadow prices (0, 3/2, 1). Find the range
    of b₂ (plant 2 hours) over which the shadow price 3/2 is valid, the new
    optimum if b₂ = 13, the range of the door profit c₁, and decide whether
    a new product using 1 hour in each plant is worth making at profit 4.
    Answer: b₂ ∈ [6, 18]; z = 37.5 at x = (5/3, 13/2); c₁ ∈ [0, 15/2];
    reduced cost 1 + 3/2 + 0 − 4 = −3/2 < 0, so yes.
    Teacher explains: The shadow price yᵢ = ∂z*/∂bᵢ: an extra hour in plant 2
    is worth 3/2, in plant 3 worth 1, in plant 1 worth 0 (plant 1 already has
    2 spare hours). From the final tableau the basic variables as functions
    of b (with b₁ = 4, b₃ = 18 fixed) are
       x₂ = b₂/2,   x₁ = (18 − b₂)/3,   s₁ = 4 − (18 − b₂)/3
    The basis stays feasible while all are ≥ 0: b₂ ≤ 18 and b₂ ≥ 6. At
    b₂ = 13: x₂ = 6.5, x₁ = 5/3, s₁ = 7/3 ≥ 0, z = 5 + 32.5 = 37.5 =
    36 + 3/2·1 ✓. Cost ranging: the vertex (2, 6) stays optimal while the
    iso-profit slope −c₁/5 lies between the slopes of the binding lines,
    0 (y = 6) and −3/2 (3x + 2y = 18): 0 ≤ c₁/5 ≤ 3/2, i.e. 0 ≤ c₁ ≤ 7.5.
    New product with column a = (1, 1, 1): it 'costs' yᵀa = 0 + 3/2 + 1 = 5/2
    in resources at shadow prices; profit 4 > 5/2, so reduced cost −3/2 < 0
    and bringing it in raises z. At profit 2 it would not be worth it. Common
    mistakes: applying a shadow price outside its range (at b₂ = 20 the
    answer is not 36 + 3); forgetting that shadow prices of nonbinding
    constraints are 0. Now you try: range of b₃ keeping the same basis?
    (x₁ = (b₃ − 12)/3 ≥ 0 and s₁ = 4 − x₁ ≥ 0: 12 ≤ b₃ ≤ 24)

D9. Define convex sets and functions. Prove: (a) the intersection of convex
    sets is convex; (b) a sublevel set {x : f(x) ≤ c} of a convex f is
    convex; (c) the maximum of convex functions is convex. Then decide by the
    Hessian whether f = x² + xy + y², g = x² − y², h = x²/y (y > 0) and
    k = log(eˣ + eʸ) are convex.
    Answer: proofs below; f convex (strictly), g not, h convex, k convex.
    Teacher explains: (a) Take x, y in every Cᵢ; each Cᵢ contains the segment
    [x, y], so the intersection does. (b) If f(x), f(y) ≤ c then
       f(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y) ≤ λc + (1 − λ)c = c.
    (c) With F = max fᵢ: fᵢ(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λfᵢ(x) + (1 − λ)fᵢ(y)
    ≤ λF(x) + (1 − λ)F(y) for each i; take the max over i. ∎ So |x| =
    max(x, −x) and every piecewise-linear max(aᵢᵀx + bᵢ) is convex. For
    twice differentiable functions use the Hessian (PSD everywhere ⇔ convex;
    for 2 × 2: diagonal entries ≥ 0 and determinant ≥ 0):
       f: H = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], det 3 > 0, trace 4 > 0   → PD, strictly convex
       g: H = [[2, 0], [0, −2]], eigenvalues ±2          → neither (a saddle)
       h: H = (2/y³)[[y², −xy], [−xy, x²]], det 0, diagonal ≥ 0 → PSD, convex
       k: H = p(1 − p)[[1, −1], [−1, 1]], p = eˣ/(eˣ + eʸ), eigenvalues
          0 and 2p(1 − p) ≥ 0                             → convex
    k is the 'soft maximum', a smooth convex approximation of max(x, y).
    Note: a convex function need not be differentiable (|x|) and a function
    with convex sublevel sets need not be convex (x³ on R). Common mistakes:
    'det ≥ 0 so PSD' without checking the diagonal ([[−1, 0], [0, −1]] has
    det 1); thinking the union of convex sets is convex. Now you try: is
    x² + 4xy + y² convex? (No: H = [[2, 4], [4, 2]] has eigenvalues 6, −2)

D10. (a) Prove that for convex f every local minimum is a global minimum, and
     that a strictly convex f has at most one minimiser. (b) Minimise
     f(x, y) = x² + 5y² by gradient descent from (5, 1) with α = 0.05, by
     exact line search, and by Newton's method. (c) Apply Newton to
     f(x) = eˣ − 2x from x₀ = 0.
     Answer: (a) proofs below. (b) GD: (4.5, 0.5), (4.05, 0.25),
     (3.645, 0.125), ...; exact line search first step α = 1/6 to
     (10/3, −2/3); Newton reaches (0, 0) in one step. (c) 1, 0.7358, 0.6940,
     0.69315 → ln 2.
     Teacher explains: (a) Let x* be a local minimum: f(x*) ≤ f(z) for
     ‖z − x*‖ < r. Suppose some y has f(y) < f(x*). Points on the segment,
     z = (1 − t)x* + ty with small t > 0, are within r of x*, and
        f(z) ≤ (1 − t)f(x*) + tf(y) < f(x*),
     a contradiction. If x ≠ y were two minimisers of a strictly convex f,
     the midpoint would give f < the minimum. ∎ (b) ∇f = (2x, 10y), so a
     gradient step with α = 0.05 is x ← x − 0.1x = 0.9x, y ← y − 0.5y = 0.5y:
        (5, 1) → (4.5, 0.5) → (4.05, 0.25) → (3.645, 0.125)
     y converges fast, x slowly: the CONDITION NUMBER 10/2 = 5 of the
     Hessian makes the level sets elongated ellipses. Convergence needs
     |1 − 2α| < 1 and |1 − 10α| < 1, i.e. α < 2/L = 0.2. Exact line search
     on ½xᵀQx with Q = diag(2, 10): g = (10, 10),
        α = gᵀg/(gᵀQg) = 200/1200 = 1/6,  new point (5 − 10/6, 1 − 10/6)
          = (10/3, −2/3),  f: 30 → 100/9 + 20/9 = 40/3
     Newton: step −Q⁻¹g = −(10/2, 10/10) = −(5, 1), landing exactly at
     (0, 0): Newton minimises a quadratic in one step. (c) f′ = eˣ − 2,
     f″ = eˣ, xₖ₊₁ = xₖ − (e^(xₖ) − 2)/e^(xₖ) = xₖ − 1 + 2e^(−xₖ):
        x₁ = 1,  x₂ = 2/e ≈ 0.7358,  x₃ ≈ 0.6940,  x₄ ≈ 0.6931475
     The number of correct digits roughly doubles each step (QUADRATIC
     convergence) near ln 2 ≈ 0.6931472. Common mistakes: stepping in the
     direction +∇f (that maximises); too large α (α = 0.25 here makes
     y ← −1.5y, diverging). Now you try: two GD steps for f = x² + y² with
     α = 0.25 from (4, 2). (x ← 0.5x: (2, 1), (1, 0.5))

D11. State the KKT conditions. Solve (a) min x² + y² s.t. x + y ≥ 2;
     (b) min (x − 3)² + (y − 2)² s.t. x + y ≤ 2, x ≥ 0; (c) min x + y s.t.
     x² + y² ≤ 2, giving the multipliers and explaining their meaning.
     Answer: (a) (1, 1), λ = 2, value 2. (b) (3/2, 1/2), λ₁ = 3, λ₂ = 0,
     value 9/2. (c) (−1, −1), λ = 1/2, value −2.
     Teacher explains: For min f s.t. gᵢ(x) ≤ 0 the KKT conditions are
        ∇f(x) + ∑λᵢ∇gᵢ(x) = 0,  gᵢ(x) ≤ 0,  λᵢ ≥ 0,  λᵢgᵢ(x) = 0.
     Geometrically, −∇f is a nonnegative combination of the gradients of the
     ACTIVE constraints. All three problems are convex, so a KKT point is the
     global minimum. (a) Write g = 2 − x − y ≤ 0. Stationarity:
        2x − λ = 0,  2y − λ = 0  ⇒  x = y = λ/2.
     If λ = 0 then x = y = 0, infeasible (0 + 0 < 2). So the constraint is
     active: x + y = 2 ⇒ λ = 2, point (1, 1), value 2. (b) g₁ = x + y − 2,
     g₂ = −x. Try g₁ active, λ₂ = 0:
        2(x − 3) + λ₁ = 0,  2(y − 2) + λ₁ = 0  ⇒  x − 3 = y − 2
     with x + y = 2: x = 3/2, y = 1/2, λ₁ = 3 ≥ 0 ✓, x ≥ 0 ✓ (so λ₂ = 0 is
     consistent). Value (3/2)² + (3/2)² = 9/2. It is the projection of (3, 2)
     onto the half-plane. (c) g = x² + y² − 2: 1 + 2λx = 0, 1 + 2λy = 0, so
     λ > 0, x = y = −1/(2λ), active: 2x² = 2, x = −1 (x must be negative),
     λ = 1/2. MEANING: λ is the shadow price of the constraint: in (a), with
     x + y ≥ c the optimum is c²/2, whose derivative at c = 2 is 2 = λ. Common
     mistakes: wrong sign of λ (check λ ≥ 0 with g ≤ 0 written correctly);
     accepting a KKT point of a NON-convex problem as a global minimum
     without checking. Now you try: min 2x² + y² s.t. x + y = 3. (4x = ν,
     2y = ν ⇒ y = 2x, x = 1, y = 2, ν = 4, value 6)

D12. Define the Lagrange dual function and prove it is concave and gives a
     lower bound. Compute the dual of (a) min x² s.t. x ≥ 1 and (b) the LP
     min cᵀx s.t. Ax ≥ b, x ≥ 0, and discuss strong duality and Slater's
     condition, including (c) min x s.t. x² ≤ 0.
     Answer: (a) g(λ) = λ − λ²/4, max at λ = 2 with d* = 1 = p*. (b) max bᵀy
     s.t. Aᵀy ≤ c, y ≥ 0. (c) p* = 0, g(λ) = −1/(4λ), d* = 0 but not
     attained; Slater fails.
     Teacher explains: For min f(x) s.t. gᵢ(x) ≤ 0 define
        L(x, λ) = f(x) + ∑λᵢgᵢ(x),   g(λ) = infₓ L(x, λ)   (λ ≥ 0).
     For each fixed x, L is AFFINE in λ, and an infimum of affine functions
     is concave — even if the original problem is not convex. Lower bound: if
     x̃ is feasible and λ ≥ 0 then ∑λᵢgᵢ(x̃) ≤ 0, so
        g(λ) ≤ L(x̃, λ) ≤ f(x̃);  hence d* = max g ≤ p* (WEAK duality).
     (a) L = x² + λ(1 − x) is minimised at x = λ/2:
        g(λ) = λ²/4 + λ − λ²/2 = λ − λ²/4
     g′ = 1 − λ/2 = 0 at λ = 2, d* = 1 = p* (x* = 1). (b) Constraints
     b − Ax ≤ 0 (multiplier y ≥ 0) and −x ≤ 0 (multiplier s ≥ 0):
        L = cᵀx + yᵀ(b − Ax) − sᵀx = bᵀy + (c − Aᵀy − s)ᵀx
     inf over x is −∞ unless c − Aᵀy − s = 0, i.e. Aᵀy ≤ c; then g = bᵀy.
     The dual is max bᵀy, Aᵀy ≤ c, y ≥ 0: LP duality falls out. (c) The only
     feasible point is 0, p* = 0. L = x + λx², minimised at x = −1/(2λ):
     g(λ) = −1/(4λ) → 0 as λ → ∞, never reaching it. SLATER's condition (a
     point with gᵢ(x) < 0 for all non-affine gᵢ) guarantees strong duality
     AND a dual optimum for convex problems; here no x has x² < 0, and the
     dual optimum is missing. For non-convex problems a DUALITY GAP d* < p*
     can occur. Common mistakes: maximising L over x instead of minimising;
     forgetting λ ≥ 0. Now you try: dual function of min x² + y² s.t.
     x + y ≥ 2. (g(λ) = 2λ − λ²/2, max 2 at λ = 2 = p*)

     l) minimiser of x − ln x (x > 0)

     n) condition number of the Hessian of x² + 5y²
     Answers:
       a) x = 2, 3                        b) (2, −1), −3
       c) (1, 1), −1                      d) x = (4/3, 7/3)
       e) (4.5, 0.5), (4.05, 0.25), (3.645, 0.125)
       f) α < 0.2 (= 2/L, L = 10)         g) (0, 0)
       h) 1, 2/e ≈ 0.7358, ≈ 0.6940       i) 2/3, 4/9; linear (factor 2/3),
                                             since f″(0) = 0
       j) 0.6; 0 (one step); −1 (oscillates, no convergence)
       k) α = 1/6, point (10/3, −2/3)     l) x = 1, value 1
       m) (2, 1), (1, 0.5)                n) 5

M11. Solve by KKT / Lagrange multipliers (point, multiplier(s), value).
     a) min x² + y²;  x + y ≥ 2
     b) min x² + y²;  x + y ≥ −1
     c) min (x − 3)² + (y − 2)²;  x + y ≤ 2
     d) min x² + y²;  x + 2y = 5
     e) min x + y;  x² + y² ≤ 2
     f) min x² + y² + z²;  x + y + z = 3
     g) min 2x² + y²;  x + y = 3
     h) min (x − 2)²;  x ≤ 1
     i) min (x − 2)²;  x ≤ 3
     j) min x² + y²;  x ≥ 1, y ≥ 2
     k) max ln x₁ + ln x₂ + ln x₃;  x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 1
     l) min w₁² + 4w₂²;  w₁ + w₂ = 1 (minimum-variance portfolio)
     m) min x² + y²;  x + y ≤ −2
     n) max xy;  x + y = 10

       a) (1, 1), λ = 2, 2                b) (0, 0), λ = 0, 0
       c) (3/2, 1/2), λ = 3, 9/2          d) (1, 2), ν = 2, 5
       e) (−1, −1), λ = 1/2, −2           f) (1, 1, 1), ν = 2, 3
       g) (1, 2), ν = 4, 6                h) x = 1, λ = 2, 1
       i) x = 2, λ = 0, 0                 j) (1, 2), λ = (2, 4), 5
       k) xᵢ = 1/3, ν = 3, −3 ln 3        l) (4/5, 1/5), ν = 8/5, 4/5
       m) (−1, −1), λ = 2, 2              n) (5, 5), ν = 5, 25
     (ν for equality constraints written ∇f = ν∇h; λ ≥ 0 for inequalities.)

M12. Lagrangian duality.
     a) dual function and d* for min x² s.t. x ≥ 1
     b) dual function and d* for min x² + y² s.t. x + y ≥ 2
     c) dual of min cᵀx s.t. Ax ≥ b, x ≥ 0 (via the Lagrangian)
     d) dual function for min x s.t. x² ≤ 0; is d* attained?
     e) dual of min ½‖x‖² s.t. Ax = b, and the resulting x*
     f) x* in e) for A = (1 2), b = 5
     g) dual function for min x² s.t. x ≥ 3; d*
     h) Slater point for b), if any
     i) T or F: the dual function is concave even for non-convex problems
     j) T or F: weak duality needs convexity
     k) Farkas: A = (1 1), b = −1: show Ax = b, x ≥ 0 has no solution by a
        certificate y
     l) min −x² s.t. −1 ≤ x ≤ 1: p*, d*
     Answers:
       a) λ − λ²/4, d* = 1                b) 2λ − λ²/2, d* = 2
       c) max bᵀy, Aᵀy ≤ c, y ≥ 0
       d) −1/(4λ); d* = 0 = p*, not attained (Slater fails)
       e) max bᵀν − ½‖Aᵀν‖²; x* = Aᵀ(AAᵀ)⁻¹b (minimum-norm solution)
       f) (1, 2)                          g) 3λ − λ²/4, d* = 9 at λ = 6
       h) e.g. (2, 2) (x + y = 4 > 2)     i) T
       j) F                               k) y = 1: Aᵀy = (1, 1) ≥ 0,
                                             bᵀy = −1 < 0
       l) p* = −1; g(λ) = −∞ for all λ, d* = −∞ (a duality gap)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always draw the two-variable picture first and label every
  vertex with its objective value — the simplex method is just a walk along
  these vertices, and each tableau can be matched to a corner of the
  drawing. Insist on the three questions of each simplex step: who enters
  (most negative), who leaves (smallest nonnegative ratio over POSITIVE
  entries), and what is the pivot. For duality, keep the sign table on the
  wall and check every dual with weak duality on one feasible pair. For
  convexity, a sketch of the function and one chord settles most questions;
  for two variables compute the Hessian and test trace and determinant.
  Harder: prove Farkas' lemma from the separating hyperplane theorem and
  deduce strong LP duality; show the simplex method can take exponentially
  many steps (Klee-Minty) while interior-point methods are polynomial;
  prove that gradient descent on an L-smooth, μ-strongly convex function
  converges linearly with factor (1 − μ/L); derive the KKT conditions from
  Farkas; and show that support vector machines and least squares with
  ℓ₁ penalty (lasso) are convex programmes with useful duals.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.39 — OPERATIONS RESEARCH: TRANSPORTATION, ASSIGNMENT, NETWORK FLOWS,
QUEUEING
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - TRANSPORTATION PROBLEM: m sources with supplies sᵢ, n destinations with
    demands dⱼ, unit costs cᵢⱼ; minimise ∑cᵢⱼxᵢⱼ s.t. ∑ⱼxᵢⱼ = sᵢ,
    ∑ᵢxᵢⱼ = dⱼ, xᵢⱼ ≥ 0. It is BALANCED if ∑sᵢ = ∑dⱼ; otherwise add a DUMMY
    source or destination with zero costs. A BFS has m + n − 1 basic cells
    (one equation is redundant) forming a TREE (no loop); fewer positive
    cells = DEGENERATE (add ε-allocations). Integer supplies and demands give
    INTEGER optimal solutions (TOTAL UNIMODULARITY).
  - INITIAL BFS: NORTH-WEST CORNER (ignores costs), LEAST-COST (cheapest
    cell first), VOGEL'S APPROXIMATION METHOD (VAM: PENALTY = difference of
    the two smallest costs in each row and column; allocate in the cheapest
    cell of the line with the largest penalty) — VAM is usually best.
  - MODI (u-v) METHOD: solve uᵢ + vⱼ = cᵢⱼ on basic cells (set u₁ = 0);
    REDUCED COSTS c̄ᵢⱼ = cᵢⱼ − uᵢ − vⱼ on the others. All c̄ᵢⱼ ≥ 0 ⇒
    OPTIMAL. Otherwise enter the most negative cell, trace its unique
    CLOSED LOOP (+ − + − alternating on basic cells), shift θ = the smallest
    '−' allocation; the cost falls by |c̄ᵢⱼ|θ. The uᵢ, vⱼ are the DUAL
    variables (uᵢ + vⱼ ≤ cᵢⱼ is dual feasibility).
  - ASSIGNMENT PROBLEM: n workers, n jobs, cost cᵢⱼ; choose a permutation
    minimising the total — a transportation problem with all sᵢ = dⱼ = 1
    (highly degenerate, so solved by the HUNGARIAN METHOD instead).
  - HUNGARIAN METHOD: (1) subtract each row minimum, then each column
    minimum; (2) cover all zeros with the MINIMUM number of lines; (3) if
    n lines are needed, an optimal assignment exists among the zeros; (4)
    otherwise subtract the smallest uncovered entry from every uncovered
    entry, ADD it at line intersections, and repeat. Correctness: adding a
    constant to a row or column changes every assignment's cost equally
    (KÖNIG: max number of independent zeros = min number of covering lines).
  - VARIANTS: MAXIMISATION (use −cᵢⱼ or max − cᵢⱼ); UNBALANCED (add dummy
    rows/columns of zeros); FORBIDDEN pairs (cost M, a huge number).
  - SHORTEST PATHS: DIJKSTRA's algorithm (nonnegative weights) makes one
    label PERMANENT per step (the smallest temporary label) and updates
    neighbours d(v) ← min(d(v), d(u) + w(u, v)); O(n²). With NEGATIVE
    weights use BELLMAN-FORD (n − 1 rounds of relaxing every edge; a further
    improvement signals a negative cycle).
  - MAXIMUM FLOW: a flow respects CAPACITIES 0 ≤ f(e) ≤ c(e) and
    CONSERVATION at every node except s and t. FORD-FULKERSON: repeatedly
    find an AUGMENTING PATH in the RESIDUAL network (forward residual
    c − f, backward residual f) and push its bottleneck. EDMONDS-KARP
    (shortest augmenting paths, BFS) runs in O(VE²). An s-t CUT (S, T) has
    capacity the sum of capacities of edges from S to T.
  - MAX-FLOW MIN-CUT THEOREM: the maximum flow value equals the minimum cut
    capacity; at termination, S = nodes reachable from s in the residual
    network gives a minimum cut. Integer capacities ⇒ an integer maximum
    flow (so bipartite MATCHING is a flow problem).
  - OTHER NETWORK MODELS: MINIMUM SPANNING TREE (KRUSKAL: add the cheapest
    edge not forming a cycle; PRIM: grow one tree by the cheapest edge
    leaving it; n − 1 edges); CRITICAL PATH METHOD (CPM): forward pass
    ES, EF = ES + duration; backward pass LF, LS = LF − duration;
    TOTAL FLOAT = LS − ES; CRITICAL activities have zero float and the
    project length is the longest path. MIN-COST FLOW generalises
    transportation, assignment and shortest paths.
  - QUEUEING BASICS: KENDALL notation A/B/c/K (M = Markovian, i.e. POISSON
    arrivals / EXPONENTIAL service; D = deterministic; G = general). A
    POISSON process of rate λ: counts in time t are Poisson(λt),
    inter-arrival times are Exp(λ) and MEMORYLESS, P(T > s + t | T > s) =
    P(T > t). LITTLE'S LAW: L = λW, Lq = λWq, and W = Wq + 1/μ.
  - M/M/1 (arrival rate λ, service rate μ, ρ = λ/μ < 1): BIRTH-DEATH balance
    λPₙ = μPₙ₊₁ gives Pₙ = (1 − ρ)ρⁿ; L = ρ/(1 − ρ), Lq = ρ²/(1 − ρ),
    W = 1/(μ − λ), Wq = ρ/(μ − λ); P(n ≥ k) = ρᵏ; the time in system is
    Exp(μ − λ). If ρ ≥ 1 the queue grows without bound.
  - M/M/c: a = λ/μ, ρ = a/c < 1,
    P₀ = [∑ₙ₌₀^(c−1) aⁿ/n! + aᶜ/(c!(1 − ρ))]⁻¹, P(wait) = aᶜP₀/(c!(1 − ρ))
    (ERLANG C), Lq = P₀aᶜρ/(c!(1 − ρ)²), L = Lq + a. POOLING servers
    beats separate queues.
  - M/M/1/K (at most K in system): Pₙ = ρⁿ(1 − ρ)/(1 − ρᴷ⁺¹) (Pₙ = 1/(K + 1)
    if ρ = 1), BLOCKING probability P_K, EFFECTIVE arrival rate
    λ_eff = λ(1 − P_K) in Little's law. M/G/1 (POLLACZEK-KHINCHINE):
    Lq = (λ²σ² + ρ²)/(2(1 − ρ)), σ² the service-time variance; M/D/1 has half
    the M/M/1 queue. COST models balance service cost against waiting cost.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Three factories S1, S2, S3 supply 7, 9, 18 units; four warehouses D1-D4
    need 5, 8, 7, 14. Unit costs:
              D1   D2   D3   D4 | supply
       S1     19   30   50   10 |   7
       S2     70   30   40   60 |   9
       S3     40    8   70   20 |  18
    demand     5    8    7   14 |  34
    Find initial basic feasible solutions by the north-west corner, least
    cost and Vogel methods and compare their costs.
    Answer: NW corner 1015; least cost 814; VAM 779 (the optimum is 743,
    see D2).
    Teacher explains: The problem is balanced (34 = 34). A BFS needs
    m + n − 1 = 6 basic cells. NORTH-WEST CORNER: start at S1D1, allocate as
    much as possible, then move right (demand still open) or down:
       S1D1 = 5, S1D2 = 2, S2D2 = 6, S2D3 = 3, S3D3 = 4, S3D4 = 14
       cost 95 + 60 + 180 + 120 + 280 + 280 = 1015
    It never looks at costs (S3D3 at 70!). LEAST COST: fill the cheapest
    available cell each time: S3D2 = 8 (cost 8), S1D4 = 7 (10), S3D4 = 7
    (20), S2D3 = 7 (40), S3D1 = 3 (40), S2D1 = 2 (70): cost 814. VOGEL: the
    PENALTY of a line is (second smallest − smallest) cost, the regret of
    not using its cheapest cell.
       step 1: rows 9, 10, 12; columns 21, 22, 10, 10. Max 22 (D2):
               S3D2 = 8 (D2 done)
       step 2: rows 9, 20, 20; columns 21, 10, 10. Max 21 (D1): S1D1 = 5
       step 3: rows 40, 20, 50; columns 10, 10. Max 50 (S3): S3D4 = 10
       step 4: rows 40, 20; columns 10, 50. Max 50 (D4): S1D4 = 2
       step 5: only S2 left: S2D4 = 2, S2D3 = 7
       cost 64 + 95 + 200 + 20 + 120 + 280 = 779
    Six cells in each case ✓. VAM is usually close to optimal because it
    avoids the choices that would later force expensive cells. Common
    mistakes: recomputing penalties with deleted rows/columns still
    included; allocating in the line with the largest penalty but not in
    its CHEAPEST cell. Now you try: NW corner for supplies 30, 20, demands
    25, 25, costs [[5, 3], [4, 7]]. (x₁₁ = 25, x₁₂ = 5, x₂₂ = 20, cost 280;
    the optimum is 180)

D2. Starting from the VAM solution of D1, use the MODI method to reach the
    optimum. Explain why the method works.
    Answer: u = (0, 50, 10), v = (19, −2, −10, 10); the cell S2D2 has reduced
    cost −18; θ = 2; new cost 779 − 36 = 743, which is optimal.
    Teacher explains: The transportation LP has dual variables uᵢ (rows),
    vⱼ (columns); complementary slackness forces uᵢ + vⱼ = cᵢⱼ on basic
    cells. Six equations, seven unknowns: set u₁ = 0.
       S1D1: v₁ = 19      S1D4: v₄ = 10      S2D4: u₂ = 60 − 10 = 50
       S3D4: u₃ = 20 − 10 = 10                S3D2: v₂ = 8 − 10 = −2
       S2D3: v₃ = 40 − 50 = −10
    Reduced costs c̄ᵢⱼ = cᵢⱼ − uᵢ − vⱼ on the nonbasic cells:
       S1D2: 30 + 2 = 32      S1D3: 50 + 10 = 60     S2D1: 70 − 69 = 1
       S2D2: 30 − 48 = −18    S3D1: 40 − 29 = 11     S3D3: 70 − 0 = 70
    S2D2 is negative: each unit sent there saves 18. Its LOOP through basic
    cells: S2D2 (+) → S2D4 (−) → S3D4 (+) → S3D2 (−) → back. The '−' cells
    hold 2 and 8, so θ = 2: S2D2 = 2, S2D4 = 0 (leaves), S3D4 = 12, S3D2 = 6.
    New cost 779 − 18·2 = 743. Recompute: u = (0, 32, 10), v = (19, −2, 8,
    10); reduced costs 32, 42, 19, 18, 11, 52, all ≥ 0: OPTIMAL,
       S1D1 = 5, S1D4 = 2, S2D2 = 2, S2D3 = 7, S3D2 = 6, S3D4 = 12, cost 743.
    Why: c̄ᵢⱼ is exactly the change in cost when one unit is pushed round the
    loop (the + and − costs along the loop sum to cᵢⱼ − uᵢ − vⱼ since the
    u's and v's cancel on basic cells); c̄ ≥ 0 everywhere means u, v are
    dual feasible, so by LP duality the plan is optimal. Common mistakes:
    loops that turn at nonbasic cells; taking θ from a '+' cell; forgetting
    that the loop must alternate row, column, row, ... Now you try: in the
    final table check the reduced cost of S2D4. (60 − 32 − 10 = 18)

D3. (a) Supplies 50, 40 and demands 30, 40: how do you balance the problem?
    (b) Supplies 20, 30, 50, demands 40, 30, 30, costs [[2, 3, 1], [5, 4, 8],
    [5, 6, 8]]. The least-cost method gives only 4 positive cells: handle the
    degeneracy and prove the solution optimal. (c) Why are optimal solutions
    integral?
    Answer: (a) add a dummy destination of demand 20 with zero costs.
    (b) S1D3 = 20, S2D2 = 30, S3D1 = 40, S3D3 = 10, plus ε in S3D2; all
    reduced costs ≥ 0; minimum cost 420. (c) total unimodularity.
    Teacher explains: (a) Total supply 90 exceeds demand 70 by 20. A dummy
    column D3 with demand 20 and cost 0 absorbs the surplus: whatever is
    'shipped' there is really left at the source (costs could instead be
    storage costs). If demand exceeds supply, add a dummy SOURCE; its
    shipments are unmet demand (costs = shortage penalties). (b) Least cost:
    S1D3 = 20 (cost 1, S1 done), S2D2 = 30 (cost 4: S2 AND D2 finish
    together), S3D1 = 40, S3D3 = 10. Only 4 cells, but m + n − 1 = 5: the
    cells {S1D3, S3D3, S3D1} and {S2D2} are not connected, so u, v cannot
    be computed. Add an allocation ε (a tiny positive amount, 0 in the end)
    in a cell joining the pieces without making a loop, say S3D2. With
    u₁ = 0:
       v₃ = 1, u₃ = 7, v₁ = −2, v₂ = 6 − 7 = −1, u₂ = 4 + 1 = 5
       c̄: S1D1 = 2 + 2 = 4, S1D2 = 3 + 1 = 4, S2D1 = 5 − 3 = 2,
          S2D3 = 8 − 6 = 2
    All ≥ 0: optimal, cost 20 + 120 + 200 + 80 = 420. (Had ε been put in
    S1D2 instead, S3D2 would have c̄ = −4 and one DEGENERATE pivot with θ = ε
    would be needed, with no change in cost.) (c) The constraint matrix
    has entries 0, 1 and each column has one 1 in a supply row and one in a
    demand row; such matrices are TOTALLY UNIMODULAR (every square
    submatrix has determinant 0, ±1), so every BFS B⁻¹b is an integer
    vector by Cramer's rule. Common mistakes: putting ε in a cell that
    closes a loop; forgetting the dummy's costs are 0 (or penalties). Now
    you try: how many basic cells does a 4 × 5 transportation problem have?
    (4 + 5 − 1 = 8)

D4. Assign four workers W1-W4 to jobs J1-J4 at minimum total cost:
              J1   J2   J3   J4
       W1     10   19    8   15
       W2     10   18    7   17
       W3     13   16    9   14
       W4     12   19    8   18
    Answer: W1-J4, W2-J1, W3-J2, W4-J3; total 15 + 10 + 16 + 8 = 49.
    Teacher explains: Row minima 8, 7, 9, 8; subtract them. Then column
    minima of the result (2, 7, 0, 5); subtract:
       W1   0  4  0  2
       W2   1  4  0  5
       W3   2  0  0  0
       W4   2  4  0  5
    Cover all zeros with as few lines as possible: column J3, row W3,
    column J1 — 3 lines < 4, so no complete zero assignment yet (W2 and W4
    both need J3). The smallest uncovered entry is 2 (W1J4). Subtract 2 from
    every uncovered entry and add 2 where lines cross (W3J1, W3J3):
       W1   0  2  0  0
       W2   1  2  0  3
       W3   4  0  2  0
       W4   2  2  0  3
    Minimum cover: column J3, rows W1, W3 — still 3 lines. Smallest
    uncovered entry 1 (W2J1); subtract from uncovered, add at crossings
    (W1J3, W3J3):
       W1   0  2  1  0
       W2   0  1  0  2
       W3   4  0  3  0
       W4   1  1  0  2
    Now 4 lines are needed. Assign where forced: W4 has one zero (J3); then
    W2 must take J1; W3 takes J2; W1 takes J4. Original costs:
    15 + 10 + 16 + 8 = 49. Why it works: subtracting a constant from a row
    lowers EVERY complete assignment by that constant, so the optimal
    assignment is unchanged, and an all-zero assignment in a nonnegative
    matrix is clearly optimal. The adjustment step is 'subtract k from the
    uncovered rows, add k to the covered columns': it keeps entries ≥ 0 and
    creates a new zero. Common mistakes: covering with more lines than
    necessary; forgetting to ADD at intersections; reading costs from the
    reduced matrix. Now you try: costs [[9, 2, 7], [6, 4, 3], [5, 8, 1]].
    (W1-J2, W2-J1, W3-J3: 2 + 6 + 1 = 9)

D5. (a) Maximise total profit for profits [[5, 7, 6], [8, 4, 9], [6, 5, 7]].
    (b) Three workers, four jobs, costs [[10, 7, 8, 9], [8, 9, 7, 6],
    [7, 8, 10, 9]]: assign to minimise cost. (c) With forbidden pairs (—),
    costs [[8, —, 6], [7, 5, —], [—, 4, 9]]. (d) Show the assignment LP has
    an integral optimum.
    Answer: (a) 22 (e.g. W1-J2, W2-J3, W3-J1). (b) W1-J2, W2-J4, W3-J1, cost
    20; J3 is left undone. (c) W1-J3, W2-J1, W3-J2, cost 17. (d) total
    unimodularity (Birkhoff).
    Teacher explains: (a) Convert to a minimisation of REGRET: subtract
    every entry from the largest, 9:
       [[4, 2, 3], [1, 5, 0], [3, 4, 2]]
    Row reduce (2, 0, 2): [[2, 0, 1], [1, 5, 0], [1, 2, 0]]; column minima
    (1, 0, 0): [[1, 0, 1], [0, 5, 0], [0, 2, 0]]. Zeros W1J2, W2J1, W2J3,
    W3J1, W3J3: assign W1-J2, then W2-J3 and W3-J1 (or W2-J1, W3-J3). Profit
    7 + 9 + 6 = 22 (or 7 + 8 + 7 = 22): two optimal answers. (b) Add a DUMMY
    worker W4 with zero costs; whichever job W4 'does' is not done. The
    Hungarian method gives W1-J2 (7), W2-J4 (6), W3-J1 (7), W4-J3 (0):
    cost 20. (c) Put M (very large) in the forbidden cells; the method will
    avoid them if a feasible assignment exists: W1-J3 (6), W2-J1 (7), W3-J2
    (4) = 17 (the only other permutation avoiding the forbidden cells is
    W1-J1, W2-J2, W3-J3 = 22). (d) The LP relaxation min ∑cᵢⱼxᵢⱼ,
    ∑ⱼxᵢⱼ = 1, ∑ᵢxᵢⱼ = 1, x ≥ 0 has as feasible set the doubly stochastic
    matrices, whose vertices are exactly the PERMUTATION matrices
    (BIRKHOFF-VON NEUMANN), so the LP optimum is attained at an assignment.
    Common mistakes: running the minimising algorithm directly on profits;
    in an unbalanced problem forgetting the dummy (the matrix must be
    square). Now you try: maximise [[16, 10, 14, 11], [14, 11, 15, 15],
    [15, 15, 13, 12], [13, 12, 14, 15]]. (W1-J1, W2-J3, W3-J2, W4-J4: 61)

D6. Find shortest distances from A to all nodes of the undirected network
    with edges AB 4, AC 2, BC 1, BD 5, CD 8, CE 10, DE 2, DF 6, EF 2, using
    Dijkstra's algorithm. Prove the algorithm correct, and show why it fails
    with negative edges.
    Answer: d(B) = 3 (A-C-B), d(C) = 2, d(D) = 8 (A-C-B-D), d(E) = 10,
    d(F) = 12 (A-C-B-D-E-F).
    Teacher explains: Keep temporary labels; each step make the smallest
    one permanent and update its neighbours.
       permanent  A 0:  temp B 4, C 2
       permanent  C 2:  B min(4, 2 + 1) = 3, D 2 + 8 = 10, E 2 + 10 = 12
       permanent  B 3:  D min(10, 3 + 5) = 8
       permanent  D 8:  E min(12, 8 + 2) = 10, F 8 + 6 = 14
       permanent  E 10: F min(14, 10 + 2) = 12
       permanent  F 12
    Record the predecessor with each improvement and trace back: F ← E ←
    D ← B ← C ← A. Correctness (induction): when u gets the smallest
    temporary label d(u), any other path to u must leave the permanent set
    at some node x with label ≥ d(u) and then add NONNEGATIVE edges, so it is
    no shorter. That argument breaks with negative weights: with edges
    s→a 4, s→b 5, b→a −3, a→t 2, Dijkstra fixes a at 4 and t at 6, but
    s-b-a-t costs 4. BELLMAN-FORD (relax every edge n − 1 times) handles
    negative weights, and a further improvement in round n reveals a
    negative cycle (then 'shortest' is undefined). Common mistakes: making
    a label permanent before it is the smallest; updating permanent
    labels; forgetting to keep predecessors. Now you try: directed edges
    S→A 7, S→B 2, S→C 3, A→D 4, B→A 3, B→D 8, C→D 6, C→E 2, D→T 3, E→T 9,
    E→D 1; shortest S→T. (9, via S-C-E-D-T)

D7. In the network with arcs (capacities) s→a 10, s→c 10, a→b 4, a→c 2,
    a→d 8, c→d 9, d→b 6, b→t 10, d→t 10, find a maximum flow by the
    Ford-Fulkerson method with shortest augmenting paths, find a minimum cut,
    and prove the max-flow min-cut theorem.
    Answer: maximum flow 19 (augmenting paths s-a-b-t 4, s-a-d-t 6,
    s-c-d-t 4, s-c-d-b-t 5); minimum cut S = {s, c}: arcs s→a and c→d,
    capacity 10 + 9 = 19.
    Teacher explains: Augment along paths with spare capacity; the amount is
    the BOTTLENECK.
       s-a-b-t: min(10, 4, 10) = 4       (a→b full)
       s-a-d-t: min(6, 8, 10) = 6        (s→a full)
       s-c-d-t: min(10, 9, 4) = 4        (d→t full)
       s-c-d-b-t: min(6, 5, 6, 6) = 5    (c→d full)
    Total 19. In the residual network from s only c is reachable (s→c has 1
    unit left, but c→d is full and a→c carries no flow to cancel), so
    S = {s, c}. Its outgoing arcs s→a (10) and c→d (9) are saturated, and
    no flow runs back from T into S: the cut capacity is 19 = the flow.
    PROOF of the theorem. For any flow f and cut (S, T), conservation gives
       value(f) = f(S → T) − f(T → S) ≤ c(S, T)          (weak duality)
    If no augmenting path exists, let S = nodes reachable from s in the
    residual network (t ∉ S). Every arc S → T is saturated (else its head
    would be reachable) and every arc T → S carries 0 (else its tail would
    be reachable through the backward residual arc). So value(f) = c(S, T):
    the flow is maximum and the cut minimum. Conversely a maximum flow has
    no augmenting path. ∎ With integer capacities each augmentation adds at
    least 1, so the method terminates with an INTEGER flow. BACKWARD residual
    arcs matter: they let later paths undo bad earlier choices. Common
    mistakes: counting arcs from T to S in the cut capacity; forgetting
    backward arcs; stopping when no FORWARD-only path exists. Now you try:
    s→a 3, s→b 2, a→b 1, a→t 2, b→t 3. (max flow 5, min cut {s})

D8. (a) Find a minimum spanning tree of the network of D6 by Kruskal's and
    Prim's algorithms and justify the greedy choice. (b) A project has
    activities A (3 days), B (2), C (4, after A), D (5, after A and B), E (2,
    after C), F (3, after D and E), G (3, after D). Find the project length,
    the critical path and the floats.
    Answer: (a) BC 1, AC 2, DE 2, EF 2, BD 5: total 12. (b) 12 days; critical
    path A-C-E-F; floats B 2, D 1, G 1, others 0.
    Teacher explains: (a) KRUSKAL: sort edges, take each unless it closes a
    cycle: BC 1 ✓, AC 2 ✓, DE 2 ✓, EF 2 ✓, AB 4 ✗ (A-C-B), BD 5 ✓ — now 5
    edges on 6 nodes, stop. Weight 12. PRIM from A: AC 2, CB 1, BD 5,
    DE 2, EF 2 — the same tree. Why greedy works (CUT PROPERTY): for any
    split of the nodes into two groups, the cheapest edge across it belongs
    to some minimum spanning tree (exchange it for a heavier crossing edge
    in any tree containing a cycle through it). Note the MST is not a
    shortest-path tree: its A-F path costs 12 here by luck, but in general
    they differ. (b) Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors):
       A 0-3,  B 0-2,  C 3-7,  D 3-8,  E 7-9,  F 9-12,  G 8-11
    Project length = max EF = 12. Backward pass (LF = min LS of
    successors, starting from 12):
       F 9-12, G 9-12, E 7-9, D LF = min(9, 9) = 9 so 4-9, C 3-7,
       B LF = LS(D) = 4 so 2-4, A LF = min(LS C, LS D) = 3 so 0-3
    Total float LS − ES: A 0, B 2, C 0, D 1, E 0, F 0, G 1. Critical path
    A-C-E-F (3 + 4 + 2 + 3 = 12), the longest path. Delaying a critical
    activity delays the project; B may slip 2 days. Common mistakes: in the
    backward pass taking the max instead of the min; confusing the longest
    path (CPM) with the shortest. Now you try: A 2, B 4, C 3 (after A), D 2
    (after A), E 5 (after B, C), F 4 (after D), G 3 (after E, F). (length 13,
    critical A-C-E-G)

D9. Customers arrive as a Poisson process of rate λ = 6 per hour.
    (a) P(no arrival in 10 minutes)? (b) P(exactly 2 arrivals in 20
    minutes)? (c) Service times are exponential with mean 4 minutes: given
    that a service has lasted 5 minutes, P(it lasts 6 more)? (d) State and
    justify Little's law and use it: 12 arrivals per hour each spend 15
    minutes in a shop; how many are inside on average? (e) Decode M/M/3/10.
    Answer: (a) e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368; (b) 2e⁻² ≈ 0.271; (c) e^(−1.5) ≈ 0.223; (d)
    L = λW = 3; (e) Poisson arrivals, exponential service, 3 servers, at
    most 10 in the system.
    Teacher explains: For a Poisson process the number of arrivals in time
    t is Poisson(λt). (a) λt = 6 × 1/6 = 1: P(0) = e⁻¹ ≈ 0.3679 — which is
    also P(inter-arrival time > 10 min), since gaps are Exp(6). (b) λt = 2:
    P(2) = e⁻²2²/2! = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707. (c) MEMORYLESS: for T ~ Exp(μ),
       P(T > s + t | T > s) = e^(−μ(s + t))/e^(−μs) = e^(−μt).
    The past 5 minutes are irrelevant: P(T > 6) = e^(−6/4) = e^(−1.5) ≈
    0.2231. This is why M/M queues are MARKOV chains: the state n (number
    in system) is all we need. (d) LITTLE: L = λW for any stable system
    (no distribution assumptions). Sketch: over a long time τ, the area
    under the 'number in system' curve counts customer-time; it equals
    both L·τ and (number of arrivals λτ) × (average time W). So
    L = 12 × 1/4 = 3. The same law applies to the queue alone (Lq = λWq) and
    to the servers (average busy servers = λ/μ). (e) Kendall A/B/c/K:
    arrival process / service distribution / number of servers / capacity;
    omitted K means infinite. Common mistakes: mixing time units (λ per
    hour, t in minutes); using Little's law with the offered λ when
    customers are turned away (use λ_eff). Now you try: L = 5, λ = 20 per
    hour: W? (15 minutes)

D10. Derive the steady state of the M/M/1 queue and its measures. Then for
     λ = 8 per hour, μ = 10 per hour find P₀, P(n ≥ 3), L, Lq, W, Wq and
     P(time in system > 1 hour).
     Answer: Pₙ = (1 − ρ)ρⁿ. With ρ = 0.8: P₀ = 0.2, P(n ≥ 3) = 0.512, L = 4,
     Lq = 3.2, W = 0.5 h, Wq = 0.4 h, P(W > 1) = e⁻² ≈ 0.135.
     Teacher explains: The number in system is a BIRTH-DEATH process: up at
     rate λ, down at rate μ (when n ≥ 1). In steady state the flow across
     the cut between n and n + 1 balances:
        λPₙ = μPₙ₊₁  ⇒  Pₙ = ρⁿP₀,   ρ = λ/μ
     ∑Pₙ = 1 needs ρ < 1 (geometric series), giving P₀ = 1 − ρ: P₀ is the
     probability the server is idle, and ρ its UTILISATION. Then
        L = ∑nPₙ = (1 − ρ)∑nρⁿ = ρ/(1 − ρ)
        Lq = ∑(n − 1)Pₙ (n ≥ 1) = L − (1 − P₀) = L − ρ = ρ²/(1 − ρ)
        W = L/λ = 1/(μ − λ),   Wq = Lq/λ = ρ/(μ − λ)   (Little)
     Numbers: ρ = 0.8, P₀ = 0.2, P(n ≥ 3) = ρ³ = 0.512, L = 0.8/0.2 = 4,
     Lq = 0.64/0.2 = 3.2, W = 1/2 h = 30 min, Wq = 0.4 h = 24 min; check
     W = Wq + 1/μ = 0.4 + 0.1 ✓. The time in system of an arriving customer
     is Exp(μ − λ) (FCFS): P(W > 1) = e^(−2) ≈ 0.1353. The formulas explode
     as ρ → 1: at λ = 9, L = 9 and W = 1 h; at λ = 9.5, L = 19. Common
     mistakes: using ρ ≥ 1 in the formulas; Lq = L − 1 (it is L − ρ). Now you
     try: λ = 3, μ = 4 per hour: L, Lq, W, Wq. (3, 2.25, 1 h, 0.75 h)

D11. Arrivals at λ = 8 per hour are served by two clerks, each with
     exponential rate μ = 5 per hour, from ONE queue (M/M/2). Find P₀, the
     probability of waiting, Lq, L, Wq, W. Compare with (a) one fast clerk of
     rate 10 and (b) two separate M/M/1 queues each receiving 4 per hour.
     Answer: P₀ = 1/9, P(wait) = 32/45 ≈ 0.711, Lq = 128/45 ≈ 2.844,
     L = 40/9 ≈ 4.444, Wq = 16/45 h ≈ 21.3 min, W = 5/9 h ≈ 33.3 min.
     (a) W = 30 min, Wq = 24 min. (b) W = 60 min, Wq = 48 min.
     Teacher explains: a = λ/μ = 1.6 (the average number of busy clerks),
     ρ = a/c = 0.8. Birth-death rates: down at rate nμ for n ≤ c and cμ
     above, so Pₙ = (aⁿ/n!)P₀ for n ≤ c and Pₙ = (aᶜ/c!)ρⁿ⁻ᶜP₀ beyond.
        P₀⁻¹ = 1 + a + a²/(2!(1 − ρ)) = 1 + 1.6 + 2.56/0.4 = 9
        P(wait) = P(n ≥ 2) = a²/(2!(1 − ρ))·P₀ = 6.4/9 ≈ 0.711  (Erlang C)
        Lq = P₀a²ρ/(2!(1 − ρ)²) = (1/9)(2.56)(0.8)/(0.08) = 25.6/9 ≈ 2.844
        L = Lq + a = 2.844 + 1.6 = 4.444
        Wq = Lq/λ ≈ 0.356 h,  W = Wq + 1/μ = 0.356 + 0.2 = 0.556 h
     (a) One clerk twice as fast (D10): W = 0.5 h, Wq = 0.4 h — shorter
     total time (service itself is quicker) but LONGER wait in the queue.
     (b) Separate queues: each M/M/1 with λ = 4, μ = 5 has W = 1/(5 − 4) =
     1 h: much worse, because one clerk can sit idle while the other has a
     queue. Lesson: POOLING (a single queue) is always better than separate
     lines. Common mistakes: using ρ = λ/μ = 1.6 > 1 and declaring the system
     unstable (the condition is λ < cμ); forgetting to add a (not ρ) to get L.
     Now you try: λ = 4, μ = 5, c = 2. (P₀ = 3/7, Lq = 16/105 ≈ 0.152,
     W = 5/21 h ≈ 14.3 min)

D12. (a) A one-chair barber with room for 3 customers in total (M/M/1/3)
     has λ = 8, μ = 10 per hour. Find P₀, the blocking probability, the
     effective arrival rate, L and W. (b) State the Pollaczek-Khinchine
     formula and find Lq for λ = 8 per hour with constant service time
     6 minutes (M/D/1), and for service with mean 12 minutes and standard
     deviation 6 minutes at λ = 4 per hour. (c) Choose the service rate μ of
     an M/M/1 system with λ = 8 to minimise 2μ + 16L per hour.
     Answer: (a) P₀ = 125/369 ≈ 0.339, P₃ = 64/369 ≈ 0.173, λ_eff ≈ 6.61,
     L = 452/369 ≈ 1.225, W ≈ 0.185 h ≈ 11.1 min. (b) M/D/1: Lq = 1.6 (half of
     M/M/1's 3.2); second case Lq = 2, Wq = 0.5 h. (c) μ* = 16, cost 48.
     Teacher explains: (a) Balance λPₙ = μPₙ₊₁ for n = 0, 1, 2 only, so
     Pₙ = ρⁿP₀ for n = 0..3 with
        P₀ = 1/(1 + 0.8 + 0.64 + 0.512) = 1/2.952 = 125/369 ≈ 0.3388
        P₃ = 0.512 × 0.3388 = 64/369 ≈ 0.1734  (arrivals finding it full leave)
     No stability condition is needed (finite states). Customers who
     actually enter arrive at λ_eff = λ(1 − P₃) = 8 × 0.8266 ≈ 6.61 per
     hour. L = 0·P₀ + 1·P₁ + 2·P₂ + 3·P₃ = (0.8 + 1.28 + 1.536)/2.952 ≈ 1.225,
     and Little with λ_eff: W = L/λ_eff ≈ 0.185 h. Using λ = 8 would be wrong.
     (b) For M/G/1 with service mean 1/μ and variance σ²,
        Lq = (λ²σ² + ρ²)/(2(1 − ρ)).
     Exponential service (σ = 1/μ) gives back ρ²/(1 − ρ). M/D/1 (σ = 0),
     ρ = 8 × 0.1 = 0.8: Lq = 0.64/0.4 = 1.6 — variability of service, not
     just its mean, creates queues. Second case: ρ = 4 × 0.2 = 0.8,
     σ = 0.1 h: Lq = (16 × 0.01 + 0.64)/0.4 = 2, Wq = Lq/λ = 0.5 h. (c)
     C(μ) = 2μ + 16·λ/(μ − λ) = 2μ + 128/(μ − 8). C′ = 2 − 128/(μ − 8)² = 0 ⇒
     μ − 8 = 8, μ* = 16; C = 32 + 16 = 48 per hour (in general
     μ* = λ + √(c_wλ/c_s)). Common mistakes: using λ instead of λ_eff; in
     P-K using the standard deviation instead of the variance. Now you try:
     M/M/1/2 with λ = 4, μ = 5: P₀ and P₂. (25/61 ≈ 0.410, 16/61 ≈ 0.262)

    k) in f), the project length if G takes 5 days
