TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: do every transportation problem in a single tableau drawn
  large, writing uᵢ down the side and vⱼ across the top, and circle the
  basic cells; count m + n − 1 before every MODI step. For the Hungarian
  method, practise covering zeros on paper with coloured lines, and always
  go back to the ORIGINAL matrix for the final cost. For networks, keep a
  table of labels (Dijkstra), draw residual arrows in a second colour (max
  flow), and do the CPM forward and backward passes in a two-row box above
  each activity. For queues, first write ρ and check ρ < 1, then compute L
  and get everything else from Little's law. Harder: prove that
  transportation matrices are totally unimodular; show the Hungarian
  method is the primal-dual algorithm for the assignment LP; prove König's
  theorem from max-flow min-cut; show that Ford-Fulkerson can fail to
  terminate with irrational capacities; derive the waiting-time
  distribution of M/M/1 (FCFS) and the Erlang C formula; and prove
  Burke's theorem that the departures of M/M/1 form a Poisson process,
  which makes tandem queues (Jackson networks) tractable.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.40 — GAME THEORY: STRATEGIC GAMES, NASH EQUILIBRIUM, ZERO-SUM GAMES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A STRATEGIC (NORMAL-FORM) GAME has PLAYERS i = 1, ..., n, STRATEGY SETS
    Sᵢ and PAYOFF functions uᵢ(s₁, ..., sₙ). Two-player finite games are
    written as a BIMATRIX: row player's strategies are rows, column player's
    are columns, and each cell shows (u₁, u₂). Players choose simultaneously,
    know the game, and are rational (maximise expected payoff).
  - DOMINANCE: sᵢ STRICTLY DOMINATES tᵢ if uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ) > uᵢ(tᵢ, s₋ᵢ) for
    every profile s₋ᵢ of the others; WEAKLY if ≥ always and > sometimes. A
    DOMINANT strategy dominates all others. ITERATED ELIMINATION OF STRICTLY
    DOMINATED STRATEGIES (IESDS) never removes a Nash equilibrium and its
    result does not depend on the order; weak elimination can remove
    equilibria and is order-dependent. A strategy may also be dominated by
    a MIXED strategy.
  - BEST RESPONSE: BRᵢ(s₋ᵢ) = argmax uᵢ(·, s₋ᵢ). A NASH EQUILIBRIUM (NE) is
    a profile s* with sᵢ* ∈ BRᵢ(s*₋ᵢ) for every i: no player gains by a
    UNILATERAL deviation. In a bimatrix, mark each column's best u₁ and each
    row's best u₂; cells with both marks are the PURE NE.
  - CLASSIC GAMES: PRISONER'S DILEMMA (dominant strategies lead to a NE that
    is not PARETO optimal), BATTLE OF THE SEXES and STAG HUNT (coordination,
    several NE), CHICKEN / HAWK-DOVE (anti-coordination), MATCHING PENNIES
    (no pure NE). A NE need not be efficient, unique or exist in pure
    strategies.
  - MIXED STRATEGY: a probability distribution σᵢ on Sᵢ; payoffs are
    expected values (for bimatrices pᵀAq and pᵀBq). MIXED NE: each σᵢ is a
    best response to σ₋ᵢ. SUPPORT (INDIFFERENCE) PRINCIPLE: in a mixed NE
    every pure strategy used with positive probability gives the SAME
    expected payoff, and unused ones give no more. Each player's mix is
    chosen to make the OPPONENT indifferent.
  - 2 × 2 RECIPE: if the row player uses T with probability p, the column
    player is indifferent when p·b₁₁ + (1 − p)b₂₁ = p·b₁₂ + (1 − p)b₂₂;
    similarly q from the row player's payoffs. SUPPORT ENUMERATION handles
    larger games: guess supports, solve the indifference equations, check
    probabilities ≥ 0 and no profitable pure deviation.
  - NASH'S THEOREM: every finite game has at least one NE in mixed
    strategies (proof: Brouwer's or Kakutani's fixed point theorem applied
    to the best-response map). Generically the number of NE is ODD.
  - CONTINUOUS GAMES: find best-response functions from first-order
    conditions and intersect them. COURNOT duopoly with price P = a − Q and
    unit cost c: qᵢ = (a − c)/3 (n firms: (a − c)/(n + 1)); BERTRAND price
    competition with equal costs: p = c (zero profit).
  - ZERO-SUM game: u₂ = −u₁, described by the payoff matrix A to the row
    player (maximiser); the column player minimises. LOWER VALUE
    v⁻ = maxᵢ minⱼ aᵢⱼ (MAXIMIN), UPPER VALUE v⁺ = minⱼ maxᵢ aᵢⱼ (MINIMAX),
    always v⁻ ≤ v⁺. A SADDLE POINT (entry smallest in its row and largest in
    its column) exists iff v⁻ = v⁺, and then the game has a VALUE in pure
    strategies.
  - VON NEUMANN'S MINIMAX THEOREM: with mixed strategies
    maxₚ min_q pᵀAq = min_q maxₚ pᵀAq = v, the VALUE of the game. Optimal
    strategies are the NE of the zero-sum game; all NE give the value v and
    are INTERCHANGEABLE. A game with A = −Aᵀ (SYMMETRIC/skew) has v = 0.
  - SOLVING: first look for a saddle point; remove DOMINATED rows (smaller
    everywhere) and columns (larger everywhere). 2 × 2 without a saddle
    [[a, b], [c, d]]: p = (d − c)/(a − b − c + d),
    q = (d − b)/(a − b − c + d), v = (ad − bc)/(a − b − c + d). 2 × n or
    m × 2: GRAPHICAL method (lower envelope of lines, highest point).
    Adding a constant k to all entries adds k to v; multiplying by λ > 0
    multiplies v by λ.
  - LP FORMULATION: after adding a constant to make v > 0, the row player
    solves min ∑xᵢ s.t. Aᵀx ≥ 1, x ≥ 0; then v = 1/∑xᵢ, p = v·x. The column
    player's problem max ∑yⱼ, Ay ≤ 1, y ≥ 0 is its LP DUAL; the minimax
    theorem is LP strong duality.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Two suspects may Cooperate (stay silent) or Defect (confess). Payoffs
    (years in prison as negative numbers):
                  C          D
       C      (−1, −1)   (−3, 0)
       D      (0, −3)    (−2, −2)
    Define a strategic game and dominance, find each player's dominant
    strategy and the Nash equilibrium, and explain why the outcome is not
    Pareto optimal. What changes if the game is repeated a known finite
    number of times?
    Answer: D is strictly dominant for both; the unique NE is (D, D) with
    (−2, −2), which is Pareto dominated by (C, C) with (−1, −1). Finite
    repetition still gives (D, D) every round (backward induction).
    Teacher explains: A strategic game lists players, strategy sets and
    payoffs; players choose at the same time. Compare the row player's
    payoffs column by column:
       against C: D gives 0 > −1;   against D: D gives −2 > −3
    So D is better whatever the other does: STRICTLY DOMINANT. By symmetry
    the same holds for the column player. Rational players therefore play
    (D, D). It is a Nash equilibrium: from (D, D) a unilateral switch to C
    gives −3 < −2. Yet both prefer (C, C): the equilibrium is not PARETO
    OPTIMAL. Individual rationality and collective rationality clash — the
    model of arms races, price wars, over-fishing. Why cooperation cannot be
    enforced by promises: at (C, C) each player gains by deviating (0 > −1).
    With a known last round, D is dominant in the last round; then in the
    second-last round the future is fixed, so D again, and so on backwards.
    (With an infinite horizon and patient players, strategies like
    TIT-FOR-TAT or GRIM TRIGGER can sustain cooperation.) Common mistakes:
    thinking a NE must be the 'best' outcome; checking only one column for
    dominance. Now you try: change (C, C) to (3, 3) and (D, D) to (1, 1),
    with (C, D) = (0, 4), (D, C) = (4, 0). Dominant strategies? (D still
    strictly dominant for both: 4 > 3 and 1 > 0; NE (D, D))

D2. Apply iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies to
                  L        C        R
       T       (4, 3)   (5, 1)   (6, 2)
       M       (2, 1)   (8, 4)   (3, 6)
       B       (3, 0)   (9, 6)   (2, 8)
    Justify the procedure, and explain why weak dominance needs care. Show
    also that a strategy can be dominated by a mixed strategy only.
    Answer: C is dominated by R; then M and B by T; then R by L. The game
    solves to (T, L) with payoffs (4, 3).
    Teacher explains: At the start NO row is dominated (M and B beat T in
    column C). But the column player's C gives (1, 4, 6), less than R's
    (2, 6, 8) in every row: remove C.
       remaining  T: (4, 3), (6, 2)   M: (2, 1), (3, 6)   B: (3, 0), (2, 8)
    Now T's payoffs (4, 6) beat M's (2, 3) and B's (3, 2): remove M and B.
    Finally the column player, facing only T, compares L = 3 with R = 2:
    remove R. Result (T, L). Justification: a rational player never uses a
    strictly dominated strategy, and if everyone KNOWS the others are
    rational (common knowledge of rationality) the reduced game is the real
    one. Strict IESDS never deletes a NE and the order is irrelevant.
    WEAK dominance: in the game [[(1, 1), (0, 0)], [(0, 0), (0, 0)]], B is
    weakly dominated by T, yet (B, R) is still a NE; eliminating weakly
    dominated strategies can delete equilibria and its result can depend on
    the order. MIXED DOMINANCE: in the zero-sum-style payoffs to the row
    player T = (3, 0), M = (0, 3), B = (1, 1), no pure strategy dominates B,
    but ½T + ½M gives (1.5, 1.5) > (1, 1), so B is strictly dominated by a
    mixture. Common mistakes: comparing the row player's payoffs across a
    ROW instead of down a column; deleting a strategy that is only better
    'on average'. Now you try: in
    [[(1, 0), (1, 2), (0, 1)], [(0, 3), (0, 1), (2, 0)]] run IESDS.
    (R dominated by C for the column player; then B by T; then L by C:
    outcome (T, C))

D3. Define Nash equilibrium and best response. Find all pure-strategy NE of
    (a) Battle of the Sexes [[(2, 1), (0, 0)], [(0, 0), (1, 2)]];
    (b) Stag Hunt [[(4, 4), (0, 3)], [(3, 0), (3, 3)]];
    (c) Chicken [[(0, 0), (−1, 1)], [(1, −1), (−10, −10)]] (rows/columns:
    Swerve, Straight); (d) Matching Pennies [[(1, −1), (−1, 1)],
    [(−1, 1), (1, −1)]].
    Answer: (a) (T, L), (B, R). (b) (Stag, Stag), (Hare, Hare). (c) (Swerve,
    Straight), (Straight, Swerve). (d) none.
    Teacher explains: s* is a NE if every player's strategy is a best
    response to the others': uᵢ(sᵢ*, s₋ᵢ*) ≥ uᵢ(sᵢ, s₋ᵢ*) for all sᵢ. Method:
    underline the row player's best payoff in each COLUMN and the column
    player's best payoff in each ROW; a cell with both underlined is a NE.
       (a) col L: best u₁ = 2 (T); col R: 1 (B). row T: best u₂ = 1 (L);
           row B: 2 (R). Double marks: (T, L), (B, R).
       (b) both (Stag, Stag) = (4, 4) and (Hare, Hare) = (3, 3): each is a
           best response to itself. (Stag, Stag) is Pareto better, but
           (Hare, Hare) is SAFER: Hare guarantees 3.
       (c) against Swerve, Straight is best (1 > 0); against Straight,
           Swerve is best (−1 > −10): NE at the two asymmetric cells.
       (d) in every cell one player wants to switch: no pure NE.
    Interpretation: a NE is a 'self-enforcing agreement' — nobody wants to
    break it alone. It is a STEADY STATE, not a prediction of how play
    starts; games with several NE need a selection argument (focal points,
    Pareto dominance, risk dominance). Common mistakes: underlining the
    column player's payoffs down columns; forgetting that both inequalities
    must hold. Now you try: [[(1, 1), (2, 0)], [(0, 2), (3, 3)]]. (Pure NE
    (T, L) and (B, R))

D4. Two firms choose quantities q₁, q₂ ≥ 0; price P = 100 − (q₁ + q₂); each
    has unit cost 10. Find the best-response functions, the Cournot-Nash
    equilibrium, price and profits, and compare with the monopoly
    (collusive) outcome and with Bertrand price competition.
    Answer: BRᵢ(qⱼ) = (90 − qⱼ)/2; q₁ = q₂ = 30, P = 40, profits 900 each
    (1800 total). Monopoly: Q = 45, P = 55, profit 2025 (1012.5 each if
    shared). Bertrand: P = 10, profits 0.
    Teacher explains: Firm 1's profit π₁ = (100 − q₁ − q₂ − 10)q₁ =
    (90 − q₂)q₁ − q₁², concave in q₁. First-order condition:
       ∂π₁/∂q₁ = 90 − q₂ − 2q₁ = 0  ⇒  BR₁(q₂) = (90 − q₂)/2
    (and 0 if q₂ ≥ 90). By symmetry BR₂(q₁) = (90 − q₁)/2. A NE is an
    intersection of the best-response curves:
       q₁ = (90 − q₂)/2, q₂ = (90 − q₁)/2  ⇒  q₁ = q₂ = 30
    Q = 60, P = 40, πᵢ = (40 − 10)·30 = 900. General formula
    qᵢ = (a − c)/3; with n firms qᵢ = (a − c)/(n + 1), so the price
    (a + nc)/(n + 1) → c as n → ∞: competition drives price to cost. A
    monopolist maximises (90 − Q)Q: Q = 45, P = 55, profit 2025 > 1800.
    Splitting it (22.5 each, profit 1012.5) is better for both, but it is
    NOT an equilibrium: BR₁(22.5) = 33.75, so each firm cheats — a
    Prisoner's Dilemma. BERTRAND: if firms set prices and the cheaper takes
    the whole market, any price above 10 can be undercut slightly, so the
    unique NE is p₁ = p₂ = 10 with zero profit (the Bertrand paradox). Common
    mistakes: differentiating with respect to Q instead of qᵢ; imposing
    symmetry before differentiating (that gives the monopoly answer). Now
    you try: a = 100, c = 10, three firms. (qᵢ = 22.5, P = 32.5, πᵢ = 506.25)

D5. Explain mixed strategies and the indifference principle, and find the
    mixed NE of Battle of the Sexes [[(2, 1), (0, 0)], [(0, 0), (1, 2)]]
    with the expected payoffs. Draw the best-response correspondences and
    show that the game has exactly three NE.
    Answer: row plays T with p = 2/3, column plays L with q = 1/3; each
    expects 2/3. Together with (T, L) and (B, R): three NE.
    Teacher explains: A mixed strategy is a probability vector over pure
    strategies; payoffs become expected values. If the row player mixes
    T and B with positive probabilities in a best response, both must give
    the SAME expected payoff (otherwise shift weight to the better one).
    So each player's mix is chosen to make the OTHER indifferent. Column
    player's payoffs when row plays T with probability p:
       L: 1·p + 0·(1 − p) = p        R: 0·p + 2(1 − p) = 2 − 2p
       indifferent: p = 2 − 2p  ⇒  p = 2/3
    Row player's payoffs when column plays L with probability q:
       T: 2q        B: 1 − q        indifferent: 2q = 1 − q  ⇒  q = 1/3
    Expected payoffs: row 2q = 2/3, column p = 2/3 — worse for both than
    either pure NE, because they miscoordinate with probability
    (2/3)(2/3) + (1/3)(1/3) = 5/9. Best responses: BR₁(q) = B for q < 1/3,
    anything for q = 1/3, T for q > 1/3; BR₂(p) = R for p < 2/3, anything
    at 2/3, L for p > 2/3. In the unit square the two 'Z'-shaped graphs
    cross at (p, q) = (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2/3, 1/3): three NE. Common
    mistakes: solving for p using the ROW player's own payoffs; reporting
    'q = 1/3' as the probability of R. Now you try: Stag Hunt
    [[(4, 4), (0, 3)], [(3, 0), (3, 3)]]: mixed NE. (Stag with probability
    3/4 each: 4p = 3; payoff 3)

D6. State Nash's existence theorem and sketch its proof. Prove the support
    characterisation: σ is a NE iff for each player every pure strategy in
    the support of σᵢ is a best response to σ₋ᵢ. Use it to verify that
    ½H + ½T for both players is the unique NE of Matching Pennies.
    Answer: Every finite game has a mixed NE (Brouwer/Kakutani). Proof and
    verification below.
    Teacher explains: Support lemma. uᵢ(σᵢ, σ₋ᵢ) = ∑ₛ σᵢ(s)uᵢ(s, σ₋ᵢ) is an
    AVERAGE of the pure payoffs uᵢ(s, σ₋ᵢ) with weights σᵢ(s). An average is
    at most the maximum, with equality iff all weight sits on maximisers.
    So σᵢ is a best response ⇔ every s with σᵢ(s) > 0 attains
    maxₛ uᵢ(s, σ₋ᵢ). ∎ Consequently the players are indifferent among the
    pure strategies they use, and it suffices to check pure deviations.
    Nash's theorem: the set Σ of mixed profiles is a product of simplices
    (compact and convex). NASH'S MAP: for each player and pure s let
    gₛ(σ) = max(0, uᵢ(s, σ₋ᵢ) − uᵢ(σ)) (the gain from switching to s) and
       σᵢ′(s) = (σᵢ(s) + gₛ(σ)) / (1 + ∑ₜ gₜ(σ)).
    This map Σ → Σ is continuous, so by BROUWER it has a fixed point. At a
    fixed point, some s in the support has uᵢ(s, σ₋ᵢ) ≤ uᵢ(σ) (not all pure
    payoffs can exceed their average), so gₛ = 0, and the fixed-point
    equation then forces ∑ₜ gₜ = 0: no strategy improves, so σ is a NE. ∎
    Matching pennies: no pure NE (D3). If the row player plays H with
    probability p > ½, the column player earns 1 − 2p < 0 from H and
    2p − 1 > 0 from T, so his unique best response is T; the row player's
    best response to T is T (p = 0), contradicting p > ½. The case p < ½ is
    symmetric. So p = ½ and similarly q = ½; then every pure
    strategy earns 0 against the opponent's mix, so both are best responses:
    NE, value 0. Common mistakes: believing a NE must be in pure strategies;
    forgetting to check strategies OUTSIDE the support (they must not do
    better). Now you try: with u = (2, −2) at (H, H) instead of (1, −1),
    find the row player's equilibrium mix. (Column indifferent:
    −2p + (1 − p) = p − (1 − p) ⇒ p = 2/5; the row player plays H with
    probability 2/5)

D7. Find all Nash equilibria of the 2 × 3 game
                  L        C        R
       T       (3, 2)   (0, 1)   (2, 0)
       B       (1, 0)   (4, 3)   (1, 4)
    Answer: three NE: (T, L); (¾T + ¼B, ⅔L + ⅓C) with payoffs (2, 3/2);
    (½T + ½B, ⅕C + ⅘R) with payoffs (8/5, 2).
    Teacher explains: Let p = P(T). The column player's expected payoffs
    are lines in p:
       L: 2p        C: p + 3(1 − p) = 3 − 2p        R: 4(1 − p) = 4 − 4p
    Their upper envelope: R is best for p < 1/2 (4 − 4p > 3 − 2p), C for
    1/2 < p < 3/4, L for p > 3/4; ties at p = 1/2 (C = R = 2) and p = 3/4
    (L = C = 3/2). So a NE needs p ∈ {0, 1/2, 3/4, 1} or pure play:
       p = 1 (T): column's best response L; row's best response to L is T
                  (3 > 1). NE (T, L), payoffs (3, 2).
       p = 0 (B): column plays R; but against R the row player prefers T
                  (2 > 1). Not a NE.
       p = 3/4:   column mixes L and C with q = P(L). Row indifferent:
                  T: 3q, B: q + 4(1 − q)  ⇒ 3q = 4 − 3q, q = 2/3.
                  Payoffs: row 3q = 2, column 3/2.
       p = 1/2:   column mixes C and R with c = P(C). Row indifferent:
                  T: 2(1 − c), B: 4c + (1 − c)  ⇒ 2 − 2c = 1 + 3c, c = 1/5.
                  Payoffs: row 8/5, column 2.
    Check the unused strategy in each mixed NE: at p = 3/4, R gives 1 <
    3/2 ✓; at p = 1/2, L gives 1 < 2 ✓. Three equilibria — an odd number, as
    Wilson's theorem predicts for generic games. This is SUPPORT
    ENUMERATION organised by a picture. Common mistakes: trying to make all
    three column strategies indifferent (impossible with one parameter p);
    skipping the check that the omitted strategy does not do better. Now you
    try: [[(2, 0), (3, 2), (0, 3)], [(1, 3), (0, 1), (2, 1)]]. (Unique NE:
    p = 2/5, column plays ⅔L + ⅓R; payoffs (4/3, 9/5))

D8. Hawk-Dove: two animals contest a resource worth V = 4; fighting costs
    C = 6. Payoffs: (H, H) = ((V − C)/2, (V − C)/2) = (−1, −1), (H, D) =
    (4, 0), (D, H) = (0, 4), (D, D) = (2, 2). Find all NE, the symmetric
    mixed NE in general (V < C), and the expected payoff. Explain why the
    mixed strategy is evolutionarily stable. Also find the mixed NE of
    Chicken from D3.
    Answer: pure NE (H, D), (D, H); symmetric mixed NE: H with probability
    V/C = 2/3, expected payoff 2/3. Chicken: Swerve with probability 9/10,
    expected payoff −1/10.
    Teacher explains: Best responses: against H, D (0 > −1); against D, H
    (4 > 2): pure NE at the asymmetric cells. Mixed: opponent plays H with
    probability p; indifference
       H: p(V − C)/2 + (1 − p)V      D: (1 − p)V/2
       p(V − C)/2 + (1 − p)V/2 = 0  ⇒  p = V/C = 4/6 = 2/3.
    Payoff: D earns (1 − p)V/2 = (1/3)(2) = 2/3 (and so does H). In a
    population where the fraction of hawks is p, hawks do better when
    p < 2/3 and doves do better when p > 2/3, so the population is pushed to
    2/3: an EVOLUTIONARILY STABLE STRATEGY (ESS): σ is ESS if, for every
    mutant μ ≠ σ, u(σ, σ) > u(μ, σ), or u(σ, σ) = u(μ, σ) and
    u(σ, μ) > u(μ, μ). With x, y the hawk probabilities of the player and
    the opponent, u(x, y) = 2 + 2x − 2y − 3xy; for a mutant playing H with
    probability m, u(m, σ) = u(σ, σ) = 2/3 (indifference), and
       u(σ, m) − u(m, m) = 4/3 − 4m + 3m² = 3(m − 2/3)² > 0  (m ≠ 2/3),
    so the mix is an ESS. Chicken: column swerves with probability q; row
    indifferent: Swerve: 0·q + (−1)(1 − q); Straight: q − 10(1 − q):
    −1 + q = 11q − 10 ⇒ q = 9/10; payoff −1 + 9/10 = −1/10. Common mistakes:
    taking p = C/V; forgetting the factor ½ in (V − C)/2. Now you try: V = 2,
    C = 8: mixed NE. (H with probability 1/4)

D9. For the zero-sum game with payoff matrix (to the row player)
       A = [[−3, −2, 6], [2, 0, 2], [5, −2, −4]]
    find the maximin and minimax values, a saddle point, and the value.
    Prove that maxᵢ minⱼ aᵢⱼ ≤ minⱼ maxᵢ aᵢⱼ for every matrix, and that a
    saddle point gives optimal pure strategies.
    Answer: maximin 0 (row 2), minimax 0 (column 2); saddle point
    (row 2, column 2); value 0.
    Teacher explains: The row player (maximiser) considers the worst case of
    each row:
       row minima: −3, 0, −4   → maximin v⁻ = 0 (row 2)
    The column player (minimiser) considers the worst case of each column:
       column maxima: 5, 0, 6  → minimax v⁺ = 0 (column 2)
    v⁻ = v⁺ = 0 and a₂₂ = 0 is the minimum of its row and the maximum of its
    column: a SADDLE POINT. Row 2 guarantees at least 0; column 2 holds the
    row player to at most 0; neither can do better, so the value is 0 and
    (row 2, column 2) is a NE. Proof of v⁻ ≤ v⁺: for any i, k,
       minⱼ aᵢⱼ ≤ aᵢₖ ≤ maxₗ aₗₖ.
    The left side does not depend on k, the right side not on i: take max
    over i on the left and min over k on the right. ∎ Saddle point (i*, j*):
    a_{i*j} ≥ a_{i*j*} ≥ a_{ij*} for all i, j, so row i* guarantees a_{i*j*}
    and column j* concedes at most a_{i*j*}: v⁻ ≥ a_{i*j*} ≥ v⁺, hence
    equality. Several saddle points always have the same value (and are
    interchangeable). If v⁻ < v⁺ there is no pure solution: whoever
    'announces' first loses, so players must MIX. Common mistakes: taking
    column MINIMA for the minimiser; confusing whose payoff the matrix
    shows. Now you try: A = [[4, 2, 3], [5, 3, 6], [1, 0, 2]].
    (Row minima 2, 3, 0; column maxima 5, 3, 6; saddle (2, 2), value 3)

D10. Solve the zero-sum game A = [[3, −1], [−2, 4]] in mixed strategies,
     derive the general 2 × 2 formulas, and explain why they fail for
     A = [[2, 1], [3, 4]].
     Answer: p = (3/5, 2/5), q = (1/2, 1/2), v = 1. The second matrix has a
     saddle point (row 2, column 1), value 3; the formula would give
     nonsense.
     Teacher explains: No saddle: row minima −1, −2 (v⁻ = −1), column maxima
     3, 4 (v⁺ = 3). Let the row player use row 1 with probability p. Against
     each column his expected payoff is
        column 1: 3p − 2(1 − p) = 5p − 2
        column 2: −p + 4(1 − p) = 4 − 5p
     He wants to maximise the smaller of the two; at the optimum they are
     equal: 5p − 2 = 4 − 5p, p = 3/5, guaranteeing 5·3/5 − 2 = 1. The column
     player with column 1 probability q:
        row 1: 3q − (1 − q) = 4q − 1      row 2: −2q + 4(1 − q) = 4 − 6q
        4q − 1 = 4 − 6q  ⇒  q = 1/2, holding the row player to 1.
     Both guarantee 1: the value is v = 1. General [[a, b], [c, d]] without
     saddle point: equating gives
        p = (d − c)/(a − b − c + d),  q = (d − b)/(a − b − c + d),
        v = (ad − bc)/(a − b − c + d);
     here (4 + 2)/10, (4 + 1)/10, (12 − 2)/10 ✓. For [[2, 1], [3, 4]]: row
     minima 1, 3, column maxima 3, 4: saddle at a₂₁ = 3. The formula gives
     p = (4 − 3)/(2 − 1 − 3 + 4) = 1/2 — wrong: row 2 dominates row 1, so
     p = 0. ALWAYS check for a saddle point first. Common mistakes: mixing
     up p (row) and q (column) formulas; forgetting to verify that 0 < p < 1.
     Now you try: A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]. (p = 1/4, q = 1/2, v = 5/2)

D11. Solve the 2 × 4 zero-sum game A = [[2, 3, 1, 5], [4, 1, 6, 0]] by the
     graphical method.
     Answer: v = 17/7; row player (5/7, 2/7); column player uses columns 2
     and 3 with probabilities 5/7 and 2/7 (columns 1 and 4 unused).
     Teacher explains: No saddle: row minima 1, 0 (v⁻ = 1), column maxima 4,
     3, 6, 5 (v⁺ = 3). If the row player uses row 1 with probability p, each
     column gives a straight line in p:
        col 1: 2p + 4(1 − p) = 4 − 2p      col 2: 3p + (1 − p) = 1 + 2p
        col 3: p + 6(1 − p) = 6 − 5p       col 4: 5p
     The column player will pick the lowest line, so the row player
     maximises the LOWER ENVELOPE. Sketch the four lines on 0 ≤ p ≤ 1. The
     envelope is col 4 on [0, 1/3] (5p = 1 + 2p at p = 1/3), col 2 on
     [1/3, 5/7] and col 3 on [5/7, 1]; it rises and then falls, so its peak
     is where col 2 and col 3 cross: 1 + 2p = 6 − 5p, p = 5/7, height
     1 + 10/7 = 17/7. Check the other lines there: col 1: 4 − 10/7 = 18/7 >
     17/7, col 4: 25/7 > 17/7 ✓. So v = 17/7 and the row player plays
     (5/7, 2/7). The column player uses only the two lines through the
     peak, columns 2 and 3; solve the 2 × 2 game [[3, 1], [1, 6]]:
        q = (6 − 1)/(3 − 1 − 1 + 6) = 5/7 for column 2,
        v = (18 − 1)/7 = 17/7 ✓.
     For an m × 2 game draw the column player's lines instead and take the
     LOWEST point of the UPPER envelope. Common mistakes: maximising the
     upper envelope; using columns that do not pass through the optimal
     point. Now you try: A = [[1, 3, −1], [2, −2, 4]]. (p = 3/5, v = 1,
     column player ½ on columns 2 and 3)

D12. State von Neumann's minimax theorem and show how it follows from LP
     duality. Then solve A = [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 1, 1], [0, 1, −1]] and reduce
     A′ = [[3, 2, 4], [1, 4, 2], [2, 1, 3]] by dominance.
     Answer: maxₚ min_q pᵀAq = min_q maxₚ pᵀAq. For A: v = 3/11,
     p = q = (4/11, 5/11, 2/11). A′ reduces to [[3, 2], [1, 4]]: v = 5/2,
     p = (3/4, 1/4, 0), q = (1/2, 1/2, 0).
     Teacher explains: The row player's guarantee with p is minⱼ (pᵀA)ⱼ (a
     pure column is always among the column player's best replies). So he
     solves: max v s.t. (pᵀA)ⱼ ≥ v for all j, ∑pᵢ = 1, p ≥ 0. Add a constant
     so that all entries are positive (then v > 0) and put xᵢ = pᵢ/v:
        (P) min ∑xᵢ s.t. Aᵀx ≥ 1, x ≥ 0          (v = 1/∑xᵢ)
     The column player similarly, with yⱼ = qⱼ/v:
        (D) max ∑yⱼ s.t. Ay ≤ 1, y ≥ 0
     (P) and (D) are dual LPs, both feasible, so by strong duality their
     optima are equal: the row player's best guarantee equals the column
     player's best concession. That is the MINIMAX THEOREM. ∎ For A (no
     saddle: v⁻ = −1 < v⁺ = 1), try all rows and columns in use: the
     equations (pᵀA)ⱼ = v, ∑p = 1:
        2p₁ − p₂ = v,  −p₁ + p₂ + p₃ = v,  p₂ − p₃ = v
     From the first and third, p₁ = (p₂ + v)/2 and p₃ = p₂ − v; substituting
     into the second gives p₂ = 5v/3, then p₁ = 4v/3, p₃ = 2v/3 and ∑p = 1
     gives 11v/3 = 1, v = 3/11: p = (4/11, 5/11, 2/11), all positive ✓. A is
     symmetric, so q = p. Check row 1 against q: (8 − 5 + 0)/11 = 3/11 ✓.
     For A′: column 3 (4, 2, 3) ≥ column 1 (3, 1, 2) everywhere, so the
     minimiser drops it; then row 3 (2, 1) ≤ row 1 (3, 2): drop it. The 2 × 2
     [[3, 2], [1, 4]]: p = (4 − 1)/(3 − 2 − 1 + 4) = 3/4, q = (4 − 2)/4 = 1/2,
     v = (12 − 2)/4 = 5/2. Common mistakes: removing columns that are
     SMALLER (those are good for the minimiser); forgetting to subtract the
     constant added for the LP. Now you try: value of RPS
     [[0, −1, 1], [1, 0, −1], [−1, 1, 0]]. (0, with (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) — the
     matrix is skew-symmetric)

M6. Continuous strategic games.
    a) Cournot, P = 100 − Q, c = 10, 2 firms: qᵢ, P, πᵢ
    b) Cournot, P = 120 − Q, c = 0, 2 firms: qᵢ, P, πᵢ
    c) Cournot, P = 100 − Q, c = 10, 3 firms: qᵢ, P, πᵢ
    d) Cournot, P = 100 − Q, c₁ = 10, c₂ = 20: q₁, q₂, P, π₁, π₂
    e) monopoly with P = 100 − Q, c = 10: Q, P, π
    f) Bertrand with equal costs c = 10: equilibrium prices, profits
    g) Cournot with n firms: limit of the price as n → ∞
    h) public goods: 4 players, endowment 10, each unit contributed returns
       0.5 to EVERY player: NE contributions and payoffs; social optimum
    i) Hotelling: two sellers choose locations on [0, 1], buyers uniform
       and go to the nearer: NE
    j) commons: n users choose gᵢ ≥ 0, payoff gᵢ(100 − G) with G = ∑gᵢ:
       symmetric NE gᵢ and total G for n = 2; the optimal total
    k) BR₁(q₂) in a)
    Answers:
      a) 30, 40, 900                     b) 40, 40, 1600
      c) 22.5, 32.5, 506.25
      d) 100/3, 70/3, 130/3 ≈ 43.33, 10000/9 ≈ 1111.1, 4900/9 ≈ 544.4
      e) 45, 55, 2025                    f) p₁ = p₂ = 10, profits 0
      g) → c (the marginal cost)
      h) contribute 0 (dominant), payoff 10 each; optimum: all contribute,
         payoff 20 each
      i) both at 1/2
      j) gᵢ = 100/3, G = 200/3; optimal G = 50
      k) (90 − q₂)/2

M7. True (T) or false (F)?
    a) Every finite game has a pure-strategy NE.
    b) Every finite game has a NE in mixed strategies.
    c) A strictly dominated strategy is never played in a NE.
    d) A weakly dominated strategy is never played in a NE.

    f) If IESDS leaves a single profile, it is the unique NE.

    l) In a non-zero-sum game NE strategies are interchangeable.
    m) maximin ≤ minimax for every matrix.

M12. Expected payoffs, guarantees and LP formulations (A = matrix to the row
     player).

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always write the game as a bimatrix with the row player's
  payoff FIRST, and practise the underline method until pure equilibria can
  be read off in seconds. For mixed equilibria repeat the slogan 'my mix
  makes YOU indifferent' and check the answer by computing both expected
  payoffs. For zero-sum games follow a fixed order: saddle point? →
  dominance → 2 × 2 formula or graph → LP. Drawing the lines of the
  graphical method on squared paper builds intuition for the lower envelope.
  Harder: prove Nash's theorem with Kakutani's fixed point theorem; prove
  the minimax theorem from the separating hyperplane theorem without LP;
  show the Lemke-Howson algorithm finds a NE of a bimatrix game and explain
  why computing one is PPAD-complete; study subgame perfection and backward
  induction in extensive-form games (Stackelberg leader q = 45, follower
  22.5 in D4's market); analyse the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma
  and the folk theorem; and verify that the mixed Hawk-Dove equilibrium is
  an ESS while the mixed Stag Hunt equilibrium is not.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.41 — CLASSICAL MECHANICS / MATHEMATICAL PHYSICS (LAGRANGIAN AND
HAMILTONIAN MECHANICS)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - GENERALISED COORDINATES q₁, ..., qₙ describe a system with n DEGREES OF
    FREEDOM; HOLONOMIC constraints (f(r, t) = 0) remove coordinates, so a
    pendulum needs only θ. The set of all q is CONFIGURATION SPACE; (q, p) is
    PHASE SPACE (dimension 2n; 6N for N free particles in space).
  - KINETIC ENERGY in standard coordinates: Cartesian ½m(ẋ² + ẏ² + ż²);
    polar ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²); cylindrical ½m(ṙ² + r²φ̇² + ż²); spherical
    ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇² + r² sin²θ φ̇²). Rigid rotation adds ½Iω²; rolling without
    slipping links v = Rω.
  - The LAGRANGIAN is L = T − V and the ACTION is S = ∫ L(q, q̇, t) dt.
    HAMILTON'S PRINCIPLE: the true motion makes S STATIONARY (δS = 0) among
    paths with fixed ends. This gives the EULER-LAGRANGE EQUATIONS
    d/dt (∂L/∂q̇ᵢ) − ∂L/∂qᵢ = 0, one for each coordinate. They have the same
    form in EVERY coordinate system; adding dF(q, t)/dt to L changes nothing.
  - GENERALISED MOMENTUM pᵢ = ∂L/∂q̇ᵢ; GENERALISED FORCE ∂L/∂qᵢ. A CYCLIC
    (ignorable) coordinate does not appear in L, and then its momentum is
    CONSERVED. NOETHER'S THEOREM: each continuous symmetry of L gives a
    conserved quantity (translation → linear momentum, rotation → angular
    momentum, time translation → energy).
  - ENERGY FUNCTION h = ∑ q̇ᵢ pᵢ − L satisfies dh/dt = −∂L/∂t, so it is
    conserved when L has no explicit t. h = T + V when T is quadratic in q̇
    and the constraints do not depend on time; otherwise (rotating hoop)
    h ≠ T + V but may still be conserved.
  - CONSTRAINT FORCES by LAGRANGE MULTIPLIERS: keep extra coordinates and use
    L + λ f(q); d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ᵢ − ∂L/∂qᵢ = λ ∂f/∂qᵢ, and λ gives the force of
    constraint (pendulum tension mg cos θ + mlθ̇²). Non-conservative forces
    enter as GENERALISED FORCES Qᵢ on the right. A charged particle has the
    velocity-dependent L = ½mv² − qφ + q v·A.
  - SMALL OSCILLATIONS: at an equilibrium q₀ (∂V/∂q = 0) write
    T ≈ ½ q̇ᵀMq̇, V ≈ ½ qᵀKq. STABLE if K is positive definite. NORMAL MODE
    frequencies solve det(K − ω²M) = 0; mode shapes solve (K − ω²M)a = 0.
    One degree of freedom: ω² = V″(q₀)/m_eff. ω = 0 means a free motion.
  - CENTRAL FORCES: L = ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²) − V(r); θ cyclic so ℓ = mr²θ̇ is
    conserved (Kepler's 2nd law: dA/dt = ℓ/(2m)). EFFECTIVE POTENTIAL
    U(r) = ℓ²/(2mr²) + V(r); circular orbits at U′(r₀) = 0, stable if
    U″(r₀) > 0. For V = −k/r: BINET u″ + u = mk/ℓ² (u = 1/r), orbit
    r = p/(1 + e cos θ), p = ℓ²/(mk), e = √(1 + 2Eℓ²/(mk²)); ellipse (E < 0),
    parabola (E = 0), hyperbola (E > 0); a = −k/(2E), T = 2π√(ma³/k).
    Two bodies reduce to one of REDUCED MASS μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂).
  - HAMILTONIAN by LEGENDRE TRANSFORM: H(q, p, t) = ∑ pᵢq̇ᵢ − L, with q̇
    written in terms of p. HAMILTON'S EQUATIONS q̇ᵢ = ∂H/∂pᵢ, ṗᵢ = −∂H/∂qᵢ
    (2n first-order equations); dH/dt = ∂H/∂t = −∂L/∂t. If T = ½q̇ᵀM(q)q̇
    then H = ½pᵀM⁻¹p + V. Charged particle: H = (p − qA)²/(2m) + qφ.
  - POISSON BRACKET {f, g} = ∑ (∂f/∂qᵢ ∂g/∂pᵢ − ∂f/∂pᵢ ∂g/∂qᵢ). It is
    antisymmetric, bilinear, obeys Leibniz {fg, h} = f{g, h} + {f, h}g and
    the JACOBI identity. df/dt = {f, H} + ∂f/∂t, so f (no explicit t) is
    conserved ⇔ {f, H} = 0. CANONICAL brackets: {qᵢ, pⱼ} = δᵢⱼ,
    {qᵢ, qⱼ} = {pᵢ, pⱼ} = 0. Angular momentum: {Lₓ, L_y} = L_z (cyclic).
    POISSON'S THEOREM: the bracket of two conserved quantities is conserved.
  - CANONICAL TRANSFORMATION (q, p) → (Q, P): keeps Hamilton's equations;
    test (one degree of freedom) {Q, P} = 1 (Jacobian determinant 1).
    GENERATING FUNCTIONS: F₁(q, Q): p = ∂F₁/∂q, P = −∂F₁/∂Q; F₂(q, P):
    p = ∂F₂/∂q, Q = ∂F₂/∂P; new Hamiltonian K = H + ∂F/∂t. F₂ = qP is the
    identity, F₁ = qQ swaps q and p. Oscillator: F₁ = ½mωq² cot Q gives
    H = ωP (ACTION-ANGLE variables).
  - LIOUVILLE'S THEOREM: the Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space AREA
    (volume), because div(q̇, ṗ) = ∂²H/∂q∂p − ∂²H/∂p∂q = 0. Friction shrinks
    areas. ACTION variable J = (1/2π)∮ p dq (area/2π); for the oscillator
    J = E/ω, and ω = dE/dJ. J is an ADIABATIC INVARIANT.
  - HAMILTON-JACOBI EQUATION (overview): ∂S/∂t + H(q, ∂S/∂q, t) = 0. For H
    without t put S = W(q) − Et with H(q, W′) = E; the constants of the
    complete solution give the motion (∂S/∂α = β). Free particle:
    S = αq − α²t/(2m).
  - TRAPS: L = T − V, NOT T + V; θ̇ in T must include every velocity term
    (moving supports, rotating frames); p = ∂L/∂q̇ is not always mv; H must be
    written in p, not q̇, before differentiating; H ≠ E for time-dependent
    constraints; sign in ṗ = −∂H/∂q.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. State Hamilton's principle and derive the Euler-Lagrange equation for a
    Lagrangian L(q, q̇, t). Use it to find the equations of motion of a free
    particle in plane polar coordinates, and explain the term mrθ̇².
    Answer: d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) − ∂L/∂q = 0. Polar: m(r̈ − rθ̇²) = 0 and
    d/dt(mr²θ̇) = 0. mrθ̇² is the centripetal term that appears because the
    coordinates are curvilinear.
    Teacher explains: Hamilton's principle: among all paths q(t) with fixed
    ends q(t₁) = a, q(t₂) = b, the actual motion makes
       S[q] = ∫_{t₁}^{t₂} L(q, q̇, t) dt
    stationary. Vary the path: q → q + εη with η(t₁) = η(t₂) = 0. Then
       dS/dε at ε = 0 = ∫ (∂L/∂q · η + ∂L/∂q̇ · η̇) dt.
    Integrate the second term by parts:
       ∫ ∂L/∂q̇ · η̇ dt = [∂L/∂q̇ · η] − ∫ d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) · η dt
    and the bracket vanishes because η = 0 at both ends. So
       0 = ∫ (∂L/∂q − d/dt ∂L/∂q̇) η dt   for EVERY such η.
    By the FUNDAMENTAL LEMMA of the calculus of variations (if ∫ fη = 0 for
    every smooth η vanishing at the ends and f is continuous then f ≡ 0),
       d/dt (∂L/∂q̇) − ∂L/∂q = 0.
    With several coordinates vary each separately: one equation per qᵢ.
    Polar coordinates: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ gives ẋ² + ẏ² = ṙ² + r²θ̇²,
    so L = ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²) (V = 0).
       r:  ∂L/∂ṙ = mṙ,     ∂L/∂r = mrθ̇²    ⇒  mr̈ − mrθ̇² = 0
       θ:  ∂L/∂θ̇ = mr²θ̇,  ∂L/∂θ = 0       ⇒  d/dt(mr²θ̇) = 0
    The particle actually moves in a straight line, but r̈ ≠ 0 along it: the
    'force' mrθ̇² is simply the price of using a curved coordinate. The
    second equation says the angular momentum is constant. Common mistakes:
    forgetting the r²θ̇² term in T; differentiating ∂L/∂q̇ partially instead
    of totally in t (d/dt(mr²θ̇) = 2mrṙθ̇ + mr²θ̈). Now you try: find the
    equation of motion for L = ½mẋ² − ½kx² − mgx. (mẍ = −kx − mg)

D2. A simple pendulum has mass m on a light rod of length l. Find L, the
    equation of motion and the conserved energy. Find the period of small
    oscillations when l = 0.5 m, g = 9.8 m/s², and estimate the period when
    the amplitude is 0.5 rad.
    Answer: L = ½ml²θ̇² + mgl cos θ; θ̈ = −(g/l) sin θ;
    E = ½ml²θ̇² − mgl cos θ. T₀ = 2π√(l/g) ≈ 1.419 s; at amplitude 0.5 rad,
    T ≈ T₀(1 + θ₀²/16) ≈ 1.441 s (exact value 1.442 s).
    Teacher explains: One coordinate θ measured from the downward vertical.
    Position (l sin θ, −l cos θ), velocity lθ̇, so
       T = ½ml²θ̇²,   V = −mgl cos θ,   L = ½ml²θ̇² + mgl cos θ.
    Euler-Lagrange:
       d/dt(ml²θ̇) − (−mgl sin θ) = 0   ⇒   θ̈ = −(g/l) sin θ.
    L has no explicit t and T is quadratic, so E = T + V is conserved:
       ½ml²θ̇² − mgl cos θ = −mgl cos θ₀ (released from rest at θ₀).
    Small angles: sin θ ≈ θ gives θ̈ = −(g/l)θ, simple harmonic with
       ω = √(g/l) = √(19.6) ≈ 4.427 rad/s,   T₀ = 2π/ω ≈ 1.419 s.
    For finite amplitude the exact period is T = 4√(l/g) K(k) with
    k = sin(θ₀/2) (complete elliptic integral), whose expansion is
       T = T₀(1 + θ₀²/16 + ...)  ⇒  1.419 × 1.015625 ≈ 1.441 s.
    Large swings are slower. Common mistakes: V = +mgl cos θ (the sign
    depends on where θ is measured from); using degrees in sin θ ≈ θ. Now
    you try: the period of a 1 m pendulum on the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s²).
    (2π/√1.62 ≈ 4.937 s)

D3. A bead of mass m slides without friction on a circular hoop of radius R
    that spins about its vertical diameter with constant angular velocity ω.
    Find the equation of motion, all equilibria and their stability, and
    the frequency of small oscillations about each stable equilibrium, for
    R = 0.5 m, g = 9.8 m/s², ω = 7 rad/s and for ω = 3 rad/s.
    Answer: θ̈ = sin θ (ω² cos θ − g/R). Equilibria θ = 0, θ = π and (if
    ω² > g/R) cos θ₀ = g/(ω²R). ω = 7: θ₀ ≈ 66.42°, stable, Ω = ω sin θ₀
    ≈ 6.416 rad/s; θ = 0 unstable. ω = 3: only θ = 0 stable (besides the
    unstable top), Ω = √(g/R − ω²) ≈ 3.256 rad/s.
    Teacher explains: θ from the bottom; the bead is at distance R sin θ
    from the axis, so it has velocity Rθ̇ along the hoop and ωR sin θ round
    the axis:
       T = ½mR²(θ̇² + ω² sin²θ),   V = −mgR cos θ.
    Euler-Lagrange (divide by mR²):
       θ̈ = ω² sin θ cos θ − (g/R) sin θ = sin θ (ω² cos θ − g/R) = f(θ).
    Equilibria: sin θ = 0 (θ = 0 or π) or cos θ₀ = g/(ω²R), which needs
    ω² > g/R = 19.6. Stability: linearise θ = θ* + x, ẍ = f′(θ*)x, with
       f′(θ) = cos θ (ω² cos θ − g/R) − ω² sin²θ.
       θ = 0:   f′ = ω² − g/R          stable iff ω² < g/R
       θ = π:   f′ = ω² + g/R > 0      always unstable
       θ = θ₀:  f′ = −ω² sin²θ₀ < 0    stable whenever it exists
    ω = 7: ω² = 49, cos θ₀ = 19.6/49 = 0.4, θ₀ ≈ 66.42°, sin²θ₀ = 0.84,
    Ω² = 49 × 0.84 = 41.16, Ω ≈ 6.416 rad/s; θ = 0 has f′ = 29.4 > 0,
    unstable. ω = 3: ω² = 9 < 19.6, θ₀ does not exist; θ = 0 has
    Ω² = 19.6 − 9 = 10.6, Ω ≈ 3.256 rad/s. This is a BIFURCATION at
    ω² = g/R: the bottom loses stability and two new equilibria ±θ₀ appear.
    Note that the energy function h = ½mR²θ̇² − ½mR²ω² sin²θ − mgR cos θ is
    conserved but is NOT T + V (the motor does work). Common mistakes:
    leaving out the ω² sin²θ term; calling h the energy. Now you try: at
    what ω does the off-axis equilibrium sit at 60° for R = 0.5 m?
    (cos 60° = 19.6/ω² ⇒ ω² = 39.2, ω ≈ 6.261 rad/s)

D4. A particle of mass m moves in a central potential V(r). Show that its
    motion is planar, that ℓ = mr²θ̇ is conserved (Kepler's second law), and
    reduce the radial motion to one dimension. For V = −k/r with m = 2, k = 8,
    ℓ = 4 find the circular orbit, its energy, and compare the frequency of
    small radial oscillations with the angular velocity.
    Answer: U(r) = ℓ²/(2mr²) + V(r). Circular orbit r₀ = ℓ²/(mk) = 1,
    E = U(r₀) = −4; ω_r = 2 = θ̇, so a slightly perturbed orbit closes (an
    ellipse).
    Teacher explains: The torque r × F is zero for a central force, so
    L = r × p is constant; r stays perpendicular to the fixed vector L, i.e.
    in a plane. Use polar coordinates in that plane:
       L = ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²) − V(r).
    θ is CYCLIC, so p_θ = mr²θ̇ = ℓ is constant. The area swept is
    dA = ½r² dθ, so dA/dt = ½r²θ̇ = ℓ/(2m), constant: Kepler II. The r
    equation is mr̈ = mrθ̇² − V′(r) = ℓ²/(mr³) − V′(r). Energy:
       E = ½mṙ² + ℓ²/(2mr²) + V(r) = ½mṙ² + U(r),
    exactly a 1-D particle in the EFFECTIVE POTENTIAL U; the ℓ² term is the
    centrifugal barrier. Numbers (m = 2, k = 8, ℓ = 4):
       U(r) = 16/(4r²) − 8/r = 4/r² − 8/r
       U′(r) = −8/r³ + 8/r² = 0  ⇒  r₀ = 1     (= ℓ²/(mk) = 16/16)
       U(1) = 4 − 8 = −4 = E
       U″(r) = 24/r⁴ − 16/r³  ⇒  U″(1) = 8,   ω_r = √(U″/m) = √4 = 2
       θ̇ = ℓ/(mr₀²) = 4/2 = 2
    ω_r = θ̇ means r returns to its value once per revolution, so nearly
    circular orbits close: a feature of 1/r (and of r²) potentials
    (BERTRAND'S THEOREM). Common mistakes: substituting θ̇ = ℓ/(mr²) into L
    before varying (that puts the centrifugal potential in with the WRONG
    sign; substitute only in the equation or the energy); dividing by m
    twice. Now you try: for V = ½kr² with m = 1, k = 4, ℓ = 2 find r₀ and
    ω_r. (r₀⁴ = ℓ²/(mk) = 1, r₀ = 1; U″ = 3ℓ²/r⁴ + k = 16, ω_r = 4 = 2θ̇)

D5. Solve the Kepler problem V = −k/r using Binet's equation, and find the
    orbit, e, a, r_min, r_max and the period for m = 1, k = 1, ℓ = 1,
    E = −3/8. Explain how the two-body problem reduces to this.
    Answer: r = p/(1 + e cos θ), p = ℓ²/(mk) = 1, e = 1/2, a = 4/3,
    r_min = 2/3, r_max = 2, T = 2π(4/3)^(3/2) ≈ 9.674.
    Teacher explains: Put u = 1/r and use θ as the variable. Since
    θ̇ = ℓu²/m, ṙ = −(ℓ/m) du/dθ and r̈ = −(ℓ²u²/m²) d²u/dθ². The radial
    equation mr̈ − ℓ²/(mr³) = F(r) becomes BINET'S EQUATION
       d²u/dθ² + u = −m F(1/u)/(ℓ²u²).
    For F = −k/r² = −ku²: u″ + u = mk/ℓ², so
       u = (mk/ℓ²)(1 + e cos θ),   r = p/(1 + e cos θ),   p = ℓ²/(mk),
    a CONIC with focus at the centre. At perihelion (θ = 0) ṙ = 0 so
       E = ℓ²/(2mr²) − k/r at r = p/(1 + e)  ⇒  e² = 1 + 2Eℓ²/(mk²).
    Numbers: e² = 1 + 2(−3/8)(1)/1 = 1/4, e = 1/2 (ellipse since E < 0).
       r_min = p/(1 + e) = 2/3,   r_max = p/(1 − e) = 2,
       a = (r_min + r_max)/2 = 4/3   (check: −k/(2E) = 1/(3/4) = 4/3 ✓)
       T = 2π√(ma³/k) = 2π(4/3)^(3/2) ≈ 9.674   (Kepler III: T² ∝ a³)
    Check with energy at perihelion: v = ℓ/(mr_min) = 3/2,
    ½(9/4) − 3/2 = −3/8 ✓. TWO BODIES: with R the centre of mass and
    r = r₁ − r₂, L = ½MṘ² + ½μṙ² − V(r) where M = m₁ + m₂ and
    μ = m₁m₂/M; R is cyclic (moves uniformly) and r obeys the one-body
    problem with mass μ. Common mistakes: sign of the force in Binet; using
    e² = 1 − 2Eℓ²/(mk²). Now you try: m = k = ℓ = 1 and E = −1/2. (e = 0,
    circle of radius 1)

D6. Prove that the energy function h = ∑ q̇ᵢ ∂L/∂q̇ᵢ − L satisfies
    dh/dt = −∂L/∂t, and that h = T + V when T is a quadratic form in q̇ and
    V = V(q). For the spherical pendulum find all conserved quantities and
    the angular speed of a conical pendulum at θ = 60° (l = 1 m, g = 9.8).
    Answer: proof below; conserved: p_φ = ml² sin²θ φ̇ and E; conical
    pendulum φ̇² = g/(l cos θ) = 19.6, φ̇ ≈ 4.427 rad/s (period ≈ 1.419 s).
    Teacher explains: Differentiate h along a motion:
       dh/dt = ∑ (q̈ᵢ pᵢ + q̇ᵢ ṗᵢ) − ∑ (∂L/∂qᵢ q̇ᵢ + ∂L/∂q̇ᵢ q̈ᵢ) − ∂L/∂t.
    With pᵢ = ∂L/∂q̇ᵢ the q̈ terms cancel, and by Euler-Lagrange
    ṗᵢ = ∂L/∂qᵢ, so the q̇ terms cancel too: dh/dt = −∂L/∂t. If T is
    homogeneous of degree 2 in q̇, EULER'S THEOREM on homogeneous functions
    gives ∑ q̇ᵢ ∂T/∂q̇ᵢ = 2T, so h = 2T − (T − V) = T + V. This is NOETHER'S
    theorem for time translations. Spherical pendulum (angles θ from the
    downward vertical and φ round it):
       L = ½ml²(θ̇² + sin²θ φ̇²) + mgl cos θ.
    φ is cyclic: p_φ = ml² sin²θ φ̇ (the vertical angular momentum) is
    constant — rotation symmetry about the vertical. t is absent: E = T + V
    is constant. θ equation:
       ml²θ̈ = ml² sin θ cos θ φ̇² − mgl sin θ.
    Conical motion θ = const ≠ 0: θ̈ = 0 ⇒ cos θ φ̇² = g/l, so
       φ̇² = 9.8/(1 × 0.5) = 19.6,  φ̇ ≈ 4.427 rad/s,  period 2π/φ̇ ≈ 1.419 s.
    Common mistakes: thinking p_θ is conserved (θ appears in L); forgetting
    that 'no explicit t' refers to L, not to the solution. Now you try: which
    momentum is conserved for L = ½m(ẋ² + ẏ² + ż²) + qBxẏ (charge in a
    uniform field B along z)? (p_y = mẏ + qBx and p_z = mż; also h = T)

D7. Use Lagrange multipliers to find the tension in a pendulum string
    (mass 2 kg, length 1 m, released from the horizontal, g = 9.8) at the
    lowest point, and the acceleration and tension in an Atwood machine.
    Answer: tension = mg cos θ + mlθ̇²; at the bottom 3mg = 58.8 N. Atwood:
    a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂), tension 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
    Teacher explains: To FIND a constraint force, do not eliminate the
    constraint; keep the extra coordinate and add λ × constraint. Pendulum in
    polar coordinates with the constraint f = r − l = 0:
       L = ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²) + mgr cos θ,   equations  EL(q) = λ ∂f/∂q.
       r:  mr̈ − mrθ̇² − mg cos θ = λ
       θ:  d/dt(mr²θ̇) + mgr sin θ = 0
    Put r = l (so r̈ = 0): λ = −(mlθ̇² + mg cos θ). λ is the generalised
    force in the r direction, i.e. the radial force of the string: it pulls
    INWARD with tension mg cos θ + mlθ̇². Released from θ = π/2 at rest,
    energy gives ½ml²θ̇² = mgl cos θ, so at the bottom mlθ̇² = 2mg and
       tension = mg + 2mg = 3mg = 3 × 2 × 9.8 = 58.8 N.
    ATWOOD: masses at depths x₁, x₂ below the pulley with x₁ + x₂ = c:
       L = ½m₁ẋ₁² + ½m₂ẋ₂² + m₁gx₁ + m₂gx₂,   f = x₁ + x₂ − c
       m₁ẍ₁ − m₁g = λ,   m₂ẍ₂ − m₂g = λ,   ẍ₂ = −ẍ₁
    Subtracting: (m₁ + m₂)ẍ₁ = (m₁ − m₂)g; then
    λ = m₁(ẍ₁ − g) = −2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂), the upward string force (tension).
    Common mistakes: forgetting that λ is a force only when f measures a
    length (λ ∂f/∂q has the units of ∂L/∂q); sign of λ. Now you try: m₁ = 3,
    m₂ = 1 kg. (a = g/2 = 4.9 m/s², tension 6g/4 = 14.7 N)

D8. Two equal masses m = 1 on a line are joined to the walls by springs
    k = 4 and to each other by a spring k′ = 2.5. Find the normal modes,
    and the motion when x₁(0) = 1, x₂(0) = 0, both at rest. Explain the
    general method of small oscillations.
    Answer: ω₁ = 2 (in phase, a = (1, 1)), ω₂ = 3 (out of phase,
    a = (1, −1)); x₁ = ½(cos 2t + cos 3t), x₂ = ½(cos 2t − cos 3t).
    Teacher explains: General method. Near a stable equilibrium put
    q = q₀ + x, keep quadratic terms:
       L ≈ ½ ẋᵀMẋ − ½ xᵀKx,    Mẍ + Kx = 0.
    Try x = a cos(ωt − φ): (K − ω²M)a = 0, nonzero a needs
       det(K − ω²M) = 0     (the secular / characteristic equation).
    Each root ω² gives a NORMAL MODE (all coordinates oscillate at one
    frequency); the general motion is a sum of modes. For our chain:
       V = ½k x₁² + ½k′(x₂ − x₁)² + ½k x₂²
       K = [[k + k′, −k′], [−k′, k + k′]] = [[6.5, −2.5], [−2.5, 6.5]],  M = I
       det = (6.5 − ω²)² − 2.5² = 0  ⇒  6.5 − ω² = ±2.5  ⇒  ω² = 4 or 9.
    ω = 2: 2.5a₁ − 2.5a₂ = 0, a = (1, 1): the middle spring is never
    stretched, so ω² = k/m. ω = 3: a = (1, −1), ω² = (k + 2k′)/m. General:
       x = A(1, 1) cos(2t − α) + B(1, −1) cos(3t − β).
    Initial conditions: at rest ⇒ α = β = 0; A + B = 1, A − B = 0 ⇒
    A = B = ½. So x₁ = ½(cos 2t + cos 3t), x₂ = ½(cos 2t − cos 3t). (Using
    cos a + cos b = 2 cos((a+b)/2) cos((a−b)/2) you see energy slosh between
    the masses when the frequencies are close: BEATS.) Common mistakes:
    writing K with +k′ off the diagonal; forgetting that M need not be the
    identity (then solve det(K − ω²M) = 0, not eigenvalues of K). Now you
    try: the same with k′ = 0. (ω = 2 twice: independent oscillators)

D9. Define the Hamiltonian by a Legendre transform and derive Hamilton's
    equations. Find H for a particle in a central potential and for the
    bead on the rotating hoop of D3, and say in each case whether H is the
    energy and whether it is conserved.
    Answer: H = ∑ pq̇ − L, q̇ = ∂H/∂p, ṗ = −∂H/∂q. Central:
    H = p_r²/(2m) + p_θ²/(2mr²) + V(r) = E, conserved. Hoop:
    H = p²/(2mR²) − ½mR²ω² sin²θ − mgR cos θ, conserved but ≠ T + V.
    Teacher explains: Given L(q, q̇, t), define p = ∂L/∂q̇ and solve for
    q̇ = q̇(q, p, t) (possible when the Hessian ∂²L/∂q̇² is non-singular).
    Then H(q, p, t) = p q̇ − L. Take the differential:
       dH = q̇ dp + p dq̇ − ∂L/∂q dq − ∂L/∂q̇ dq̇ − ∂L/∂t dt.
    The dq̇ terms cancel since p = ∂L/∂q̇, and ∂L/∂q = ṗ by Euler-Lagrange:
       dH = q̇ dp − ṗ dq − ∂L/∂t dt.
    Comparing with dH = ∂H/∂p dp + ∂H/∂q dq + ∂H/∂t dt:
       q̇ = ∂H/∂p,   ṗ = −∂H/∂q,   ∂H/∂t = −∂L/∂t,
    and along a motion dH/dt = ∂H/∂t. Central force: p_r = mṙ, p_θ = mr²θ̇,
       H = p_r ṙ + p_θ θ̇ − L = p_r²/(2m) + p_θ²/(2mr²) + V(r).
    Hamilton's equations: ṙ = p_r/m, θ̇ = p_θ/(mr²), ṗ_θ = 0,
    ṗ_r = p_θ²/(mr³) − V′(r). Hoop: p = mR²θ̇ and
       H = p²/(2mR²) − ½mR²ω² sin²θ − mgR cos θ,
    which has no explicit t (conserved) but its middle term has the WRONG
    sign for T + V: the term ½mR²ω² sin²θ in T has degree 0 in θ̇, so
    Euler's theorem does not give h = T + V. Common
    mistakes: writing H = T + V automatically; forgetting to eliminate q̇
    (H must be a function of p). Now you try: L = ½m(ẋ² + ẏ²) + qBxẏ.
    (H = p_x²/(2m) + (p_y − qBx)²/(2m))

D10. Define the Poisson bracket, list its properties, and prove that
     df/dt = {f, H} + ∂f/∂t. Compute {x, p_x}, {x, L_z}, {L_x, L_y}, and show
     that L_z is conserved when V = V(r).
     Answer: {x, p_x} = 1, {x, L_z} = −y, {L_x, L_y} = L_z; {L_z, H} = 0
     for central V.
     Teacher explains: For functions of (q, p, t),
        {f, g} = ∑ᵢ (∂f/∂qᵢ ∂g/∂pᵢ − ∂f/∂pᵢ ∂g/∂qᵢ).
     Properties: {f, g} = −{g, f} (so {f, f} = 0); bilinear; Leibniz
     {fg, h} = f{g, h} + g{f, h}; JACOBI {f, {g, h}} + {g, {h, f}} +
     {h, {f, g}} = 0. Along a motion, by the chain rule and Hamilton,
        df/dt = ∑ (∂f/∂qᵢ q̇ᵢ + ∂f/∂pᵢ ṗᵢ) + ∂f/∂t
              = ∑ (∂f/∂qᵢ ∂H/∂pᵢ − ∂f/∂pᵢ ∂H/∂qᵢ) + ∂f/∂t = {f, H} + ∂f/∂t.
     So f without explicit t is conserved ⇔ {f, H} = 0. Computations
     (L_x = yp_z − zp_y, L_y = zp_x − xp_z, L_z = xp_y − yp_x):
        {x, p_x} = 1·1 − 0 = 1
        {x, L_z} = ∂x/∂x · ∂L_z/∂p_x = 1 · (−y) = −y
        {L_x, L_y}: only z and p_z are shared. Using Leibniz,
          {yp_z − zp_y, zp_x − xp_z} = {yp_z, zp_x} + {zp_y, xp_z}
                                     = yp_x{p_z, z} + xp_y{z, p_z}
                                     = −yp_x + xp_y = L_z.
     Central force: H = |p|²/(2m) + V(r). {L_z, |p|²} = 0 and
     {L_z, r²} = 0 (both are rotation-invariant; check: ∂L_z/∂p_x = −y,
     ∂L_z/∂p_y = x, so {L_z, x² + y²} = −[(−y)(2x) + x(2y)] = 0), so
     {L_z, H} = 0. POISSON'S THEOREM (from Jacobi): if f, g are conserved
     so is {f, g}; e.g. L_x, L_y conserved ⇒ L_z conserved. Common
     mistakes: the sign convention (some books use the opposite order: be
     consistent); forgetting ∂f/∂t. Now you try: {q², p²}. (4qp)

D11. What is a canonical transformation? Show that q = √(2P/(mω)) sin Q,
     p = √(2mωP) cos Q is canonical, find its generating function F₁(q, Q),
     transform the oscillator H = p²/(2m) + ½mω²q², and solve for m = 1,
     ω = 2, q(0) = 1, p(0) = 0.
     Answer: {Q, P} = 1; F₁ = ½mωq² cot Q; K = ωP; P = E/ω = 1,
     Q = 2t + π/2, q(t) = cos 2t, p(t) = −2 sin 2t.
     Teacher explains: A transformation (q, p) → (Q, P) is CANONICAL if for
     every H the equations stay Hamiltonian (with some new K). For one
     degree of freedom this happens iff {Q, P}_{q,p} = 1, i.e. the Jacobian
     ∂(Q, P)/∂(q, p) = 1 (area preserving); equivalently {q, p}_{Q,P} = 1.
     Here compute with (Q, P) as variables:
        ∂q/∂Q ∂p/∂P − ∂q/∂P ∂p/∂Q
          = √(2P/(mω)) cos Q · √(mω/(2P)) cos Q
            − sin Q/√(2mωP) · (−√(2mωP) sin Q) = cos²Q + sin²Q = 1 ✓.
     Generating function: p/q = mω cot Q, so p = ∂F₁/∂q with
     F₁ = ½mωq² cot Q; then −∂F₁/∂Q = ½mωq² csc²Q = P gives back
     q² = (2P/(mω)) sin²Q ✓. New Hamiltonian (F₁ has no t, so K = H):
        K = (2mωP cos²Q)/(2m) + ½mω²(2P/(mω)) sin²Q = ωP.
     Q is cyclic: Ṗ = −∂K/∂Q = 0, Q̇ = ∂K/∂P = ω, so P = E/ω and
     Q = ωt + Q₀. Numbers: E = p²/2 + 2q² = 2 at t = 0, P = 1,
     q = √(2P/(mω)) sin Q = sin(2t + Q₀); q(0) = 1 ⇒ Q₀ = π/2, so
     q = cos 2t, p = √4 cos Q = −2 sin 2t ✓. Common mistakes: checking
     {Q, P} = 1 with Q, P as the independent variables (then it must be
     {q, p}_{Q,P}); forgetting ∂F/∂t when F depends on t. Now you try: is
     Q = q², P = p/(2q) canonical? Give F₂. (Yes, {Q, P} = 2q/(2q) = 1;
     F₂ = q²P)

D12. State and prove Liouville's theorem, sketch the phase portrait of a
     pendulum, and outline the Hamilton-Jacobi method for a free particle
     and the harmonic oscillator. Compute the action variable of the
     oscillator.
     Answer: Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space area/volume. Pendulum:
     centres at (0, 0), saddles at (±π, 0), separatrix E = mgl.
     Free particle S = αq − α²t/(2m) ⇒ q = q₀ + αt/m. Oscillator
     J = E/ω.
     Teacher explains: LIOUVILLE: phase points move with velocity
     v = (q̇, ṗ) = (∂H/∂p, −∂H/∂q). Its divergence is
        ∂q̇/∂q + ∂ṗ/∂p = ∂²H/∂q∂p − ∂²H/∂p∂q = 0.
     A region Ω(t) moving with the flow has d|Ω|/dt = ∫_Ω div v = 0 (the
     Reynolds transport / divergence theorem), so its area (2n-volume) is
     constant. Contrast: damped q̇ = p, ṗ = −q − γp has divergence −γ, so
     areas shrink like e^(−γt). PENDULUM H = p²/(2ml²) − mgl cos θ: level
     curves are closed loops (libration) around the CENTRES (2kπ, 0) for
     E < mgl, open wavy curves (rotation) for E > mgl, separated by the
     SEPARATRIX E = mgl through the SADDLES (±π, 0). HAMILTON-JACOBI: look
     for a generating function S(q, α, t) making the new Hamiltonian zero:
        ∂S/∂t + H(q, ∂S/∂q, t) = 0.
     Then the new momenta α and the new coordinates β = ∂S/∂α are constants.
     Free particle: ∂S/∂t + (∂S/∂q)²/(2m) = 0; try S = αq − Et gives
     E = α²/(2m); β = ∂S/∂α = q − αt/m, so q = β + αt/m. Oscillator:
     S = W(q) − Et with W′ = √(2mE − m²ω²q²); β = ∂S/∂E = ∫ m dq/W′ − t
     = (1/ω) arcsin(q√(mω²/(2E))) − t, so q = √(2E/(mω²)) sin ω(t + β).
     ACTION: the orbit is an ellipse with semi-axes √(2E/(mω²)) and √(2mE),
     area π·2E/ω, so J = (1/2π)∮p dq = E/ω, and dE/dJ = ω is the frequency.
     Common mistakes: thinking Liouville says points do not spread (areas
     are kept, shapes are stretched into filaments); forgetting the minus in
     ṗ = −∂H/∂q when finding the divergence. Now you try: under H = qp the
     unit square [1, 2] × [1, 2] moves to what at time t, and what is its
     area? ([eᵗ, 2eᵗ] × [e^(−t), 2e^(−t)], area 1)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Write the Lagrangian L = T − V (g is gravity, angles from the downward
    vertical unless stated).
    a) mass m on a spring k along x
    b) free particle, plane polar (r, θ)
    c) particle in potential V, cylindrical (r, φ, z)
    d) free particle, spherical (r, θ, φ)
    e) simple pendulum (m, l, θ)
    f) projectile (x, y), y upward
    g) bead on helix x = R cos φ, y = R sin φ, z = cφ, gravity along −z
    h) particle on cone z = r (cylindrical r, φ), gravity along −z
    i) spherical pendulum (m, l, θ, φ)
    j) Atwood machine, x = depth of m₁, rope length c
    k) block on smooth incline, angle α, s = distance down the slope
    l) uniform disc (M, R) rolling without slipping down the incline, s
    m) pendulum whose support moves as x_s = a cos γt (horizontal)
    n) charged particle q in fields φ(r, t), A(r, t)
    o) double pendulum, equal masses m and lengths l
    p) two masses on a line joined by a spring (k, natural length a)
    q) particle in the plane seen from a frame rotating with rate Ω
    r) elastic pendulum: spring k, natural length l₀, polar (r, θ)
    Answers:
      a) ½mẋ² − ½kx²          b) ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²)
      c) ½m(ṙ² + r²φ̇² + ż²) − V(r, φ, z)
      d) ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇² + r² sin²θ φ̇²)
      e) ½ml²θ̇² + mgl cos θ    f) ½m(ẋ² + ẏ²) − mgy
      g) ½m(R² + c²)φ̇² − mgcφ  h) ½m(2ṙ² + r²φ̇²) − mgr
      i) ½ml²(θ̇² + sin²θ φ̇²) + mgl cos θ
      j) ½(m₁ + m₂)ẋ² + m₁gx + m₂g(c − x)  (= ½(m₁ + m₂)ẋ² + (m₁ − m₂)gx
         + const)
      k) ½mṡ² + mgs sin α      l) ¾Mṡ² + Mgs sin α
      m) ½m(l²θ̇² − 2aγl sin γt cos θ θ̇ + a²γ² sin²γt) + mgl cos θ
      n) ½m|ṙ|² − qφ + q ṙ·A
      o) ml²θ̇₁² + ½ml²θ̇₂² + ml²θ̇₁θ̇₂ cos(θ₁ − θ₂) + 2mgl cos θ₁ + mgl cos θ₂
      p) ½m₁ẋ₁² + ½m₂ẋ₂² − ½k(x₂ − x₁ − a)²
      q) ½m[(ẋ − Ωy)² + (ẏ + Ωx)²] − V(x, y)
      r) ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²) + mgr cos θ − ½k(r − l₀)²

M2. Write the Euler-Lagrange equation(s).
    a) L = ½mẋ² − ½kx²                 b) L = ½mẋ² − mgx
    c) L = ½ml²θ̇² + mgl cos θ          d) L = ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²) − V(r)
    e) L = ½ẋ² − ½x⁴                   f) L = ½(ẋ² + ẏ²) − xy
    g) L = e^(γt)(½mq̇² − ½kq²)         h) L = ½q̇² + qq̇ − ½q²
    i) L = ¾Mṡ² + Mgs sin α            j) L = ½(m₁ + m₂)ẋ² + (m₁ − m₂)gx
    k) elastic pendulum M1 r)          l) rotating frame M1 q)
    m) L = −mc²√(1 − ẋ²/c²) − V(x)     n) spherical pendulum M1 i)
    o) L = ½m|ṙ|² − qφ + qṙ·A          p) L = ½(q̇₁² + q̇₂²) − ½(q₁² + q₂²)
                                          − αq₁q₂
    Answers:
      a) mẍ = −kx                b) ẍ = −g
      c) θ̈ = −(g/l) sin θ        d) mr̈ = mrθ̇² − V′(r),  d/dt(mr²θ̇) = 0
      e) ẍ = −2x³                f) ẍ = −y,  ÿ = −x
      g) mq̈ + γmq̇ + kq = 0 (a damped oscillator)
      h) q̈ + q = 0 (qq̇ = d/dt(q²/2) is a total derivative)
      i) s̈ = (2/3)g sin α        j) ẍ = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂)
      k) mr̈ = mrθ̇² + mg cos θ − k(r − l₀),  rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇ + g sin θ = 0
      l) mẍ = 2mΩẏ + mΩ²x − ∂V/∂x,  mÿ = −2mΩẋ + mΩ²y − ∂V/∂y
         (Coriolis and centrifugal terms)
      m) d/dt [mẋ/√(1 − ẋ²/c²)] = −V′(x)
      n) θ̈ = sin θ cos θ φ̇² − (g/l) sin θ,  d/dt(sin²θ φ̇) = 0
      o) mr̈ = q(E + ṙ × B), E = −∇φ − ∂A/∂t, B = ∇ × A
      p) q̈₁ = −q₁ − αq₂,  q̈₂ = −q₂ − αq₁

M3. Find the generalised momenta, the cyclic coordinates and the conserved
    quantities.
    a) L = ½m(ẋ² + ẏ² + ż²) − mgz
    b) L = ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²) − V(r)
    c) spherical pendulum (M1 i)
    d) L = ½m(ẋ² + ẏ² + ż²) + qBxẏ
    e) L = ½m(ṙ² + r²φ̇² + ż²) − V(r)
    f) bead on helix, L = ½m(R² + c²)φ̇² − mgcφ
    g) L = ½(ẋ² + ẏ²) − V(x − y)
    h) L = ½m(ẋ² + ẏ²) − V(x² + y²)
    i) L = e^(γt)(½mq̇² − ½kq²)
    j) energy function h for L = ½mq̇² − V(q)
    k) energy function h for the rotating hoop (D3)
    l) Kepler problem in 3-D, V = −k/r
    m) L = ½m(ṙ² + r²φ̇² + ż²) − V(r, z − cφ)   (screw symmetry)
    n) free particle L = ½mẋ², Galilean boost
    o) two bodies, V(|r₁ − r₂|)
    p) pendulum whose length l(t) is changed by pulling the string
    Answers:
      a) x, y cyclic: p_x = mẋ, p_y = mẏ; also E = T + V
      b) θ cyclic: p_θ = mr²θ̇; E
      c) φ cyclic: p_φ = ml² sin²θ φ̇; E
      d) y, z cyclic: p_y = mẏ + qBx, p_z = mż; h = ½m|v|²
      e) φ, z cyclic: p_φ = mr²φ̇, p_z = mż; E
      f) none cyclic; E = ½m(R² + c²)φ̇² + mgcφ
      g) x + y direction: p_x + p_y = ẋ + ẏ; E
      h) rotation: L_z = m(xẏ − yẋ); E
      i) p = me^(γt)q̇; nothing conserved from t (∂L/∂t ≠ 0)
      j) h = ½mq̇² + V
      k) h = ½mR²θ̇² − ½mR²ω² sin²θ − mgR cos θ (conserved, ≠ T + V)
      l) Lₓ, L_y, L_z, E (and the Runge-Lenz vector, a hidden symmetry)
      m) p_φ + c p_z = mr²φ̇ + cmż; E
      n) mx − pt = mx − mẋt (the centre of mass starts at x(0))
      o) total momentum, total angular momentum, E
      p) E not conserved (∂L/∂t ≠ 0: the pulling force does work); no
         cyclic coordinate

      e) x = 0 stable, ω = 1; x = π unstable
      f) x = 1 stable, V″ = 1, ω = 1
      g) x = 0 stable, ω = √2 ≈ 1.414; x = 2 unstable (V″ = −2e^(−2))
      h) x = 1 stable, V″ = 2, ω = √2

      j) x = 2^(1/6) stable, V″ = 36·2^(2/3), ω = 6·2^(1/3) ≈ 7.560

M8. Write Hamilton's equations, and solve where initial data are given.
    a) H = p²/(2m) + ½kq²              b) H = p²/(2m) + mgq

M10. Is the transformation canonical? (test {Q, P} = 1)
     a) Q = p, P = −q                    b) Q = p, P = q
     c) Q = 2q, P = p/2                  d) Q = 2q, P = p
     e) Q = q + p, P = p                 f) Q = ln(sin p/q), P = q cot p

M12. Phase space, Liouville, action variables, Hamilton-Jacobi.
     a) phase curve and enclosed area of H = p²/(2m) + ½mω²q² at energy E

     c) particle in a box of length a: J(E) and E(J)
     d) pendulum H = p²/(2ml²) − mgl cos θ: separatrix energy and its

     f) H = qp: image of [1, 2] × [1, 2] after time t and its area
     g) free particle m = 1: image of [0, 1] × [0, 1] after time t; area
     h) damped q̇ = p, ṗ = −q − γp, γ = 0.5: area factor after t = 2
     i) dimension of phase space for 5 particles in space
     j) HJ solution S for the free particle

     n) the box has E = cJ² (c constant): frequency ω(J) = dE/dJ
