          ≈ 1.414
       n) ω = dE/dJ = 2cJ

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always follow the same four steps — choose coordinates, write
  the positions, differentiate to get T (square every velocity carefully,
  moving supports included), write V with a clear zero level — and only then
  apply d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ − ∂L/∂q = 0. Check each equation against Newton in a
  simple limit (ω = 0, small angles). For Hamiltonians, insist on writing
  q̇ as a function of p before forming H, and on the minus sign in ṗ. Draw
  phase portraits by plotting level curves of H. Harder: derive the Coriolis
  force from the rotating-frame Lagrangian; show that the Runge-Lenz vector
  A = p × L − mk r/r is conserved and use it to get the Kepler orbit in two
  lines; prove that the Jacobi identity implies Poisson's theorem; prove that
  the transformation generated by F₂ = qP + εG(q, P) is an infinitesimal
  canonical transformation with δf = ε{f, G}, so that G generates a symmetry
  iff {G, H} = 0 (Noether in Hamiltonian form); separate the Hamilton-Jacobi
  equation for the Kepler problem in polar coordinates; and show that the
  action J = (1/2π)∮p dq of a pendulum tends to 0 near the bottom as E/ω.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.42 — CALCULUS OF VARIATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A FUNCTIONAL assigns a number to a function: J[y] = ∫ₐᵇ F(x, y, y′) dx,
    over ADMISSIBLE y (C¹ or C², with fixed ends y(a) = A, y(b) = B unless
    the problem says otherwise). Examples: length ∫√(1 + y′²) dx, time of
    descent, area of a surface of revolution, the action ∫(T − V) dt.
  - FIRST VARIATION: with y + εη (η(a) = η(b) = 0),
    δJ = d/dε J[y + εη] at ε = 0 = ∫ (F_y η + F_{y′} η′) dx. y is an EXTREMAL
    (stationary) when δJ = 0 for every η. A minimiser is always an extremal;
    an extremal need not be a minimiser.
  - FUNDAMENTAL LEMMA: if g is continuous and ∫ₐᵇ gη dx = 0 for every smooth
    η vanishing at a and b, then g ≡ 0. With integration by parts this gives
    the EULER-LAGRANGE EQUATION  F_y − d/dx F_{y′} = 0, i.e.
    F_{y′y′} y″ + F_{y′y} y′ + F_{y′x} − F_y = 0 (second order, two constants).
  - FIRST INTEGRALS: F without y ⇒ F_{y′} = C. F without x ⇒ BELTRAMI
    IDENTITY F − y′F_{y′} = C. F depending on y′ only ⇒ straight lines.
    A total derivative (NULL LAGRANGIAN, e.g. yy′, y′) changes nothing.
  - CLASSIC PROBLEMS: shortest path in the plane — straight line;
    BRACHISTOCHRONE (fastest descent, F = √((1 + y′²)/y), y downward) —
    CYCLOID x = a(θ − sin θ), y = a(1 − cos θ), time θ√(a/g); MINIMAL
    SURFACE OF REVOLUTION (F = y√(1 + y′²)) — CATENARY y = c cosh((x − d)/c)
    (or no smooth solution: Goldschmidt discs); GEODESICS — great circles
    on a sphere, helices on a cylinder, straight lines after unrolling a
    cone; CLAIRAUT r sin ψ = const on surfaces of revolution.
  - SEVERAL FUNCTIONS y₁, ..., yₙ: one Euler-Lagrange equation for each.
    HIGHER DERIVATIVES F(x, y, y′, y″): EULER-POISSON equation
    F_y − (F_{y′})′ + (F_{y″})″ = 0 (fourth order; needs y and y′ at both
    ends). SEVERAL INDEPENDENT VARIABLES: ∬ F(x, y, u, u_x, u_y) gives
    F_u − ∂/∂x F_{u_x} − ∂/∂y F_{u_y} = 0 (DIRICHLET PRINCIPLE: ∬|∇u|² ⇒
    Laplace Δu = 0; area ⇒ MINIMAL SURFACE EQUATION).
  - NATURAL BOUNDARY CONDITIONS: if y(b) is free, add F_{y′} = 0 at x = b
    (with an end cost G(y(b)): F_{y′} + G′ = 0). If the end moves on a curve
    y = φ(x): TRANSVERSALITY [F + (φ′ − y′)F_{y′}] = 0 there; for
    F = n(x, y)√(1 + y′²) this means the extremal meets the curve at a right
    angle.
  - ISOPERIMETRIC PROBLEMS: extremise J = ∫F subject to K = ∫G = ℓ. Unless y
    is an extremal of K, there is a LAGRANGE MULTIPLIER λ with y an
    extremal of ∫(F − λG). Results: DIDO — fixed length encloses the most
    area as a circular arc (closed curve: circle, area L²/(4π)); HANGING
    CHAIN — catenary. Pointwise constraints g(x, y, z) = 0 (geodesics) use a
    multiplier function λ(x).
  - SECOND VARIATION: δ²J = ∫ (F_{yy}η² + 2F_{yy′}ηη′ + F_{y′y′}η′²) dx.
    LEGENDRE'S NECESSARY CONDITION for a minimum: F_{y′y′} ≥ 0 along y.
    JACOBI: with P = ½F_{y′y′}, Q = ½(F_{yy} − (F_{yy′})′), the ACCESSORY
    equation −(Ph′)′ + Qh = 0, h(a) = 0, h′(a) = 1; a zero at c ∈ (a, b] is a
    CONJUGATE POINT. Strengthened Legendre (F_{y′y′} > 0) + no conjugate
    point in (a, b] ⇒ WEAK LOCAL MINIMUM. Example ∫(y′² − y²): y = 0 is a
    minimum iff the length is < π (conjugate point π).
  - CONVEXITY: if F(x, y, y′) is convex in (y, y′) jointly, every extremal is
    a GLOBAL minimiser (the problem is 'nice'). Existence can fail:
    WEIERSTRASS' example ∫₋₁¹ x²y′² dx, y(±1) = ±1 has infimum 0, never
    attained. Broken extremals obey the WEIERSTRASS-ERDMANN CORNER
    conditions: F_{y′} and F − y′F_{y′} are continuous at corners.
  - EIGENVALUE PROBLEMS and the RAYLEIGH QUOTIENT: minimising
    ∫(py′² + qy²)dx subject to ∫ry²dx = 1 gives the Sturm-Liouville equation
    −(py′)′ + qy = λry with λ the minimum. R[y] = ∫y′²/∫y² on [0, 1] with
    y(0) = y(1) = 0 has minimum π² (y = sin πx); any trial function gives an
    UPPER BOUND (x(1 − x) gives 10). RAYLEIGH-RITZ: minimise over
    y = ∑ cₖφₖ to get approximate solutions.
  - HAMILTON'S PRINCIPLE: mechanics is the calculus of variations with
    F = L = T − V and x = t (see 10.41).
  - TRAPS: forgetting the minus sign or the TOTAL derivative d/dx in
    Euler-Lagrange; using Beltrami when F depends on x; assuming an
    extremal is a minimum without checking; ignoring natural boundary
    conditions when an end is free; losing the λ term in isoperimetric
    problems.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Derive the Euler-Lagrange equation for J[y] = ∫ₐᵇ F(x, y, y′) dx with
    fixed ends, including a proof of the fundamental lemma. Then find the
    extremal of J = ∫₀¹ (y′² + 12xy) dx with y(0) = 0, y(1) = 1.
    Answer: F_y − d/dx F_{y′} = 0; extremal y = x³.
    Teacher explains: Let y be an extremal and η any C¹ function with
    η(a) = η(b) = 0, so y + εη is admissible. Put Φ(ε) = J[y + εη]; Φ must
    be stationary at ε = 0:
       Φ′(0) = ∫ₐᵇ (F_y η + F_{y′} η′) dx = 0.
    Integrate the second term by parts (assuming y ∈ C²):
       ∫ F_{y′}η′ dx = [F_{y′}η]ₐᵇ − ∫ (d/dx F_{y′}) η dx,
    and the bracket is 0 since η vanishes at both ends. So
       ∫ₐᵇ g(x) η(x) dx = 0 for all such η,  g = F_y − d/dx F_{y′}.
    FUNDAMENTAL LEMMA: suppose g(c) > 0 at some c ∈ (a, b). By continuity
    g > 0 on some (c − δ, c + δ). Take η = (x − c + δ)²(c + δ − x)² there and
    0 elsewhere (C¹, vanishing at the ends). Then ∫gη > 0, a contradiction.
    Similarly g(c) < 0 is impossible, so g ≡ 0:
       F_y − d/dx F_{y′} = 0.
    Example: F = y′² + 12xy, F_y = 12x, F_{y′} = 2y′, so
       12x − 2y″ = 0  ⇒  y″ = 6x  ⇒  y = x³ + c₁x + c₂.
    y(0) = 0 gives c₂ = 0; y(1) = 1 gives c₁ = 0. So y = x³. Is it a
    minimum? F is convex in (y, y′) (y′² convex, 12xy linear), so yes, a
    global minimum. Common mistakes: writing F_y + d/dx F_{y′}; treating
    d/dx F_{y′} as a partial derivative (it is total: it differentiates the
    y and y′ inside too). Now you try: extremal of ∫₀¹ (y′² + 2y) dx,
    y(0) = 0, y(1) = 1. (y″ = 1, y = (x² + x)/2)

D2. Prove the Beltrami identity (F − y′F_{y′} = C when F does not depend on
    x). Use the appropriate first integral to show that the shortest curve
    between two points of the plane is a straight line, and find the
    extremals of J = ∫ y y′² dx.
    Answer: proof below; straight lines; y^(3/2) = Ax + B.
    Teacher explains: Compute along any C² function:
       d/dx (F − y′F_{y′}) = F_x + F_y y′ + F_{y′} y″ − y″F_{y′} − y′ d/dx F_{y′}
                           = F_x + y′(F_y − d/dx F_{y′}).
    On an extremal the bracket is 0, so d/dx(F − y′F_{y′}) = F_x. If F has
    no explicit x, F − y′F_{y′} is constant: that is BELTRAMI (in mechanics
    it is energy conservation, with x as time). The shortest path:
       J = ∫ √(1 + y′²) dx,   F depends on y′ only.
    Then F_y = 0, so F_{y′} = y′/√(1 + y′²) = C, which forces y′ = constant:
    a straight line y = mx + c through the two points. It really is the
    minimum since F_{y′y′} = (1 + y′²)^(−3/2) > 0 and F is convex. For
    F = y y′² (no x), Beltrami:
       yy′² − y′(2yy′) = −yy′² = C  ⇒  √y y′ = k  ⇒  (2/3) y^(3/2) = kx + d
    so y^(3/2) = Ax + B. Common mistakes: applying Beltrami when F contains
    x; losing solutions such as y = constant when dividing by y′ (check
    them separately). Now you try: extremals of ∫ (y′² + y²) dx using
    Beltrami. (y² − y′² = C; the solutions are y = A cosh x + B sinh x)

D3. Solve the brachistochrone problem: a bead slides from rest at the origin
    to (π, 2) (y measured downward) under gravity g = 9.8 m/s². Show that the
    fastest curve is a cycloid, find it, and compare its time with the
    straight line.
    Answer: x = θ − sin θ, y = 1 − cos θ (a = 1, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π); time
    π/√g ≈ 1.004 s against ≈ 1.190 s along the straight line.
    Teacher explains: Energy: ½mv² = mgy, so v = √(2gy). Time =
    ∫ ds/v:
       T[y] = ∫₀^{x₁} √((1 + y′²)/(2gy)) dx.
    F has no x, so Beltrami: F − y′F_{y′} = C gives
       1/(√(2gy) √(1 + y′²)) = C  ⇒  y(1 + y′²) = 2a   (2a = 1/(2gC²)).
    Substitute y = a(1 − cos θ) = 2a sin²(θ/2). Then y′² = 2a/y − 1
    = cot²(θ/2), y′ = cot(θ/2), and
       dx = dy/y′ = a sin θ dθ · tan(θ/2) = 2a sin²(θ/2) dθ = a(1 − cos θ) dθ,
    so x = a(θ − sin θ) (starting at 0): a CYCLOID, the curve traced by a
    point on a rolling wheel of radius a. Endpoint: at θ = π the point is
    (πa, 2a) = (π, 2) ⇒ a = 1. Time: along the cycloid ds = 2a sin(θ/2) dθ
    and v = √(2gy) = 2√(ga) sin(θ/2), so dt = √(a/g) dθ and
       T = π√(1/9.8) ≈ 1.0035 s.
    Straight line: length ℓ = √(π² + 4) ≈ 3.724, constant acceleration
    g × 2/ℓ along it, so ℓ = ½(2g/ℓ)t², t = ℓ/√g ≈ 1.1896 s. The cycloid wins
    because it drops steeply first to gain speed. Common mistakes: measuring y
    upward (then v = √(−2gy)); forgetting that the time on a cycloid is
    θ√(a/g), not the arc length over g. Now you try: time along the same
    cycloid from θ = 0 to θ = π/2 (the point (π/2 − 1, 1)). ((π/2)/√9.8
    ≈ 0.502 s)

D4. Find the curve y(x) > 0 through (−1, cosh 1) and (1, cosh 1) whose
    rotation about the x-axis gives the least area. Compute the area of the
    catenoid(s) and compare with the Goldschmidt solution (two discs).
    Answer: catenaries y = c cosh(x/c) with c cosh(1/c) = cosh 1: c = 1 (area
    π(2 + sinh 2) ≈ 17.677) and c ≈ 0.7021 (area ≈ 17.734). The two discs
    have area 2π cosh²1 ≈ 14.961, less than either: the global minimum is
    the discs; y = cosh x is only a local minimum.
    Teacher explains: The area is A[y] = 2π ∫ y √(1 + y′²) dx. No x, so
    Beltrami:
       y√(1 + y′²) − y′ · yy′/√(1 + y′²) = y/√(1 + y′²) = c
       ⇒  y′ = √(y² − c²)/c  ⇒  arccosh(y/c) = (x − d)/c
       ⇒  y = c cosh((x − d)/c)          (CATENARY)
    Symmetry gives d = 0; the end condition is c cosh(1/c) = cosh 1. The
    function f(c) = c cosh(1/c) has a minimum ≈ 1.509 at c ≈ 0.834 (where
    tanh(1/c) = c) and cosh 1 ≈ 1.543 lies above it, so there are TWO roots:
    c = 1 and c ≈ 0.7021. For c = 1:
       A = 2π ∫₋₁¹ cosh²x dx = 2π [x/2 + sinh 2x/4]₋₁¹ = π(2 + sinh 2) ≈ 17.677.
    The deeper catenary (c ≈ 0.702) has area ≈ 17.734 and is not even a
    local minimum (it has a conjugate point). The GOLDSCHMIDT solution —
    the two end discs of radius cosh 1 joined along the axis — has area
    2π cosh²1 ≈ 14.961, which is smaller. It is not a smooth graph, so
    Euler-Lagrange cannot find it. If the rings are pulled further apart
    (so that the height lies below the minimum of f) no catenary exists at
    all: the soap film breaks. Lesson: the Euler-Lagrange equation finds
    candidates; it does not guarantee a global minimum. Common mistakes:
    finding one root of c cosh(1/c) = h and stopping; forgetting the factor
    2π. Now you try: which c makes y = c cosh(x/c) pass through (±1, 1.6)?
    (Solve c cosh(1/c) = 1.6: two roots, c ≈ 0.634 and c ≈ 1.126; the second
    is the shallower, locally minimising film.)

D5. Find the geodesics of a sphere of radius R using spherical coordinates,
    and those of a cylinder. Compute the shortest distance on the unit sphere
    between (lat 60°N, long 0°) and (lat 60°N, long 180°) and compare with the
    path along the parallel.
    Answer: great circles; helices (including lines and circles) on the
    cylinder; distance π/3 ≈ 1.047 against π/2 ≈ 1.571 along the parallel.
    Teacher explains: On the sphere ds² = R²(dθ² + sin²θ dφ²) (θ polar
    angle). Describe the curve as φ(θ):
       L = R ∫ √(1 + sin²θ φ′²) dθ,   F has no φ ⇒ F_{φ′} = C:
       sin²θ φ′/√(1 + sin²θ φ′²) = C.
    Solve for φ′: φ′ = C/(sin θ √(sin²θ − C²)). With u = cot θ,
    du = −dθ/sin²θ, this integrates to
       φ − φ₀ = −arcsin(C cot θ/√(1 − C²)),  i.e.  cot θ = k sin(φ₀ − φ).
    Multiply by R sin θ and expand sin(φ₀ − φ): with x = R sin θ cos φ,
    y = R sin θ sin φ, z = R cos θ this reads z = k(x sin φ₀ − y cos φ₀),
    a plane through the ORIGIN. The sphere meets such planes in GREAT
    CIRCLES. (Quick check: C = 0 gives φ = const, a meridian.) Cylinder:
    unroll it onto a plane (the metric dz² + R²dφ² is flat), where
    geodesics are lines z = aRφ + b, which roll back up to HELICES (a = 0
    circles, vertical lines). The numbers: the two points lie on the
    meridian plane through long 0°/180°, so the great circle runs over the
    North Pole, through the
    angle 30° + 30° = 60°, length π/3 ≈ 1.047. Along the parallel of radius
    cos 60° = ½ the half turn is π × ½ = π/2 ≈ 1.571. Common mistakes: the
    parallels (other than the equator) are NOT geodesics; forgetting sin²θ
    in the metric. Now you try: on the unit cylinder, the shortest distance
    from (φ = 0, z = 0) to (φ = π/2, z = 1). (Unroll: √((π/2)² + 1) ≈ 1.862)

D6. Among curves y(x) ≥ 0 from (−1, 0) to (1, 0) with length π, find the one
    enclosing the greatest area with the x-axis. Explain the Lagrange
    multiplier rule for isoperimetric problems.
    Answer: the semicircle x² + y² = 1, area π/2.
    Teacher explains: RULE: to extremise J = ∫F subject to K = ∫G = ℓ, if y
    is not an extremal of K there is a constant λ such that y is an
    extremal of ∫(F − λG) dx. (Reason: vary with two functions, y + ε₁η₁ +
    ε₂η₂; the ε₂ direction keeps K = ℓ, and the ordinary Lagrange multiplier
    rule in (ε₁, ε₂) gives ∇J = λ∇K.) Here F = y, G = √(1 + y′²). The new
    integrand y − λ√(1 + y′²) has no x, so Beltrami:
       y − λ√(1 + y′²) + λy′²/√(1 + y′²) = C  ⇒  y − C = λ/√(1 + y′²).
    Put y′ = −tan t, so √(1 + y′²) = sec t and y − C = λ cos t. Then
    dy = −λ sin t dt, dx = dy/y′ = λ cos t dt, x = λ sin t + d. So
       (x − d)² + (y − C)² = λ²,
    a CIRCULAR ARC. Ends (±1, 0) give d = 0 and λ² = 1 + C²; the length is
    π, exactly half the circumference of a unit circle through (±1, 0) with
    centre (0, 0). So C = 0, λ = 1: the upper unit semicircle, area π/2 ≈
    1.571. Compare a triangle with the same perimeter π: sides π/2 each,
    height √(π²/4 − 1) ≈ 1.211, area ≈ 1.211 < π/2. This is DIDO'S problem;
    with a closed curve of length L the answer is a circle of area L²/(4π).
    Common mistakes: dropping λ (then F = y alone has no extremal);
    forgetting to apply the length constraint to find λ. Now you try: a rope
    of 100 m has both ends on a straight beach. Maximum area enclosed?
    (A semicircle, 100²/(2π) ≈ 1591.5 m²)

D7. A uniform chain of length 3 hangs between (−1, 0) and (1, 0). Show that
    it takes the shape of a catenary and find how far it sags.
    Answer: y = c cosh(x/c) − c cosh(1/c) with 2c sinh(1/c) = 3, c ≈ 0.6165;
    sag c(cosh(1/c) − 1) ≈ 1.005.
    Teacher explains: The chain minimises its potential energy
    ∫ ρgy ds = ρg ∫ y√(1 + y′²) dx subject to fixed length
    ∫ √(1 + y′²) dx = 3. Multiplier: extremals of ∫ (y − λ)√(1 + y′²) dx.
    Put Y = y − λ: the integrand is Y√(1 + Y′²), exactly the minimal
    surface integrand of D4, so
       y − λ = c cosh((x − d)/c).
    Symmetry: d = 0. Length:
       ∫₋₁¹ √(1 + sinh²(x/c)) dx = ∫₋₁¹ cosh(x/c) dx = 2c sinh(1/c) = 3.
    This transcendental equation has one root; Newton's method from
    c = 0.5 gives c ≈ 0.61647 (check 2 × 0.61647 × sinh(1.6222) ≈ 3.000).
    y(1) = 0 fixes λ = −c cosh(1/c). The lowest point is x = 0, so
       sag = y(±1) − y(0) = c cosh(1/c) − c ≈ 1.005.
    (If the length were exactly 2 the chain would be tight and straight; a
    shorter chain cannot reach.) Common mistakes: confusing the chain
    (catenary, minimising energy) with a parabola (the shape of a
    suspension bridge cable loaded uniformly per horizontal length); using
    λ = 0. Now you try: the sag of a chain y = cosh x − cosh 1 on [−1, 1].
    Its length? (sag cosh 1 − 1 ≈ 0.543; length 2 sinh 1 ≈ 2.350)

D8. Minimise J = ∫₀¹ (y′² + y²) dx with y(0) = 1 and y(1) FREE. Derive the
    natural boundary condition, and state the transversality condition when
    the right end moves along a curve y = φ(x); apply it to the shortest
    line from (0, 0) to the line y = 2 − x.
    Answer: y = cosh(1 − x)/cosh 1, J_min = tanh 1 ≈ 0.7616; F_{y′} = 0 at a
    free end; shortest line y = x meeting y = 2 − x at (1, 1), length √2.
    Teacher explains: Now η(1) need not vanish, so the boundary term stays:
       δJ = [F_{y′}η]₀¹ + ∫ (F_y − d/dx F_{y′}) η dx = 0.
    First take η(1) = 0: the Euler-Lagrange equation still holds. Then the
    integral is 0 and F_{y′}(1)η(1) = 0 for arbitrary η(1), so
       F_{y′} = 0 at x = 1    (NATURAL BOUNDARY CONDITION).
    Here F_{y′} = 2y′, so y′(1) = 0. Euler-Lagrange: 2y − 2y″ = 0,
    y = A cosh x + B sinh x. y(0) = 1 ⇒ A = 1; y′(1) = sinh 1 + B cosh 1 = 0
    ⇒ B = −tanh 1. So y = cosh x − tanh 1 sinh x = cosh(1 − x)/cosh 1. The
    value: using y″ = y, y′² + y² = (yy′)′, so
       J = [yy′]₀¹ = 0 − y(0)y′(0) = tanh 1 ≈ 0.7616.
    Freeing the end can only lower the minimum, since every competitor of
    a fixed-end problem is still allowed. TRANSVERSALITY: if the
    right end (b, y(b)) must lie on y = φ(x), varying b too gives
       [F + (φ′ − y′)F_{y′}] = 0 at x = b.
    For F = √(1 + y′²): √(1 + y′²) + (φ′ − y′)y′/√(1 + y′²) = 0 ⇒
    1 + φ′y′ = 0: the extremal meets the curve at a RIGHT ANGLE. With
    φ = 2 − x (φ′ = −1): y′ = 1, the line y = x hits y = 2 − x at (1, 1),
    distance √2 ≈ 1.414. Common mistakes: imposing y(1) = 0 (or anything)
    at a free end; forgetting the φ′ term. Now you try: minimise
    ∫₀¹ (y′² + 2y) dx with y(0) = 0, y(1) free. (y = x²/2 − x, J = −1/3)

D9. Show that y = 0 is an extremal of J = ∫₀ᵇ (y′² − y²) dx with
    y(0) = y(b) = 0. Using Legendre's and Jacobi's conditions, decide for
    which b it is a minimum, and confirm with the trial function
    sin(πx/b).
    Answer: minimum iff b ≤ π (strict minimum for b < π); for b > π,
    J[sin(πx/b)] = (b/2)(π²/b² − 1) < 0 (e.g. b = 4: π²/8 − 2 ≈ −0.766).
    Teacher explains: Euler-Lagrange: −2y − 2y″ = 0, y″ + y = 0; y = 0
    satisfies it with the boundary values. SECOND VARIATION: expand
    J[εη] = ε²∫(η′² − η²) (J is quadratic), so y = 0 is a minimum iff
       ∫₀ᵇ (η′² − η²) dx ≥ 0 for all η with η(0) = η(b) = 0.
    LEGENDRE: F_{y′y′} = 2 > 0: necessary condition holds, no decision yet.
    JACOBI: P = ½F_{y′y′} = 1, Q = ½F_{yy} = −1; accessory equation
       −h″ − h = 0,  h(0) = 0, h′(0) = 1  ⇒  h = sin x,
    whose first zero after 0 is x = π: the CONJUGATE POINT. If b < π there
    is no conjugate point in (0, b] and y = 0 is a (strict) minimum; indeed
    WIRTINGER'S inequality ∫η′² ≥ (π/b)²∫η² ≥ ∫η² holds. At b = π the minimum
    value 0 is attained also by sin x (not strict). If b > π take
    η = sin(πx/b):
       ∫₀ᵇ η′² = (π²/b²)(b/2),  ∫₀ᵇ η² = b/2,  J = (b/2)(π²/b² − 1) < 0.
    For b = 4: J = 2(π²/16 − 1) = π²/8 − 2 ≈ −0.766 < 0 = J[0]. Beyond the
    conjugate point the extremal stops being a minimum (on a sphere a great
    circle arc longer than π is not the shortest path). Common mistakes:
    thinking Legendre's condition alone is sufficient; forgetting that the
    trial function must satisfy the boundary conditions. Now you try: is
    y = 0 a minimum of ∫₀¹ (y′² − 4y²) dx? (Jacobi h = sin 2x, conjugate
    point π/2 ≈ 1.571 > 1: yes)

D10. Derive the Euler-Poisson equation for ∫ F(x, y, y′, y″) dx, and find the
     curve minimising the bending energy ∫₀¹ y″² dx with y(0) = 0,
     y′(0) = 0, y(1) = 1, y′(1) = 0. Also find the extremals of the system
     ∫₀^{π/2} (y′² + z′² + 2yz) dx with y(0) = z(0) = 0, y(π/2) = 1,
     z(π/2) = −1.
     Answer: F_y − (F_{y′})′ + (F_{y″})″ = 0; y = 3x² − 2x³, J = 12;
     y = sin x, z = −sin x.
     Teacher explains: Vary y + εη with η = η′ = 0 at both ends:
        δJ = ∫ (F_y η + F_{y′} η′ + F_{y″} η″) dx.
     Integrate the η′ term by parts once and the η″ term twice; all
     boundary terms vanish because η and η′ vanish at the ends:
        δJ = ∫ (F_y − (F_{y′})′ + (F_{y″})″) η dx = 0,
     and the fundamental lemma gives the EULER-POISSON equation. It is of
     order four, so four conditions are needed: y and y′ at both ends. For
     F = y″²: (2y″)″ = 0 ⇒ y⁗ = 0 ⇒ y cubic. y(0) = y′(0) = 0 ⇒
     y = ax³ + bx²; y(1) = 1: a + b = 1; y′(1) = 0: 3a + 2b = 0. So a = −2,
     b = 3, y = 3x² − 2x³ (the smoothstep curve), and
        J = ∫₀¹ (6 − 12x)² dx = 36 − 72 + 48 = 12.
     (Physically: an elastic beam clamped horizontally at both ends.)
     SEVERAL FUNCTIONS: one equation per function.
        y:  2z − 2y″ = 0 ⇒ y″ = z,     z:  2y − 2z″ = 0 ⇒ z″ = y.
     So y⁗ = y: y = A eˣ + B e^(−x) + C cos x + D sin x, z = y″. Try the
     trigonometric part: y = sin x gives z = y″ = −sin x, and these meet all
     four conditions (the other constants are forced to 0 since the system
     has a unique solution here). Common mistakes: the sign of the (F_{y″})″
     term (+); prescribing only two conditions for a fourth-order equation.
     Now you try: minimise ∫₀¹ y″² dx with y(0) = y′(0) = 0, y(1) = y′(1) = 1.
     (y = 2x² − x³, J = 4)

D11. Derive the Euler-Lagrange equation for a functional of a function of two
     variables, ∬_D F(x, y, u, u_x, u_y) dx dy with u fixed on ∂D. Apply it
     to the Dirichlet integral, to ∬(½|∇u|² − fu), and to the area of a
     graph (minimal surfaces). Check that Scherk's surface
     u = ln(cos y/cos x) is minimal.
     Answer: F_u − ∂/∂x F_{u_x} − ∂/∂y F_{u_y} = 0; Δu = 0; −Δu = f;
     (1 + u_y²)u_xx − 2u_xu_yu_xy + (1 + u_x²)u_yy = 0; Scherk satisfies it.
     Teacher explains: Vary u + εη with η = 0 on ∂D:
        δJ = ∬ (F_u η + F_{u_x} η_x + F_{u_y} η_y) dx dy.
     The last two terms are the vector field (F_{u_x}, F_{u_y}) dotted with
     ∇η. The divergence theorem (Green) moves the derivative:
        ∬ V·∇η = ∮ η V·n ds − ∬ (div V) η,
     and the boundary integral is 0. So
        F_u − ∂/∂x F_{u_x} − ∂/∂y F_{u_y} = 0.
     DIRICHLET: F = u_x² + u_y² ⇒ −2u_xx − 2u_yy = 0 ⇒ Δu = 0 (harmonic
     functions minimise energy). F = ½|∇u|² − fu ⇒ −f − Δu = 0 ⇒ −Δu = f
     (POISSON; the membrane under load). AREA: F = √(1 + u_x² + u_y²) = W;
        ∂/∂x (u_x/W) + ∂/∂y (u_y/W) = 0,
     which after expanding and multiplying by W³ is the MINIMAL SURFACE
     EQUATION (1 + u_y²)u_xx − 2u_xu_yu_xy + (1 + u_x²)u_yy = 0 (mean
     curvature 0). SCHERK: u = ln cos y − ln cos x, u_x = tan x,
     u_y = −tan y, u_xx = sec²x, u_yy = −sec²y, u_xy = 0:
        (1 + tan²y) sec²x + (1 + tan²x)(−sec²y) = sec²y sec²x − sec²x sec²y = 0 ✓.
     Common mistakes: partial vs total derivatives (∂/∂x F_{u_x} is TOTAL in
     x, through u too); forgetting that if u is free on part of ∂D a natural
     condition F_{u_x}n₁ + F_{u_y}n₂ = 0 (Neumann ∂u/∂n = 0 for Dirichlet)
     appears there. Now you try: the equation from ∬∫ (u_t² − c²u_x²) dx dt.
     (u_tt = c²u_xx, the wave equation)

D12. Show that minimising ∫₀¹ y′² dx subject to ∫₀¹ y² dx = 1,
     y(0) = y(1) = 0, gives an eigenvalue problem, and that the minimum is
     the least eigenvalue π². Estimate it with the Rayleigh quotient of
     x(1 − x) and with a two-term Rayleigh-Ritz trial. Then use Ritz with
     y = ax(1 − x) to approximate the minimiser of
     J = ∫₀¹ (y′² − y² − 2xy) dx, y(0) = y(1) = 0.
     Answer: −y″ = λy, λₙ = n²π², min π² ≈ 9.8696; R[x(1 − x)] = 10; two-term
     Ritz ≈ 9.8697. a = 5/18, so y(½) ≈ 0.0694 vs the exact
     sin(½)/sin 1 − ½ ≈ 0.0697.
     Teacher explains: Multiplier rule: extremals of ∫(y′² − λy²) satisfy
     −2λy − 2y″ = 0, i.e. −y″ = λy with y(0) = y(1) = 0: a STURM-LIOUVILLE
     problem. Solutions y = sin nπx, λ = n²π². On an extremal, multiply
     −y″ = λy by y and integrate by parts: ∫y′² = λ∫y² = λ, so the value of J
     IS the eigenvalue; the minimum is the smallest, π². Equivalently, the
     RAYLEIGH QUOTIENT R[y] = ∫y′²/∫y² ≥ π² for all admissible y ≠ 0, with
     equality only for sin πx. Any trial gives an UPPER bound:
        y = x(1 − x):  ∫y′² = ∫(1 − 2x)² = 1/3,  ∫y² = 1/30,  R = 10.
     10 is within 1.3% of π² ≈ 9.8696. RAYLEIGH-RITZ with
     y = c₁x(1 − x) + c₂x²(1 − x)²: minimising R over (c₁, c₂) means solving
     det(A − λB) = 0 with Aᵢⱼ = ∫φᵢ′φⱼ′, Bᵢⱼ = ∫φᵢφⱼ; the lower root is
     ≈ 9.8697, excellent. RITZ for J: with y = ax(1 − x),
        ∫y′² = a²/3,  ∫y² = a²/30,  ∫xy = a/12,
        J(a) = (3/10)a² − a/6,  J′(a) = 0 ⇒ a = 5/18 ≈ 0.278.
     Exact: Euler-Lagrange −2y − 2x − 2y″ = 0 ⇒ y″ + y = −x, y = sin x/sin 1
     − x. At x = ½: exact 0.0697, Ritz a/4 = 0.0694. Common mistakes:
     choosing trial functions that break the boundary conditions (then the
     'bound' is meaningless); thinking Ritz gives a lower bound (it gives
     an upper bound for a minimum). Now you try: R[y] for y = x²(1 − x).
     (∫y′² = 2/15, ∫y² = 1/105, R = 14)

M1. Write and simplify the Euler-Lagrange equation for F(x, y, y′).
    a) y′²                        b) y′² + y²
    c) y′² − y²                   d) y′² + 2y
    e) y′² + 2xy                  f) y′² + y² + 2yeˣ
    g) x²y′²                      h) xy′²
    i) (1 + x)y′²                 j) y′²/x
    k) eˣy′²                      l) √(1 + y′²)
    m) y√(1 + y′²)                n) √((1 + y′²)/y)
    o) y′² + 2yy′ + y²            p) y′² − y² − 2y sin x
    q) y²y′²                      r) y′³
    Answers:
      a) y″ = 0                   b) y″ = y
      c) y″ + y = 0               d) y″ = 1
      e) y″ = x                   f) y″ − y = eˣ
      g) (x²y′)′ = 0              h) (xy′)′ = 0
      i) ((1 + x)y′)′ = 0         j) (y′/x)′ = 0
      k) y″ + y′ = 0              l) y″ = 0
      m) yy″ = 1 + y′²            n) 2yy″ + 1 + y′² = 0
      o) y″ = y (2yy′ is a null Lagrangian)
      p) y″ + y = −sin x          q) yy″ + y′² = 0, i.e. (y²)″ = 0
      r) 6y′y″ = 0 ⇒ y″ = 0 (where y′ ≠ 0)

M12. First variation, first integrals, corners.
     a) δJ for J = ∫₀¹ y′² at y = x in the direction η = x(1 − x)
     b) δJ for J = ∫₀¹ y² at y = x, η = 1
     c) δJ for J = ∫₀¹ (y′² + y²) at y = x, η = x(1 − x)
     d) Beltrami constant F − y′F_{y′} for F = y√(1 + y′²) on y = cosh x
     e) cycloid (a = 1) to the point (π/2 − 1, 1): θ₁ and time (g = 9.8)
     f) minimise ∫₀² y′²(1 − y′)², y(0) = 0, y(2) = 1
     g) action ∫₀^{π/2} ½(ẋ² − x²) dt along x = sin t
     h) is F = y′² + y⁴ jointly convex? is y′² − y²?
     i) J = ∫ₐᵇ yy′ dx depends only on what?
     j) J = ∫ₐᵇ y′ dx
     k) Weierstrass-Erdmann: which quantities are continuous at a corner?
     l) H = y′F_{y′} − F for F = √(1 + y′²)
     Answers:
       a) 2∫(1 − 2x) dx = 0 (y = x is an extremal)
       b) 2∫x dx = 1
       c) 2∫[(1 − 2x) + x²(1 − x)] dx = 1/6
       d) y/√(1 + y′²) = cosh x/cosh x = 1
       e) θ₁ = π/2, t = (π/2)/√9.8 ≈ 0.502 s
       f) 0, e.g. y = 0 on [0, 1], y = x − 1 on [1, 2] (slopes 0 and 1)
       g) ½∫₀^{π/2} cos 2t dt = 0
       h) yes; no
       i) the end values: (y(b)² − y(a)²)/2
       j) y(b) − y(a)
       k) F_{y′} and F − y′F_{y′}
       l) −1/√(1 + y′²)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: drill the three-line routine — write F, compute F_y and
  F_{y′}, form F_y − d/dx F_{y′} = 0 — before any theory; then spot the
  shortcuts (no y: F_{y′} = C; no x: Beltrami) because they turn a second-
  order equation into a first-order one. Always check boundary conditions
  last and ask 'is it really a minimum?' by testing one nearby function
  numerically. Draw the brachistochrone and the catenary. Harder: prove the
  du Bois-Reymond lemma (∫gη′ = 0 for all η ⇒ g constant) and derive the
  integrated Euler-Lagrange equation for C¹ extremals; show that the
  catenoid ceases to exist when the rings are more than about 1.3255 radii
  apart; prove Wirtinger's inequality ∫η′² ≥ π²∫η² on [0, 1] with Fourier
  series; derive Snell's law from Fermat's principle; show that the Jacobi
  equation is the linearisation of Euler-Lagrange about the extremal; and
  explain why the direct method (lower semicontinuity + compactness) proves
  existence for convex F with growth ≥ |y′|², while the Weierstrass example
  fails at x = 0 where the coefficient x² degenerates.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.43 — COMBINATORICS: INCLUSION-EXCLUSION, PÓLYA COUNTING, DESIGNS,
RAMSEY THEORY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - INCLUSION-EXCLUSION (PIE): |A₁ ∪ ... ∪ Aₙ| = S₁ − S₂ + S₃ − ... +
    (−1)ⁿ⁺¹Sₙ, where Sₖ = ∑ over k-subsets of |Aᵢ₁ ∩ ... ∩ Aᵢₖ|. COMPLEMENT
    form: the number with NONE of the properties is N − S₁ + S₂ − ... =
    ∑ (−1)ᵏSₖ (S₀ = N). If the intersections depend only on k, Sₖ = C(n, k)Nₖ.
    Truncating gives the BONFERRONI inequalities (alternately upper and
    lower bounds).
  - EXACTLY m properties: Eₘ = ∑_{k≥m} (−1)^(k−m) C(k, m) Sₖ; AT LEAST m:
    Lₘ = ∑_{k≥m} (−1)^(k−m) C(k − 1, m − 1) Sₖ.
  - STANDARD PIE COUNTS: EULER φ(n) = n∏(1 − 1/p) over primes p | n;
    SURJECTIONS from an n-set onto a k-set ∑ⱼ (−1)ʲC(k, j)(k − j)ⁿ = k!S(n, k)
    (STIRLING numbers of the 2nd kind); DERANGEMENTS
    Dₙ = n!∑ₖ (−1)ᵏ/k! = round(n!/e) (n ≥ 1), with Dₙ = (n − 1)(Dₙ₋₁ + Dₙ₋₂);
    permutations with exactly k fixed points C(n, k)Dₙ₋ₖ; integer solutions
    with UPPER BOUNDS (x₁ + ... + xₘ = n, 0 ≤ xᵢ ≤ c):
    ∑ⱼ (−1)ʲC(m, j)C(n − j(c + 1) + m − 1, m − 1); arrangements with no two
    equal/adjacent objects; FORBIDDEN POSITIONS via the ROOK POLYNOMIAL
    R(x) = ∑ rₖxᵏ: the count is ∑ (−1)ᵏrₖ(n − k)!.
  - GROUP ACTIONS: a group G acts on a set X; ORBIT of x, STABILISER Gₓ,
    ORBIT-STABILISER |Gx|·|Gₓ| = |G|. Two colourings are 'the same' when a
    symmetry maps one to the other, so we count ORBITS.
  - BURNSIDE'S LEMMA (Cauchy-Frobenius): number of orbits
    = (1/|G|) ∑_{g∈G} |Fix(g)|: the AVERAGE number of fixed points.
    A colouring with k colours is fixed by g iff it is constant on each
    CYCLE of g, so |Fix(g)| = k^(c(g)), c(g) = number of cycles.
  - CYCLE INDEX Z(G) = (1/|G|) ∑_g x₁^(j₁) x₂^(j₂) ... (jᵢ = number of i-cycles
    of g). PÓLYA'S THEOREM: number of k-colourings = Z(G; k, k, ..., k);
    PATTERN INVENTORY: substitute xᵢ = r^i + b^i + ... and the coefficient
    of r^a b^c ... counts the orbits with a red, c blue, ....
  - STANDARD CYCLE INDICES: Cₙ: (1/n)∑_{d|n} φ(d) x_d^(n/d) (NECKLACES
    N(n, k) = (1/n)∑φ(d)k^(n/d)); Dₙ adds n reflections: n odd x₁x₂^((n−1)/2)
    each; n even (n/2)x₂^(n/2) + (n/2)x₁²x₂^((n−2)/2) (BRACELETS). Cube
    rotations (24) on faces: (x₁⁶ + 3x₁²x₂² + 6x₁²x₄ + 6x₂³ + 8x₃²)/24, giving
    (k⁶ + 3k⁴ + 12k³ + 8k²)/24 colourings. Graphs on 4 vertices = 11 (S₄ on
    the 6 edges).
  - BLOCK DESIGNS: a 2-(v, k, λ) design / BIBD(v, b, r, k, λ) has v points,
    b blocks of size k, every point in r blocks and every PAIR of points in
    exactly λ blocks. Counting: bk = vr and λ(v − 1) = r(k − 1). Incidence
    matrix N (v × b): NNᵀ = (r − λ)I + λJ. FISHER'S INEQUALITY b ≥ v (so
    r ≥ k); b = v is SYMMETRIC (then any two blocks meet in λ points).
    BRUCK-RYSER-CHOWLA: a symmetric (v, k, λ) with v even needs k − λ to be
    a square (v odd: x² = (k − λ)y² + (−1)^((v−1)/2) λz² has a nonzero
    integer solution).
  - STEINER TRIPLE SYSTEMS STS(v) (k = 3, λ = 1) exist iff v ≡ 1 or 3
    (mod 6), with b = v(v − 1)/6, r = (v − 1)/2. FANO plane STS(7).
    PROJECTIVE PLANE of order n: 2-(n² + n + 1, n + 1, 1), symmetric (any two
    lines meet in one point); exists for every prime power n; none for n = 6
    (BRC) or n = 10 (computer search). AFFINE plane of order n: 2-(n², n, 1),
    n² + n lines in n + 1 parallel classes.
  - LATIN SQUARES: n × n arrays with each symbol once per row and column.
    Two are ORTHOGONAL if the n² ordered pairs are all different. At most
    n − 1 MUTUALLY ORTHOGONAL LATIN SQUARES (MOLS); n − 1 exist for prime
    powers (Lₐ(i, j) = ai + j in GF(n), a ≠ 0) and n − 1 MOLS ⇔ a projective
    plane of order n. Order 6: no pair (EULER'S 36 OFFICERS, Tarry 1900).
  - RAMSEY THEORY: R(s, t) is the least N such that every red/blue colouring
    of the edges of K_N has a red K_s or a blue K_t. PIGEONHOLE is the base.
    R(3, 3) = 6 (the pentagon shows R > 5). R(s, t) ≤ R(s − 1, t) + R(s, t − 1)
    (strict if both are even), so R(s, t) ≤ C(s + t − 2, s − 1). Known:
    R(3, 4) = 9, R(3, 5) = 14, R(4, 4) = 18, R(3, 3, 3) = 17; 43 ≤ R(5, 5) ≤ 46.
    ERDŐS (probabilistic): R(k, k) > 2^(k/2) for k ≥ 3.
  - RAMSEY-TYPE THEOREMS: ERDŐS-SZEKERES — every sequence of n² + 1 distinct
    reals has a monotone subsequence of length n + 1 (sharp); SCHUR — any
    finite colouring of {1, ..., N} (N large) has a monochromatic x + y = z
    (S(2) = 4, S(3) = 13); VAN DER WAERDEN — monochromatic arithmetic
    progressions (W(2, 3) = 9); happy ending: 5 points in general position
    contain a convex quadrilateral.
  - TRAPS: forgetting the alternating signs or the S₀ term; double counting
    because Sₖ counts ordered choices; counting colourings instead of
    orbits (not dividing by |G|, or dividing without Burnside); wrong cycle
    types (a 180° face rotation of a cube has two FIXED faces); checking only
    necessary conditions for designs and claiming existence.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Prove the inclusion-exclusion principle by counting how often each
    element is counted. Use it to find how many integers in 1, ..., 1000 are
    divisible by none of 2, 3, 5, and derive the formula for φ(n).
    Answer: 266; φ(n) = n∏_{p|n}(1 − 1/p).
    Teacher explains: Let x ∈ A₁ ∪ ... ∪ Aₙ lie in exactly m ≥ 1 of the sets.
    In Sₖ it is counted once for every k-subset of those m sets, i.e. C(m, k)
    times. Its total count on the right side is
       C(m, 1) − C(m, 2) + ... + (−1)^(m+1)C(m, m) = 1 − (1 − 1)ᵐ = 1,
    by the binomial theorem. An element in none of the sets is counted 0
    times on both sides. So each element of the union is counted exactly
    once: PIE is proved. Numbers: Aₚ = multiples of p in [1, 1000],
    |Aₚ| = ⌊1000/p⌋, and Aₚ ∩ A_q = multiples of pq (coprime):
       S₁ = 500 + 333 + 200 = 1033
       S₂ = ⌊1000/6⌋ + ⌊1000/10⌋ + ⌊1000/15⌋ = 166 + 100 + 66 = 332
       S₃ = ⌊1000/30⌋ = 33
       none = 1000 − 1033 + 332 − 33 = 266.
    EULER φ: for n = p₁^a₁ ... pᵣ^aᵣ, the integers in [1, n] sharing a factor
    with n are those divisible by some pᵢ, and |A_{pᵢ} ∩ ...| = n/(pᵢ...)
    exactly (divisors of n), so
       φ(n) = n − ∑ n/pᵢ + ∑ n/(pᵢpⱼ) − ... = n(1 − 1/p₁)...(1 − 1/pᵣ).
    Example φ(360) = 360 × ½ × ⅔ × ⅘ = 96. Common mistakes: using 1000/6 =
    166.7 without the floor; forgetting that multiples of 2 and 3 are the
    multiples of 6 only because 2, 3 are coprime (for 4 and 6 use lcm 12).
    Now you try: how many integers in [1, 1000] are divisible by 4, 6 or 9?
    (250 + 166 + 111 − 83 − 27 − 55 + 27 = 389)

D2. Derive the derangement formula Dₙ = n!∑ₖ₌₀ⁿ (−1)ᵏ/k!, the recurrence
    Dₙ = (n − 1)(Dₙ₋₁ + Dₙ₋₂), and compute D₅. Five letters are put at random
    into five addressed envelopes: find the probability that none is right
    and that exactly one is right.
    Answer: D₅ = 44; P(none) = 44/120 = 11/30 ≈ 0.367; P(exactly one)
    = 45/120 = 3/8.
    Teacher explains: Let Aᵢ = permutations fixing i. Fixing k chosen points
    leaves (n − k)! permutations, so Sₖ = C(n, k)(n − k)! = n!/k!. By PIE
    (complement form)
       Dₙ = ∑ₖ (−1)ᵏ n!/k! = n!(1 − 1 + 1/2! − 1/3! + ... + (−1)ⁿ/n!).
    For n = 5: 120(1/2 − 1/6 + 1/24 − 1/120) = 60 − 20 + 5 − 1 = 44.
    RECURRENCE: in a derangement, 1 goes to some j ≠ 1 (n − 1 choices). Either
    j goes back to 1 (swap; the other n − 2 form a derangement: Dₙ₋₂), or
    not (then rename 'j must not go to 1' as 'j must not be fixed' and we
    have a derangement of n − 1 things: Dₙ₋₁). So Dₙ = (n − 1)(Dₙ₋₁ + Dₙ₋₂):
       D₁ = 0, D₂ = 1, D₃ = 2·1 = 2, D₄ = 3·3 = 9, D₅ = 4·11 = 44, D₆ = 265.
    Probabilities: P(none) = D₅/5! = 44/120 ≈ 0.3667, already close to
    1/e ≈ 0.3679 (the series for e^(−1)); indeed Dₙ = round(n!/e).
    EXACTLY ONE correct: choose it (5 ways), derange the other 4:
    5 × D₄ = 45, probability 45/120 = 0.375. Common mistakes: thinking the
    probability of no match tends to 0 as n grows (it tends to 1/e);
    computing 'exactly one' as 5 × 4! (the others must all be wrong). Now you
    try: how many permutations of 6 objects have exactly 2 fixed points?
    (C(6, 2)D₄ = 15 × 9 = 135)

D3. Count the surjections from a 6-set onto a 3-set and find S(6, 3). Then
    count the ways of rolling a total of 15 with three dice, using PIE on
    integer solutions with bounds.
    Answer: 540 surjections, S(6, 3) = 90; 10 ways.
    Teacher explains: Let Aⱼ = functions missing value j. Missing a given set
    of i values leaves (3 − i)⁶ functions, so
       surjections = 3⁶ − C(3, 1)2⁶ + C(3, 2)1⁶ − C(3, 3)0⁶
                   = 729 − 192 + 3 − 0 = 540.
    A surjection is a partition of the 6 elements into 3 non-empty blocks
    (the fibres) together with a labelling of the blocks by the 3 values, so
    540 = 3! S(6, 3), S(6, 3) = 90. DICE: we want x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 15 with
    1 ≤ xᵢ ≤ 6. Put yᵢ = xᵢ − 1: y₁ + y₂ + y₃ = 12, 0 ≤ yᵢ ≤ 5. Without the
    upper bound, STARS AND BARS gives C(12 + 2, 2) = C(14, 2) = 91. Let Aᵢ:
    yᵢ ≥ 6; substitute yᵢ = 6 + zᵢ: sum 6, C(8, 2) = 28 each; two violators:
    sum 0, C(2, 2) = 1 each; three: impossible.
       91 − 3 × 28 + 3 × 1 − 0 = 10.
    Check by listing (as multisets with orderings): {6, 6, 3} 3 orders,
    {6, 5, 4} 6 orders, {5, 5, 5} 1 order: 3 + 6 + 1 = 10 ✓. So
    P(total 15) = 10/216. Common mistakes: forgetting the shift to yᵢ ≥ 0;
    stopping after the first correction (91 − 84 = 7 is wrong); using
    C(n + k − 1, k) with n and k swapped. Now you try: surjections from a
    5-set onto a 3-set. (243 − 96 + 3 = 150 = 6 × S(5, 3), S(5, 3) = 25)

D4. For the integers 1, ..., 100 and the properties 'divisible by 2, 3, 5',
    find how many have exactly 0, 1, 2, 3 of the properties, using the
    formula for Eₘ. Then use a rook polynomial to count the assignments of
    three workers A, B, C to three jobs 1, 2, 3 when A cannot do job 1, B
    cannot do jobs 1 or 2, and C cannot do job 3.
    Answer: E₀ = 26, E₁ = 48, E₂ = 23, E₃ = 3; one assignment (A2, B3, C1).
    Teacher explains: S₀ = 100, S₁ = 50 + 33 + 20 = 103,
    S₂ = 16 + 10 + 6 = 32 (multiples of 6, 10, 15), S₃ = 3 (multiples of 30).
    An element with exactly j properties is counted C(j, k) times in Sₖ, and
    one checks ∑ₖ (−1)^(k−m)C(k, m)C(j, k) = [j = m], giving
       Eₘ = Sₘ − C(m + 1, m)Sₘ₊₁ + C(m + 2, m)Sₘ₊₂ − ...
       E₀ = 100 − 103 + 32 − 3 = 26
       E₁ = S₁ − 2S₂ + 3S₃ = 103 − 64 + 9 = 48
       E₂ = S₂ − 3S₃ = 32 − 9 = 23
       E₃ = S₃ = 3
    Check: 26 + 48 + 23 + 3 = 100 ✓. ROOKS: the forbidden squares of the
    3 × 3 board are A1, B1, B2, C3. rₖ = number of ways to put k
    non-attacking rooks on forbidden squares. The square C3 shares no row
    or column with the others, so the rook polynomial factorises:
       board {A1, B1, B2}: r₁ = 3, r₂ = 1 (A1 with B2)  →  1 + 3x + x²
       board {C3}:                                      →  1 + x
       R(x) = (1 + 3x + x²)(1 + x) = 1 + 4x + 4x² + x³.
    PIE with Sₖ = rₖ(3 − k)!:
       3! − 4·2! + 4·1! − 1·0! = 6 − 8 + 4 − 1 = 1.
    Direct check: B must do 3, then C (not 3) and A (not 1) force A2, C1 ✓.
    Common mistakes: letting two rooks share a row (that is not a valid
    partial assignment); multiplying rook polynomials of boards that share a
    row or column. Now you try: how many of 1, ..., 100 are divisible by at
    least two of 2, 3, 5? (E₂ + E₃ = 26)

D5. State and prove Burnside's lemma. Use it to count the necklaces of 6
    beads in 2 colours (rotations only), and the bracelets (rotations and
    reflections).
    Answer: orbits = (1/|G|)∑|Fix(g)|; 14 necklaces; 13 bracelets.
    Teacher explains: Count the pairs (g, x) with gx = x in two ways:
       ∑_g |Fix(g)| = ∑_x |Gₓ| = ∑_x |G|/|Gx|    (orbit-stabiliser).
    Group the x by orbits: an orbit O contributes ∑_{x∈O} |G|/|O| = |G|. So
    the sum equals |G| × (number of orbits). Divide by |G|. ∎
    NECKLACE: G = C₆ (rotations by 0, 1, ..., 5 places). A rotation by r
    places has gcd(r, 6) cycles, each of length 6/gcd(r, 6); a colouring is
    fixed iff constant on cycles, so |Fix| = 2^gcd(r, 6):
       r = 0: 2⁶ = 64    r = 1, 5: 2¹ = 2 each    r = 2, 4: 2² = 4 each
       r = 3: 2³ = 8
       orbits = (64 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 4 + 2)/6 = 84/6 = 14.
    BRACELET: G = D₆ adds 6 reflections. Three pass through two opposite
    beads (2 fixed beads + 2 swapped pairs: 4 cycles, 2⁴ = 16 each); three
    pass between beads (3 swapped pairs: 2³ = 8 each):
       orbits = (84 + 3 × 16 + 3 × 8)/12 = 156/12 = 13.
    Only one pair of necklaces merges into a bracelet: the chiral pair
    BBWBWW and its mirror image BBWWBW (read around the ring). Common
    mistakes: dividing 2⁶ = 64 by 6 (not an integer — orbits have different
    sizes); miscounting the cycle structure of reflections. Now you try:
    necklaces of 5 beads in 3 colours. ((3⁵ + 4 × 3)/5 = 255/5 = 51)

D6. Find the cycle index of the rotation group of the cube acting on its
    faces, and hence the number of ways to colour the faces with k colours.
    Evaluate for k = 2, 3, and use the pattern inventory to find how many
    colourings have 3 red and 3 blue faces, and 2 red, 2 blue, 2 green.
    Answer: Z = (x₁⁶ + 3x₁²x₂² + 6x₁²x₄ + 6x₂³ + 8x₃²)/24; count
    (k⁶ + 3k⁴ + 12k³ + 8k²)/24 = 10 (k = 2), 57 (k = 3); 2 with 3R3B; 6 with
    2R2B2G.
    Teacher explains: The 24 rotations and their action on the 6 faces:
       identity                              1    x₁⁶
       90°/270° about face axes (3 axes)     6    x₁²x₄   (2 faces fixed)
       180° about face axes                  3    x₁²x₂²
       120°/240° about vertex axes (4 axes)  8    x₃²     (two 3-cycles)
       180° about edge-midpoint axes (6)     6    x₂³
    1 + 6 + 3 + 8 + 6 = 24 ✓. PÓLYA: put every xᵢ = k:
       (k⁶ + 6k³ + 3k⁴ + 8k² + 6k³)/24 = (k⁶ + 3k⁴ + 12k³ + 8k²)/24.
       k = 2: (64 + 48 + 96 + 32)/24 = 240/24 = 10
       k = 3: (729 + 243 + 324 + 72)/24 = 1368/24 = 57
    PATTERN INVENTORY: substitute xᵢ = rⁱ + bⁱ. The coefficient of r³b³:
       x₁⁶ → C(6, 3) = 20;  x₁²x₄ → (r + b)²(r⁴ + b⁴): no r³b³ term, 0;
       x₁²x₂² → (r + b)²(r² + b²)²: r³b³ needs r¹b¹ × r²b²: 2 × 2 = 4, times 3
       = 12;  x₃² → (r³ + b³)²: 2, times 8 = 16;  x₂³ → (r² + b²)³: 0
       total (20 + 0 + 12 + 16 + 0)/24 = 48/24 = 2.
    (The two: three red faces meeting at a corner, or forming a 'band'.)
    With three colours, r²b²g²: from x₁⁶: 6!/(2!2!2!) = 90. For a 180° face
    rotation (x₁²x₂²) each swapped pair is one colour, using two colours
    twice, so the two fixed faces must both get the third colour: 3 × 2 = 6
    colourings, times 3 rotations = 18. Edge rotations (x₂³): the three
    pairs get the three colours, 3! = 6, times 6 = 36. Others 0.
    (90 + 18 + 36)/24 = 144/24 = 6. Common
    mistakes: forgetting the edge rotations; thinking a 90° rotation fixes
    no face. Now you try: colour the faces with 6 different colours, each
    used once. (720/24 = 30, since only the identity fixes such a colouring)

D7. Count the simple graphs on 4 unlabelled vertices by applying Pólya's
    theorem to S₄ acting on the 6 edges of K₄, and find how many have
    m edges for each m.
    Answer: Z = (x₁⁶ + 9x₁²x₂² + 8x₃² + 6x₂x₄)/24; 11 graphs; by edges
    1, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 1 (m = 0, ..., 6).
    Teacher explains: A graph is a 2-colouring of the edges of K₄ (edge
    present / absent); isomorphic graphs are in the same S₄-orbit. Work out
    how each vertex permutation moves the 6 edges 12, 13, 14, 23, 24, 34:
       identity (1): all 6 fixed                         x₁⁶
       transposition (12) (6 of them): 12, 34 fixed;
         13 ↔ 23, 14 ↔ 24                                x₁²x₂²
       double transposition (12)(34) (3): 12, 34 fixed;
         13 ↔ 24, 14 ↔ 23                                x₁²x₂²
       3-cycle (123) (8): 12 → 23 → 13, 14 → 24 → 34    x₃²
       4-cycle (1234) (6): 12 → 23 → 34 → 14, 13 ↔ 24    x₂x₄
    So Z = (x₁⁶ + 9x₁²x₂² + 8x₃² + 6x₂x₄)/24. Number of graphs:
       (64 + 9 × 16 + 8 × 4 + 6 × 4)/24 = 264/24 = 11.
    Inventory with xᵢ = 1 + tⁱ (t marks an edge): the coefficient of t³ is
       [C(6, 3) + 9 × (coeff of t³ in (1 + t)²(1 + t²)² = 4)
        + 8 × 2 + 6 × 0]/24 = (20 + 36 + 16 + 0)/24 = 3
    (triangle + isolated vertex, path P₄, star K₁,₃). The full list
    1, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 1 is symmetric because complementing swaps m and
    6 − m. Common mistakes: using the cycle index of S₄ on VERTICES (that
    counts vertex colourings); forgetting that (12) fixes edge 34. Now you
    try: graphs on 3 vertices. (S₃ on 3 edges acts like on vertices:
    (8 + 3 × 4 + 2 × 2)/6 = 4)

D8. Define a BIBD(v, b, r, k, λ). Prove bk = vr and λ(v − 1) = r(k − 1), and
    Fisher's inequality b ≥ v. Find the parameters of the design of lines of
    the affine plane of order 3, and describe the Fano plane.
    Answer: proofs below; AG(2, 3): (9, 12, 4, 3, 1); Fano (7, 7, 3, 3, 1).
    Teacher explains: DOUBLE COUNTING. (1) Count pairs (point, block) with
    the point in the block: by blocks bk, by points vr, so bk = vr. (2) Fix a
    point P and count pairs (Q, B) with Q ≠ P and P, Q ∈ B: each of the
    v − 1 points Q lies with P in λ blocks, giving λ(v − 1); each of the r
    blocks through P has k − 1 other points, giving r(k − 1). FISHER: let N
    be the v × b incidence matrix (N_{P,B} = 1 if P ∈ B). Entry (P, Q) of NNᵀ
    counts blocks containing both P and Q: r on the diagonal, λ off it:
       NNᵀ = (r − λ)I + λJ   (J = all-ones matrix).
    Its eigenvalues are r − λ + λv = rk (on the all-ones vector) and r − λ
    (v − 1 times), so det = rk(r − λ)^(v−1). Since k < v, λ(v − 1) = r(k − 1)
    gives r > λ, so det ≠ 0 and NNᵀ has rank v. But rank(NNᵀ) ≤ rank N ≤ b.
    Hence b ≥ v. ∎ AFFINE PLANE AG(2, 3): points Z₃ × Z₃ (v = 9), lines are
    the solutions of ax + by = c (k = 3); any two points determine one line
    (λ = 1). Then r = λ(v − 1)/(k − 1) = 8/2 = 4 and b = vr/k = 36/3 = 12:
    four parallel classes (slopes 0, 1, 2, ∞) of three lines each. FANO:
    points 1, ..., 7, lines {1,2,4}, {2,3,5}, {3,4,6}, {4,5,7}, {5,6,1},
    {6,7,2}, {7,1,3} (translates of {1, 2, 4} mod 7, because the differences
    of {1, 2, 4} give every nonzero residue exactly once: a DIFFERENCE SET).
    v = b = 7, r = k = 3, λ = 1: SYMMETRIC, the projective plane of order 2.
    Common mistakes: confusing r (blocks per point) with k (points per
    block); assuming the necessary conditions guarantee existence. Now you
    try: does a 2-(16, 6, 1) design exist? (r = 15/5 = 3, b = 16 × 3/6 = 8 < 16:
    violates Fisher, no)

D9. Prove that a Steiner triple system STS(v) can exist only if v ≡ 1 or 3
    (mod 6). Construct STS(9). Find the parameters of a projective plane of
    order n and explain why there is none of order 6.
    Answer: v ≡ 1, 3 (mod 6) from integrality of r, b; STS(9) = the 12 lines
    of AG(2, 3); projective plane: v = b = n² + n + 1, k = r = n + 1, λ = 1;
    order 6 is excluded by Bruck-Ryser-Chowla.
    Teacher explains: For k = 3, λ = 1: r = (v − 1)/2 must be an integer, so v
    is ODD; b = vr/3 = v(v − 1)/6 must be an integer, so 3 | v(v − 1), i.e.
    v ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 3). Odd and ≡ 0, 1 (mod 3) means v ≡ 3 or 1 (mod 6).
    (Kirkman 1847 proved these v all work.) STS(9): write the points as a
    3 × 3 grid
       1 2 3
       4 5 6
       7 8 9
    Triples: 3 rows, 3 columns, 3 'diagonals' {1,5,9}, {2,6,7}, {3,4,8} and
    3 anti-diagonals {3,5,7}, {1,6,8}, {2,4,9}: 12 = 9 × 8/6 triples, and
    every pair appears once (e.g. 1 and 6 only in {1,6,8}). PROJECTIVE PLANE
    of order n: every line has n + 1 points, any two points on one line, any
    two lines meet in one point. Through a point P there are n + 1 lines,
    each with n further points, so v = 1 + (n + 1)n = n² + n + 1 = b. Order 6:
    v = 43, k = 7, λ = 1 symmetric with v odd; BRC requires a nonzero
    solution of x² = 6y² − z² (since (v − 1)/2 = 21 is odd), i.e.
    x² + z² = 6y². Take a solution with gcd(x, y, z) = 1. Squares are 0 or
    1 mod 3, so x² + z² ≡ 0 (mod 3) forces 3 | x and 3 | z; then 9 | 6y²,
    so 3 | y, contradicting gcd 1. No solution, so no plane of order 6 —
    matching Tarry's result that there are not even two orthogonal Latin
    squares of order 6. Common mistakes:
    writing v ≡ 1, 3 (mod 6) as 'v odd'; forgetting that STS(3) (one block)
    also counts. Now you try: how many triples in STS(15), and through each
    point? (b = 15 × 14/6 = 35, r = 7)

D10. Define orthogonal Latin squares. Prove that there are at most n − 1
     mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order n, and construct a complete
     set of MOLS of order 5. Explain the link with projective planes.
     Answer: at most n − 1; Lₐ(i, j) = ai + j (mod 5), a = 1, 2, 3, 4.
     Teacher explains: L and M (n × n, symbols 0, ..., n − 1) are ORTHOGONAL
     when the pairs (L(i, j), M(i, j)) run through all n² pairs exactly once.
     Renaming symbols in one square keeps orthogonality, so we may make the
     FIRST ROW of every square 0, 1, ..., n − 1. Now look at cell (2, 1)
     (second row, first column). In each square it cannot be 0 (column 1
     already has 0 at the top). If two squares had the same symbol s there,
     the pair (s, s) would occur twice: at (1, s + 1) and at (2, 1). So
     the squares have DIFFERENT symbols from {1, ..., n − 1} there: at most
     n − 1 squares. ∎ CONSTRUCTION for a prime p: Lₐ(i, j) = ai + j mod p
     (a ≠ 0) is Latin (a ≠ 0 is invertible mod p). For a ≠ b, given a pair
     (s, t), the system ai + j = s, bi + j = t has the unique solution
     i = (s − t)(a − b)⁻¹, j = s − ai: orthogonal. For p = 5 this gives 4 MOLS;
     for instance L₁ has rows 01234, 12340, 23401, ... and L₂ has rows
     01234, 23401, 40123, 12340, 34012. Over GF(q) the same works for prime
     powers. LINK: n − 1 MOLS of order n exist ⇔ a projective plane of order
     n exists (rows, columns and each square's symbols give the n + 1
     parallel classes of an affine plane of order n). Mod 4 the recipe fails
     (a = 2 is not invertible), but GF(4) gives 3 MOLS of order 4. Euler
     conjectured no pair for n ≡ 2 (mod 4); true only for n = 2 and 6
     (Bose-Shrikhande-Parker 1959). Common mistakes: using Z₄ or Z₆ as if
     they were fields; normalising rows but forgetting cell (2, 1) is
     restricted. Now you try: are L₁ and L₃ (ai + j mod 4) orthogonal of
     order 4? (No: a − b = 2 is not invertible mod 4; e.g. pairs repeat)

D11. Prove R(3, 3) = 6. Prove R(s, t) ≤ R(s − 1, t) + R(s, t − 1) and deduce
     R(s, t) ≤ C(s + t − 2, s − 1). Show that R(3, 4) ≤ 9.
     Answer: proofs below; R(3, 4) ≤ 9 (in fact = 9).
     Teacher explains: R(3, 3) ≤ 6: in a red/blue K₆ take a vertex v; it has
     5 edges, so by PIGEONHOLE at least 3 have the same colour, say red to
     a, b, c. If any of ab, bc, ca is red, it forms a red triangle with v;
     otherwise abc is a blue triangle. R(3, 3) > 5: colour the pentagon's
     5 sides red and its 5 diagonals blue: the red graph is a 5-cycle and
     the blue graph is another 5-cycle (the pentagram), and neither contains
     a triangle. RECURRENCE: let N = R(s − 1, t) + R(s, t − 1) and colour K_N.
     A vertex v has N − 1 neighbours, so it has either at least R(s − 1, t)
     red neighbours or at least R(s, t − 1) blue ones (else
     N − 1 ≤ R(s − 1, t) − 1 + R(s, t − 1) − 1). In the first case the red
     neighbours contain a red K_{s−1} (add v: red K_s) or a blue K_t; the
     second case is symmetric. Since R(2, t) = t = C(t, 1) and Pascal's rule
     C(s + t − 2, s − 1) = C(s + t − 3, s − 2) + C(s + t − 3, s − 1), induction
     gives R(s, t) ≤ C(s + t − 2, s − 1). R(3, 4) ≤ R(2, 4) + R(3, 3) = 4 + 6
     = 10. Improve to 9: suppose K₉ has no red K₃ and no blue K₄. Each vertex
     has ≤ 3 red neighbours (4 red neighbours: if two are joined red we have
     a red triangle, otherwise they form a blue K₄) and ≤ 5 blue neighbours
     (6 blue neighbours contain a red K₃ or a blue K₃, giving a blue K₄ with
     v). Degree 8 forces exactly 3 red and 5 blue at every vertex; but then
     the red graph has 9 × 3/2 red edges, not an integer. Contradiction.
     (The circulant graph on Z₈ with red differences ±1, 4 shows R(3, 4) > 8.)
     Common mistakes: in R(3, 3) taking only 2 same-coloured edges; mixing
     up which colour is required for which clique. Now you try: bound
     R(4, 4) by the recurrence. (R(3, 4) + R(4, 3) = 18, and R(4, 4) = 18)

D12. Prove Erdős's lower bound R(k, k) > 2^(k/2) (k ≥ 3) by the
     probabilistic method, and the Erdős-Szekeres theorem: every sequence
     of n² + 1 distinct real numbers has a monotone subsequence of length
     n + 1. Show the latter is sharp for n = 3.
     Answer: proofs below; 3, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4, 9, 8, 7 has no monotone
     subsequence of length 4.
     Teacher explains: ERDŐS: colour the edges of K_N red/blue at random,
     independently with probability ½. A fixed k-set is monochromatic with
     probability 2 × 2^(−C(k,2)) = 2^(1 − C(k,2)). The expected number of
     monochromatic k-sets is
        C(N, k) 2^(1 − C(k,2)) < (N^k/k!) 2^(1 − k(k−1)/2).
     Take N = ⌊2^(k/2)⌋: N^k ≤ 2^(k²/2), so the bound is
        2^(1 + k/2)/k! < 1   for k ≥ 3.
     Expected number < 1 means SOME colouring has no monochromatic K_k, so
     R(k, k) > N. (k = 10: R(10, 10) > 32; nobody knows an explicit
     colouring nearly as good.) ERDŐS-SZEKERES: to each term aᵢ attach
     (uᵢ, dᵢ) = lengths of the longest increasing / decreasing subsequences
     ENDING at aᵢ. For i < j: if aᵢ < aⱼ then uⱼ > uᵢ; if aᵢ > aⱼ then dⱼ > dᵢ.
     So the n² + 1 pairs are all different. If every uᵢ, dᵢ were ≤ n there
     would be only n² possible pairs: PIGEONHOLE gives a contradiction, so
     some uᵢ or dᵢ ≥ n + 1. ∎ SHARP: 3, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4, 9, 8, 7 (n² = 9 terms):
     an increasing subsequence takes at most one term from each block
     (length ≤ 3); a decreasing one stays in one block (length ≤ 3).
     Common mistakes: in Erdős' argument forgetting the factor 2 (two
     colours); in Erdős-Szekeres labelling with lengths of subsequences
     STARTING at aᵢ but comparing in the wrong direction. Now you try: a
     sequence of 10 distinct numbers must contain a monotone subsequence of
     what length? (4, since 10 = 3² + 1)
