M12. Pigeonhole and Ramsey-type results.
     a) longest monotone subsequence guaranteed in 10 distinct numbers
     b) longest sequence of distinct numbers with no monotone subsequence of
        length 4
     c) Schur number S(2) (largest N with a 2-colouring of 1..N with no
        monochromatic x + y = z)
     d) S(3)
     e) van der Waerden W(2, 3)
     f) least number of points in general position forcing a convex
        quadrilateral; a convex pentagon
     g) 5 points in a unit square: two are within what distance?
     h) people needed to guarantee two born in the same month
     i) from n + 1 numbers in {1, ..., 2n}: guaranteed pair that is coprime?
     j) from n + 1 numbers in {1, ..., 2n}: one divides another?
     k) smallest group guaranteeing 4 mutual friends or 4 mutual strangers
     l) can K₁₆ be 3-coloured with no monochromatic triangle?
     m) a 2-colouring of {1, 2, 3, 4} with no monochromatic x + y = z
     n) any 2-colouring of the plane: two points at distance 1 of the same
        colour?
     Answers:
       a) 4               b) 9               c) 4
       d) 13              e) 9               f) 5; 9
       g) √2/2 ≈ 0.707    h) 13              i) yes (two consecutive)
       j) yes (same odd part)                k) 18
       l) yes (since R(3, 3, 3) = 17)        m) red {1, 4}, blue {2, 3}
       n) yes (an equilateral triangle of side 1 has two vertices alike)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: write PIE as a table with columns k, Sₖ, sign, and compute
  every intersection by describing it in words first ('multiples of 6');
  check small cases by listing (D₃ = 2, 3 dice totalling 15). For symmetry
  counting, physically list the rotations of a cube with a real die and
  write the cycle type of each before substituting; a Burnside sum that is
  not divisible by |G| signals an error. For designs, drill the two counting
  identities until automatic. Harder: prove the Möbius inversion formula
  on the lattice of subsets and show that PIE is its special case; derive
  the ménage formula Uₙ = ∑(−1)ᵏ(2n/(2n − k))C(2n − k, k)(n − k)!; count
  necklaces with Möbius to get the number of irreducible polynomials of
  degree n over GF(q); prove that an affine plane of order n gives n − 1
  MOLS; prove Schur's theorem from R(3, 3, ..., 3); and show via Goodman's
  formula that every 2-colouring of K₆ has at least two monochromatic
  triangles.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.44 — MATHEMATICAL LOGIC: PROPOSITIONAL AND PREDICATE LOGIC,
COMPLETENESS, GÖDEL'S INCOMPLETENESS THEOREMS (OVERVIEW)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - PROPOSITIONAL SYNTAX: formulas are built from ATOMS p, q, r, ... by the
    connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔ (and ⊥); unique readability lets us define
    things by recursion on formulas and prove them by INDUCTION on formulas.
  - SEMANTICS: a VALUATION v assigns T/F to the atoms and extends by truth
    tables. φ is a TAUTOLOGY (⊨ φ) if true under every v, a CONTRADICTION if
    under none, SATISFIABLE if under some. SEMANTIC CONSEQUENCE Γ ⊨ φ: every
    v making all of Γ true makes φ true. φ ≡ ψ iff ⊨ φ ↔ ψ. Γ ⊨ φ iff
    Γ ∪ {¬φ} is unsatisfiable.
  - NORMAL FORMS: every truth function is given by a DNF (OR of the true
    rows' MINTERMS) and a CNF (AND of clauses ruling out the false rows).
    There are 2^(2ⁿ) truth functions of n atoms. FUNCTIONALLY COMPLETE sets:
    {¬, ∧}, {¬, ∨}, {¬, →}, {NAND ↑}, {NOR ↓}, {→, ⊥}. NOT complete: {∧, ∨}
    and {∧, ∨, →, ↔} (they preserve 'all true'), {¬, ↔} (only affine
    functions). POST'S criterion: complete iff not inside one of the five
    classes (0-preserving, 1-preserving, monotone, self-dual, affine).
  - PROOF SYSTEMS: HILBERT system with axioms A1 φ → (ψ → φ),
    A2 (φ → (ψ → χ)) → ((φ → ψ) → (φ → χ)), A3 (¬ψ → ¬φ) → (φ → ψ) and the
    single rule MODUS PONENS. Γ ⊢ φ means there is a derivation. DEDUCTION
    THEOREM: Γ ∪ {φ} ⊢ ψ ⇔ Γ ⊢ φ → ψ. Natural deduction and RESOLUTION
    (clauses; from C ∨ p and D ∨ ¬p infer C ∨ D; a set of clauses is
    unsatisfiable iff the empty clause □ can be derived) are alternatives.
  - SOUNDNESS (Γ ⊢ φ ⇒ Γ ⊨ φ) and COMPLETENESS (Γ ⊨ φ ⇒ Γ ⊢ φ) of
    propositional logic. COMPACTNESS: Γ is satisfiable iff every finite
    subset is (consequence: an infinite graph is k-colourable iff every
    finite subgraph is). SAT is decidable (by truth tables; NP-complete).
  - FIRST-ORDER (PREDICATE) LANGUAGE: constant, function and relation
    symbols, =, variables, ∀, ∃. TERMS and FORMULAS; FREE and BOUND
    occurrences; a SENTENCE has no free variables. SUBSTITUTION φ(x := t)
    is allowed only if t is FREE FOR x (no variable of t gets captured):
    rename bound variables first.
  - STRUCTURES: a structure M has a non-empty DOMAIN and interprets each
    symbol; M ⊨ φ[s] (satisfaction under an assignment s) is defined by
    recursion; M ⊨ ∀xφ iff φ holds for every value of x. φ is VALID if true
    in every structure; M is a MODEL of a theory T if M ⊨ every sentence of
    T; T ⊨ φ if every model of T satisfies φ.
  - LAWS: ¬∀xφ ≡ ∃x¬φ; ∀x(φ ∧ ψ) ≡ ∀xφ ∧ ∀xψ; ∃x(φ ∨ ψ) ≡ ∃xφ ∨ ∃xψ; but
    ∀x(φ ∨ ψ) ⊭ ∀xφ ∨ ∀xψ and ∃xφ ∧ ∃xψ ⊭ ∃x(φ ∧ ψ). ∃x∀yφ ⊨ ∀y∃xφ, not
    conversely. If x is not free in ψ: ∀x(φ → ψ) ≡ ∃xφ → ψ. Every formula has
    an equivalent PRENEX form Q₁x₁...Qₙxₙ φ (φ quantifier-free); SKOLEM form
    replaces each ∃y by a new function of the preceding ∀-variables
    (equisatisfiable, not equivalent).
  - GÖDEL'S COMPLETENESS THEOREM (1929): for first-order logic Γ ⊨ φ ⇔
    Γ ⊢ φ; equivalently every CONSISTENT set of sentences has a MODEL
    (HENKIN's proof: add witnesses, extend to a maximal consistent set, build
    the term model). The valid sentences are recursively enumerable, but by
    CHURCH-TURING (1936) not decidable.
  - COMPACTNESS (first order): Γ has a model iff every finite subset does.
    LÖWENHEIM-SKOLEM: a countable theory with an infinite model has models of
    every infinite cardinality (in particular a countable one: SKOLEM'S
    PARADOX for ZFC). Consequences: 'finite', 'connected', 'torsion',
    'well-ordered' are not first-order expressible; PA and Th(N) have
    NONSTANDARD models; an infinite structure is never characterised up to
    isomorphism by first-order sentences.
  - ARITHMETIC: PEANO ARITHMETIC PA (0, S, +, ·, with the induction scheme)
    and the weak finite theory Q. GÖDEL NUMBERING codes symbols, formulas and
    proofs as numbers (e.g. 2^(a₁)3^(a₂)5^(a₃)...); 'x codes a proof of the
    formula coded by y' is a computable relation, REPRESENTABLE in Q, giving
    a provability formula Prov_T(y). DIAGONAL LEMMA: for every ψ(x) there is
    a sentence G with T ⊢ G ↔ ψ(⌜G⌝).
  - FIRST INCOMPLETENESS THEOREM (Gödel 1931, Rosser 1936): if T is
    CONSISTENT, EFFECTIVELY AXIOMATISED (recursively enumerable) and contains
    Q, then T is INCOMPLETE: some sentence G has T ⊬ G and T ⊬ ¬G (G 'says'
    'I am not provable', and is true in N if T is sound). SECOND
    INCOMPLETENESS THEOREM: such T (extending PA) does not prove its own
    consistency Con(T). TARSKI: arithmetical truth is not definable in
    arithmetic.
  - LIMITS OF THE HYPOTHESES: true arithmetic Th(N) is complete (but not
    r.e.); PRESBURGER arithmetic (no ·) and real closed fields / Tarski's
    geometry are complete and DECIDABLE. Natural independent statements:
    Con(PA), GOODSTEIN'S theorem and PARIS-HARRINGTON (true, unprovable in
    PA); CH and AC are independent of ZF(C).
  - TRAPS: 'p → q' is true when p is false; ⊨ (semantic) vs ⊢ (syntactic);
    completeness (of a logic: provable = valid) vs completeness (of a
    theory: decides every sentence); 'unprovable' vs 'false'; Gödel's
    theorems do not say every theory is incomplete (they need the
    hypotheses), nor that mathematics is inconsistent.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Use truth tables to show that ((p → q) ∧ (q → r)) → (p → r) and Peirce's
    law ((p → q) → p) → p are tautologies. Decide whether
    (p → q) → r ⊨ p → (q → r) and whether p → (q → r) ⊨ (p → q) → r.
    Answer: both tautologies; the first consequence holds; the second fails
    at p = q = r = F.
    Teacher explains: A tautology must be T in all rows. For the first,
    the only way an implication X → (p → r) is false is X true and p → r
    false, i.e. p = T, r = F. Then X = (T → q) ∧ (q → F) = q ∧ ¬q = F. So no
    row makes it false: tautology (the TRANSITIVITY of →). Peirce's law:
       p  q  | p → q | (p → q) → p | ((p → q) → p) → p
       T  T  |   T   |      T      |         T
       T  F  |   F   |      T      |         T
       F  T  |   T   |      F      |         T
       F  F  |   T   |      F      |         T
    Consequence 1: we need every row with (p → q) → r true to make
    p → (q → r) true. The conclusion is false only at p = T, q = T, r = F;
    there p → q = T, so the premise is T → F = F. So no counter-row: the
    consequence HOLDS. Consequence 2: try to make the premise true and the
    conclusion (p → q) → r false: need r = F and p → q = T. Take p = q = F:
    premise p → (q → r) = F → ... = T, conclusion (F → F) → F = T → F = F.
    Counter-valuation found, so it FAILS. The method: to test Γ ⊨ φ look
    only for rows where φ is false. Common mistakes: filling truth tables
    with 'F → anything = F'; declaring a consequence valid after checking a
    few rows. Now you try: is (p → q) ∨ (q → p) a tautology? (Yes: if q = T
    the first disjunct is T, if q = F the second is T)

D2. Prove that every truth function has a DNF and a CNF. Find both for the
    majority function maj(p, q, r) (true when at least two arguments are
    true) and for (p ∨ q) → r.
    Answer: maj: DNF (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r) ∨ (q ∧ r), CNF (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r) ∧
    (q ∨ r). (p ∨ q) → r: CNF (¬p ∨ r) ∧ (¬q ∨ r), DNF (¬p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r.
    Teacher explains: Let f be a truth function of p₁, ..., pₙ. For each row
    ε = (ε₁, ..., εₙ) with f(ε) = T form the MINTERM ℓ₁ ∧ ... ∧ ℓₙ, where ℓᵢ
    is pᵢ if εᵢ = T and ¬pᵢ otherwise; the minterm is true in that row only.
    The OR of all these minterms is true exactly in the rows where f is
    true: a DNF (if f is never true use p₁ ∧ ¬p₁). Dually, for each FALSE
    row form the clause that is false only in that row (ℓᵢ negated), and
    AND them: a CNF (or apply the DNF result to ¬f and push the negation
    in with De Morgan). Majority: the true rows are TTT, TTF, TFT, FTT; the
    full DNF has 4 minterms, which simplify (TTT is covered by any pair):
       maj = (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r) ∨ (q ∧ r).
    The false rows are FFF, FFT, FTF, TFF; each false row has at least two
    F's, and 'at least two true' fails iff some pair is both false:
       maj = (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r) ∧ (q ∨ r).
    (p ∨ q) → r ≡ ¬(p ∨ q) ∨ r ≡ (¬p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r (DNF), and distributing ∨ over
    ∧: (¬p ∨ r) ∧ (¬q ∨ r) (CNF). Common mistakes: in a CNF writing the
    clause for a false row with the literals NOT negated; forgetting that a
    DNF can be exponentially long (CNF/DNF conversion can blow up). Now you
    try: DNF and CNF of p ↔ q. ((p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q); (¬p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ ¬q))

D3. Show that {↑} (NAND) is functionally complete, but that {∧, ∨, →, ↔}
    and {¬, ↔} are not. How many binary connectives are there?
    Answer: ¬p ≡ p ↑ p and p ∧ q ≡ (p ↑ q) ↑ (p ↑ q), so {↑} can express the
    complete set {¬, ∧}. The other two sets cannot express ¬ and ∧
    respectively. There are 2⁴ = 16 binary connectives.
    Teacher explains: By D2 every truth function is a DNF, which uses only
    ¬, ∧, ∨; and p ∨ q ≡ ¬(¬p ∧ ¬q), so {¬, ∧} is complete. Now NAND:
       p ↑ p = ¬(p ∧ p) = ¬p
       (p ↑ q) ↑ (p ↑ q) = ¬(p ↑ q) = p ∧ q
       (p ↑ p) ↑ (q ↑ q) = ¬(¬p ∧ ¬q) = p ∨ q
    so {↑} is complete (so is {↓}; these are the only two complete single
    binary connectives). {∧, ∨, →, ↔}: prove by INDUCTION on formulas that
    any formula built from atoms with these connectives is TRUE under the
    valuation making every atom true (T ∧ T, T ∨ T, T → T, T ↔ T are all T).
    ¬p is false there, so ¬ is not expressible. {¬, ↔}: identify T = 1,
    F = 0; then ¬p = 1 + p and p ↔ q = 1 + p + q (mod 2). By induction every
    formula over p, q in these connectives is AFFINE: a + bp + cq (mod 2),
    which has an EVEN number (0, 2 or 4) of true rows. p ∧ q has exactly one
    true row, so it is not expressible. Counting: a binary connective is a
    function {T, F}² → {T, F}: 2^(2²) = 16 (with n atoms, 2^(2ⁿ): 256 for
    n = 3). Common mistakes: 'showing' incompleteness by failing to find an
    expression (you need an INVARIANT, as above); forgetting that constants
    can matter ({→, ⊥} is complete since ¬p ≡ p → ⊥). Now you try: express
    p → q with NAND only. (p ↑ (q ↑ q), since p ↑ ¬q = ¬(p ∧ ¬q))

D4. In the Hilbert system (A1, A2, A3, modus ponens) give a formal proof of
    p → p. State the deduction theorem and sketch its proof, and use it to
    show ⊢ (p → q) → ((q → r) → (p → r)).
    Answer: five-line proof below; Γ ∪ {φ} ⊢ ψ ⇔ Γ ⊢ φ → ψ.
    Teacher explains: The five lines:
       1. (p → ((p → p) → p)) → ((p → (p → p)) → (p → p))   A2
       2. p → ((p → p) → p)                                 A1
       3. (p → (p → p)) → (p → p)                           MP 2, 1
       4. p → (p → p)                                       A1
       5. p → p                                             MP 4, 3
    DEDUCTION THEOREM. (⇐) If Γ ⊢ φ → ψ then from Γ ∪ {φ} add φ and use MP.
    (⇒) Let ψ₁, ..., ψₙ = ψ be a derivation from Γ ∪ {φ}; show by induction
    on i that Γ ⊢ φ → ψᵢ. If ψᵢ is an axiom or in Γ: ψᵢ, then A1
    ψᵢ → (φ → ψᵢ), MP. If ψᵢ = φ: use ⊢ φ → φ (above). If ψᵢ comes by MP from
    ψⱼ and ψₖ = ψⱼ → ψᵢ: by induction Γ ⊢ φ → ψⱼ and Γ ⊢ φ → (ψⱼ → ψᵢ); A2
    gives (φ → (ψⱼ → ψᵢ)) → ((φ → ψⱼ) → (φ → ψᵢ)), and two MPs give
    Γ ⊢ φ → ψᵢ. ∎ APPLICATION: from the hypotheses p → q, q → r, p:
       p, p → q ⊢ q (MP);  q, q → r ⊢ r (MP).
    So {p → q, q → r, p} ⊢ r; apply the deduction theorem three times:
    ⊢ (p → q) → ((q → r) → (p → r)). The theorem turns 'assume and derive'
    (how mathematicians argue) into a formal proof. Common mistakes: using
    the deduction theorem in first-order logic after generalising on a
    variable free in the hypothesis; writing MP in the wrong order (MP needs
    φ and φ → ψ). Now you try: which axiom instance and MP give q ⊢ p → q?
    (A1: q → (p → q), then MP with q)

D5. Use resolution to show that {p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r, ¬q ∨ r, ¬r} is
    unsatisfiable, and hence that p ∨ q, p → r, q → r ⊨ r. Explain why
    resolution is sound, and decide satisfiability of
    {p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r, ¬q ∨ ¬r, ¬p ∨ ¬r}.
    Answer: derivation of □ below; the second set is satisfiable with
    p = F, q = T, r = F.
    Teacher explains: RESOLUTION RULE: from clauses C ∨ ℓ and D ∨ ¬ℓ infer
    C ∨ D. SOUND: any valuation satisfying both makes ℓ true or false; if ℓ
    is true, D must be true, if false, C must be; either way C ∨ D is true.
    So if □ (the empty clause, never true) is derived, the set was
    unsatisfiable. Derivation:
       1. p ∨ q     2. ¬p ∨ r     3. ¬q ∨ r     4. ¬r
       5. q ∨ r     (1, 2 on p)
       6. r         (5, 3 on q)
       7. □         (6, 4 on r)
    The four clauses are the CNF of {p ∨ q, p → r, q → r, ¬r}; they are
    unsatisfiable, so every valuation satisfying the first three makes r
    true: p ∨ q, p → r, q → r ⊨ r ('proof by cases'). Resolution is also
    REFUTATION COMPLETE: every unsatisfiable finite clause set yields □.
    Second set: resolve ¬p ∨ r with ¬p ∨ ¬r to get ¬p; with p ∨ q get q;
    with ¬q ∨ ¬r get ¬r. Nothing more gives □ (the set of all resolvents
    closes without it), and indeed p = F, q = T, r = F satisfies all four
    clauses: p ∨ q = T, ¬p ∨ r = T, ¬q ∨ ¬r = T, ¬p ∨ ¬r = T. Common
    mistakes: resolving on two literals at once (from p ∨ q and ¬p ∨ ¬q you
    may NOT infer □); forgetting to negate the conclusion before refuting.
    Now you try: show {p, ¬p ∨ q, ¬q ∨ r, ¬r} unsatisfiable. (p with ¬p ∨ q
    gives q, with ¬q ∨ r gives r, with ¬r gives □)

D6. State soundness, completeness and compactness for propositional logic,
    sketch why completeness holds, and use compactness to prove that an
    infinite (countable) graph is 3-colourable if every finite subgraph is.
    Answer: statements below; the graph result follows by encoding
    colourings as satisfying valuations.
    Teacher explains: SOUNDNESS: Γ ⊢ φ ⇒ Γ ⊨ φ, by induction on derivations
    (axioms are tautologies; MP preserves truth). COMPLETENESS: Γ ⊨ φ ⇒
    Γ ⊢ φ. Sketch (Lindenbaum): it suffices that every CONSISTENT Γ (not
    deriving both ψ and ¬ψ) is satisfiable. List all formulas φ₁, φ₂, ...;
    add φₙ to Γ if that keeps consistency, otherwise add ¬φₙ (one of them
    always does). The limit Γ* is MAXIMAL consistent: for each φ exactly one
    of φ, ¬φ is in Γ*. Define v(p) = T iff p ∈ Γ*; induction on formulas
    shows v(φ) = T iff φ ∈ Γ*, so v satisfies Γ. COMPACTNESS: Γ satisfiable
    iff every finite subset is — because a proof of ⊥ from Γ uses only
    finitely many hypotheses. GRAPH: for each vertex v and colour
    i ∈ {1, 2, 3} take an atom p_{v,i} ('v has colour i'). Let Γ contain, for
    every vertex v, p_{v,1} ∨ p_{v,2} ∨ p_{v,3} and ¬(p_{v,i} ∧ p_{v,j})
    (i ≠ j), and for every edge uv and colour i, ¬(p_{u,i} ∧ p_{v,i}). A
    valuation satisfying Γ is exactly a proper 3-colouring. A finite subset
    of Γ mentions finitely many vertices; the finite subgraph on them is
    3-colourable, so that subset is satisfiable. By compactness Γ is
    satisfiable: the whole graph is 3-colourable (DE BRUIJN-ERDŐS). Common
    mistakes: confusing 'Γ is consistent' (syntactic) with 'Γ is
    satisfiable' (semantic) — completeness says they coincide; thinking
    compactness is about finite sets only. Now you try: use compactness to
    show every partial order on a countable set extends to a linear order.
    (Atoms p_{a<b}; the linear-order axioms plus the given relations are
    finitely satisfiable because finite partial orders extend (topological
    sort))

D7. For each formula list the free variables, and say whether it is a
    sentence: (a) ∀x (x < y); (b) ∀x ∃y (x < y); (c) ∀x R(x, y) → ∃y R(y, x);
    (d) ∃y (y + y = x). Explain when a term t may be substituted for x, using
    ∃y (y > x) with t = y. Translate into first-order logic: 'x is prime',
    'there are infinitely many primes', 'f is injective' and 'there is
    exactly one x with P(x)'.
    Answer: (a) {y}; (b) none, sentence; (c) {x, y} (y free in the
    antecedent, x in the consequent); (d) {x}. y is NOT free for x in
    ∃y (y > x). Translations below.
    Teacher explains: An occurrence of x is BOUND if it lies inside a
    quantifier ∀x or ∃x, FREE otherwise; the same letter can occur both
    ways, as in (c): in ∀x R(x, y) the y is free, and in ∃y R(y, x) the x is
    free. Such a formula is legal but confusing: rename to
    ∀u R(u, y) → ∃w R(w, x). SUBSTITUTION: ∃y (y > x) says 'something is
    bigger than x' (true in N for every x). Naively putting y for x gives
    ∃y (y > y), which is FALSE: the y got CAPTURED. The rule: t is free for
    x in φ if no free occurrence of x lies within the scope of a quantifier
    on a variable of t. Fix by renaming: ∃z (z > x), then substitute:
    ∃z (z > y). Translations (language of arithmetic, variables over N):
       x | y (divides):  ∃z (y = x · z)
       Prime(x):  1 < x ∧ ∀y ∀z (x = y · z → (y = 1 ∨ z = 1))
       infinitely many primes:  ∀x ∃p (x < p ∧ Prime(p))
       f injective:  ∀x ∀y (f(x) = f(y) → x = y)
       exactly one:  ∃x (P(x) ∧ ∀y (P(y) → y = x))
    Common mistakes: 'every student loves some course' written as
    ∀x (S(x) ∧ ∃y (C(y) ∧ L(x, y))) (that says everything is a student; use
    →: ∀x (S(x) → ∃y (C(y) ∧ L(x, y)))); and 'some student ...' written
    with → (∃x (S(x) → ...) is true if there is a non-student). Now you try:
    translate 'no student loves every course'. (¬∃x (S(x) ∧ ∀y (C(y) →
    L(x, y))), equivalently ∀x (S(x) → ∃y (C(y) ∧ ¬L(x, y))))

D8. Decide the truth of these sentences (language <) in N, Z, Q and R:
    σ₁ = ∀x ∃y (x < y), σ₂ = ∃x ∀y (x ≤ y), σ₃ = ∀x ∀y (x < y → ∃z (x < z ∧
    z < y)), σ₄ = ∀x ∃y (x < y ∧ ∀z (x < z → y ≤ z)). Then show that
    ∃x ∀y R(x, y) → ∀y ∃x R(x, y) is valid but its converse is not.
    Answer: σ₁: T T T T. σ₂: T F F F. σ₃: F F T T. σ₄: T T F F. Counter-model
    for the converse: N with R(x, y) meaning x > y.
    Teacher explains: σ₁ (no largest element): take y = x + 1 in each. σ₂
    (a least element): 0 in N; none in Z, Q, R. σ₃ (DENSITY): between 0 and
    1 there is no integer, so false in N and Z; in Q and R take
    z = (x + y)/2. σ₄ (every element has an IMMEDIATE SUCCESSOR): y = x + 1
    in N and Z; in Q, R there is no least element above x (if y > x then
    (x + y)/2 is smaller). Note that no first-order sentence in < separates
    Q from R (both are dense linear orders without end points, and that
    theory is complete); completeness of R needs quantification over sets.
    VALIDITY: suppose M ⊨ ∃x ∀y R(x, y): some a has R(a, b) for every b.
    Then for each b we can take x = a, so M ⊨ ∀y ∃x R(x, y). Valid, in every
    structure. CONVERSE: in N with R(x, y) := x > y, '∀y ∃x (x > y)' is true
    (x = y + 1) but '∃x ∀y (x > y)' is false (x > x fails). One structure
    where the premise is true and the conclusion false shows the
    implication is NOT valid. Common mistakes: evaluating σ₃ in Z as true
    ('take z between'—there may be none); believing a sentence true in all
    familiar structures must be valid. Now you try: is ∀x ∃y (y · y = x)
    true in R, C, [0, ∞) (with ·)? (F, T, T)

D9. Convert ∀x (∃y R(x, y) → ∃y S(y, x)) ∧ ¬∀z T(z) to prenex normal form,
    then Skolem form, and explain why the Skolem form is equisatisfiable
    but not equivalent.
    Answer: prenex ∃z ∀x ∀y ∃w ((R(x, y) → S(w, x)) ∧ ¬T(z)); Skolem
    ∀x ∀y ((R(x, y) → S(f(x, y), x)) ∧ ¬T(c)).
    Teacher explains: Use the rules (x not free in ψ):
       ∃xφ → ψ ≡ ∀x(φ → ψ)       φ → ∃xψ ≡ ∃x(φ → ψ)
       ¬∀xφ ≡ ∃x¬φ               (Qx φ) ∧ ψ ≡ Qx(φ ∧ ψ)
    and rename bound variables so that no clash occurs. Inside:
       ∃y R(x, y) → ∃y S(y, x)
         ≡ ∀y (R(x, y) → ∃w S(w, x))      (antecedent ∃ becomes ∀)
         ≡ ∀y ∃w (R(x, y) → S(w, x))
    so the first conjunct is ∀x ∀y ∃w (R(x, y) → S(w, x)); the second is
    ∃z ¬T(z). Pull out, first ∃z (z does not occur in the first part):
       ∃z ∀x ∀y ∃w ((R(x, y) → S(w, x)) ∧ ¬T(z)).
    SKOLEMISE from left to right: ∃z has no ∀ in front, so z becomes a new
    CONSTANT c; ∃w lies after ∀x ∀y, so w becomes f(x, y):
       ∀x ∀y ((R(x, y) → S(f(x, y), x)) ∧ ¬T(c)).
    EQUISATISFIABLE: if M satisfies the prenex form, choose (axiom of
    choice) a witness w for each (x, y) and call the choosing function f,
    and a witness c: M expanded by f, c satisfies the Skolem form;
    conversely the Skolem form clearly implies the prenex form. Not
    EQUIVALENT: the Skolem form has new symbols, and ∃z ¬T(z) does not imply
    ¬T(c) for an arbitrary interpretation of c. Skolem forms feed automatic
    theorem provers (resolution with unification). Common mistakes: turning
    the ∃ in an antecedent into ∃ (it becomes ∀); Skolemising ∃ with
    functions of ALL universal variables instead of only those before it.
    Now you try: Skolem form of ∀x ∃y ∀z ∃w S(x, y, z, w). (∀x ∀z S(x, f(x),
    z, g(x, z)))

D10. State Gödel's completeness theorem and outline Henkin's proof. Deduce
     the compactness theorem, and use it to show (a) there is no set of
     first-order sentences whose models are exactly the finite structures,
     and (b) there is a nonstandard model of true arithmetic Th(N).
     Answer: Γ ⊨ φ ⇔ Γ ⊢ φ (equivalently: consistent ⇒ has a model); (a) and
     (b) by compactness as below.
     Teacher explains: COMPLETENESS (Gödel 1929). Soundness (⊢ ⇒ ⊨) is easy.
     For the converse it suffices: every consistent Γ has a model (if
     Γ ⊬ φ then Γ ∪ {¬φ} is consistent, has a model, and that model shows
     Γ ⊭ φ). HENKIN: (1) add new constants and, for every formula φ(x), a
     WITNESS axiom ∃x φ(x) → φ(c_φ); this keeps consistency. (2) Extend to a
     MAXIMAL consistent set Γ* (Lindenbaum, as in D6). (3) Build the TERM
     MODEL: domain = closed terms modulo t ~ s iff (t = s) ∈ Γ*, with
     relations read off Γ*. By induction on formulas, M ⊨ φ iff φ ∈ Γ*; the
     witnesses handle ∃. COMPACTNESS: if every finite subset of Γ has a model
     it is consistent (a proof uses finitely many sentences and soundness
     applies), so Γ is consistent and has a model. (a) Let λₙ say 'there are
     at least n elements': ∃x₁...∃xₙ ⋀_{i<j} xᵢ ≠ xⱼ. If Σ had exactly the
     finite structures as models, Σ ∪ {λ₁, λ₂, ...} would be finitely
     satisfiable (a large finite model of Σ satisfies finitely many λₙ) but
     have no model (a model would be infinite). Contradiction. (b) Add a new
     constant c and the sentences c > 0, c > 1, c > 2, ... (numerals
     S...S0) to Th(N). Each finite subset holds in N (interpret c as a big
     number), so the whole set has a model M: it satisfies every sentence
     true in N, yet contains c larger than every standard number — a
     NONSTANDARD model (its order type is N followed by densely many copies
     of Z). Common mistakes: confusing this completeness (of the LOGIC) with
     the completeness of a theory (which Gödel's 1931 theorem denies for
     PA); thinking (b) contradicts induction (the set of standard numbers is
     not definable in M). Now you try: why does a theory with arbitrarily
     large finite models have an infinite model? (Add all λₙ: finitely
     satisfiable, so it has a model, necessarily infinite)

D11. Outline Gödel's first incompleteness theorem for a consistent,
     recursively axiomatised theory T ⊇ Q: Gödel numbering, representability,
     the diagonal lemma and the Gödel sentence. Why is G true (in N) if T is
     sound, and why are the hypotheses needed?
     Answer: T ⊢ G ↔ ¬Prov_T(⌜G⌝); if T is consistent T ⊬ G, and if T is
     ω-consistent (Rosser: consistent suffices with a modified sentence)
     T ⊬ ¬G. G is true because it says truly that it is unprovable. Without
     r.e. axioms (Th(N)) or without enough arithmetic (Presburger) the
     conclusion fails.
     Teacher explains: (1) GÖDEL NUMBERING: give each symbol a code and a
     string s₁...sₙ the number 2^(c₁)3^(c₂)...pₙ^(cₙ); proofs (sequences of
     formulas) are coded the same way. Unique factorisation lets us decode.
     (2) 'p codes a proof in T of the formula coded by y' is a DECIDABLE
     relation Prf_T(p, y), since T's axioms can be listed (r.e.) and checking
     a proof is mechanical. Every decidable relation is REPRESENTABLE in Q,
     so there is a formula Prf_T(p, y), and Prov_T(y) := ∃p Prf_T(p, y). If
     T ⊢ φ then T ⊢ Prov_T(⌜φ⌝) (the proof is a real number p, and Q proves
     true Σ₁ facts). (3) DIAGONAL LEMMA: for every formula ψ(y) there is a
     sentence G with T ⊢ G ↔ ψ(⌜G⌝) (built from the computable function
     taking the code of φ(x) to the code of φ(⌜φ⌝)). Take ψ = ¬Prov_T:
        T ⊢ G ↔ ¬Prov_T(⌜G⌝)      'G says: I am not provable in T'.
     (4) If T ⊢ G then T ⊢ Prov_T(⌜G⌝) by (2), and T ⊢ ¬Prov_T(⌜G⌝) by (3):
     T is INCONSISTENT. So a consistent T does not prove G. If T ⊢ ¬G then
     T ⊢ Prov_T(⌜G⌝), i.e. T ⊢ ∃p Prf(p, ⌜G⌝) while (as G is unprovable) for
     each actual n, T ⊢ ¬Prf(n, ⌜G⌝): ω-INCONSISTENT. Rosser's sentence ('for
     every proof of me there is a shorter proof of my negation') needs only
     consistency. TRUTH: in N, G ↔ 'no number codes a proof of G', which is
     the case: G is TRUE but unprovable (if T is sound). HYPOTHESES: Th(N),
     the set of all true sentences, is complete and consistent but not r.e.
     (no algorithm lists it); Presburger arithmetic (N, 0, S, +) is complete
     because it cannot represent multiplication/decidable relations.
     Common mistakes: 'Gödel showed there are true statements that can
     never be proved' (G is provable in the stronger T + Con(T); the claim
     is always relative to a fixed T); forgetting 'consistent'. Now you try:
     decode the Gödel number 1500 of a sequence coded as 2^(a₁)3^(a₂)5^(a₃).
     (1500 = 2² · 3 · 5³: (2, 1, 3))

D12. State Gödel's second incompleteness theorem, Tarski's undefinability
     theorem and Church's theorem, and explain how they relate to Hilbert's
     programme. Give examples of natural statements independent of PA or
     ZFC.
     Answer: If T ⊇ PA is consistent and r.e., T ⊬ Con(T); truth in N is not
     arithmetically definable; first-order validity is undecidable.
     Examples: Con(PA), Goodstein's theorem, Paris-Harrington (PA); CH,
     AC over ZF (set theory).
     Teacher explains: Let Con(T) := ¬Prov_T(⌜0 = 1⌝). The first theorem's
     argument 'if T is consistent then T ⊬ G' can itself be formalised in
     PA (using the Hilbert-Bernays-Löb derivability conditions), giving
       T ⊢ Con(T) → G.
     If T proved Con(T), MP would give T ⊢ G, contradicting the first
     theorem. So T ⊬ Con(T): the SECOND INCOMPLETENESS THEOREM. It ends
     HILBERT'S PROGRAMME of proving the consistency of mathematics by finite,
     elementary means inside mathematics itself (Gentzen proved Con(PA) in
     1936 but needed induction up to the ordinal ε₀, beyond PA). TARSKI: if
     some formula True(y) satisfied True(⌜φ⌝) ↔ φ for all sentences φ in N,
     the diagonal lemma with ψ = ¬True gives L with L ↔ ¬True(⌜L⌝) ↔ ¬L: the
     LIAR paradox, a contradiction. So truth is not definable (though
     provability is). CHURCH (and Turing): the set of valid first-order
     sentences is r.e. (by completeness, enumerate proofs) but NOT
     decidable; one encodes the HALTING PROBLEM — 'machine M halts' becomes
     'axioms of Q plus a description of M imply a halting sentence'.
     INDEPENDENT STATEMENTS: Con(PA); GOODSTEIN'S theorem (every Goodstein
     sequence reaches 0: true, unprovable in PA, Kirby-Paris 1982); the
     PARIS-HARRINGTON strengthening of finite Ramsey's theorem; in set
     theory the CONTINUUM HYPOTHESIS is neither provable (Cohen 1963) nor
     refutable (Gödel 1940) in ZFC. Common mistakes: 'PA + Con(PA) is
     complete' (no: it is still r.e. and consistent, so incomplete, with its
     own Gödel sentence); 'PA + ¬Con(PA) is inconsistent' (it is consistent
     if PA is, but UNSOUND: it has only nonstandard models). Now you try:
     which theories escape the incompleteness theorems: (i) Th(N), (ii)
     Presburger arithmetic, (iii) ZFC? ((i) complete, not r.e.; (ii) complete
     and decidable; (iii) incomplete if consistent)

M1. Classify as T (tautology), C (contradiction) or S (satisfiable but not a
    tautology).
    a) p ∨ ¬p                          b) p ∧ ¬p
    c) p → (q → p)                     d) (p → q) → (q → p)
    e) ((p → q) → p) → p               f) (p → q) ∨ (q → p)
    g) (p ∧ q) → (p ∨ q)               h) (p ∨ q) → (p ∧ q)
    i) ¬(p → q) ∧ q                    j) (p ↔ q) ↔ (¬p ↔ ¬q)
    k) ((p → q) ∧ (p → ¬q)) → ¬p       l) (p → (q → r)) → ((p → q) → (p → r))
    m) ((p → q) ∧ (q → r)) → (r → p)   n) (p ↔ q) ∧ (p ↔ ¬q)
    o) ((p ∨ q) ∧ (¬p ∨ r)) → (q ∨ r)  p) (p → q) ↔ (¬q → ¬p)
    q) p → (p ∧ q)                     r) (p ∧ (p → q)) → q
    s) (¬p → p) → p                    t) (p ⊕ q) ∧ (p ↔ q)

M2. Does the consequence hold? (Y, or N with a counter-valuation.)
    a) p, p → q ⊨ q                    b) q, p → q ⊨ p
    c) ¬q, p → q ⊨ ¬p                  d) ¬p, p → q ⊨ ¬q
    e) p ∨ q, ¬p ⊨ q                   f) p → q, q → r ⊨ p → r
    g) p ∨ q ⊨ p                       h) p → q ⊨ ¬q → ¬p
    i) p → (q ∨ r), ¬q ⊨ p → r         j) (p ∧ q) → r ⊨ (p → r) ∨ (q → r)
    k) (p ∨ q) → r ⊨ p → r             l) p → r ⊨ (p ∨ q) → r
    m) ∅ ⊨ p ∨ ¬p                      n) p ∧ ¬p ⊨ q
    o) p ↔ q, q ↔ r ⊨ p ↔ r            p) p → q, ¬p → q ⊨ q
    q) p ∨ q, p → r, q → s ⊨ r ∨ s     r) p → q, r → s, ¬q ∨ ¬s ⊨ ¬p ∨ ¬r
    s) p → q, r → s, q ∨ s ⊨ p ∨ r     t) (p → q) → r ⊨ p → (q → r)
    Answers:
      a) Y (modus ponens)        b) N (p = F, q = T; affirming the consequent)
      c) Y (modus tollens)       d) N (p = F, q = T; denying the antecedent)
      e) Y                       f) Y
      g) N (p = F, q = T)        h) Y
      i) Y                       j) Y
      k) Y                       l) N (p = F, q = T, r = F)
      m) Y                       n) Y (anything follows from a contradiction)
      o) Y                       p) Y
      q) Y (constructive dilemma) r) Y (destructive dilemma)
      s) N (p = q = r = F, s = T) t) Y

M3. Give a DNF and a CNF (simplified).
    a) p → q                           b) p ↔ q
    c) p ⊕ q                           d) ¬(p ∨ (q ∧ r))
    e) (p ∨ q) → r                     f) p → (q → r)
    g) maj(p, q, r)                    h) (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ r)
    i) ¬((p → q) → r)                  j) full DNF of p ⊕ q ⊕ r
    k) number of minterms in the full DNF of p ∨ q ∨ r; of maj; of p ⊕ q ⊕ r
    l) number of clauses in the full CNF of p ∧ q ∧ r (3 atoms)

      f) ¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ r (both forms)
      g) (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r) ∨ (q ∧ r);  (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r) ∧ (q ∨ r)
      h) as given (DNF);  (¬p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r)

      j) (p ∧ q ∧ r) ∨ (p ∧ ¬q ∧ ¬r) ∨ (¬p ∧ q ∧ ¬r) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q ∧ r)

M5. Resolution: derive □ (UNSAT) or give a satisfying valuation (SAT).
    a) {p}, {¬p}
    b) {p, q}, {¬p}, {¬q}
    c) {p, q}, {¬p, r}, {¬q, r}, {¬r}
    d) {p, q}, {¬p, q}, {p, ¬q}, {¬p, ¬q}
    e) {p, q}, {¬p, q}, {p, ¬q}
    f) {¬p, q}, {¬q, r}, {¬r, p}
    g) {p}, {¬p, q}, {¬q, r}, {¬r}
    h) {p, q, r}, {¬p, ¬q}, {¬q, ¬r}, {¬p, ¬r}
    i) {p, q}, {¬p, r}, {¬q, ¬r}, {¬p, ¬r}
    j) {p}, {¬p, q}, {¬p, ¬q, r}, {¬r, s}, {¬s, ¬q}
    k) {p, q}, {¬p, q}, {¬q, r}, {¬r, ¬q}
    l) pigeonhole: pᵢⱼ (pigeon i in hole j), i = 1, 2, 3, j = 1, 2
    Answers:
      a) UNSAT (□ at once)
      b) UNSAT ({p, q} + {¬p} → {q}, + {¬q} → □)
      c) UNSAT ({q, r}, {r}, □)
      d) UNSAT ({q} from the first two, {¬q} from the last two, □)
      e) SAT p = q = T
      f) SAT (all T, or all F)
      g) UNSAT ({q}, {r}, □)
      h) SAT (exactly one of p, q, r true)
      i) SAT p = F, q = T, r = F
      j) UNSAT (unit propagation p, q, r, s contradicts {¬s, ¬q})
      k) UNSAT ({q} from the first two; with {¬q, r}: {r}; with {¬r, ¬q}:
         {¬q}; with {q}: □)
      l) UNSAT (3 pigeons cannot fit injectively into 2 holes)

M9. Valid (V) or not (N, with a counter-model)?
    a) ∀x P(x) → ∃x P(x)
    b) ∃x P(x) → ∀x P(x)
    c) ∃x ∀y R(x, y) → ∀y ∃x R(x, y)
    d) ∀y ∃x R(x, y) → ∃x ∀y R(x, y)
    e) ∀x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) ↔ (∀x P(x) ∧ ∀x Q(x))
    f) ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)) → (∀x P(x) ∨ ∀x Q(x))
    g) ∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) → (∃x P(x) ∧ ∃x Q(x))
    h) (∃x P(x) ∧ ∃x Q(x)) → ∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x))
    i) ∃x (P(x) → ∀y P(y))
    j) ¬∀x P(x) ↔ ∃x ¬P(x)
    k) ∀x (P(x) → Q) ↔ (∃x P(x) → Q)   (x not free in Q)
    l) ∀x ∀y (R(x, y) → R(y, x)) → ∀x R(x, x)
    m) ∀x R(x, x) → ∀x ∃y R(x, y)
    n) (∀x ∃y R(x, y) ∧ ∀x ∀y ∀z ((R(x, y) ∧ R(y, z)) → R(x, z))) → ∃x R(x, x)
    o) ∃x (P(x) ∧ ¬P(x)) → Q
    p) ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) → (∀x P(x) → ∀x Q(x))
    q) (∀x P(x) → ∀x Q(x)) → ∀x (P(x) → Q(x))
    Answers:
      a) V (domains are non-empty)       b) N (N, P = even)
      c) V                               d) N (N, R(x, y): x > y)
      e) V                               f) N (N, P = even, Q = odd)
      g) V                               h) N (N, P = even, Q = odd)
      i) V (the 'drinker paradox')       j) V
      k) V                               l) N (R empty)
      m) V (take y = x)                  n) N (N with <)
      o) V                               p) V
      q) N (domain {0, 1}, P = {0}, Q = ∅: ∀x P(x) is false so the premise
         is true, but P(0) → Q(0) fails)

M10. Prenex and Skolem normal forms.
     a) ∀x P(x) → ∃y Q(y)
     b) ∃x P(x) → ∀y Q(y)
     c) ¬∀x ∃y R(x, y)
     d) ∀x ∃y R(x, y): Skolem form
     e) ∀x ∃y ∀z ∃w S(x, y, z, w): Skolem form
     f) ∃x ∀y ∃z R(x, y, z): Skolem form
     g) ∀x P(x) ∨ ∀x Q(x)
     h) (∀x P(x)) → Q   (x not free in Q)
     i) ∀x (P(x) → ∃y R(x, y)) ∧ ∃z Q(z): prenex and Skolem
     j) ∃x ∀y (x ≤ y): Skolem form
     k) ¬∃x ∀y ∃z R(x, y, z): prenex and Skolem
     l) is φ equivalent to its Skolem form?
     Answers:
       a) ∃x ∃y (P(x) → Q(y)); Skolem P(c) → Q(d)
       b) ∀x ∀y (P(x) → Q(y))
       c) ∃x ∀y ¬R(x, y); Skolem ∀y ¬R(c, y)
       d) ∀x R(x, f(x))
       e) ∀x ∀z S(x, f(x), z, g(x, z))
       f) ∀y R(c, y, f(y))
       g) ∀x ∀y (P(x) ∨ Q(y))
       h) ∃x (P(x) → Q)
       i) ∃z ∀x ∃y ((P(x) → R(x, y)) ∧ Q(z)); ∀x ((P(x) → R(x, f(x))) ∧ Q(c))
       j) ∀y (c ≤ y)
       k) ∀x ∃y ∀z ¬R(x, y, z); ∀x ∀z ¬R(x, f(x), z)
       l) no, only equisatisfiable

M11. True or false?
     a) Propositional logic is sound and complete.
     b) If Γ ⊨ φ then Γ₀ ⊨ φ for some finite Γ₀ ⊆ Γ.
     c) Every consistent first-order theory has a model.
     d) Every consistent theory in a countable language has a countable model.
     e) Some first-order sentence is true exactly in the finite structures.
     f) Some first-order theory has exactly the infinite structures as models.
     g) The class of connected graphs is first-order axiomatisable.
     h) First-order PA has nonstandard models.
     i) Second-order PA is categorical (all models ≅ N).
     j) Th(R, +, ·, 0, 1, <) has a countable model.
     k) A theory with arbitrarily large finite models has an infinite model.
     l) The class of torsion groups is first-order axiomatisable.
     m) The completeness theorem says every sentence true in N is provable
        in PA.
     n) The set of valid first-order sentences is r.e.; is it decidable?
     o) Propositional satisfiability is decidable.
     p) An infinite graph is 3-colourable iff every finite subgraph is.
     q) If ZFC is consistent it has a countable model.
     r) Soundness says: if Γ ⊢ φ then Γ ⊨ φ.
     Answers:
       a) T   b) T   c) T   d) T   e) F   f) T   g) F   h) T   i) T
       j) T (the real algebraic numbers)     k) T   l) F   m) F
       n) T; no (Church-Turing)              o) T (NP-complete)
       p) T   q) T (Skolem's 'paradox')      r) T

M12. Gödel numbering and incompleteness. Sequences are coded as
     2^(a₁)3^(a₂)5^(a₃)7^(a₄)... with every aᵢ ≥ 1.
     a) code of (1, 2, 3)               b) code of (2, 2, 2)
     c) decode 360                      d) decode 1500
     e) decode 1050                     f) is 70 a code?
     True or false (T, F):
     g) PA is complete (if consistent).
     h) Presburger arithmetic (N, 0, S, +) is complete and decidable.
     i) Th(N, +, ·) is complete but not recursively enumerable.
     j) If PA is consistent then PA ⊬ Con(PA).
     k) If PA is sound, its Gödel sentence G is true in N.
     l) If PA is consistent, so is PA + ¬Con(PA).
     m) The halting problem is decidable.
     n) The theory of real closed fields is decidable.
     o) Goodstein's theorem is provable in PA.
     p) ZFC proves CH or ¬CH (if ZFC is consistent).
     q) Truth in N is definable by a formula of arithmetic.
     r) The first incompleteness theorem applies to every consistent r.e.
        theory containing Robinson's Q.
     s) Tarski's elementary Euclidean geometry is complete.
     t) PA + Con(PA) is complete.
     Answers:
       a) 2 · 9 · 125 = 2250     b) 4 · 9 · 25 = 900
       c) 2³ · 3² · 5: (3, 2, 1) d) 2² · 3 · 5³: (2, 1, 3)
       e) 2 · 3 · 5² · 7: (1, 1, 2, 1)
       f) no (70 = 2 · 5 · 7 has exponent 0 at 3)
       g) F   h) T   i) T   j) T   k) T   l) T   m) F   n) T   o) F
       p) F   q) F   r) T   s) T   t) F

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep ⊨ and ⊢ in two separate columns on the board and never
  let them merge until the completeness theorem is stated; test every
  consequence by hunting for a counter-valuation (or counter-model) first;
  translate English into logic in two stages (restricted quantifiers
  'for all students x', then ∀x (S(x) → ...)); read Gödel's theorem through
  the sentence 'I am not provable' and ask which hypotheses each step uses.
  Harder: prove that Horn-SAT is decidable in linear time by unit
  propagation; prove Craig's interpolation theorem for propositional logic;
  use compactness to build a non-Archimedean ordered field containing R;
  prove that the theory of dense linear orders without end points is
  ω-categorical (Cantor's back-and-forth) and hence complete; show the
  Hilbert-Bernays-Löb conditions yield Löb's theorem (T ⊢ Prov(⌜φ⌝) → φ
  implies T ⊢ φ); and prove that the set of Gödel numbers of theorems of PA
  is r.e. but not recursive.


================================================================================
TOPIC 10.45 — THEORY OF COMPUTATION: AUTOMATA, COMPUTABILITY, COMPLEXITY
(P VS NP)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - An ALPHABET Σ is a finite set of symbols; a STRING (word) is a finite
    sequence of symbols, ε is the EMPTY string, |w| is the length, Σ* is the
    set of all strings, and a LANGUAGE is any subset L ⊆ Σ*. Operations:
    union, CONCATENATION L₁L₂ = {uv : u ∈ L₁, v ∈ L₂}, KLEENE STAR
    L* = {ε} ∪ L ∪ LL ∪ ..., complement Σ* − L, reversal.
  - A DETERMINISTIC FINITE AUTOMATON (DFA) is M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F): finite
    set of STATES Q, TRANSITION FUNCTION δ : Q × Σ → Q, START state q₀,
    ACCEPTING states F ⊆ Q. M accepts w if the run from q₀ ends in F. L(M)
    is the language RECOGNISED by M; languages recognised by DFAs are called
    REGULAR.
  - A NONDETERMINISTIC FA (NFA) has δ : Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → P(Q); it accepts if
    SOME run ends in F. SUBSET CONSTRUCTION: every NFA with n states has an
    equivalent DFA with at most 2ⁿ states (states = sets of NFA states), and
    this bound can be needed ('k-th symbol from the end is 1' needs 2ᵏ).
  - REGULAR EXPRESSIONS: ∅, ε, a, R₁ ∪ R₂ (also written R₁ | R₂), R₁R₂, R*.
    KLEENE'S THEOREM: L is regular ⇔ L is described by a regular expression
    ⇔ L is accepted by an NFA ⇔ L is accepted by a DFA. Regular languages
    are CLOSED under union, intersection (PRODUCT CONSTRUCTION), complement
    (swap F and Q − F in a DFA), concatenation, star, reversal.
  - PUMPING LEMMA (regular): if L is regular there is p ≥ 1 such that every
    w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p splits as w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1 and
    xyⁱz ∈ L for ALL i ≥ 0. Used by CONTRADICTION to prove non-regularity
    ({0ⁿ1ⁿ}, palindromes, {a^(n²)}, {aᵖ : p prime}). It is a necessary, not
    sufficient, condition.
  - MYHILL–NERODE: u ≡ v iff for all z, uz ∈ L ⇔ vz ∈ L. L is regular ⇔ ≡
    has finitely many classes, and the number of classes is the number of
    states of the MINIMAL DFA (unique up to renaming). MINIMISATION: remove
    unreachable states, then refine the partition {F, Q − F} until stable.
  - A CONTEXT-FREE GRAMMAR (CFG) G = (V, Σ, R, S) has rules A → α; L(G) is
    the set of terminal strings DERIVABLE from S. Context-free languages
    (CFLs) = languages of PUSHDOWN AUTOMATA (NFA + stack). {aⁿbⁿ} is
    context-free but not regular. A grammar is AMBIGUOUS if some string has
    two parse trees. CHOMSKY NORMAL FORM: A → BC or A → a (S → ε allowed).
    CFL pumping lemma (w = uvxyz, |vxy| ≤ p, |vy| ≥ 1, uvⁱxyⁱz ∈ L) shows
    {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is not context-free. CFLs are closed under ∪, concatenation,
    star, but NOT under ∩ or complement.
  - A TURING MACHINE (TM) has a finite control, an infinite tape and a
    read/write head; δ : Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}, with ACCEPT and REJECT
    states. On an input it accepts, rejects or LOOPS for ever. L is
    RECOGNISABLE (recursively enumerable) if some TM accepts exactly L; L is
    DECIDABLE (recursive) if some TM accepts L and HALTS on every input.
    Multitape and nondeterministic TMs recognise the same languages.
  - CHURCH–TURING THESIS: 'algorithm' (effective procedure) = Turing
    machine. It is a thesis (a definition backed by evidence: λ-calculus,
    recursive functions, register machines all give the same class), not a
    theorem.
  - UNDECIDABILITY: there are countably many TMs but uncountably many
    languages, so most languages are not even recognisable. The HALTING
    PROBLEM HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w} and A_TM = {⟨M, w⟩ : M accepts w}
    are recognisable but UNDECIDABLE (proof by DIAGONALISATION). L is
    decidable ⇔ L and its complement are both recognisable, so the
    complement of A_TM is not recognisable.
  - REDUCTIONS: A ≤ₘ B (mapping reduction: w ∈ A ⇔ f(w) ∈ B, f computable).
    If A ≤ₘ B and B is decidable then A is decidable; so if A is
    undecidable, B is undecidable. RICE'S THEOREM: every non-trivial
    property of the LANGUAGE L(M) of a TM is undecidable. Other undecidable
    problems: E_TM, EQ_TM, Post correspondence, ambiguity of CFGs, EQ_CFG,
    Hilbert's tenth problem (integer roots of polynomials).
  - ASYMPTOTICS: f = O(g) if ∃c > 0, n₀ with f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for n ≥ n₀;
    Ω is the reverse, Θ = both. TIME(t(n)) = languages decided by a
    single-tape TM in O(t(n)) steps; input size n = number of SYMBOLS (bits),
    not the size of the numbers.
  - P = ⋃ₖ TIME(nᵏ): problems solvable in POLYNOMIAL time (the 'tractable'
    problems; robust across reasonable models). Examples: sorting, shortest
    paths, 2-colouring, 2-SAT, matching, linear programming, PRIMES (AKS
    2002), gcd (Euclid, O(n) divisions for n-bit numbers).
  - NP = problems whose YES-instances have a CERTIFICATE (witness) of
    polynomial length checkable in polynomial time by a VERIFIER;
    equivalently decided by a NONDETERMINISTIC TM in polynomial time.
    P ⊆ NP. coNP = complements of NP problems. P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME, and
    P ≠ EXPTIME by the TIME HIERARCHY THEOREM.
  - A ≤ₚ B: polynomial-time mapping reduction. B is NP-HARD if every NP
    problem reduces to B; NP-COMPLETE if also B ∈ NP. COOK–LEVIN THEOREM
    (1971): SAT is NP-complete. Chain of reductions: SAT ≤ₚ 3-SAT ≤ₚ
    INDEPENDENT SET ≤ₚ CLIQUE, VERTEX COVER; 3-SAT ≤ₚ 3-COLOURING, SUBSET SUM,
    HAMILTONIAN CYCLE ≤ₚ TSP. To show a new problem X NP-complete: (1) X ∈ NP,
    (2) a known NP-complete problem ≤ₚ X.
  - P VS NP: is every problem with quick-to-check answers also quick to
    solve? Open (a Clay Millennium Problem). If ANY NP-complete problem is
    in P, then P = NP. Most believe P ≠ NP; much of cryptography assumes it
    (and more). Pseudo-polynomial algorithms (subset sum in O(nT)) do not
    show P = NP, because T is exponential in its number of bits.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Design a DFA over Σ = {0, 1} that accepts exactly the binary strings
    whose value is divisible by 3 (read ε as 0). Give the formal 5-tuple,
    trace it on 10110, and explain why it works.
    Answer: Q = {r₀, r₁, r₂} (rᵢ = 'remainder i so far'), q₀ = r₀,
    F = {r₀}, δ(rᵢ, b) = r_((2i + b) mod 3). On 10110 the run is
    r₀ → r₁ → r₂ → r₂ → r₂ → r₁: rejected (10110₂ = 22 = 3·7 + 1).
    Teacher explains: A DFA can only remember a finite amount, so ask:
    'what must I remember about the part already read?' Reading a binary
    number left to right, appending bit b turns value v into 2v + b. We do
    not need v itself, only v mod 3, because
       (2v + b) mod 3 = (2(v mod 3) + b) mod 3.
    So three states suffice, one per remainder. The table:
          state |  0   |  1
          → r₀* |  r₀  |  r₁        (2·0 + 0 = 0,  2·0 + 1 = 1)
            r₁  |  r₂  |  r₀        (2·1 + 0 = 2,  2·1 + 1 = 3 ≡ 0)
            r₂  |  r₁  |  r₂        (2·2 + 0 = 4 ≡ 1, 2·2 + 1 = 5 ≡ 2)
    (→ marks the start state, * an accepting state.) Trace 10110:
       read 1: 2·0 + 1 = 1   r₁        prefix 1     = 1
       read 0: 2·1 + 0 = 2   r₂        prefix 10    = 2
       read 1: 2·2 + 1 = 5   r₂        prefix 101   = 5 ≡ 2
       read 1: 2·2 + 1 = 5   r₂        prefix 1011  = 11 ≡ 2
       read 0: 2·2 + 0 = 4   r₁        prefix 10110 = 22 ≡ 1
    It ends in r₁ ∉ F, so 10110 is rejected. Correctness is an INDUCTION on
    the length of the input: 'after reading u the machine is in r_(u mod 3)'
    (base: ε, value 0, state r₀; step: the table above). The same idea
    gives a k-state DFA for 'divisible by k' with δ(rᵢ, b) = r_((2i+b) mod k).
    Every DFA must have a transition for EVERY state and EVERY symbol; a
    missing arrow means an extra non-accepting DEAD (trap) state. Common
    mistakes: reading the string right to left; forgetting that the empty
    string must be decided too (here it is accepted, as 0). Now you try: run
    the DFA on 1001 and 111. (1001: r₁, r₂, r₁, r₀, accept, 9 = 3·3; 111:
    r₁, r₀, r₁, reject, 7 ≡ 1.)

D2. Let N be the NFA over {0, 1} with states p (start), q, r (accepting),
    transitions p –0,1→ p, p –0→ q, q –1→ r. Describe L(N), convert N to a
    DFA by the subset construction, and explain why the DFA for 'the third
    symbol from the end is 1' needs 8 states.
    Answer: L(N) = strings ending in 01. The DFA has 3 reachable states
    {p} (start), {p, q}, {p, r} (accepting). The 'third from the end'
    language has 2³ = 8 Myhill–Nerode classes.
    Teacher explains: The NFA 'guesses' when the final 01 begins: it loops
    in p and at some 0 jumps to q, then needs a 1 to reach r with the input
    finished. A string is accepted if SOME guess works, i.e. if it ends in
    01. SUBSET CONSTRUCTION: a DFA state is the SET of NFA states the NFA
    could be in. Start with {p} and compute only reachable sets:
       {p}     on 0 → {p, q}         on 1 → {p}
       {p, q}  on 0 → {p, q}         on 1 → {p} ∪ {r} = {p, r}
       {p, r}  on 0 → {p, q}         on 1 → {p}
    A subset is accepting iff it contains an accepting NFA state: here
    {p, r}. Three states instead of the 2³ = 8 possible. Check on 1101:
    {p} →1 {p} →1 {p} →0 {p, q} →1 {p, r}: accept ✓. (If there are
    ε-arrows, replace each set by its ε-CLOSURE at every step.) Now the
    blow-up example: for L₃ = {w : |w| ≥ 3 and the 3rd symbol from the end is
    1} an NFA needs only 4 states (guess the position), but a DFA must
    remember the last three symbols. Any two different 3-letter strings u, v
    differ in some position, say position j from the left, where u has 1;
    appending j − 1 symbols pushes that position to 'third from the end',
    so one extension is accepted and the other not. Hence the 8 strings of
    length 3 are pairwise distinguishable, and a DFA needs at least 8
    states (8 suffice: remember the last three symbols). In general 'k-th
    from the end is 1' needs 2ᵏ DFA states: the 2ⁿ bound is sharp. Common
    mistakes: forgetting that the DFA must be COMPLETE (every set has both
    arrows); marking only {r} as accepting. Now you try: how many DFA states
    does 'the second symbol from the end is 1' need? (4 = 2²)

D3. (a) Prove that regular languages are closed under complement and
    intersection. (b) Use the product construction to build a DFA for
    L = {w ∈ {0, 1}* : w has an even number of 0s and an odd number of 1s}.
    (c) Find a regular expression for 'an even number of 1s' and state
    Kleene's theorem.
    Answer: (a) complement: swap accepting and non-accepting states;
    intersection: product DFA with F = F₁ × F₂. (b) 4 states (parity of 0s,
    parity of 1s), start (E, E), accepting (E, O). (c) 0*(10*10*)*.
    Teacher explains: (a) Let M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) be a DFA for L. Since a
    DFA has exactly ONE run on each w, the DFA (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, Q − F) accepts
    precisely the strings M rejects: its language is Σ* − L. (This fails
    for an NFA: swapping states of an NFA does not complement it; convert
    to a DFA first.) For M₁, M₂ run both at once: states Q₁ × Q₂,
       δ((s, t), a) = (δ₁(s, a), δ₂(t, a)),  start (q₁, q₂),  F = F₁ × F₂.
    After reading w the product is in (state of M₁, state of M₂), so it
    accepts iff both do: L(M₁) ∩ L(M₂). With F = (F₁ × Q₂) ∪ (Q₁ × F₂) it
    gives the union. (b) M₁ tracks the parity of 0s (E or O), M₂ the parity
    of 1s. Product table (first letter = 0s, second = 1s):
          state    |   0    |   1
          → (E,E)  | (O,E)  | (E,O)
            (E,O)* | (O,O)  | (E,E)
            (O,E)  | (E,E)  | (O,O)
            (O,O)  | (E,O)  | (O,E)
    Check 10101 (two 0s, three 1s): (E,E) → (E,O) → (O,O) → (O,E) → (E,E)
    → (E,O): accept ✓. (c) For 'even number of 1s' the string is some 0s,
    then any number of blocks '1, some 0s, 1, some 0s': 0*(10*10*)*. Check
    0110 = 0·(1·ε·1·0): matches; 010 has one 1 and cannot match. KLEENE'S
    THEOREM: a language is regular (DFA) ⇔ it is accepted by an NFA ⇔ it is
    the language of a regular expression. Regex → NFA by gluing small NFAs
    with ε-arrows (Thompson), NFA → DFA by subsets, DFA → regex by
    eliminating states one at a time (arrows labelled by expressions).
    Common mistakes: complementing an NFA by swapping states; writing
    (11)* for 'even number of 1s' (that forbids 0s). Now you try: how many
    states does the product DFA for 'length divisible by 2' ∩ 'length
    divisible by 3' have, and how many does the minimal DFA have? (6 in the
    product; also 6 minimal, since the language is 'length divisible by 6'.)

D4. State the pumping lemma for regular languages and use it to prove that
    (a) L₁ = {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0} and (b) L₂ = {a^(n²) : n ≥ 0} are not regular.
    Explain why the lemma cannot be used to prove that a language IS
    regular.
    Answer: Proofs below; the lemma gives a property every regular language
    has, but some non-regular languages also have it.
    Teacher explains: WHY the lemma is true: a DFA with p states reading
    w with |w| ≥ p visits p + 1 states in the first p steps, so some state
    repeats (PIGEONHOLE); the part y between the two visits is a loop that
    can be traversed any number of times i ≥ 0. The proof pattern is a GAME
    against an opponent:
       1. suppose L regular; opponent gives the pumping length p
       2. YOU choose w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p (choose cleverly)
       3. opponent splits w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1 (you must handle
          EVERY split)
       4. YOU choose i with xyⁱz ∉ L: contradiction.
    (a) Choose w = 0ᵖ1ᵖ. Since |xy| ≤ p, x and y lie inside the block of
    0s, so y = 0ᵏ with k ≥ 1. Pump down (i = 0): xz = 0^(p−k)1ᵖ has fewer 0s
    than 1s, so xz ∉ L₁. Contradiction; L₁ is not regular.
    (b) Choose w = a^(p²). Any split has y = aᵏ with 1 ≤ k ≤ p. Take i = 2:
       |xy²z| = p² + k,   and   p² < p² + k ≤ p² + p < p² + 2p + 1 = (p + 1)²
    so p² + k lies strictly between consecutive squares and xy²z ∉ L₂.
    Contradiction. The lemma is only NECESSARY: e.g.
    L = {aⁱbʲcʲ : i ≥ 1} ∪ {bʲcᵏ : j, k ≥ 0} satisfies the pumping condition
    (pump the first letter) but is not regular. To prove regularity build a
    DFA, NFA or regular expression; to prove non-regularity use pumping,
    closure properties or Myhill–Nerode. Closure trick: if
    E = {w : #0 = #1} were regular then E ∩ 0*1* = L₁ would be regular. Common
    mistakes: choosing the split yourself ('let y = 01'); choosing a w that
    CAN be pumped (w = 0^(2p) for 'even length'); only checking one i when
    another would work. Now you try: prove that the palindromes over {0, 1}
    are not regular. (w = 0ᵖ10ᵖ; y = 0ᵏ lies in the first block; xz =
    0^(p−k)10ᵖ is not a palindrome.)

D5. Minimise the DFA with states A (start), B, C, D, E, accepting state E,
    and transitions
          state | 0 | 1
            A   | B | C
            B   | B | D
            C   | B | C
            D   | B | E
            E   | B | C
    Also state the Myhill–Nerode theorem and use it to show the result is
    minimal.
    Answer: A and C merge; the minimal DFA has 4 states {A, C}, B, D, E and
    accepts the strings ending in 011.
    Teacher explains: TABLE-FILLING / PARTITION REFINEMENT. Two states are
    equivalent if no suffix z leads one to accept and the other to reject.
    Start with the split accept / non-accept and keep splitting blocks whose
    states go to different blocks on some symbol:
       P₀ = {A, B, C, D} {E}
       on 1: A→C, B→D, C→C, D→E. D goes to block {E}, the others do not.
       P₁ = {A, B, C} {D} {E}
       on 1: A→C, B→D, C→C. B goes to {D}, A and C stay in {A, B, C}.
       P₂ = {A, C} {B} {D} {E}
       on 0: A→B, C→B (same); on 1: A→C, C→C (same). Stable.
    So A ≡ C. The minimal DFA:
          state   | 0 | 1
          → {A,C} | B | {A,C}
            B     | B | D
            D     | B | E
            E*    | B | {A,C}
    B means 'last symbol 0', D 'last two 01', E 'last three 011'. MYHILL–
    NERODE: define u ≡ v ⇔ (∀z: uz ∈ L ⇔ vz ∈ L). L is regular iff there
    are finitely many classes, and the minimal DFA has exactly one state
    per class. Here ε, 0, 01, 011 are pairwise distinguishable: the suffix
    z = 11 separates 0 (0 11 ∈ L) from ε (11 ∉ L); z = 1 separates 01 from ε
    and 0; z = ε separates 011 from all. Four classes ⇒ at least 4 states,
    and we have 4, so the DFA is minimal. Common mistakes: forgetting to
    delete unreachable states first; stopping after one round of
    splitting. Now you try: minimise the DFA over {0, 1} with states 1, 2, 3
    (start 1, accepting 2 and 3) and δ(1, x) = 2, δ(2, x) = 3, δ(3, x) = 3 for
    both symbols x. (2 ≡ 3; two states, language = non-empty strings.)

D6. (a) Give context-free grammars for {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} and for balanced
    parentheses, and derive aaabbb and (()()). (b) Show that the grammar
    E → E + E | E × E | a is ambiguous and give an unambiguous grammar.
    (c) Describe a pushdown automaton for {aⁿbⁿ}. (d) Explain why
    {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is not context-free.
    Answer: (a) S → aSb | ε;  S → (S)S | ε. (b) a + a × a has two parse
    trees; unambiguous: E → E + T | T, T → T × F | F, F → a. (c) push on
    each a, pop on each b, accept on empty stack at the end. (d) CFL pumping
    lemma with w = aᵖbᵖcᵖ.
    Teacher explains: (a) A derivation replaces one variable at a time:
       S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aaaSbbb ⇒ aaabbb
    The rule S → aSb keeps the numbers of a's and b's equal and the a's in
    front. For parentheses, S → (S)S splits a balanced string at the
    bracket matching the first '(':
       S ⇒ (S)S ⇒ (S) ⇒ ((S)S) ⇒ (()S) ⇒ (()(S)S) ⇒ (()()S) ⇒ (()())
    (b) Two different PARSE TREES for a + a × a:
       E ⇒ E + E with the right E ⇒ E × E      means a + (a × a)
       E ⇒ E × E with the left E ⇒ E + E       means (a + a) × a
    Ambiguity is a property of the GRAMMAR; the layered grammar with T
    (terms) and F (factors) forces × to bind tighter and makes the parse
    unique. (Some CFLs are INHERENTLY ambiguous, e.g.
    {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j or j = k}.) (c) A PDA is an NFA with a stack. For aⁿbⁿ:
       state q₁: read a, push A (repeat)
       on the first b move to q₂: read b, pop A (repeat)
       accept if the input ends in q₂ (or q₁ with nothing read) with the
       stack empty; a b with empty stack, or an a in q₂, rejects.
    The stack is an unbounded counter, which a DFA lacks. Every CFG can be
    turned into a PDA and back. (d) CFL PUMPING LEMMA: long w ∈ L splits as
    uvxyz with |vxy| ≤ p, |vy| ≥ 1 and uvⁱxyⁱz ∈ L for all i. For
    w = aᵖbᵖcᵖ the window vxy has length ≤ p, so it cannot touch both a's and
    c's. Pumping up then increases at most two of the three letters, and
    the counts are no longer equal: contradiction. Hence CFLs are not
    closed under ∩: {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} ∩ {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, and (by De Morgan) not
    under complement. CHOMSKY HIERARCHY: regular ⊂ context-free ⊂
    context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable. Common mistakes: S → aSb
    without S → ε (then no finite string is generated); thinking an
    ambiguous grammar means an ambiguous language. Now you try: give a CFG
    for the palindromes over {a, b}. (S → aSa | bSb | a | b | ε)

D7. Describe a Turing machine that adds 1 to a binary number written on the
    tape, give its transition table, trace it on 1011, and state the
    Church–Turing thesis.
    Answer: states q₀ (go right), q₁ (carry), halt. On 1011 it halts with
    1100 after 8 steps. Thesis: every effectively computable function is
    Turing-computable.
    Teacher explains: A TM step: in state q reading symbol s, write s′,
    move L or R, go to state q′. Plan: walk to the right end, then add 1
    with carries moving left (1 + 1 = 10: write 0, carry left).
       q₀, 0 → 0, R, q₀        q₀, 1 → 1, R, q₀        q₀, ⊔ → ⊔, L, q₁
       q₁, 1 → 0, L, q₁        q₁, 0 → 1, halt         q₁, ⊔ → 1, halt
    (⊔ = blank.) Trace on 1011 (head position shown by [ ]):
       q₀ [1]011   q₀ 1[0]11   q₀ 10[1]1   q₀ 101[1]   q₀ 1011[⊔]
       q₁ 101[1]   → 1010, move L:  q₁ 10[1]0  → 1000, move L:  q₁ 1[0]00
       write 1, halt: 1100
    Steps: 4 moves right + 1 turn at the blank + 2 carries + 1 final write =
    8. In general, for n bits ending in t ones (not all ones) the machine
    uses n + t + 2 steps; for 11...1 the carry runs off the left end onto a
    blank, which becomes 1 (111 → 1000). CONFIGURATIONS (state, tape, head
    position) change deterministically; a TM may also run for ever. Many
    variants (several tapes, two-way infinite tape, nondeterminism, RAM
    machines) compute exactly the same functions; they differ only in speed
    (e.g. a k-tape machine running in time t is simulated by one tape in
    time O(t²)). CHURCH–TURING THESIS: the informal idea 'computable by a
    step-by-step algorithm' coincides with 'computable by a TM'. It cannot
    be proved, because 'algorithm' is informal, but every proposed model
    (Church's λ-calculus, Gödel–Kleene recursive functions, Post systems)
    has turned out equivalent. Common mistakes: forgetting the all-ones
    case; moving the head without saying where; confusing 'halt' with
    'accept'. Now you try: what does the machine produce on 10011, and in
    how many steps? (10100 in 5 + 2 + 2 = 9 steps)

D8. (a) Show that some languages over {0, 1} are not recognisable by any
    Turing machine. (b) Prove that the halting problem is undecidable.
    Answer: (a) countably many TMs, uncountably many languages. (b) The
    diagonal machine D gives a contradiction.
    Teacher explains: (a) A TM is a finite object, so it can be encoded as
    a finite string ⟨M⟩; there are only COUNTABLY many strings, hence
    countably many TMs and countably many recognisable languages. But the
    set of all languages P(Σ*) is UNCOUNTABLE (Cantor: Σ* is countably
    infinite and |P(N)| > |N|). So almost all languages have no TM.
    (b) HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on input w}. Suppose, for a contradiction,
    that a TM H decides HALT: H(⟨M, w⟩) = 'yes' if M halts on w, 'no'
    otherwise, and H always halts. Build D:
       D on input ⟨M⟩:  run H on ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩;
                        if H says 'yes', loop for ever;
                        if H says 'no', halt.
    Now run D on its own code ⟨D⟩:
       D halts on ⟨D⟩  ⇔  H says 'no' on ⟨D, ⟨D⟩⟩  ⇔  D does not halt on ⟨D⟩
    Contradiction, so H cannot exist. This is Cantor's DIAGONAL argument:
    list machines M₁, M₂, ... down the side and inputs ⟨M₁⟩, ⟨M₂⟩, ...
    across the top; D is built to differ from every Mᵢ on the diagonal
    entry ⟨Mᵢ⟩, so D is not in the list, yet D would be a TM if H existed.
    HALT is still RECOGNISABLE: simulate M on w and accept if it halts (a
    'semi-decision': no answer when M loops). Consequences: no program can
    check all programs for infinite loops, and many mathematical questions
    (e.g. Goldbach: 'does the search for a counterexample halt?') would be
    settled by a halting decider. Common mistakes: saying 'just run M and
    see' (you cannot tell 'still running' from 'never halts'); thinking the
    proof shows particular programs are hard to analyse (it shows no single
    decider works for all). Now you try: prove that A_TM = {⟨M, w⟩ : M
    accepts w} is undecidable the same way. (D(⟨M⟩) = opposite of what the
    decider says about ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩; D accepts ⟨D⟩ ⇔ D does not accept ⟨D⟩.)

D9. (a) Prove: L is decidable ⇔ both L and its complement are recognisable,
    and deduce that the complement of A_TM is not recognisable.
    (b) Using a reduction from A_TM, show that
    E_TM = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅} is undecidable. (c) State Rice's theorem and
    apply it.
    Answer: proofs below; Rice: every non-trivial property of L(M) is
    undecidable.
    Teacher explains: (a) (⇒) a decider for L also decides the complement
    (swap answers), and deciders are recognisers. (⇐) Let M₁ recognise L
    and M₂ recognise the complement. On input w run M₁ and M₂ in parallel,
    one step each in turn. w is in exactly one of the two languages, so
    exactly one of them eventually accepts; answer accordingly. This always
    halts, so L is decidable. Since A_TM is recognisable but not decidable,
    its complement cannot be recognisable. (b) REDUCTION: assume R decides
    E_TM; we build a decider for A_TM, which is impossible. Given ⟨M, w⟩,
    construct (without running anything) the machine
       M_w on input x:  if x ≠ w reject;  otherwise run M on w and accept
                        if M accepts.
    Then L(M_w) = {w} if M accepts w, and ∅ otherwise. So
       M accepts w  ⇔  L(M_w) ≠ ∅  ⇔  R rejects ⟨M_w⟩.
    That decides A_TM: contradiction. The direction matters: we reduce the
    KNOWN undecidable problem TO the new one (A_TM ≤ E_TM, via complement).
    (c) RICE'S THEOREM: let P be a property of languages that is
    NON-TRIVIAL (some TM languages have it, some do not). Then
    {⟨M⟩ : L(M) has P} is undecidable. Examples, all undecidable: 'L(M) is
    empty', 'L(M) is regular', 'L(M) contains 101', 'L(M) is finite',
    'L(M) = Σ*'. Rice does NOT apply to properties of the MACHINE rather
    than its language: 'M has 7 states' or 'M halts on ε within 100 steps'
    are decidable. Common mistakes: reducing in the wrong direction (showing
    E_TM ≤ A_TM proves nothing); applying Rice to trivial properties ('L(M)
    is recognisable' is true for all M, so decidable). Now you try: is
    {⟨M⟩ : L(M) contains exactly 3 strings} decidable? (No, by Rice: some TM
    languages have 3 strings, some do not.)

D10. (a) Prove from the definition that 3n² + 5n + 7 = O(n²) and that
     n³ ≠ O(n²). (b) Explain why the input size for arithmetic problems is
     the number of digits, and compare trial division with Euclid's
     algorithm. (c) Compute gcd(1071, 462) and count the division steps.
     (d) Define P and explain why it is taken as 'efficient'.
     Answer: (a) c = 15, n₀ = 1 works; n³ ≤ cn² fails for n > c. (b) trial
     division takes about √N ≈ 2^(n/2) steps for an n-bit N (exponential);
     Euclid takes O(n) divisions. (c) gcd = 21 after 3 divisions.
     (d) P = ⋃ₖ TIME(nᵏ).
     Teacher explains: (a) For n ≥ 1, 5n ≤ 5n² and 7 ≤ 7n², so
        3n² + 5n + 7 ≤ 3n² + 5n² + 7n² = 15n²
     giving c = 15, n₀ = 1. If n³ ≤ cn² for all n ≥ n₀ then n ≤ c for all
     large n, false. Only the LEADING term matters, and constants are
     ignored. Ladder of growth: 1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ <
     2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ. (b) A number N is written with n ≈ log₂ N bits. Trial
     division up to √N = 2^(n/2) is EXPONENTIAL in n: for a 200-digit N it is
     hopeless. (c) Euclid:
        1071 = 2 × 462 + 147
         462 = 3 × 147 + 21
         147 = 7 × 21 + 0      ⇒ gcd = 21 (last non-zero remainder)
     Every two steps the remainder at least halves (Lamé: at most about
     5 × (number of decimal digits) steps), so Euclid is polynomial, in
     fact O(n) divisions. Primality is also in P (Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena,
     2002), but no polynomial FACTORING algorithm is known. (d) P is the
     class of decision problems solvable by a (deterministic, single-tape)
     TM in time O(nᵏ) for some fixed k. Reasons: polynomials are closed
     under sum, product and composition (a polynomial algorithm calling a
     polynomial subroutine is polynomial); all reasonable models simulate
     each other with polynomial overhead, so P does not depend on the
     model; and the gap with exponentials is huge: at 10⁹ steps per
     second, n³ with n = 100 takes 10⁻³ s but 2ⁿ takes about 4 × 10¹³
     years. Common mistakes: calling trial division 'O(N), hence linear';
     writing O(2n²) instead of O(n²). Now you try: find gcd(252, 198) with
     Euclid. (252 = 198 + 54, 198 = 3·54 + 36, 54 = 36 + 18, 36 = 2·18:
     gcd 18)

D11. (a) Define NP by certificates and explain why P ⊆ NP. (b) State the
     Cook–Levin theorem and define NP-complete. (c) Carry out the
     reduction 3-SAT ≤ₚ INDEPENDENT SET on
     φ = (x ∨ y ∨ ¬z) ∧ (¬x ∨ ¬y ∨ z), and show how CLIQUE and VERTEX COVER
     follow.
     Answer: (a) L ∈ NP iff there is a polynomial-time verifier V and a
     polynomial bound so that w ∈ L ⇔ some short certificate c has
     V(w, c) = accept. (b) SAT is NP-complete. (c) 6 vertices, two
     triangles plus 3 conflict edges; independent set of size 2 ⇔ φ
     satisfiable.
     Teacher explains: (a) Think 'hard to find, easy to check'. For SAT the
     certificate is a truth assignment, checked by evaluating the formula;
     for HAMILTONIAN CYCLE it is the order of the vertices; for COMPOSITES
     it is a factor. A problem in P is in NP with the empty certificate
     (the verifier ignores c and solves the problem), so P ⊆ NP. The name
     means 'Nondeterministic Polynomial': an NTM guesses c then verifies.
     (b) COOK–LEVIN: SAT is NP-complete, i.e. SAT ∈ NP and every L ∈ NP
     satisfies L ≤ₚ SAT. (Idea: the computation table of a polynomial-time
     verifier is a polynomial-size grid; 'this grid is a valid accepting
     computation' is a polynomial-size Boolean formula.) Once one problem
     is NP-complete, others follow by reductions, since ≤ₚ is transitive.
     (c) Vertices: one per literal occurrence, grouped in a triangle per
     clause:
        clause 1: x₁ = x, y₁ = y, z₁ = ¬z      (triangle)
        clause 2: x₂ = ¬x, y₂ = ¬y, z₂ = z     (triangle)
        conflict edges: x—¬x, y—¬y, ¬z—z (complementary literals)
     Target k = number of clauses = 2. An independent set of size k takes
     exactly one vertex per triangle (triangle edges) and never both x and
     ¬x (conflict edges), so setting those literals true is consistent and
     satisfies every clause. Conversely a satisfying assignment gives one
     true literal per clause, and these are pairwise non-conflicting. E.g.
     {x in clause 1, z in clause 2} is independent ⇒ x = T, z = T (y free)
     satisfies φ. Building the graph takes polynomial time (3m vertices for
     m clauses). Then: S is independent in G ⇔ S is a CLIQUE in the
     complement graph Ḡ ⇔ V − S is a VERTEX COVER of G. So
     IS ≤ₚ CLIQUE and IS ≤ₚ VC (with k ↦ |V| − k), all NP-complete. Common
     mistakes: reducing the new problem TO SAT (that shows only X ∈ NP);
     forgetting to check X ∈ NP. Now you try: in a graph with 10 vertices
     the largest independent set has 4 vertices. What is the smallest
     vertex cover? (10 − 4 = 6; e.g. the Petersen graph)

D12. (a) Is there a subset of {3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2} with sum 9? With sum 30?
     Use dynamic programming and explain why its running time O(nT) does
     not prove P = NP. (b) Explain the P vs NP question, NP-hard, coNP, the
     chain P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME, and what would follow if P = NP.
     Answer: (a) 9: yes (4 + 5, also 3 + 4 + 2); 30: no (without 34 the total
     is 26 < 30, and 34 > 30). (b) below.
     Teacher explains: (a) DP: keep the set R of reachable sums (≤ T), add
     one number at a time. For T = 9:
        start      R = {0}
        add 3      R = {0, 3}
        add 34     (too big) R = {0, 3}
        add 4      R = {0, 3, 4, 7}
        add 12     (too big) unchanged
        add 5      R = {0, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9}      9 reached ✓
     A table of n rows and T + 1 columns: O(nT) work. But T is written with
     log₂ T bits, so nT can be EXPONENTIAL in the input length (T = 2¹⁰⁰
     has 101 bits). Such an algorithm is PSEUDO-POLYNOMIAL; SUBSET SUM
     stays NP-complete. (b) P vs NP asks whether every problem whose
     solutions can be CHECKED quickly can also be FOUND quickly. NP-HARD:
     at least as hard as every NP problem (need not be in NP, e.g. the
     halting problem is NP-hard). coNP: complements of NP problems, e.g.
     TAUTOLOGY, 'N is prime' (certificate for 'no' is a factor). Known:
        P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME,   P ⊊ EXPTIME (time hierarchy)
     so at least one inclusion is strict, but we do not know which. If
     P = NP: every NP-complete problem (scheduling, TSP, protein folding
     models, theorem proving with short proofs) would be solvable in
     polynomial time, and public-key cryptography based on hard NP
     problems (factoring-based RSA) would break, since factoring is in NP.
     If P ≠ NP (the common belief): NP-complete problems have no
     polynomial algorithm, and NP-intermediate problems exist (Ladner);
     candidates are factoring and graph isomorphism. It is one of the
     seven Clay Millennium Problems ($1,000,000). Practical responses to
     NP-hardness: approximation algorithms (2-approximation for vertex
     cover), heuristics, SAT solvers, parameterised and exponential-but-
     faster algorithms. Common mistakes: 'NP = not polynomial'; 'NP-complete
     problems have been proved to need exponential time'. Now you try: why
     does a polynomial algorithm for 3-COLOURING prove P = NP? (3-COLOURING
     is NP-complete: every L ∈ NP reduces to it in polynomial time, and a
     composition of polynomials is a polynomial.)

M5. How many states does the MINIMAL complete DFA have? (Σ = {0, 1}; dead
    states count.)
    a) length divisible by 3              b) strings ending in 01
    c) strings containing 011             d) strings ending in 011
    e) binary value divisible by 3 (ε = 0)
    f) binary value divisible by 5 (ε = 0)
    g) binary value divisible by 4 (ε = 0)
    h) second symbol from the end is 1    i) third symbol from the end is 1
    j) even #0s and odd #1s               k) no 11

M12. Classify each decision problem: P (known polynomial algorithm),
     NPC (NP-complete), NPI? (in NP, not known to be in P or NP-complete),

     k) contains a triangle (k = 3 fixed)

     n) 0-1 integer programming      o) PRIMES
     p) 'N has a factor ≤ k'         q) graph isomorphism
     r) SUBSET SUM                   s) TSP (tour of length ≤ k)
     t) halting problem              u) minimum spanning tree ≤ k
     v) TQBF (quantified Boolean formulas)
     w) generalised chess on n × n boards
